2step.arrangement: Two formats coexist. The radio version: 3 minutes, 16-bar verse, 16-bar chorus, bridge, chorus, with the vocal as the common thread. The club version: 5 to 6 minutes, 32-bar intro with drums and bass, vocal hook at bar 32, 16-bar breakdown where only the vocal and chords remain, snare comes back with a roll. Blocks are 16 bars. The high points come from drums returning, not from build-ups. A classic trick: cut the bass for 2 bars before the chorus. Always plan an instrumental dub version for DJs.
2step.basse: The bass fills the holes left by the missing kicks. Sine or triangle sub in Operator, attack 0, decay 150 to 300 ms, played in short, syncopated notes. Write a melodic line in minor that lands on the positions where there is no kick: for example the “a” of 1, beat 3, the “and” of 4. For the dark side à la El-B, layer a filtered saw with the cutoff at 250 Hz and a slight glide between two notes. The relationship with the kick is a dialogue: kick, bass, snare, bass. Avoid long notes, except on the first beat of a 4-bar phrase to anchor the key.
etapes: Set Ableton to 135 BPM and an MPC 16 Swing 62% groove on every drum track.
Place a kick on 1 and 2.5, a snare on 2 and 4, a ghost snare at the end of beat 3, and swung hats.
Write a short sine bass in minor that only lands where there is no kick.
Chop an R'n'B vocal into syllables in Simpler, pitch it and turn it into a rhythmic motif.
Add syncopated Rhodes chords and arrange in 16-bar blocks with a 16-bar breakdown.
Compress the snare with a slow attack, keep the sub clean and mono, master toward -9 LUFS.
2step.mix: Transients are sacred: the snare and the kick must crack. Compressor on the snare with a slow 30 ms attack, 100 ms release, 4:1 ratio, to keep the attack and fatten the tail. Clean sub, no saturation, mono below 100 Hz, cut below 35 Hz. Kick cut below 45 Hz to leave the sub alone at the bottom. Vocals up front, de-esser, gentle 3:1 compression, short plate reverb. Hi-hats processed in mid-side to widen them without touching the center. Less saturation than in speed garage, more clarity. Master around -9 LUFS, 2-step lives through its dynamics.

outils.pourquoi: The 12-bit sampler of 2-step: dry snares, timestretched R'n'B vocals with artifacts. Today Redux at 12 bits in Ableton gives that crunch.
The Atari ST sequencer used by MJ Cole and the 1998 studios, to place kicks on 1 and 2.5 and set the swing by hand.
The stereo sampler used on Sincere: vocals taken from sample CDs, strings and chords chopped and then replayed on the keyboard.
Sine or triangle sub, attack 0, decay from 150 to 300 ms, for the short notes that fill the holes left by the kicks.
Chop an R'n'B vocal into syllables, pitch it in Complex Pro and turn it into a rhythmic motif, the move inherited from Todd Edwards.
A Rhodes for syncopated chords, played short and slightly compressed, in place of old romplers.

outils.nom: Akai Professional, 2 Step Garage MPC Expansion
outils.pourquoi: Drum kits, vocal chops and chords designed after MJ Cole, El-B and Artful Dodger, in 24 bits, to get started fast.

reperes: Dem 2: Destiny (1998): the pure 2-step skeleton, kick on 1 and 2.5, a snare that carries everything.
Groove Chronicles: Stone Cold (1998): the dark side, filtered bass and space, before dubstep.
Sweet Female Attitude: Flowers (2000): the vocal chopped into a rhythmic motif and the perfect radio version.
Wookie: Battle (2000): the bass in dialogue with the drums, chords that stay minimal.
2step.rythme: The skeleton: kick on beat 1 and on the “and” of beat 2 (position 2.5 in Ableton), or on the “a” of beat 2 for a heavier feel. Snare or rimshot on 2 and 4, velocity 110, with a ghost note on the last sixteenth of beat 3. No kick on 2 and 4. Swung sixteenth-note hi-hats, velocities alternating 100 and 50, open hat just before the snare. Shaker in eighth notes to smooth things out. Add rimshots and a doubled clap on the 4 every other bar. Dry, short samples, Akai S950 spirit: a bit of 12-bit crunch on the snare with Redux. The snare is bright and snappy, it is what carries the groove.
2step.sons: Female R'n'B vocals, chopped and pitched, timestretched in Simpler with a bit of grainy artifact. Each vocal phrase becomes a rhythmic motif. Syncopated Rhodes or electric piano chords, string stabs, a discreet pad with a filter that opens. Bells and marimbas for the pop color, Cubase and Akai S950 era. A few FX: vinyl noise, filter sweep, a very short siren. The contrast with 4/4 UK garage: less M1 organ, more vocals and harmony, a softer, more radio-friendly sound. The dark version swaps the vocals for low stabs and dub delays.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, MJ Cole on the making of UKG classic Sincere
Internet Tattoo, UKG VST: The Best Synth Plugins for UK Garage
KVR Audio, 2 Step Garage by Akai
2step.tempo: Between 130 and 138 BPM, most classics sit at 134 or 136. 2-step is defined by what it takes away: the kicks on beats 2 and 4 disappear, and the groove turns limping and sensual. The swing is pushed further than in 4/4 UK garage: 60 to 66% on a sixteenth-note grid. The feel should sound like it is falling forward and then catching itself. In Ableton, try the MPC 16 Swing 62 or 66 grooves and apply them to every drum track, kick included. The rhythmic signature fits in two bars: the first bar plants the foot, the second moves it. This imbalance is the rule, not the exception.

acidhouse.arrangement: An acid track is a single idea that transforms. 32-bar intro with drums alone or the 303 alone with the filter closed, then the kick comes in and the filter starts to open. Move the cutoff in 16-bar waves: opening, plateau, sudden closing at the breakdown. The breakdown cuts the kick for 8 bars while the 303 rises in resonance, then everything drops back. Change the sequence once or twice over the whole track, no more, by modifying only the accents and slides. Length 7 to 10 minutes. The long format is not a flaw, it is what allows the trance: the DJ will mix half of it.
acidhouse.basse: The bass is the track. A real TB-303 or an emulation (AudioRealism ABL3, D16 Phoscyon, Roland Cloud's 303) with a 16-step sixteenth-note sequence on one note, two at most, with accents and slides placed by hand. The typical pattern: repeated root, an octave jump on an accented step, a slide down a semitone. Then the part that matters: automate the cutoff frequency and the resonance live over dozens of bars, slowly, with sudden openings on the accents. Env Mod around 60 to 70%, short decay when you want it to snap, long when you want it to smear. Record the performance rather than drawing curves.
etapes: Load a 303 emulation and program 16 sixteenth-note steps on a single note, with two accents and a slide.
Add an 808 or a 909 in four-on-the-floor with snare on 2 and 4, hats in sixteenth notes, no swing.
Record 4 minutes of live cutoff and resonance automation on the 303 by playing with your hands, then keep the best passages.
Put a soft distortion after the filter and a 3/16 delay on the acid line.
Build the track over 8 minutes around the waves of filter opening, with a kickless breakdown where the resonance rises.
Compress the 303, cut it below 80 Hz, and put a dynamic EQ on the resonance peak before exporting.
acidhouse.mix: The 303 must dominate the mids, between 200 Hz and 3 kHz, where the filter sings. Cut it below 80 Hz and leave the 808 kick alone in the low end. Compress the acid line fairly hard (4:1 ratio, 5 ms attack) so the accents don't poke out and the slides stay audible. Distortion comes before compression. Dry drums, with no reverb or almost none, a very short plate on the snare. On the master, light tape saturation flattens the resonance peaks and makes the whole thing warm. Always check the resonance on headphones: a 2 kHz peak at full can hurt on a big system, a dynamic cut (dynamic EQ or Pro-Q in dynamic mode) tames it without killing the character.

outils.pourquoi: The instrument of the genre: 16-step sequence with accents and slides, cutoff and resonance turned by hand for minutes on end.
The 303 emulation reputed to be the most faithful, with the original step sequencer; the course cites it for writing the acid line in the DAW.
Another software 303, with built-in distortion and effects: handy for making the resonance grind without adding a plugin after it.
Roland's official version, modeled by the manufacturer; same pattern, accent and slide logic as the machine, for those with the subscription.
The drums of the first acid records, long kick and syncopated cowbell; D16 Nepheton 2 or Roland Cloud TR-808 for the software version.
Takes over from the 808 around 1988 with a wider clap and metallic hats, on Acid Thunder and the English records of the Second Summer of Love.
The distortion after the 303's filter, so the resonance peak grinds; place it before the compressor, as the course explains.
Recent 303 emulation with added modulation and effects, chosen by producers who want an acid line more mobile than the original.

reperes: Phuture: Acid Tracks (1987): twelve minutes of a single sequence where only the filter moves, the lesson in patience.
Sleezy D: I've Lost Control (1986): the 303 turning menacing as the resonance rises under a raving vocal.
Adonis: No Way Back (1986): acid bass serving a real house groove, with an 808 rolling under the cowbells.
acidhouse.rythme: On the first records, the 808 dominates: long 808 kick with the decay wide open, dry 808 snare on 2 and 4, closed hats in sixteenth notes lightly accented on the eighths, cowbell and clave in syncopation. Later the 909 takes over with a wider clap. The pattern stays minimal to leave room for the 303. A trick from the era: program the 808 toms descending on the last bar of each 8-bar block, or a triplet rim, to mark transitions without adding anything. No breakbeat, no ride: the drums are a metronome, all the movement is in the bass.
acidhouse.sons: Few other sounds, on purpose. A second 303 an octave higher and more closed to answer the first, a sampled synth stab or a held Juno chord, a filtered or spoken vocal treated with a dotted-eighth delay. The squelch itself is the signature timbre: a saw or square run through an 18 dB per octave resonant filter, with distortion after it (Saturator or a pedal overdrive) so the resonance grinds. Add a short 3/16 delay on the acid line to double it and a slow flanger or phaser at the end of the track for the psychedelic side. Nothing melodic in the classic sense.
sourcesOutils: Plugin Boutique, The Best TB-303 Plugins
Integraudio, The 8 Best 303 & Acid VST Plugins
acidhouse.tempo: Between 118 and 128 BPM, a little slower than the acid techno that would follow. The 303 imposes its own feel: it plays in sixteenth notes with an internal swing, and its slide links certain notes in a glissando that stretches time. Keep the drum machine dead straight (808 or 909, swing at 50%) so the acid line is the only thing that wobbles. The track lives in duration: Acid Tracks runs almost twelve minutes, and the trance feeling comes from the fact that nothing moves except the filter. Count your sections in 16 bars but think of changes over 32 or 64 bars.

acidtechno.arrangement: Six to seven minutes. The 303 comes in from bar 1 or 17, filter closed, and opens over 32 bars: the cutoff automation is your arrangement. Prepare two or three 303 patterns and alternate them every 8 bars. Central 16-bar breakdown: kick cut, 303 alone with the resonance rising, then the kick returns without a complicated build-up. Second 303 in dialogue after the first breakdown. Hardfloor version: long plateaus, filters opening slowly over 64 bars, a nine-minute track. London version: shorter, dry drops, sirens. End on 32 bars of drums and closed 303 for the DJ. Record the cutoff tweaks live rather than drawing curves.
acidtechno.basse: The 303 is the bass. In AudioRealism ABL3, D16 Phoscyon or a real TB-303: a sixteenth-note sequence on four or five notes maximum, root, octave, minor third, fifth, with accents on the strong beats and slides between two neighboring notes. Cutoff between 30 and 50%, high resonance, env mod at 70%, medium decay. The signature of the genre is two 303s in dialogue: a low one that lays down the line, a higher, more distorted one that answers on the even bars. After the 303, a distortion: Overdrive or Pedal in Fuzz, then an EQ to remove the peaks at 2 or 3 kHz. If you add a sine sub, cut the 303 at 80 Hz.
etapes: At 138 BPM, lay down a four-on-the-floor 909 kick and toms a few dB behind.
Program the three closed hats in a 36, 107, 36 pyramid and the open hat in sixteenth notes with rising velocities.
Load ABL3 or Phoscyon, write a sixteenth-note sequence on four notes with accents and slides.
Add Overdrive then EQ after the 303, and a dotted-eighth delay at 20%.
Duplicate the 303 with another pattern, higher and more distorted, for the dialogue.
Record the cutoff automation live over six minutes, with a 16-bar breakdown in the middle.
acidtechno.mix: Mix around the kick, at -12 dB peak in the center, toms at -16, snare around -13 panned 10%, open hat and rim at -17 in the center. The drum bus gets Glue at ratio 4 with fast attack, auto release, 3 dB of reduction in parallel at 65%, followed by a soft saturation at 2 dB. The distorted 303 creates aggressive peaks: a 3 to 5 dB notch where it whistles, often between 2 and 4 kHz. If it carries the low end, leave it alone below 100 Hz and cut everything else at 100. The distortion raises the perceived level, so you can stay at -8 LUFS without an aggressive limiter. Stay dirty but readable: the kick must come through two 303s.

outils.pourquoi: The bass and the melody of the genre, often two machines in dialogue; the Cyclone Analogic TT-303 and Behringer TD-3 clones hold today's scene.
The most faithful 303 emulation on slides and accents: sixteenth-note sequence on four notes, cutoff between 30 and 50%, high resonance.
A software 303 with built-in distortion and effects, handy for the second, higher and dirtier instance that answers on the even bars.
Hard four-on-the-floor kick, rimshot and clap rolls; the sixteenth-note open hat with rising velocities replaces the sidechain.
Right after the 303, at 30% with the filter around 1.5 kHz, then an EQ that removes the peaks around 3 kHz; Pedal in Fuzz for the squat sound.
A soft spectral clipper on the drum bus, about 2 dB of drive, to gain level without the kick disappearing behind two 303s.

outils.nom: UNDRGRND Sounds They Call It Acid
outils.pourquoi: Pack of already saturated 303 and 909 loops and one-shots, useful to lay down a skeleton quickly before programming your own line.
4:1 ratio, fast attack, auto release, 3 dB of reduction in parallel at 65% on the drums for the retro pumping of the London scene.

reperes: Hardfloor: Acperience 1 (1992): two 303s opening over ten minutes, the widescreen version
Plastikman: Spastik (1993): almost nothing but drums and a ghost 303, proof that the groove is enough
Emmanuel Top: Acid Phase (1995): the 303 as the only line, the cutoff as the only melody
999999999: Rave 4 Love (2021): acid brought into today's hard techno, saturated 303 and huge kick
acidtechno.rythme: Hard 909 kick, four-on-the-floor, with the 909 toms a few dB behind. The closed hat plays only three hits per bar: on beat 2, on the last sixteenth of beat 2, on the offbeat of beat 3, with velocities 36, 107, 36 in a pyramid. The open hat plays every sixteenth with velocities between 1 and 105, accented on the offbeat of beat 1, and 10% random panning. A 909 rimshot falls on the fourth sixteenth of beats 1 and 3, and a clap roll answers at the end of the bar. For the squat version, add a saturated 909 snare on 2 and 4 and a crash at the start of each 16-bar phrase.
acidtechno.sons: Everything revolves around the 303 and its distortion. Typical chain: 303, then Overdrive at 30% with the filter at 1.5 kHz, then EQ, then a dotted-eighth delay mixed at 20%. Two instances with different patterns, one distorted, the other almost clean. Hardware sequencers bring the feel: if you don't have one, program the accents and slides by hand rather than leaving it to an arpeggiator. Around the 303, not much: a few rave stabs on Alpha Juno, a 909 crash, hoover sirens for the breakdowns. On the drum bus, Glue Compressor at 4:1 in parallel at 65% and a soft clipper at 2 dB of drive. Nothing else melodic: the 303 already fills the mids.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
acidtechno.tempo: From 130 to 145 BPM. Hardfloor stays around 130 for its widescreen version, the London squat scene pushes to 140 or 145. The period groove comes from a light swing on the sixteenths, a Swing 16 at 15% in Ableton, applied to the hi-hats and the 303 but not to the kick. What replaces the sidechain is the programming: the hi-hat velocities rise between each kick, which creates a very retro natural pumping. The 303 imposes its own feel with its slides and accents: if you quantize it too hard, it loses its glide. Keep the 303 10 to 20 ms behind the grid, it will sound more alive.

acidtrance.arrangement: Acperience 1 lasts more than 10 minutes and rests on one line. 32-bar intro with drums alone, then the 303 comes in with the cutoff closed and spends 64 bars rising. The first breakdown removes the kick and leaves the 303 alone with the pad for 16 bars: the resonance keeps climbing. Return with the filter wide open, then introduction of a second, higher acid line. Each plateau lasts 32 bars. A second, longer breakdown, with the pad changing chord once. Return, then the filter closes over the last 64 bars while the drums pull out. The track is a single curve that rises and then comes back down.
acidtrance.basse: Here the 303 is often the bass itself. Write a 16-step line on the root and the octave, with two or three accents and one slide per bar, cutoff closed at the start. Under it, a discreet sine on each kick holds the bottom of the spectrum below 80 Hz. When two acid lines coexist, as with Hardfloor, one stays low and closed, the other climbs into the highs. High-pass the low line at 50 Hz and saturate it slightly so it stays audible when the filter is down. The kick and the 303 share the low end: the kick takes the hit, the 303 takes the note.
etapes: Project at 138 BPM, 909 drums: kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeat, ride in eighth notes.
Open a 303 (ABL3, Phoscyon or Roland Cloud) and write 16 steps on the root and the octave with two accents and a slide, cutoff closed.
Add a sine under the kick to hold the low end, and a long minor pad filtered low.
Automate the 303's cutoff and resonance as a single curve that rises over 64 bars.
Build 9 minutes: drum intro, 303 rise, kickless breakdown, return with a second acid line, come-down.
Contain the resonance peaks with a fast compressor on the 303, then set the kick level first.
acidtrance.mix: The 303's resonance peaks are the danger of the mix: they jump out by 3 to 6 dB when the filter passes between 1 and 4 kHz. Put a dynamic EQ or a fast compressor, 6:1 ratio, 1 ms attack, on the 303 track to contain those spikes. Saturate before the filter rather than after. 909 kick in the center around -8 dB peak, low 303 in mono, high 303 slightly widened by its delay. Pads are wide and cut at 250 Hz. Light compression on the master bus, 2:1 ratio, then a limiter toward -8 LUFS. Check in mono that the acid line doesn't disappear when the filter is closed.

outils.pourquoi: The machine of the genre: acid line in a resonance rise over 32 to 64 bars, accents and slides. Cyclone Analogic TT-303 or Roland TB-03 for hardware clones.
Modeled 303 emulation, three oscillator models, sequencer with accents and slides: the most faithful replacement for long acid lines.
Another 303 emulation with built-in distortion and delay, useful for thickening the line before the filter without leaving the plugin.
Official Roland version, same envelope and resonance behavior, handy if you already subscribe to Roland Cloud.
Straight kick in the center, open hat on the offbeats, under the 303. 909 samples or D16 Drumazon are enough, the grain matters less than the acid line.
In dynamic mode on the 303 track to contain the resonance peaks between 1 and 4 kHz, which jump out by 3 to 6 dB when the filter opens.
Light saturation placed before the 303's delay, Analog Clip mode, drive 3 to 6 dB: thickens the sound without crushing the accents.

outils.nom: UNDRGRND Sounds They Call It Acid
outils.pourquoi: Pack of 303 loops and sequences cited in Attack's book for acid techno, usable as is for secondary acid layers.

reperes: Hardfloor: Acperience 1 (1992): two 303 lines rising one after the other for ten minutes, the absolute reference for the resonance rise
Emmanuel Top: Turkish Bazar (1995): the 303 as an oriental melody, high resonance and short delay
Kai Tracid: Dance For Eternity (1998): acid trance at the end of the decade, with harder kicks and bigger pads
acidtrance.rythme: The 909 is a carpet, not a show. Kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeat, ride in eighth notes from the first plateau. The difference from parent trance: the kick is a little shorter, decay around 250 ms, to let the 303's low end through. Snare rolls follow the resonance rises: when the filter climbs, the snare doubles into sixteenth notes and then thirty-second notes. A 909 tom tuned to the root can punctuate the end of the 16-bar blocks. No tribal percussion, no shakers: the 303 already fills the sixteenths.
acidtrance.sons: The central sound is the 303 in a resonance rise: cutoff opening over 32 to 64 bars, resonance rising at the same time, up to a whistle. On a real machine or on AudioRealism ABL3, D16 Phoscyon, Roland Cloud TB-303, what matters is the link between accent, envelope and resonance. A light distortion before the delay thickens the sound without crushing the peaks. Behind it, floating pads, long, filtered low, holding a minor chord without moving. Dotted-eighth synced delay on the 303, 35% feedback, high-pass at 400 Hz on the return. Automate the cutoff as a long curve, not with an LFO: the rise should feel played by hand.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
acidtrance.tempo: Between 135 and 145 BPM, a little faster than parent trance, always without swing. What replaces the groove is the TB-303: its accents and glides create an internal pulse that the straight grid lacks. Keep quantization at 100% on the drums, and let the 303 do the rest with its slides. An acid line is felt over 16 bars, not 4: the resonance rise is the real tempo of the track. Count in 32-bar blocks for each filter stage. If you are writing for the floor, 138 BPM is a good compromise between Hardfloor's hypnosis and the energy of the 1995 raves.

afrohouse.arrangement: A long ceremony. 32-bar intro with kick, shaker and one percussion in 12/8, then the layers come in every 16 bars: bass, pad, second percussion, vocal. The main chant arrives around bar 65 and repeats in call and response. 32-bar breakdown: kick cut, vocal and pad, percussion that keeps going, a gentle filter rise, the kick returns with the choirs. Second plateau with a melodic instrument added (kora, kalimba), long 32-bar outro where the layers pull out. Length 7 to 9 minutes. No drop, only one real arrival: the vocal's.
afrohouse.basse: A supple deep house bass: round synth (Massive with a sine and a bit of saw, or Analog) filtered at 200 to 300 Hz, in eighth notes with rests, on the roots of the progression and with passing notes. The line follows the ternary sway of the percussion: place notes on the triplets, not only on the eighths. Light sidechain with the kick. On more percussive tracks, the bass is a tuned tom or a low log drum playing the root. Stay on one or two notes per phrase, the richness is in the rhythm and the vocals, not in the bass harmony.
etapes: Project at 121 BPM, round kick on every beat, rim on 2 and 4, continuous sixteenth-note shaker with 55% swing.
Program a djembe part in 12/8 on the 4/4 grid and a low dundun in triplets, humanized.
Round bass in eighth notes with rests on the roots, a few notes placed on the triplets, light sidechain.
Massive or Juno pad on held minor 9 chords, and a 4-bar kalimba or kora motif.
Record or sample a call-and-response chant, place it at bar 65, and build 8 minutes around its arrival.
Mix warm and wide, percussion spread with room reverb, vocal up front with a long hall, master at -10 LUFS.
afrohouse.mix: A warm, deep, wide mix. Round kick in the center, cut above 5 kHz to avoid the click. Bass in the center, below 200 Hz. Percussion spread in stereo, each with a short room reverb, filtered so they don't mask each other. The vocal up front, with gentle (opto) compression, long reverb and dotted-quarter delay. Wide pads filtered below 200 Hz. Gentle bus compression, light tape saturation. Master at -9 to -10 LUFS with dynamics: the style is played in clubs but also listened to, and a crushed track loses its ternary breathing. Check that the triplets stay readable when everything plays together.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the South African scene, where most afro house tracks are programmed, humanized percussion and triplets on the 4/4 grid.
The scene's other DAW, for producers in Lisbon and Berlin; Black Coffee and Keinemusik projects circulate built with Ableton stock plugins.
Round sine bass with a bit of saw filtered at 250 Hz, and held minor 9 pads, as the course describes.
Round kick on every beat, mixed low, cut above 5 kHz; a rim or a snap plays the role of the clap.
Djembe, dundun, shekere, udu, log drum: Loopmasters Afro House or Native Instruments' West Africa Kontakt library, in 12/8 patterns.
Long, filtered hall on the Zulu vocals and the pads, plus a short room on the percussion; the Beatportal tutorial cites it.
Dotted-quarter delay on the call-and-response chants, with a bit of saturation, for a recorded-in-a-room feel.

reperes: Black Coffee: Superman (2009): Bucie's voice over 12/8 percussion and a deep bass, the formula that made the style global.
Culoe De Song: Webaba (2009): the darker, more percussive side, where tension rises through drums and silence.
Black Motion: Rainbow (2013): live-played djembe and choirs, the ceremonial side fully embraced.
Osunlade: Envision (2003): afro house seen from the diaspora, Yoruba percussion and deep house pads, before the South African wave.
afrohouse.rythme: The 909 kick or a round, deep kick on every beat, not too loud. Little clap: a rim, a snap or a wooden percussion on 2 and 4. Light sixteenth-note hats with swing. The heart: sampled or played African percussion, djembe, dundun, shekere, udu, in 12/8 patterns or in triplets on the 4/4 grid, with a continuous sixteenth-note shaker. A discreet log drum, less central than in amapiano, answering the kick. Fills are djembe or low tom rolls, never a 909 snare. On the breakdown, the kick is cut, the percussion and a chant keep going. Every percussion part is humanized.
afrohouse.sons: Deep house pads: Juno or Massive on held minor 7 and 9 chords, chorus, filter opening slowly. A Rhodes or a piano in long chords. Sampled traditional instruments: kora, mbira, kalimba, flute, balafon, played in 2- or 4-bar motifs. The vocals: chants in Zulu or Xhosa, call and response, choirs, often recorded rather than sampled, with a long reverb. Shouts, breaths, field recordings. Signature effects: dotted-quarter delay on the vocals, long filtered hall reverb, low-pass filter on the pads. The style is produced in FL Studio or Ableton with African percussion banks and a Massive for basses and pads.
sourcesOutils: Beatportal, Step-by-Step Guide to Creating an Afro House Track
The Producer School, How to Make Afro House Like Black Coffee
afrohouse.tempo: Between 118 and 124 BPM, slower than the tribal house it descends from, and above all more patient. The feel comes from polyrhythm: a straight four-on-the-floor kick, but percussion in 6/8 or 12/8 on top, which gives that ternary sway over a binary base. Program your shakers and log drums in eighth-note triplets or in 12/8 on a 4/4 grid and let them rub. Moderate swing on the hats, 54 to 56%. Phrases are long, 16 or 32 bars, and tracks last 7 to 9 minutes. Nothing is rushed: the track settles in like a ceremony.

aggrotech.arrangement: A 4- to 5-minute club song. Short 8- to 16-bar intro with a horror sample and the kick coming in fast. Screamed verse over the bass and hi-hats. Pre-chorus: roll, build-up. Chorus: the trance lead comes in, the voice screams the hook, the kick is at full. Second verse, chorus. 8- to 16-bar breakdown without kick with the filtered lead and a sample, then a thirty-second-note kick roll and a drop where everything returns. Last chorus doubled. Short outro. The track must be playable in a goth-industrial club: DJs chain choruses there, so keep them identifiable and loud.
aggrotech.basse: A distorted, rolling bass. Massive, cited in the brief, or Wavetable: saw with an aggressive wavetable, low-pass filter at 600 Hz with resonance, internal distortion, in sixteenth notes on the steps without a kick, or in continuous sixteenth notes with the EBM accent. Strong sidechain on the kick, 8 dB, 100 ms release: the pumping is audible and intended. The lines follow minor chords, often with the minor second or the tritone for aggression. A sine sub layer held on the root. Compared with dark electro, the bass is twice as loud and twice as dirty: it rivals the kick instead of supporting it.
etapes: At 140 BPM, program a club kick saturated at 6 dB on every beat, snare and clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, open hat on the offbeats.
Create a distorted bass on Massive or Wavetable in sixteenth notes, filter at 600 Hz with resonance, 8 dB sidechain on the kick.
Record a screamed vocal, then Overdrive 20 dB, pitch shift an octave down at 50%, Vocoder at 40%, delay.
Write a minor trance lead on Massive in Unison for the chorus, and bitcrush a few percussion hits on the offbeats.
Program a thirty-second-note kick roll and a snare build-up before each drop.
Arrange over 4 minutes 30: short intro with a horror sample, verse, chorus, 16-bar breakdown, drop, last chorus doubled.
aggrotech.mix: Loud, bright, dirty but readable. The kick and the bass share the low end through sidechain rather than EQ: the kick holds 40 to 100 Hz, the bass pumps above. The distorted voice is risky in the highs: de-esser, cut at 10 kHz, and 6:1 compression before the distortion to keep every word audible. The leads spread wide, cut below 300 Hz. Bitcrushed percussion filtered at 5 kHz so it isn't harsh. Master: 2:1 compression, then a soft clipper, then a limiter. Aim for -6 LUFS, the genre is one of the loudest in the family. Check that the chorus stays louder than the verse despite the limiting, with a 1 dB automated gain.

outils.pourquoi: Distorted sixteenth-note bass, aggressive wavetable, filter at 600 Hz with resonance, and minor trance leads in Unison.
Mixed at 40% after an Overdrive at 20 dB and a pitch shift an octave down: the robotic growl that defines the genre.
Multiband distortion recommended on the forums for harsh vocals: saturates the mids while keeping every word audible below 10 kHz.
Aggressive analog filter with distortion, cited by Vlaysin in the book and by harsh EBM producers for vocals and basses.
Synthetic club kick with a 50 ms pitch envelope and built-in distortion, to be run afterward through a Saturator at 6 dB.
The DAW of the Out of Line and NoiTekk scene, for thirty-second-note kick rolls and drops at 140 BPM.
The scene's leads and short pads, in very bright saw, inherited from the dark electro the genre descends from.
8 bits on the percussion and some leads, then filtered at 5 kHz so it isn't harsh: the bitcrush from the brief.

reperes: Combichrist: This Shit Will Fuck You Up (2005): the club kick, the growled voice, the chorus built for the floor.
Hocico: Born to Be Hated (2002): the dirty bass, the horror samples, excess fully embraced.
Grendel: Zombie Nation (2006): the minor trance lead on a club song structure.
Suicide Commando: Bind Torture Kill (2006): the vocoded screamed voice and the build-up before the drop.
aggrotech.rythme: A heavy club kick, saturated but not destroyed: a 909 or a synthetic kick with a 50 ms pitch envelope, run through a Saturator at 6 dB and a 4:1 compressor. On every beat. Snare and clap layered on 2 and 4, with a short reverb and a layer of white noise. Sixteenth-note hi-hats, velocities 100 and 60, open hat on the offbeats. Thirty-second-note kick rolls before the drops, a 4-bar snare build-up. A variation borrowed from the scene's forums: on some passages, replace the third kick of the bar with a synth hit or a silence, to break the monotony. Bitcrushed percussion on the offbeats.
aggrotech.sons: The voice is the emblem: screamed, then run through a distortion chain (Overdrive at 20 dB), a pitch shift an octave down mixed at 50%, a Vocoder at 40% and a delay. The result is a robotic growl. Another approach, described on the scene's forums: sing on a single note, correct the pitch all the way, then drop it an octave. The leads are minor trance melodies on Massive, saw in Unison, very bright. Bitcrush (Redux at 8 bits) on the percussion and some leads. Horror film samples and sirens. Dark but short pads. Everything is excessive, that is the definition of the genre.
sources: KVR Audio and Gearspace forums (threads on harsh EBM and aggrotech vocals)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros: Favourite bit of kit)
KVR Audio (threads Harsh EBM/aggrotech vocal effects and Vocal Effects Industrial/Harsh EBM)
Gearspace (thread What are you guys harsh EBM guys doing for vocals)
aggrotech.tempo: Between 130 and 150 BPM, most often 140, straight, no swing. What sets aggrotech apart from the dark electro it descends from: the tempo rises by 10 to 15 BPM and everything is designed for the dancefloor, with club kicks and club-style lifts. The feel is that of hard trance: massive four-on-the-floor, rolls, drops. In your DAW, start at 140 BPM, full quantization. The only off-grid elements are the screams and the horror samples, placed by hand. The track should make you want to stomp from the first bar: no long atmospheric intro, the kick arrives fast.

amapiano.arrangement: A long wait, then a party. 32- to 64-bar intro (up to 2 minutes) with kick, shakers, piano and vocals, without log drum, the filter opening. At bar 65 or later, the log drum comes in: that is the amapiano drop, often announced by a silence or a roll. 32-bar plateau with the log drum, then a 16-bar breakdown where it pulls out, return, second plateau with a denser log drum pattern or a vocal. 32-bar outro where the layers pull out. Length 6 to 8 minutes, sometimes more. The log drum doesn't play all the time: its absences matter as much as its arrivals.
amapiano.basse: The log drum: a hollow percussive bass sound, between a tuned tom and a sub, with a wooden attack and a low resonance. In Serum or Massive: a sine or a triangle with a fast pitch envelope (a drop of a few semitones in 30 to 60 ms), an amplitude envelope with a medium decay (300 to 500 ms), light distortion and saturation. It plays syncopated: 2-bar patterns in eighth and sixteenth notes, with rests, on the root, the third and the fifth, with octave jumps. The log drum is the bass, the percussion and the melody in a single instrument. Light sidechain. A held sine sub underneath on the deeper tracks.
etapes: Project at 112 BPM, round kick on every beat, rim on 2 and 4, three layered shakers in sixteenth notes with 58% shuffle.
Write a 4-chord jazz progression (minor 9, major 7) over 8 bars, played on piano with syncopation, with a held pad.
Create a log drum in Serum: sine, fast pitch envelope, 400 ms decay, light distortion.
Write a syncopated 2-bar log drum pattern on root, third and fifth, with rests and octave jumps.
Build 7 minutes with a 64-bar intro without log drum, its arrival at bar 65, a breakdown where it pulls out, and a second plateau.
Mix the log drum in the center between 50 and 300 Hz, wide shakers, piano with hall, and check on a phone.
amapiano.mix: A warm, wide mix with the log drum in the center. The log drum occupies 50 to 300 Hz, lightly saturated to come through on a phone, cut above 5 kHz. Kick in the center, round, light sidechain on the log drum. Wide, bright shakers, filtered below 500 Hz, with compression for the shuffle. Piano left and right, with a 2 to 3 s hall reverb. Vocals up front, gentle compression, long reverb and delay. Gentle bus compression, light tape saturation. Master at -8 to -9 LUFS: the style is listened to on small speakers and phones, the log drum must stay audible without sub. Check on a phone.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of Pretoria and Johannesburg: shakers shuffled at 58% in the step sequencer, log drum programmed in the piano roll, 64-bar intro.
The log drum: sine with a fast pitch envelope, 400 ms decay, light distortion, as in the course; Serum 2 today.
The other synth for the log drum and held deep house pads, very widespread among South African producers.
Gates and rhythmic repeats on the log drum and vocals, for syncopated patterns that stutter without redrawing everything.
Preset pianos, organs and saxophones for minor 9 jazz chords, common in amapiano studios that lack a pianist.
Pre-tuned log drums, layered shakers, whistles and bottle sounds; Transmission Samples or Modern Producers offer them for FL Studio.
When a musician plays the syncopated jazz chords, a real piano or a Rhodes with a 2 to 3 s hall replaces the rompler.

reperes: Kabza De Small & DJ Maphorisa ft. Ami Faku: Abalele (2021): the jazz piano, the vocal and the log drum arriving late, the classic form of the style.
Young Stunna: Adiwele (2021): the log drum as melody, syncopated under a friendly vocal, the hit that swept everything.
MFR Souls ft. Major League DJz, Kamo Mphela & Bontle Smith: Amanikiniki (2020): the more danceable side, shakers up front and dense log drum.
Mapara A Jazz: John Vuli Gate (2020): the festive, sung side, with the piano up front and a song structure.
amapiano.rythme: Round, short kick on every beat, often doubled with a lower kick, not too loud. A rim, a snap or a discreet clap on 2 and 4. The shakers are the engine: a continuous shaker in shuffled sixteenth notes, often two or three shakers layered at different speeds, with accents. Sixteenth-note hats with shuffle, rare open hat. Sampled African percussion, congas, bells in 12/8. Whistle sounds, tongue clicks, bottles. Fills are percussion rolls, never a 909 snare. During the intro, the drums are almost complete but the log drum is missing, and that absence is what builds the anticipation.
amapiano.sons: The piano: played jazz chords, minor 9, major 7, in quarter notes and syncopated, with a slightly bright acoustic or electric piano sound. Jazz keys: Rhodes, organ, soft synths. Held deep house pads (Massive, Juno). Friendly vocals, sung or spoken in Zulu, Sotho or English, often in call and response, with choirs and ad libs. Sampled saxophones or flutes. Whistles, crowd sounds. Signature effects: long reverb on the piano and vocals, dotted-quarter delay, low-pass filter opening over the intro, and the log drum arriving clean. The style is produced in FL Studio with South African percussion banks.

amapiano.tempo: Between 110 and 115 BPM, 112 on average: that is slow for house, and it is what gives the log drum room to bounce between two hits. The feel is supple, with a marked shuffle on the shakers and hats (56 to 60%) and a straight kick. The percussion is often in 12/8 or in triplets over the 4/4, a legacy of afro house. The log drum plays syncopated, never on every beat. Tracks are long, 6 to 8 minutes, with 2-minute intros where the log drum is not there yet. Don't rush: amapiano is music of patience, and the arrival of the log drum is the event.

ambientdub.arrangement: Long tracks of 8 to 15 minutes. 2-minute intro of pads and samples without kick, the bass comes in, then the drums, in 32-bar sections. No drop: the high points are breakdowns where only the delays and the reverb remain, then the return of the bass. The dub mix is the composition itself: record a 10-minute pass where you play mutes and sends on the console or on a controller, keep the best moments, and edit. The track can change pad and sample every 4 minutes without changing the bass. Last Train to Lhasa works like a journey: the landscapes roll by, the rhythm stays.
ambientdub.basse: The bass matters here, unlike in the rest of the family. A deep, round sub, sine or triangle in Operator or Trilian, low-pass filter at 120 Hz, long notes. The pattern comes from reggae: silence on the first beat, a note on the offbeat of the second, root and fifth, one or two notes per bar, in minor or Dorian. It doesn't move much: two chords over 16 bars are enough. A little Saturator (4 dB drive) so you can feel it on small speakers. It is not sidechained to the kick, the two coexist because the kick is weak. With Banco de Gaia, it carries the journey; with Dreadzone, it comes from the dub sound system.
etapes: Set the tempo to 80 BPM and create an Echo delay in tape mode synced to the dotted eighth, 60 percent feedback, high-pass at 300 Hz: that is your grid.
Write a sine bass in Operator, two notes (D and A) in Dorian, silence on 1, a note on the offbeat of 2, filtered at 120 Hz.
Lay down a soft 808 kick filtered at 100 Hz with a rimshot on the third beat, and an isolated percussion hit sent into the delay.
Add a Juno pad with chorus and a one-second attack, and a radio voice or flute sample sent into the same delay.
Record 10 minutes of mutes and sends live on a controller, then edit the best passages into 10 minutes with a kickless intro.
Mix with the bass in mono in front of the kick, delays behind, final level around -13 LUFS.
ambientdub.mix: The bass in mono, louder than the kick, which stays buried. Delays and reverbs on sends with a high-pass at 300 Hz and a low-pass around 4 kHz, so they stay behind. A long reverb (Valhalla Room, 6 seconds) on the pads, a short spring on the percussion. Very light bus compression, 1.5:1 ratio. Dynamics preserved, final level around -12 to -14 LUFS: louder than pure ambient, but far from club. The dub trick: when a delay runs away, let it almost saturate, then cut it dead, the ear loves it. Check the bass on a system with a sub, it must stay round and free of distortion.

outils.pourquoi: The tape delay of dub: repeats that darken, feedback pushed to the edge of self-oscillation. Ableton Echo in tape mode or Roland Cloud RE-201 replace it.
The sampler for the radio, NASA and flute voices with The Orb and Banco de Gaia, also on S900 and S3200; Simpler does this today.
You play the console: mutes and delay sends recorded live over ten minutes, like The Orb on their big Soundcraft. A MIDI controller is enough in Ableton.
Pads with slow chorus and a one-second attack, the harmonic base of the genre; TAL-U-NO-LX or Ableton Analog with Chorus-Ensemble give the same roundness.
The multi-effects unit The Orb owned a dozen of: pitch-shift, diatonic delays, strange reverbs. Eventide H3000 Factory brings it to plugin form.
6-second reverb on the pads and a short spring on the percussion; high-pass at 300 Hz and low-pass at 4 kHz on the returns.
Delay synced to the dotted eighth, 60 percent feedback, tape mode, high-pass filter at 300 Hz: that is your rhythmic grid even before the kick.
Pure sine bass on two notes, filtered at 120 Hz, in mono and in front of the buried 808 kick; the harmonics stay at the console, not in the synth.

reperes: The Orb: Towers of Dub (1992): 15 minutes of dub bass, runaway delays and dialogue samples, the model of the genre.
Higher Intelligence Agency: Speech (1993): bass and pads breathing together at the tempo of the delay, more restrained than The Orb.
Banco de Gaia: Last Train to Lhasa (1995): travel samples, flutes and a rhythm that moves forward, the traveling side.
Dreadzone: Zion Youth (1995): the sound system in ambient dub, heavier bass and vocals, the door to the club.
ambientdub.rythme: The kick is soft and buried: an 808 filtered at 100 Hz or a reggae drum sample, in one drop (kick and rimshot together on the third beat) or kick on 1 and 3 with a rimshot on 3. The hi-hats are sparse sixteenth notes, sometimes just one per beat, and a sporadic percussion hit (bongo, shaker, block) goes off into the Space Echo. What sets this genre apart from parent ambient is that the drums appear and disappear: dub is done at the console, by cutting the snare for 8 bars and then throwing it back into the delay. Record these mutes live rather than drawing them, you can hear the gesture. No clap, no tight closed hat.
ambientdub.sons: The brief names the Roland RE-201 Space Echo, the mixing console and the Akai S1000. The Space Echo lives on in Ableton's Echo in tape mode or in a dedicated emulation: synced delay, feedback pushed to the edge of self-oscillation, high-pass at 300 Hz and low-pass at 4 kHz on the repeats. A spring reverb on the percussion. The pads come from a Juno-106 or Analog with slow chorus, one-second attack. The samples make the identity: radio and NASA dialogue with The Orb, flutes and tablas with Banco de Gaia, travel voices with Loop Guru. The delay sends are automated like an instrument. It is the only genre in the family where you play the console.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, The Orb's Thomas Fehlmann's Berlin studio
KVR Audio (forum), The Orb / early KLF sound
ambientdub.tempo: Here, at last, a pulse. Between 70 and 100 BPM, the tempo of slowed-down dub reggae, or 120 BPM played half-time as with The Orb, where the kick falls once per bar in half-time. What defines the feel is the delay: a delay synced to the dotted eighth (3/16) or the dotted quarter, with 50 to 70 percent feedback, becomes the real grid of the track. The pads breathe at that tempo. A light swing, 54 to 56 percent, on the hi-hats and percussion. Check that the delay on your pad and the one on the percussion share the same subdivision, otherwise the track loses its breathing. Towers of Dub holds 15 minutes on this principle.

ambientgenre.arrangement: There is no verse and no drop. An ambient piece lasts between 6 and 20 minutes and is built layer by layer: each element enters with a 30 to 60 second fade, stays, then fades away the same way. Attack's book advises gently automating the entry and exit of a drone's layers to make it organic: apply that to the whole track. One or two harmonic zones at most, no spectacular modulation. The track must go nowhere, that is the listening contract: 1/1 holds 17 minutes on a single motif. Think in slow shapes rather than bars, note your intentions in seconds. End by disappearing, never with a hard cut.
ambientgenre.basse: No bassline. The low end comes from the root of the pads: a note held one or two octaves below the chord, between C1 and C2, low-pass filtered around 200 Hz, at a modest level. It is a root pedal rather than a bass: it stays while the chords move above, which gives that feeling of harmony floating without ever resolving. Harold Budd's Rhodes gives a warm low end without any sub at all. No sidechain, no kick to respect. The trap is accumulation: every pad brings low end, and long reverbs add more. Cut the reverb returns below 150 Hz and keep a single low-end source, otherwise everything turns to mud.
etapes: Choose a key and two slow chords (for example F major 7 and D minor 9). Create a pad in Wavetable with a 2 s attack and an 8 s release, and record each chord into a looping clip of a different length (7 and 11 bars).
Add a root pedal an octave below, filtered at 200 Hz, at -12 dB, that never changes.
Record a few piano or Rhodes notes by hand, off the grid, without a metronome, then send them into a 10-second reverb with 80 ms of pre-delay.
Bring the pads to life: a slow LFO on the cutoff (30 s period) and another on the volume (8 s period), low depth.
Add a field recording or discreet tape noise, then arrange over 8 to 12 minutes by drawing 45-second fades for every entry and every exit.
Mix at -15 LUFS, cut the reverb returns below 200 Hz, and listen to the whole thing at low volume: if it works in the background, you've got it.
ambientgenre.mix: Keep the dynamics. Target -14 to -16 LUFS integrated, peak at -1 dB, with no limiter crushing it. Light compression or none: 2:1 ratio, 30 ms attack, release above 500 ms so it doesn't pump. Reverbs go on sends, with a high-pass at 200 Hz and a low-pass around 6 to 8 kHz on the return, otherwise the tail swallows everything: Attack's book also advises cutting the low end of reverb and delay returns to avoid mush. Pads wide in stereo, but everything below 150 Hz in mono. Over a 15-minute listen, the 2 to 5 kHz range gets tiring: lower it by 2 dB. A light tape or vinyl noise at -40 dB glues the layers together.

outils.pourquoi: Eno's suitcase synth: drifting oscillators and a pin matrix for unstable pads. Today the XILS-lab XILS 3 emulation or Ableton Analog captures the gesture.
Two linked Revoxes form the tape loop of Discreet Music: a delay of several seconds that accumulates. In Ableton, Echo in tape mode with feedback at 70 percent.
Harold Budd's electric piano: spaced notes, soft attack, drowned in a 10-second reverb. Ableton Electric or a sampled Rhodes replaces it easily.
Basic pad synth: 2-second attack, 8-second release, two slightly detuned oscillators and a very slow LFO on the cutoff, 30-second period.
Thick analog pads with built-in chorus, a filter that heats up when you push the resonance. u-he Zebra is better suited to moving textures and spectral drones.
A huge library of ready-to-use pads, bowls and granular textures; useful to find a color quickly and then slow it down with the envelopes.
Free reverb with near-infinite tails, on a send with a high-pass at 200 Hz on the return, 80 ms pre-delay; Gemini mode makes a single note float.
Free Max for Live instrument that reads a sample in slow grains; Attack's book uses it for two layers of a textured drone, low end and high crackle.

reperes: Brian Eno: 1/1 (1978): loops of different lengths crossing each other, the piano arriving when you don't expect it, never the same twice.
Harold Budd: The Pearl (1984): piano and Rhodes drowned in reverb, a warm low end without any sub.
Hiroshi Yoshimura: Blink (1986): lightness, short clear sounds with lots of air between them, ambient that breathes.
Aphex Twin: Rhubarb (1994): a single pad rising and falling over 7 minutes, proof that a track can hold on almost nothing.
ambientgenre.rythme: No drums, and that is the point. What stands in for rhythm: the beating of two close notes, the slow attack of a piano or a Rhodes that surfaces every 20 seconds, the cycle of a 0.1 Hz LFO on the volume of a pad. On 1/1, the pulse is the irregular return of the same piano notes over the synth carpet. If you want breathing, put an Auto Pan or a Max for Live LFO on the gain of a pad, period 6 to 12 seconds, depth 20 percent. A ping-pong delay at 500 ms with 30 percent feedback gives a slight float without marking time. Field recordings (rain, a distant city) also add a sense of time to the texture.
ambientgenre.sons: The brief names the EMS Synthi AKS, the tape recorder, the modular and the Fender Rhodes. Today, Wavetable or Analog in Ableton, Omnisphere, u-he Diva or Zebra, an electric piano (Electric) do the job. The Eno/Lanois move is the processing: 8 to 15 second reverb with 80 ms pre-delay, tape delay (Ableton's Echo or an RE-201 emulation), slow chorus, then an EQ that removes what gets in the way. Envelope attacks of 1 to 3 seconds, releases of 5 to 10 seconds. Attack's book builds a drone in distinct layers spread across the spectrum, from the low end to the air above 4 kHz, with Granulator II and Operator: a good recipe for a pad that lives. For generativity, random Follow Actions and a Random MIDI device.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Textural Drone and Movement & Change)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Textural Drone and Movement & Change)
eMastered, 13 Best VST Plugins for Ambient Music
Magnetic Magazine, Best VST Plugins for Ambient Electronic Music Production
KVR Audio (forum), What are some good plugins for creating ambient music
ambientgenre.tempo: There is no tempo in the club sense. What replaces the pulse is duration: notes of 10 to 30 seconds, cycles that never land back on their feet. Eno's method on Music for Airports is tape loops of different lengths slowly drifting out of phase. In Ableton, do the same: clips of 7, 11 and 13 bars looping, each with a held note, and let them drift. If you set a BPM anyway, take 60 to 70 only to sync the delays and LFOs. No swing, no quantization: you place your notes by ear, slightly before or after the grid. Time should feel suspended, as if the music was there before you pressed play.

ambienthouse.arrangement: Tracks are long, 8 to 18 minutes, and built like a journey: 2 minutes of pads and samples, the kick coming in through a filter over 32 bars, a 4- to 6-minute plateau where samples come and go, a long 2-minute breakdown without kick, then a return and a 2-minute come-down. Changes arrive every 32 bars, never faster. No chorus: repetition and delay make the memory. Plan a 4-minute radio version by cutting the plateau, and a long version for the album. The listener should be able to fall asleep and wake up without losing the thread.
ambienthouse.basse: The bass is a low pad more than a line: a Juno-106 or a Korg M1 on a filtered square or triangle wave, a note held over 4 or 8 bars, root then fourth or minor seventh, 1-second release. On some tracks, a simple house line in eighth notes appears for 16 bars and then melts back into the pad. Dub delays on the bass are typical: a send to a dotted-quarter delay with feedback at 40%, filtered at 500 Hz, that makes the notes spin. Gentle sidechain on the kick, 3 dB, 200 ms release, so the pulse breathes. It stays below 150 Hz and leaves the mids to the samples.
etapes: Lay down a Korg M1 or Juno pad in major seventh chords, 3-second attack, over 8 bars at 118 BPM.
Add a bass held over 4 bars, root then fourth, with a send to a dotted-quarter delay at 40% feedback.
Program a 909 kick filtered at 150 Hz mixed at -16 dB, open hats on the offbeat, clap far back in the reverb.
Cut 6 or 8 voice, radio or nature samples in Simpler and trigger them every 8 or 16 bars into a dub delay.
Arrange over 10 minutes: 2 minutes without kick, entry through a filter over 32 bars, plateau, 2-minute breakdown, come-down.
Mix huge: 8-second reverb on a send, small kick, automate the delay feedback, master at -12 LUFS.
ambienthouse.mix: The mix is huge and soft: pads across the whole stereo field, samples placed in ping-pong delay, kick in the center and small. 6 to 8 second reverb on a send for the samples and pads, high-pass at 300 Hz. The drums are lightly compressed, 2:1, and the master bus has only a compressor that does nothing, or almost. Cut the pads at 120 Hz to leave the held bass alone. Automate the delay sends on the samples: a sample going into 70% feedback for 8 bars is an event. Master at -12 or -14 LUFS, with room: an ambient house track that is too loud loses its sky.

outils.pourquoi: The sampler that loads radio voices, birds and minimalist guitars. The Orb started on an Akai S700 in a bedroom, then in the studio.
Major seventh pads with a 3-second attack, and the house organ if you want it. Korg Collection M1 is the official emulation.
The held bass on a filtered square or triangle over 4 bars, 1-second release, with the chorus. Softube Model 84 in software.
Softened kick, attack cut, low-pass at 150 Hz, mixed at -16 dB, filtered open hats. D16 Drumazon 2 or Roland Cloud TR-909.
The dub delay with long, filtered feedback that turns each sample into a cloud. Ableton Echo with feedback at 70% does the same job.
To cut 6 or 8 voice or nature phrases and trigger them every 8 or 16 bars into the delay.

outils.nom: BBC Sound Effects and NASA archives
outils.pourquoi: Water sounds, animals, radio and space mission voices, freely available, as raw material for the travel samples.
Free, 6 to 8 second reverb on a send for the pads and samples, high-pass at 300 Hz to keep the low end clean.

reperes: 808 State: Pacific State (1989): the saxophone, the birds and the soft house beat, the pastoral version of the genre.
The Orb: Little Fluffy Clouds (1990): the interview laid over a guitar sequence, the travel samples and the discreet kick.
The Orb: A Huge Ever Growing Pulsating Brain That Rules from the Centre of the Ultraworld (1989): the long journey, dub delays and voice samples.
The KLF: Last Train to Trancentral (1991): the pad, the 909 kick and the voice samples becoming almost pop.
ambienthouse.rythme: The kick is a softened TR-909: attack cut, low-pass filter at 150 Hz, medium decay, mixed at -16 dB, far below what you would do in house. 909 open hats on the offbeat, filtered at 8 kHz and drowned in a dub delay. Snare or clap almost absent, or a 909 clap far back with 2 seconds of reverb. Add percussion in dotted-eighth ping-pong delay, a rimshot, a tambourine, that spin and disappear. On 808 State's Pacific State, the beat is that of a calm house track under a saxophone and birds. Automate the drum bus filter: the beat must come in from far away over 32 bars and leave just as slowly.
ambienthouse.sons: The wide pads come from the Korg M1 and the Juno-106: major seventh or ninth chords, 3-second attack, chorus, covered in reverb. Travel samples are the hallmark of the genre: NASA voices, interviews, radio, birdsong, water sounds, excerpts from classical records or minimalist guitars, as on Little Fluffy Clouds, which lays an interview over a guitar sequence. Load them into Simpler, cut them into phrases and trigger them every 8 or 16 bars. Dub delays, Space Echo or Ableton's Echo, with long feedback and a filter, turn each sample into a cloud. Add a slow arpeggiated sequence and a sampled saxophone or flute for the pastoral version.
sourcesOutils: Sound On Sound (Classic Tracks: The Orb Little Fluffy Clouds)
Wikipedia (The Orb's Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld)
ambienthouse.tempo: It is the only genre in the family that keeps a real house tempo: 110 to 125 BPM, in straight 4/4. What changes compared with Chicago house is the weight: the kick is there but it doesn't drive, it pulses under pads. Low swing, 50 to 53%, a steady pulse that lets the journey happen on top. The Orb's tracks often run past 10 minutes and the tempo serves as a thread, not an engine. Think of a tempo of 118 BPM and a kick you could almost forget: if the listener notices the drums before the pad, they are too loud.

ambienttechno.arrangement: Six to ten minutes. Open on the pads and a delay, 32 bars without a beat. The bass comes in, then the kick at bar 49 or 65, gently. Add the melody over 16 bars, then let it repeat with tiny variations: a changed note, a delay that lengthens. A long central breakdown of 32 or 64 bars without drums where the pads evolve through filter automation. The beat returns without announcement. End by removing the elements in the reverse order of their entry, down to the pads alone. No build-up, no drop, no roll. The track must be able to serve as a set closer or a chill-out piece: each section must stand on its own.
ambienttechno.basse: A warm analog bass: SH-101, Juno or Ableton's Analog, triangle or saw wave filtered at 300 Hz, long release. It plays one note per bar or soft eighth notes on the chord roots, and follows the harmonic progression rather than hammering the root. Very light sidechain or none. A sine sub can double it an octave below at -12 dB. Add a light chorus on the main bass (not on the sub) for width. It can play a descending melody over 8 bars as in B12's tracks. Cut it below 35 Hz, keep the sub mono, and let the bass stop during the breakdowns so the pads take up all the space.
etapes: At 115 BPM, write a progression of four minor chords on a Juno or Diva pad, slow attack, chorus.
Send the pad into a dotted-quarter delay and an 8 s reverb on returns cut below 300 Hz.
Add a soft analog bass that follows the roots, one note per bar.
Lay down a softened 909 kick (faded attack, low-pass at 3 kHz) and eighth-note hi-hats, all under the pads.
Create a filtered noise layer in Analog with automated cutoff and auto-pan for movement.
Arrange over eight minutes: 32 bars without a beat, gentle entry, long central breakdown, mirrored exit.
ambienttechno.mix: Space is the subject. Reverbs and delays on returns, cut below 300 Hz and above 8 kHz to avoid mush. Pads wide in stereo, bass and kick mono. The beat is mixed low, kick around -14 dB, under the pads which peak around -8. No bus compression or very gentle (Glue 2:1, 1 dB). A master around -12 or -14 LUFS with all the dynamics preserved: the genre is played at moderate volume, on hi-fi speakers as much as in clubs. Check that the reverb tails don't mask the melody's attacks; if they do, add 20 ms of pre-delay. The light grain of a 1 dB saturation unifies the layers.

outils.pourquoi: Softened: kick attack faded over 20 ms, low-pass at 3 kHz, eighth-note hi-hats cut at 10 kHz, all mixed under the pads.
Sampled strings played as chords, filtered congas and rims, the 12-bit grain of the Warp records from the Artificial Intelligence series.
Two detuned saw pads with chorus, 500 ms attack, 2 s release; u-he Diva is the usual emulation.
Warm analog bass, triangle or saw filtered at 300 Hz, one note per bar following the chord roots.
1980s reverb on clap and snare, decay 1.3 s, pre-delay 12 ms, mix 17%, and a 5 to 10 s reverb on a return for the pads.
Analog for the filtered noise with auto-pan, Echo on the dotted quarter at 50% feedback, Granulator II for granular backgrounds.
The dark, muddy multi-effects of Aphex Twin's first records, delays falling into the reverb with a slight pitch shift.
The polyphonic rack believed to be behind the pads of Selected Ambient Works II, for thick pads that a slow filter opens over 64 bars.

reperes: The Orb: Little Fluffy Clouds (1990): the voice sample, the slow beat and the pads, the founding English chill-out
Biosphere: Baby Interphase (1991): the softened 909 under arctic textures
Aphex Twin: Xtal (1992): the patient melody, the ethereal voice and the receding beat, the model of the genre
Barker: Paradise Engineering (2019): the kickless version, where only melodies and textures carry the track
ambienttechno.rythme: A softened TR-909: kick with the attack faded over 20 ms, low-pass filtered at 3 kHz, sent into a short plate reverb, at a low level. Soft four-on-the-floor or a broken pattern with varying velocities. Snare or clap drowned in a 1980s reverb (Valhalla VintageVerb, decay 1.3 s, pre-delay 12 ms, mix 17%). 909 closed hats in eighth notes on the offbeats, cut above 10 kHz. A few Akai S950 sampler percussion sounds: congas, rims, filtered fragments. Add a layer of filtered white noise in Analog, short envelope (attack 5 ms, decay 300 ms), automated cutoff and auto-pan at 1 Hz, which plays the sixteenths in place of the hi-hats. The beat always stays under the pads.
ambienttechno.sons: Analog pads: Juno-106 or Diva, two detuned saws, chorus, 500 ms attack, 2 s release, low-pass filter opened slowly. Strings sampled in an Akai S950 and played as chords. Patient melodies, four or five notes on a minor or Dorian scale, played on an electric piano or a soft pluck. The delays are long: Echo on the dotted quarter, 50% feedback, filtered, on almost everything. 5 to 10 second reverb on a return, cut below 300 Hz. Granular textures (Granulator II on a synth sample) for the backgrounds. Stack eight drone layers if you like, each on a different frequency zone, then mix them along a Fletcher-Munson curve: the lows louder.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
ambienttechno.tempo: From 100 to 125 BPM, often around 115 like Xtal. The kick is not the reason for the track, so the tempo can be slow without the piece collapsing. Minimal or no groove; it is the long delays, locked to the dotted quarter or the half note, that give the sway. A half-time beat (snare on beat 3 only) works well and lets the pads breathe. Sixteenth-note hi-hats become useless: prefer soft eighth notes or nothing. The track is built on 8- or 16-bar melodic cycles rather than on a pulse. The tempo must let an 8-second reverb die out before the next chord.

anthemtrance.arrangement: Eight minutes built around six passes of the theme. 32-bar intro with kick, bass and a pluck. The theme arrives filtered at bar 33, opens over 16 bars. 32-bar plateau. First short breakdown. Return. Then the big breakdown, 48 to 64 bars: the theme is played bare, over pad and strings, once slowly, then with the filtered bass, then with the roll. Drop: kick, bass, theme in full supersaw, 32 bars. Second pass with an octave variation, then a gradual pull-out, the theme being the last to leave. The breakdown is long because it is the moment the anthem becomes unforgettable.
anthemtrance.basse: Offbeat bass, JP-8000 or Virus saw, 120 ms decay, 400 Hz cutoff, 5:1 sidechain. It follows the theme's chords, often three or four chords over 8 bars, in minor with a resolution to the relative major. It is simple, with no sixteenth-note layer: the theme is melodic, the bass is an engine. Sine sub below 60 Hz. In the breakdown, it leaves and lets the pad hold the harmony. At the drop, it returns at the same time as the kick and the theme, on the same first beat. Cut at 90 Hz.
etapes: Project at 138 BPM, restrained uplifting drums: kick, clap and snare, open hat, ride.
Compose an 8-bar theme in minor with long notes and an interval of a fifth or a sixth, one you remember on first listen.
Play it on a 7-voice monophonic supersaw with portamento, in octaves, with a dotted-eighth delay and a 5-second reverb.
Lay down the offbeat bass on the theme's chords, with sub and 5:1 sidechain, and a wide pad behind.
Arrange 8 minutes around six passes of the theme, including a 48-bar breakdown where it is played bare.
Make the lead dominate the mix, compress it at 4:1 and let it come up 2 dB in the breakdown.
anthemtrance.mix: The lead dominates: around -8 dB peak, wide, with 2 dB at 3 kHz and a long reverb on a return. Kick in the center around -6 dB, sub in mono. The pad is cut at 200 Hz and lightly sidechained. The pluck is low and on the sides. Sidechain on the lead too, 2:1 ratio, 80 ms release, so it pumps with the kick without disappearing. 4:1 compression on the lead so it stays constant on the long notes. Master: glue compressor at 2:1, limiter toward -6 LUFS. In the breakdown, the lead can come up 2 dB: bare, it must fill the room.

outils.pourquoi: The monophonic anthem lead: a supersaw in octaves, 50 ms portamento, cutoff at 800 Hz then wide open. Arturia Jup-8000 V in software.
The wide pad holding the chords behind the lead, and the discreet arpeggio plucks, on the Hooj Choons and Deviant records.
Breakdown strings and pianos, for the bare passage where the lead must fill the room. Korg Triton in software in the Korg Collection.
On the anthem lead: cutoff automated from 800 Hz to fully open over 16 bars, the theme's first filtered appearance before the drop.
To replay the anthem lead today: 7 unison voices, portamento, 4:1 compression to hold the long notes at a constant level.
The DAW of anthem trance studios, with a long arrangement where the filtered theme returns three times before the final drop.
Long 5-second reverb on a return for the lead, with a dotted-eighth delay, so the theme stays suspended in the breakdown.

reperes: Three Drives: Greece 2000 (1997): a theme of a few notes repeated endlessly, filtered then open, the model of the anthem
Paul van Dyk: For an Angel (1998): the monophonic lead in octaves and the long breakdown where the theme is played bare
Binary Finary: 1998 (1998): the arpeggio that becomes an anthem, with the long reverb and the crash at each entry
Cosmic Gate: Exploration Of Space (Cosmic Gate's Third Contact Remix) (2019): the same theme twenty years later, with a modern mix
anthemtrance.rythme: Clean 909 kick on every beat, clap and snare on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeat, ride in eighth notes: the uplifting base. What changes is the restraint: snare rolls are shorter, 4 to 8 bars, and don't accelerate up to thirty-second notes, because the anthem does the work. A crash on the first beat of each entry of the theme. During the breakdown, a one-bar reversed cymbal and an isolated kick on the last beat before the drop. No decorative percussion: the theme must have all the space. The pattern can stay identical from start to finish.
anthemtrance.sons: The monophonic anthem lead: a JP-8000 supersaw as a single melodic voice, 7 detuned saws, 50 ms portamento, played in octaves for thickness. The theme is in minor, with long notes and a memorable interval, often a fifth or a sixth. It is first heard filtered, cutoff at 800 Hz, then wide open. Behind it, a wide Virus pad holding the chords, Triton strings on the breakdown. A sixteenth-note pluck arpeggio, discreet. Long 5-second reverb and dotted-eighth delay on the lead. No vocals, or a single repeated word. Everything serves the theme.
anthemtrance.tempo: 136 to 140 BPM, the same zone as the uplifting trance it is the shadow of. Straight grid. The feel is dictated by a single theme of 8 or 16 bars, huge, repeated until the floor sings it. The whole tempo is organized around this theme: 16-bar blocks where it appears, disappears, comes back. Greece 2000 and For an Angel sit in this zone. The difference from uplifting: the anthem doesn't climb step by step toward a climax, it arrives complete and repeats. Count repetitions rather than bars: the theme must pass at least six times, filtered, bare, then at full power.

balearic.arrangement: A balearic track or edit lasts 6 to 9 minutes, with a long mixable opening of 32 bars of percussion and pads. The track proper, pop or instrumental, then arrives: verse, chorus, guitar or saxophone solo. Around two thirds of the way in, a long 16- to 32-bar breakdown removes the kick and leaves the delayed guitar and the sea. The return is gentle, no aggressive build-up: the kick comes back alone with a pad, then everything else. End with 32 bars of percussion and pads for the DJ. The art of the edit is patience: you cut nothing, you extend everything, you give the sunset time.
balearic.basse: The bass is round, played, almost slow disco: electric bass played with the fingers, or a Juno-106 on a square wave filtered at 400 Hz with a bit of chorus. It plays melodic lines in eighth notes, root, octave, fifth, with chromatic passages toward the next chord, as in 1980s pop. It is more melodic and more mobile than in chill-out. Add a 3:1 compressor with a slow attack to keep the attack of the fingers. On edits, the original bass is often kept and reinforced with a sine doubled underneath. The kick is soft, so sidechain is unnecessary: the bass and kick share the low end without conflict.
etapes: Choose a tempo of 102 BPM, a soft 808 kick mixed low and slightly swung eighth-note hi-hats.
Record or loop congas, bongos and shaker over 4 bars, and humanize the velocities by 15%.
Write a played, melodic bass in eighth notes with chromatic passages, on a Juno-106 or an electric bass.
Add a clean guitar into a dotted-eighth tape echo and a Juno pad in major seventh chords.
Arrange over 7 minutes: 32-bar mixable intro, song or theme, long kickless breakdown, percussion outro.
Mix bright and wide, high shelf at +2 dB, 4-second reverb, discreet kick.
balearic.mix: The mix is bright and wide, with generous stereo: guitar on the left, echo on the right, pads everywhere. The kick stays small, -14 dB, with no dominant sub. A 3 to 4 second reverb on a send for guitar, vocals and percussion, with 30 ms of pre-delay. Gentle compression, 2:1, no heavy saturation: the grain comes from the original record if it is an edit, or from a bit of tape. A high shelf at +2 dB above 8 kHz brings the sun. Master around -10 LUFS to hold up against house records in a mix, but keep the breakdown's dynamics. Listen outdoors if you can: balearic is judged in the open air.

outils.pourquoi: Major seventh pads with the chorus, and a square-wave bass filtered at 400 Hz. Softube Model 84 or Roland Cloud JUNO-106 emulate it.
The signature: slow arpeggios or soft chicken-scratch, a bit of chorus, panned left with the echo answering on the right.
Dotted-eighth tape echo with 3 or 4 repeats on the guitar and the sax. Ableton Echo or Roland Cloud RE-201 in software.
Discreet kick mixed at -14 dB, soft clap or rimshot: the drums of 1980s fusion records. Samples in a Drum Rack.
Free, the Juno chorus on the guitar, the bass or a pad that doesn't come from a Juno.
Latin percussion played by hand in tumbao, or a sampled loop humanized by 15% in velocity.
For patient edits: warp an entire record, keep the best passage looped for 4 minutes, add a kick and a conga for the DJ.
3 to 4 second reverb with 30 ms of pre-delay on guitar, vocals and percussion: the sun in the sound.

reperes: Sueno Latino: Sueno Latino (1989): Manuel Göttsching's guitar sequence replayed under a soft kick and vocals, the perfect balearic edit.
A Man Called Adam: Barefoot in the Head (1990): piano, saxophone and Latin percussion over a light 4/4.
Chris Rea: Josephine (1985): a mid-tempo pop rock song adopted by Ibiza DJs, proof that the spirit matters more than the genre.
Penguin Cafe Orchestra: Music for a Found Harmonium (1984): the harmonium and joyful repetition, no kick, played at sunrise anyway.
balearic.rythme: The kick is a discreet 4/4, often an 808 or a LinnDrum, mixed low. Open hi-hats in eighth notes, a little swing. On top, hand-played Latin percussion: congas in tumbao, bongos, shaker, cabasa, bell on the offbeat, as on a 1980s fusion record. Record them yourself or sample a conga loop and humanize the velocities by 15%. The snare is a soft clap or a rimshot, never a rock snare. An edit trick: keep the drums of the original record and add only a looped conga and a kick under its own, to give the DJ a mixable entry. The rhythm must be able to host a guitar, a piano and a saxophone without getting in their way.
balearic.sons: The electric guitar in delay is the signature: a clean sound, a bit of chorus, a dotted-eighth tape echo with 3 or 4 repeats, and slow arpeggios or soft chicken-scratch chords. The Juno-106 provides the pads with its chorus and major seventh chords. Add an electric piano, a saxophone or a flute, a steel drum or a marimba, soft female vocals with lots of reverb. Nature sounds, waves, birds, often come in at the intro. Patient edits sample an entire record and keep only its best passage, looped for 4 minutes. What matters is the sun in the sound: everything is bright, open, a little naive, with no tension at all.
sourcesOutils: Gearnews (Recreating the classic Roland Juno sound with plug-ins)
balearic.tempo: Balearic runs between 95 and 115 BPM, the tempo of the sea: slower than house, faster than chill-out, with a light 4/4 groove. What changes is that the tempo is a DJ doctrine before it is a production rule: a rock record, a slowed-down italo track, some odd pop, anything works if it lands around 100. The feel is straight, almost slow disco, with a 52 to 55% swing. If you make an edit, slow the original record down by 5 to 10% without changing the pitch, or change it, the hazy effect is intentional. The kick is soft and steady, and the Latin percussion brings the life around it.

balearictrance.arrangement: A balearic track starts without a kick: 32 bars of pad, guitar and sea. The kick comes in gently, filtered, then the bass. The guitar theme is the chorus: it comes back three times, each time with one more layer. The breakdown is a sunset, 32 to 48 bars with piano and pads, without an aggressive build-up: no roll, just a reversed cymbal and the kick coming back. Length 7 to 9 minutes in the club version, 4 minutes in the radio version. Plan an ending that fades out on the guitar alone rather than a DJ outro, or make both versions.
balearictrance.basse: The balearic bass is round and singing, closer to pop than to the trance offbeat. Juno-106 with saw and square, cutoff at 400 Hz, 300 ms release. It follows the roots of the chord progression, four chords over 8 bars, in eighth notes or dotted quarters, sometimes with a passing note toward the next chord. No pumping sidechain: gentle compression, 3:1 ratio, is enough. The kick doesn't dominate the low end, it shares. When the guitar plays its theme, the bass simplifies into whole notes. High-pass it at 40 Hz and give it sustain.
etapes: Project at 126 BPM, choose a four-chord progression in major (C, G, A minor, F) over 8 bars.
Record or program a clean guitar with a dotted-eighth delay and chorus, playing an 8-bar theme over these chords.
Lay down a softened kick, a soft clap on 2 and 4, congas and a shaker swung at 10%.
Write a round Juno bass that follows the roots in dotted quarters, without a marked sidechain.
Add an M1 piano in wide chords and a warm Juno pad, then build 8 minutes with a kickless intro and a sunset breakdown.
Mix warm: plate reverb, tape saturation, little limiting.
balearictrance.mix: A warm, wide mix, less compressed than club trance. Kick around -10 dB peak, the bass almost at the same level, which is unusual in the family. Guitar and piano wide, with their plate reverb on separate returns. Pads filtered at 300 Hz to let the piano breathe. Light tape saturation on the mix bus to round off the transients. Gentle master compression, 1.5:1 ratio, and a limiter that barely works, around -11 LUFS. Dynamics are part of the style: the breakdown must be truly softer than the drop. Add a bit of background noise, vinyl or hiss, for warmth.

outils.pourquoi: Played clean, single-coil pickup, then sampled: the echoed guitar is the timbre that defines Chicane. A virtual amp like Ableton Amp is enough.
The 1990s sampler for freezing a guitar or piano phrase and replaying it on the keyboard. Ableton Simpler or Sampler do the same today.
The M1 piano in open chords with seventh or ninth, and its choirs. Korg M1 Software in the Korg Collection reproduces the original presets.
Warm pads, chorus maxed, 2-second attack. TAL-U-NO-LX or Roland Cloud Juno-106 so you don't depend on a temperamental machine.
Plate reverb on the guitar and piano, 2.5-second decay, on separate returns to keep depth without blurring.
Dotted-eighth delay, 40% feedback, tape mode to round off the guitar's repeats. Ableton Echo gives a close result.
The stereo enhancer Chicane uses on his pads: width and brilliance without classic EQ. As a plugin, Plugin Alliance's Vitalizer MK2-T.

reperes: Energy 52: Cafe Del Mar (1993): the club version of balearic, faster, but listen to the theme that stays pop and the breakdown that breathes
Jam & Spoon: Stella (1992): the held chords and the soft kick, trance slowing down for the first time
Chicane: One Foot In The Past, One Foot In The Future (2021): the delayed guitar and the open piano, thirty years later, same recipe
balearictrance.rythme: The 909 kick is softened: low-pass filter at 8 kHz, short decay, sometimes replaced by a rounder 808 kick. The snare is light, often a soft clap or a rimshot on 2 and 4.
