What matters is the percussion: congas in eighth notes with ghost notes, shaker in swung sixteenth notes, tambourine on the offbeat, discreet bongos. The open hat stays on the offbeat but at low volume. Fills are not snare rolls but conga rolls or a reversed cymbal. Keep drums that could accompany a song: not a rave, a terrace.
balearictrance.sons: The clean electric guitar, played or sampled through the Akai S1000, with a dotted-eighth delay, 40% feedback, and a light chorus: that is the sound that defines Chicane. The open piano, often a Korg M1 or a sampled piano, plays chords in wide voicing with the seventh or the ninth. The Juno-106 pads are warm, chorus maxed, 2-second attack. Sampled voices, a breath, the sea. Arpeggios exist but in eighth notes and filtered, never up front. Plate reverb on the guitar and piano, 2.5-second decay. All in a major key or a gentle relative minor.
balearictrance.tempo: Slower than the rest of the family: 120 to 130 BPM, often around 126. The feel is relaxed, and it is the only trance subgenre where a bit of swing is welcome, 8 to 12% on the hi-hats and shakers. The kick stays straight. You think in 8-bar phrases but with breaths: a bar of silence, a held chord, a beat where the kick pulls back. The tempo must allow a hand-played guitar without it sounding rushed. Energy 52's Cafe Del Mar is a borderline case, faster and more club, but the balearic feel is in the half-time moments and the lingering chords.

baltimoreclub.arrangement: 3 to 4 minutes, no nuance. Intro on the break alone, 8 to 16 bars, with the clap. The 808 kick comes in all at once, often after a minute in the classics. The vocal sample arrives on loop, cuts out, comes back. 8-bar blocks, each block changes one thing: the break stops, a new shout, a fill. No melodic breakdown: at most, 4 bars of voice alone before the kick returns. Abrupt ending. A Baltimore club track is a DJ and dance tool: it must hold up on loop and survive the cuts.
baltimoreclub.basse: The 808 kick serves as the bass: long, muffled, with a 400 to 600 ms decay, it fills the sub on its own. Many tracks have no other bass. If you add one, a simple sine or a funk bass sample, on the roots, in short notes that double the kick on certain positions. A minor key or no key at all. The bass must never take the break's place: it stays under the kick, very simple. Cut it while the kick plays if the two clash, with a fast sidechain.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM, sample the Think break or an equivalent break, chop it in Simpler in Slice mode.
Add disco shakers in sixteenth notes and an 808 clap on 2 and 4.
Program a muffled 808 kick in a syncopated pattern, with a 500 ms decay that serves as the bass.
Loop a rap syllable or a crowd shout in sixteenth notes, cut it and restart it.
Arrange in 8-bar blocks: break alone, kick entry, shouts, cuts, abrupt ending.
Mix raw: kick up front in mono, saturated break, compressed voice, clipper on the master.
baltimoreclub.mix: Raw, unpolished, almost clipped. 808 kick around -3 dB peak, mono, cut below 35 Hz, it dominates everything. Break saturated and compressed hard, 8:1 ratio, 1 ms attack, so it hits. Dry, loud clap, no reverb. Shouted voice compressed at 6:1 and pushed up front, with a high-pass at 300 Hz. No spatial effects, everything is mono or nearly so. A clipper on the master rather than a limiter, target around -6 LUFS. Don't try to clean it up: the grain of the sample and the clip of the 808 are the sound. Only check that the kick doesn't mask the voice.

outils.pourquoi: The Think break and the Sing Sing shakers sliced and replayed on the pads, cut dead and restarted.
Muffled 400 to 600 ms kick that serves as the bass, clap on 2 and 4; a sampled 808 kit is enough.
The sampler of the first Baltimore producers: phrases taken from vinyl and CD, looped down to a syllable.
The turntables for sampling breaks, crowd shouts and funk horns on the fly, then playing them in the club.

outils.nom: Think (About It) and Sing Sing breaks
outils.pourquoi: The two source breaks, Lyn Collins and Gaz: chopped in Simpler in Slice mode, they bring their recorded shuffle.
Simpler in Slice mode for the break, Drum Rack for the syncopated 808 kick, clipper on the master, 8-bar blocks.

reperes: Frank Ski: Whores in This House (1992): the looped shout over the break, the template of the genre.
DJ Class: Tear Da Club Up (1995): the muffled 808 kick and the hammered Think break.
Rod Lee: Dance My Pain Away (2005): the more melodic version, with a sung vocal on the same mechanics.
Blaqstarr: Get Off (2006): the transition to a more synthetic sound that leads to today's club music.
baltimoreclub.rythme: Lyn Collins' Think break and the shakers from Gaz's Sing Sing, sampled, chopped and replayed in an MPC or in Simpler in Slice mode. On top, a huge, muffled 808 kick, played in a syncopated pattern: for example kick on 1, 2, the “a” of 3 and the “and” of 4, a starting point that Jersey club guides also give. 808 clap on 2 and 4. The breaks are cut, repeated, stopped dead and restarted. A sixteenth-note snare fill every 8 bars. No programmed hi-hats: the break's shakers do that job. Repetition and pounding.
baltimoreclub.sons: Shouted vocal samples, a rap phrase or a crowd shout, cut down to a syllable or two and looped in sixteenth or eighth notes. Sirens, horns sampled from a funk record, a whistle, a DJ shout. Clips from cartoons or TV. A very simple synth stab, one or two notes. Turntables and MPC, an 808 kit for the kick and clap. No sound design: everything comes from samples grabbed on the fly and played fast. The energy is in the voice yelling on loop and in the break that never lets go.
sources: Red Bull Music Academy Daily, Sing Sing: A Loop History
Orphiq, What Is Jersey Club? Sound, BPM, and Kick Pattern (orphiq.com)
sourcesOutils: Red Bull Music Academy Daily, Sing Sing: A Loop History
Melodics, Classic Breaks: Sing Sing, Think & Doggone
Baltimore Sun, What makes a Baltimore Club hit?
baltimoreclub.tempo: Between 125 and 135 BPM, 130 is the historic center. The feel is straight, with no programmed swing: the groove comes from the Think and Sing Sing breaks looping and bringing their own recorded shuffle. The kicks are hard and repeated, the music never stops. What changes compared with the Chicago house it descends from: the rawness, the speed, the absence of melody, and the hip-hop culture of the shouted sample. What sets it apart from the Jersey club that follows it: the kicks are straighter and less in triplets, the vocal samples are crowd shouts more than sung hiccups.

bangintechno.arrangement: Six to seven minutes, functional. 32-bar intro of kick and hi-hats. Acid loop at 33, stab at 49, ride at 65. Changes happen every 16 bars by adding or removing an element and with a low-pass filter that closes and then opens over 8 bars. A 16-bar breakdown in the middle: kick cut, acid loop and rumble alone, snare roll over the last 4, kick returns at full power. No second breakdown: the second half is a plateau. 32-bar outro of kick, hi-hats and rumble. Everything is built so a DJ can come in and out anywhere.
bangintechno.basse: The kick and its rumble are the bass. The sidechained reverb carpet, low-pass filtered at 150 Hz and saturated, fills the low end between hits. On top, a short acid loop: a 303 or a 303 sample in sixteenth notes on two notes, filter closed, cut at 100 Hz, looping without ever really opening. It acts as a rhythmic bass rather than a melody. The Advent version: a synth bass in eighth notes on the root, saturated, very short. Tune the rumble and the loop to the kick's fundamental (F# here), reading the kick's note with Tuner. Mono below 120 Hz, no reverb on the acid loop.
etapes: At 140 BPM, lay down a 909 kick with Glue, EQ (cut at 39 Hz, boost at 45 Hz, dip at 560 Hz) and Saturator.
Route the kick to a 100% reverb track (decay 9 s, low cut at 71 Hz) sidechained by the dry kick.
Add 909 hi-hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats, dry clap on 2 and 4.
Program a short 303 acid loop on two notes, filter closed, cut at 100 Hz.
Sample a rave stab and play it on an offbeat every two bars.
Arrange over six minutes in 16-bar blocks, a breakdown in the middle, Glue at 10:1 on the drum bus.
bangintechno.mix: Aggressive compression is the signature. Drum bus with Glue at ratio 10, fast attack, auto release, 5 dB of reduction, 60% mix; then Saturator Analog Clip at 3 dB. Kick at -6 dB peak, everything else around -10. Rumble mono below 150 Hz, cut above. Bright hi-hats, cut below 500 Hz, at -12 dB. Centered stab, short reverb. The master goes up to around -7 LUFS with a limiter, but the bus pumping must stay audible: it is what gives the feel. Check that the kick's reverb tail doesn't build up low end between hits; if it does, shorten the sidechain release to 50 ms.

outils.pourquoi: Up front and undressed: kick, dry clap, hi-hats, ride and crash, all saturated; 909 samples processed in Simpler do the job.
Rave stabs and repitched one-bar percussion loops, the tool of the era for the English warehouse scene, alongside Cubase.
The sequencer of 1990s London studios, to drive the Akai and the 909 over MIDI; Ableton has taken over.
The signature: ratio 10, fast attack, auto release, 5 dB of reduction, 60% mix on the drum bus, audible pumping.
On an audio track that receives the kick, 100% mix, decay 9 s, low cut at 71 Hz, sidechained by the dry kick: that is the rumble.
Short acid loop on two notes, filter closed, cut at 100 Hz, serving as a rhythmic bass; AudioRealism ABL3 in software.
Analog Clip at 3 dB after the Glue on the bus, and on every group, for the aggressive compression that makes the sound.
A 909 recorded through consoles and tape, already dirty, so you don't start from a kick that is too clean.

reperes: Joey Beltram: Game Form (1993): the kick up front and the pounding loop, post-Energy Flash but harder
The Advent: Farencounters (1995): the short saturated bass and the stabs, the 1990s London sound
Umek: Lanicor (1999): the acid loop and the bus pumping, the Slovenian take on warehouse
VTSS: Goin' Nuts (2020): the current reinterpretation, kick up front, stabs, raw energy
bangintechno.rythme: The kick in three layers, warehouse style: a 909 sample run through Glue Compressor (threshold -19 dB, ratio 4, mix 50%), EQ with a low cut at 39 Hz, a 4 dB boost on the fundamental at 45 Hz (F#) and a 6 dB dip at 560 Hz to remove the knock; a second reverb layer on an audio track that receives the kick, 100% mix, size 50, decay 9 s, low cut at 71 Hz, sidechain-compressed by the dry kick; a third click layer. 909 hi-hats in sixteenth notes at fixed velocities, open on the offbeats, clap on 2 and 4 with no reverb, ride on the strong phrases. 909 snare roll over 2 bars before each change.
bangintechno.sons: The TR-909 up front, undressed: kick, clap, hi-hats, ride, crash, all saturated. Short acid loops on a 303. Rave stabs sampled into an Akai S3000, played on an offbeat every two bars, with a short room reverb. One-bar percussion loops, repitched. Cubase and Akai were the tools of the era; in Ableton, Simpler and Saturator do it all. No pads, no melody, a single stab and an acid loop are enough. A white noise riser over 8 bars before a change, a hoover siren in the breakdown if you want the rave color. Aggressive compression on every group: that is the sound.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
bangintechno.tempo: From 135 to 145 BPM, no swing. Banging is English warehouse techno in its most direct form: the grid is straight, the kick is up front, and the only movement comes from the pumping compression. At 140 BPM, your kick and your kick reverb must be set so the reverb tail dies just before the next hit: set the decay by listening, not by reading. Unlike hard techno, you don't go past 145; unlike schranz, stabs and acid loops remain. The feel is that of a DJ tool: every bar must be mixable with the previous one.

basshouse.arrangement: A bass music structure on a house base. 16- to 32-bar DJ intro with kick, hats and a vocal chop. 16-bar build-up: the pad comes in, the chop becomes a melody, snare roll, white noise, one-beat silence. 32-bar drop: the growl bass in the clear, kick and clap, metallic percussion. 16-bar breakdown: kick cut, chop and pad, a second filtered bass pattern. Second 8-bar build-up, second 32-bar drop with a different bass or a denser pattern. 16-bar outro. Length 4 to 6 minutes. The second drop must be heavier than the first: new modulation, new octave, or half-time for 4 bars.
basshouse.basse: The modulated growl bass, made in Serum: two saw or wavetable oscillators with tight unison, a low-pass or notch filter modulated by a synced LFO (1/4, 1/8) or by an envelope, then distortion, an OTT (multiband compression) and a formant or phaser for the talking quality. The pattern is in quarter and eighth notes, with held notes that the LFO works on, rests and octave jumps. Rewrite the LFO rhythm every bar for variety. A clean sine sub underneath on the same notes, heavily sidechained, holds the low end that the saturated growl has lost. Cut the growl below 100 Hz.
etapes: Project at 128 BPM, short, compressed kick on every beat, layered clap on 2 and 4, hats with accents.
In Serum, create a growl bass: two saws in unison, filter modulated by a 1/8 LFO, distortion, OTT, phaser, cut below 100 Hz.
Write a bass pattern in quarter and eighth notes with rests and an octave jump, and a sine sub on the same notes, heavily sidechained.
Pitch a vocal, slice it into syllables and play a chop melody on the build-up.
Build 5 minutes with intro, build-up with roll and silence, 32-bar drop, breakdown, heavier second drop, outro.
Mix the bass up front in near mono, OTT and distortion except below 100 Hz, clipper and limiter at -7 LUFS.
basshouse.mix: The bass up front, the short kick cutting through it. Strong sidechain on the growl and the sub (8:1 ratio, 100 ms release). Clean sine sub below 100 Hz, growl above, with an EQ that scoops 200 to 300 Hz from the growl to make room for the clap. OTT on the bass and the chops, moderate distortion, but everything cut below 100 Hz except the sub. Clap and snare with short reverb and a snap at 4 kHz. Hard bus compression, clipper before the limiter. Master at -6 to -7 LUFS. Check the bass in mono: stereo modulations that are too wide cancel out on a club system, keep the growl almost mono and only spread the upper layers.

outils.pourquoi: The growl: two oscillators in tight unison, filter modulated by a 1/8 LFO, distortion and formant inside the synth; Serum 2 since 2025.
Free multiband compression on the bass and vocal chops, set hard, for the metallic density the style demands.
The DAW of most Night Bass and Confession projects, with its racks for stacking growl, sub and upper layers.
Modulated basses inherited from dubstep, with its LFOs and its Performer for rewriting the wobble rhythm every bar.
Multiband distortion on the growl, cut below 100 Hz to keep the sine sub clean; iZotope Trash plays the same role.
Pitched vocals cut into syllables, impacts and industrial percussion; Splice and W. A. Production supply most of these elements.
A clipper before the limiter to hold -6 to -7 LUFS, and a mono check: stereo modulations that are too wide cancel out in the club.

reperes: Jauz: Feel the Volume (2015): the growl bass played like a dubstep drop over a house kick, the manifesto of the style.
AC Slater: Fly Kicks (2016): the Night Bass side, drier and more UK, with a garage shuffle on the hats.
Joyryde: Hot Drum (2017): industrial percussion and cuts, bass house as festival music.
Chris Lorenzo: California Dreamin' (2019): the sampled vocal and the modulated bass, the tech house version of the style that conquered the charts.
basshouse.rythme: Short, heavily compressed kick, with a marked click and little sustain, on every beat: it must leave room for the bass in the low end. Layered clap or snare on 2 and 4, with a snap and a short reverb. Closed hats in eighth or sixteenth notes with accents, open on the offbeats, often replaced by metallic percussion or shakers. Snare fills in sixteenth and thirty-second notes on the build-ups, with white noise and rising pitch, and a one-beat silence before the drop. On the drop, industrial percussion (sheet metal, clicks) syncopated. The drums are thinner than the bass: they frame, they don't fill.
basshouse.sons: Serum, Massive and Ableton racks for the basses. Vocal chops: a pitched voice, cut into syllables, played as a melody on the build-ups and as an accent on the drop, with formant shift. Metallic synth stabs, sirens, machine noises, impacts. A rare lead. A pad on the build-up. Signature effects: OTT on almost everything, distortion, phaser and flanger on the basses, fast-moving filter, bitcrush, eighth-note delay on the chops. The style also descends from UK bass and garage: a hat skip or a 2-step shuffle can appear on a breakdown. The sound is clean and hard, designed for big systems.
sourcesOutils: W. A. Production, Making Power House Bass In Xfer Serum
Plugg Supply, Bass House Production Guide 2026
Rekkerd, Bass House Driver sample pack
basshouse.tempo: Between 125 and 130 BPM, like the electro house it grew out of, but with a different reading: the bass is played like a dubstep drop, in heavy quarter and eighth notes, with rests and accents, not as a continuous riff. The feel is square and heavy, no swing. The sidechain is short and strong. Think in 16-bar sections with a drop at bar 33 or 65, and structure the track like a bass music track: build-up, drop, a different second drop. The house tempo keeps it mixable in a tech house set, the vocabulary comes from dubstep and UK bass.

bassline.arrangement: Two formats. Radio: 3 minutes, vocal chorus first, verse, chorus with the bass, bridge, chorus. Club: 5 to 6 minutes, 32-bar intro with kick, hats and filtered vocal, bass drop at 32, vocal hook every 16, 16-bar breakdown with the vocal alone over a pad, snare roll, bass returns with the kick. The drop is the moment the warp bass arrives after a one-beat silence. 16-bar blocks, quick variations: a new bass note every 8, a new vocal chop every 16. 16-bar outro for the DJ.
bassline.basse: The warp bass, up front and moving. In Massive or Serum: a mix of square and saw, medium 20 ms attack, long decay, an LFO or envelope that bends the pitch down a semitone, and a low-pass filter modulated by an envelope. The “wah” quality comes from the filter modulation, an envelope with a 200 ms decay on the cutoff. Notes on the offbeats, in eighth notes, with octave jumps and glides. According to Syntorial, it is FM modulation that gives the most recognizable warp character. Separate sine sub, on the roots, sidechained by the kick.
etapes: Set Ableton or FL Studio to 138 BPM, dry four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats.
Build a warp bass in Massive: square and saw, envelope on the pitch, envelope on the filter.
Write the bass on the offbeats in eighth notes with octave jumps, separate sine sub.
Chop an R'n'B vocal, pitch it up +4 semitones, make it into a 4-bar hook.
Arrange: 32-bar intro, bass drop, 16-bar breakdown with the vocal alone, snare roll, return.
Boost the bass at 150 Hz, saturate, sidechain on the kick, loud master around -6 LUFS.
bassline.mix: The warp bass lives between 100 and 400 Hz, that is where it must be loud: a 2 dB boost at 150 Hz, saturation with Saturator or an amp at 30% mix. Mono sub below 90 Hz, sidechained by the kick, 6:1 ratio, 70 ms release. Clean kick with the click around 3 kHz pushed forward, cut below 45 Hz. Bright vocal, +3 dB shelf at 10 kHz, de-esser, 4:1 compression. Cut the organ and synths below 250 Hz. Loud master, around -6 LUFS, limiter with 4 dB of reduction. Bassline is played on powerful club systems, the bass must hold up in mono.

outils.pourquoi: The warp bass: square and saw, envelope bending the pitch down a semitone, envelope on the filter, FM for the wah quality.
The other synth for the warp, with a separate sine sub on the roots, sidechained by the kick, 70 ms release.
The DAW of Niche and Sheffield: direct club production, chopped vocal hook, everything done fast in patterns.
Dry four-on-the-floor kick, clap and open hat on the offbeats, snare roll at the end of the phrase. Samples or D16 Drumazon 2.
Organ 2 and house piano for the garage side of the genre, as stabs on the offbeats. Korg Collection plugin.
R'n'B vocal pitched up +3 to +6 semitones, chopped and repeated as a 4-bar hook.
Warp basses, kicks and vocals for bassline and 4x4, in two volumes, to spot the typical settings of a warp.

reperes: T2: Heartbroken (2007): the pitched R'n'B vocal over a warp bass, the genre's radio model.
DJ Q: You Wot (2008): the bass moving on the offbeats, dry four-on-the-floor kick.
Wideboys: Sambuca (2001): the bridge between speed garage and bassline, organ and hard bass.
Skepsis: Goes Like (2019): the revival, with modern sound design and the same bounce.
bassline.rythme: TR-909 kick or a dry kick sample, short, on all four beats, no sub. Clap on 2 and 4, often doubled with a 909 snare. 909 open hat on every offbeat, closed hat in sixteenth notes at low velocity. Sixteenth-note snare roll on the last bar of each 8-bar phrase. Few extra percussion parts: a shaker, sometimes a conga from garage. The drums are simple and clean because the bass takes up all the offbeat space. Classic trick: cut the kick one bar before the drop and leave the bass alone for a beat.
bassline.sons: Female R'n'B vocals pitched up 3 to 6 semitones, chopped and repeated in Simpler. M1 organ stabs for the garage side, house piano for the euphoria. Sirens, sweeps, a simple synth lead doubling the vocal. Orchestral “hits” at the ends of phrases. FL Studio and Massive as the scene's typical tools. Everything is done fast and direct: the sounds are not worked in depth, they serve the club function. The contrast: soft, sugary vocal on top, aggressive bass at the bottom, dry kick in the middle.
sources: Syntorial, How To Make A UK Bassline tutorial (syntorial.com)
sourcesOutils: Syntorial, How To Make A UK Bassline
Whipped Cream Sounds, How To Make A UK Bassline Synth Patch
Rekkerd, Producer Pack Bassline & 4x4 UK Garage Sample Pack
bassline.tempo: Between 135 and 142 BPM, faster than the speed garage it descends from. Four-on-the-floor kick is mandatory, hence the genre's other name, 4x4. The swing is low, 52 to 55% on the hats only: the bounce comes from the bass, which plays on the offbeats. Rhythmic signature: the kick lands on the beats, the warp bass on the “ands”, the vocal on the sixteenths. The feel is straight, euphoric, direct, made for a club in the north of England where everyone jumps. What changes compared with speed garage: the tempo goes up, the bass is harder and further forward, the R'n'B vocal is the second character.

belgiantechno.arrangement: Think in three acts like Energy Flash. Act 1: kick, hi-hats and sub from bar 1, then one element every 4 bars (rim at 5, clap at 9, second clap at 13, crash at 17), bass riff at 25, tambourine at 33, rides at 49. Act 2 around bar 57: the riff disappears, the reversed strings take its place, then the voice, two mini kick breaks at 71 and 77, two-note strings at 81, choir, an 8-bar breakdown. Act 3 at 109: the beat returns over 4 bars, crash, bass riff, percussion one by one, claps going out of sync at 145, final strings at 153. No drop: a tension that prowls. Five minutes fifty.
belgiantechno.basse: Two layered basses. A sub that holds the root permanently, Ab1 at about 52 Hz, never leaving the mix or changing note: it is the weight of the track. On top, from bar 25, the hoover bass riff: a single note in pulsing sixteenth notes, generated by a synth with a nasty filter (SH-2, Pro-One, or Alpha Juno), with a resonant filter whose cutoff moves in question-and-answer phrases, never at random. Tight, metallic reverb on the riff, plus a delay panned right. Cut the riff at 100 Hz so the sub stays alone underneath. Sidechain is unnecessary: the sub and the kick are tuned to the same note.
etapes: At 123 BPM, lay down a straight 909 kick, sixteenth-note hi-hats, and a sub held on Ab1 without interruption.
Add a 909 clap on 2 and 4 with fills at the end of every 4 bars, then a second clap pitched high, on the right, in a long reverb.
Program a single-note riff in sixteenth notes on a synth with a resonant filter, with cutoff phrases.
Create a hoover on Alpha Juno or Serum and a minor organ stab for the offbeats.
Sample strings, reverse them and loop them as a descending phrase for the central section.
Arrange in three acts, one element every 4 bars, no drop, over five minutes thirty.
belgiantechno.mix: A mix of contradictory space: dry percussion in the center, a single clap hard right with a huge reverb, the riff in a tight reverb with a delay on the right. The sub dominates, around -6 dB, mono. Kick at -8 dB, riff at -10, claps at -12. No heavy bus compression: the track holds through its space, not its density. Cut the organ stabs below 200 Hz, the hoovers below 150 Hz. The master stays modest, around -10 LUFS; what hits is the sub, not the volume. Check on a subwoofer that the 52 Hz sub and the kick don't cancel each other: shift the kick by 5 ms if necessary.

outils.pourquoi: Straight kick from the first bar, two claps including one pitched high on the right with a long reverb, sixteenth-note tambourine, martial crash.
The siren hoover on the breakdowns, WhatThe preset; recreate it in Serum or Diva if you don't have the machine.
Beltram's sampler: a JX-3P bass sampled and then replayed in sixteenth notes with the filter moved by hand, the riff of Energy Flash.
Mono synth with a nasty filter for the resonant single-note riff; a Roland SH-2 or an SH-101 play the same role.
The dark organ stabs as a minor chord on an offbeat, short, with a room reverb; Korg M1 Software in software.
Reversed strings looped as a descending phrase, whispered voice pitched down, everything sampled in the central section.
Dry, bright rimshot that sits above the riff, clearer than the 909's, entering at bar 5 and gone at 17.
Sequencer and drum sampler in Beltram's New York studio to drive the FZ-1 and the 909 samples.

reperes: Joey Beltram: Energy Flash (1990): the continuous sub, the filtered single-note riff, the three-act structure
Outlander: Vamp (1991): the gloomy organ stabs and the heavy kick, the R&S anthem
CJ Bolland: Horsepower (1991): the rising riff and the continuous pressure, without a breakdown
Charlotte de Witte: Formula (2020): the current Belgian reinterpretation, kick up front and resonant riff
belgiantechno.rythme: Straight 909 kick, four-on-the-floor, from the first bar. 909 closed hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats for the lift. No snare: only claps. A first 909 clap on 2 and 4 with fill claps at the end of each 4-bar cycle. A second clap pitched higher, panned hard right, with a long reverb with a delayed onset that doesn't mask the transient. A TR-707 rimshot, dry and bright, that comes in at bar 5 and disappears at bar 17 never to return. A 909 crash in a martial pattern on the build-ups. A 909 tambourine in insistent sixteenth notes. All the percussion is dry, except the second clap.
belgiantechno.sons: The Alpha Juno hoover: PWM saws, chorus, descending pitch envelope, played as a siren on the breakdowns. Dark organ stabs: a sampled organ or an M1 organ preset, played as a minor chord on an offbeat, short, with a room reverb. A string sample reversed and looped as a descending phrase for the central section, slowed to tempo. A whispered male voice, pitched down, triggered at two pitches. A synthesized string line on two neighboring notes (F and G#) for claustrophobia. A resonant filter riser drowned in a metallic reverb. Akai S1000 sampler for everything sampled, Juno-106 for the pads.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
belgiantechno.tempo: From 118 to 128 BPM, the legacy of slowed-down new beat: Energy Flash runs at 123. Slower than euro techno and English rave, and that is what gives the heaviness. No swing: the 909 is straight, so is the bass, and the rolling sensation comes from the continuous sub and the heavy kicks. The feel is that of a stadium: every element is massive and spaced out. A slower tempo allows longer reverbs on the claps without clutter. If you want the faster 1991 version (T99, Praga Khan), go up to 128 but keep the heavy organ stabs. Never go past 130: beyond that you tip into the hardcore that Belgium would invent right after.

bigbeat.arrangement: A big beat track lasts 4 to 6 minutes and is built like a rock song with verses and a chorus. 8-bar intro on the break alone or the riff alone. 16-bar verse: break, bass, riff. 16-bar chorus: everything, plus the catchy vocal and a stab. 8-bar bridge: low-pass filter closing on everything, then a roll and the explosion. Second verse, second chorus, and a 16-bar breakdown where only the vocal remains, stuttered by Beat Repeat, before the final return. The track must have an obvious “drop” moment, a crowd shout, and an ending that slams on a cymbal.
bigbeat.basse: The big beat bass is a riff, not a line. Often sampled from a rock or funk record (distorted electric bass), or played on a raw analog synth: a square or a saw on a Juno or on Analog, with a low-pass filter at 400 Hz and distortion (Overdrive 40%). It plays the same riff as the main sample, in eighth notes, on three or four notes, with rock rests (root, root, minor third, fifth). It is mixed loud and dirty, and fights with the kick rather than submitting to it: no sidechain, or very light. A sine sub underneath is not mandatory, it is the distortion that makes the bass audible.
etapes: Set Ableton to 128 BPM with an MPC groove at 58%. Import a funk or rock break and play it almost in full.
Layer a 909 kick on 1 and 3 and a 909 snare on 2 and 4, plus a second high-pass filtered break for the sixteenths.
Sample a riff (guitar, organ or horns) over two bars, and create a distorted bass on Analog that plays the same riff.
Sample a catchy vocal phrase and prepare a clip with Beat Repeat for the breakdown.
Arrange: 8-bar intro, 16-bar verse, 16-bar chorus, 8-bar bridge with a closing filter, verse, chorus, vocal breakdown, final return.
Compress the drum bus at 10:1 until it pumps, saturate, and aim for -7 LUFS.
bigbeat.mix: The intentionally pumping compression from the brief: the drum bus goes into a Glue Compressor at a 10:1 ratio, 1 ms attack, 100 ms release, with 6 to 10 dB of reduction, so the hi-hats and ghost notes swell between the kicks. Then tube saturation (Saturator Analog Clip, Drive 8 dB). The 909 kick reinforces the sampled kick at 60 Hz, the snare is boosted at 3 kHz. The riff samples go through a high-pass filter at 200 Hz and a soft distortion. Reverbs are short, chamber type, on the snare. Master at -7 LUFS, with a bit of clipping: big beat must sound louder than the neighboring house records.

outils.pourquoi: The Chemical Brothers' sampler, with an Atari ST: rock and funk breaks played almost in full, pitched riffs and vocals.
The 58 or 62% swing on the sixteenths and the grain of the pads; Ableton's MPC groove reproduces the feel.
Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, layered over the sampled break for stadium weight; 909 samples are enough.
The turntables of Fatboy Slim and the Skint DJs: scratches, lifting riffs and vocal phrases from vinyl.
Square or saw bass filtered at 400 Hz with distortion that doubles the sampled riff; Ableton Analog does the same job.
Intentionally pumping compression on the drum bus, slow attack, fast release, to swell hi-hats and ghost notes between the kicks.
Classic mode without warp to pitch riffs and vocals as on an Akai, with Beat Repeat for the vocal stutters.
Crackle and groove distortion on the record samples, with Saturator Analog Clip at 8 dB after it on the bus.

reperes: The Chemical Brothers: Block Rockin' Beats (1997): the huge compressed break, the sampled bass riff, the vocal shout as a chorus.
Fatboy Slim: The Rockafeller Skank (1998): the stuttered, pitched vocal phrase, the surf guitar riff, the song structure.
The Prodigy: Firestarter (1996): breakbeat turned punk, sampled guitars and a shouted vocal, stadium big beat.
Propellerheads: Spybreak! (1997): the funk break and the spy movie organ, the more elegant version of the genre.
bigbeat.rythme: The huge compressed breaks from the brief: a funk or rock break (Funky Drummer, a Led Zeppelin break, a garage rock break) sampled on an Akai S1000 or an MPC, played almost in full at 128 BPM, with a 909 kick on beats 1 and 3 and a 909 snare on 2 and 4 on top for weight. Add a second, faster break, in sixteenth notes, high-pass filtered, for movement, and a crash cymbal on the first beat of each section. Fills are sampled snare rolls or rock drums. The swing comes from the MPC: 58 to 62% on the sixteenths, never quantized at 100%.
bigbeat.sons: The brief cites the Akai MPC, the S1000, the TR-909 and the turntables. The MPC gives the swing and the grain, the S1000 the time-stretch and the stabs, the 909 the weight, the turntables the scratches. Sampled rock riffs: guitar, organ, horns, a singer's shout, cut to one or two bars and looped. Advertising-style hooks: a catchy vocal phrase repeated, pitched, filtered. Add sirens, rave stabs, crowd noise, scratches. In Ableton, Simpler in Classic mode with warp off to pitch the samples, Vinyl Distortion for the crackle, and Beat Repeat for Fatboy Slim-style vocal stutters.
sourcesOutils: Wikipedia (The Chemical Brothers, Akai S950, Big beat)
bigbeat.tempo: Big beat runs between 115 and 140 BPM, with a few faster exceptions like The Rockafeller Skank around 153. The center is 125 to 130 BPM. The feel is rock: the breaks are heavy, ahead of the beat, with a hip-hop swing (MPC at 58%) that drags just enough. What sets it apart from root breakbeat is the size: every hit sounds like a stadium drum hit, and the track is built like a rock song, with a riff. Slow a funk break down to 128 BPM, compress it until it pumps, and you are in the right feel.

birminghamtechno.arrangement: Seven to nine minutes of stubborn loops. A 32-bar intro of kick and one loop. The second loop comes in at 33, the rim at 65. The changes are 4-bar mutes and filters closing on one loop while the other keeps going. A single 8-bar breakdown, without kick, where the loops run alone and distorted. No build-up, no fill. The modern version lightens things up: less percussion, more room for a synth, which moves closer to the industrial sound. The 5/4 version changes everything without adding anything: keep the same loop but count five. End on the kick and a single loop, 32 bars.
birminghamtechno.basse: Almost no separate bass. The loops supply the low mids; cut them below 400 Hz with an EQ at the end of the chain to leave the kick alone underneath. If you want a sub, a very short sine on the root, only on beats 2 and 4, at -14 dB, to thicken without melody. Tune the loops by ear: the pack says A, but the harmonics are so complex that the label means nothing. Transpose by a semitone until it locks with the kick. The bass, when it exists, is a synth drone over 8 bars, filtered at 150 Hz, without movement. Mono below 120 Hz, no reverb.
etapes: At 130 BPM, lay down a dry, straight 909 kick, no reverb, and a discreet closed hi-hat on the offbeats.
In an eight-bar sample, isolate two beats that catch, loop them in Warp Beats and transpose by ear.
Add a second two-beat loop that pushes against the first, group the two.
Process the group with multiband VolumeShaper (crossover 3 kHz) triggered by the kick, then cut below 400 Hz.
Add a metallic rim on beat 4 and a dry distortion on the bus, no reverb.
Arrange over eight minutes with mutes and filters, one 8-bar breakdown, try a version in 5/4.
birminghamtechno.mix: Dry, gray, no space. No long reverb anywhere, at most a 0.3 s ambience on the percussion. The multiband VolumeShaper on the loop group pumps the lows and mids below 3 kHz in response to the kick while leaving the highs intact. A final EQ that cuts below 400 Hz on the loops. Kick at -8 dB, loops at -12, hi-hats at -18. A dry distortion on the drum bus (Saturator Analog Clip 2 dB) rather than compression. The master stays around -9 LUFS, dense but not crushed. Almost fully mono: the style does not live in width but in pounding. Compare with Surgeon: everything seems to come from a single point.

outils.pourquoi: Stripped down: dry, straight kick with no reverb, closed hi-hats barely audible on the offbeats, metallic rim on beat 4.
Two-beat loops isolated from an eight-bar sample, with the 12-bit grain; Redux at 12 bits and a low-pass at 8 kHz imitate it.
In multiband mode, crossover at 3 kHz on the loop group: lows and mids pump with the kick, the highs stay intact.
Dry distortion with the Hard Curve shape on the loops, Analog Clip at 2 dB on the bus, in place of any compression and any reverb.
The analog mono of 1990s Downwards setups, for a drone filtered at 150 Hz or three repeated notes without movement.
Cheap rack multi-effects unit of the Downwards studios, for a 0.3 s ambience or an austere distortion, never a ping-pong delay.
The sequencer of the first Surgeon and Regis records, with the Akai and the 909 over MIDI; Ableton's Warp Beats handles the loops today.
The alternative to the 909 for a rounder kick and drier rims, often sampled into the S950 and then transposed by a semitone.

reperes: Regis: Speak to Me (1994): the gray loop that never lets go, the dry kick and the Downwards pounding
Surgeon: Magneze (1996): short metallic loops rubbing against each other, no melody
Surgeon: Atol (1997): the texture that turns like a machine, the pumping on the loops
British Murder Boys: Learn Your Lesson (2004): Surgeon and Regis together, stripped-down loops and a distant voice
birminghamtechno.rythme: A stripped-down TR-909 or a TR-808, four-on-the-floor kick, dry, no reverb. The percussion comes from short loops: in an eight-bar sample (acoustic percussion, djembe, texture), you isolate two beats that sound good and loop them. Two loops are enough, one that pulls (the chop) and one that pushes (the broken melody); group them, then process with VolumeShaper in multiband mode, crossover at 3 kHz, so that only the lows and mids pump in response to the kick. Closed 909 hi-hats on the offbeats, barely audible. No clap, or a dry clap with no reverb. Fixed velocities: variation comes from muting and filtering, not from programming. A metallic rim on beat 4 for the stubbornness.
birminghamtechno.sons: Short metallic loops: two beats of a mysterious texture taken from the second half of a bar of a sample, in Warp Beats mode, transposed by -1 semitone, looped endlessly. The effects chain is austere: a dry distortion (Saturator Hard Curve, Amp Clean with gain), an EQ, a VolumeShaper, and that's it. No long reverb, no ping-pong delay. An Akai S950 brings the 12-bit grain; in Ableton, Redux at 12 bits and a gentle low-pass at 8 kHz. For a melodic motif, a modulation-rich synth (Wavetable with an LFO on the table position) played on three repeated notes. The sound must be gray, not colorful.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
birminghamtechno.tempo: From 123 to 140 BPM. The book works through an example at 123; the Downwards records of the 1990s often climb toward 135 or 140. No groove applied: the style is gray and stubborn, the grid is straight. What moves is the friction between two-beat loops and a four-beat bar: a loop one and a half beats long only realigns after three bars and creates a constant pull. Dare odd time signatures, 5/4 or 9/8, with a kick on every beat: that is the Downwards tradition. The tempo has to stay low enough for the saturated loops to keep their grain; above 140 they turn into noise.

bleeptechno.arrangement: Five to six minutes. A 16-bar intro of drums and shaker, then the bleep pattern comes in alone for 16 bars. The sub arrives at bar 33 like a drop in pressure. After that you change almost nothing: add or remove a hi-hat, transpose the pattern by a fifth halfway through, cut the sub 4 bars before each return. A single 16-bar central breakdown without kick, with the bleeps in delay. No white-noise build-up, no roll: the tension comes from the silence of the sub. Stay with five elements. End on 32 bars of drums without bass for the DJ. Warp tracks hold up because they are empty; respect that emptiness.
bleeptechno.basse: The bass is the subject of the genre: a pure sine sub, very low, often in octave 0 or 1 (E1 around 41 Hz). One or two notes, held for a quarter or a half note, on the root and sometimes the fifth. No distortion, no filter, absolute mono. In Operator, a single sine oscillator, envelope attack 0, release 50 ms. To make it come through on small speakers, add a discreet layer one octave up at -12 dB, or a hint of Saturator at 2 dB. Shorten the kick so that the sub alone fills the zone below 60 Hz. Listen to Unique 3: the bass arrives as an event, not as a background. Cut it before a breakdown, bring it back, that's your drop.
etapes: At 125 BPM, lay down a short four-on-the-floor 909 kick, then a snare one sixteenth note before beats 2 and 4.
Program two hi-hats alternating eighth notes and a sixteenth-note shaker, MPC swing at 55%.
Create a sine sub in Operator and play a held E1 note, mono, no effects.
Write a three-note bleep pattern at C5, decay 80 ms, ping-pong delay on the eighth note.
Cut the kick below 40 Hz and the bleeps below 1 kHz to clear the hole between them.
Arrange over six minutes, bringing the sub in and out as the only event.
bleeptechno.mix: Everything is in the extremes. The sub is the loudest element in the mix, around -6 dB peak, strictly mono. The bleeps are thin: low cut at 1 kHz, they need nothing below. Between 150 and 800 Hz there should be almost nothing: that hole is what gives the feeling of space. Kick at -10 dB, toms at -16, hi-hats at -18. The drum bus gets a short reverb on an aux send, never on the sub. A Glue at 4:1 with 3 dB of reduction is enough. Check on a sound system or a subwoofer: if the sub disappears, turn it up further rather than saturating it. Reference: LFO, whose sub shakes the walls without ever distorting.

outils.pourquoi: Sheffield's 12-bit sampler: bleeps, vocal snippets and test tones came out of the S900 or the S950; Simpler followed by Redux recreates the grain.
Short, dry four-on-the-floor kick, alternating hi-hats; 909 samples are enough, the kick must leave the zone below 60 Hz to the sub.
Toms shortened with a 118 ms fade and a low cut at 90 Hz, dry, bright accents that never become basses.
The pure sine sub of the genre: a single sine oscillator, attack 0, release 50 ms, a held E1 note, strictly mono.
To replay the sampled bleeps and test tones on two or three pentatonic notes, decay from 50 to 100 ms, played high around C5.
Small ambience on the drum bus, decay 0.45 s and high cut at 6 kHz: tight, never washed out, to keep the emptiness between bleeps and sub.
Ping-pong delay on the eighth note, 15 to 20% mix, to bounce the bleeps across the stereo field while the sub stays in the center.

reperes: Unique 3: The Theme (1989): the sub that arrives like an earthquake under a tiny pattern
Sweet Exorcist: Testone (1989): test tones as melody, nothing but kick, bleeps and sub
LFO: LFO (1990): Sheffield's most famous sine bass, and bleeps in delay in the void
Special Request: Vortex (2019): the modern reading, sub intact, more urgent drums
bleeptechno.rythme: 909 kick on all four beats, short and dry. The snare is not on 2 and 4 but one sixteenth note earlier, a systematic anticipation: that is the detail that makes the style. Two eighth-note hi-hats answer each other in strict alternation, except on the last sixteenth of each two-beat group where they double up to push forward. A sixteenth-note shaker ties it all together. The 707 toms are cut to less than half of the sample, with a 118 ms fade and a low cut at 90 Hz: they must stay dry accents, never basses. A single clap on the last sixteenth of the bar. Keep eight voices at most; the emptiness is part of the pattern.
bleeptechno.sons: The bleeps: short synth notes, square or sine wave, decay from 50 to 100 ms, played high (C5 to C6), on two or three notes of a pentatonic scale. Operator or any monosynth will do; an Akai S900 for the 12-bit grain of the era, or Redux in Ableton. Ping-pong delay on the eighth note, 15 to 20% mix, so the bleeps bounce across the stereo field. Add sampled and pitched vocal snippets, a very short piano stab, a test tone (Testone) in the Sweet Exorcist manner. On the drum bus, a send to a small ambience like Valhalla Room, decay 0.45 s, high cut at 6 kHz: tight, never washed out. Avoid pads and anything that fills the mids.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
bleeptechno.tempo: Between 118 and 135 BPM. LFO and Nightmares on Wax stay under 125, the club version climbs to 135. The groove comes from the sampler era: apply an MPC 16 swing around 55% on the hi-hats and the shaker, not on the kick. The feel is stiff and clean, almost naive: the bleeps land right on the grid, and so does the sub. What moves is the high sixteenth notes. Unlike Detroit, you are not after the warmth of a jam, you are after the contrast between a precise machine up top and an earthquake down below. A slow tempo lets the sub breathe: at 120 BPM, a quarter-note sub note lasts half a second, long enough to feel it in your gut.

boogie.arrangement: Boogie keeps the R&B song format, stretched for the 12-inch: 5 to 7 minutes. An intro of 8 to 16 bars with the full groove or just bass and drums, a 16-bar verse, an 8- or 16-bar chorus, a second verse, chorus, then an instrumental break: a synth, talkbox or clavinet solo over 16 bars with the rhythm section. Last chorus with stacked backing vocals, then a final 32-bar vamp where the groove turns with vocal ad-libs. No string build-up, no disco-style percussion break: the tension comes from the bass varying its patterns every 4 bars.
boogie.basse: The bass moves to the keyboard: a Minimoog, or sometimes a Prophet-5. The sound is a sawtooth or a square with a resonant filter that opens on the attack, short release, a bit of glide between some notes. The rhythm is funky, syncopated, in sixteenth notes with rests: root on 1, a note on the “e” of 2, an octave jump, a fifth on the “a” of 3. Imitate slap: short, percussive notes, strongly contrasting velocities. The model is Bounce Rock Skate Roll or Kashif's bass. It converses with the kick: when the kick plays, it goes silent or doubles; when the kick is silent, it fills. Today: Arturia Mini V or Ableton's Monark.
etapes: Set 110 BPM with a 58% swing on the sixteenth notes, load LinnDrum and 808 samples.
Program a syncopated kick (1, “and” of 2, 3), snare and clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats with accents.
Write a syncopated sixteenth-note Minimoog bass with rests, octave jumps and a bit of glide, over two 7th chords.
Add a Rhodes playing 9th chords with chorus, a chicken-scratch clavinet, and synth brass stabs.
Record or program an R&B vocal with stacked backing vocals, and an instrumental break on talkbox or synth.
Mix warm: compressed bass in front of the kick, tape on the drum bus, light bus compression.
boogie.mix: The boogie mix is warm and round, with the bass and the kick well aligned. The Minimoog bass is compressed at 4:1 with a 10 ms attack, and it sits slightly in front of the kick. The Linn or 808 kick is cut below 40 Hz and slightly saturated. The hi-hats are softer than in Hi-NRG. The Rhodes is widened with a chorus and a short reverb. The snare gets a short 1-second plate. The voice is up front, with a short delay and a plate. Saturate the drum bus with a tape emulation. Bus compression on the master at 2:1, slow attack, medium release, for the bounce. Aim for -12 LUFS with dynamics.

outils.pourquoi: The keyboard bass that replaces the bass player: sawtooth, resonant filter opening on the attack, glide between some notes, contrasting velocities.
The common Minimoog emulation for the funky sixteenth-note bass; Ableton's Monark also does the job with its ladder filter.
The drum machine that plays funk: kick on 1 and the and of 2, snare doubled with a clap, hi-hats with 58% swing.
The round kick, the cowbell and the clave for color, often mixed with the Linn sounds in the same Drum Rack.
Seventh and ninth chords with chorus or tremolo; Ableton's Electric replaces it for the block-chord parts.
Sixteenth-note chicken-scratch parts run through an auto-wah, the rhythmic backbone of the midrange.
Roger Troutman's talkbox in Zapp: a synth that sings through the tube; get close to it with Ableton's Vocoder on a sawtooth.
The synth strings and brass that replace the orchestra, sometimes the bass; today TAL-U-NO-LX or Arturia Prophet-5 V for the pads.

reperes: Vaughan Mason & Crew: Bounce Rock Skate Roll (1979): the syncopated synth bass that replaces the electric bass.
Evelyn King: Love Come Down (1982): Kashif's production, Minimoog, Rhodes and R&B vocals.
One Way: Cutie Pie (1982): the drum machine playing funk and the groove at 108 BPM.
Parcels: Comingback (2021): the current reading, same pocket, same clavinet.
boogie.rythme: The LinnDrum or the TR-808 replaces the drummer, but it plays funk. Kick on 1, on the “and” of 2 and sometimes on 3, never a plain four-on-the-floor. Linn snare doubled with a clap on 2 and 4. Sixteenth-note hi-hats with an accent on each eighth note and an open hat on the “and” of 4. Rimshot on some offbeats. 808 cowbell or clave for color. In your DAW, a Drum Rack with LinnDrum and 808 samples, swing at 58%, hi-hat velocities alternating between 100 and 60. A tom fill or a sixteenth-note snare roll every 8 bars.
boogie.sons: The Fender Rhodes plays 7th and 9th chords, with chorus or tremolo. The Hohner clavinet does the sixteenth-note chicken-scratch parts, often with an auto-wah. Zapp's talkbox turns a synth into a singing voice. Synth brass replaces real brass, Prophet-5 or Oberheim synth strings replace the orchestra. A chicken-scratch guitar can stay. The vocals are R&B, warm, often with stacked backing vocals. Today: Ableton's Electric for the Rhodes, a clavinet sample, Ableton's Vocoder on a sawtooth synth to get close to the talkbox, TAL-U-NO-LX for the pads.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (80s Boogie Post Disco Drum Machine)
boogie.tempo: Boogie slows disco down: 100 to 118 BPM, centered around 108 to 112. The feel is funk, with a clear swing on the sixteenth notes, 56 to 60%, and a pocket feel: everything is slightly late except the kick. Set 110 BPM with an MPC swing of 58% on the sixteenth notes. Where disco pushes forward, boogie pulls back and bounces. The signature is syncopation: the kick is no longer on all four beats, the synth bass plays between the beats, and the snare on 2 and 4 is the only fixed point. Count in 4-bar phrases.

bouncytechno.arrangement: Tracks run 4 to 6 minutes, in very regular 16-bar blocks. A 32-bar intro of kick and hi-hats, the bass enters, the stab enters, 16 bars each. A 16-bar breakdown without kick where the stab and the hoover play with the filter opening, snare roll, return of the kick and bass. Two or three cycles, with a new stab pattern each time. End on kick and bass, 32 bars. No key change, no sung chorus: variation comes from the stabs and the filter. What makes the track playable is the constant kick-bass bounce, never to be interrupted during the drops.
bouncytechno.basse: The offbeat bass, even more central than in happy hardcore. On every “and”, a short, fat note, sawtooth or square wave with a bit of distortion, low-pass filtered at 500 Hz with a little resonance. In Analog or Operator: sawtooth, filter at 500 Hz, resonance at 20 percent, decay 100 ms. It is this alternation, kick on the beat, bass on the offbeat, at 170 BPM, that makes the “bounce”. The bass often stays on a single note (the root) for 8 bars, then goes up to the fourth or the fifth for the change. No sidechain needed. A light saturation so it stays audible on small systems.
etapes: Tempo 170 BPM. 909 kick with Saturator at 8 dB, decay 120 ms, on every beat.
Offbeat bass on every “and”: sawtooth filtered at 500 Hz, light resonance, decay 100 ms, on the root.
Dry snare on 2 and 4, open hat on every offbeat, closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes.
Rave stab: three-note Juno sawtooth chord, syncopated 2-bar pattern, filter opening over 16 bars.
Softened hoover (low-pass at 3 kHz) as a two-note riff, plus a one-word vocal sample.
Arrange in 16-bar blocks: intro 32, bass, stab, breakdown 16, drop, new stab, breakdown, drop, outro 32. Dry, clear mix.
bouncytechno.mix: The bouncy techno mix is simple and dry: kick at minus 4 dB peak, bass just below, both in mono. The kick and the bass never overlap in time, so there is no need for sidechain, but cut the bass below 60 Hz so the kick keeps the sub. Dry snare, a bit of compression (ratio 4:1, attack 5 ms) so it cracks. Stabs and hoover in stereo with an eighth-note delay and a short reverb. No heavy bus processing: a light Glue Compressor on the drums. Master: limiter toward minus 8 LUFS. The genre was pressed on vinyl for modest clubs; it has to sound clear on a small system.

outils.pourquoi: The softened hoover, filter slightly closed, played as a two-beat stab on the downbeats: the signature between gabber and happy hardcore.
Bouncing kick: 909 with a short decay, light overdrive, snare on 2 and 4, open hats on every offbeat.
Rave stabs and vocals sampled at 12 bits, played as simple four-note riffs. The sampler of the Scottish studios of the Rezerection era.
The MIDI sequencer of 1993-1996 on Atari ST or PC: driving the 909, the Alpha Juno and the S950, arranging in 16-bar blocks.
On the drum bus, ratio 4:1, attack 10 ms, release Auto: that is what makes the kick and the hi-hats bounce together.
Sawtooth rave stabs and a simple offbeat bass on the root; replaces the Juno and the sampler for the stabs.
Drive of 4 to 6 dB on the kick, never more: the kick stays bouncy, not crushed like in Rotterdam.

reperes: Ultra-Sonic: Annihilating Rhythm (1993): the kick and the offbeat bass, the stab that carries the whole track.
Ultra-Sonic: Obsession (1994): the bounce at maturity, with a softened hoover and a repeated vocal sample.
Bass X: Hardcore Disco (1993): simplicity, kick, bass, stab, and nothing else.
Q-Tex: Power of Love (1994): the more melodic fringe, between bouncy and happy hardcore.
bouncytechno.rythme: Saturated 909 kick, harder than happy hardcore, softer than gabber: a Saturator at 8 dB of Drive, no clipping. Short decay, 120 ms, to leave room for the bass. Kick on every beat. 909 snare on 2 and 4, dry, with no reverb or almost none. Open hats on the offbeats, as in happy hardcore, but less up front. Closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes. The pattern is very regular and barely changes across the whole track: variation comes from the stabs and the breakdowns. Snare rolls of 1 or 2 bars before the drops, shorter than in happy hardcore. Occasional descending 909 toms.
bouncytechno.sons: Simple rave stabs: a two- or three-note chord on a Juno or Alpha Juno sawtooth, played very short, on a syncopated 2-bar rhythm, with a filter that opens gradually over 16 bars. A softened hoover, less aggressive than in gabber, with a low-pass at 3 kHz, played as a two-note riff. Short vocal samples, often a word or an MC shout, repeated. Sirens. Few elements: kick, bass, stab, hoover, a vocal sample, that's often all. What makes the genre is simplicity: each sound must be instantly identifiable and play a 1- or 2-bar pattern.
sources: Micro Genre Music, What is Bouncy Techno? (microgenremusic.com)
sourcesOutils: Micro Genre Music, What is Bouncy Techno? (microgenremusic.com)
bouncytechno.tempo: Bouncy techno is played between 160 and 180 BPM, with most of the Scottish tracks from 1994-1996 around 170. What sets it apart from happy hardcore, at the same tempo, is that melody matters less and bounce matters more: there is no piano, no sung vocal, only the kick, the offbeat bass and stabs. What sets it apart from gabber is that the kick is hard but not crushed, and the bass bounces instead of disappearing. No swing. Program at 170 BPM, eighth-note grid: the genre lives almost entirely in eighth notes, kick on the beats, bass on the offbeats.

braindance.arrangement: A tune format of 3 to 5 minutes, shorter than IDM: intro, melody stated, acid section where the 303 takes over, breakdown, return with both together, ending. What makes the genre is the sharp turns: a tempo change, an 8-bar passage in another style, a childlike melody popping up in the middle of the acid. Hasty Boom Alert strings breaks together like gags; Come To Daddy flips between aggression and lullaby. Plan a surprise every 32 bars, but keep a thread: the main melody has to come back. The listener should smile at least once and dance all the way through.
braindance.basse: The TB-303 from the brief, played off the rails. A sixteenth-note sequence with slides and accents, high resonance, automated cutoff, but with out-of-scale notes, octave jumps, a 7- or 11-step pattern running over 16, a note held too long. On an emulation (ABL3, TAL-BassLine-101, D16 Phoscyon, or Operator set to sawtooth with Auto Filter on resonance), push the drive hard enough to make it scream. The SH-101 from the brief serves as a round bass under the melodies, slightly detuned. Unlike acid techno, the braindance bass changes pattern every 4 bars and allows itself melodies. I Love Acid is the reference: the 303 as a voice that is comic and serious at the same time.
etapes: Program a straight 808 electro pattern at 110 BPM: kick, 808 snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, cowbell on the offbeat.
Write a 303 line on an emulation (or Operator with Auto Filter on resonance): 7 notes on a grid of 16 sixteenth notes, with slides, accents, one out-of-scale note.
Compose a naive melody on an FM bell or Casio sound, two voices detuned by 15 cents, in major.
Break the rhythm in two places per bar with repeated slices and a different fill every 4 bars.
Arrange over 4 minutes with a surprise every 32 bars: a tempo change, a breakdown in another style, a return of the melody.
Mix the saturated 303 in the center, the drums compressed hard, the melodies wide, a low-pass at 14 kHz on the master, level around -11 LUFS.
braindance.mix: Dirty and happy. The 303 goes through Overdrive or Saturator with heavy drive, then an EQ cutting below 80 Hz to leave room for the kick. Drums compressed firmly (ratio 4:1, attack 5 ms, release 50 ms) so they crack, a Drum Buss with boosted transients. The detuned melodies go wide in stereo with chorus, the 303 in the center. Final level around -10 to -12 LUFS; it's club music even if it's laughing. A low-pass at 14 kHz on the master gives the 1990s Rephlex patina. No long reverb, everything stays dry and close. Check that the 303 and the kick don't fight: a light sidechain, 2 dB, is enough.

outils.pourquoi: Rephlex's twisted acid: 7 notes over 16 steps, slides, accents, one out-of-scale note. Roland TB-03, Arturia Acid V or D16 Phoscyon 2 as emulations.
Internal sequencer for stuttering lines and sawtooth basses; the common software version is TAL-BassLine-101.
Straight electro pattern at 110 BPM, snare on 2 and 4, cowbell on the offbeat; D16 Nepheton 2 or Roland Cloud TR-808 for the software studio.
8-bit toy keyboard sampler for naive melodies and cartoon voices, the off-key, happy side of the genre. Redux roughly simulates it.
FM bells in two voices detuned by 15 cents for the major-key themes; Dexed, free, loads the original cartridges, and so does Arturia DX7 V.
303 emulation with sequencer, slides and built-in distortion; push the drive and cut below 80 Hz to leave room for the kick, light 2 dB sidechain.
Boosted transients and medium drive on the hard-compressed drums, ratio 4:1, attack 5 ms, so the electro cracks under the detuned melodies.
Bitcrush and downsample for the toy sound on the melodies and the humorous samples; Erosion adds whistling aliasing, Chorus widens it all.

reperes: µ-Ziq: Hasty Boom Alert (1997): breaks strung together like gags, the melody that always comes back.
Cylob: Cut the Midrange Drop the Bass (1998): humor in the title and in the sound, Rephlex electro.
Luke Vibert: I Love Acid (2003): the 303 as a voice, comic and serious at the same time, the genre's acid manifesto.
Aphex Twin: Come To Daddy (1997): the brutal flip between aggression and softness, braindance that refuses to choose.
braindance.rythme: The kick often stays in 4/4, which is what separates braindance from broken IDM: you can dance, but you get jostled. An 808 electro base (kick, 808 snare, sixteenth-note hi-hats, cowbell) or 909 acid, then edited breaks on top, playful rather than clever: a slice repeated 8 times, a pitched snare roll that rises, a missing hit on the downbeat. Fills every 4 bars, never the same. Cylob and Vibert keep the rhythm readable; µ-Ziq stacks the breaks; Bogdan Raczynski mangles them. First program a straight, solid pattern, then break it in 2 or 3 places per bar. No more, or you fall back into IDM.
braindance.sons: The brief gives the TB-303 and the SH-101. Around them: the TR-808 for electro, the 909 for acid, a Juno for pads, cheap keyboards like the Casio SK-1 and DX7 FM bells for naive melodies. The melodies are deliberately detuned: two voices 15 or 20 cents apart, or a pitch bend that doesn't quite come back. The samples are humor: cartoon voices, jingles, mouth noises, a child talking. Effects: Redux for the toy side, Erosion, wide Chorus, a short reverb. The sound must be happy and slightly off, like a broken toy that still plays in tune. Nothing clean, nothing serious, but everything precise.
sourcesOutils: Gearnews, Acid Sound: This Gear is a Perfect Match
ADSR Sounds, Arturia Acid V Review
braindance.tempo: More danceable than generic IDM, that's what the name means. Two tempos dominate: 130 to 150 BPM for twisted acid, and 100 to 115 BPM for DMX Krew's playful electro, with jungle excursions at 165 from Squarepusher. The grid is straight, in 4/4, but it gets booby-trapped: a 7-step pattern on a 16-step grid, a sudden tempo change, a break that doubles the speed for 2 bars. The swing comes from the TB-303 slides, not from quantization. With Aphex Twin, a track can go from a 90 BPM ballad to a 160 BPM assault in a single bar: surprise is a rule. Always keep a readable tempo so people can dance between the jokes.

breakbeat.arrangement: The original breakbeat is a music of collage, not of build-ups. Basic structure: an 8-bar intro on the break alone, then the bass and main stab come in at bar 9, an 8-bar bridge with a vocal sample or a scratch, return of the full break. Change the vocal sample every 16 beats to hold attention. A track fits into 4 to 5 minutes. The 1992 Prodigy trick: cut all the drums for 2 bars, leave a pad or a vocal, then relaunch the break with a sampled snare roll on the last bar. End on 8 bars of break alone to make mixing easier for DJs.
breakbeat.basse: On the first breakbeat records, the bass is often a sample too: a funk line cut on one note, or a very simple synth sub. Today, take an Operator with a single sine wave, or a Trilian set to a Moog preset, and play quarter or eighth notes on the root, with a passing note on the fifth or the octave on the fourth beat. What matters is the relationship with the sampled kick: a break's kick already has low end around 60 to 80 Hz, so let the bass stop with the note and avoid long sustains. A light sidechain (ratio 4:1, release 80 ms) from the kick is enough to line everything up.
etapes: Set Ableton to 120 BPM and import a royalty-free break (or the Amen to practice). Warp in Beats mode, Preserve Transients.
Slice it in Simpler in Slice mode by transients and replay a pattern: kick on 1 and the “and” of 2, snare on 2 and 4, ghost notes at velocity 45.
Add a 909 kick under the sampled kick and an Operator sine wave playing the root in eighth notes, light sidechain from the kick.
Choose three samples: a stab, a vocal snippet, a noise. Place them every 2 or 4 bars to create a call-and-response game.
Build an 8-16-8-16-8 bar structure with a 2-bar drum cut before each return.
Run the drum bus through Redux (12 bits) then Saturator, and check that the break stays the loudest element of the track.
breakbeat.mix: A sampled break arrives already mixed: the reverb, compression and color of the original console are in it. Your job is to reinforce it, not to clean it. High-pass filter around 40 Hz, a hit of compression with a fast attack (1 ms) and a short release (50 ms) to bring out the ghost notes, and a bit of tube saturation (Saturator in Analog Clip mode, Drive 6 dB) to weld it all together. The stabs and vocals go on a separate bus, with a short plate reverb. Put the break at -10 dB on the master, the sub just below, and aim for -8 LUFS integrated for club versions, without limiting further: the old records breathed.

outils.pourquoi: The 12-bit sampler that chopped the first breaks: its metallic time-stretch and grainy conversion are the grain of the genre, imitated today by Redux.
Its 16-bit successor, cleaner and stereo, for stabs and vocals; it is the one that speeds up the 1992 Prodigy breaks.

outils.nom: Original funk breaks (Amen Brother, Funky Drummer, Think, Apache)
outils.pourquoi: The raw material: two to four bars of recorded drums that you chop, pitch and replay; always start from a break rather than a grid.
In Slice mode by transients, it replaces chopping on the Akai: every hit of the break becomes a pad you replay on the keyboard.
Downsample toward 22 kHz and 12 bits on the drum bus to get the S950 grit back without owning the machine.
A short kick doubled under the break's kick so it carries in the club; 909 samples or the D16 Drumazon emulation are enough.
A single sine wave for the sub under the loop: quarter or eighth notes on the root, light sidechain from the sampled kick.
For a played funk bass or a round Moog preset when you don't want to sample a line off a record.

reperes: The Winstons: Amen Brother (1969): at 1 min 26, the four bars of solo drums that the whole family chopped up; listen to the snare ghost notes.
James Brown: Funky Drummer (1970): Clyde Stubblefield's break around 5 min 20, open hats on the offbeats, it's all in the hands.
Coldcut: Beats and Pieces (1987): the English collage, a drum break under a rain of vocal and brass samples.
The Prodigy: Out of Space (1992): a sped-up break, a slowed-down reggae sample, and the contrast between the two that makes the track.
breakbeat.rythme: Everything starts from two to four bars of recorded drums: Amen, Funky Drummer, Think, Apache. Load the break into Simpler in Slice mode (the modern equivalent of chopping on the Akai S950), slicing by transients. You get a kick, a snare, a hi-hat and ghost notes already played. Replay them on your keyboard: kick on beat 1 and the “and” of 2, snare on beats 2 and 4, and above all keep the snare ghost notes at velocity 40 or 50 between the beats. Double the break's kick with a short TR-909 kick so it carries, and the snare with a discreet clap.
breakbeat.sons: The machines in the brief are the Akai S950 and S1000: 12 bits for the first, 16 bits for the second. Their conversion and their time-stretch give the metallic grain of the old records. In Ableton, you get that grain back by running the break through Redux (Downsample toward 22 kHz, Bit Depth 12) or by turning on warp in Beats mode with Preserve set to Transients and a short grain loop. The rest is collage: brass or piano stabs sampled off a record, vocal snippets cut at the word, sirens, and scratches. Coldcut and Bomb the Bass stacked dozens of sources on a single loop this way. Do the same, but choose three or four strong samples, not thirty.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (Slicing Breakbeats Like Nia Archives)
breakbeat.tempo: Basic breakbeat has no fixed tempo: it has the tempo of the loop you sample. Funky Drummer runs around 100 BPM, Amen Brother around 136 BPM. In the late 1980s, English producers played them between 110 and 130 BPM, then The Prodigy pushed them toward 140. The feel comes from the drummer, not from your grid: the hi-hats never land exactly on the sixteenth note, the snare drags a little. Keep that looseness. If you quantize everything to 100%, you lose exactly what you came for. Set your DAW to 120 BPM, import a break, and let it dictate its swing to you rather than the other way around.

breakbeatgarage.arrangement: A club track of 5 to 6 minutes. A 32-bar intro: the filtered break and a stab, the 909 kick comes in at 16. The warp bass arrives at 32, the MC hook at 48. 16-bar blocks. Breakdown in the middle: the breakbeat stops, only the bass and the hook remain, then the break returns with a roll and a rewind. Second half with a new chop of the break or a second stab. A 32-bar outro with the break and the kick. The rewind is an arrangement tool: simulate it by reversing one bar of the whole mix before the bass returns.
breakbeatgarage.basse: The speed garage warp bass, kept intact: in Massive or Serum, sawtooth and square, a pitch envelope going down a semitone, a low-pass modulated by an envelope with a 200 ms decay, a bit of glide. Notes on the break's offbeats, in eighth notes, with octave jumps. A separate sine sub on the roots. The bass answers the break's slices: when the break rolls, the bass holds a note; when the break stops, the bass does a fill. Minor key, two or three notes. A bit of saturation so the warp cuts through the break.
etapes: Set Ableton to 135 BPM, slice a funk break in Simpler in Slice mode, high-pass at 200 Hz.
Add a 909 kick on 1 and 2.5 and a 909 snare on 2 and 4 on top of the break.
Build a warp bass in Massive with pitch and filter envelopes, separate sine sub.
Lay down a 2-bar sampled MC hook, M1 organ stabs and a siren.
Arrange: 32-bar intro with the filtered break, bass at 32, hook at 48, breakdown in the middle with a rewind.
Separate the break and the bass with EQ, compress the break, sidechain the bass, master around -8 LUFS.
breakbeatgarage.mix: The break and the bass share the middle of the spectrum, so you have to separate them: break high-passed at 200 Hz, warp bass concentrated between 80 and 400 Hz with a 2 dB bump at 150 Hz. Short 909 kick, cut below 45 Hz, mono sine sub below 90 Hz. Break compressed at a 4:1 ratio, 10 ms attack, to keep its punch, then lightly saturated. The added 909 snare up front, with a short reverb. Bass sidechained by the kick, ratio 4:1. MC vocal compressed and high-passed at 300 Hz. Master around -8 LUFS with a Glue Compressor at 2 dB. Check that the break doesn't muddy the bass in mono.

outils.pourquoi: Funk break sliced at 12 bits with grainy time-stretch, like the Barry White break under 138 Trek.
Kick added on 1 and 2.5, snare doubled on 2 and 4 on top of the break, to hold the club. Samples or D16 Drumazon 2.
The 2001 sequencer of Menta and Agent X, for stacking the break, the 909 kick, the warp bass and the MC hook.
Simpler in Slice mode for the break, a reversed slice every 4 bars, rewind simulated by reversing one bar.
The speed garage warp bass: saw and square, pitch envelope, filter modulated by an envelope, a bit of glide.
Same warp recipe with a separate sine sub on the roots, saturated to cut through the break.
Organ 2 stabs to keep the link with garage, played short with a delay. Korg Collection plugin.

reperes: Zed Bias: Neighbourhood (2000): the break under a garage bass, MC hook and club energy.
Agent X: Decoy (2002): the warp bass cutting through a chopped breakbeat.
Stanton Warriors: Right Here (2004): the nu-skool breaks side, bounce and vocal hook.
Menta: Snake Charmer (2001): the break and the sub starting to look toward dubstep.
breakbeatgarage.rythme: A funk breakbeat or a sampled drum break, sliced in Simpler in Slice mode or in an Akai S950, looped at 135 BPM with a bit of grainy time-stretch. On top, a 909 kick added on 1 and on the “and” of 2, to keep a garage foot, and a 909 snare doubled on 2 and 4 to hold the club. The break is reordered every 4 bars: a reversed slice, a repeated slice. The break's hats are left as they are, a programmed shaker in swung sixteenth notes on top. Snare roll and rewind at the end of a phrase. The break is high-pass filtered at 200 Hz to leave room for the kick.
breakbeatgarage.sons: MC hooks sampled from a pirate radio station, a two-bar phrase repeated in every 16-bar block. Korg M1 organ stabs, to keep the link with garage. Sirens, rewinds, crowd shouts. Short rave synth stabs, a disco brass or string sample. A pitched R'n'B vocal on one section. Roland TR-909 for the added kick and snare, Akai S950 for the break, Cubase back then, Ableton today. The blend: a hip-hop break, a speed garage bass, a pirate radio MC. No long reverb, a short delay on the stabs and the vocal.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, How to create classic house sounds with the Korg M1
breakbeatgarage.tempo: Between 132 and 138 BPM, the garage tempo. The feel keeps the UK garage swing, 58 to 62%, but it is carried by a full breakbeat rather than by programmed hats. The energy is festive and bouncy, closer to nu-skool breaks than to early dubstep. What changes compared to the UK garage it descends from: the 4/4 kick disappears under a chopped break, the warp bass stays. What sets it apart from breakstep, its dark neighbor: the MC hooks, the organ and the light remain, the sub does not yet sink into the dark at 140. This is garage relearning the syncopation of breaks.

breakbeathardcore.arrangement: A 1992 hardcore track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and strings surprises together. A 16-bar intro on kick and hi-hats, first drum break at bar 17 with the sub, then the first “drop” with piano and stab at bar 33. After that, alternating 16-bar sections: piano section, stab and break section, pitched vocal section. The middle breakdown removes everything except the piano and a vocal, over 16 bars, before a roll and everything returning at once. DJs played these records on white labels with a 16-bar kick-only intro and ending: keep that convention.
breakbeathardcore.basse: Two basses coexist, sometimes in the same track. The first is a reggae sub: a sine or a filtered square, played in dotted quarter notes or with a dub pattern (root, rest, fifth, root), one octave below the kick, between 40 and 60 Hz. The second is a rave line in eighth notes on a Juno or an M1, higher, with a bit of release (150 ms). For the sub, stick it to the break's notes: it plays on beat 1 and on the “and” of 3, never continuously. To tie the kick and the sub together, a sidechain compressor at a 6:1 ratio and 100 ms release on the sub, triggered by the 909 kick.
etapes: Set Ableton to 145 BPM. Lay down a 909 kick in 4/4, a clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Import a hip-hop break, turn off warp and transpose it by +5 semitones in Simpler so it fits the tempo: that's the S1000 sound.
Create a sub with Operator (sine, release 200 ms) on a dub pattern, then sidechain at 6:1 from the kick.
Program an M1 piano in major chords on dotted eighth notes and a minor hoover stab on the offbeats, on two separate tracks.
Pitch an a cappella up by +7 semitones in Sampler and cut it into short phrases.
Arrange 16 bars per section, with a piano and vocal breakdown in the middle and a snare roll before each return.
breakbeathardcore.mix: Rave hardcore is not clean and does not try to be. The pitched break occupies the midrange and goes to the front, the 909 kick reinforces it without dominating it. Compress the drum bus with a Glue Compressor (ratio 4:1, attack 3 ms, release Auto) and let it pump a little. The M1 piano likes a short reverb (1.2 s) and a bit of chorus, no surgical EQ. The pitched vocals get a high-pass at 300 Hz so they don't clog the sub. Aim for a bright master: a 2 dB bump at 10 kHz on the main bus reproduces the aggressiveness of the pressings of the era. The sub, for its part, must stay mono and below 80 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: The sampler of the 1991-1992 raves: time-stretched sped-up breaks, Belgian stabs and pitched vocals, everything goes through it, often from records.
The piano and organ presets of the euphoric anthems: major chords in eighth notes, short release; the Korg Collection M1 software version does the same.
Source of the hoover, the Mentasm stab: a chord with portamento and chorus; today sampled or reproduced with Chorus-Ensemble on two saws.
The MIDI sequencer of the English bedroom studios that made the white-label wave possible; it drives sampler and synths, with no audio.
Amen, Think and Funky Drummer sped up toward 140 BPM, plus lifted stabs and sirens; today's hardcore break packs draw on that stock.
Fixed pitch for the chipmunk vocals and the a cappellas raised by +7 semitones and cut into short phrases.
On the breaks bus, ratio 4:1 and short release, to glue the sped-up break to the added kick.
Sine wave for the reggae sub between 40 and 60 Hz, stuck to the notes of the rave line playing above it.

reperes: The Prodigy: Charly (1991): sped-up break, a sample from a road-safety cartoon, rave stab, the whole vocabulary in one track.
Altern 8: Activ 8 (1991): hoover stabs on dotted eighth notes over a 4/4 kick, the Belgian techno touch of hardcore.
Acen: Trip II the Moon (1992): sampled piano and strings, break and reggae sub, rave at its peak of euphoria.
2 Bad Mice: Bombscare (1992): the breakdown with a sampled explosion then the return, the genre's model of tension and release.
breakbeathardcore.rythme: Two stacked layers. Underneath, a 909 kick or a sampled kick on all four beats, for the house energy. On top, a hip-hop break (Funky Drummer, Amen, Think) sped up to 145 BPM by pitching it without time-stretch, which makes it higher and more nervous: that's the Akai S1000 sound from the brief. Add a 909 clap on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes with velocities alternating 100 and 60, and an open hat on the “and” of each beat. On the last 4 bars of a section, replace the break with a sixteenth-note snare roll rising in velocity from 60 to 127.
breakbeathardcore.sons: Three sounds sign the genre. The rave piano is the Korg M1 (Piano 16 preset or an emulation), played as block major chords in dotted eighth notes, one octave above the midrange. The rave stabs come from the Alpha Juno hoover or from Mentasm samples: a minor chord with portamento and chorus. The pitched vocals are soul or reggae a cappellas transposed by +5 to +7 semitones on the sampler, without formant correction, for the chipmunk effect. Add police sirens, crowd shouts and a spoken intro. In Ableton, Sampler with fixed pitch reproduces the effect, and Chorus-Ensemble gives the hoover its fatness.
breakbeathardcore.tempo: Between 1990 and 1992, the tempo climbs year after year: 125 BPM for the first house-breaks records, 140 in 1991, 150 in early 1992. Take 145 BPM as a starting point. The feel is that of a hip-hop break sped up by 30%, so a swing that comes from the sample, not from the sequencer. What changes compared to root breakbeat is the energy of house: a steady 4/4 kick can coexist with the break during the choruses, and the stabs fall on dotted eighth notes as in Belgian techno. Think of an open-air rave, not a club: everything is bigger, faster, happier.
