breakcore.arrangement: A breakcore track lasts 3 to 6 minutes and works by ruptures. No 32-bar intro: start with a vocal sample or a burst of Amen from the very first second. Alternate blocks of 4 to 16 bars in different styles: Amen in 7/4, gabber in 4/4, ragga over a break, a strings section alone. Each block arrives without a build-up, or with a build-up that lies (an 8-bar build-up that leads into silence). A Venetian Snares track can contain a slow, melancholic 16-bar section before taking off again. End on a hard cut or on the vocal sample from the beginning. The principle is collage: you build a track the way you edit a film.
breakcore.basse: The breakcore bass is secondary and brutal. Often it is the gabber kick that plays the role of bass: a saturated 909 with a long tail, going down to 50 Hz and holding the note. Otherwise, a distorted square on Operator or Roar, in short notes following the kicks, or a sampled ragga bass pitched without respect. No clean separate sub: everything is saturated together. The relationship with the kick is fusion: bass and kick go through the same distortion and the same compressor, and the whole forms a single mass. If you want a readable note, keep a sine sub at -12 dB under the rest, for the systems that can handle it.
etapes: Set Ableton (or Renoise) to 200 BPM. Import the Amen, slice it into 32 pieces, and write a pattern over 7 beats.
Add snare bursts with Beat Repeat (or the tracker's retrigger command) that speed up until they become noise.
Create a gabber kick: 909 with a long decay, Overdrive 100%, Saturator Digital Clip, playing 4/4 for 4 bars in a row.
Sample three unrelated things (a cartoon voice, a metal riff, a ragga phrase) and pitch them.
Arrange in blocks of 4 to 16 bars that change style without transition, with a strings section alone in the middle.
Crush the drum bus through distortion, a 20:1 compressor and a clipper, and push the master to -5 LUFS.
breakcore.mix: The breakcore mix is a wall. The whole drum bus goes through a distortion, then a compressor at a 20:1 ratio and 0.1 ms attack, then a clipper. The stacked Amens are distinguished by their pitch and their frequency band, not by level. The gabber kick is the loudest, saturated until its tail becomes a note. The melodic samples (strings, voices) sit behind with a long reverb, and leap forward when the drums go quiet. No sidechain, no surgical EQ: it's the opposite of neurofunk. Master at -4 or -5 LUFS, crushed, with a pumping limiter: that's the intended sound. Bloody Fist pressed records that distorted on playback.

outils.pourquoi: Venetian Snares' modern tracker: Amen typed line by line, pitch rolls, bursts and odd time signatures without effort.
The first breakcore of Digital Hardcore and of Venetian Snares on the Amiga 500, before the MED Soundstudio port to Windows.
Hardware tracker for composing breaks live or on the move, in the same logic as Renoise and the Dirtywave M8.
Amen in Slice mode, each slice repitched and replayed off the grid; Redux after it to crush everything to 8 bits.
Random stutters on the breaks at 200 BPM, high Chance, short Gate, for collages without permission.
Amen saturated to the point of fusion: Roar after Overdrive and Saturator, in series, until the break becomes a wall.
8 bits and brutal downsampling to get back the sound of Amiga trackers and the netlabels of 1999.
Sine sub or gabber kick synthesized with a pitch envelope, under the breaks for the hardcore side.

reperes: Venetian Snares: Szamar Madar (2005): sampled classical strings and Amen in 7/4, beauty and violence in the same bar.
Venetian Snares: Hajnal (2005): snare bursts shifting against the bar, the odd time signature pushed all the way.
Bong-Ra: Killergram (2003): ragga, metal and distorted Amen in the same meat grinder, squat breakcore.
Atari Teenage Riot: Deutschland (Has Gotta Die!) (1996): Berlin digital hardcore, breaks and punk screams, the direct ancestor.
breakcore.rythme: The crushed, distorted Amen from the brief: load the Amen into Renoise or Simpler, slice it into 32 pieces, and write patterns of 7 or 14 lines instead of 8 or 16. An example: kick on line 1, snare on 3, kick on 5, snare on 6 and 7, on a loop of 7. Use tracker commands (retrigger, reverse, pitch slide) on the snare slices to create bursts. Add a gabber kick (distorted 909, long) that takes over in 4/4 for 4 bars, then disappears. Stack two or three Amens at different pitches, each with its own distortion. The fills are snare “retrigs” that speed up until they become noise.
breakcore.sons: The brief cites Renoise and Amiga trackers: the tracker is the instrument, not just the sequencer. Its per-line commands (0Bxx for retrigger, 0Exx for delay, pitch slides) make the bursts. Sample collages without permission: cartoons, metal, ragga, pop songs, film dialogue, everything is sampled, pitched, saturated. The distortions are extreme: Overdrive at 100%, Saturator in Digital Clip, Redux at 8 bits, often in series. Add a screamed metal or gabber vocal, hoover stabs, sirens, and sampled passages of classical music or jazz for contrast. Venetian Snares mixes strings and Amen: beauty and noise together.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (5 of the Best Software and Hardware Trackers)
breakcore.tempo: Breakcore runs between 180 and 220 BPM, and the tempo can change in the middle of a phrase. What sets it apart from drill and bass is the violence and the odd time signatures: Venetian Snares writes in 7/4 or 5/4, and the Amen pattern constantly shifts against the bar. The feel is that of a punk collage: a gabber section in 4/4, then a burst of Amen in 7/8, then a ragga section, without transition. Set your DAW to 200 BPM and, if you use Renoise or a tracker, count in lines per bar rather than in beats: that is how odd patterns become natural.

breakstep.arrangement: A DJ tool of 5 to 6 minutes. A 32-bar intro: the filtered break, a few percussion parts, a sample. The drop at 32: sub, Reese, 2-step snare. 16-bar blocks, variations by subtraction: the break stops for 4 bars, the bass changes note every 8. A 16-bar breakdown in the middle with the sub alone and a delay spinning, then the snare returns. Second half with a new element, a stab or a sample. A 32-bar drum outro. The structure of Zinc's 138 Trek is a good model: few elements, each with its entrance and its exit.
breakstep.basse: A deep sine sub, in long half notes, played on the roots in minor, with slides down a fourth. On top, a jungle Reese: two sawtooths detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide on, low-pass filter around 300 Hz with a slow LFO, as in the recipe from the Attack Magazine book. The bass alternates with the kick: kick on 1, the bass comes in on the “and” of 1 and holds until 2.5. A few eighth-note sub notes for pressure. No melody, two or three notes, the root, the fifth below, the minor seventh.
etapes: Set Ableton to 138 BPM, lay down a 2-step skeleton with the kick on 1 and 2.5, heavy snare on 2 and 4.
Chop a funk break in Simpler in Slice mode, high-pass at 300 Hz, Redux at 12 bits.
Create a sine sub in long notes and a detuned Reese with glide, filter at 300 Hz.
Add rimshots with a dub delay, a filtered minor stab and a pirate MC sample.
Arrange: 32-bar intro with the filtered break, drop at 32, 16-bar breakdown with the sub alone, 32-bar outro.
Mix the sub mono and clean, saturate the Reese and the break, master around -8 LUFS.
breakstep.mix: Raw and heavy. Mono sub below 90 Hz, clean, around -6 dB peak. Reese saturated with Saturator drive at 30% to carry the mid bass. Kick cut below 50 Hz, short, it leaves the sub alone at the bottom, the same rule as in dubstep. Break saturated and compressed hard, ratio 6:1, attack 5 ms, for the S950 side. Snare up front, with a short reverb. Bass sidechained by the kick, discreetly. Controlled lo-fi: a filter at 10 kHz on the master bus or a light Redux. Master around -8 LUFS, no more. Check the low end on a subwoofer: the Reese and the sub must not cancel each other out.

outils.pourquoi: The funk break run through 12 bits, sliced and replayed, the grain of 138 Trek. Redux at 12 bits in Ableton gives the equivalent.
Simpler in Slice mode to chop the break into sixteenth notes, high-pass at 300 Hz, slices reordered every 4 bars.
The jungle Reese from the book: two oscillators detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide, low-pass around 300 Hz with a slow LFO.
Reduction to 12 bits on the break and a filter at 10 kHz on the master, the gray sound of a pirate tape.
Held, filtered minor chord for the dark stabs; TAL-U-NO-LX as a plugin does the job.
Tape delay on the dotted eighth note, feedback at 45%, on the rimshots and wood blocks for the dub spirit.
Drive at 30% on the Reese to carry the mid bass, break compressed and saturated hard for the S950 side.

reperes: DJ Zinc: 138 Trek (2000): the model of the genre, a break under a garage skeleton, jungle bass, DJ tool structure.
Zed Bias: Neighbourhood (2000): dark 2-step with a break and a sliding bass.
El B: Buck and Bury (2001): the sub and the space that herald dubstep, snare still on 2 and 4.
Horsepower Productions: Gorgon Sound (2002): the dub version, percussion and delay, the transition almost complete.
breakstep.rythme: Two layers. Underneath, the 2-step skeleton: kick on 1 and 2.5, heavy snare on 2 and 4, a ghost snare at the end of beat 3. On top, a funk break chopped into sixteenth-note slices in Simpler, Slice mode, looped with a few slices reordered, high-pass filtered at 300 Hz so it doesn't fight the kick. The break goes through an Akai S950 in spirit: Redux at 12 bits, a bit of crunch. Rimshots and wood blocks syncopated with a dub delay. Snare layered with a clap for weight. Snare roll at the end of each 16-bar phrase.
breakstep.sons: Dark synth stabs, a held, filtered minor chord, in Massive or on a Juno. Dub sirens, rewind noises, an MC shout sampled from a pirate radio station, a ragga phrase cut short. Tape delay on the dotted eighth note on the percussion, feedback at 45%. Pads mixed low with a high-pass at 500 Hz. A film dialogue sample, an isolated piano note. Everything goes through a filter that removes the brightness: the sound is gray, as if off a pirate tape. No sung vocals, no M1 organ. The spirit is that of a dark DJ tool, prepared for a sound system.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter Basslines Reese bass (wavetable)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter Basslines Reese bass (wavetable)
breakstep.tempo: Between 135 and 140 BPM, the 2-step tempo tipping over into the dubstep tempo. The feel keeps the garage swing, 58 to 62%, but the tone is dark and heavy. The signature: a 2-step skeleton under which a chopped breakbeat brings jungle syncopation. The perceived tempo is double: the break runs fast, the bass and the kick are slow. What changes compared to 2-step: the vocals disappear, the sub goes lower, the breaks replace the sixteenth-note hats. What sets it apart from the dubstep that follows: the snare is still on 2 and 4, halfstep has not yet imposed its slowness.

bristolsound.arrangement: Tracks run 4 to 5 minutes and follow a simple song form: an intro of 4 to 8 bars of break alone, the bass and the vocal come in, chorus with the sampled strings. What comes from the sound system is the dub version: after 2 minutes, the vocal disappears, the delay takes the snare and the bass carries on alone for 16 bars. Transitions are abrupt: you cut, you bring back, no filtered build-up. Think of two versions of the same track, the vocal and the dub, as on a 12-inch single of the era. The rap, if there is any, is delivered low, without shouting, and leaves room for the singer.
bristolsound.basse: The bass is the sound system bass: deep, played on an electric bass or a synth, in reggae lines that leave holes. The model is the lovers rock line: root on 1, jump to the fifth on 3, silence on 4. It is mixed very loud, more than anywhere else in the family, because it is made for a wall of speakers. Low-pass at 150 Hz, almost no harmonics, heavy compression at a 6:1 ratio for a constant level. On Smith & Mighty's covers, the bass outright replaces the original orchestral accompaniment: it carries the harmony, the voice sings on top, and the rest is scenery.
etapes: Choose a tempo of 95 BPM and loop a 2-bar funk break, with no added swing, as is.
Lay down a drum machine kick on every beat and a snare with spring reverb on 2 and 4, plus a rimshot on the offbeat.
Write a reggae bassline, root on 1 and fifth on 3, silence on 4, very loud and compressed.
Add a sampled string or piano stab, one chord per bar, and a soft vocal sung in the lovers rock style.
Create a dub version: cut the vocal after 2 minutes, send the snare into a tape delay and let the bass run.
Mix bass up front, vocal in the center, run everything through a cassette simulation and cut above 12 kHz.
bristolsound.mix: The mix is made for a sound system: bass up front, vocal in the center, everything else behind. Cut the low end of everything that isn't the bass at 120 Hz. The break is compressed hard to hold its level, ratio 4:1, but without modern saturation: the grain comes from the sampler and the cassette. The spring reverb on the snare is short, under one second. The vocal is clean, a bit of 3:1 compression and a short plate. No sidechain, no limiter: the master is simply loud and without effects. If your mix sounds too clean, run the whole track through a cassette simulation and cut at 12 kHz: 1988 Bristol never had shiny highs.

outils.pourquoi: The 12-bit samplers of the Bristol home studios in 1987 and 1989: short funk breaks, string stabs, everything goes through their grain. Decimort 2 to emulate it.
The 16-bit version that arrived in 1988, cleaner, where the break loops with fixed outputs to the console.
To play the break and the drum machine kick together on the pads, with the snare cracking on 2 and 4.
The cassette recorder of the Ashley Road studio: hiss, natural compression and highs cut at 12 kHz. A cassette simulation reproduces this.
Tape delay and spring reverb in the same box: the dub snare and the offbeat rimshot go through it. Ableton Echo imitates it.
Turntables for the soul and pop samples, and discreet scratches. Smith & Mighty covered Bacharach starting from the record.
The Wild Bunch's wall of speakers: the mix is judged on the bass pushed up front, cut at 150 Hz, compressed at a 6:1 ratio.
Set gently on the master bus, plus pink noise at minus 50 dB, to get the cassette back without owning one.

reperes: Smith & Mighty: Walk On By (1988): the Bacharach cover where the dub bass replaces the whole orchestra under a dry break.
Fresh 4: Wishing on a Star (1989): the lovers rock vocal, the hip-hop break and the deep bass, produced by Smith & Mighty.
Massive Attack: Daydreaming (1990): the laid-back rap, the short samples and the singer, the bridge between the Wild Bunch and trip-hop.
Massive Attack: Teardrop (1998): the harpsichord and the heavy kick, where Bristol's slowness became a language of its own.
bristolsound.rythme: Two layers coexist: a sampled funk drum break, looped on an Akai S1000 or an MPC60 with fixed outputs, and on top a very dry drum machine kick on every beat. It is this break plus digital reggae blend that defines the sound: the break's hi-hats, the drum machine snare cracking on 2 and 4 with a spring reverb. Add a rimshot on the offbeat, like a reggae skank, on the “and” of each beat. The percussion comes from dub: a wood block or a bell in delay on the dotted eighth note, running for 4 bars then disappearing. Keep it simple: two bars that loop, and the effects create the variation.
bristolsound.sons: The gear is that of a 1988 home studio: a sampler, a four-track cassette recorder, turntables. The samples are soul and pop: Smith & Mighty covered Burt Bacharach, with reggae singers. So the sound is a clear, soft voice, sung like lovers rock, over a bed of short samples: a string chord, a piano stab cut dry. The effects are those of dub: spring reverb, tape delay, a sweeping high-pass filter. The cassette adds a light hiss and natural compression: in Ableton, a gentle Saturator and pink noise at minus 50 dB imitate this. Scratches are present but discreet. The whole thing is raw, not yet cinematic.
sourcesOutils: The Vinyl Factory (Life Has A Way: The Smith & Mighty story)
The Wire (Smith & Mighty, Ashley Road Sessions)
bristolsound.tempo: 1980s Bristol is faster and brighter than the trip-hop that will come out of it: 90 to 105 BPM, a hip-hop breakbeat or lovers rock tempo, not yet the dragging half-time. The swing comes from the sampled breaks, not from a setting: the first samplers had no swing, you played the loops as they were and laid things on top. So program on the grid, 50%, and let the break bring its feel. The kick is straight, often on every beat as in digital reggae, with a snare on 2 and 4. The feel is that of a sound system: steady, danceable; the slowness will come later.

brokenbeat.arrangement: A broken beat track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and is built like a jazz-funk piece recorded in the studio. An 8-bar intro on the Rhodes alone or on the percussion. The swaying drums and the bass come in at bar 9. A 16-bar theme A with the chords, a 16-bar theme B with a change of harmony (often a modulation by a third). An 8-bar bridge where the drums stop and the Rhodes improvises. Return of theme A, then a 32-bar solo (synth, vocal or bass) over the loop. A 16-bar outro with a fade. No drop, no build-up: sections that answer one another, like musicians passing the word around.
brokenbeat.basse: The played basses from the brief: an electric bass or a Moog played by hand, or an Electric Bass and Trilian patch with varied velocities and legato. The line is a jazz-funk line: root, fifth, sixth, minor seventh, octave, in syncopated sixteenth notes that follow the sway of the drums, with glissandi and ghost notes at velocity 30. It changes every bar, over a chord progression of four to eight bars. The Attack Magazine book, in its chapter on broken beat techno, shows the value of separating a clean sine sub and a processed main bass that follows the same pattern: apply this principle, but without the distortion, with a bit of tape saturation.
etapes: Set Ableton to 125 BPM with an MPC 16 Swing groove at 66%. Program a kick on 1, the “a” of 2 and the “and” of 4, rimshot on the “e” of 2 and on 4.
Add sixteenth-note hi-hats with shifted accents, and congas in a 2-bar loop. Change the kick every 2 bars.
Write a progression of four ninth chords on Electric (Rhodes) and play them by hand, light tremolo and phaser.
Create a played bass (Electric Bass or Trilian) in syncopated sixteenth notes with ghost notes, and a sine sub under it.
Add a unison Moog lead and a soul vocal, then arrange as theme A, theme B, bridge, solo, outro.
Mix warm: tape saturation on the drums, no sidechain, -10 LUFS.
brokenbeat.mix: The broken beat mix is warm and dynamic. The programmed drums are compressed gently (ratio 3:1, attack 10 ms) and go through tape saturation (Saturator Soft Sine, Drive 3 dB) to glue the samples together. The Rhodes is wide and up front, high-passed at 120 Hz, with a 2 s reverb. The played bass is compressed at 4:1 with a slow attack (30 ms) to keep the finger attacks, and the sub underneath is mono. No sidechain: musicians don't pump. The percussion is panned wide. Master at -10 LUFS, with dynamics: this is musicians' music, the master has to breathe like a jazz record.

outils.pourquoi: Bugz in the Attic's machine: swing pushed to 65-70% on the sixteenth notes, kicks and snares placed off the beats.
Rich four-note chords played by hand, tremolo and light phaser; Ableton Electric or samples if you don't have one.
Hand-played bass and unison leads; Arturia Mini V or Moog Model D in software give the same fatness.
Groove Pool with MPC 16 Swing at 66% on the drum tracks, to get the MPC3000 sway back without the machine.
Electric bass played with varied velocities and ghost notes in syncopated eighth notes, under a sine sub.
Unison leads and analog synth stabs when the Moog isn't there, two saws and a soft filter.
Light Analog Clip on the drum bus to give the programmed hits a console grain.
Sampled brass, flute and vibraphone for the themes, played with human velocities and without quantization.

reperes: 4hero: Hold It Down (2001): the swaying drums, the Rhodes and the strings, Dego and Marc Mac moving from jungle to jazz.
Bugz in the Attic: Booty La La (2004): club broken beat, funky played bass and a rhythm that's impossible to count.
Seiji: Loose Lips (2002): the pushed swing and the played keyboards, the Co-Op sound.
Kaidi Tatham: An Insight to All Minds (2021): Kaidi's keyboards solo, broken beat twenty years later, still alive.
brokenbeat.rythme: The swaying programmed drums from the brief: program on an MPC3000 or in Ableton with an MPC 16 Swing groove at 66%. Kick on beat 1, on the “a” of 2 (the sixteenth before 3) and on the “and” of 4. Snare or rimshot on the “e” of 2 (the sixteenth after 2) and on 4, or the other way around in the next bar. Sixteenth-note hi-hats with shifted accents (velocity 110 on the second sixteenth of each beat). Add Latin and African percussion (congas, shakers, agogô) in a 2-bar loop with its own swing. Change the kick placement every 2 bars. The sounds are short, dry, often acoustic drum samples.
brokenbeat.sons: The played Fender Rhodes, cited in the brief, is the central instrument: ninth and thirteenth chords, jazz voicings, played with a tremolo and a bit of phaser, in Electric or as samples. Add a Moog or Analog for unison leads, sampled or played brass, a flute, a vibraphone. The vocals are soul, sung or spoken, with harmonies. Kaidi Tatham and IG Culture layer played keyboards over programmed rhythm sections: the contrast between the human hand and the machine is the sound. Use samples from Brazilian jazz-funk and soul records for textures, and a bit of dub (dotted-eighth delay, spring reverb) on the percussion.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapter Broken Beat Techno, for the separation of sub and main bass)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapter Broken Beat Techno)
Attack Magazine (DAW and Drum Machine Swing)
brokenbeat.tempo: Broken beat is played between 120 and 130 BPM, but the tempo matters less than the sway. The feel comes from a swing pushed to the extreme on the MPC3000 (65 to 70% on the sixteenth notes) and from kick and snare placements that fall beside the beats: the snare arrives one sixteenth note late on 2, or early on 4, and the kick moves from one bar to the next. What sets it apart from the rest of the family is that it's impossible to count by tapping your foot, yet the body understands it. The model is jazz-funk and afrobeat, not rave.

brokentechno.arrangement: Five to six minutes. To stay playable, keep one stable element throughout the track: the sub or a straight hi-hat. A 16-bar intro with the sub and one percussion part, then the broken kick comes in at 17. Beat variations every 8 bars: move a kick, add a ghost. The breakdown arrives around 65: 8 to 16 bars without kick where only the main bass screams with its delays, then the return with a denser variation. Change the bass pattern halfway through. Overmono's anthems add a vocal and a build-up; Objekt and Blawan prefer clean cuts, a bar of silence, a return. A 16-bar outro with the sub and the hi-hats.
brokentechno.basse: Two twin basses on the same pattern. A sub: Operator, oscillator A at coarse 0.5 at 0 dB, oscillator B at coarse 1 at -30 dB, a sound close to an organ, F notes lasting an eighth note on syncopated positions (the second one on the third sixteenth of beat 2). A screaming main bass that follows the same pattern: Analog with two saws an octave apart and a tiny detune, noise at -7 dB, LP24 filter at 50 Hz with 24% resonance, envelope at 5, LFO at 0.15 on the cutoff, attack 5 ms, decay 45 ms, sustain 20%, release 250 ms. Then Saturator at +20 dB, eighth-note ping-pong Echo cut at 200 Hz, Devastor. Group and compress the two together.
etapes: At 135 BPM, program a kick on syncopated positions (1, offbeat of 2, 3, last sixteenth) and a snare on 2 and 4.
Slice a break loop, replay it with the slices moved around, extract its groove and apply it to the hi-hats.
Create an FM sub in Operator (coarse 0.5 and 1) on syncopated F notes lasting an eighth note.
Duplicate the pattern on Analog (two saws an octave apart, LP24 at 50 Hz), then Saturator +20 dB, Echo, Devastor.
Add two impact layers (cut at 80 Hz and a 150 Hz to 12 kHz band) and ghost notes at velocity 30.
Arrange over six minutes keeping the sub stable, beat variations every 8 bars, a breakdown without kick.
brokentechno.mix: The sub is mono and dominant, around -6 dB. The distorted main bass is cut below 80 Hz and occupies the low mids and mids; the two are grouped and compressed together with Glue at 4:1. The break stays in the background, at -16 dB, filtered; if you push it up, the bass must step back. Impacts and high percussion wide in stereo, kick and snare in the center. Heavy sidechain on the high percussion and the rim, triggered by the broken kick, not by a straight LFO. A master around -8 LUFS, but the transients of the ghosts must survive: avoid clipping. Check in mono that the displaced kicks stay readable.

outils.pourquoi: Replaying and pitching the slices of a resampled sequence, chopping vocals into sixteenth notes; the pivot of Overmono's live set.
At Blawan's, Cwejman QMMF-4 filters and a Bugbrand delay: sounds broken and then rebuilt, which seem ready to collapse at every bar.
The swing between 55 and 62% on the percussion, inherited from Detroit electro; an MPC One or Ableton's MPC 16 groove is enough.
Slice to New MIDI Track to extract the groove of a real break, Simpler in Slice mode to reprogram the slices, Analog for the screaming bass.
Organ-like sub: oscillator A at coarse 0.5, B at coarse 1 at -30 dB, syncopated F notes, the only element that never moves.
Last stage on the main bass after Saturator at +20 dB and a ping-pong Echo cut at 200 Hz, then grouped with the sub.
Eighth-note ping-pong on the bass and a dotted-eighth delay on the fragmented rave stabs; everything high-pitched moves in the stereo field.

reperes: Blawan: Why They Hide Their Bodies Under My Garage (2012): the chopped vocal, the displaced kick and the screaming bass
Objekt: Theme from Q (2017): the reprogrammed break and the metallic impacts, the precision of the writing
Batu: Marius (2017): UK bass swing under club techno, stable sub and floating percussion
Overmono: So U Kno (2021): the broken anthem, pitched vocal, syncopated kicks and a rave build-up
brokentechno.rythme: The kick refuses four-on-the-floor: beat 1, the offbeat of beat 2, beat 3 and the last sixteenth of the bar, for example, with variations every 2 bars. Snare on 2 and 4 for anchoring, with ghost notes at velocity 30 around it. A reprogrammed break: slice a loop, replay it by moving the slices around, push it into the background. Two impact layers: one cut hard at 80 Hz, the other isolated between 150 Hz and 12 kHz. Swung sixteenth-note hi-hats with lots of velocity variation, a displaced open hat. A metallic percussion or a pitched rim. Every bar should feel like it is falling and then catching itself.
brokentechno.sons: Modular and resampling: record a sequence, slice it, replay the slices on an Octatrack or in Simpler in Slice mode, pitch the slices, re-record. An MPC for the swing. Wobbling UK basses (LFO on the filter of a saw). Fragmented rave stabs, a note held then cut. Metallic impacts pitched down -15 semitones, a hangar reverb then an EQ to frame it. Vocals chopped into sixteenth notes. A short mechanical reverb for the impacts, a dotted-eighth delay for the stabs. Everything high-pitched moves around in the stereo field. The sub never moves.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
brokentechno.tempo: From 125 to 140 BPM. Overmono around 130 to 135, Blawan and Objekt up to 140. Swing is central: an MPC groove or a break template between 55 and 62% on the percussion, with low-velocity ghost notes filling the holes. The feel comes from Detroit electro and UK bass: the grid is there, but the kick doesn't follow it. Extract the groove from a real break loop (Slice to New MIDI Track in Ableton) and apply it to your own samples. The tempo can feel doubled: at 135 BPM, a snare on 2 and 4 with syncopated kicks sounds like sped-up garage. Keep one straight element for the track.

brostep.arrangement: Short format, 3 minutes 30 to 4 minutes 30. A melodic intro of 16 to 32 bars with a vocal or a lead. A 16-bar build-up: snare roll, riser, filter opening, the drums stop on the last bar. A 32-bar drop, split in two: the second half changes bass or doubles the density. Return of a calm 16-bar verse, second build-up, second drop with new sounds. A dry ending or a short outro. Everything is written for listening and festivals, not for DJ mixing. The drop must hold up in 8 bars if you cut it; every bar brings a change.
brostep.basse: The growl is the heart of the genre. In Serum or Massive: a rich wavetable, a bit of FM from a second oscillator, a formant filter or a comb filter, and several LFOs synced to 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 modulating cutoff, wavetable position and FM. Change the LFO speed on each note for the roller-coaster side. Always keep the sub separate: a mono sine on its own track, following the growl's notes. Resample the growl to audio, then chop it and rearrange the pieces. Run it through OTT and a distortion. The notes stay on one or two scale degrees; the movement comes from the timbre, not from the melody.
etapes: Set Ableton to 140 BPM, kick on 1, layered snare on 3, with sixteenth-note ghost kicks.
Build a growl in Serum: wavetable, FM, formant filter, three LFOs synced at different speeds.
Put a mono sine sub on its own track, following the growl's notes.
Resample the growl, chop it into sixteenth-note pieces and rearrange them as call and response.
Write a 16-bar melodic intro, a 16-bar build-up with a snare roll, then a 32-bar drop.
Run the basses through OTT, sidechain everything to kick and snare, limit the master to around -6 LUFS.
brostep.mix: A war mix. OTT on the mid basses with depth at 40%, a clipper on the drum bus, multiband on the master. Sidechain everything that isn't drums from the kick and the snare, with a short 60 ms release. Mono sub below 100 Hz, growl widened above it with a bit of Haas or unison. Snare around -4 dB peak, it's the loudest element along with the sub. Cut the growls below 120 Hz so the sub stays clean. Limiter on the master with 4 to 6 dB of reduction, target between -5 and -6 LUFS. Check in mono; the growls often lose width.

outils.pourquoi: The growl: rich wavetable, FM from oscillator 2, formant filter, three LFOs synced to 1/4, 1/8 and 1/16 on cutoff and position.
The synth of the 2010 growls, with its aggressive wavetables and its modulation matrix; Skrillex and Rusko put it everywhere.
Free multiband compression, depth around 40% on the mid basses, to flatten and bring out every movement of the timbre.
Per-band saturation: distortion on the growl's mids, sub left clean, a bit of tape on the top.
Multiband distortion and convolution to dirty up a resampled growl before chopping it into sixteenth-note pieces.
Master limiter with 4 to 6 dB of reduction, target between -5 and -6 LUFS, the genre's war-level loudness.
Resample the growl to audio, chop it, reorder the slices as call and response and automate the eighth-note stops.

outils.nom: Splice, brostep packs and Serum presets
outils.pourquoi: Growl presets, impacts, risers and sub drops to compare your sound design with the references and complete a drop.

reperes: Rusko: Cockney Thug (2008): the shift from dubstep wobble to the midrange growl, still with humor.
Skrillex: Scary Monsters and Nice Sprites (2010): sugary intro, build-up, roller-coaster drop, the complete manual.
Flux Pavilion: Bass Cannon (2011): a single bass in call and response, power in simplicity.
Excision: Robo Kitty (2011): the heaviest version, stacked growls and weighty drums.
brostep.rythme: Kick on 1, snare on 3, but both are layered to hit heavy: kick with a 909 click and a short sub, snare with a clap, white noise and an acoustic snare, plus a short 0.5 s reverb. Between the two, syncopated ghost kicks on the sixteenth notes, always answering the bass. The hi-hats matter little, often simple eighth notes or nothing. The build-up: a snare roll going from eighth notes to sixteenths then thirty-seconds over 16 bars, with a riser. Pitched tom fills before the drop. In the drop, the drums often stop for an eighth note to leave a bass scream alone.
brostep.sons: Massive and Serum for the growls, with aggressively named wavetables. Robot screams obtained by modulating the wavetable position with a fast envelope. Vocals pitched up yelling “yeah” or a phrase, cut into stutters. A supersaw lead for the melodic intro, with a four-chord minor progression. Lasers, impacts, sub drops, white-noise risers climbing over 8 bars. The drop works as call and response: one bass sound states a 2-beat phrase, another answers it. Maximum compression on everything that moves.
sourcesOutils: ADSR Sounds, How to Make a Skrillex Growl in Xfer Serum
EDM Templates, How To Make Dubstep Growls In Serum 2
brostep.tempo: 140 BPM, like the dubstep it comes from, with the snare on beat 3. But halfstep becomes a pretext: the drop is filled with sixteenth notes, triplets and sudden silences in the bass. The swing almost disappears, everything is quantized, the grid is in sixteenth notes and sometimes thirty-second notes for the fills. The feel is that of a video game: nervous, mechanical, full of sudden stops. What changes compared to dubstep: the rhythmic density of the drop, and the 16-bar build-ups with snare rolls that didn't exist in Croydon. The contrast between a melodic intro and a brutal drop is the signature.

chicagohouse.arrangement: Think in blocks of 8 and 16 bars, with a 32-bar DJ intro containing only drums and bass. The track lasts 5 to 7 minutes. There is no verse and chorus, there are entrances and exits: the bass arrives at bar 17, the piano at 33, the voice at 49. A breakdown in the middle removes the kick for 8 or 16 bars, keeps the clap and the voice, then everything comes back at once, with no white-noise build-up. A 1986 track has no drop, it has a kick return. End with an outro symmetrical to the intro, drums alone, so the next DJ can mix.
chicagohouse.basse: The Chicago bass is synthetic, monophonic and short. A Juno-106 or a Poly-61 with a sawtooth, low-pass filter at 300 to 600 Hz, a touch of resonance, fast envelope (attack 0, decay 200 ms, low sustain). In a DAW, Operator or Analog will do the job. The typical pattern is a bouncing octave: root on the beat, octave above on the “and”, in eighth or sixteenth notes, as on On and On. Stay on one or two chords, with jumps of a fifth or a minor seventh for section changes. Cut everything below 40 Hz and let the kick own the 60 Hz: the bass lives between 80 and 250 Hz.
etapes: Open a project at 122 BPM, load a 909 kit into a Drum Rack and program a four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hats with the open hat on the offbeats.
Create a sawtooth bass in Analog or Operator, filter at 400 Hz, and write the root-octave pattern in eighth notes on one note for 4 bars.
Add a piano or a Rhodes playing a minor 7 chord on the offbeats, then a Juno pad with chorus on two held notes.
Record or sample one spoken word, repeat it in a loop with a dotted-eighth delay, and place it like a percussion part.
Spread everything over 6 minutes in 16-bar blocks, with a drums-only intro and outro and a breakdown without kick in the middle.
Compress the drum bus, saturate kick and bass, cut above 14 kHz and check that the track holds up in mono.
chicagohouse.mix: The Chicago sound is narrow, somewhat mono, with a kick in front of everything. Put fairly firm bus compression (ratio 4:1, attack 10 ms, release 100 ms) on the drum group to make it pump slightly. Saturate the kick and the bass with a gentle distortion (Saturator in Analog Clip mode) to simulate a pushed mixing desk. Cut the top above 14 kHz on the mix: the recordings of the era had no air. A short, single reverb, a 1 s plate on the clap and the voice only. Don't chase modern loudness: aim for -12 LUFS integrated and let the transients breathe; the record should sound like a slightly dusty Trax pressing.

outils.pourquoi: The long kick, the clap and the toms that carry Move Your Body and Jack Your Body; today Roland Cloud TR-909 or D16 Drumazon 2 do the same job.
The dry, digital box of the first Trax records: short hats, thin clap, cowbell; a 707 kit in a Drum Rack is enough to get it back.
Filtered sawtooth bass and chorused pads, the color of Larry Heard and Marshall Jefferson; emulated by TAL-U-NO-LX or Roland Cloud JUNO-106.
A cheap polyphonic synth from the early Chicago days, used for short basses and block-chord stabs, colder and rawer than a Juno.
The course relies on its native instruments: Drum Rack with a 909 kit, Analog or Operator for the bass, Saturator in Analog Clip on kick and bass.
For the house piano playing block minor 7 chords on the offbeats, with a slightly cold Rhodes sound reminiscent of the 1986 digital keyboards.
The Trax records sound narrow and saturated because everything went through a small, pushed console; gentle saturation on the bus reproduces that grain.

reperes: Jesse Saunders: On and On (1984): the bouncing octave bass and the bare drum machine, the model for everything that follows.
Marshall Jefferson: Move Your Body (1986): the block-chord piano in eighth notes that becomes a rhythmic instrument, the voice repeating an instruction.
Steve Silk Hurley: Jack Your Body (1986): absolute economy, a vocal sample, a 909 and a bass, and how the breakdown without kick relaunches the track.
chicagohouse.rythme: The 909 kick on every beat, long and a little boomy, tuned around 50 to 60 Hz. 909 clap or snare on beats 2 and 4, often both layered, with the clap shifted by one sixteenth note for the “jack” effect. Closed hi-hats in eighth notes, open hat on the offbeat of each beat, short release (150 to 250 ms) to keep the dry 707 feel. Add a rimshot or a 909 cowbell in syncopation, for example on the “a” of beat 2, to sign the pattern. The fills are simple 909 tom rolls every 8 bars. Resist the urge to pile things on: four or five elements are enough, repetition is the point.
chicagohouse.sons: The house piano playing block major or minor 7 chords, in eighth notes on the offbeats, played with a Rhodes preset or a slightly cold digital piano. Juno-106 pads with the chorus on, two or three notes held over eight bars. A voice, often a single repeated word (“jack”, “move”) or a spoken line, processed with a dotted-eighth delay. Organ or string stabs sampled on an old 12-bit sampler for a dirty grain. No layer is rich: every sound is simple, almost poor, and it is that economy that sounds like Chicago. Use Ableton's native emulations (Drum Rack with a 909 kit, Analog for the synths) rather than overly clean modern presets.
sourcesOutils: MusicTech, Best Roland Juno emulation plugins
chicagohouse.tempo: Aim for 120 to 124 BPM, the zone where disco was replaced by a machine. The feel is square, almost stiff: the TR-909 or TR-707 plays without swing, or with a very light swing (52 to 54% in Ableton). What gives the groove is not humanization but the contrast between the four-on-the-floor kick and elements that fall beside it: offbeat hats, a doubled clap, a bass that pushes on the “and”. Keep a strict sixteenth-note grid for everything that comes from the machines and save the micro-offsets for the vocal or piano samples. The track must stay mixable: a DJ should be able to beatmatch it with their eyes closed.

chillout.arrangement: Chill-out is a journey more than a song: 6 to 12 minutes, or a whole continuous album. Start with 1 to 2 minutes of pads and field recordings without pulse. Introduce the beat with a filter opening over 32 bars. Let it live for 3 to 4 minutes, with a vocal or radio sample coming in and out, then remove the kick and let the pads finish alone for 1 to 2 minutes. Transitions are long fades, never cuts: automate the volume over 16 bars. Think about the segue: the track should be able to start where the previous one ends, as in a back room at 5 in the morning.
chillout.basse: The bass is soft and melodic, often an electric bass played with the fingers or a sine Moog with a long release. It plays little: notes held over 2 bars, root then fourth, sometimes a small descending line reminiscent of soul. On Air's La Femme d'Argent, the electric bass carries the whole track with a funky line played softly. Cut it at 200 Hz, add a light chorus to widen it, and keep it a little quieter than in downtempo: here it accompanies, it doesn't lead. On the beatless passages, it can disappear entirely and let the pads hold the low end with a low octave.
etapes: Record or gather 5 minutes of field recordings, radio voices, city or nature, and band-pass them from 300 Hz to 5 kHz.
Create a wide pad on a Juno or Wavetable, oscillators detuned by 10 cents, 2-second attack, and play two chords over 8 bars.
Program a soft drum machine at 92 BPM, kick filtered at 2 kHz, light rimshot and hi-hats, inside a closed low-pass.
Add an electric or Moog bass in held notes, root and fourth, and a guitar with a dotted-quarter delay.
Arrange over 8 minutes: 2 minutes without beat, filter opening over 32 bars, beat for 4 minutes, ending on the pads.
Mix wide, 8-second reverb on a send, almost no compression, master at minus 14 LUFS.
chillout.mix: The mix is open and wide, the complete opposite of trip-hop. The pads take up the whole stereo field, the beat stays in the center and small. A long reverb of 6 to 10 seconds on a send, with a high-pass at 300 Hz so it doesn't drown the low end. Very light compression, ratio 1.5:1, or none: dynamics are part of the journey. Cut the pads at 100 Hz, leave the bass alone at the bottom. The field recordings are band-pass filtered, 300 Hz to 5 kHz, so they sound like a distant radio. Master at minus 14 or minus 16 LUFS, with real silences: a chill-out track that sounds loud has missed its point.

outils.pourquoi: Softened drum machine: kick filtered at 2 kHz, rimshot in place of the snare, low-velocity hi-hats. Samples in a Drum Rack.
Wide chorused pads, oscillators detuned by 10 cents, 2-second attack. Softube Model 84 as a common emulation.
Two detuned oscillators, cutoff at 3 kHz moving very slowly via LFO: the pad that holds 8 bars without getting tiresome.
To capture trains, seagulls, street voices, then band-pass from 300 Hz to 5 kHz. A phone does the job to start with.
The KLF assembled Chill Out live between two DATs, cassettes, a turntable and a 12-track: collage as an instrument.
Replaces the KLF's pedal steel: clean sound, dotted-quarter delay, 6-second reverb, two notes per bar.
Free, 6 to 10-second reverb on a send with a high-pass at 300 Hz, to open up the stereo field around the beat.

reperes: The KLF: Madrugada Eterna (1990): the pedal steel, the radio samples and the gridless journey, the genre's manifesto.
Air: La Femme d'Argent (1998): the soft electric bass, the Rhodes and the Moog, chill-out turned instrumental pop.
Zero 7: In The Waiting Line (2001): softly played drums, string pads and the voice, the song version.
Jose Padilla: Agua (1998): soft percussion and oceanic pads, the sound of Café del Mar at sunset.
chillout.rythme: The drums are a softened drum machine: a TR-808 or a 707 with the kick filtered at 2 kHz, the snare replaced by a rimshot or a clap drowned in reverb, eighth-note hi-hats at low velocity. No sampled break: it is clean, regular, almost naive. Put the whole thing through a low-pass that opens slowly over 32 bars so the beat seems to arrive from far away. Add natural percussion: a shaker, a softly played conga, rain sticks. Most tracks benefit from the beat coming in after 2 minutes and disappearing before the end. On later tracks like those of Zero 7, drums played with brushes do the same job.
chillout.sons: Wide pads are the main material: a Juno or a Wavetable with two oscillators detuned by 10 cents, 2-second attack, 4-second release, chorus, cutoff at 3 kHz moving very slowly. On top, radio samples and field recordings: announcer voices, train noise, seagulls, snippets of old songs, like the KLF with their pedal steel guitar and their Elvis samples. Record your own city or nature sounds with a phone. A clean electric guitar with a dotted-quarter delay and a 6-second reverb replaces the pedal steel. Add a piano or a Rhodes in held chords. Everything must be soft, with no hard transients.
sourcesOutils: Classic Album Sundays (The KLF Chill Out)
chillout.tempo: Here, the tempo matters less than time: 80 to 100 BPM when there is a beat, and often no beat for minutes. What sets chill-out apart from downtempo is that freedom: the rhythm can appear, fade out, come back slower. The KLF recorded Chill Out as one continuous journey, with no fixed grid. In your DAW, choose 92 BPM as a reference to sync the delays, but let the pads and the samples float without quantization. When a beat arrives, it is simple, straight, without marked swing, like a drum machine left running in the next room.

chillwave.arrangement: Chillwave is a pop song of 3 to 4 minutes: an intro of 4 to 8 bars with the synth and the drum machine, a verse of 8 or 16 bars, an 8-bar chorus, second verse, chorus, an 8-bar bridge where the drums stop, a doubled final chorus. The chorus is recognizable by a rising major chord and a louder vocal. No filtered build-up or club breakdown: these are chamber pop codes. Transitions are drum machine rolls or a hit of reversed reverb. End with a fade or a cassette stop: a pitch slowdown on the last bar does the job very well.
chillwave.basse: The bass is synthetic, often a Juno or a Prophet, or a software synth with a square wave filtered at 500 Hz and chorus. It plays 1980s pop lines: eighth notes on the root with an octave jump, or a melodic line following the vocal. On Toro y Moi's more danceable tracks, a sampled funk bass or a gently slapped one. Cut it at 250 Hz, but it has little sub: chillwave is listened to on a laptop and the low end is absent by nature. Add the same cassette wow as the master so it undulates with everything else. No sidechain; the tape compression ties it to the kick.
etapes: Choose 96 BPM and program the simplest drum machine pattern possible: kick on 1 and 3, clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hats, in 8 bits.
Create a synth detuned by 20 cents with thick chorus and a low-pass at 3 kHz, and play a 4-chord pop progression over 8 bars.
Write a synth bass in eighth notes with octave jumps, filtered at 500 Hz, no sub.
Record a soft vocal, double it, drown it in a 5-second reverb and a delay, and filter it at 5 kHz.
Arrange as a 3 minute 30 song: intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, bridge without drums, final chorus.
Run the master through a cassette simulation with wow, hiss and saturation, low-pass at 8 kHz.
chillwave.mix: The mix is hazy, saturated and small, like a rediscovered cassette. Master low-pass at 8 kHz, tape saturation on each bus, and a bit of parallel compression on the drums to fatten them up. The vocal is mixed under the synths, 3 dB below the usual pop level, which creates the drowned effect. A long 4 to 6-second reverb shared by everything, with a high-pass at 200 Hz. The stereo comes from the chorus, not from panning. Master around minus 12 LUFS, with light tape clipping rather than a limiter. Add cassette hiss at minus 45 dB across the whole track. If your mix sounds clean, you've missed it: add more wow.

outils.pourquoi: The model for hazy detuned synths: two oscillators 20 cents apart, thick chorus, low-pass at 3 kHz. TAL-U-NO-LX as an emulation.
Everything but the kick goes into it, sometimes at 100% wet, 4 to 6-second reverb: the 2009 Washed Out sound lives there.
Cassette simulation on the master: wow, hiss at minus 45 dB, gentle saturation, low-pass at 8 kHz.
Tape saturation and doubling pedal seen on Toro y Moi's pedalboard, on the guitar with chorus and tremolo.
Cheap drum machines, kick on 1 and 3, clap on 2 and 4. Samples in a Drum Rack run through Redux at 8 bits.
Simple analog synth to get the Juno pad without a third-party plugin: two oscillators, detune, low-pass filter, chorus after it.
Toro y Moi's stage and studio keyboard for the Rhodes, organs and pianos of his more danceable records.
Causers of This was made almost entirely in it, with the NN-XT sampler and the Thor synth. Ableton works just as well.

reperes: Washed Out: Feel It All Around (2009): the slowed-down Italo sample, the drowned vocal and the cassette, the founding track.
Neon Indian: Deadbeat Summer (2009): the detuned synths, the cheap drum machine and the pop song structure.
Toro y Moi: Blessa (2010): the chopped samples, the funkier groove and the vocal filtered into the reverb.
Memory Tapes: Bicycle (2009): the rising synth bassline, the layers of synths and the chorus that is slow to arrive.
chillwave.rythme: The drum machine is cheap and lo-fi: Casio, Boss DR-55, TR-505, or a Drum Rack with samples from these machines run through Redux at 8 bits. Kick on 1 and 3, snare or clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hats: the simplest pattern possible, like chamber pop. Add a tambourine or a shaker drowned in reverb. No sampled break, no MPC swing: that's what separates it from lo-fi hip hop. The whole kit goes through a spring reverb or a short plate, then a low-pass at 6 kHz. On Washed Out's Feel It All Around, the beat comes from a slowed-down Italo record: keep this idea of the whole sample as rhythm.
chillwave.sons: Hazy detuned synths are the signature: two oscillators 15 or 20 cents apart, thick chorus, a low-pass at 3 kHz, a 4-second reverb. The Juno-106 and its chorus are the model; Drift or Analog in Ableton imitate it well. The vocal is drowned: sung softly, doubled, in a long reverb and a delay, filtered at 5 kHz, often barely intelligible, with a slight pitch shift. Samples of forgotten pop or disco, slowed down, bring the nostalgia. Add an electric guitar with chorus and tremolo. Everything goes through a simulated cassette: hiss, wow, gentle saturation. The VHS aesthetic is not an effect, it is the material.
sourcesOutils: Logic Pro Help (Toro Y Moi, Glo-Fi, Chillwave production techniques)
chillwave.tempo: Between 85 and 110 BPM, with the feel of slowed-down 1980s pop. What changes compared to the rest of the family is the form: chillwave is song, verse and chorus, sung. The groove is straight, drum machine at 50% swing, but the whole track floats because the tempo itself wavers: a 0.3% cassette wow on the master makes pitch and time undulate. Program at 96 BPM, then add a cassette simulation with wow and flutter on the master bus. A disco or pop sample slowed down by 10 to 20% is a common starting point.

clickscuts.arrangement: The pieces last between four and nine minutes and don't follow the DJ structure. The form is often additive: a click pattern runs alone for 30 seconds, a sub appears, a texture comes in, then everything withdraws to leave a single click. There is no breakdown because there is never a full section. Work in 16-bar layers, but vary the lengths: a 5-sixteenth pattern against a 16-step one creates cycles that only realign after 80 steps. Vladislav Delay stretches slowly shifting pads over 15 minutes. Akufen, on the contrary, arranges like house, with a real drop. Decide first whether your piece is for the dance floor or for headphones.
clickscuts.basse: With Pole, the bass comes from dub: a round sine sub, two notes per bar, with a long dotted-eighth delay at 40% feedback that makes it bounce. With SND or Jelinek, the bass is almost absent or reduced to a very low drone, a sine at 45 Hz held over 4 bars with a slow tremolo. The common point: the bass never plays a dense rhythmic pattern, it leaves room for the clicks. 5 ms attack, 200 ms release, no harmonics above 200 Hz. A resonant low-pass filter in Auto Filter, cutoff at 120 Hz, resonance 20%, modulated very slowly, gives the underwater side. No sidechain: the bass floats under the clicks.
etapes: Build a bank of errors: cut samples without fades, reduce to 4 bits in Redux, keep the artifacts of a noise reducer pushed all the way.
Tempo 120 BPM, 60 ms sine kick on 1 and 3, clicks on irregular sixteenth notes, one empty eighth note per bar.
Add a two-note sub with a dotted-eighth dub delay, or a 45 Hz drone without a pattern.
Lay down three sines held between 200 Hz and 3 kHz as a spectral backdrop, panned to the extremes.
Layer a 5-step pattern against the 16-step grid and let it run for 80 steps before changing.
Mix with no compression on the clicks, an empty spectrum in the middle, a safety limiter at -1 dBFS.
clickscuts.mix: The mix is clinical. Every click must be audible in detail: no compression on the short elements, no reverb on them, except for a deliberate dub choice. The spectrum is empty between 300 Hz and 2 kHz, which is what gives the laboratory impression: sub at the bottom, clicks and sines at the top. High-pass at 2 kHz on the clicks, low-pass at 100 Hz on the sub. Extreme panning, 100% left or right, to create dialogues. Low overall level, -14 LUFS, with lots of dynamics. Watch out for real clicks that damage speakers: run the master through a limiter at -1 dBFS with no output gain. Export at 24 bits; this genre lives on low-level details.

outils.pourquoi: Oval's Markus Popp stores and replays his click libraries in it; buffers read without an envelope produce the clicks themselves.
Patches of impulses, pure sines and counters; the software laboratory of Raster-Noton and Frank Bretschneider.
Reduction to 4 bits without dither and downsampling: quantization noise becomes your snare.
Grid at 1/32, Chance at 30%, on an isolated click: random stutters that sound like a skipping CD.
Stefan Betke's broken filter, which gave Pole its name: its crackles make the rhythm of Tanzen.
Oval damaged discs with a marker and recorded the playback skips; the founding method of the genre.
The German sequencer of the Mille Plateaux era: sample-accurate edits, zoom in to the points and cut without fades.
Sine or Noise mode on a sub or a pad for discreet digital artifacts, in place of the broken filter.

reperes: Pole: Tanzen (1998): the crackle of a broken filter becomes rhythm, the bass is pure dub.
Jan Jelinek: Tendency (2001): jazz grains reduced to pops, a groove that seems to breathe.
Akufen: Deck The House (2002): hundreds of radio fragments arranged into danceable house.
Alva Noto: Xerrox Voyage (2020): the same digital material without rhythm, stretched into a pad.
clickscuts.rythme: The kick can be a short 60 ms sine or a DC click, a digital pop a few samples long. The snare is a fragment of error: a skipping CD, a dropout, a quantization noise. Make them yourself: take a sample, cut it right in the middle of a waveform without a fade; the resulting click is your material. Rhythmically, the loop stays in four but fragmented: kick on 1 and 3 only, clicks on irregular sixteenth notes, an empty eighth note in the middle. In Ableton, Beat Repeat with Grid at 1/32 and Chance at 30% generates stutters. Edit at the sample level: zoom in until you see the points and move the hits one by one.
clickscuts.sons: The raw material is digital error. Oval damaged CDs with a marker and recorded the skips. You can: reduce a sound to 4 bits in Redux without dither, cut samples without fades to create clicks, push a noise reducer all the way to hear only the artifacts, export a file at the wrong sample rate. Max/MSP and Reaktor are used to build patches that generate random impulses or modulated pure sines. A string of static harmonics, a few sines held between 200 Hz and 3 kHz, serves as a spectral backdrop. With Pole, a broken Waldorf filter produced crackles; Ableton's Erosion or Vinyl Distortion gives an approximation. No traditional synth, no presets.
sourcesOutils: Cycling '74 forums (Approaches to Composing Glitch Music using Max MSP)
Gearspace (Glitch Electronic music from late 90's / early 2000's, how did they do it?)
clickscuts.tempo: The tempo varies more than in microhouse: from 100 BPM for Pole's dub pieces to 130 for Akufen. The feel is often deliberately irregular: the grid exists, but some clicks fall off the grid, shifted by a few milliseconds or several samples, like read errors. Moderate swing, around 55%, or no swing at all and manual placements. With Villalobos, the tempo is slow, 122 BPM, but the groove comes from triplet percussion against the binary grid. A useful technique: program in sixteenth notes, then remove 20% of the notes at random. Silence is a rhythmic element in its own right.

coldwave.arrangement: Short song format, 3 to 4 minutes. Intro on the bass riff and the drum machine, 8 bars. Verse, chorus, verse, chorus, an instrumental bridge where the mono synth takes the melody, last chorus, dry ending or fade. No build-up, no breakdown: the drum machine never stops before the end. The sections are distinguished by instruments: the synth comes in on the chorus, the guitar drops out in the verse. Write the bass riff first, then the vocal melody, then the rest. Simplicity is the strength of the genre: three or four tracks are enough, and the poverty of means is the charm.
coldwave.basse: The electric bass is the main instrument. Played with a pick, in eighth notes, with a chorus (Boss CE-2 or Ableton's Chorus-Ensemble, rate 0.5 Hz, medium depth), it often carries the main melody rather than the harmony. The lines move: root, minor third, fifth, seventh, back and forth over two bars. It is mixed up front, almost at the level of the vocal. A light saturation (Overdrive at 5 dB) and 4:1 compression hold it. If you don't have a bass, a mono sawtooth synth with a filter at 800 Hz, played by hand without quantization, will do. Don't double it with a sub: the low end stays thin, on purpose.
etapes: At 126 BPM, load TR-606 or DR-55 samples and program a fixed pattern: kick, snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hat, with no fills at all.
Record or program an eighth-note bass with chorus, playing a two-bar melodic line.
Write an eight-note mono synth line on Analog in mono mode, sawtooth filtered at 800 Hz.
Sing a text in your own language, without vibrato, dry vocal with a 100 ms slapback.
Arrange a 3 minute 30 song: bass intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, synth bridge, chorus.
Group everything into four buses with tape saturation and cut at 12 kHz for the cassette grain.
coldwave.mix: A deliberately lo-fi mix. Group everything into four buses, as on a four-track: drums, bass, synths and guitar, vocal. Run each bus through a tape emulation or a gentle Saturator, then cut above 12 kHz. The mix is almost mono: bass and vocal in the center, synth slightly left, guitar slightly right. The vocal is dry, with a 100 ms slapback, no long reverb. The bass is loud, the drums set back. Little compression on the master, ratio 2:1. Add cassette hiss at minus 45 dB. Aim for minus 14 LUFS: the genre isn't after volume, but cold intimacy.

outils.pourquoi: Thin kick, a snare that cracks like a tick, eighth-note hi-hat, no fills: the clock of the genre. 606 or CR-78 samples are enough.
The 100-dollar drum machine of the French bands of 1982, four sounds and rigid presets, to be left running without touch-ups.
On the pick-played electric bass, rate 0.5 Hz, medium depth: the genre's main instrument, which often carries the melody.
The most widespread mono synth in the cold wave scene, for four- to eight-note lines in filtered sawtooth, no effects.
The other cheap mono of the era, a simple line that comes in on the chorus and drops out in the verse, a short delay at most.
The four-track cassette recorder as an instrument: hiss, tape compression, cut highs. In Ableton, Saturator in Analog Clip and a low-pass at 12 kHz.
The string machine for the chorus pads, or a Juno in strings mode with chorus. Arturia Solina V is its emulation.
In mono mode, sawtooth filtered at 800 Hz, played by hand without quantization: the native replacement for the cheap mono synth.

reperes: KaS Product: So Young But So Cold (1982): the rigid drum machine, the flat vocal, the mono synth up front.
Martin Dupont: Inside Out (1985): the chorused bass carrying the melody, the poor and charming recording.
Trisomie 21: The Last Song (1984): dry spleen, repetition without variation, the string machine in the choruses.
coldwave.rythme: A cheap drum machine, with its presets: Roland CR-78, TR-606, Boss DR-55, or an organ Rhythm Ace. Thin kick, a snare that cracks like a tick, eighth-note hi-hat. No fills, no variation: the pattern runs from start to finish. In Ableton, take 606 or DR-55 samples and barely process them, except for a Redux at 12 bits and a gentle tape saturation for the cassette grain. Sometimes a real drum kit plays on top, but then with the same rigidity. A Casio tambourine or clap can double the snare. The rhythm is a clock, nothing more.
coldwave.sons: A cheap monophonic synth: SH-101, MS-10, Korg MS-20, or Analog in mono mode. Simple four- or eight-note lines, filtered sawtooth, no effects apart from a short delay. A string machine (Solina, or a Juno in strings mode with chorus) for the chorus pads. A clean, high guitar, in arpeggios or block chords, with chorus and a bit of spring reverb. The vocal is flat, sung without vibrato, in your native language, a little detached. Four-track cassette recording is an instrument: in Ableton, a Saturator in Analog Clip mode on each track, a low-pass at 12 kHz and a bit of pink noise.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (thread First hardware synth for coldwave/darkwave/post-punk)
Treble Zine (Hold On to Your Genre: Coldwave / Minimal Wave)
NoiseGun (The Hidden Story of French Coldwave Music)
Wikipedia (Cold wave, Martin Dupont, KaS Product)
coldwave.tempo: Between 100 and 140 BPM, most often 120 to 130. The feel is that of a cheap drum machine holding the tempo without any nuance, with punk energy on top. No swing. What sets cold wave apart from the industrial it descends from: there are songs, verses, choruses, and a constant tempo. What sets it apart from neighboring darkwave: it is drier, faster, poorer in reverb. In your DAW, choose 126 BPM, quantize everything, but play the bass and the guitar by hand: the contrast between the rigid box and the human instruments is the heart of the sound.

cosmic.arrangement: A cosmic track is built like a DJ set: long, 8 to 10 minutes, without a drop, with soft transitions. Start with 32 bars of percussion and echoes, bring in the synth sequence, then the bass, then the kick at bar 33. The changes are echo feedback swells, filters opening, a percussion part coming in or going out. No chorus, no euphoric build-up: a hypnotic plateau that moves slowly. In the middle, a 16-bar dub-out where everything goes into the echo except the percussion. The ending dissolves by subtraction. Leave 32 bars of clean rhythm at each end for mixing.
cosmic.basse: The bass is often that of a slowed-down funk record: round, deep, with long notes that seem to drag. If you create it, play notes held for a quarter or a half note on the root, with an occasional glissando, on a virtual Moog with a low-pass filter at 200 Hz and a long 300 ms release. The rhythm is simple, one or two notes per bar, in the manner of dub. The bass and the kick share the bottom of the spectrum: cut the bass below 40 Hz and let the pitched kick occupy 50 to 80 Hz. A German synth line in slow eighth notes, in the spirit of the Berlin sequences, can replace the played bass.
etapes: Set 100 BPM with a 55% swing, import a funk or disco drum break and slow it down in Re-Pitch mode so it becomes deep.
Add sampled African percussion in loose sixteenth notes and send it into a tape echo with 40% feedback.
Write a round bass in held notes, one or two per bar, on a virtual Moog with a filter at 200 Hz.
Create a slow eighth-note arpeggio sequence on an analog synth, and let a low-pass filter move over 32 bars.
Build 9 minutes without a drop: gradual entrances, an echo dub-out in the middle, a final dissolution.
Tape-saturate the drum bus and the master, automate the echo feedback in the transitions.
cosmic.mix: The cosmic mix is warm and dirty. Tape saturation is everywhere, on the drum bus and on the master: a tape emulation with a bit of wow and flutter. The tape echoes have their feedback automated, up to self-oscillation during transitions. The slowed-down samples lose the top of their spectrum: don't try to recover it, add fresh percussion for brightness instead. Compress the drum bus at 3:1 with a slow attack to keep the transients. Leave the Afro percussion wide in stereo and the kick and bass in mono. Aim for modest loudness, -13 LUFS, with dynamics: slowness needs air.

outils.pourquoi: Daniele Baldelli's turntables, played at the wrong speed to slow down funk and German electronic music; an SL-1200 with the pitch at minus 8% gets close.
The tape echo on the percussion and the voices, feedback at 40% then into self-oscillation in the transitions; Roland Cloud offers an emulation.
Simpler in Re-Pitch mode to slow down a funk break while lowering its timbre, Echo in tape mode, and transpose automation for rewound-tape effects.
Baldelli's sampler, four seconds of memory, three units to hold twelve seconds of repeated phrases over the records.
The drum machine triggered in the booth over the slowed-down records, kick on 1 and 3, to hold the tempo between 90 and 110.
Congas, djembes, bells and shakers in loose sixteenth notes, for the brightness that the slowed-down samples have lost.
The tape emulation with wow and flutter on the drum bus and the master, for the dirty warmth and the drifting echoes.

reperes: Tullio De Piscopo: Stop Bajon (Primavera) (1984): deliberate slowness, the percussion and the round bass.
Casco: Cybernetic Love (1983): an Italo record that becomes cosmic as soon as you play it slower.
Daniele Baldelli: Cosmic Drag (2014): the founder producing himself what he used to play, echoes and slow sequences.
Prins Thomas: Fra Miami til Chicago (2019): the Norwegian version, hypnotic plateau and saturated tape.
cosmic.rythme: The cosmic rhythm section is a slowed-down disco or funk drum part, with a kick that becomes round and deep because of the pitch, and a snare that thickens. On top, African percussion: congas, djembes, shakers, bells, rototoms, in loose sixteenth notes. In your DAW, take a funk drum break and slow it down with warp turned off or in Re-Pitch mode so the timbre drops too. Add sampled percussion and run it through a tape echo (Ableton's Echo in tape mode, or an RE-201 emulation) with 40% feedback. Kick on all four beats, but not mandatory: a kick on 1 and 3 is sometimes enough.
cosmic.sons: Cosmic is made of records: funk, German electronic music, Italo, African music, all slowed down. The sounds that come out of it: tape echo everywhere, Afro percussion, slow and repetitive synth sequences, floating pads, voices pitched down that become strange. Rewound tapes and speed effects are tools: in your DAW, automate the transpose parameter of a Simpler or use a tape-stop type effect. The Roland RE-201 or its emulation is the central effect, with its drifting repeats. Take slow arpeggio sequences in the manner of Klaus Schulze or Space Art, and let them run with a filter moving over 32 bars.
sourcesOutils: Red Bull Music Academy (Daniele Baldelli lecture)
cosmic.tempo: Cosmic is slow: 90 to 110 BPM, often around 100. This tempo comes from a DJ practice: playing disco or Italo records meant for 120 or 130 at 33 rpm instead of 45, or with the pitch at its minimum. The feel is heavy, thick, hypnotic, with a slight human float because the original records were played by musicians. Set your project to 100 BPM and work with samples pitched down by 20 to 30%: that's where the low end and the slowness appear. A 55% swing on the sixteenth notes helps. The signature is not a pattern, it is a slowness that transforms everything it touches.

crossbreed.arrangement: A crossbreed track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and follows a DnB form with double drops. 32-bar intro: drone, percussion, an isolated hardcore kick that sets the tone. 8-bar build-up with a roll. First 32-bar drop in neuro two-step with bass. Switch at bar 33 of the drop: hardcore 4/4 kick for 16 bars, then both together for 16 bars. 32-bar breakdown with vocals and drone. Second drop that starts straight on the 4/4 kick, then moves to two-step. 32-bar outro. The hardcore DJ and the DnB DJ must both be able to mix the same record: keep a clear intro and outro.
crossbreed.basse: The hardcore kick already fills the low end with its tuned tail, so the bass has to work around it. The neuro basses from the brief: a resampled Reese or an FM bass from Serum, high-passed at 120 Hz, playing in the midrange during the two-step passages, and falling silent or holding a note during the 4/4 kick passages. Tune the hardcore kick to the track's root (for example a kick whose tail sounds in F) and have the bass play the same note or the fifth. A sine sub can fill in under the two-step, but cut it as soon as the hardcore kick arrives: the two together clog everything. Heavy sidechain, 8:1 ratio, from the kick onto the bass.
etapes: Set Ableton to 178 BPM. Program a hardened neuro two-step over 4 bars, then a 4/4 kick over 4 bars, in two clips.
Create the hardcore kick in Operator (3-octave pitch envelope over 30 ms, 400 ms decay), then Saturator and Overdrive, tuned to F.
Create a resampled Serum bass, cut at 120 Hz, that plays over the two-step and falls silent over the 4/4 kick.
Add an industrial screech, impacts, a drone and a sampled shouted vocal.
Arrange a 32-bar intro, 8-bar build-up, a drop of 32 bars two-step then 16 bars 4/4 kick then 16 together, a 32-bar breakdown, a reversed second drop, a 32-bar outro.
Clip the drum bus and the master, limiter after that, and check the kick tail at the end.
crossbreed.mix: The loudness production from the brief: crossbreed is mixed to be the loudest record of the night. The hardcore kick is the loudest thing in the track and it is clipped even before the master. The snare is just below it. The basses are high-passed at 120 Hz and compressed by band (Multiband Dynamics, 4:1 ratio on the mids). Sidechain everything except the kick. A clipper on the drum bus, another on the master, then a limiter: aim for -4 to -5 LUFS. The low end is mono, the rest wide. Check that the hardcore kick does not lose its tuned tail going through the limiter: if it disappears, turn down the bass, not the kick.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the PRSPCT scene: neuro breaks at 175, resampled gabber kicks, everything as audio for loudness production.
Modulated, resampled neuro basses, serial filter and audio export, as in hard drum and bass.
The synth Katharsys and The Outside Agency used in the early 2010s for moving basses and leads.
The starting kick, lengthened and distorted into the gabber kick, then resampled into a single hit.
On the kick and the bass: multiband distortion after Overdrive and Saturator for a hardcore kick that keeps its low end.
OTT on the neuro bass and band compression on the drum bus, to hold the loudness without losing the sub.
Sine sub that follows the bass, and a fast pitch envelope to synthesize a kick when the 909 is not enough.
Digital Clip on the kick before Roar, Analog Clip on the breaks bus, to harden the DnB to hardcore level.

reperes: The Outside Agency: Motherfucking Ants (2011): the hardcore kick coming in under the two-step, the canonical example of the crossover.
Katharsys: Zero (2012): the neuro bass and the gabber kick in the same drop, the French school of crossbreed.
The Outside Agency & Current Value: They Are Human (2011): the master of darkstep and the master of industrial hardcore, the junction in one track.
Sinister Souls: Beat the Drum Hard (2012): kick rolls and two-step alternation, the PRSPCT sound.
crossbreed.rythme: Two drum kits in one. The first is a hardened DnB two-step: short, dry kick, stacked, cracking snare, sixteenth-note hi-hats, as in neurofunk. The second is the hardcore kick: a 909 with its decay pushed to 400 ms, run through Overdrive or Roar until the tail becomes a distorted note, played in 4/4. In the drop, alternate: 4 bars of two-step, 4 bars of 4/4 kick, then both together, the hardcore kick on the beats and the break on top. Add metallic percussion, saturated rides, and kick rolls (sixteenth-note kicks) on the last bar before a change.
crossbreed.sons: The brief cites Ableton Live, Massive and Serum: the same kit as neurofunk, plus the gabber kick. The kick is made in Operator (sine with a 3-octave pitch envelope over 30 ms, 400 ms decay), then into a Saturator, Overdrive, EQ chain to emphasize 100 Hz and 2 kHz. The basses come from Serum with resampling. Add industrial hardcore screeches (a square wave with resonance maxed out, pitched high), shouted vocals or war film samples, metallic drones, and impacts. The Outside Agency uses a lot of filtered white noise in build-ups and industrial "stabs". No melody: textures and impacts.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable chapter)
crossbreed.tempo: Crossbreed is played between 175 and 180 BPM, a little above DnB, so the hardcore kicks keep their violence. What sets it apart from breakcore is order: the bars are square, in 4/4, and the track is made to be mixed. The feel alternates two engines within the same track: neurofunk two-step passages (kick on 1 and the "and" of 3, snare on 2 and 4), and gabber 4/4 kick passages, often inside the same drop, in blocks of 4 or 8 bars. No swing. The tension comes from this switch between the break and the hammer.

darkambient.arrangement: Pieces of 8 to 15 minutes, often conceived as an album that tells the story of a place. The form is in plateaus: three or four successive states, each 2 to 4 minutes long, joined by 1 to 2 minute crossfades. The background never stops: unlike lowercase, total silence does not exist here. One rare event (impact, distant voice, door) every two or three minutes is enough to hold attention. No build-up to a peak: the track sinks rather than rises. Open with the drone alone, add the resonances, then remove everything but the sub to finish. Twin Flames shows that a voice can come in without breaking the contract.
darkambient.basse: The bass is the low drone, and it dominates everything. Aim for 30 to 60 Hz: A0 or E1. A sine for weight, plus a sawtooth low-passed at 120 Hz for body, with a very slow pitch modulation of 5 cents. Two oscillators detuned by 3 to 7 Hz produce a slow beating that makes the room vibrate, the Lustmord effect. A layer an octave up with light saturation (Saturator, 6 dB drive) helps you hear the sub on small speakers. No kick, no sidechain, but watch the level: a sub held at -12 dB RMS eats all the headroom. Unlike bright ambient, the low end here is not a discreet pedal tone, it is the subject of the track.
etapes: Record or download the sound of a real space (parking garage, cellar, stairwell) and stretch it 20 times with Paulstretch: that is your background.
Create a sub drone: a sine at 41 Hz (E1) plus a sawtooth filtered at 120 Hz, two voices detuned by 5 Hz, at -12 dB.
Take a metallic sample, run it through Granulator II with long grains and slow playback, then into a convolution reverb with a cistern IR.
Place a dull impact roughly every 30 seconds, each with a 15-second reverb, and let the tails overlap.
Automate very slow free LFOs on the filters and pans, then arrange three plateaus over 10 minutes joined by one-minute crossfades.
Mix with the low end in mono, a high-pass on the reverbs, and a final level around -18 LUFS.
darkambient.mix: The low end is the danger. Everything below 120 Hz in mono, a high-pass at 100 Hz on every reverb return, and a single element occupying the sub. The Attack book points out that in a layered drone, low sounds are mixed louder than high ones, but each layer must have its own frequency zone. Don't chase loudness: -18 LUFS, -1 dB peak, slow bus compression (30 ms attack, 1 s release, 2:1 ratio). Tape saturation or Roar on the bus adds harmonics that make the sub audible on headphones. Test on a subwoofer and on cheap earbuds: if the track disappears on the latter, bring up the octave layer.

outils.pourquoi: To capture cellars, parking garages and stairwells, the raw material of the genre since Lustmord's Heresy was recorded in underground spaces. High gain, XY mic, keep the hiss.
Extreme, free stretching: the sound of a real space stretched 20 to 50 times becomes a continuous background. Factor 30, long window size, then a high-pass at 40 Hz.
Convolution section that accepts your own impulse responses of cisterns or caves; Audio Ease Altiverb does the same with its bank of real spaces.
Free infinite reverb tails, on a send for the impacts spaced 30 seconds apart, with a high-pass at 100 Hz on the return so the sub does not drown.
Slow granulation of a metallic sample: long grains, nearly static playback, position spray; the result then goes into the convolution reverb.
Atrium Carceri and raison d'être build their textures on modular; a Morphagene or a Mutable Instruments Clouds granulates and freezes any source into a drone.
For synthetic drones: noisy wavetables swept by hand, two voices detuned by 5 Hz below 120 Hz, a sine at 41 Hz to reinforce the sub.
Saturation on the bus to create harmonics that make the sub audible on headphones and small speakers, light drive, multiband mode on the low end only.

reperes: Lustmord: Heresy Part I (1990): the reverb of real underground places as an instrument, the sub vibrating under everything.
Raison D'Etre: Prospectus I (1993): crypt resonances and distant choirs, the sacred side of the genre.
Lustmord: Black Star (1994): the drone spreading out in plateaus, almost no attack, time abolished.
Atrium Carceri: The Untold (2003): cinematic dark ambient, with impacts and object noises that tell the story of a place.
darkambient.rythme: No regular percussion. What structures time is isolated impacts: a dull thud every 20 to 40 seconds, a drip, a dragging chain, metal slowed to half speed. Field recordings in basements, parking garages or cisterns serve as the backdrop: Lustmord recorded Heresy in real underground spaces. A simple technique: take a metallic percussion sample, put it in Granulator II with 200 to 500 ms grains, a little spray and a playback position that advances very slowly. You get a texture that scrapes without ever hitting. Each impact goes through a 15 to 20 second reverb, and its tail becomes the background of the track.
darkambient.sons: The brief gives the modular, the field recorder and the granulator. The basic tools: a convolution reverb with impulse responses of real spaces (Ableton's Hybrid Reverb accepts your own IRs, look for cisterns or caves), Valhalla Supermassive for infinite tails, Paulstretch to stretch a sample 20 to 50 times, Granulator II for slow granulation. A -24 semitone pitch-shift on a voice or a choir gives crypt resonances. Pink noise filtered by a slow Auto Filter becomes wind. Reverb freeze turns any sound into a drone. In the modular or Serum, noisy wavetables swept by hand. Everything is dark, nothing is clean.
