sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone and Movement & Change chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone chapter)
Gearspace (forum), Let's talk dark ambient / industrial / neoclassical
darkambient.tempo: Still no tempo, but time moves even more slowly than in classic ambient: a drone that takes 45 seconds to rise, one event every two minutes. If you set a BPM, take 50 to 60, only so the delays land right. The big difference from the parent genre is the absence of melodic events: nothing sings, everything rumbles. Movement comes from free, unsynced LFOs at 0.03 or 0.05 Hz (a period of 20 to 30 seconds), on the filter, pitch and pan. Since no cycle ever lines up with another, nothing ever repeats exactly. Listen to Heresy: the sense of time comes from the reverb of the space, not from a pulse.

darkcore.arrangement: A darkcore track lasts 6 minutes and plays on anticipation. 32-bar intro: pad alone, then fragments of break that appear and disappear, a dialogue sample. First entry of the full break and the sub at bar 33, with no build-up, almost cold. Then 32-bar sections where only one element changes at a time. The middle of the track is a long breakdown where the break disappears and the pad rises a semitone, as in Valley of the Shadows. The last third adds the 909 kick under the break for the final weight. The ending is brutal: a cut on a vocal sample, or a fade of the pad alone over 8 bars.
darkcore.basse: The darkcore sub is menacing because it moves little and goes low. A sine or a triangle from Operator, between 35 and 50 Hz, played in long notes of one or two bars, with a slight glide between two notes a descending fourth or fifth apart. It is the opposite of the bouncing dub sub of hardcore. A second layer, a square wave low-passed at 200 Hz, follows the same note but with a 30 ms attack and light distortion, so the bass can be heard on small systems. The break's kick sits above this sub in the spectrum: filter the kick around 60 Hz and leave the sub below.
etapes: Set Ableton to 155 BPM. Import an Amen or Think break, warp in Beats mode, short Loop Back, and listen to the artifacts appear.
Split the break into two tracks: the full break, and kick and snare slices replayed for doublings.
Create an Operator sub around 40 Hz in long notes with glide, and a second square wave filtered at 200 Hz, lightly saturated.
Lay down a minor pad on Analog (two detuned saws) and automate the cutoff over 8 bars.
Sample two film dialogues, pitch -5, 4 s reverb, and place them in the intro and the breakdown.
Arrange in 32-bar blocks, add the 909 kick in the last third, and finish with a clean cut.
darkcore.mix: Everything should sound heavy and veiled. The break goes through a low-pass filter at 8 kHz with light resonance, then through a slow compressor (30 ms attack, 300 ms release, 3:1 ratio) to round it off, the opposite of bright hardcore. The pads get a 6-second reverb with a 40 ms pre-delay, at -12 dB under the break. The sub stays mono, untreated, and it is the only uncompressed element. Tape saturation on the main bus (Saturator in Soft Sine, Drive 4 dB) takes off the edge. Aim for -9 LUFS, and accept a master quieter than average: darkcore sounds loud because it is dark, not because it is limited.

outils.pourquoi: Breaks pitched down and slowed voices: its 12-bit conversion is what darkened the hardcore of winter 1992.
The 8-bit tracker of London bedrooms: you type the breaks column by column, which gives the dry chopping of the Reinforced era.
Kick and snare placed under the break so the track holds up in a rave; 909 samples or D16 Drumazon today.
The MIDI sequencer of better-equipped studios, to sync the sampler, the 909 and the pad synth.
Held minor pads, third and fifth without the root, filter opened slowly over 8 bars; Ableton Analog or TAL-U-NO-LX do the same job.
12 bits and downsampling on the break to veil the cymbals and get back the dirty grain of the Akai.
On the drum bus after Redux, to weld the pitched break and the 909 kick into a single dark mass.
Menacing sine sub under the break, with a second square wave filtered at 200 Hz, lightly saturated.

reperes: 4hero: Mr Kirk's Nightmare (1990): the death announcement sample and the heavy break, the birth certificate of the dark side.
Rufige Kru: Terminator (1992): time-stretch as an effect, stretched and grinding voices, Goldie invents a sound by abusing a function.
Origin Unknown: Valley Of The Shadows (1993): the “long dark tunnel” dialogue, the rising pad, the sub holding everything.
Doc Scott: Here Come the Drumz (1992): the transition to jungle, doubled breaks and sampled brass stabs.
darkcore.rythme: The break is time-stretched on the Akai S950: instead of transposing it to fit the tempo, you stretch it, which creates grain and metallic artifacts on the cymbals. In Ableton, warping in Beats mode with Transient Loop Mode set to Loop Back and a short Transient Envelope reproduces the effect; in Complex or Texture mode, you get a more watery blur, typical of Goldie. Program the break in two layers: a full version for the body, and short cuts (kick alone, snare alone) replayed to create doublings. Add a TR-909: kick as reinforcement on beat 1 and on the "and" of 3, sparse sixteenth-note rimshots, ride crash cymbal on the changes.
darkcore.sons: Pads replace pianos. A held minor chord, often a minor third and a fifth without the root, played on a Juno or on Analog with two detuned sawtooths, low-pass filter opened slowly over 8 bars. On top, horror film samples: dialogue, screams, breaths, creaking doors, loaded into Simpler with a long reverb (4 s) and a pitch of -5 semitones. The brief cites the Commodore Amiga: trackers like OctaMED gave a grainy 8-bit sound that you can get back with Redux (Bit Depth 8, no downsample). Add a voice pitched down rather than up, a single repeated word, and a brass stab sampled from a soundtrack record.
darkcore.tempo: Darkcore keeps the tempo of 1992 hardcore but pushes it: 150 to 160 BPM, the zone where the break starts running on its own. The feel changes completely: where hardcore bounces, darkcore glides. The breaks are no longer pitched up but time-stretched, sometimes pitched down, which gives them a dragging, cold quality. No continuous 4/4 kick under the break: it appears in sections, for weight. Count in bars of 4 but think in blocks of 32: the pads change slowly, the breaks quickly. The contrast between the two speeds is the heart of the style.

darkdisco.arrangement: A dark disco track is a DJ tool: 6 to 7 minutes, on a plateau. 32-bar intro with kick, hi-hats and bass, then the toms at bar 17. Main section of 32 to 48 bars where the riff loops and the synths come in one by one. 16-bar breakdown in the middle: the kick stops, the bass remains along with a delay whose feedback rises, a spoken vocal passes through. The return happens without a massive drop, just the kick coming back with a tom. Second section, 32-bar outro. There is no chorus and no euphoric build-up: the tension comes from what enters and what remains, and from the hypnosis of the riff.
darkdisco.basse: The bass is often played on an electric bass or on a Korg MS-20, then processed: saturation, chorus, heavy compression. The riff is in eighth or sixteenth notes with held notes, in minor, over two or four bars, and it almost never changes. A typical pattern: root repeated in eighth notes, a minor seventh on the "and" of 4, back again. The MS-20 sound: sawtooth, low-pass filter at 400 Hz with resonance, a little glide. On an electric bass, play with a pick, compress at 6:1 with a fast attack, then chorus and amp saturation. It doubles the kick on the beats and fills the offbeats, closer to rock than to funk.
etapes: Set 120 BPM with no swing, load 808 samples into a Drum Rack with a Drum Buss for weight.
Program the kick on the beats, clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hats with an open one on the offbeats, 808 toms in eighth notes at the end of the bar.
Record or program an eighth-note bass riff on a virtual MS-20 or an electric bass, in minor, then saturate, compress at 6:1 and add a chorus.
Add an acid MS-20 lead, a Juno pad in minor chords, a spoken vocal with a dotted-quarter delay at 50% feedback.
Build 6 minutes on a plateau: 32-bar intro, main section, breakdown without kick with a rising delay, return without a drop, outro.
Mix dark: soften the highs, saturate the drum bus and the bass, long reverbs on sends, low end in mono.
darkdisco.mix: The dark disco mix is dark and heavy. The kick and the bass share the low end: kick at 50 Hz, bass cut below 45 Hz and saturated so it exists in the 100 to 300 Hz range. The hi-hats are softened, pull everything above 10 kHz down by one or two dB. The toms get a short reverb. The synths and vocals go into long delays and 4-second reverbs, on sends. Saturate the drum bus and the bass with a tape emulation or a Saturator in analog clip mode. Compress the master at 2:1 with a bus compressor. Keep the low end in mono, open the delays very wide. Aim for -9 LUFS.

outils.pourquoi: Acid, nasal bass and lead: sawtooth, low-pass at 400 Hz with resonance, a little glide; the MS-20 mini or the Korg Collection can replace it.
The round, slightly long kick, the dry saturated clap and the tribal eighth-note toms; today TR-8S, Roland Cloud TR-808 or D16 Nepheton 2.
Cold pads in minor chords, reduced chorus, and eighth-note arpeggios over one octave, inherited from cold wave.
The virtual Juno for pads and arpeggios; Ableton Analog will do for the MS-20 style lead if you have no Korg emulation.
Long delays at a quarter note or dotted quarter with 50% feedback, on sends for the synths, vocals and guitars.
The 4 to 6 second reverbs that carve out the dark space, on sends, with the delays opened very wide.
The bass played with a pick then processed: 6:1 compression, chorus and amp saturation, a riff that almost never changes.
Drum Buss for the weight of the 808s, Saturator in analog clip mode on the bass and the drum bus, toms moving in the stereo field.

reperes: Pardon Moi: Power To The People (Damon Jee Remix) (2017): the founding track, chug bass and cold synths with no build-up.
Darlyn Vlys: Modelo 303 (2020): the hypnotic plateau and the recurring 808 toms.
Red Axes: Sun My Sweet Sun (2020): the reverberated guitar and the spoken vocal over a steady chug.
Damon Jee: Revolte (2022): the processed bass riff, heavy and saturated, at 120 BPM.
darkdisco.rythme: A TR-808 clone holds the kick, round and a little long, on all four beats. The snare or clap on 2 and 4 is dry, often an 808 with a little saturation. The hi-hats are closed eighth notes, with an open one on the offbeat of 2 and 4 for drive. The 808 toms play eighth-note patterns on the second half of the bar, and they come back often: that is the tribal color of the genre. A shaker or cabasa in sixteenth notes, a rimshot on offbeats. In your DAW, a Drum Rack of 808 samples with Drum Buss for weight, and toms that move in the stereo field.
darkdisco.sons: The synths are cold, inherited from cold wave: an acid, nasal MS-20 lead, Juno-106 pads in minor chords with no chorus or little, eighth-note arpeggios over one octave. The vocals are spoken, low, reverberated, sometimes in French or German. Guitars with lots of delay and reverb, played in single notes. Long delays, at a quarter note or dotted quarter with 50% feedback, and 4 to 6 second reverbs create the dark space. Today: a virtual Korg MS-20 or Ableton Analog, TAL-U-NO-LX, Ableton's Echo and Hybrid Reverb, and an 808 clone for the rhythm section.
sources: Beatportal, A Guide to Dance Music's Devious New Genre, Dark Disco (beatportal.com)
darkdisco.tempo: Dark disco is a chug: 115 to 125 BPM, most tracks between 118 and 122. The feel is heavy and steady, no swing, or 52% at most. Set 120 BPM. The difference from indie dance is not the tempo but the absence of a euphoric build-up: the track moves forward on a plateau, hypnotic, dark, with no exploding chorus. The rhythmic signature is a four-on-the-floor with pounding eighth-note percussion, toms, and a bass that repeats a minor riff for the whole duration. Think of a slow train: everything pushes in the same direction, nothing takes off.

darkelectro.arrangement: Count on 5 to 7 minutes, with a long intro: 30 seconds of pad, samples and whispered voice before the first kick. Song structure: whispered verse, chorus with the lead melody and sometimes a more shouted voice, second verse, chorus, then an instrumental bridge where the pad and the arpeggio loop alone for 16 bars. Transitions are made with reverb: cut the kick and let the tails fill 2 bars before bringing it back. The ending returns to the intro: pad alone, last sample. The slowness of the setup is essential. The track should feel like a cold room closing in.
darkelectro.basse: A minor arpeggio in sixteenth notes, rather than a repeated note. On a JP-8000 or on Wavetable, a sawtooth with a low-pass filter at 600 Hz that opens slowly over 8 bars. The typical pattern descends: root, fifth, minor third, minor second, which gives the shiver. In the low register, around A1. No heavy saturation: the bass should stay round and a little sad, unlike aggrotech, which would later make it scream. Gentle sidechain from the kick, 2 dB. You can double the arpeggio with a sine sub layer on the root, held in half notes, to ground the whole thing.
etapes: At 128 BPM, program a short 909 kick and a thin snare with a 3-second reverb filtered at 3 kHz. Sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Write a descending minor arpeggio in sixteenth notes on Wavetable or a JP-8000, filter at 600 Hz opening over 8 bars.
Create a sawtooth pad with chorus and an 8-second reverb, on two minor chords.
Record a whispered voice, then Overdrive 15 dB, 10:1 compression, formant lowered by a whole tone.
Add three medical or film samples, placed off the grid, in the intro and the bridge.
Arrange over 6 minutes with a 30-second intro without kick and a 16-bar instrumental bridge.
darkelectro.mix: Clean up the low mids: cut between 200 and 400 Hz on the pads and the voice, to let the bass arpeggio breathe. The distorted whispered voice is dangerous in the highs: a de-esser and a cut at 9 kHz calm it down. Dark reverbs everywhere, low-pass at 3 or 4 kHz on the returns, otherwise the mix turns to mush. The kick stays dry, centered, the only element with no space. The pads open wide. Moderate master compression, 2:1 ratio. Aim for -10 LUFS. The coldness comes from the contrast between a dull kick and everything else drowned: keep that contrast sharp.

outils.pourquoi: The descending minor arpeggio in sixteenth notes, sawtooth, filter at 600 Hz opening over eight bars. Roland Cloud JP-8000 reproduces it.
Icy sawtooth pads, wide chorus, filter at 2 kHz, and four-note leads with a glass sound: the synth of Zoth Ommog and Off Beat.
The sequencer of the 1990s German scene, where medical samples sit off the grid while the kick stays metronomic.
The half-rack multi-effect cited by harsh EBM producers to lower the pitch and formant of a whispered voice by a whole tone, before the distortion.
Multiband distortion on the murmured voice: saturate the mids, leave the highs alone, which the course's 15 dB Overdrive does more brutally.
White noise carrier, a little distortion after it: the whispered voice becomes a menacing breath, a technique shared on the scene's forums.
The native equivalent of the JP-8000 for the bass arpeggio, with a gentle 2 dB sidechain from the kick and a sub layer in half notes.
Synthetic sine kick with a 40 ms pitch envelope, dry and with no reverb, plus the FM bells of the minor melodies.

reperes: yelworC: Trinity (1992): icy pads, the murmured, distorted voice, the dry kick in the middle.
Wumpscut: Soylent Green (1993): the film sample as a hook, the minor arpeggio, the cold room.
Suicide Commando: Hellraiser (2000): the transition toward the dancefloor, a more present kick, a more assertive melody.
darkelectro.rythme: A drier, tighter kick than in the parent genre: a short 909 with no reverb, or a synthetic kick on Operator (sine, 40 ms pitch envelope). A thin snare with a long, dark reverb, 3 seconds, low-passed at 3 kHz: that is what creates the autopsy room. Sixteenth-note hi-hats, alternating velocities of 100 and 50, very clean. Few extra percussion sounds; instead, rare glitches and clicks. The pattern barely varies over the whole track. A few kicks doubled as thirty-second notes before the choruses are enough as a lift. The rhythm is a skeleton, everything else is cold flesh.
darkelectro.sons: The voice is whispered, then distorted: record it as a murmur, 10 cm from the mic, then Overdrive at 15 dB, 10:1 compression, formant lowered by a whole tone with a pitch shifter. The result is intimate and menacing. The pads are icy: Nord Lead or JP-8000 sawtooth with wide chorus, filter at 2 kHz, 8-second reverb. The lead melodies are minor and simple, four notes, with a glass or FM bell sound. Medical or horror film samples punctuate: heart monitor, artificial respiration, a doctor's phrase. Every sound has reverb, except the kick.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (thread What are you guys harsh EBM guys doing for vocals)
KVR Audio (threads Vocal Effects Industrial/Harsh EBM and VST and DAW for dark electro/aggrotech)
darkelectro.tempo: Between 120 and 140 BPM, straight, metronomic, no swing. Some tracks drop toward 100 for the liturgical passages. Compared with electro-industrial, the rhythm simplifies and stiffens: fewer syncopations, more icy regularity. The atmosphere does not come from the groove but from the sounds. In your DAW, start at 128 BPM, full quantization, and focus your effort on the synths and the voice. A trick: keep the kick perfectly regular and let all the irregularity come from noise samples placed off the grid, a slamming door, a medical instrument, a breath.

darkpsy.arrangement: No drop in the full-on sense. An intro of 16 to 32 bars sets up kick, bass and a texture. Then the track moves forward in sections of 16 or 24 bars, each bringing a micro-event: a vocal sample, a change in bass pattern (triplets to sixteenths), a percussion fill. The breakdowns are short, 4 to 8 bars, and brutal: the kick disappears, a granular texture alone, and the kick returns with no build-up. Some tracks have a long breakdown in the middle, with a film monologue. Aim for 8 minutes. For playability, keep 32 bars of intro and outro with a stable kick and bass, because the DJ will be mixing in the dark.
darkpsy.basse: The twisted triplet bass from the brief: kick on the first triplet of each beat, bass on the other two, each note 50 ms long. The sound starts from a square wave or a sawtooth on a Virus or FM8, with clear distortion in the low mids (around 200 to 500 Hz) that gives the grinding side, and a low-pass filter whose envelope opens very fast. Alternate triplet bars and sixteenth-note bars to create the twist. Add pitch variations: a note a semitone up every 4 beats, or a descending glide at the end of the phrase. Root in F# or G, but the bass moves more than in classic psytrance. Separate the sub, a clean sine, from the grit.
etapes: Project at 155 BPM. Make a short kick in Operator (pitch 150 down to 65 Hz, 90 ms decay) with a noise click.
Write the triplet bass on F#1: kick on the first triplet, bass on the other two, 50 ms notes, square sound distorted around 300 Hz.
Add a rimshot on 2 and 4, irregular sixteenth-note hi-hats and three triplet micro-percussion parts with random velocities.
Program a grinding FM8 patch with a non-integer ratio and feedback, play sixteenth-note blips into a short ping-pong delay.
Stretch a vocal sample in Granulator or Absynth, filter it with a random LFO, place it in the background.
Arrange 8 minutes in 16-bar sections with brutal 4-bar breakdowns, no build-ups, stable intro and outro.
darkpsy.mix: Darkpsy is mixed tight and dry: little reverb, short filtered delays, all the low end centered and mono. The kick and the bass share a bus with a fast compressor and light saturation. Since the kick is short, the bass can be louder than in full-on, with a peak around 300 Hz for the grit. High-pass at 250 Hz on everything else. Textures go to the sides, with a stereo utility, but stay below the kick in level. No crushing limiter: the genre wants clean transients, aim for -7 to -8 LUFS with a fast limiter. Check that the micro-percussion stays audible on a festival system by listening at low volume.

outils.pourquoi: The broken machine sound: a modulator at a non-integer ratio like 2.37 and high feedback. Twisted basses and metallic blips come straight out of it.
Anxiety-inducing granular pads: a stretched voice or metal sample, filtered by a random LFO, under the kick at 155 BPM.
Square or sawtooth bass with distortion in the low mids; darkpsy Serum and Virus banks circulate among producers.
Historical DAW of the Russian and German darkpsy scene; tight editing of the bass triplets and the offset fills.
For the current generation, it replaces FM8 for the bass: FM between oscillators, clear distortion, very fast filter envelope.
The dry darkpsy kick: sine, pitch from 150 down to 65 Hz in 15 ms, 90 ms body, 5 ms noise click added alongside.
Micro-percussion and grinding textures from horror film samples; Corpus completes it for metallic resonances.

reperes: Kindzadza: Born to Grit (2023): current darkpsy, precise, with bass patterns that change every 8 bars.
Absolum: Inside the Sphere (2002): the twist between triplets and sixteenth notes, and FM textures very far forward.
Xenomorph: Hallucinatory Spheres (1998): proto-darkpsy, horror samples and black humor, to understand the spirit.
Tristan: Mind Over Matter (1999): the speed and dryness of the kick, before the genre had a name.
darkpsy.rythme: The darkpsy kick is dry, short, tailless: a click and a body of 80 ms maximum, tuned high, around 65 to 70 Hz, because at 155 BPM a long tail would turn the low end to mush. Make it in Operator: sine, pitch from 150 down to 65 Hz in 15 ms, 90 ms decay, click added with a 5 ms noise transient. Thin, dry snare on 2 and 4, often replaced by a rimshot or a metallic noise sample. The hi-hats play irregular sixteenth notes, with gaps. The percussion is micro-sounds: drips, clicks, crackles, placed in triplets and sixteenth notes with random velocities. Program 1-beat fills every 4 bars that land off.
darkpsy.sons: Absynth and FM8 are the historical tools, and they do exactly what is needed: metallic FM textures, grinding noises, synthetic voices that seem to speak. An FM8 patch with a modulator at a non-integer ratio (2.37 for example) and high feedback gives the broken machine sound. Absynth is for anxiety-inducing granular pads: a stretched voice or metal sample, filtered by a random LFO. Short horror film samples go through a filter delay and a downward pitch shifter. Leads are rare and short: more like resonant sixteenth-note blips bouncing in a ping-pong delay. In Ableton, Granulator and Corpus complete the palette.
sourcesOutils: KVR Audio, Sound Design forum (darkpsy and hi-tech FM leads)
Bandcamp, Gnosis Darkpsy and Hitech pack for Serum and FM8
darkpsy.tempo: Darkpsy starts where full-on stops: 148 BPM minimum, most tracks between 150 and 158, some at 160 and above. At this speed, the rolling sixteenth-note bass becomes a vibration: that is why the genre uses a lot of triplet patterns, kick then two triplet notes, which breathe better. No swing. What also changes is the relationship to the cycle: darkpsy likes 3- or 6-beat patterns laid over 4/4, and phrases that don't land where you expect them. The track doesn't build to a drop, it drifts: each section is a room in an 8 to 10 minute labyrinth.

darkstep.arrangement: A darkstep track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and works by accumulation. 32-bar intro: horror drone, whispers, an isolated kick that drops now and then, a snare that starts to run. Drop at bar 33: saturated Amen, doubled kicks, Reese, all at once, over 64 bars, with elements accumulating every 16 (a second snare, a screech, a roll). 16-bar breakdown, short, with the drone and a scream. Second 64-bar drop, even denser, with the bass more distorted. 32-bar outro that leaves the drone alone. The track should feel like it never catches its breath.
darkstep.basse: The distorted basses from the brief: a Reese, as in the Reese chapter of the Attack Magazine book (two oscillators detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide), but pushed further than in techstep: serial distortion (Overdrive then Saturator Digital Clip then Roar), resampling, and a fast LFO (eighth note) on the filter that makes it growl. It plays long notes on the root, with descending glides of a fifth at the end of phrases, and short accents on the doubled kicks. A separate sine sub, mono, below 60 Hz. The doubled kick is short and sits above 80 Hz. Sidechain the Reese from the kick at a 6:1 ratio, 40 ms release, so the hammering gets through.
etapes: Set Ableton to 180 BPM. Program a two-step, then double each kick one sixteenth note after it.
Import an Amen, warp in Beats mode, Overdrive 60%, and play it in bursts: 2 full bars, 1/32 cuts, silence.
Create a Reese (two saws detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide) and run it through Overdrive, Saturator Digital Clip and Roar, then resample.
Add an eighth-note LFO on the Reese filter, a mono sine sub, and a 6:1 sidechain from the kick.
Sample a horror drone, whispers and a scream, pitched down, 8 s reverb.
Arrange a 32-bar intro, a 64-bar drop accumulating every 16, a 16-bar breakdown, a second 64-bar drop, a 32-bar outro, master at -6 LUFS with a clipper.
darkstep.mix: The darkstep mix is dirty, dense and dark, the opposite of neurofunk. The breaks bus is saturated and compressed hard (10:1 ratio, 0.5 ms attack, 30 ms release). The doubled kicks are clipped. The Reese occupies the entire midrange, from 100 Hz to 4 kHz, with an EQ that scoops 500 Hz to let the snare through. The sub is mono, alone below 80 Hz. The atmospheres are wide and in the back, with a long reverb and a high-pass at 400 Hz. A general low-pass filter at 12 kHz removes the shine: darkstep is not bright. Master at -6 LUFS, with a clipper before the limiter, and a little tape saturation to weld everything together.

outils.pourquoi: Sped-up, saturated Amen, doubled kicks and horror film atmospheres sampled on the Position Chrome records.
The hostile starting Reese, two saws detuned in opposite directions, mono with glide, before the distortion chain.
The sequencer Panacea and Technical Itch used in the late 1990s for breaks in bursts at 180 BPM.
Modern Reese with a fast eighth-note LFO on the filter that makes it growl, then resampling.
First distortion in the chain on the Reese as audio, before Saturator and Roar.
Digital Clip as the second stage on the bass, Analog Clip on the fast saturated Amen.
Last multiband distortion stage on the Reese, then resampling, for a bass more hostile than techstep.
The break played in bursts at 175-180 BPM, saturated and doubled with kicks, on the border of breakcore.

reperes: Panacea: Torture (1997): the screaming Reese, the saturated Amen and the German industrial atmosphere, the founding act.
Technical Itch: The Rukus (2003): doubled kicks and breaks in bursts, hardened English darkstep.
Bad Company UK: The Nine (1999): the bass rising and falling over a heavy two-step, the hinge between techstep and darkstep.
Dylan: Fabrication (2003): density and speed, the Freak Recordings sound.
darkstep.rythme: The fast saturated Amen and the doubled kicks from the brief. Base: a two-step with the kick on 1 and the "and" of 3, snare on 2 and 4. Then the doubling: a second kick one sixteenth note after each kick (the "e" of 1 and the "a" of 3), for a hammering effect. On top, an Amen at 180 BPM, saturated (Overdrive 60%), played in bursts: 2 full bars, then 1/32 snare cuts on the last beat, then one beat of silence. Add a second snare pitched down an octave, every other bar on the "and" of 4. The fills are sixteenth-note kick rolls and reversed cymbals.
darkstep.sons: The brief cites the Akai S3000, the Nord Lead and Cubase: the techstep studio, pushed into the red. The Nord Lead gives the Reese and screaming resonant sawtooth leads. The horror atmospheres: horror film samples, breaths, whispers, screams, metal doors, filtered pink noise drones with moving resonance, all pitched down and drowned in an 8 s reverb. Add metallic impacts, factory sirens, a shouted, distorted metal or gabber vocal, and "screeches" (square wave with resonance maxed out). Panacea used industrial textures from the German scene: noise, distortion, cold.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Basslines chapter, Reese bass)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable chapter)
darkstep.tempo: Darkstep is played between 175 and 185 BPM, the highest tempo in drum and bass before breakcore. What sets it apart from techstep, its parent, is density: where techstep leaves silences, darkstep fills everything with bursts of Amen and doubled kicks. The feel is that of a race: the breaks run in saturated sixteenth notes, the kick hits twice where techstep hits once. No swing, no soft ghost notes. Set your DAW to 180 BPM and think of a damp cellar rather than a club: the track should oppress.

darkwave.arrangement: Song format, 4 to 5 minutes. 8-bar intro on the pad alone or the arpeggio, then the drum machine and the bass come in together. Verse with voice, bass, pad. Chorus: the pad opens up, the arpeggio comes in, the guitar doubles. Second verse, chorus, 16-bar instrumental bridge where the pad modulates to another chord, last chorus, outro on the pad fading out. Transitions go through tom fills and the opening of the pad's filter. No brutal breaks: everything flows. Write the chord progression first, four minor chords, then the bassline, then the voice.
darkwave.basse: Two options, often combined. Electric bass with chorus, played in eighth notes or in melodic lines that rise and fall over the chord: root, fifth, octave, seventh. That is the cold wave legacy, and with Lebanon Hanover, it carries the main riff. Or a bass on a Juno-106: sawtooth, filter at 500 Hz, in eighth notes, with the Juno's chorus on. Both can play together, the Juno an octave lower. No saturation, a light 3:1 Compressor. The bass is forward in the mix, almost at the level of the voice. It follows a minor chord progression, often four chords over 8 bars.
etapes: At 118 BPM, write a progression of four minor chords over 8 bars and play it as a pad on Analog with Chorus-Ensemble, 300 ms attack.
Program a LinnDrum or 707 drum machine: kick on the beats, snare on 2 and 4 with a 0.5-second gate, eighth-note hi-hat, tom fill every 8 bars.
Record a bass with chorus that plays a melodic line over the chords, or program it on a Juno emulator.
Add a sixteenth-note arpeggio with a dotted-eighth delay, and a clean guitar in arpeggios.
Sing a deep vocal with a 2.5-second plate reverb, over a melancholic text.
Arrange over 4 minutes 30 with a modulating instrumental bridge, and an outro on the pad alone.
darkwave.mix: A warm, wide mix. Chorus is everywhere: bass, pad, guitar, which widens everything. The pads spread out in stereo, the bass and voice stay in the center, the drum machine is centered with the toms slightly panned. Plate reverb on the voice, 2.5 seconds, with a 40 ms pre-delay to keep it intelligible. Short gated reverb on the snare. The bass is mixed forward. Gentle compression on the master, 2:1, and light tape saturation for 1980s warmth. Aim for -12 LUFS. The low end stays round, cut below 40 Hz, with no aggressive sub.

outils.pourquoi: Sawtooth pads with the built-in chorus, filter at 1.5 kHz, 300 ms attack, and bass filtered at 500 Hz. TAL-U-NO-LX is its emulation.
Kick on the beats, snare on 2 and 4 with a 0.5-second gate, descending toms every 8 bars. Samples with a gentle Compressor are enough.
The other clean 1980s drum machine, which Helena Hauff still programs: clap doubled on the snare in the choruses.
Colder strings than the Juno, for the funereal pads of the verses, over four minor chords in 8 bars.
Lebanon Hanover's chorused bass, carrying the main riff in eighth notes, mixed almost at the level of the voice.
Clean, round 8-bit drum samples, the American alternative to the LinnDrum for the genre's backbeat.
On the bass, the pad and the guitar at once: chorus everywhere widens the warm, wide mix described in the course.
To recreate the Juno or the Poly-61 without hardware: sawtooth, 300 ms attack, Chorus-Ensemble after it, 2.5-second plate reverb.

reperes: Clan of Xymox: A Day (1985): the clean drum machine, the pads opening up, the deep voice, the genre's entire vocabulary.
Lebanon Hanover: Gallowdance (2013): the chorused bass carrying the riff, the minimalism of the revival.
Boy Harsher: Fate (2019): the current version, darker and more club-oriented, between darkwave and EBM.
darkwave.rythme: A 1980s drum machine: LinnDrum, Oberheim DMX, TR-707, or Drumatix. Kick on the beats, sometimes with an extra kick on the offbeat of 3. Snare on 2 and 4 with a 0.5-second gated reverb, the sound of the decade. Eighth-note hi-hat, open on the last offbeat. Descending tom fills every 8 bars. Clap doubled on the snare in the choruses. The pattern is simple and clean, with no distortion: darkwave is the only branch of the family where the drums are not mistreated. In Ableton, LinnDrum or 707 samples with a gentle Compressor are enough.
darkwave.sons: The Juno-106 is the central instrument: sawtooth pads with the built-in chorus, filter at 1.5 kHz, 300 ms attack, on minor chords sometimes with a seventh or a ninth. The Poly-61 gives colder strings. Recreate this with Analog or Wavetable plus Chorus-Ensemble. Sixteenth-note arpeggios over a held chord, with a dotted-eighth delay. Clean guitar with chorus and delay, in arpeggios. The voice is deep, baritone, sung with a 2 to 3 second plate reverb. The lyrics are melancholic, often in English with an accent. Few samples, no noise: darkwave is clean and sad.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros: Favourite bit of kit)
Gearspace (thread First hardware synth for coldwave/darkwave/post-punk)
Cold War Night Life (Guide to Darkwave)
darkwave.tempo: Between 90 and 130 BPM, most danceable tracks around 110 to 125. The feel is straight, driven by a 1980s drum machine, but rounder and broader than the cold wave darkwave descends from: reverb and pads slow down the perception. What distinguishes the genre from cold wave: more polyphonic synths, more space, a deeper, more sung voice. Some ballads drop to 80 BPM. In your DAW, start at 118 BPM, quantize the drum machine, but let the bass and guitar sit a little ahead of the beat, that is the romantic tension of the style.

deconstructedclub.arrangement: Nonlinear, 3 to 5 minutes. No DJ intro and no drop: sections that collide, an 8-bar club fragment, a silence, a 30-second pad, an explosion. The dynamics go from a whisper to an explosion. A motif can come back transformed at the end. Think film editing more than club track: hard cuts, contrasts, false starts. A more regular "club edit" version can exist for the DJ, with a pulse held for 3 minutes. In the main version, each section must surprise the one before it. Silence is a section in its own right.
deconstructedclub.basse: The sub is an impact more than a line: sine explosions at 40 Hz with a pitch envelope that drops an octave in 200 ms, isolated, one every 4 bars. Distorted basses that appear for one bar and disappear. An 808 pitched out of key. No continuous bassline, or else a sub drone holding for 16 bars under fragments fighting each other. Contrast is the rule: a sub alone in silence, then nothing. In Serum or Operator, with violent distortion followed by a clean cut. The kick and the sub ignore each other or collide, never a clean sidechain.
etapes: Set Ableton to 135 BPM, import a dembow pattern, a gabber kick and a grime snare, keep 4 bars of each.
Sample found impacts: metal, glass, doors, and place them off the grid in the arrangement.
Create sub explosions at 40 Hz with a falling pitch envelope, one every 4 bars.
Stretch a voice in Granulator and make a pad out of it, then cut it into rhythmic grains.
Edit the sections like a film: club fragment, silence, pad, explosion, transformed return.
Mix by section, keep the transients, limit the impacts, leave the quiet passages very low.
deconstructedclub.mix: Extreme dynamics, fully embraced. The impacts are limited hard, at -1 dB peak, the quiet passages stay at -25 dB. No global bus compression: each section has its own processing. Transients intact, no conventional sidechain. Violent stereo: a sound alone on the left, a reverb alone on the right, brutal mono on the impacts. Distortion and clipping on chosen elements, clinical cleanliness on others. Convolution reverb on a send with odd impulses, a stairwell, a tunnel. Master with a transparent limiter, no loudness target, more like -10 to -12 LUFS integrated with very loud peaks.

outils.pourquoi: Impacts placed off the grid in the arrangement view, tempo automation, sections edited like a film.
SOPHIE's machine: five synthesis engines, six mono voices, waveforms pushed into materials, plastic, latex, bubble.
Extreme FM, fast pitch modulation, hyperrealistic sounds and 40 Hz sub explosions with an octave drop.
Stretches a voice into a granular cloud, then cuts it into rhythmic grains; the device behind the genre's vocal sound design.
Custom patches for gridless collages, polymeters in 5 sixteenth notes and processing that is impossible elsewhere.
Textures, metallic impacts and physical modeling synthesis, every sound resampled several times with no preset.
Convolution with strange impulses, stairwell or tunnel, on a single send, next to raw mono impacts.
Four-operator FM sequenced step by step, for synthetic snaps and bells in the spirit of the Monomachine.

reperes: Arca: Xen (2014): off-grid fragments and impact subs, fragility and violence.
SOPHIE: Lemonade (2015): hyperrealistic synthesis, plastic and bubble sounds, torn-up pop.
Lotic: Hunted (2018): metallic impacts and silences, extreme dynamics.
Amnesia Scanner: AS Going (2020): inhuman voices and rave collage, the most recent version.
deconstructedclub.rythme: Fragments: a saturated gabber kick for 4 bars, a dembow pattern for 2, an isolated grime snare, then silence. Sampled metallic impacts, breaking glass, gunshots, slamming doors, treated as drums. Place them off the grid in the arrangement view rather than in MIDI clips. Use polymeters: a percussion part in 5 sixteenth notes over a grid of 4. Snare rolls that speed up until they become noise. Complete silences of a whole bar. The pattern exists only to be interrupted. A huge snare with 3 seconds of reverb, then a dry clap with nothing on it.
deconstructedclub.sons: Granular synthesis: Ableton's Granulator or a Max for Live patch that stretches a voice into a cloud. Serum in extreme FM, Reaktor for textures. Voices pitched to the inhuman, up and down, cut into grains. Found sounds: metal, water, breathing, a crowd. Hyperrealistic synthesized sounds in the style of SOPHIE: a plastic snap, latex, a bubble, made with FM and fast pitch modulation. Pop chords run through a reversed reverb. Rave sirens and chopped reggaeton shouts. Every sound is both shiny and menacing. No presets, everything is resampled several times.
sourcesOutils: Elektronauts, SOPHIE's sound design (Digitone or Monomachine?)
deconstructedclub.tempo: There is no fixed tempo, and that is the point. Take a base of 130 to 140 BPM to converse with grime and dembow, then break it: tempo automation, sections at 90 then at 160, passages with no pulse. The rhythmic fragments come from rave, reggaeton, grime and ballroom, but they don't last more than 4 bars. The feel alternates violence and fragility, impact and silence. What changes compared with the UK bass it descends from: the grid is no longer a constraint, and the track is no longer a DJ tool, it is a piece that can also be played in a club.

deeptech.arrangement: Seven to eight minutes, designed for mixing. 32-bar intro with kick, hats and a rolling percussion part. The bass comes in at 33, the vocal or the chord at 65. A single short breakdown, 8 or 16 bars, where only the sub and one percussion part remain, with a high-pass filter rising on the percussion. No complete silence: the kick comes back without fanfare. The second half adds a new element, often a second bass or a chord. 32-bar outro that steps back down to the hats and kick. The secret is to change one detail every 8 bars: a hi-hat that skips a sixteenth note, a tom that changes step, without the listener noticing the moment it changes.
deeptech.basse: The UK sub bass is the center: a sine with a touch of saturation, very low, F0 or G0, playing a note held for two beats then a short note, as in 2000s garage. Add a second triangle oscillator an octave up at -12 dB so it reads on small speakers. The pattern is simple, two or three notes per bar, often with a glide (60 ms portamento) between the root and the minor seventh. Sidechain from the kick, 1 ms attack, 150 ms release, 4 dB of reduction. Cut everything above 200 Hz. Unlike tech house, the bass doesn't play the offbeats, it carries the downbeats with the kick.
etapes: Tempo 127 BPM, short 909 kick with click, thin clap on 2 and 4, tight sixteenth-note closed hi-hat with 57% swing.
Program the UK sub: saturated sine on F0, one held note then a short one, 60 ms portamento, 4 dB sidechain.
Add two rolling percussion parts (tom, shaker) in sixteenth notes with gaps on the beats, and a block on three steps.
Place a filtered minor chord every 4 bars and a vocal fragment in a short echo, both very low.
Arrange over eight minutes with a single short 16-bar breakdown and one detail changing every 8 bars.
Mix with the mono sub up front, tightly compressed percussion group, limiter around -8 LUFS, check on a subwoofer.
deeptech.mix: The sub is the center of the mix, louder than in tech house: kick and bass level with each other around -10 dBFS, the bass in strict mono, controlled by a dedicated limiter on its track. The percussion is grouped into a compressor with a fast attack (3 ms), 60 ms release, 4:1 ratio, for tightness. High-pass at 150 Hz on everything that is not kick or bass. Little reverb: a 0.5 s plate on the clap, nothing elsewhere. Light saturation on the kick for the click. On the master, an EQ that scoops 1 dB at 300 Hz to clear the sub, then Glue at 2:1 and a limiter around -8 LUFS. Check on a subwoofer: the sub should stay clean, with no distortion.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the FUSE scene: MPC 16 Swing groove at 57% on hats and percussion, one detail changed every 8 bars.
The UK sub: sine on F0 with a triangle an octave up at -12 dB, 60 ms portamento, 4 dB sidechain.
Dry 200 ms kick with a click at 3 kHz, thin clap, tight hi-hats; samples or the Roland Cloud emulation.
Rolling percussion played on the pads with the machine's swing, more alive than the DAW's perfect grid.
Drum machine sampler with trig conditions and per-track LFOs, for toms and shakers that vary on every cycle.
Dedicated analog kick, tunable, with adjustable attack; used in recent deep tech sample packs.
Dotted eighth at 30% wet on the wood and metal percussion, reverb in the feedback loop, for the basement atmosphere.
Pack inspired by Enzo Siragusa and Archie Hamilton: dry percussion, subs and vocal fragments ready for this groove.

reperes: Michael Bibi: Hanging Tree (2019): a gliding sub, a chopped vocal, percussion rolling nonstop.
Baby Ford: Normal (1989): the prehistory of the sound, British house already reduced to a groove and a bass.
Losoul: Overland (1998): Playhouse's rolling percussion, a model of a loop that runs for ten minutes.
Little Green Men: Time Changes (1999): the Wiggle spirit, dry groove and round bass, before the name deep tech existed.
deeptech.rythme: Dry 909 kick, shorter than in tech house, 200 ms, with a pronounced click at 3 kHz to cut through on big systems. Clap or rimshot on 2 and 4, thin, no reverb. The closed hi-hat plays every sixteenth note, very tight, 40 ms decay, velocities of 110 on the beats and 70 elsewhere. The open hi-hat on the eighth-note offbeats, 150 ms decay. Rolling percussion is the signature: a tom or a conga in sixteenth notes with gaps on the beats, plus a shaker in sixteenth notes, plus a block on a three-step pattern. Together they make a turning wheel. Remove one percussion step every 4 bars to create a snag.
deeptech.sons: The textures stay discreet. A two- or three-note minor chord, on Analog or Juno, with a 500 ms attack and plenty of filter, appearing every 4 bars and disappearing. A garage vocal fragment, a syllable or a word, pitched down 3 semitones, in a short echo. Recorded club noises or field recordings, very low in the mix, for the basement atmosphere. The organic percussion (wood, metal) goes through an Echo set to a dotted eighth at 30% wet with the reverb in the feedback loop. A short tonal beep, a sine at 800 Hz, on an offbeat, serves as a marker. No lead, no white noise build-up: the percussion does the build-ups.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Deep Techno chapter, fake sidechain and rolling toms technique)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Deep Techno chapter, fake sidechain and rolling toms)
Data Transmission (Lighting The Fuse: Enzo Siragusa)
deeptech.tempo: 125 to 128 BPM, a little faster than minimal tech, with a groove inherited from UK garage: 55 to 58% swing on the sixteenth notes, but with accents that fall on the offbeat eighth notes. The feel is rolling and dark, made for basements and long sets. In Ableton, an MPC 16 Swing groove at 57% on the hats and percussion is enough; the kick and the bass stay straight. What changes compared with tech house is continuity: each track must be mixable for three minutes with the previous one, so the tempo does not move and the breakdowns stay short. An MPC or its emulation brings the grain.

detroitelectro.arrangement: The tracks are short for the family, four to six minutes, and work by layering sequences: 808 intro and low bass 16 bars, melodic bass 16, lead 16, pads 16, then gradual removal. The breakdowns are subtractions: cut the kick for 8 bars, keep the bass and the polyrhythmic percussion, relaunch without a roll. There is no chorus and no vocal, the bass melody plays the role of the chorus. Variations come from filter automation and sequence length, not from new elements. Plan two bass patterns and one lead, and make them enter, exit and combine on an 8-bar grid. The ending is often abrupt, with no outro.
detroitelectro.basse: The bass is analog and moving: SCI Pro-One, Oberheim OB-8 in mono, SH-101. Today Repro-1, Ableton Analog or Diva. Sawtooth and square mixed, low-pass filter at 250 Hz with a fast envelope, 120 ms decay, and above all a slow cutoff automation over 8 bars for movement. It plays sixteenth notes in octave and fifth jumps, on minor scales with chromatic notes, in the manner of the SH-101 pluck the Attack book recreates for Detroit minimal. Often two basses: a low one held on the root, and a staccato higher one that carries the melody. Cut the melodic bass below 100 Hz, let the low one go down to 45 Hz.
etapes: Tempo at 132 BPM, 808: kick on 1, the "and" of 2 and step 12 with a 200 ms decay, snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats with a velocity ramp.
Add a percussion part on a 5-step loop and a tuned tom pattern on the even bars.
Program a low bass held on the root, then a staccato sixteenth-note bass with octave jumps and a slow cutoff automation.
Write an eight-note mono lead with portamento and an OB pad in two-note chords.
Create an aquatic sound effect with white noise through a resonant band-pass modulated by a slow LFO.
Arrange by adding and removing sequences every 16 bars, with no reverb, and a breakdown by subtraction.
detroitelectro.mix: Dry, with no reverb: that is the most striking trait. Each sound is mixed naked, at most a short eighth-note delay on the lead at 15% dry/wet. 808 at -8 dBFS, low bass just behind, melodic bass and lead 6 dB lower. Moderate panning, basses in the center, pads slightly opened. Light tape saturation on the drum bus, 2 dB drive, to recall cassette and vinyl. No bus compression, or a Glue at 1.5:1 that barely acts. Mono below 120 Hz. Let the peaks breathe: a master at -13 LUFS with dynamics sounds truer than a crushed master, precision gets lost in compression.

outils.pourquoi: Dry 808, snapping kick with a 200 ms decay, high snappy on the snare, tuned toms in a three-note pattern; Drexciya pitched it on tape.
The main mono synth of Drexciya and Dopplereffekt: moving basses in octave jumps and leads with short portamento; u-he Repro-1 emulates it directly.
The other central synth of the school, four oscillators for thick basses and sequences; Korg Collection Mono/Poly is the software version.
Cold pads with slight detune and no chorus, in two-note minor chords, and a held bass in mono mode on the root.
Sixteenth-note bass pluck with chromatic notes, the sound the Attack book recreates for Detroit; TAL-BassLine-101 or Roland SH-01A.
The cold chords answering the basses in Dopplereffekt, played dry, with no reverb; TAL-U-No-LX today.
Sawtooth and square mixed, filter at 250 Hz with a 120 ms decay and slow cutoff automation over 8 bars; u-he Diva for more grain.
Not for samples but for the sonar blips: a sine with a descending pitch envelope, and white noise through a resonant band-pass.

reperes: Model 500: Night Drive (1985): the dry 808 and the sixteenth-note analog bass, the starting point of Detroit.
Drexciya: Bubble Metropolis (1993): sonar blips, moving basses and a mix with no reverb.
Drexciya: Wavejumper (1995): the precision of the 808 pattern and the layering of two basses.
Dopplereffekt: Pornoactress (1995): the coldness, a slower tempo, a vocoder on isolated words.
detroitelectro.rythme: A precise 808, with no layers and no breakbeat samples. Kick on 1, on the "and" of 2 and on step 12, short 200 ms decay: the Detroit kick snaps, it doesn't linger, the bass provides the sub. 808 snare on 2 and 4 with high snappy, sometimes a rimshot instead on beat 4. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes with a velocity that ramps across the bar, open hi-hat on a single offbeat per bar. Tuned 808 toms play a three-note melodic pattern on the even bars. No cowbell, no Miami rolls. Add a percussion part on a 5- or 7-step loop for the polyrhythmic drift. Program in 16 steps, think like a machine.
detroitelectro.sons: SCI and Oberheim synths: cold OB-8 pads with slight detune, no chorus, played as two-note minor chords. Mono Pro-One leads with short portamento, playing four- to eight-note patterns in sixteenth notes, with a filter that opens at the ends of phrases. Aquatic sound effects in Drexciya: white noise filtered by a band-pass with high resonance, modulated by a slow LFO, and sonar blips (a sine with a descending pitch envelope). Vocoder rare but present, on isolated words. No samples, no orch hits, no rapped vocals. Everything is played by oscillators, and every sound moves a little thanks to an LFO or an envelope.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Step-sequences and Detroit Techno chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Step-sequences and Detroit Techno chapters)
detroitelectro.tempo: Between 125 and 140 BPM, Drexciya often around 130 to 135, Dopplereffekt slower. A rigorous grid, zero swing, every note quantized: the obsessive precision is part of the sound. What sets Detroit apart from the rest of the family is the sequencer feel: the patterns are conceived as 16-step loops that shift against one another. The Attack book points out that an odd pattern length, five or nine steps, creates a polyrhythm that only realigns after several bars. Use this idea on a percussion part or a bass: the track seems to move without a single note changing. Start at 132 BPM.

detroittechno.arrangement: Count on six to eight minutes. Open with 16 or 32 bars of drums alone for the DJ, then add an element every 8 bars: toms, open hi-hat, clap, sub. The chords arrive around bar 33 and set up the melancholy. Avoid big build-ups: Detroit doesn't do drops, it brings elements in and out as in a jam. A central 16-bar breakdown with the strings alone is enough. Think in three acts like Beltram: exposition, a more harmonic central section, return of the modified patterns. Finish with 32 bars of drums for the next mix. Play the mutes live in Session view and record the result: you get a living structure, not a drawn-up plan.
detroittechno.basse: In Detroit, the bass is often played by the toms: tune the low tom to the root, send the tom group into a RE-201-style echo at a dotted eighth with 15% feedback, then compress it all with sidechain from the kick. If you want a real bass, use a DX7, an ESQ-1 or Operator: one note per beat or staccato eighth notes on the root, an octave up now and then, no distortion. Beltram's track shows another way: a sub held permanently on the root (A flat 1, about 52 Hz), which never leaves the mix. In every case, tune the kick, tom and sub to the same note.
etapes: Load Ableton's 909 Core kit, lay the kick in four-on-the-floor at 128 BPM and shorten its decay.
Program three toms tuned to the root, on the second and fourth sixteenth notes, then shift them by hand.
Add a sixteenth-note closed hi-hat with a 45% groove, an open hi-hat on the offbeats, a sparse clap.
Write a two-chord minor progression with a strings or ESQ-1 patch, each held for two bars.
Send the toms into Echo in RE-201 mode then into a sidechain, and saturate the drum bus with Pedal and Glue.
Arrange by playing the mutes live over eight minutes, then trim the lengths.
detroittechno.mix: The sound should seem to have gone through tape and a slightly tired console. On the drum bus: Pedal Distort at 35% mix with Sub engaged, then Glue Compressor at a 10:1 ratio, fast attack, auto release, threshold around -25 dB, 30% mix. Sum everything below 200 Hz to mono. Push the kick to around -12 dB peak and keep 6 dB of headroom on the master: a Detroit track isn't played loud, it is played wide. Cut the hi-hats below 2 kHz and scoop 4 to 5 dB around 4.7 kHz to remove the metallic edge. Short reverb on the toms, measured delay on the strings. No brickwall limiter: keep the dynamics.

outils.pourquoi: The four-on-the-floor kick and above all the tuned toms that play the bass; Ableton's 909 Core kit or D16 Drumazon replace it very well.
The Underground Resistance version: congas, rimshot and electro-style broken beat, with a clock that never lands on a round BPM. Common emulation: D16 Nepheton.
Electric piano and dry FM basses for the rhythmic patterns; Operator in Ableton or NI FM8 take on its presets easily.
Derrick May's melancholic synth strings, minor chords held for two bars; a Korg Poly-800 or a Kurzweil K2000 give the same kind of pad.
Chord stabs and strings sampled then pitched across the keyboard, with the 12-bit grain; Simpler with Redux does the same job today.
In tape mode, RE-201 style, at a dotted eighth with 15% feedback on the tom group, then sidechained from the kick.
Distort mode at 3% gain on every sound, and at 35% mix on the drum bus, to simulate the tape and tired console of the era.
SSL-style bus compression on the drums: 10:1 ratio, threshold around -25 dB, 30% mix, to glue the toms to the kick without crushing.

reperes: Cybotron: Clear (1983): the dry drum machine and the vocoder, the robotic funk that precedes everything
Model 500: No UFO's (1985): the 909 kick and the minimal bass, the cold strings on top
Rhythim Is Rhythim: Strings of Life (1987): the sampled strings and piano, a track with no real bass that holds together through its chords
Underground Resistance: The Final Frontier (1992): all on 808, broken beat, a 303 lead with gated reverb and strings in A-flat minor
detroittechno.rythme: The TR-909 kick plays four-on-the-floor, with a shortened decay (around 30 ms in Simpler) to leave the low end of the spectrum to the toms. The 909 toms are the heart of the signature: three or four toms tuned to each other, placed on the second and fourth sixteenth notes of beats 1, 2 and 3, plus a last tom on the third sixteenth of beat 4 to announce the restart. Pull the toms on the fourth sixteenth back slightly for a lazy feel. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes with groove, open hi-hat on the offbeats, a discreet snare and a clap that acts as a fake fill. UR version: all on TR-808, mid and hi congas, snare on 2 and 4 with a double hit before the end of the bar, and an electro-style broken beat.
detroittechno.sons: The synth strings do everything: a strings patch on a Poly-800, ESQ-1 or a Kurzweil K2000 (UR), minor chords with a seventh or ninth, held for two bars, slow attack. Add a DX7 electric piano for the rhythmic patterns, and a Juno pad for the pads. The effects are vintage: Ableton's Echo in RE-201 mode, a short plate reverb, a light phaser on the hi-hats. On the Akai samplers, pitched chord stabs. The grain matters as much as the notes: run every sound through Pedal in Distort mode at 3% gain, or through Saturator, to simulate tape and console. One hi-hat too clean, one pad too smooth, and you leave the style.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
detroittechno.tempo: Aim for 120 to 136 BPM. The Cybotron and Model 500 classics run around 120 to 128, Underground Resistance goes up to 136 with a TR-808 clock that never lands on a round number. The feel comes from funk: the grid is straight, but the toms and hi-hats are shifted by hand, never 100% quantized. In Ableton, apply a Cabasa or MPC 16 groove at 40 or 45% on the hi-hats only, and leave the kick perfectly straight. The swing should not be seen, it should be felt: the track rolls a little behind the beat, like a machine breathing. If you quantize everything, you lose Detroit.

digitalhardcore.arrangement: The tracks are short, 2 to 4 minutes, structured like punk songs: 4- to 8-bar intro with a sample or a riff, 8- to 16-bar verse with the break and the shouted vocal, 8-bar chorus with the kick on every beat, the guitar and the repeated slogan, verse, chorus, a 4- to 8-bar break with a political sample or feedback, last chorus, brutal ending, cut clean. No DJ intro, no 8-bar build-up, no silence before the drop: those are club codes, and digital hardcore is not club music. What makes the track work is the slogan: a shouted, memorable phrase, repeated.
digitalhardcore.basse: There is rarely a written bassline: the low end comes from the distorted 909 kick and the sampled electric guitar, played in power chords and run through a saturated amp, which fills the low mids. When there is a bass, it is a heavily distorted square or sawtooth wave, playing a held note or a two- or three-note punk riff in eighth notes, in the same key as the guitar, often in E or A. In Operator: sawtooth, no filter, Saturator at 20 dB, Overdrive after it. Sidechain is pointless: cleanliness is not the goal. Still, cut below 40 Hz on everything so the limiter doesn't saturate on sub.
etapes: Tempo 175 BPM. Load an Amen or a funk break into Simpler, speed it up without preserving pitch, Saturator at 25 dB then Redux at 8 bits.
Distorted 909 kick on 1 and 3, 909 snare on 2 and 4 doubling the break, sixteenth-note snare bursts at the end of each block.
Sampled or played electric guitar riff, two power chords in eighth notes, Amp and Cabinet then Overdrive.
Record a shouted vocal, a slogan of 4 to 8 words, any mic, heavy compression and distortion.
Add a political sample (speech, news) in the break and a dirty resonant sawtooth synth.
Punk structure: intro 8, verse 16, chorus 8, verse 16, chorus 8, break 8, chorus, ending cut clean. Distortion on the master before the limiter.
digitalhardcore.mix: The digital hardcore mix refuses the rules of mixing. Everything is saturated, including the master bus, with a Saturator or an Overdrive before the limiter. The break and the kick fight in the low mids and that's intended. As the Attack book notes, distortion creates new frequencies: here you let it take over everything, and only fix what really hurts, a high-pass at 40 Hz and a narrow cut around 3 kHz if the screams become unbearable. Vocals very far forward, compressed at a 10:1 ratio, distorted. Master: limiter pushed hard, -6 LUFS, with audible distortion. Listen to Atari Teenage Riot: it saturates everywhere, and it works.

outils.pourquoi: Alec Empire's sequencing computer in the 1990s: MIDI to the sampler, saturated 8-bit breaks, tempo pushed to 180 and beyond.
Breaks and screams sampled at 12 bits then distorted on the way back into the desk; the political samples and guitar riffs go through it.
909 kick under the breaks, distorted until it merges with them: hardcore techno remains the backbone of the genre.
Punk riffs played or sampled, run through a distortion pedal then into the sampler; the rage comes from there more than from the synths.
Amp then Cabinet on the breaks and on the shouted vocals: guitar distortion makes the breakbeat dirty and the scream believable.
Saturator, Overdrive, then Redux at 8 bits on the drum bus: distortion on everything, including the hi-hats, as on the DHR records.
Chopping breaks and screams, transposing down for the tape effect; Operator adds the sawtooth sirens.

reperes: Atari Teenage Riot: Start the Riot (1995): the saturated break, the 909 kick, the shouted slogan, the complete manifesto.
Atari Teenage Riot: Deutschland (Has Gotta Die!) (1996): the sampled guitar and punk structure on machines.
Ec8or: AK-78 (1995): the more abstract version, 8-bit samples and distortion on everything.
Alec Empire: The Destroyer (1996): the founder solo, closer to breakcore, listen to the distortion on the master.
digitalhardcore.rythme: Breakbeats sampled on an Atari ST (or any break in Simpler), sped up to 175 BPM without preserving pitch (the pitch goes up, that's intended), chopped roughly, and distorted to the maximum: Saturator at 25 dB then Redux at 8 bits. On top, a distorted 909 kick on beats 1 and 3, or on every beat in the hardest passages, and a 909 snare doubled on 2 and 4 to hammer along with the break. Sixteenth-note snare retrigs like machine-gun bursts. Blast beat passages: kick and snare in alternating eighth notes. Brutal cuts. Everything punk does with a drum kit, done with samples.
digitalhardcore.sons: Punk screams: shouted vocals, often political slogans in English or German, recorded with a cheap mic, distorted, with a short delay. Electric guitars sampled in two-bar riffs, run through Amp and Cabinet, then through extra distortion. Political samples: speeches, TV news, demonstrations, police sirens. Dirty synth sounds, resonant sawtooth, broken hoover style. White noise, feedback, 8-bit Atari ST sounds. Everything is distorted, without exception: Alec Empire put distortion on the master. No sound should be clean, that is the manifesto.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
digitalhardcore.tempo: Digital hardcore runs between 160 and 200 BPM, often 170-180 with Atari Teenage Riot, but the tempo matters less than the energy: it is punk played with machines. What sets it apart from everything else in the family is the grid: no regular 4/4, but saturated breakbeats, often the Amen or a funk break, sped up and distorted, with 909 kicks falling on top. The feel is that of a punk gig: raw, shouted, unpolished. A little natural swing from the break, no forced quantization. Program at 175 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, and leave the mistakes in: they are part of the sound.

disco.arrangement: The 12-inch single was invented for this music: aim for 6 to 8 minutes. Open with 16 to 32 bars of rhythm section alone, drums, percussion and bass, so the DJ can mix. Then a 16-bar verse, an 8- or 16-bar chorus, second verse, chorus, then the break: the strings and vocals disappear, congas, hi-hats and bass remain for 16 bars, before a string build-up brings everything back. Finish with a long 32-bar instrumental vamp that fades out by subtraction. Each 8-bar section should add or remove an element. The chorus should arrive with all the strings: that is the moment of euphoria.
disco.basse: The bass is electric, played fingerstyle, often a Fender Precision or Jazz Bass. It is syncopated: it states the root on beat 1, then dances between the kicks in sixteenth notes with octave jumps and muted notes. Think of Bernard Edwards in Chic: two-bar patterns, ghost notes, a chromatic run up before the chord change. In a DAW, an electric bass sampler or Spectrasonics Trilian does the job if you write short notes, varied velocities and small muted notes between the real ones. The relationship to the kick is simple: it lines up on the 1, then it grooves on its own, it never doubles the kick on all four beats.
etapes: Set the project to 120 BPM with 54% swing and load an acoustic drum kit into a Drum Rack.
Program the kick on all four beats, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hat closed on the beats and open on the offbeats, then add sixteenth-note congas and tambourine.
Write a syncopated two-bar electric bass part with octave jumps and ghost notes, over a two-chord minor progression.
Add the sixteenth-note chicken-scratch guitar, a Rhodes in block chords, then staccato eighth-note strings and brass stabs on the offbeats.
Build the extended version: rhythm intro, verses, choruses, percussion and bass break, string build-up, final vamp.
Mix with gentle compression on the drum bus, a plate on the snare and strings, and tape saturation on the master.
disco.mix: A disco mix keeps its dynamics. No aggressive limiter: aim for -14 LUFS for listening, a little louder for the club. The kick is round, cut below 40 Hz, with no huge sub. The bass sits in front, compressed at 3:1 with a 20 ms attack to let the finger attack through. The drum bus gets slow glue compression, 2:1 ratio, 30 ms attack, 100 ms release. A plate reverb on the snare and strings, a short chamber on the brass. Lightly saturate the master with a tape emulation to tie everything together. Keep everything below 120 Hz in mono, and open the strings and guitars wide.

outils.pourquoi: The fingerstyle bass that dances between the kicks. A Precision or a Jazz Bass, roundwound strings, compressed at 3:1 with a slow attack to keep the attack.
The chicken-scratch guitar in muted sixteenth-note chords, Nile Rodgers style: clean single-coil, often plugged straight into the console, with a little phaser.
The electric piano that fills the middle with seventh and ninth chords, a light tremolo and a short plate behind it.
The virtual electric bass that replaces a bassist if you write short notes, ghost notes and widely varied velocities.
An acoustic drum kit played with the open hi-hat on the offbeats, not quantized to 100%, velocities between 70 and 110 to avoid the machine effect.

outils.nom: Spitfire Audio BBC Symphony Orchestra Discover
outils.pourquoi: A free string library for staccato eighth-note lines and chromatic runs before the choruses, with brass stabs on the offbeats.
The plate reverb of the studios of the era, on the snare and strings; today Hybrid Reverb in plate mode or the Universal Audio EMT 140 emulation.
The Drum Rack for a sampled acoustic kit, Orchestral Strings for the strings, and the console driven by mute and send automation as on a 12-inch single.

reperes: The Trammps: Disco Inferno (1976): the open hi-hat on the offbeats and the strings rising before each chorus.
Chic: Everybody Dance (1978): Bernard Edwards' bass dancing between the kicks without ever doubling them.
Sister Sledge: Lost In Music (1979): Nile Rodgers' chicken-scratch guitar and the break where only the rhythm section remains.
Sylvester: You Make Me Feel (Mighty Real) (1978): the transition between the disco orchestra and the machine, with the vocal staying huge.
disco.rythme: The kick falls on every beat, round and not too hard. The snare is on beats 2 and 4, often doubled by a tambourine. The real signature is the hi-hat: closed on the beats, open on the eighth-note offbeats, Earl Young's famous pattern with MFSB and the Trammps. Add sixteenth-note congas with simple tumbaos, a continuous shaker and a snare roll at the end of the phrase. Use a Drum Rack filled with acoustic drum samples, or a virtual drum kit like Addictive Drums. Vary the velocities between 70 and 110 to avoid the machine effect. The sixteenth-note tambourine gives the shine at the top of the spectrum.
disco.sons: Disco is an orchestra in a studio. The strings play staccato eighth-note lines and chromatic runs up before the choruses: a good-quality string library (Spitfire, Kontakt, or even Ableton's Orchestral Strings) is enough if you write short, rhythmic parts. The brass punctuates with stabs on the offbeats. The guitar plays chicken scratch, chords muted in sixteenth notes with a wah or a phaser, on a clean single-coil sound. The Fender Rhodes and the clavinet fill the middle. The mixing console is an instrument: the extended version lives through mutes, plate reverb sends and wide panning. Record real guitars if you can, that is what no sample replaces.
sourcesOutils: Guitar World (Nile Rodgers' sound on Le Freak)
disco.tempo: Classic disco runs between 110 and 125 BPM, with a center of gravity around 118 to 122. The feel is played, not sequenced: a human drummer who pushes the hi-hats a little and lets the congas float. In your DAW, don't quantize to 100%. Set a swing of 52 to 56% on the sixteenth notes and shift the hi-hats 5 to 10 milliseconds late. The signature stays in regular 4/4, but everything around the kick breathes: that is the difference from the house music that descends from it. Think in 8-bar phrases and accents on the fourth beat, where the drummer opens the hi-hat.

discodub.arrangement: A dub version is long, 8 to 10 minutes, and is built by revelation. 32-bar intro of percussion and drums alone, the bass comes in, then the chicken-scratch guitars. A first complete section with the vocal, but short. Then the dub proper: mutes on the vocal and strings, the brass heads into the echo, the bass and drums stay alone for 16 bars. A vocal fragment comes back, drowned in echo. A plate swell on the strings brings back the full version for 32 bars. 32-bar outro with the rhythm section. The structure is that of a performance at the console, recorded in a single take if possible.
discodub.basse: The original's electric bass is the common thread of the dub version: when everything is muted, it stays with the drums. Push it forward, compressed at 4:1 with a 20 ms attack to keep the fingers, and an EQ with a slight boost at 100 Hz. Occasionally, send a note or two into the tape echo to create a bounce, as Jamaican dub does. If you produce the bass yourself, write it syncopated as in disco, in sixteenth notes with octave jumps, but plan bars where it falls silent so the mute can exist. The bass and kick stay dry: it is the other elements that head off into space.
etapes: Prepare a multitrack: your own disco track with drums, congas, bass, guitar, brass, strings and vocal on separate tracks, at 120 BPM.
Create two return tracks: a dotted-eighth tape echo with automatable feedback, and a 3-second plate reverb.
Build the intro by revelation: 32 bars of percussion, then kick, then bass, then guitar.
Automate the mutes and sends over a 32-bar section: cut the vocal, send the brass into the echo, keep bass and drums.
Record a real-time console performance with a controller, over 8 minutes, then correct the automation.
Finish with gentle bus compression and preserved dynamics, with no aggressive limiter.
discodub.mix: The mix is the composition. Automate the sends to the echo and the plate instead of leaving them fixed: one snare hit in four goes into the echo, one word in two of the vocal. Let the echo feedback climb to 80% during transitions then come back down. The mutes are clean, on the beat or just before. The EQ is played: a high-pass filter rising on the strings over 8 bars, then dropping back in one go. Compress the drum bus at 3:1 to keep a constant body when elements disappear. The plate reverb is long, 3 seconds. Aim for -13 LUFS, dynamics are part of the style.

outils.pourquoi: The main instrument: clean mutes, aux sends automated by hand, EQ played live while mixing the extended version.
The tape echo on the snare, the brass and the vocal fragments, feedback climbing to 80% into controlled howl; Roland Cloud offers an emulation.
The 3-second plate that turns brass and strings into distant pads; Hybrid Reverb in plate mode or the Universal Audio emulation.
The 16- or 24-track multitrack the remixer starts from: every track of the original becomes a source to mute or send into the echo.
Tape mode with automated feedback, on a return track, so one snare hit in four heads off into space.
The long plate on a send for the strings and brass, with a high-pass filter rising over 8 bars then dropping back in one go.
Return tracks and send automation that replace hands on the console, on a real or fake multitrack of your own disco track.

reperes: Double Exposure: Ten Percent (1976): the first commercial 12-inch single, Walter Gibbons and the stretched percussion intro.
Loleatta Holloway: Love Sensation (1980): the extended version where the vocal becomes a fragment and the rhythm section stays.
Taana Gardner: Heartbeat (1981): Larry Levan, slow tempo, bass up front and space around it.
Khruangbin: Time (You and I) (2020): the dub method applied today, mutes and echoes on a played groove.
discodub.rythme: The rhythm section is that of the vocal version, but isolated and pushed forward. Walter Gibbons opened Ten Percent with minutes of congas and drums alone. In your DAW, start from a multitrack, or build a "fake multitrack" with your own disco track: drums, congas, tambourine, bass on separate tracks. The work is to mute and reveal: 16 bars of congas alone, then the kick comes in, then the hi-hats. Send the snare into a tape echo at a dotted eighth on certain hits only, by automating the send. The percussion breaks are long, 32 bars, and the snare fills trigger an explosion of echo.
discodub.sons: The main instrument is the mixing console: mutes, aux sends, live EQ. The Roland RE-201 Space Echo is the central effect, with its drifting repeats and its feedback rising into controlled howl. The plate reverb takes the brass and strings, which become distant pads. The vocal is cut into fragments: a word, a phrase, sent into the echo. In Ableton, Echo in tape mode with automated feedback, a Hybrid Reverb in plate mode, and return tracks that you drive with send automation. Every track of the original version becomes a source to process.
sourcesOutils: Red Bull Music Academy Daily (Walter Gibbons: The First DJ's DJ)
discodub.tempo: Disco dub keeps the tempo of the track it reworks: 110 to 125 BPM, played by the original band. So the feel is that of disco, human and pushed, but the dub version stretches it out and lets it breathe. Set your project to the multitrack's tempo, often 118 to 122 BPM, with Ableton's warp mode to lock the played drums to the grid without stiffening them. The rhythmic signature is not a new pattern: it is the disco pattern laid bare, with silences and holes the engineer creates at the console. Time becomes elastic through the echo, not through the tempo.

discohouse.arrangement: The structure follows the filter. 16-bar intro with the loop heavily filtered (cutoff at 300 Hz) and the kick, the filter opens over 16 bars up to the full loop. 32-bar plateau with the bass and vocal. 16-bar breakdown: kick cut, filtered loop slowly reopening, then the kick returns with the filter wide open and a crash. Second cycle with a different sample or an added stab. 16-bar drum outro. Length 5 to 7 minutes. Some tracks, like Da Funk, are built around a played riff rather than a loop, but the logic stays the same: a short pattern, filtered, repeated.
discohouse.basse: Two options, often together: the sample's bass, if it is good, isolated with a low-pass at 200 Hz and looped; or a synth or sampled bass that replays the disco line in eighth notes with octaves. The line is funky, syncopated, with anticipations before the beat, the way a bassist really played. When you program it, write eighth notes with rests on beat 1 and octave jumps on the "and" of 4. A sine sub underneath, on the root, for the club pressure disco didn't have. Light sidechain from the kick, just enough to clear things up.
etapes: Choose a disco record, isolate two bars with strings and brass, lock them to 125 BPM with warp or as slices.
Put a 909 underneath, four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, and filter the loop below 120 Hz.
Replay or isolate the bass in syncopated eighth notes with octaves, and add a sine sub on the root.
Put a resonant low-pass Auto Filter on the loop and automate it opening over 16 bars, with a slow phaser.
Build 6 minutes around the filter opening and closing, with a breakdown where the loop breathes without the kick.
Mix with a sidechain pumping on the samples, light saturation, a loud and round master.
discohouse.mix: The sample brings its own mix, often warm and compressed, and you build around it. Cut the loop below 120 Hz so the kick and sub are yours. The 909 kick is clean and dry, louder than in the original disco. The resonant filter creates peaks: a compressor after it (4:1) holds them. A little saturation on the loop to glue the slices back together. The bus compression should pump slightly, sidechain on the sample group with a 150 ms release. Short reverb, the loop already has some. The master is loud and round, -8 to -10 LUFS, with full lows and highs that keep the shine of the disco strings.

outils.pourquoi: The 16-bit sampler sequencer of Armand Van Helden and DJ Sneak: two bars of disco cut across the pads, loop played with the filter.
The rack sampler of New York studios for string and brass stabs and a bass isolated from a record, replayed on the keyboard.
Dry kick under the loop filtered below 120 Hz, clap on 2 and 4: the 909 is the only kick in the track, the disco keeps its hats.
24 dB low-pass with 30% resonance, automated over 16 or 32 bars: the signature move of filter house, followed by a slow phaser.
The sequencer of French and New York studios from 1995 to 2000 for arranging MPC loops; Ableton Live and its warp today.
To give a clean loop the grain of an old sampler, with noise and loss of fidelity; Splice recommends it for filter house.
A sampling plugin common among today's disco house producers for finding, locking and slicing a record passage directly in the DAW.
The raw material: strings, brass and guitars from 1977 to 1982 digitized from vinyl; the sample must stay recognizable once transformed.

reperes: Daft Punk: Da Funk (1995): the riff as a loop, the filter and the pumping compression, before the style had a name.
Stardust: Music Sounds Better With You (1998): four bars of Chaka Khan filtered until they become a new chorus, the peak of the genre.
Deee-Lite: Groove Is In The Heart (Meeting Of The Minds mix) (1990): the disco bass sampled and replayed, the sample celebrated rather than hidden.
