Fire Island: There But For The Grace Of God (1993): the English side, where the disco vocal sample is replayed over harder drums.
discohouse.rythme: A solid 909 under the loop: kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, closed hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats, plus the drums already contained in the disco sample. The trick is to line the two up: filter the loop below 120 Hz so the 909 kick is the only kick, and let the sample's hats and shaker bring the swing. Add a sampled conga or tambourine on the choruses. The fills are cuts in the loop or a filter closing in one go, more than a tom roll. On the breakdown, cut the 909 and let the full disco loop breathe, with its original drums.
discohouse.sons: The filtered disco loop is the main instrument: two or four bars of strings, brass, guitar and vocals, lifted from a record, cut into slices on the MPC2000 or in Simpler. The resonant low-pass filter (Auto Filter at 24 dB, 30% resonance) opening and closing over 16 or 32 bars is the signature move. A slow phaser on top. Brass and string stabs cut from elsewhere, played as chords. A sampled vocal or a sung chorus that takes up the title of the sample. A house piano can round it out. The sample is not hidden: you should recognize the source and hear it transformed.
sourcesOutils: Splice Blog, The history, ingredients, and techniques behind filter house
discohouse.tempo: Between 122 and 128 BPM, above the original disco, which ran around 110 to 120. The sample dictates its feel: a disco loop played by a real band has its own swing, and that is what you have to respect. Lock the loop to the tempo with warp (Complex Pro or Beats in Ableton) or cut it into slices, but keep the 909 drums straight underneath: the contrast between the swinging loop and the steady machine gives the groove. Don't put swing on the 909. Choose your tempo according to the loop: beyond 6% stretching, the strings start to sound odd.

discopunk.arrangement: Disco punk keeps a rock song structure, but stretched out by repetition: 4 to 7 minutes. 8- to 16-bar intro with the bass and cowbell alone, then the drums come in. 16-bar verse with vocals, 8- or 16-bar chorus with the guitar scratching harder. Second verse, chorus. 16-bar break with percussion and bass alone, a build-up by accumulation, a shout. Long last chorus, outro that cuts clean or loops for 32 bars. There are no strings and no filter sweeps: the tension comes from the playing, from the intensity rising on the same riff, and from the dry cuts between sections.
discopunk.basse: The electric bass is dry, played with a pick, often with a Precision Bass sound and no studio compression. The riff is repeated: one or two notes, the root in eighth notes with an octave or fourth jump, like Liquid Liquid's Cavern or ESG's UFO. No slap, no walking: a two-bar pattern that doesn't move for four minutes. Record it if possible; otherwise an electric bass sampler with short notes and a little amp saturation. It lands with the kick on the beats and pushes on the offbeats: it is more rock than funk, but it has to make people dance, not headbang.
etapes: Set 128 BPM with no swing, load an acoustic drum kit with a small-room sound and a sampled cowbell.
Program or record the kick on the beats, dry snare on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats in eighth notes, cowbell in eighth notes.
Record an electric bass with a pick on a one- or two-note riff in eighth notes, repeated without variation.
Record a guitar playing muted chords in sixteenth notes through a clean amp, and congas or claves on top.
Add a shouted or spoken vocal with a short slapback, then build verse, chorus, percussion and bass break, long chorus.
Mix dry and alive: little reverb, aggressive compressed drum bus, loud bass, light tape saturation.
discopunk.mix: The disco punk mix is dry and alive, with the energy of a live take. Little reverb: a small room on the drums, an 80 ms slapback on the vocal. Compress the drum bus at 4:1 with a fast attack for aggression, and leave some room sound. The bass is loud and dry, cut below 50 Hz, with amp saturation. The guitar is panned to one side, the cowbell to the other, the vocal in the center. The kick has no sub: it is a rock kick. Lightly saturate the master with tape. Aim for -11 LUFS with dynamics. If it sounds too clean, add room noise and remove an EQ.

outils.pourquoi: The dry bass played with a pick, no studio compression, a two-bar riff that doesn't move for four minutes, Liquid Liquid style.
The cheap guitar LCD Soundsystem proudly used: muted sixteenth-note chords, clean or slightly overdriven single-coil.
The cowbell in eighth or sixteenth notes, played and mixed loud, with congas and claves: the rhythmic signature of the genre.
The virtual amp for a real recorded guitar, set dirty, with an 80 ms slapback on the vocal via Echo.
The pad or discreet mono synth of the second wave, alongside the Roland SH-101, in James Murphy's DFA studio.
The short slapback on the shouted or spoken vocal, and a short delay on the guitar, with no long reverb.
The mic for the snare and the guitar amp, for a small-room sound and a live take, lightly compressed.

reperes: Liquid Liquid: Cavern (1983): the one-note bass riff, the cowbell and the percussion, the most sampled record of the genre.
ESG: UFO (1981): three elements, dry drums, bass and a grating guitar.
Gang of Four: Damaged Goods (1978): the guitar that scratches instead of singing, over a danceable, tense rhythm section.
Radio 4: Dance to the Underground (2002): the second wave, same cowbell and same edginess, DFA production.
discopunk.rythme: The drums are played, tight, recorded with no frills. Kick on all four beats or on a simple disco pattern, dry, punchy snare on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats in eighth notes, rarely open. The cowbell in eighth or sixteenth notes is the signature, with hand percussion: congas, claves, tambourine. No long fills, clean cuts. In your DAW, an acoustic drum kit with a small-room sound, little compression on the cymbals, a sampled cowbell in eighth notes with varied velocities. If you can record a real drummer or a real cowbell, do it: this is the least programmable genre in the family.
discopunk.sons: The guitar scratches: muted chords in sixteenth notes, clean or slightly overdriven single-coil sounds, sometimes a short delay, sometimes a simple two-note riff that grates. It is a rhythmic instrument, not a melodic one. The vocals are shouted, spoken, or sung out of tune with confidence, with few effects, sometimes a slapback. The percussion, congas and cowbell, is mixed loud. There is almost no synth in the first wave; the second wave (DFA) adds a pad or a discreet mono synth. Today: record a real guitar with Ableton's Amp and Cabinet, a real cowbell, and keep everything a little dirty.
discopunk.tempo: Disco punk goes fast and pushes: 120 to 135 BPM, often 125 to 130. The feel is played, tense, with a drummer who pulls forward: no swing, rather a slight lead of a few milliseconds on the hi-hats and snare. Set 128 BPM and, if you program, shift the hi-hats 5 ms early and let the velocities vary. The signature is a disco four-on-the-floor played with punk economy: few elements, all of them edgy, an eighth-note cowbell and a bass that repeats a figure until it becomes hypnotic. Nothing floats: everything is tight and a little aggressive.

doomcore.arrangement: The tracks are long, 6 to 9 minutes, and evolve slowly. Intro of 32 to 64 bars with pads and bass, no kick, like an overture. The kick arrives with no build-up, just on beat 1 of a block, and stays. Then elements are added one by one every 16 or 32 bars. A breakdown in the middle, 32 bars, where the kick stops and the pads take over everything. The kick returns, then a long descent: elements leave one by one until only the pads remain. No drop, no roll, no one-beat silence: that would be a lapse in taste. What makes the track playable is its stability: a DJ can mix it for 3 minutes.
doomcore.basse: Basses from beyond the grave: a very low note, held, in sawtooth or square wave, low-passed around 150 Hz, droning under the whole track. In Operator or Analog: a sawtooth on the root two octaves below the midrange, filter at 150 Hz with a little resonance, 2-second release so the notes overlap. One note per 4 or 8 bars, in minor: root, then minor sixth, then fifth, then root. Light sidechain from the kick, 3:1 ratio, 200 ms release, just so the kick stays clean. No extra sine sub: the reverberated kick and this bass are enough, adding more low end would muddy everything.
etapes: Tempo 138 BPM. 909 kick in Simpler, Saturator at 12 dB, then a long Reverb (4 s) mixed at 25%, high-pass at 100 Hz on the reverb.
Kick on all four beats, reverberated snare on 2 and 4, one open hi-hat per bar.
Held sawtooth bass filtered at 150 Hz, one note per 8 bars, in minor.
Pads: a string sample in Simpler, pitched down, 500 ms attack, huge reverb, minor chord held for 4 bars.
Add a slow hoover, one note held for 2 bars with a long release, like a lament.
Arrange over 8 minutes: 48-bar intro without kick, kick entry, additions every 32, 32-bar breakdown, long descent. Gentle limiter.
doomcore.mix: The doomcore mix is the only one in the family that leaves space. The kick is distorted but pushed back by the reverb, at -6 dB peak, and it shares the low end with the held bass. As the Attack book describes, reverb and delay lengthen the perceived shape of a drum: here it is the heart of the sound, the kick seems to hit inside a cathedral. Cut the kick reverb below 100 Hz so as not to drown the low end. Wide stereo pads, bass and kick in mono. Gentle compression on the bus, 2:1 ratio, slow release, 500 ms. Master: light limiter, around -10 LUFS, lower than the rest of hardcore. Dynamics are part of the mourning.

outils.pourquoi: 909 kick with a long decay, moderately distorted then drowned in a reverb lasting several seconds: cavernous rather than crushed.
PCP's sampler in Frankfurt: sampled string and choir pads, transposed down at 12 bits, which gives the funereal color.
The period sequencer on Atari ST to drive the 909 and the S950; the long filter automations over 32 bars were done there.
Layered sawtooth pads with the chorus, filter closed slowly over 16 bars. The apocalyptic backdrop under the kick.
Decay of 4 to 8 seconds, Predelay 40 ms, on a send shared by the kick and the pads: that is the genre's empty cathedral. Valhalla VintageVerb also does the job.
Bass from beyond the grave, a sine one octave below the kick, long release, plus slow FM pads when you don't have a Juno.
Moderate drive, 6 to 8 dB, on the kick before the reverb: enough for presence, not enough for gabber. Simpler reloads the resampled kick.

reperes: Mescalinum United: Symphonies Of Steel (1992): string pads over the PCP kick, the birth of the tone.
The Mover: Waves of Life (1994): the reverberated kick and the held bass, listen to the deliberate slowness.
Pilldriver: Apocalypse Never (1997): the darkest version, pads and cavernous kick over 8 minutes.
Low Entropy: Doomcore Records (2013): the descendants, same vocabulary with modern tools.
doomcore.rythme: The doomcore kick is a distorted 909 as in hardcore techno, but with a long, dark reverb applied to it, which is forbidden everywhere else in the family. In Ableton: Reverb with Size at maximum, Decay 3 to 5 seconds, low-pass at 2 kHz on the reverb, mixed at 25%. Kick on all four beats, sometimes only on 1 and 3 in the heaviest passages. A distant 909 snare on 2 and 4, also reverberated, or a clap with a long plate. Rare hi-hats, one open hi-hat per bar at most. 909 toms pitched low, in slow eighth-note rolls, at the end of 16-bar blocks. The grid stays simple, it is the space that is complex.
doomcore.sons: Apocalyptic pads: strings sampled in an Akai S950 (or any orchestral sample in Simpler), pitched down, filtered, with a huge reverb. Choirs. Organs. All in minor, in two- or three-note chords, held for 4 bars. Juno sawtooths with chorus, 500 ms attack, very dark. The hoover is there but slow, played like a lament, with a long release. Samples from war or science fiction films, distant voices, drowned in reverb. Bells. The vocabulary is that of PCP's hardcore techno, but slowed down, reverberated and darkened. Nothing bright: cut everything above 8 kHz on the pads.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
doomcore.tempo: Doomcore slows hardcore down to between 130 and 150 BPM, often 135-140 with The Mover. It is the only branch of hardcore where the tempo drops below fast techno, and that slowdown is the subject: each kick has time to resonate, and the space between hits becomes a place. No swing, but heaviness: everything is slightly late, from the kicks to the pads. You can delay the pads by 20 to 30 ms for this dragging effect. Program at 138 BPM, eighth-note grid. The feel is that of a funeral march, not a dance. Many tracks keep the same pattern for 8 minutes: patience is a technique.

downtempogenre.arrangement: A track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and is built in layers, not drops. 16-bar intro with the sample and a little percussion, kick and bass at bar 17, full theme at 33. Then alternate two 16-bar sections, A and B: B changes a chord or adds the flute. The breakdown comes around the middle: remove the kick and bass for 8 bars, leave the hi-hats and a long reverb, then come back with everything. Add a new element every 8 bars so the ear has a reason to stay. Finish with a 16-bar outro with kick and hi-hats alone so the DJ can blend in the next track. The track should be able to play in a bar without anyone jumping.
downtempogenre.basse: The bass is round and short, played or sampled, never aggressive. A fingerstyle electric bass, a Moog or an Operator with a sine plus a little triangle, 200 to 400 ms release so the notes don't touch. It plays the root and the fifth, with slides to the minor third, in quarter notes and dotted eighths that follow the kick and then move away from it on the "and" of 4. Stay within a 40 to 120 Hz range, low-pass filter at 300 Hz with a little tube saturation so the note stays audible on a small system. The kick and the bass share the low end: tune the kick to the root and have the bass play just after it, not at the same time.
etapes: Choose a tempo between 88 and 98 BPM and set the global swing to 60% on the sixteenth notes before writing anything.
Cut 2 or 4 bars from a jazz or soul sample, pitch it down a semitone and loop it cleanly.
Program the kit over 2 bars: round kick, muted snare on 3, swung eighth-note hi-hats, humanized shaker.
Write the bass in Operator or with an electric bass, root and fifth, letting the notes breathe after the kick.
Add a Rhodes in ninth chords with tremolo, then the dub effects on sends: dotted-eighth delay and plate.
Arrange over 6 minutes in 16-bar layers with a breakdown in the middle, then mix warm, dynamic, with no aggressive limiter.
downtempogenre.mix: The mix is warm and a little dark. Kick around -10 dB, bass 2 dB below, everything else lower. Cut the low end of the pads and the Rhodes at 150 Hz to leave the bass alone. Light tape saturation on the drum bus and on the Rhodes, then a bus compressor at a 2:1 ratio, 30 ms attack, 100 ms release, reducing by only 1 or 2 dB. Very gentle sidechain between kick and bass, 2 dB maximum, 150 ms release: the pumping should be felt, not heard. Shared reverb on sends, a short room for the drums, a long plate for the snare and vocals. Master around -12 to -10 LUFS, never crushed: the genre lives on its dynamics.

outils.nom: Akai MPC (MPC3000, MPC One, MPC Live II)
outils.pourquoi: That is where the groove comes from: swing set between 58 and 64% on the sixteenth notes, jazz samples chopped on the pads. Ableton with its Groove Pool does the same today.
Kruder & Dorfmeister's sampler in their early days, 20 seconds of memory: one perfect 4-bar loop and you build everything around it.
Ninth chords with slow tremolo and a little overdrive. In software, Spectrasonics Keyscape or AAS Lounge Lizard give the same keyboard.
To chop a flute phrase or four bars of strings and pitch it down a semitone without time-stretching.
The round bass: a sine plus a little triangle, 200 to 400 ms release, low-pass filter at 300 Hz, light saturation.
The muffled kick tuned low with a short tail. 808 samples in a Drum Rack are enough, you don't need the machine.
Slow-chorus pads cut at 2 kHz behind the Rhodes. Softube Model 84 or TAL-U-NO-LX emulate it faithfully in the DAW.
The plate reverb on a send for the snare and the vocal, with a dotted-eighth delay alongside for the dub touch.

reperes: Kruder & Dorfmeister: High Noon (1993): the MPC swing sitting behind the beat and the bass gliding under a brass sample.
Thievery Corporation: Lebanese Blonde (1998): the looped sitar, the nice round dub bass and a beat that never builds tension.
Nightmares On Wax: Les Nuits (1999): the sampled strings, the dusty break and the way the bass anchors the track.
Bonobo: Kiara (2010): layers added every 8 bars and humanized sampled percussion.
downtempogenre.rythme: The kick is round and muffled, often an 808 tuned low or a kick sampled from a soul break, with a short tail. No snap: cut above 4 kHz. The snare is muted: rimshot, a clap doubled with a break snare run through a low-pass filter at 6 kHz. The hi-hats play swung eighth or sixteenth notes with velocities alternating strong and weak, plus a shaker played by hand or humanized by 10% in velocity. Add a slowed-down, filtered jazz or funk drum break under the programmed kit: that is what gives the dust. Basic 2-bar pattern: kick on 1 and the "and" of 2, snare on 3, snare ghost notes at velocity 40 before the 3.
downtempogenre.sons: The Fender Rhodes is the signature instrument: seventh and ninth chords, slow tremolo at 4 Hz, a little overdrive. Jazz and soul samples do the rest: a flute phrase, a trumpet riff or four bars of strings, chopped on an MPC or in Simpler, pitched down one or two semitones. Add a very low vinyl crackle, barely audible, across the whole track. Dub effects are everywhere: dotted-eighth delay on the percussion, plate reverb send on the snare, a filter opening on the pads. The pads come from a Juno or Wavetable, slow chorus, cutoff at 2 kHz. The vocal, if there is one, is a short phrase repeated and drowned in a delay.
sourcesOutils: Gearnews (How To Sound Like Kruder & Dorfmeister)
downtempogenre.tempo: Aim for 85 to 105 BPM, and think of the groove as hip-hop with time on its hands. Swing is the key: on an MPC or in Ableton, set a swing of 58 to 64% on the sixteenth notes, never anything 100% quantized. The feel is laid back, slightly late: shift the hi-hats and percussion 5 to 15 ms after the grid, keep the kick on the beat. The feel is often half-time: the snare falls on 3 rather than on 2 and 4, which makes the track seem to float twice as slowly. Choose a tempo, then test the half-time version and the normal version on the same loop: the right one is the one that makes your head nod without effort.

dreamtrance.arrangement: The structure is that of an instrumental song. Intro on the piano theme alone or with the pad, 16 bars. The kick comes in, then the bass, then the theme returns in full. A 32-bar breakdown with piano and strings, where the theme is played in full, often with a variation. Short roll, return with everything. Second breakdown, shorter, then the finale. The radio version lasts 3 minutes 50, the club version 6 to 7 minutes with a 32-bar drum intro and outro. The theme must come back at least four times: it is what people remember.
dreamtrance.basse: The bass is round, not on the offbeat: it follows the roots of the piano progression in eighth or quarter notes, a Juno-106 or a square wave filtered at 300 Hz, 200 ms release. The progression is typically minor, four chords over 8 bars, with movement from the root to the major sixth then the seventh. A sine sub doubles the roots below 60 Hz. Gentle compression, 3:1 ratio, light sidechain from the kick, 150 ms release. The kick and bass form a warm whole, without pumping. On the breakdown, the bass can play whole notes or disappear with the kick.
etapes: Project at 136 BPM, choose a four-chord minor progression over 8 bars and write an 8-bar piano melody with rests.
Program the piano (M1 Piano or sampled piano) as melody plus broken chords, with an eighth-note delay and hall reverb.
Lay down a simple rhythm: softened 909 kick, soft clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats on eighth notes and offbeats.
Write a round bass that follows the roots in eighth notes, with a sub, no pumping.
Add held strings and a filtered choir, then arrange like a song: piano intro, drop, 32-bar breakdown with the theme, return, finale.
Mix clear and soft, piano up front, master around -10 LUFS.
dreamtrance.mix: The piano is up front, bright, at about -12 dB peak, with a bump at 3 kHz and a hall reverb on a return. The kick is lower than in the rest of the family, around -10 dB. Wide strings cut at 250 Hz. The bass warm, in mono, never distorted. Light compression everywhere, 2:1 or 3:1 ratio, and a master that keeps the dynamics of the breakdown: around -10 LUFS. No saturation, no crushed drum bus. The mix should sound like a 1990s pop record: clean, clear, a little soft in the highs. Check that the piano melody stays readable on a small speaker.

outils.pourquoi: M1 Piano and M1 strings: the melancholic piano as a monophonic melody and the pads behind it. Korg M1 Software in the Korg Collection.
The 16' Piano patch of this Korg workstation is generally cited for Robert Miles' Children, with a short delay and hall reverb.
To sample a real piano or a string ensemble and play it from the keyboard. Ableton Sampler or Kontakt today.
Softened kick, lower than in the rest of the family, clap on 2 and 4. 909 samples with a light low-pass for roundness.
Round bass and warm pads, Juno chorus. TAL-U-NO-LX as an emulation for the dream trance bass, never distorted.
Free sampled piano, soft in the highs, that suits the dream trance piano melody if you don't have an M1.
3-second hall reverb on a return for the piano and strings, Concert Hall mode, for the 1990s pop record feel.

reperes: Robert Miles: Children (1995): the minor piano melody, with its rests, over a simple rhythm, the whole genre in one track
Robert Miles: Fable (1996): the same recipe with a vocal and more prominent strings
Voyager: City Of Light (1994): the Italian version from before Children, more club-oriented, piano and pads
Robert Miles: Children (Tinlicker Remix) (2021): how the theme survives a modern production, bass and drums rewritten
dreamtrance.rythme: The 909 is softened: kick low-passed at 6 kHz, 250 ms decay, soft clap on 2 and 4, often blended with a light acoustic snare. Open hi-hat on the offbeat at low volume, closed hi-hat in eighth notes. It is a simple house-trance rhythm, almost eurodance, with no metallic percussion or aggressive rolls. The snare roll before the drop exists but is short, 2 bars, with a reversed cymbal. Sometimes an eighth-note tambourine for warmth. The drums should never compete with the piano: keep them simple and steady, like an accompaniment.
dreamtrance.sons: The piano lead is everything: a Korg M1 Piano or a piano sampled in the Akai S3000, played as a monophonic melody in the upper register, with a broken-chord accompaniment. Write a melancholic 8-bar melody, in minor, with held notes and rests. Behind it, M1 string pads or a sampled string ensemble, 1-second attack, holding the chords. A filtered choir for thickness. Short delay on the piano, an eighth note, 20% feedback, and a 3-second hall reverb. Trance synths, arpeggio or supersaw, are absent or far in the background: dream trance is a piano over drums.
dreamtrance.tempo: 130 to 140 BPM, in club trance territory, but the feel is that of a song: the tempo serves the piano, not the other way around. Straight grid, no swing. You count in 8-bar phrases that match the piano melody, often 16 bars for a complete theme. The track breathes through breakdowns where the kick disappears and the piano holds the tempo alone. Robert Miles' Children has a piano theme played in eighth and quarter notes, with rests: that breathing is what distinguishes dream trance from uplifting, where everything is filled in.

drillnbass.arrangement: A drill and bass track follows no club form. It lasts between 3 and 8 minutes and is built like a piece: a melody stated over 16 bars, drums coming in with bursts, a development where the drums run wild while the melody stays calm, a passage in 7/8, a return to the theme, a coda with drums alone or melody alone. The changes are abrupt, often every 4 bars. There is no drop, only accumulations and cuts. Squarepusher likes to end with a played bass passage without drums; Aphex Twin with a melody that fades out. Write the melody first, then make it explode with the drums.
drillnbass.basse: Two schools. Squarepusher's: a played electric bass, slap or walking, very fast, recorded live or sampled note by note into Sampler with glissandi and harmonics. If you don't play, a Trilian bass or an Electric Bass in fingered mode, with jazz fusion lines in eighth and sixteenth notes. Aphex Twin's: a TB-303 or an emulation, in an acid sequence with accent and slide, or a simple sine sub under complex melodies. The relationship to the kick is free: the bass plays its own line, often in counterpoint with the melody, and the kick of the break adapts. No sidechain, this isn't club music.
etapes: Set Ableton to 170 BPM. First write a soft IDM melody on Operator (FM bells) with rich chords, 16 bars.
Import an Amen, slice it into 32 slices per bar in Simpler and write a basic two-step.
Add snare bursts in 1/32 over 1 beat, with a per-slice transpose automation.
Create a played bass (Electric Bass or Trilian) as a jazz line, or an acid 303, without sidechain.
Slip in a bar of 7/8 every 8 bars, and send a sound through a cascade resampling chain.
Arrange it like a piece: theme, explosion, development, return, coda with bass or melody alone.
drillnbass.mix: The drill and bass mix is raw and detailed at the same time. The breaks are compressed hard and saturated, with per-slice pitch and volume edits that replace EQ. No sidechain, no rigid bus: each sound lives its own life. The IDM melodies get a long reverb (4 s) and chorus, and sit in front of the drums in level, which is unusual in the family. The played bass is compressed at a 4:1 ratio with a little tube saturation. Allow clips and artifacts: Aphex Twin went looking for them. Master at -10 LUFS, without a brutal limiter, to keep the snare bursts sharp.

outils.pourquoi: Squarepusher's early sampler: breaks resampled in cascade, a sound reloaded and reworked several times in a row.
Aphex Twin's acid lines with accent and slide; an emulation like D16 Phoscyon, or Roar plus Auto Filter on a square.

outils.nom: Commodore Amiga with OctaMED or ProTracker
outils.pourquoi: Trackers for editing breaks in thirty-second notes and slipping in bars of 7/8; Renoise is their direct heir.
The MIDI sequencer of the Rephlex era, for slice tracks transposed automatically bar by bar.
Bursts and stutters on the breaks, with Grain Delay behind it for vertigo; the effects are extreme, not decorative.
Pitched acoustic instruments and glissandi, one note per key, with FM harmonics from Operator for the bells.
Jazz fusion bass in fingered mode for those who don't play Squarepusher's electric bass, in eighth and sixteenth notes.
Squarepusher's lab for his own synthesis and processing patches, alongside his hardware Eventide Orville.

reperes: Squarepusher: Port Rhombus (1996): played bass and bursting breaks, the soft melody on top, the manifesto.
Aphex Twin: Girl/Boy Song (1996): strings and piano against crazy drums, the contrast that defines the style.
u-Ziq: Hasty Boom Alert (1997): childlike melodies and breaks that speed up without warning.
Aphex Twin: Windowlicker (1999): drill and bass turning pop, pitched vocals, breaks both precise and deranged.
drillnbass.rythme: The manic break edits of the brief: start from an Amen or a jazz break, slice it into 32 or 64 slices per bar, and write the patterns note by note in the piano roll, in thirty-second notes. Alternate recognizable two-step passages with bursts of 8 to 16 hits in 1/32 on the snare, raising or lowering the pitch of each slice by a semitone (transpose automation). Use trackers as a method: each slice has its own pitch, volume and effect. Add 808 percussion sounds (cowbell, clap) in counterpoint. Squarepusher sometimes plays the pattern on a real kit or a pad: record by hand, then quantize to 1/32.
drillnbass.sons: The brief cites Amiga trackers, the Akai S950, the TB-303 and Cubase. Cascade resampling is Aphex Twin's method: a sound is recorded, transformed, re-recorded, until it becomes unrecognizable, then replayed on the keyboard. The melodies are IDM: soft pads, music boxes, detuned pianos, synthetic strings, with rich chords and childlike melodies that contrast with the violence of the drums. Use Operator for FM bells, a Sampler for pitched acoustic instruments, a 303 (or Roar plus Auto Filter on a square) for the acid lines. The effects are extreme: Beat Repeat in bursts, Grain Delay, real-time pitch shift.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (5 of the Best Software and Hardware Trackers)
drillnbass.tempo: Drill and bass has no club tempo: between 150 and 200 BPM, often with tempo changes inside the track, and bars in 7/8 or 5/4 slipped in without warning. The feel is that of a virtuoso drummer who has had too much coffee: the breaks are edited in thirty-second and sixty-fourth notes, with rolls that are impossible to play. What sets it apart from jungle is the lack of function: it isn't made for mixing, it's made for listening. Set your DAW to 170 BPM to start, but allow yourself to change time signature every 4 bars.

drone.arrangement: The form is a single gesture: a rise over 5 to 8 minutes then a descent, or a plateau that thickens. Add one harmonic per minute (one more voice, a partial opening up in the filter), then remove them in reverse order. The Attack book builds a drone in eight layers spread from the low end to the air and advises bringing them in and out gently with automation: that is exactly a drone arrangement. Length 10 to 20 minutes, never silence, never a cut. Requiem for Dying Mothers moves this way: the strings rise so slowly that you only notice the peak after you've passed it. The only event is the appearance of a new note.
drone.basse: The drone is the bass. Its fundamental is low, A1 at 55 Hz or E1 at 41 Hz, and everything else is its harmonics. Work the intervals in just intonation rather than equal temperament: fifth 3:2, major third 5:4. In Operator or Wavetable, set the fine pitch of each voice in cents (the just third is 14 cents below the tempered third), or use the microtuning in Surge XT. A pure fifth doesn't beat, a tempered fifth beats slowly: that's a compositional choice. Sunn O))) tune their guitars two whole tones down on tube amps, and the sub comes from the amp's saturation, not from a synth. No sidechain, obviously.
etapes: Choose a low fundamental (E1, 41 Hz) and record a guitar note with an EBow, or an Operator sine, lasting 30 seconds, then loop it without a click.
Layer a second copy of the same note detuned by 8 cents, and a fifth in just intonation (2 cents above the tempered fifth).
Run everything through Amp and Cabinet with moderate drive, then into a 20-second reverb with a high-pass at 200 Hz on the return.
Add two high layers: a filtered partial around 2 kHz and a granular crackle above 4 kHz, each at a level well below the low end.
Arrange over 12 minutes: each layer comes in with a 90-second fade, one minute apart, then goes out in reverse order.
Mix without compression, low end in mono below 300 Hz, final level around -18 LUFS.
drone.mix: No compression, or a very slow one with release above one second, and manual gain riding on the rises. The Attack book notes that in a layered drone, low sounds are mixed louder than high ones, following the ear's equal-loudness curve, and advises summing to mono everything below 300 Hz to avoid phase issues between layers. A high-pass on the reverb returns at 200 Hz. Tube saturation thickens without raising the level. Aim for -16 to -20 LUFS, peak -1 dB. Over 15 minutes, 2 to 4 kHz gets tiring: keep it below the low end. Listen once all the way through before exporting, at real volume.

outils.pourquoi: The EBow makes the string vibrate endlessly: a single note held for 30 seconds, the basis of Stars of the Lid before the strings and piano.
The amp that gave Sunn O))) its name: slow saturation at huge volume, low end that moves air. Guitar Rig 7 or Neural DSP imitate it in the DAW.
Moderate drive on the low layers, Bass or Heavy model, then a 4x12 Cabinet; thickens the drone without raising the level, before the 20-second reverb.
Free long reverb with a high-pass at 200 Hz on the return; the freeze turns a guitar chord into a continuous carpet for Tim Hecker or Kali Malone.
Stretches a piano, organ or string note 10 to 50 times to make a layer that barely moves anymore; use it on acoustic sources.
For the high layers: granular crackle above 4 kHz from a percussive sample, like the eight-layer drone in the Attack book.
Tube saturation on the drone bus, style A or N, drive at 3, to glue the layers and bring out the beating harmonics.
Éliane Radigue's modular, oscillators beating over hours; with no common emulation, an Operator sine detuned by 8 cents conveys the idea.

reperes: Stars of the Lid: Requiem for Dying Mothers Part 1 (2001): strings and guitars rising for minutes, the crescendo as the only form.
Sunn O))): It Took the Night to Believe (2005): guitars tuned very low on tube amps, one chord every 20 seconds, the sub coming from the saturation.
Tim Hecker: Chimeras (2006): the digital drone, granulated and saturated, with the melody surfacing beneath the material.
Stars of the Lid: Dungtitled (in A major) (2007): a single sustained major chord, the beating between voices as the only movement.
drone.rythme: No percussion. The rhythm is the inner life of the sound: the beating of the harmonics, the tremolo of a tube amp, the bow passing over the string again every 8 seconds, the tape loops coming back around. To build it in the DAW, layer two copies of the same sound detuned by 5 to 15 cents: the slow beating appears on its own. A very slow Auto Pan (0.1 Hz) gives a rotation. The Attack book suggests a cymbal run through an arpeggiator with randomized velocity, playback position and pan, then a Grain Delay: this produces a generative crackle that replaces percussion without marking time. With Sunn O))), the rhythm is a guitar chord struck every 20 seconds.
drone.sons: The brief lists electric guitar, tube amp, tape and bow. In the DAW: Ableton's Amp and Cabinet, Guitar Rig 7 or Neural DSP for amp saturation, an EBow or a bow on the string for infinite sustain. Stars of the Lid drown guitars and real strings in a long reverb, then stretch them. Éliane Radigue worked on an ARP 2500, Kali Malone on a pipe organ, Tim Hecker on granulated and saturated piano and organ. Tools: Paulstretch, Granulator II, Valhalla Supermassive, Decapitator, Chow Tape Model, a reverb's freeze. The Attack book points out that a more minimal drone is built with a single synthesis technique, granular or FM.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Textural Drone and Movement & Change)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone chapter)
Artists in DSP, Best VST Plugins for Ambient and Drone Music
drone.tempo: No tempo, and time is counted in minutes: a drone piece is a single note or a single chord held for 10 or 20 minutes. The difference from Eno's ambient is that there aren't even events: the movement is entirely in the timbre. With Stars of the Lid, a crescendo lasts 2 or 3 minutes. Set a BPM of 40 only for synced LFOs, otherwise work in seconds. What gives a sense of pulse is beating: two close notes, for example A2 at 110 Hz and a second voice at 113 Hz, produce 3 beats per second. Change the gap and you change the rhythm. It's the only metronome in the genre.

drumandbass.arrangement: A club drum and bass track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and follows a form that has become standard. A 32-bar intro with pad, light percussion and a white noise riser over the last 8. First drop at bar 33, 32 or 64 bars, with all the elements. A 32-bar breakdown: the drums stop, the pad and a vocal remain, a build-up announces the second drop. Second drop, often with a bass variation or a note “switch” halfway through. A 32-bar outro that removes elements one by one. Mark each 16-bar block with a fill or an FX. The DJ counts in 32s: respect that.
drumandbass.basse: Two basses, always. The sub is an Operator sine wave, between 40 and 55 Hz, played in half-bar notes or syncopated eighth notes, with no processing at all. The Reese is the second layer, the one detailed in the Attack Magazine book: two sawtooth oscillators detuned a few cents in opposite directions, in mono mode with a short glide, 4 to 6 unison voices spread in stereo, and a low-pass filter that moves by envelope then by slow LFO. High-pass the Reese at 100 Hz to leave the sub alone at the bottom. The kick is light and short so the bass dominates the low end. Typical notes: root, fifth, and a passing minor seventh.
etapes: Set Ableton to 174 BPM and program a two-step: kick on 1 and the “and” of 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Stack the snare (break, 909, clap) and add an Amen break high-pass filtered at 300 Hz in the background.
Create the sub on Operator (sine, 45 Hz) and the Reese on Serum or Wavetable: two saws detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide, 6-voice unison.
High-pass the Reese at 100 Hz, sidechain the sub from the kick, and check the low end in mono.
Add a cold minor pad and riser FX every 16 bars.
Arrange intro 32, drop 64, breakdown 32, drop 64, outro 32, with parallel compression on the drum bus.
drumandbass.mix: The DnB mix is surgical. Kick and sub don't overlap: kick high-passed at 50 Hz with a peak at 80 Hz, sub alone below, mono. The Reese is cut at 100 Hz and spread in stereo above. Every drum element has its own EQ: snare boosted at 200 Hz and 5 kHz, hi-hats cut below 500 Hz. The drum bus gets parallel compression and light saturation. Short reverbs (0.8 s) on the snare, long ones on the pads only. Sidechain the sub from the kick at a 4:1 ratio, release 60 ms, so the two don't step on each other. Master at -7 LUFS with a two-stage limiter, for big systems.

outils.pourquoi: The sampler of the Metalheadz and RAM studios: breaks edited to the step, 16-bit resolution cleaner than the S950.
The red synth of the 1996-2002 years: Reese from two detuned saws, stabs and cold pads; Nord Lead A1 or Analog can replace it.
The sequencer of classic DnB, still used by part of the UK scene for MIDI editing of breaks.
Short kick and snare layered over the Apache, Think or Amen breaks for club punch at 170 BPM.
The genre's standard synth since 2015: Reese, wavetable basses and resampling, with two oscillators detuned in opposite directions.
The native alternative to Serum for the Reese: unison, LFO on wavetable position, mono output with short glide.
Pure sine for the sub at 40 or 50 Hz, separate from the Reese, which keeps only the midrange.
The Reese documented in the book: Monster wavetables, 6-voice unison, glide, Monark LP4 filter, no external effects.

reperes: Goldie: Inner City Life (1994): Diane Charlemagne's voice, breaks that transform over seven minutes, DnB as album music.
Adam F: Metropolis (1997): the Reese growling under sharp breaks, the Metalheadz sound at its peak.
Roni Size: Brown Paper Bag (1997): double bass played then sampled, jazz breaks, Bristol DnB.
Andy C: Body Rock (1999): the dry two-step and the bass that switches in the middle, the quintessential club record.
drumandbass.rythme: Build the beat in layers, not from a whole break. A short, dry kick (909 or sample, 60 to 90 Hz) on beat 1 and the “and” of 3. A stacked snare: a break sample for the body, a 909 snare for the attack, a discreet clap for width, on 2 and 4. Only then, a break (Amen, Think, Apache) in the background, high-pass filtered at 300 Hz, which brings the hi-hats and ghost notes. Hi-hats programmed in sixteenth notes with alternating velocities of 100 and 55, and an open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4. The brief talks about breaks edited to the step: shift some sixteenth notes by 10 to 20 ms to humanize.
drumandbass.sons: The brief cites the Akai S3000, the Nord Lead and the TR-909. The Nord Lead gives cold pads and sawtooth leads heard on Goldie and Adam F records. Today, Serum or Ableton's Wavetable do the Reese; Operator does the sub. The pads are wide and dark: minor chord with a ninth, low-pass filter at 2 kHz, 5-second reverb. Transition FX (filtered white noise risers, impacts, reversed cymbals) are essential for marking the 16 bars. The parallel drum processing cited in the brief is a signature: a copy of the drum bus crushed by a compressor at a 20:1 ratio, blended at 30% under the original.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Basslines chapter, Reese bass)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable chapter)
Attack Magazine (Reese Bass Redux, Techno Reese Bass with Massive X)
drumandbass.tempo: Drum and bass settles between 170 and 174 BPM, with 174 as the standard since the late 1990s. What changes compared with jungle is regularity: the break is no longer played whole but rebuilt on a grid, step by step, and the groove comes from precise placement rather than the drummer's swing. The basic pattern is the two-step: kick on beat 1, snare on beats 2 and 4, kick again on the “and” of 3. At 174 BPM, this structure sounds like a heavy 87 BPM, which explains why the genre has held up through thirty years of clubs. The DAW swing stays at 0; the movement comes from the ghost notes.

drumfunk.arrangement: A drumfunk track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and is arranged like a jazz piece. A 16-bar intro: one break alone, filtered, with an ambient sample. The sub comes in at bar 17. Then the breaks take turns: a new break every 8 or 16 bars, sometimes two at once, with transitions by a one-bar cut or by a fill taken from the break itself. The breakdown in the middle removes all breaks but one, filtered, over 16 bars. There is no drop in the club sense: there are changes of drummer. The ending is a last break alone for 16 bars. The structure follows the attentive listener, not the DJ.
drumfunk.basse: The drumfunk bass is a pure sine sub, almost always, as on Paradox's Reinforced records: an Operator or a sampled sine, between 40 and 55 Hz, playing few notes, long ones, on the root and a passing fifth or fourth. It is there to give the breaks a floor, not to draw attention. No Reese, no distortion. A variant, with Photek, uses a sampled double bass or a played electric bass, with grit. The relationship to the kick is particular: since the kicks in the breaks are light and variable, the sub holds the bottom on its own, without sidechain, and it is cut clean before the break changes.
etapes: Set Ableton to 168 BPM. Find three rare funk or jazz-rock breaks, import them without warping and transpose them toward the tempo.
Cut each break hit by hit, by hand, right at the transient, and put the slices in one Drum Rack per break.
Recompose a 4-bar pattern with hits from the three breaks, keeping their original placement.
Add an Operator sine sub, long notes, root and fourth, without sidechain.
Run one of the breaks through Redux at 12 bits and Saturator, leave the others clean, slow compression on each.
Arrange by passing the baton between breaks every 8 or 16 bars, a breakdown with a single break, and a master at -9 LUFS.
drumfunk.mix: The breaks are the mix. Each break has its own EQ (high-pass at 40 Hz, a 2 dB cut at 300 Hz if needed), its slow compression, and sometimes its saturation. The breaks are panned slightly differently (one 10% left, one right) to tell them apart. The sub is mono, alone below 80 Hz, unprocessed. No reverb on the breaks, except what's on the record. Gentle parallel compression on the breaks bus (30% mix) adds density. Master at -9 or -10 LUFS: drumfunk needs dynamics so the hits keep their relief. It's the quietest genre in the family, and that's a choice.

outils.pourquoi: The 12-bit grit on rare breaks, kept on purpose by Paradox and Fanu for the color of 1970s studio records.
Hit-by-hit editing: each hit of a whole break assigned to a key, replayed in polyrhythm.
Photek's sequencer in the Ni Ten Ichi Ryu era: MIDI tracks of slices edited to the tick.
Paradox still uses it in the studio and on stage; the tracker enforces the discipline of hit-by-hit placement.
One pad per hit of the sliced break, to recompose a whole drum part without a loop, with Simpler in each cell.
12 bits on the main break only, with a Saturator Analog Clip behind it; the other breaks stay clean.
Slow 1176 or LA-2A style compression on each break, 4:1 ratio, release 200 ms, to make the cymbals breathe.
A discreet sub under the breaks, one held note per bar, to leave all the room to the drums.

reperes: Photek: Ni Ten Ichi Ryu (1997): breaks edited into polyrhythms, silence as an instrument, the absolute reference.
Paradox: A Certain Sound (2003): a rare break played whole, a sub, almost nothing else, and it holds up.
Source Direct: Snake Style (1995): hits that take turns and answer each other, drumfunk before the name.
Fanu: Siren Song (2005): the Finnish school, recomposed breaks with a more modern grit.
drumfunk.rythme: The rare whole breaks of the brief: dig for funk, jazz-rock and 1970s soundtrack records, and sample breaks nobody uses. Load each break into Ableton, cut it hit by hit (not bar by bar), by hand, placing each cut at the exact start of the transient. Then recompose: a kick from one break, a snare from another, a hi-hat from a third, keeping each hit's original placement relative to the beat, which preserves the feel. Paradox insists on respecting the break: the pattern must stay audible. No 909 kick, no stacked snare: the hits are the drummers' own. Change pattern every 2 or 4 bars.
drumfunk.sons: The brief cites the Akai S950 for grit and the Akai S3000 for precision, a real combination in Paradox's setup: the S950 to dirty things up, the S3000 to edit. In Ableton, run the breaks through Redux (12 bits, light downsampling) and a Saturator in Digital Clip mode for the first one, and leave the others clean. The rest is sparse: a Rhodes or jazz flute sample, a vibraphone chord, Japanese film dialogue, rare percussion sounds (tabla, congas) taken from the same records. The vintage compression of the brief is a slow compressor on each break, 1176 or LA-2A style (Glue Compressor, 4:1 ratio, release 200 ms), which makes the cymbals breathe.
sources: Drum&BassArena, interview “Paradox: A Lesson In Breakbeats” (breakbeat.co.uk)
drumfunk.tempo: Drumfunk is played between 165 and 172 BPM, a bit slower than standard DnB, to let the breaks breathe. The feel lies entirely in the original drummer's playing: the swing isn't a setting, it's that of the 1972 take you sampled. What sets it apart from DnB is the absence of a grid: the patterns change constantly, bar after bar, with polyrhythms (three against two) that come from the breaks themselves. Set your DAW to the tempo of the break once sped up, and add no quantization. The track is a conversation between several drummers who never played together.

drumstep.arrangement: A drumstep track lasts 4 to 5 minutes and follows a festival form. A 16-bar intro on a synth theme. A 16-bar build-up in DnB two-step with supersaw and roll. A 32-bar half-time drop with the talking bass. A 32-bar breakdown: piano or supersaw, vocal, build-up. A 32-bar second drop, often in DnB two-step this time, or in half-time with a different bass. A 16-bar outro. Alternating DnB then half-time is the trump card: Pendulum and Knife Party play it both ways. A “switch” from half-time to two-step in the middle of the drop makes a crowd jump.
drumstep.basse: The brostep basses at 87/174 from the brief: in Serum or Massive, a wavetable with an LFO synced to the cutoff or to the wavetable position, at changing divisions (quarter note, eighth note, eighth-note triplet) to give the talking “wub”. Record several versions and alternate them bar by bar in the drop. A separate sine sub holds the root, low-pass filtered at 80 Hz. The bass plays the half-time rhythm: it's active between the kick on 1 and the snare on 3, in eighth or quarter notes, then goes quiet or holds a note on 4. Sidechain the bass from the kick and the snare, 5:1 ratio, release 80 ms.
etapes: Set Ableton to 174 BPM. Program two drum clips: a DnB two-step, and a half-time with the snare on 3 only.
Stack the half-time snare with a 909, a clap, a break and white noise, short reverb.
Create three basses in Serum or Massive with LFOs at different divisions on the cutoff, and record them to audio.
Alternate the basses bar by bar in the drop, with a sine sub below 80 Hz and a sidechain from kick and snare.
Add a 7-voice unison supersaw for the build-up and the breakdown, plus an 8-bar white noise riser.
Arrange intro 16, build-up 16 in DnB, drop 32 half-time, breakdown 32, second drop 32 in two-step, outro 16.
drumstep.mix: The drumstep mix is the EDM mix: very loud, very wide, very clean. The kick is a stack with lots of transient, high-passed at 40 Hz, and the half-time snare is the loudest thing in the track along with the kick. The basses are mono below 150 Hz and very wide above (Utility or a chorus in Mid/Side). Sidechain everywhere: everything that isn't drums ducks 4 to 6 dB on every kick and every snare. Multiband Dynamics on the bass bus to contain the midrange. Master at -5 LUFS with a clipper and a limiter, and a high-end exciter on the main bus. Compare with a Monstercat reference at the same level.

outils.pourquoi: The genre's DAW: half-time drops at 174 BPM, Drum Buss and Track Delay on the drums, resampling the bass to audio.
Brostep basses at 87/174: modulated wavetables, FM, filters in series, then audio export and reloading for the growls.
The synth of the first Knife Party and Pendulum drops: wobbles from an LFO synced to the filter, Dimension Expander.
Festival supersaw in 8-voice unison for the breakdown leads, and native wavetable basses.
OTT on the bass and leads for EDM aggression, with a mono Utility below 120 Hz after it.
FM basses and layering in a single instrument for the half-time drops, as in Attack's halftime tutorials.
Trap and hip-hop kicks, snares and fills for the half-time drop; the quality of the one-shots matters more than how many you have.
Mono below 120 Hz on the bass, width pushed on the supersaws, output gain controlled before the limiter.

reperes: Pendulum: The Vulture (2010): the half-time drop laid on a 174 grid, going from DnB to dubstep in the same track.
Knife Party: Bonfire (2012): the talking bass, the huge snare, the festival format pushed all the way.
Camo and Krooked: All Fall Down (2011): melodic drumstep, pop vocal and supersaw, the radio side.
Delta Heavy: Get By (2012): the switch between half-time and two-step in the middle of the drop.
drumstep.rythme: Two beats in one track. For the DnB sections: classic two-step, kick on 1 and the “and” of 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenth notes. For the half-time drop: kick on 1, snare on 3, and that's it for the skeleton. The drop snare is huge, stacked: a 909 snare, a clap, a break sample, a layer of white noise, with a short, wide reverb. The hi-hats stay in sixteenth notes at 174 BPM to keep the energy, which creates the contrast. Add tom fills and snare rolls in thirty-second notes over the last 2 bars before each drop.
drumstep.sons: The brief cites Ableton Live, Massive and Serum: the EDM toolkit of the 2010s. Massive gives the “growl” basses (Scrapyard wavetable, Scream filter, LFO on position and cutoff). Serum gives the FM basses and the leads. The festival supersaws come from a Wavetable or a Serum in 7-voice unison, 30% detune, as block major chords during the build-ups and breakdowns. Add impacts, 8-bar white noise risers, chopped vocals with a vocoder or transposition, “lasers” and crowd screams. The EDM production of the brief also means a broad palette: breakdown piano, strings, a pop vocal.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (Halftime Drops In The Style Of Nikki Nair)
drumstep.tempo: Drumstep is played at 174 BPM for the grid, but the drop is half-time: the snare lands on beat 3 only, which gives an 87 BPM feel, the feel of dubstep. The trick is that the intro and build-ups are in DnB two-step, then the drop switches to half-time, and sometimes returns to DnB for a second drop. This interplay between the two speeds is the genre's only subject. No swing, everything is quantized. If you write at 174 BPM with a snare on 3 and a kick on 1, you're in drumstep; add the snare on 2 and 4 and you're back in DnB.

dub.arrangement: A dub is the version of a song: first compose or source a complete riddim of 3 to 4 minutes, with vocals, then create the dub by deconstructing it. The structure comes from the mutes: 8 bars of bass and drums, the skank comes in sent into the echo, a vocal fragment cascades away, the drums cut for 2 bars with only the echo, then return. Every time an element comes in, it's sent into the delay; every time it goes out, its tail remains. The climax is feedback rising until it screams, then cut dead. Length 3 to 5 minutes, 6 to 7 for an extended version. Record the dub in a single take of console automation, mistakes included: the spontaneity of the live mix is part of the style.
dub.basse: The dub bass is the foundation, the only thing that never goes into the echo. An electric bass played fingerstyle, low, round, with 2-bar lines that leave silences and come back on 1 or 3: root, fifth, octave, a pass through the minor seventh. Use a fingerstyle bass sample with the top cut at 1.5 kHz, or a sine plus triangle synth if you want a more electronic bass. Compress it hard (6:1 ratio, attack 20 ms, release 200 ms, 6 dB of reduction) for constant sustain, and boost 3 dB at 60 Hz. It has to be felt in the body on a sound system: monophonic, no effects, huge. King Tubby would drop it out and bring it back: automate 2-bar mutes, never longer.
etapes: Build a riddim at 70 BPM: one drop on an acoustic kit, fingerstyle bass over 2 bars with silences, organ skank on the offbeats.
Add a melodica or a horn in short phrases and a few vocal fragments.
Create an Echo return in tape mode, dotted eighth, feedback 70%, Wobble on, Saturator in the loop, high-pass at 300 Hz.
Create a second return with a short spring reverb for the snare and stabs.
Record in one take the automation of the sends, mutes and a high-pass on the mix, playing it as you would a console.
Check the bass in mono on a subwoofer, cut below 35 Hz, master at -12 LUFS.
dub.mix: Dub is a mix you perform: the mixing is the composition. The low end is huge and mono, cut clean below 35 Hz, with the bass and kick touching without sidechain. High-pass filters are used as instruments: an EQ Eight automation that cuts everything below 500 Hz for 2 bars, then opens again, is a classic move. The Space Echo has to saturate: put a Saturator or a Drive in the return loop, and a high-pass at 300 Hz in the return so the echo doesn't muddy the low end. The spring reverb stays short and metallic. Little master compression, a Glue at 2 dB, and a limiter with headroom: aim for -12 LUFS, but above all weight below 100 Hz, to be checked on a subwoofer.

outils.pourquoi: The three-head tape echo with built-in spring, on the skank, the vocal and the snare; feedback pushed up to self-oscillation, then cut dead.
The main instrument: aux sends, mutes, brutal high-pass played live; recreate it by recording one take of EQ Eight and send automation.
Tubby's tube spring reverb, for big snare splashes; hit the unit for the crash, u-he Twangström imitates it.
The spring of Lee Perry's Black Ark, short and metallic on stabs and vocals, one of the keys to the studio's dirty, spongy sound.
The native Space Echo: tape mode on a return, dotted eighth, feedback 50 to 90%, Wobble on, Saturator in the loop, high-pass at 300 Hz.
The most faithful RE-201 emulation: three heads, spring and all twelve routing modes, for when you want the exact behavior of runaway tape.
The spring on the second return, for the snare and stabs: Spring algorithm, or Convolution with a spring impulse, very short.
Dedicated spring reverb, with three models and an LFO on tension: closer to the Fisher than generic reverbs for snare splashes.

reperes: Augustus Pablo: King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown (1976): the melodica in the echo, the bass holding everything, Tubby's console slicing it up.
King Tubby: Dub Fi Gwan (1976): the brutal mutes, the snare in the spring, empty space as an instrument.
The Upsetters: Blackboard Jungle Dub (1973): Lee Perry in the studio, the dirty, saturated Black Ark sound.
Scientist: Dance of the Vampires (1981): the next generation's dub, cleaner, with more spectacular effects.
dub.rythme: The drums are played, then torn apart at the console. The one drop: kick and rimshot or snare together on 3, hi-hat in eighth or sixteenth notes with an open hat on the and of 4. The steppers beat, later on, puts the kick on all four beats. Program on a dry acoustic kit, then process: the snare gets a spring reverb (Spring mode in Hybrid Reverb, or Convolution Reverb with a spring impulse) and a Space Echo delay in dotted eighths, feedback 60%. The dub move is to cut the drums all at once and leave only the echo tail: automate the track mute and let the delay return keep spinning. Add occasional percussion, timbales, bell, with every hit sent into the echo.
dub.sons: The brief names the console, the Roland RE-201 Space Echo, tape echo, spring reverb and the sound system. The console is the instrument: aux sends, mutes, brutal high-pass EQ. In Ableton, put Echo in tape mode on a return, feedback between 50 and 90%, time in dotted eighths or triplets, with the Wobble function for tape instability, and automate the feedback live for flights up to self-oscillation. A second return track with a short spring reverb for snares and stabs. The musical material comes from a reggae riddim: guitar or organ skank on the offbeats, melodica as with Augustus Pablo, horns in short phrases, vocals in fragments of half a word.
sourcesOutils: Sound On Sound (Lee Perry, Back On The Controls)
Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (dub techno chapter)
dub.tempo: Dub takes the reggae tempo, 60 to 80 BPM in feel, or 120 to 160 if you count double, with the one drop: the kick and the snare land together on 3, the first beat stays empty. What changes compared with reggae: the tempo doesn't move, but time is warped by the echoes. A delay in triplets or dotted eighths turns a single snare hit into a rhythmic cascade. In Ableton, set 70 BPM, grid in eighth notes, and think in 4-beat bars with the pulse on 3. The swing is light, 52 to 54%, played by the drummer; the guitarist and the keyboard player hit the skank on the offbeats of 2 and 4 (the ands), always a little ahead.

dubstep.arrangement: A 5 to 6 minute track for the DJ. A 16 to 32-bar intro: atmosphere, dub percussion, a vocal sample. The drop at bar 32 or 48: the sub arrives with the snare on 3, no build-up, just one bar of silence before. 32 bars of drop where the bass changes every 8: a note change, the LFO opening up, one more percussion. A 16-bar break with the reverb and the sample, then a second drop. A 16-bar outro with drums alone. No build-up with a riser: the contrast comes from emptiness. Keep holes of a whole bar, that's where the subwoofer breathes.
dubstep.basse: The bass is the subject. First a pure sine sub between 40 and 60 Hz, long notes of a half or whole note, in Operator or a simple Massive oscillator. Then, on a second track, a mid bass: sawtooth or square through a low-pass with a slow LFO on the cutoff, synced at 1/2 or 1/4, for the meditative wobble. The notes follow the root and the fifth, in minor. For the darker side, a Reese with two oscillators detuned in opposite directions, mono, with glide, as in the Reese chapter of the Attack Magazine book. Kick and sub don't double each other: the kick hits, the sub settles in after.
etapes: Set Ableton to 140 BPM, place a kick on 1 and a huge snare on 3, nothing else.
Add sparse dub percussion with a dotted-eighth delay and a spring reverb.
Create a sine sub in long notes, then a mid bass with a slow LFO on the cutoff, at 1/2 or 1/4.
Place a vocal sample or an instrument on a 4-second reverb, one note every 4 bars.
Arrange: 32 bars of intro, drop with no build-up, a 16-bar break, second drop.
Mix the sub in mono and clean, lighten the kick, master around -9 LUFS, check on a subwoofer.
dubstep.mix: Everything is built for a sound system. Sub in mono, cut below 30 Hz, never saturated, around -6 dB peak. The kick is short and light, high-passed at 50 Hz, it leaves the sub alone at the bottom: the Attack Magazine book points out that against a Reese, the kick has to stay thin and tight. Snare compressed hard, 6:1 ratio, then long reverb on a send. Gentle sidechain of the mid bass from the kick. Mid bass lightly saturated to come through on small systems. Moderate master, around -9 LUFS, no brutal limiter. Listen on a subwoofer or closed-back headphones, checking that the sub is there and that nothing masks 40 to 80 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: The wobble synth: sawtooth into a low-pass, LFO synced at 1/2 or 1/4 on the cutoff, long notes in minor.
Skream made Midnight Request Line in FruityLoops with four plugins; Benga and Coki also worked in it, in Croydon.
Pure sine sub between 40 and 60 Hz, half or whole notes, on a track separate from the mid bass.
For assembly: grid in eighth notes, almost empty bars, reverb and delay sends for the dub space.
Tape delay in dotted eighths, feedback at 40% and filtering, sent in touches on the snare and the rimshots.
Long reverb of 3 to 6 seconds on a send, high-pass before it, for the tail that follows the snare on beat 3.
For today's dubstep: sub, mid bass and a Reese with two detuned oscillators, mono glide, as in the book's recipe.

reperes: Skream: Midnight Request Line (2005): melodic halfstep, snare on 3 and a gently undulating bass.
Loefah: Mud (2005): emptiness as an instrument, minimal sub and isolated percussion.
Digital Mystikz: Anti War Dub (2006): dub reverb and subwoofer meditation, every sound has its place.
Commodo: Kibosh (2019): the original strain still alive, with finer sound design.
dubstep.rythme: Kick on beat 1, often a second one on the “and” of 2 or the “a” of 2. Snare on beat 3, huge, layered with a clap and a rimshot, with a long reverb. No snare on 2 and 4. Sparse hi-hats: every other eighth note, or a triplet pattern that appears then disappears. Dub percussion: rimshots, wood blocks, sidesticks run through a dotted-eighth delay with feedback at 40%. An isolated percussion hit with a spring reverb. Short, dry kick, trimmed so it doesn't fight the sub. Variable velocities on the percussion so it breathes. The silence after the snare is part of the pattern.
dubstep.sons: Dub space: a long reverb of 3 to 6 seconds on a send, a tape delay in dotted eighths with filtering, sent in touches on the snare and the percussion. Massive for the basses, Ableton or Cubase for assembly. Short samples: a Jamaican vocal phrase, an Eastern instrument, a gust of wind, a dub siren. Heavily filtered pads, almost inaudible, to set the mood. A piano or a bell playing one note every 4 bars. Everything is treated in gray and dark. The rule: few elements, each with its place and its reverb tail. This isn't yet the aggressive sound design of brostep.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter, Reese bass (wavetable), and its note on the kick against the Reese
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, Skream on how he made Midnight Request Line
Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter, Reese bass (wavetable)
dubstep.tempo: 140 BPM, no argument: that's the genre's tempo, inherited from 2-step. But the feel is halfstep: the snare lands on beat 3 only, which gives the impression of a track at 70 BPM. That's what your 2-step parent doesn't have: the felt slowness. The swing is light, 52 to 56%, sometimes replaced by a triplet feel on the hats. The spaces matter as much as the hits. In Ableton, set the grid to eighth notes and leave bars almost empty. A 2-bar loop is enough, the variation comes from the bass and the dub space, not the drums.

dubstyle.arrangement: A dubstyle track follows the hardstyle structure but with a dubstep drop: a 16 to 32-bar intro with the hardstyle kick, a 32-bar break with the supersaw lead and the vocal, an 8-bar build-up, then the half-time drop, 32 bars, with the wobble and the snare on 3, often alternating with 4 or 8-bar passages where the 4/4 hardstyle kick comes back. Second break, second drop that can be the reverse (hardstyle drop with wobbles in the background). Ending on the hardstyle kick. What makes the track playable for a hardstyle DJ is the constant tempo at 150 and the 4/4 intro.
dubstyle.basse: Two basses as well. The hardstyle reverse bass: the kick tail reversed (or a tail sample with a slow 100 ms attack) played on the offbeats, which seems to suck toward the next kick. And the dubstep wobble: in Massive, a sawtooth or a wavetable, low-pass filter modulated by an LFO synced in eighth or sixteenth notes (1/8, then 1/16, then dotted 1/8 for variety), with distortion after the filter. The wobble is played in long notes, one per bar or per half bar, on the root and the fifth. Sidechain both basses from the kick, 6:1 ratio, release 60 ms. Cut the wobble below 40 Hz and add a separate sine sub if the mix lacks low end.
etapes: Tempo 150 BPM. Build a hardstyle kick (short tok plus a saturated, tuned tail), kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4.
Make the reverse bass: reverse the kick tail, trim it to an eighth note, place it on every offbeat.
Create a wobble in Massive: sawtooth, low-pass filter modulated by an LFO at 1/8 then 1/16, distortion after. One note per bar, root.
Program the dubstep section: kick on 1 and the “and” of 2, big snare on 3, wobble in the background, over 8 bars.
Make a supersaw lead for the break, 8 bars of a simple melody in minor.
Arrange: hardstyle intro 16, break 32 with lead, build-up 8, dubstep drop 32 alternating with 8 bars of 4/4, second cycle, ending. Limiter.
dubstyle.mix: The problem with dubstyle is the low end: the hardstyle kick with its tuned tail, the reverse bass, the wobble and sometimes a sub all fight between 40 and 150 Hz. Solve it by alternation: when the wobble plays, cut it below 60 Hz and leave the kick alone underneath; when the reverse bass plays, no wobble. Kick at -3 dB peak. Wobble compressed hard (6:1 ratio) then distorted so the modulation stays audible in the midrange. Master: limiter around -6 LUFS, like hardstyle. Check in mono that the wobble doesn't disappear: stereo wideners on the basses are forbidden.

outils.pourquoi: The dubstep wobble: sawtooth and Scrawl, low-pass filter, quarter or eighth-note LFO automated on the Rate. The sound of every dubstyle drop of 2010-2011.
Hardstyle leads and supersaw for the breakdowns, plus the reverse bass as a filtered sawtooth: the Scantraxx scene's synth at the time.
The DAW of Dutch hardstyle producers: kick and reverse bass in the Piano roll, wobble as automation on Massive.
The basis of the hardstyle kick, sampled then lengthened and tuned; at dubstyle's half-time it keeps more tail than in hardstyle.
Hand-drawn sidechain on the wobbles and pads to let the kick through, plus the rhythmic volume shapes of the drop.
Carves the wobble between 60 and 120 Hz so kick and bass don't fight, and cuts the reverse bass below 40 Hz.

reperes: Headhunterz & Brennan Heart: The MF Point of Perfection (Original Dubstyle Mix) (2010): the hardstyle kick giving way to the half-time wobble, the manifesto.
Headhunterz & Brennan Heart: MF Point of Lento (2011): the same idea pushed toward slow motion.
Obsidia: Fallin' (2011): the more dubstep version, growls and snare on 3 with a hardstyle kick.
Excision & Downlink: Existence VIP (2011): on the dubstep side, listen to the growls that dubstyle borrows.
dubstyle.rythme: Two drum parts in the same track. In hardstyle mode: kick on every beat, reverse bass on every offbeat, clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes. In dubstep mode: kick on beat 1 and on the “and” of beat 2, huge snare on beat 3, hi-hats in sixteenth notes with rolls, all over a bar that feels twice as slow. Dubstyle alternates these two modes, often 8 bars of one then 8 of the other, or layers the half-time wobble over the hardstyle kick. The kick stays the hardstyle kick (tok and tuned tail), even in the dubstep sections; that's what sets dubstyle apart from classic dubstep.
dubstyle.sons: Hardstyle screeches and supersaw leads for the melodies: sawtooths stacked at 7 voices in Sylenth1 or Massive, long reverb, for the breaks. Dubstep growls and wobbles for the drops: Massive wavetables with LFO on the filter and on the wavetable position, formants, distortion. Pitched vocals, MC shouts, risers. Rap or dubstep samples. The transition FX come from both worlds: reverse cymbals, rising white noise, hardstyle kick roll. The contrast of textures is the subject: a bright supersaw lead that stops dead to let a dirty growl take its place.
sources: Beatport, release pages for The MF Point of Perfection (beatport.com)
sourcesOutils: Beatport, release pages for The MF Point of Perfection (beatport.com)
dubstyle.tempo: Dubstyle is played at 140-150 BPM, most often at the hardstyle tempo, 150, which is also dubstep speed if you count its half-time at 70-75. That's the key to the hybrid: the hardstyle kick and reverse bass hold the 4/4 at 150, and on top, or in alternation, the dubstep wobbles are written in half-time, with the snare on beat 3 only. So the feel switches between the pounding of hardstyle and the half-time heaviness of dubstep. No swing. Program at 150 BPM, grid in sixteenth notes, and think of each section either as full 4/4 or as half-time.

dubtechno.arrangement: Seven to ten minutes, with no trajectory: it's a state that transforms. A 32-bar intro of echoed chords alone, kick at bar 33 or later. The changes are mixing gestures: a delay send rising over 4 bars then falling back, a filter opening over 64 bars, a shaker coming in unannounced. A single break, where the kick stops and the echoes spin on their own for 16 bars. Record the mixdown as a performance: play the sends, mutes and cutoffs live across the whole length, then keep the take. End by letting the echoes dissolve over 32 bars. No drop, no roll, ever.
dubtechno.basse: A sine sub on the root (F in the book's example), long, in whole or half notes, mono, no effects. On the kick, Drum Buss with Boom at 45% tuned to F0 (43.7 Hz) and a gentle drive at 20%: it's the kick that brings the weight. For a dub bass, an offbeat line on MS-20 or Operator, one or two notes, low-pass filter closed at 200 Hz, long release, gliding from one note to the next. It can disappear for 8 bars and come back through an echo throw. Never put the bass in the reverb; it stays dry while everything else dissolves. Cut it below 30 Hz and check that it doesn't beat against the kick.
etapes: At 122 BPM, place a muffled kick transposed to the key, click cut at 1 kHz, ghost kicks before beats 3 and 4.
Program a snare transposed 18 semitones down, saturated, doubled with a wood block.
Play a minor ninth chord as a stab on an offbeat, send it into Echo in tape mode at 50% feedback.
Place a resonant filter after the echo and automate its cutoff over 32 bars.
Add a sustained sine sub on the root and a Drum Buss on the kick with Boom on F0.
Record the mixdown as a performance of sends and mutes over nine minutes.
dubtechno.mix: A dark, warm mix. Cut almost everything above 10 kHz, the ride included. Grain matters: Vinyl Distortion, Saturator at 2 dB, a bit of tape noise. Sends to the spring reverb and the delay are dosed between 25 and 50% on snare, wood block, hi-hats and chords, never on the kick or the sub. Cut the reverb returns below 300 Hz. Modest levels: kick around -10 dB, chords around -14, the bass in between. Mono sub, chords wide in stereo thanks to the ping-pong delay. A master around -12 LUFS with plenty of dynamics: the style lives in the micro-variations that compression destroys.

outils.pourquoi: The tape echo on the chords, feedback 40 to 60% at the dotted eighth; Ableton's Echo in tape mode or AudioThing Outer Space can replace it.
The genre's instrument: the sends to delay and reverb are played live, the mixdown is recorded as a performance.
Chord stabs and offbeat dub bass, low-pass filter closed at 200 Hz; the MS-20 mini or Ableton's Analog give the same character.
A minor chord with a seventh or ninth played short on an offbeat, before the echo and the resonant filter; a Korg Polysix does the same thing.
Spring preset at 25 or 50% on the percussion bus, the spring reverb that gives the snare and wood block their Jamaican grain.
Closed hi-hat on the offbeats transposed 5 semitones; the kick itself is often muffled and acoustic rather than 909.
Echo in tape mode, Filter Delay, Vinyl Distortion for the hiss, Drum Buss with Boom on F0 and Simpler with an MS2 filter on the kick.
The Pete kit and muffled acoustic samples, transposed to the key, for a kick and snare that don't sound like a machine.

reperes: Basic Channel: Quadrant Dub I (1994): the echoed chord dissolving, the absolute model
Basic Channel: Octaedre (1994): the distant kick and the filtered chords turning for fifteen minutes
Fluxion: Thumb (1998): echoes becoming rhythm, the more percussive Chain Reaction version
Gombeen & Doygen: D'Americana / Auto-Lies (2021): the contemporary lineage, tape grain and patience
dubtechno.rythme: A soft kick, often acoustic or muffled (Ableton's Pete kit), transposed to land on the key, with the click cut above 1 kHz by an MS2 filter at 50% resonance. Ghost kicks at low velocity on the sixteenth-note grid, before beats 3 and 4, filtered at 2 kHz. A snare transposed 17 or 18 semitones down, saturated at 8 dB, placed just ahead of beats 3 and 1 and on beat 4, doubled with a wood block. Shakers alternating on beats 1 and 3 and their neighbors. A closed 909 hi-hat on the offbeats, transposed 5 semitones, doubled with a ride filtered at 10 kHz with a 400 ms fade-in that simulates heavy compression.
dubtechno.sons: The echoed filtered chord is the sound of the genre: a minor chord with a seventh or ninth on a Juno, Polysix, MS-20 or Ableton's Analog, played as a short stab on an offbeat, sent into a Space Echo RE-201 (Ableton's Echo in tape mode) with 40 to 60% feedback, then into a resonant low-pass or band-pass filter whose cutoff moves slowly over 32 bars. The console is the instrument: automate the sends to the delay and the reverb so the chords appear and disappear. Add tape hiss (Vinyl Distortion, low-density crackle), a spring reverb on the percussion bus (H9 Spring preset, 25 to 50%), heavily filtered pads.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
dubtechno.tempo: From 118 to 126 BPM, slower than Detroit and much slower than 2010s Berlin. The groove is gentle: a Maschine or MPC template at only 10%, because the movement comes from the echoes, not the swing. Every delay is locked to the tempo (dotted eighth, quarter note) and that's what creates the sway. At 122 BPM, a dotted eighth is 369 ms: set your Space Echo to that and everything starts to roll. The percussion can float: a kick and an open hat placed every three sixteenth notes give a triplet feel that hovers above the four-on-the-floor. The tempo is a state, not a pulse.

dungeonsynth.arrangement: Songs without words, 3 to 6 minutes long, with a theme that sticks. Simple form: an A theme of 8 or 16 bars, a B theme, a return of A with one more voice (the choir, the flute), and a coda. Each repetition adds or removes a layer, like in a 90s video game where the music loops. An album tells a story: titles of fortresses, strongholds, kingdoms, and the tracks flow as atmospheres, a march, a crypt, a banquet. No build-up or drop: the emotion comes from the melody and the change of mode. Fra Fjelltronen is a good model for form.
dungeonsynth.basse: The bass is a left hand: GM pizzicato double basses, organ in the low octave or low strings, one note per strong beat, in quarter or half notes. It follows the root of each chord, sometimes the fifth, never playing an independent line. The harmonies are modal and simple: A minor, Aeolian or Dorian mode, i, VII, VI, VII cadences, with a resolution to the root every 8 bars. No sub at all: GM banks don't go below 60 Hz and that's just fine, the cassette couldn't have kept up anyway. If your bass sounds too modern and too clean, it isn't in the genre.
etapes: Load a General MIDI SoundFont into Sforzando or Simpler and choose four sounds: strings, flute, choir, organ, plus a pizzicato double bass.
Compose an 8-bar theme in A minor at 80 BPM in 3/4, left hand in half notes on the roots, flute melody on top, everything quantized with no swing.
Write a B theme in C major or in Dorian mode, then return to the A theme adding the choir.
Send all tracks to a single 8-second Hall reverb and let it soak at 40%.
Put a cassette emulation on the master with wow, flutter, low-pass at 8 kHz and hiss, or actually record to cassette and redigitize.
Give your piece a fortress title and export at -16 LUFS without a limiter.
dungeonsynth.mix: Unapologetically lo-fi. Everything goes through the same reverb, a single send channel, no individual processing. Narrow stereo or mono, a tape emulation on the master, a low-pass at 10 kHz, a bit of saturation. No multiband compression, no transparent limiter, a low final level around -16 LUFS. The cassette hiss must stay audible in the silences. If you record to a real cassette, keep the defects (wow, dropouts) instead of fixing them. The mix is done when it sounds like a 1995 demo found in a box, but the melody comes through effortlessly. A clean mix kills the genre.

outils.nom: General MIDI arranger keyboard (Casio CT-X700, Roland JUNO-DS)
outils.pourquoi: The genre was born on cheap keyboards: strings, flute, Aah choir, church organ played straight from the factory presets, untouched.
Free banks that reproduce the naive GM sounds of the 90s; the harpsichord, the horn and the pizzicato double bass come from there, as is.
Free SoundFont and SFZ player to load FluidR3 into the DAW; Ableton's Simpler does the job for a single sound.
Actually recording to cassette and then redigitizing remains the most faithful method: wow, dropouts and hiss become part of the composition.
Cassette emulation cited by Sweetwater for the genre: wow and flutter, low-pass around 8 kHz, hiss at -45 dB, placed on the master.
A free alternative for tape patina: gentle saturation, adjustable high-end loss and flutter, useful if you want to keep the hiss audible in the silences.
