A single Hall preset of 6 to 10 seconds, no fine-tuning, on a send channel that all tracks go through: the cheap reverb is the aesthetic.

reperes: Wongraven: Fra Fjelltronen (1995): the keyboards of Satyr from Satyricon, solemn melodies and naive orchestral banks, the source of the whole genre.
Depressive Silence: Mourning (1996): choir and string pads in the reverb, the most melancholic side.
Old Tower: The Rise of the Specter (2017): the Bandcamp revival, closer to dark ambient, drones and crypt organs.
Erang: The Kingdom Is Ours (with Fief) (2024): today's warm, melodic dungeon synth, themes you hum.
dungeonsynth.rythme: Often no drums at all, and when there are some, they come from cheap orchestral banks: timpani on the first and third beats, a roll at the end of each 8-bar phrase, a tambourine on the weak beats, a marching bass drum. Fixed velocity, no variation, on purpose. The real rhythm is carried by the keyboard's left hand: quarter or half notes in the bass marking the meter, like a folk song played on an organ. In pieces without percussion, it's the harpsichord or harp arpeggio in steady eighth notes that keeps time. No hi-hat, no clap, nothing from club music.
dungeonsynth.sons: The brief lists the General MIDI keyboard, the cassette recorder and digital reverb. Free SoundFonts (FluidR3, Arachno) loaded into Sforzando or Simpler are enough: flute, strings, Aah choir, harpsichord, church organ, horn. The reverb should be cheap and long, 6 to 10 seconds, a Hall preset in Ableton's Reverb with no fine-tuning. The cassette is simulated with a tape emulation (the Sweetwater article cites Klevgrand DAW Cassette; Chow Tape Model is free): wow and flutter, low-pass at 8 kHz, hiss at -45 dB. Actually recording to a cassette Walkman and then redigitizing remains the most faithful method. The naive orchestral banks are the instrument, not a flaw.
sources: Sweetwater InSync, Genres You've (Probably) Never Heard: Dungeon Synth
sourcesOutils: Sweetwater InSync, Genres You've (Probably) Never Heard: Dungeon Synth
dungeonsynth.tempo: This is the exception in the family: here there is a meter and a pulse. Between 60 and 100 BPM, often in 3/4 or 6/8, like a medieval march or dance, sometimes in slow 4/4 for crypt pieces. The charm comes from the stiffness: strict quantization to the quarter or eighth note, no swing, no humanization. It's the General MIDI keyboard's sequencer playing, not a musician. Tempos change from one track to the next on an album (a march at 90, a lullaby at 65) but never within a piece. Old Tower leans toward pulseless dark ambient, Erang toward melody that moves forward.

earlyindustrial.arrangement: There's no song structure: an industrial piece is a block, 3 to 10 minutes, that starts abruptly and ends the same way. What holds the listener is tension: an element that slowly rises in volume and distortion for 5 minutes, never resolving. You can organize the block in three states: the drone alone, the drone plus the rhythm loop, then the voice and tapes invading everything. Add violent interruptions: a two-second cut, a return with the loop shifted by an eighth note. Cabaret Voltaire leaned more toward the punk format, 3 minutes, shouted verse and repeated chorus. For a club set, a 125 BPM version with an uninterrupted drum machine stays mixable, the brutality does the rest.
earlyindustrial.basse: The bass is often absent or replaced by a drone. When there is one, it's an electric bass played in quarter notes by someone who isn't a bassist, on a single note, run through distortion. Reproduce it with a bass sample or Analog with a square wave, a low held note, Overdrive all the way up, then Auto Filter as a low-pass at 500 Hz. The alternative drone: an oscillator from a modular synth or an organ, held for the whole track, with slow modulation that makes it drift by a semitone. With Throbbing Gristle, the low end also came from down-tuned guitar and slowed-down tapes. Don't aim for cleanliness: a rumble that masks everything is an aesthetic choice. Still, cut below 35 Hz so you don't blow the speakers.
etapes: Load a preset drum machine pattern and let it run at 120 BPM through Pedal in Fuzz and a low-pass at 3 kHz.
Build a low drone with Analog on a square wave, held for the whole track, drifting by a semitone via a slow LFO.
Record three metal impacts and loop them in Simpler with slight offsets.
Drop in slowed-down radio voice excerpts, run through a saturated Echo and Frequency Shifter in Ring mode.
Organize three states over 6 minutes, drone, loop, invasion, with two brutal cuts.
Crush the master: Saturator, 10:1 compression at 10 dB of reduction, low-pass at 8 kHz.
earlyindustrial.mix: The original industrial mix sounds like a bad rehearsal recording, and that's intentional: little top end, lots of dirty midrange, crushing compression by accident. To get it, saturate the master with Saturator in Digital Clip mode or Roar, then a Compressor at a 10:1 ratio, attack 1 ms, release 50 ms, 10 dB of reduction, which makes the whole mix pump. Then a low-pass at 8 kHz and a high-pass at 60 Hz for the cassette feel. Use Vinyl Distortion or constant tape noise under everything. The stereo is narrow, almost mono. No target level: what matters is that the track is unpleasant in the right dose. Just check that it doesn't sit steadily below -10 LUFS with no dynamics, so a DJ can play it.

outils.pourquoi: Throbbing Gristle's homemade effect, an LFO tremolo-filter built by Chris Carter; Endangered Audio Research sells a reissue, and Auto Filter and Auto Pan modulated fast imitate it.
Chris Carter's semi-modular: sweeping white noise, screaming oscillators, drifting drones; Analog on a square wave with a slow LFO is enough.
The preset drum machine left in its dumbest state, Rock 1 or Bossa, then run through distortion; a CR-78 sample pack in Drum Rack.
Loops of radio, TV and speeches slowed down and layered; today, looped audio clips, Warp off, transposed down.
The distortion pedal on everything: Fuzz mode, drive at 70%, followed by a low-pass at 3 kHz that chokes the drum machine.
Digital dirt on top of analog dirt: 8 bits on the drum machine, a few kHz on the vocals, for the cassette and bad-rehearsal feel.
The dehumanized voice: saturated Echo with 80% feedback, then Frequency Shifter in Ring mode for the ring modulator of the processed vocals.
To crush the master like a rehearsal recording: saturation in series before a 10:1 Compressor that pumps by 10 dB.

reperes: Throbbing Gristle: United (1978): the dumb drum machine under what looks like a pop song, the unease beneath the surface.
Cabaret Voltaire: Nag Nag Nag (1979): punk on a drum machine, screamed and distorted vocals, three minutes of saturation.
SPK: Slogun (1979): metal impacts and white noise, violence without groove.
Einstürzende Neubauten: Kollaps (1981): percussion on sheet metal and pipes, rhythm played on objects.
earlyindustrial.rythme: The rhythm comes out of a cheap drum machine or tape loops. Take a preset pattern (Rock 1, Bossa) from a vintage sample pack, or build one with Operator, and let it run without variation. Then put it through a distortion pedal: Pedal in Fuzz mode, drive at 70%, then a low-pass filter that chokes everything above 3 kHz. A Redux at 8 bits dirties it further. Another route: record metal impacts, sheet metal, a drum can, a pipe, and loop them in Simpler without lining them up perfectly, like Einstürzende Neubauten and SPK. A tape loop that repeats with a slight offset creates an unstable mechanical rhythm. No hi-hat or snare: impacts and clatter.
earlyindustrial.sons: The brief lists: tape recorder, drum machine, modular synth, distortion pedal, prepared instruments and vocals processed to the extreme. Tape is used to loop recordings of radio, TV, speeches, to slow them down and layer them: in Ableton, drop spoken excerpts into looped audio clips, Warp off, transposed several semitones down. The voice goes through a saturated tape delay (Echo, feedback 80%, high drive) and a Ring Modulator that dehumanizes it. The modular synth makes filtered white noise sweeping slowly and screaming oscillators. Distortion is on everything, often in series: Overdrive then Erosion then Vinyl Distortion. The Gristleizer, a homemade TG effect, was an LFO tremolo-filter: imitate it with Auto Filter and Auto Pan modulated fast.
sourcesOutils: Industrial Music Library (Throbbing Gristle's stage gear)
earlyindustrial.tempo: Early industrial rejects groove as it rejects everything else: either a primitive drum machine ticking over, monotonous, between 100 and 130 BPM, or no tempo at all. Throbbing Gristle's United sits on a drum machine pulse at around 120, Cabaret Voltaire's Nag Nag Nag is punk at 150 BPM on a drum machine. No swing, no velocity nuance: the machine is left in its dumbest state. The difference from neighboring proto-techno: the grid isn't an ideal, it's a hostile constraint. You can derail it, let a loop drift, change the tempo abruptly in the middle. Test Dept, later on, would beat metal by hand at martial tempos around 110 BPM.

ebm.arrangement: EBM keeps a song format: intro on the bass sequence alone (8 bars), kick comes in, chanted verse, chorus with a repeated slogan, percussive break on the toms and metals, second verse, chorus, dry ending. Count on 4 to 5 minutes. Transitions don't go through opening filters: you cut elements all at once, you bring them back all at once. Use mutes as your main arrangement tool. The middle break removes the bass for 8 bars and leaves the metallic percussion alone. For a club-playable version, extend the intro to 16 bars of kick and bass. The track has to stay tense from start to finish, with no soft breathing room.
ebm.basse: This is the heart of the genre. Take a square wave on a Korg MS-20 or on Analog, a single note, and sequence sixteenth notes. The low-pass filter cuts between 300 and 800 Hz, medium resonance, with a short envelope (decay 120 ms) that makes each note snap. The typical pattern: the root on the first three sixteenths, then the octave above on the fourth, which gives the characteristic bounce. No portamento. The bass stays on one or two notes per section: a move to the fourth or the minor seventh is enough to mark the chorus. No sidechain on the kick: the bass hits at the same time, and the two reinforce each other. A light saturation at the output, 4 dB, is enough.
etapes: Set Ableton to 124 BPM, swing at zero. Sequence a square bass on Analog in sixteenth notes: three times the root, then the octave, on a single note.
Add an 808 kick on every beat, a clap on 2 and 4 with a 0.3-second gated reverb, a hi-hat in eighth notes.
Sample a metal object, run it through Redux at 8 bits and play it on the offbeats as percussion.
Record a chanted vocal twice, 80 ms slapback, 8:1 compression. Write a four-word slogan for the chorus.
Arrange over 4 minutes 30 with hard mutes: bass-only intro, verse, chorus, metal break, chorus, dry ending.
ebm.mix: The EBM mix is dry, centered, upfront. Little stereo: the kick, the bass and the voice are in the center, and only the metals and stabs are panned. The bass sequence is almost as loud as the kick, one or two dB below. Compression on the drum bus, 4:1 ratio, attack 10 ms, release 80 ms, for even punch. The voice is compressed hard (8:1) and doubled, which makes it massive without a long reverb. The gated reverb on the snare stays short, 0.3 seconds, cut clean. Little sub: cut below 45 Hz, the energy is between 60 and 150 Hz. A gentle Saturator on the master, 3 dB, glues it all together.

outils.pourquoi: Square wave sequenced in sixteenth notes, low-pass filter between 300 and 800 Hz, short decay: the EBM bass. The MS-20 mini or the Korg Collection plugin can replace it.
Bon Harris says the early Nitzer Ebb tracks were 90% made with it: internal sequencer, accent, bass jumping to the octave. TAL-BassLine-101 is the common emulation.
Dry kick with short Decay on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, toms in kick-start rolls. D16 Nepheton 2 or Roland Cloud TR-808 for the software version.
The semi-modular lent to Nitzer Ebb by Daniel Miller, with the ARP sequencer keeping the march going. Behringer 2600 or Arturia ARP 2600 V today.
Front 242's 8-bit sampler for brass stabs, orchestra hits and metal hits. Recreate it with Simpler and a Redux at 8 bits, 22 kHz.
Doubled on the SH-101 bass, it adds the plucky, bright attack of the transients. The free Dexed plugin reproduces its patches exactly.
The native equivalent for the square sequence: one note, 120 ms decay, medium resonance, three roots then the octave, 4 dB of saturation at the output.
The descending electronic percussion used by Front 242 and Nitzer Ebb, played on the offbeats like metal hits.

reperes: Nitzer Ebb: Join In The Chant (1987): the square bass in sixteenth notes, the voice chanted like a slogan, the metallic percussion.
Front 242: Headhunter (1988): the sequence jumping to the octave, the sampled stabs, the tense song structure.
Liaisons Dangereuses: Los Ninos Del Parque (1981): the primitive version, a sequencer and a voice, almost nothing else.
ebm.rythme: The TR-808 is the brief's machine, and its dry kick, with no long resonance, is perfect: set the Decay short. Kick on every beat. 808 clap or snare on beats 2 and 4, with a short gated reverb (0.3 seconds) that gives the military slap. Closed hi-hat in eighth notes, sometimes sixteenths with a strong accent on the beat (velocity 110) and weak in between (velocity 60). 808 toms in sixteenth-note rolls serve as a kick-start before each section. Add metallic percussion: a drum can, an anvil, a pipe, sampled and played on the offbeats. That's the Nitzer Ebb sound. No cymbal, no rock drum fill: transitions are made by cutting everything.
ebm.sons: EBM sounds are few but sharp. The analog sequencer (ARP, MS-20) provides the bass and sometimes a second square pattern an octave above. The Emulator II brings the brass stabs, orchestra hits and metal hits: recreate it with Simpler and a Redux at 8 bits, 22 kHz, to get the grain back. The voice is chanted, shouted, not sung: record it twice to double it, add an 80 ms slapback and a short plate reverb. The kick-start shouts (“Hey!”) are sampled and played like percussion. Few or no pads: if you add one, keep it dark and filtered below 2 kHz. The empty space between sounds is part of the style.
sourcesOutils: Vintage Synth Explorer (Nitzer Ebb Synths forums)
Gearspace (threads Front242 drum machine sounds and What Synth to choose for EBM/Industrial)
ebm.tempo: Between 120 and 130 BPM, with a perfectly straight groove: swing at 0%, no humanization. The feel is martial, that of a march. Everything plays in rigid sixteenth notes, sequenced, never played by hand. What sets EBM apart from its industrial parent is precisely this grid: where industrial drifts, EBM keeps step. In your DAW, quantize everything at 100% and avoid Ableton's grooves. Nitzer Ebb sits around 125 BPM, Front 242 sometimes climbs toward 130. If in doubt, start at 124: fast enough to stomp to, slow enough for the sixteenth-note bass to stay readable. The tempo never moves within a track.

electroacoustic.arrangement: An electroacoustic piece is composed like architecture: you first write a plan of durations, then fill it in. Sketch on paper: section A of 90 seconds, B of 40, a 10-second transition, C of 150, and so on. Each section has a type of energy (mass, isolated points, line, silence). The great pieces alternate densities: after a saturated mass, a single isolated impulse in silence sounds louder than anything. Transitions are prepared by an element that announces what comes next, for example a grain from section C that briefly appears in section B. Total length ranges from 4 to 30 minutes; for a club audience, stick to 8 minutes and include at least one pulsed passage to offer a way in.
electroacoustic.basse: The bass is often a sustained mass rather than a line. Build it with a sine oscillator (Operator, a single operator) between 30 and 60 Hz, then make it beat against a second oscillator offset by 1 to 3 Hz: the beating produces a slow, very physical pulse. This laboratory oscillator technique is the school's signature. Add a ring modulator (Ring in Operator or the Frequency Shifter device in Ring mode) to create inharmonic metallic sounds in the low end. For a bass that moves, draw its pitch with continuous automation rather than notes: a three-octave glissando over 40 seconds is a typical gesture. Filter the partials above 150 Hz to keep the weight without the mud.
etapes: Sketch on paper an 8-minute plan with five sections and one type of energy per section.
Build three synthesized sounds in Operator: an impulse, a beating low sine, a ring-modulated pad.
Record a voice or an instrument, cut it into fragments and transpose them into an artificial choir.
Create the rhythm-to-pitch passage by automating the repetition rate of a click.
Place each element in space with two reverbs of different depth and automated panning.
Assemble the sections in Arrangement, let the silences breathe, export without compression.
electroacoustic.mix: Space is composed, not added. Plan from the start where each sound lives: close and dry in the center, distant and reverberant on the sides. Use two different reverbs on returns, a short one (0.8 seconds, room) and a very long one (10 seconds, Hybrid Reverb in convolution), and automate the sends to move a sound from one to the other. Huge dynamics are intended: quiet passages can drop to -40 dBFS. Don't compress the master. Check your mix on headphones and on speakers, because sine basses are easily misleading. If you're aiming for multichannel diffusion in a hall, export separate stems per depth plane. A surgical EQ (high Q) is for removing annoying resonances, not for coloring.

outils.pourquoi: The big modular of institutional studios (WDR, BBC Radiophonic Workshop, IPEM): 12 oscillators, pin matrix and sequencer, for written masses of synthesis.
Test oscillators repurposed as instruments: two sines a few hertz apart give the low beating that the course reproduces with Operator.
Editing and layering: several synchronized tapes, variable speed, reverse playback, the basis of Kontakte and of four-track spatialization.
Today's composers' patching environment: real-time synthesis, processing and control, with Spat for multichannel diffusion in concert.
Spatialization as a compositional parameter: source trajectories in a virtual space, room reverb, output to eight speakers or binaural.
Additive and FM synthesis with four operators: the one-millisecond click that, repeated 40 times per second, becomes a pitch, as in Kontakte.

outils.nom: Ableton Spectral Resonator and Spectral Time
outils.pourquoi: The spectral transformations that replaced lab vocoders: freeze, per-partial transposition, stretching, to melt a voice into synthesis.
Xenakis's granular mass: Spray all the way up and random Pitch on an impulse, hundreds of events whose density makes the rhythm.

reperes: Karlheinz Stockhausen: Gesang der Jünglinge (1956): the boy's voice melted into synthesis, the first great marriage of the two schools.
Karlheinz Stockhausen: Kontakte (1960): the moment when a repeated impulse speeds up until it becomes a note.
Iannis Xenakis: Bohor (1962): the granular mass, thousands of events forming a crushing texture.
Edgard Varèse: Poème électronique (1958): composed for 400 speakers, spatialization as the subject of the work.
electroacoustic.rythme: Rhythm is made through synthesis and editing. The founding technique is to take a very short impulse (a 1 ms click made with Operator, attack and release at zero) and repeat it at varying speeds. Below 20 repetitions per second you hear a rhythm, above it you hear a note. Automate the rate of a Beat Repeat or of an LFO triggering the click to cross that boundary. Another tool: multichannel spatialization, which here is a rhythmic element. A sound rotating between four speakers at 1 Hz imposes a pulse even without an attack. In stereo, reproduce it with Auto Pan synced to the quarter note. Xenakis, in Bohor, built granular masses: hundreds of small events whose density makes the rhythm.
electroacoustic.sons: The timbres come from three sources: synthesis (pure oscillators, filtered noise, ring modulation), voice or instruments recorded then transformed, and the computer for algorithmic generation. In Ableton, Operator covers additive and FM synthesis, Wavetable the filtered noises, and Spectral Resonator or Spectral Time the spectral transformations that replaced lab vocoders. The voice, as with Stockhausen and the boy in Gesang der Jünglinge, is processed by cutting it into phonemes, transposing and layering it into an artificial choir. Grain Delay with random pitch and high Spray gives Xenakis's granular burst. Tape echoes are reproduced with Echo in tape mode and 60% feedback that degrades the signal on each pass.
electroacoustic.tempo: Electroacoustic music thinks of duration through form, not pulse. A piece can have no tempo for eight minutes and then bring in a regular pulse as an event. What replaces BPM is the relationship between smooth time (continuous textures) and striated time (impulses). In your DAW, work in Arrangement at 60 BPM so the grid matches seconds: a bar of 4/4 then lasts 4 seconds, which makes duration math easier. The feel comes from written accelerations and decelerations: a series of impulses going from 2 per second to 40 per second becomes a pitch, as Stockhausen demonstrated in Kontakte. This continuity between rhythm and timbre is the central idea of the genre.

electroclash.arrangement: Club pop song structure: a 16-bar intro with bass and drums, a 16-bar spoken verse, a 16-bar sung or chanted chorus, second verse, chorus, an 8 to 16-bar break where the bass runs alone with a filter closing then opening, final chorus. Four to five minutes, six for the 12-inch with drum intro and outro. The break is the only moment of tension, with no white noise riser. Muting the drums under a spoken line is a trick of the genre. Repeat the same bassline from start to finish and only move the filter and the layers. A chorus has to be memorable on first listen.
electroclash.basse: The italo bass: a mono synth with a sawtooth or square, playing eighth or sixteenth notes alternating root and octave, across the whole bar, with no silence. It's the engine of the track. SH-101, Pro-One or Juno in mono back then, Ableton Analog or TAL-BassLine-101 today. Filter at 500 Hz, medium resonance, a short 90 ms envelope, and a cutoff automation that opens on the choruses. Simple progressions in minor, two or four chords, often i, VI, III, VII. The Attack book gives a method for varying an arpeggio: duplicate a bar and transpose a few notes by an octave in the copy. Apply it to this bass. Cut below 50 Hz, the kick is short.
etapes: Tempo at 128 BPM, 808 and 606 kits mixed: kick on every beat, 808 clap on 2 and 4, 606 hi-hats in eighth notes, cowbell on even bars.
Write a mono sawtooth bass in sixteenth notes alternating root and octave, over i, VI, III, VII, cutoff 500 Hz.
Add a square lead with slow vibrato and a Juno arpeggio in octaves, with chorus.
Record a cheeky spoken vocal, compress it and add an eighth-note delay.
Arrange as a song: intro, verse, chorus, break where the bass runs alone with the filter, final chorus.
Mix dry, bass as loud as the kick, tape saturation on the bus.
electroclash.mix: Dry, flat, a bit lo-fi: that's the charm. 808 or 606 drums with no reverb, kick at -8 dBFS, italo bass at the same level as the kick, which is unusual, with a light 2 dB sidechain. Spoken vocal up front, compressed at 4:1 and doubled with an eighth-note delay at 25% dry/wet. A bit of tape saturation on the main bus, 3 dB of drive, and a high-pass filter at 30 Hz. Chorus on the pads for width, everything else in the center. Bus compression at 3:1 with a 3 ms attack for audible pumping on the choruses. Master around -10 LUFS. Don't polish too much: a mix that's too clean kills the irony.

outils.pourquoi: Short 250 ms kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, cowbell on even bars, no reverb; an 808 kit in Drum Rack is enough.
Thin snare and metallic hi-hats mixed with the 808 for the cheap side; Roland TR-06 or 606 samples today.
The Hacker's mono for square leads with slow vibrato and aggressive basses; Korg Collection MS-20 or MS-20 Mini.
The italo bass in eighth or sixteenth notes alternating root and octave, played as a live sequence; TAL-BassLine-101 today.
The Hacker's polysynth for thin string pads and stabs; Arturia Jup-8 V gives a similar color.
Octave arpeggios and pads with the Juno chorus, the italo color of Miss Kittin & The Hacker; TAL-U-No-LX emulates it faithfully.
For the mono bass: sawtooth, filter at 500 Hz, 90 ms envelope, cutoff automation that opens on the choruses.
A cheap synthesis drum machine in The Hacker's studio, for the genre's cheap synthetic noises and percussion.

reperes: Miss Kittin and The Hacker: Frank Sinatra (1998): the cheeky spoken vocal over an octave italo bass and a bare 808.
Miss Kittin & The Hacker: 1982 (1998): raw monophonic synths and an instant chorus.
Fischerspooner: Emerge (2001): the showbiz version, slower, with pads and a chanted chorus.
Ladytron: Destroy Everything You Touch (2005): the cold synth-pop that inherits the movement, arpeggios and a detached vocal.
electroclash.rythme: Bare TR-808 or TR-606, or both mixed: the short 808 kick with a 250 ms decay, the thin 606 snare, the metallic 606 hi-hats. Kick on every beat, or in electro syncopation on the verses for variety. 808 snare or clap on 2 and 4, with no reverb or a very short plate. Closed hi-hat in eighth notes, open hat on the offbeats, in sixteenth notes for the choruses. An 808 cowbell or a rimshot on even bars. No elaborate fills, at most a two-beat 606 snare roll before a chorus. The pattern is deliberately poor: it's an aesthetic choice, not a limitation. The groove comes from the contrast between these drums and a very busy bass.
electroclash.sons: Monophonic synths everywhere, with raw sounds: square leads with a slow vibrato, octave arpeggios on a Juno, thin synth string pads, a single piano note now and then. The vocal is spoken, cheeky, with an accent, processed with an eighth-note delay and sometimes a vocoder or a downward pitch shifter. Add a 606 noise or a cheap synth drum machine for the cheap side. The effects are deliberately old: Juno chorus, flanger, a tape delay. With Vitalic and The Hacker, distortion on the lead and pumping compression bring the dance side. No orchestral samples, no talkbox, no Fairlight.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Arpeggios chapter)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Arpeggios and Ask The Pros chapters)
Vintage Synth Explorer (forum, The Hacker - What synths?)
electroclash.tempo: Between 125 and 135 BPM, Frank Sinatra and 1982 around 130, Emerge a bit slower. Rigid grid, zero swing, like the italo and synth-pop it replays. What changes compared with electro-funk and Detroit is the attitude: the feel is that of a club pop track, simple, almost lazy, where the spoken vocal falls slightly behind the beat. Don't go for Drexciya's precision or Miami's heaviness: go for the straight line. A four-on-the-floor kick for the whole length is common here, which is rare elsewhere in the family. Start at 128 BPM.

electrofunk.arrangement: The 12-inches of the era last six to seven minutes and are built in 8-bar blocks. Intro: the 808 alone for 8 to 16 bars, then the bass comes in, then the melody. The vocoded chorus comes back every 32 bars, between rapped or sung verses. The central break removes the kick and leaves claps, cowbell and vocoder for 8 bars, before the 808 returns with a tom roll. No filtered build-up, no white noise: transitions are made by adding or removing an element, and by 808 fills. End with a 16-bar outro of drums and bass, for the DJs. An instrumental version on the B-side is part of the tradition.
electrofunk.basse: The bass is a monophonic synth, Minimoog, ARP Odyssey or SH-101 style: today Ableton Analog, Repro-1 or Diva will do. A single sawtooth, low-pass filter at around 400 Hz, light resonance, filter envelope with a short 150 ms decay and sustain at zero for the plucky side. Write eighth or sixteenth notes on the root, with octave jumps on the offbeats: the electro-funk bass bounces, it doesn't hold notes. Stay in minor, often in E or F. Let the 808 kick take the sub-bass: cut your synth bass below 60 Hz and let it live between 80 and 300 Hz. It answers the kick, it doesn't double it.
etapes: Load an 808 kit into Drum Rack, set the tempo to 118 BPM and program two bars: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and the “and” of 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenth notes.
Add cowbell, claves and an open hat on the last offbeat, then a descending tom fill at the end of each 8-bar block.
Write a mono sawtooth bass, eighth notes on the root in E minor with octave jumps, filter decay at 150 ms.
Compose a four-note melody for a mono synth and place an orch hit on the first beat of every other bar.
Record a chanted phrase and run it through a vocoder whose carrier plays the melody's chord.
Arrange in 8-bar blocks: 808 alone, bass, melody, vocoded chorus, break without kick, return, outro for the DJs.
electrofunk.mix: The mix is dry and upfront. The 808 dominates: kick at about -6 dBFS peak, the synth bass 4 to 6 dB below, the vocals at the kick's level. Only the snare gets reverb, short, plate or gated, 300 to 500 ms. Run all the drums through gentle tape saturation (Ableton's Saturator in Analog Clip mode, 3 dB of drive) to recall the analog multitrack. Sum everything below 150 Hz to mono. Light bus compression, 2:1 ratio, attack 30 ms, release 100 ms, glues it together without pumping. Keep the dynamics: 1982 productions don't go above -12 LUFS integrated, no need to crush it.

outils.pourquoi: The whole drum kit: a kick with a long decay around 400 ms that serves as the sub, cowbell, claves, toms for fills; today Roland Cloud TR-808 or D16 Nepheton.
The vocoder of the chanted choruses, sawtooth carrier on the chord; replaced today by Ableton's Vocoder, TAL-Vocoder or Arturia Vocoder V.
Source of the ORCH2 orchestra hit placed on the strong beats of Planet Rock; you'll find it in Arturia CMI V or in any pack under the name orch hit.
Sampler for the chopped vocals, lasers and sound effects of the 1982 12-inches; recreate them with filtered white noise and a falling pitch envelope in Simpler.
The step sequencer that drove Planet Rock: it's what imposes the square grid at 0% swing, quantized to the sixteenth note.
The mono sawtooth bass bouncing in octave jumps, filter around 400 Hz and short decay; ARP Odyssey and SH-101 play the same role.
To recreate that bass today: a single sawtooth, filter decay 150 ms, sustain zero; u-he Repro-1 or Diva give the same pluck.
On the 808 bus in Analog Clip mode with 3 dB of drive, to recall the analog multitrack of the Tommy Boy studios.

reperes: Afrika Bambaataa & Soulsonic Force: Planet Rock (1982): the syncopated 808 kick, the orch hit and the transposed Kraftwerk theme, the model for the whole genre.
Man Parrish: Hip Hop Be Bop (1982): the dark instrumental version, where Emulator effects and claps take the place of the rap.
Hashim: Al-Naafiysh The Soul (1983): the 808 almost alone with an octave-jumping bass, a lesson in electro minimalism.
Newcleus: Jam On It (1984): the vocoder as the lead voice, with 808 toms as fills.
electrofunk.rythme: Everything starts from the TR-808, or an 808 kit in Drum Rack. Kick on beat 1, on the “and” of beat 2 (step 7 of 16) and on the “and” of beat 3 (step 11): this jump avoids the four-on-the-floor and gives the electro march. 808 snare on 2 and 4, often doubled with a handclap with a little reverb. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, velocity 100 on the beats, 60 in between. Open hat on the last “and” of the bar. Add 808 cowbell and claves in two-bar patterns, rimshot for kick-starts. Set the 808 kick decay long, around 400 ms, it stands in for the sub. Fills are done with descending 808 toms every 8 bars.
electrofunk.sons: Three colors define the style. The vocoder first: Roland VP-330 or SVC-350 back then, today Ableton's Vocoder, TAL-Vocoder or Arturia's Vocoder V, with a sawtooth carrier playing the chord and a chanted voice, not a sung one. Next, the Fairlight CMI orchestra hit: an orchestral sample played on the strong beats, which you'll find in every pack under the name orch hit or in Arturia's Fairlight kit. Finally, mono synth melodies borrowed from Kraftwerk: a sawtooth with a slow vibrato, playing a simple four-note theme in eighth notes. The Emulator is used for chopped vocals and laser noises, which you can recreate with filtered white noise and a falling pitch envelope.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Step-sequences chapter, sidebar on sequencers and Planet Rock)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Step-sequences chapter)
electrofunk.tempo: Aim for between 110 and 130 BPM: Planet Rock runs around 126, Jam On It and Al-Naafiysh slower, around 112 to 115. The feel is square, no swing: back then, patterns came out of a step sequencer (the Attack book points out that Planet Rock was sequenced on a Roland MC-4), so quantize everything to the sixteenth note, at 0% swing. The sense of slowness comes from the snare on beats 2 and 4, not from the tempo. The groove is born from syncopated kicks falling between the beats, never from micro-timing. If you add an Ableton groove, keep it under 10%: the style is robotic by choice, not for lack of means.

electrohop.arrangement: The structure is that of a rap track: an 8-bar 808 intro with the cowbell, the bass and chords come in, a vocoded or chanted chorus, then 16-bar verses. Tracks last five to six minutes, with long instrumental stretches where the DJ scratches. The break comes around the middle: kick cut, snare and hi-hat alone, a scratch answering the vocoder, then the kick returns. Variations come mostly from mutes: drop the bass one bar in four, cut the hi-hat for two beats. End with a 16-bar solo 808, like at the start. The track has to stay mixable on two turntables from start to finish.
electrohop.basse: The bass is played by a Roland polysynth of the era, Juno-106 or Jupiter style, in mono mode, with a square wave or a filtered sawtooth. Today, take TAL-U-No-LX or Cherry Audio's Juno. It plays eighth notes on the root with a rising figure at the end of the bar, a bit funky, a bit naive: for example root, root, octave, minor seventh, root. Filter at 500 Hz, no resonance, light Juno chorus for width. It stays above the 808 kick: cut below 80 Hz. Unlike electro-funk, the bass is often doubled by a pad of held chords on the same synth, which gives the impression that everything comes out of a single keyboard. Which is often the case.
etapes: Tempo at 125 BPM, 808 kit in Drum Rack, one bar: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and step 12, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenth notes, cowbell in eighth notes.
Write a mono Juno bass in eighth notes with a rising figure at the end of the bar, filter at 500 Hz, light chorus.
Add a held chord on the same synth and a mono Eastern melody with portamento in harmonic minor.
Record a two-word chorus, run it through the vocoder, then create two or three scratches with a vocal sample and the Warp tool.
Arrange like a rap track: 808 intro, chorus, 16-bar verses, break without kick with scratches, outro with the 808 alone.
electrohop.mix: Even drier than electro-funk: no reverb at all, except a short delay on the vocoder or a voice. The 808 comes out direct, each sound on its own track, moderate panning: snare in the center, cowbell slightly right, hi-hat left. Aim for the kick at -8 dBFS peak, the snare at the same level, the rap 2 dB above everything. A bit of tape saturation on the 808 bus rounds off the transients. Compress the vocal alone, 4:1 ratio, attack 10 ms, so it stays up front. No bus compression. Mono below 120 Hz. The result should sound like a well-recorded cassette: honest, a bit grainy, no frills.

outils.pourquoi: Played bare and live by Egyptian Lover, short kick around 250 ms, cowbell in eighth notes; Roland Cloud offers its TR-808 Egyptian Lover pattern and kit collection.
Egyptian Lover's polysynth for held chords and Eastern melodies with portamento; Arturia Jup-8 V captures its grain.
Mono bass and synth lines of the Los Angeles scene, with a handy internal sequencer on stage; TAL-BassLine-101 or Roland SH-01A today.
Juno-60 emulation for the eighth-note bass with the Juno chorus and the chord pad played on the same keyboard; Cherry Audio DCO-106 is the alternative.
The rack vocoder for one or two-word choruses, the rest being rapped; TAL-Vocoder or Ableton's Vocoder give the same result.
The turntable for the scratches, the genre's second instrument with the World Class Wreckin' Cru, to be recorded over the running 808.
To make scratches without a turntable: a short vocal sample, back-and-forths drawn with Warp, a clean cut at the end.

reperes: Egyptian Lover: Egypt Egypt (1984): the bare 808, the mono Eastern melody and the rap sitting on the eighth notes.
World Class Wreckin' Cru: Surgery (1984): scratches as the main instrument, with a young Dr. Dre on the turntables.
Unknown DJ: 808 Beats (1984): a whole track built on the machine, a reference for programming.
Uncle Jamm's Army: Dial-A-Freak (1983): the cowbell and the continuous hi-hat pushing the tempo.
electrohop.rythme: The 808 is dry and bare, with no layers on top at all. Kick on 1, on the “and” of 2 and on step 12 (just before beat 4), short decay, around 250 ms: here the kick is more percussive than sub, the West Coast wasn't after the subwoofer yet. 808 snare on 2 and 4, with the snappy turned up for the crack. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, all at the same velocity, and open hat on the offbeats of 2 and 4. 808 cowbell in eighth notes every other bar, it's almost a signature. Handclap layered on the snare. Fills use the toms and the rimshot, never snare rolls. A scratch on a strong beat often replaces the crash.
electrohop.sons: The vocoder remains central, but it's used as an effect rather than the lead voice: one vocoded word or chorus, the rest rapped naturally. Scratches are the real second instrument: record a short vocal sample, move it with a DJ controller or with Ableton's Warp tool by drawing the back-and-forths, then cut it clean. The lead is a mono synth with portamento, playing an Eastern melody on the harmonic minor scale, that's Egyptian Lover's trademark. Add a held Juno chord with chorus, lasers and bursts of filtered white noise, and voices pitched down for the interjections. No Fairlight, no orch hit: the Los Angeles budget was more modest than New York's.
sourcesOutils: Roland Cloud (TR-808 Egyptian Lover Patch Collection)
electrohop.tempo: Livelier than Bronx electro-funk: between 120 and 130 BPM, Egypt Egypt runs around 125. No swing: Egyptian Lover played his 808 live on stage, but the machine quantizes everything to the sixteenth note. What changes compared with the parent is density: the pattern stays busy from start to finish, with a continuous closed hi-hat pushing the tempo forward. The rap sits on the eighth notes, almost sung, which gives that sprightly feel. First program a single bar, let it run for a long time, then think in 4-bar variations: repetition is part of the fun, as at a block party where the 808 keeps running while the DJ scratches.

electrohouse.arrangement: Rock song structure. A 16-bar intro with drums and a filtered riff. First drop at bar 17 or 33: the bass riff in the clear, 16 bars. A 16-bar verse with the filtered riff and a vocal or a stab. An 8-bar build-up: snare roll, white noise, filter opening, one beat of silence. A 16-bar drop with the full riff and a crash. A 16-bar break: kick out, vocal or piano, the riff with the filter closed. Second build-up, a final 32-bar drop, a 16-bar outro. Length 4 to 6 minutes. Drops are frequent, every 32 bars, and each one is louder than the last.
electrohouse.basse: The saturated sawtooth bass: Sylenth1 or Massive, two or three detuned sawtooths in unison, low-pass filter between 500 Hz and 2 kHz with resonance at 20%, then distortion (Saturator in Hard Curve mode, or an overdrive) and heavy compression. The riff is played in eighth notes, over 1 or 2 bars, with passing notes, octave jumps and sometimes power chords: it's a guitar riff played on a synth. Automate the cutoff or an LFO on the filter for a light “wobble”. Heavy sidechain from the kick. A clean sine sub underneath, to hold the low end that the saturated bass no longer has.
etapes: Project at 128 BPM, a short saturated kick on every beat, layered clap on 2 and 4, bright hats.
Sylenth1 or Massive bass with three detuned sawtooths, filter at 800 Hz, distortion and compression, heavy sidechain, sine sub underneath.
Write a 2-bar bass riff in eighth notes, like a guitar riff, with octave jumps.
Add a saturated string or synth stab and a pitched vocal as a chorus.
Build 5 minutes in rock structure: intro, drop, verse, build-up with roll and silence, drop, break, final drop.
Mix hard: parallel compression, distortion everywhere except below 100 Hz, clipper and limiter at -7 LUFS.
electrohouse.mix: A hard, loud mix, full in the mids. The saturated bass occupies 100 Hz to 3 kHz and the sine sub holds the bottom. Kick up front, with heavy sidechain on bass and stabs (release 120 ms). Parallel compression on the drums for density. Distortion and saturation everywhere, but cut them below 100 Hz to keep a clean low end. Clap and snare with short reverb, spread wide. Master compressed hard and limited to -6 to -7 LUFS, with a maximizer working. A clipper before the limiter for the transients. It's a mix that has to sound loud at low volume: aggressive in the 2 to 5 kHz range, merciless.

outils.pourquoi: Detuned sawtooths in unison for the riff bass and supersaw leads, the reference synth of electro house from 2006 to 2012.
Modulated basses with an LFO on the filter for the light wobble and the saturated stabs; Massive X replaces it but the original is still everywhere.
The wavetable synth that took over after 2014 for the same saturated basses, with distortion and filter inside the synth.
Hard Curve mode on the bass after the filter, then heavy compression: distortion is on everything, except below 100 Hz.
Free distortion and compression widely used on basses and stabs in the Ed Banger era; iZotope Trash or FabFilter Saturn today.
Heavy sidechain from the kick on bass and stabs, release 120 ms, plus parallel compression on the drums for rock density.
A clipper before FabFilter Pro-L 2 or a maximizer to hold -6 to -7 LUFS without losing the transients, as the course describes.

reperes: Justice: D.A.N.C.E. (2007): the saturated riff bass under children's voices, the crushing compression and the pop song structure.
Justice: Genesis (2007): strings and brass compressed to death like riffs, the hardest Ed Banger sound.
Who Da Funk feat Jessica Eve: Shiny Disco Balls (2002): the synth bass replacing the disco sample, electro house before the name.
David Guetta Feat Sia: Titanium (David Guetta & Morten Future Rave Remix) (2021): what the style becomes at festivals, with the same saturated basses and a sung drop.
electrohouse.rythme: A 909 or sampled kick, short, heavily compressed, with a click at 3 to 5 kHz and saturation, on every beat. A wide layered clap (two or three claps stacked) on 2 and 4, with a short reverb. Closed hats in eighth or sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats, nice and bright. A sampled rock snare layered in on the drops. The fills are snare rolls in sixteenth then thirty-second notes, with rising pitch, over 2 or 4 bars before the drop, and one beat of silence. Add crashes on beat 1 of the drops. The drums are louder and harder than in classic house, mixed like rock.
electrohouse.sons: The lead is often the bass itself, an octave up. Add distorted synth chord stabs, saturated string sounds (the Justice sound: string and brass samples compressed to death), pitched or vocoded vocals for a pop chorus. Massive for modulated basses, Sylenth1 for leads and supersaw pads. Signature effects: distortion on everything, parallel compression, light bitcrush, eighth-note delay, rising white noise. A piano can show up in a break. The sound is compressed, bright, saturated, cut for a big system. Fidget adds chopped vocal samples and fast-moving filters.
sourcesOutils: House of Tracks, Best software for producing electro house
Samplephonics, Electro House Plugin Presets (Massive & Sylenth)
electrohouse.tempo: Between 125 and 130 BPM, faster than the French touch it comes from. The feel is square, aggressive, read in eighth notes: the bass plays riffs like a guitar, on the eighth notes, and that riff defines the track, not the kick. No swing. The sidechain is very heavy but shorter than in French house: release at 100 to 150 ms, so it slaps rather than breathes. The phrases are short, the riff lasts 1 or 2 bars, the structure follows a rock song: intro, riff, break, riff. The drops are the riff returning at full power.

electroindustrial.arrangement: Count on 5 to 6 minutes. The intro is long, 30 to 45 seconds of film samples and textures, before the rhythm settles in. The structure keeps verse and chorus, but each section adds a layer: the first chorus has a pad, the second has the pad plus a second bass pattern plus a percussion. The middle contains a break that changes tempo or goes half-time, with a sampled dialogue at its center. Sections don't cut clean like in EBM: they overlap, melt into reverb tails. The finale piles everything up then collapses into a noise texture that lasts 20 seconds.
electroindustrial.basse: The EBM sequence, thickened. Keep the square pattern in sixteenth notes, but layer a second one: the same pattern played on a Nord Lead with a sawtooth, an octave above, run through an Overdrive at 10 dB. The line moves more than in EBM: it includes minor second or tritone jumps that create unease. The notes are sometimes longer, in eighth notes, for the slow sections. The filter has an envelope with high resonance (60%) that pinches the start of each note. The kick and the bass share fundamentals around E1. A light sidechain, 3 dB of reduction, keeps everything readable despite the density.
etapes: At 118 BPM, program a syncopated kick (beat 1, offbeat of 2, beat 4) and a snare doubled with a metallic impact with a 2-second reverb.
Sequence a square bass in sixteenth notes with a tritone jump, then double it with a Nord Lead or Analog on a saturated sawtooth, an octave higher.
Sample three dialogue excerpts and two machine noises in Simpler, play them as a detuned loop over the rhythm.
Record a vocal, run it through Overdrive then Vocoder at 40%, then into a filtered delay.
Bounce your drum loop, slice it, repitch fragments and replay them as a second rhythmic layer.
Arrange over 5 minutes 30 with a 40-second sample intro, a half-time break and a finale that collapses into noise.
electroindustrial.mix: With so many layers, the mix is a job of subtractive EQ. Every element gets a high-pass: bass at 40 Hz, pads at 200 Hz, film samples at 400 Hz, secondary percussion at 300 Hz. The distorted vocal is compressed at 6:1 then placed up front, with the long reverb on a send rather than an insert. The kick holds the center, the textures spread wide with a Utility at 130% width. Parallel compression on the drum bus to keep the punch under the layers. Dark reverbs: cut their highs at 4 kHz. Aim for -10 LUFS. Multi-stage saturation glues the layers, but keep one clean stage for the bass.

outils.pourquoi: The sampler for Skinny Puppy's horror film dialogue, screams and laboratory noises. Simpler and your own excerpts make the same collage today.
Front Line Assembly's 16-bit sampler for repitched and replayed percussion loops, the course's resampling technique.
Sawtooth an octave above the square bass, run through an Overdrive at 10 dB, and dark pads filtered at 1.2 kHz with chorus.
Bill Leeb and Rhys Fulber's multitimbral analog for heavy pads and thick sequences. Arturia Matrix-12 V shares the same architecture.
On Atari ST then on PC, the sequencer that stacks the scene's rhythmic and MIDI layers, still a standard among the genre's producers.
Kick on beat 1, the offbeat of 2 and beat 4, rather than a flat four-on-the-floor: the syncopation that sets the genre apart from EBM.
After an Overdrive, mix the vocoder at 40% then a filtered delay: the voice distorted in stages, readable despite the layers.
Ratio 11 on operator B for the metallic FM textures that fill the gaps between the film samples.

reperes: Skinny Puppy: Worlock (1990): the density of the layers, the film samples, the distorted vocal that stays readable.
Front Line Assembly: Mindphaser (1992): the thickened EBM sequence, the dark pads, the stretched song format.
Haujobb: Dead Market (1995): the cleaner, more rhythmic side, where each layer has its place in the spectrum.
electroindustrial.rythme: The rhythm is a stack. An 808 kick or an industrial kick sample, on beat 1, the offbeat of 2 and beat 4, rather than a flat four-on-the-floor. Snare doubled by a metallic impact and a dark 2-second reverb. Hi-hats in sixteenth notes, but often replaced by looped machine noises. Rolls made by retriggering a sample every thirty-second note with velocity rising from 40 to 127. Add a second sampled percussion loop, detuned, played on top. The resampling technique described for processed techno applies: bounce your drum loop, slice it, repitch fragments and replay them.
electroindustrial.sons: The Emulator in the brief is used to sample dialogue from horror and science fiction films, screams, laboratory noises. Recreate this approach with Simpler and royalty-free film excerpts or your own recordings. The pads are dark: Nord Lead sawtooth, filter at 1.2 kHz, chorus, 6-second reverb. The voice is distorted in several stages: Overdrive, then Vocoder at 40% mix, then a filtered delay. Add metallic FM textures with Operator, ratio 11 on operator B. Everything is stacked in layers, then re-bounced and reworked: that's the layered production inherited from industrial.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Processed Techno chapter: resampling and stacked processing)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Processed Techno chapter)
Vintage Synth Explorer (Bill Leeb/Rhys Fulber thread, Transitions in Equipment)
Reverb (The Mean Synths and Fast Drums of Skinny Puppy)
electroindustrial.tempo: Between 110 and 130 BPM, often slower than EBM. Skinny Puppy frequently runs under 120. The groove is straight, but the rhythm is more twisted: syncopated kicks, half-time sections, tempo breaks within the same track. What changes compared with EBM is density: there are always two or three rhythmic layers answering each other. In your DAW, work at 118 BPM and allow yourself sections where the kick drops to half notes. No swing, but deliberate offsets: a percussion sample nudged 20 ms early creates the genre's mechanical unease.

electromodern.arrangement: A six to seven-minute club format, mixable: a 32-bar intro with drums and one element, the body in 16-bar sections, a break around the middle with a white noise riser and filter over 8 to 16 bars, a return on a roll or one beat of silence, a 32-bar outro. Alternate syncopated electro sections and four-on-the-floor sections to change the energy without changing the sounds. Cutoff and distortion automations make the build-ups. Plan a second, shorter break three quarters of the way through. The vocoder comes back like a chorus every 32 bars. It's more dramatic than Detroit and much more structured than electro-funk.
electromodern.basse: An analog electro bass, bigger than in Detroit: sawtooth with a sine sub underneath, on Analog, Repro-1 or a VCO module. Cutoff at 350 Hz, medium resonance, filter envelope with a short 100 ms decay, and distortion after the synth: Saturator or Roar, 8 dB of drive, for grit. Sixteenth notes in octave jumps on the root, with chromatic passing notes at the end of the phrase, in minor, often in A or F. The Attack book describes a bass where the cutoff is automated a little every bar and more before each 4-bar turn: that's exactly the movement to give it here. Sidechain from the kick, 4 dB, release 150 ms.
etapes: Tempo at 134 BPM, 808: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and step 12 into a Drum Buss with 20% drive, clap and snare stacked on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenth notes.
Program a B pattern where the kick lands on every beat, for the techno sections.
Build a sawtooth plus sine sub bass, cutoff 350 Hz, 8 dB saturation, sixteenth notes in octave jumps, 4 dB sidechain from the kick.
Add a mono or modular lead in a 16-step sequence with two ratcheted steps, and a minor stab into a dotted-eighth delay.
Record a vocoded phrase with chorus that will come back every 32 bars.
Arrange in club format: 32-bar intro, 16-bar sections, break with white noise and filter, electro and four-on-the-floor alternating, 32-bar outro.
electromodern.mix: Busier and louder than the rest of the family, calibrated for club systems. Kick at -6 dBFS, sidechained bass behind it, mono sub down to 35 Hz. Saturation on almost everything, distortion on the bass and leads, Drum Buss on the drums. Reverb is allowed, but short on the drums (300 ms) and medium on the stabs (1.2 s), with a 20 ms pre-delay. Glue bus compression at 2:1, attack 10 ms, auto release, 2 dB of reduction. A dynamic EQ on the bass at 200 Hz avoids mud. Master around -8 LUFS integrated with a limiter, the style can take the pressure. Check in mono: wide Legowelt-style basses collapse otherwise.

outils.pourquoi: Affordable analog 808 clone of the 2010s wave, kick with a 350 ms decay then run into Drum Buss; Roland TR-8S is the digital alternative.
Helena Hauff names it as her favorite tool, fun to program and useful as a master controller for the rest of the setup.
Semi-modular cited in the Attack book, for saturated leads in 16-step sequences with ratcheting and for modular percussion.
Analog electro bass in sixteenth notes and octave jumps, with the cutoff moving at each 4-bar turn; TAL-BassLine-101 today.
Sawtooth plus sine sub, cutoff at 350 Hz, decay 100 ms, before a distortion; Ableton Analog or a modular VCO do the same.
On the drum bus with 20% drive and a light Boom at 50 Hz, the processing that makes the 808 harder and dirtier than Detroit.
Distortion with 8 dB of drive after the bass and on the leads for club grit; Saturator does the job in older versions of Live.
The vocoder back as the lead voice, cold lyrics, doubled with a chorus to widen it, as a chorus every 32 bars.

reperes: I-F: Space Invaders Are Smoking Grass (1997): dirty italo, vocoder and octave bass, the starting point of the revival.
DMX Krew: You Can't Hide Your Love (1997): 1982-style keyboards and arpeggios replayed with precision.
DJ Stingray: Sphere of Influence (2013): the speed, the saturated sounds and the club format of the 2010s wave.
Gesloten Cirkel: Submit X (2014): the huge bass and the brutal mix, between techno and electro.
electromodern.rythme: 808 or a clone (Behringer RD-8, Roland TR-8S, 808 kits in Drum Rack) with harder processing than Detroit. Kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and step 12, decay 350 ms, run through a Drum Buss with 20% drive and a light Boom at 50 Hz. Clap or snare on 2 and 4, often both stacked with a short reverb and a transient shaper. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes with alternating velocities, open hat on the offbeats, sometimes a thinner 606 hi-hat on top. Add modular percussion or short FM noises on unexpected offbeats, and 808 toms as fills. Program a B pattern in four-on-the-floor for the techno sections.
electromodern.sons: The vocoder is back as the lead voice, often with cold lyrics and a wider sound, doubled with a chorus. The leads come from a modular or a saturated mono synth, with sixteenth-note sequences and ratcheting on some steps (repeat a note in thirty-second notes). The minor chord stabs are short and run through a dotted-eighth delay. With I-F and Legowelt, an italo color: octave arpeggios, Juno pads, a sine lead in echo. The Attack book advises having arpeggios play short, plucky sounds, instant attack, brief decay, so they don't swamp the mix. Add rising white noise, absent in Detroit, for club transitions.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Arpeggios chapter, Melodic techno arp walkthrough)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros and Arpeggios chapters)
electromodern.tempo: Modern electro is played in techno clubs: 128 to 140 BPM, I-F around 130, Helena Hauff and DJ Stingray often above 135. The grid stays strict but, unlike Detroit, the feel is heavier and dirtier: the kicks have more sub, the sounds are saturated. What also changes is the role of the four-on-the-floor: many tracks alternate syncopated electro sections with sections where the kick lands on every beat, to mix with techno. Pick 134 BPM as a starting point, and plan both kick variants from the programming stage so you can switch.

elektronischemusik.arrangement: The form follows from the system: if your series of durations is 3, 5, 8, 13, your sections will last 13, 21, 34 and 55 seconds, or their multiples. Each section explores a different frequency band, from low to high for example, then comes back. There's no build-up or drop, only densities: one section can contain a single sustained sound, the next thirty impulses per second. To make the piece feel alive to modern ears, place a memorable event at one third and two thirds of the length, a complete three-second silence for example. Five to ten minutes is a good length. Spatialization, five channels in Gesang der Jünglinge, translates in stereo into hand-drawn panning trajectories.
elektronischemusik.basse: The bass is a pure sine, Cologne's basic building block. A single operator in Operator, sine waveform, on notes that follow your pitch system rather than the tempered scale. Stockhausen in Studie I used fixed frequency ratios: start from 100 Hz and multiply by 1.25 or 1.6 to find your other notes, then set Operator's fine Pitch to reach them. Make each note last a very long time, 20 to 60 seconds, with slow volume swells. To give it life, layer a second sine a few hertz apart: the slow beating acts as a low pulse. No sidechain, no saturation: the low end must stay clean and be judged on a meter, on speakers that go low.
etapes: Choose a series of numbers and derive your durations and frequency ratios from it.
Build three additive timbres from sines in Operator (an impulsive one, a sustained one, a low beating one).
Create two narrow-band filtered noise sounds with Wavetable and Auto Filter as a band-pass.
Write the events in MIDI according to your series, without relying on feel, then listen and adjust the density.
Add panning trajectories and an automated reverb send for depth.
Export without compression, with 12 dB of headroom, and listen on real speakers.
elektronischemusik.mix: Pure sounds are unforgiving: every sine must sit exactly in its place, with no distortion. Keep 12 dB of headroom on the master, no saturation, no limiter. Check with Spectrum that your frequency bands don't overlap where you didn't intend them to. Reverb is used as a compositional parameter: dry means close, wet means distant, and you automate the send to move a sound. A Reverb at 3 seconds on a return is enough. Low sines can cause phase cancellation between left and right; keep them mono below 120 Hz with Utility. Export at 24 bits, without aggressive dither, so the silences stay black.

outils.nom: WDR studio sine, impulse and noise generators
outils.pourquoi: Cologne's gray boxes: every timbre in Studie I is built sine by sine, at calculated fixed frequencies, then mixed on tape.
The monophonic keyboard of the studio's early days, alongside the Trautonium, soon replaced by pure generators; any single-oscillator mono synth can replace it.

outils.nom: Laboratory ring modulator and band-pass filters
outils.pourquoi: The ring modulator hardens attacks and creates inharmonic spectra, the filters carve white noise into narrow bands for Studie II.
The studio's tape machine: layering of sine layers, editing to the millisecond, speed changes to transpose intermediate mixes.
The voltage-controlled modular installed at the WDR in the early 1970s to Stockhausen's specifications, with its sine, square, sawtooth and noise generators.
Additive with four sines (parallel algorithm): metallic impulse with an 80 ms decay, breath with a 400 ms attack, low beating between two operators.
The native ring modulator: set to 300 Hz, it hardens the attacks and makes pure sounds inharmonic, like the Cologne boxes.
The subtractive approach of Studie II: Wavetable in noise mode, then Auto Filter as a band-pass with a Q of 8 or more for narrow noise bands.

reperes: Karlheinz Stockhausen: Studie I (1953): only sines, calculated frequency ratios, the purity of the Cologne program.
Karlheinz Stockhausen: Studie II (1954): noise bands and impulses organized by a graphic score.
Karlheinz Stockhausen: Gesang der Jünglinge (1956): the recorded voice finally enters the studio, spatialized over five channels.
Herbert Eimert: Klang im unbegrenzten Raum (1952): the studio's first attempt, electronic timbres and boundless space.
elektronischemusik.rythme: There are no drums and no percussion: rhythmic events are envelopes applied to synthesized sounds. In Operator, create a sound made of four sines (four additive operators, no modulation) and give it a 0 ms attack and an 80 ms decay: you get a metallic impulse. Make a second one with a 400 ms attack and a long decay, which becomes a breath. The rhythmic structure is born from alternating these two types according to your series of durations. Program the notes in MIDI on a sixteenth-note grid, then remove everything that falls on the strong beats: the sense of pulse disappears, the order remains. A Ring Modulator (Frequency Shifter in Ring mode) set to 300 Hz hardens the attacks further.
elektronischemusik.sons: The brief names frequency generators, the ring modulator, band-pass filters and the multitrack tape recorder: each sound is built additively, sine by sine, or subtractively, from white noise filtered into narrow bands. In Ableton, additive is done with Operator (four sines, parallel algorithm) or by stacking several instances; subtractive with Wavetable in noise mode and Auto Filter as a band-pass, Q at 8 or higher. The Melochord, a monophonic keyboard in the studio, can be replaced by any single-oscillator mono synth. Tape editing translates into cutting audio clips to the millisecond. Gesang der Jünglinge adds the boy's voice: fragments of words transposed, mixed with sines until you can no longer tell which is which.
elektronischemusik.tempo: What sets Cologne apart from Paris is the refusal of recording: everything is calculated. Durations are set by series of numbers, not by feel. To get close to it, pick a small series, for example 3, 5, 8, 13 (Fibonacci), and turn it into your durations in seconds or sixteenth notes. A tempo of 120 BPM makes the sixteenth note a 125 ms unit, handy for the math. No groove, no swing: rhythm is a structure. Studie II, in 1954, went as far as publishing the score as a graph of durations and frequency bands. Your track can have a pulse, but it must derive from the same system of proportions as the pitches.

eurodisco.arrangement: Euro disco loves long formats, sometimes a whole side of an LP. The principle is the sequence that never stops: it is the chords changing underneath, the filter opening, a layer added every 8 or 16 bars. Start with the bass sequence alone, add the kick at bar 9, the hi-hats at 17, the strings at 33. The vocals come in late. The breakdowns remove the drums but never the sequence. Plan build-ups of filtered white noise and upward key changes at one third and two thirds of the track. Aim for 7 to 9 minutes for a club version, with 32 clean bars at each end.
eurodisco.basse: This is where the sequenced bass is born. The modular Moog plays eighth or sixteenth notes in octaves, with a dotted delay that creates the galloping feel. The model is I Feel Love: a repeated eighth note, sent into a dotted-eighth delay, which gives the octave pattern that seems to go faster than it really does. Reproduce it with Operator or a Moog emulation (Arturia Modular V, Cherry Audio), a sawtooth wave, a low-pass filter at 300 Hz with a touch of resonance, a short 80 ms envelope. The note holds on the root, then the chord changes and the note follows. The kick and the bass land together on every beat: it is a fusion, not a dialogue.
etapes: Set 126 BPM with no swing, create an Operator track or a Moog emulation with a sawtooth and a low-pass filter at 300 Hz.
Write an eighth-note bass on the root, add a dotted-eighth delay to create the octave gallop.
Program dry drums: kick on the beats, clap and snare on 2 and 4, even sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Add a string synth with chorus playing long chords, then an ARP-style lead that answers the vocals.
Build by accumulation over 8 minutes: the sequence runs, the chords change, the filter opens, a key change around the middle.
Compress the bass and the master heavily, stereo delay on the vocals, long plate on the strings.
eurodisco.mix: The studio compression is heavy and deliberate. Compress the sequenced bass at 4:1 with a fast 5 ms attack so it pumps slightly. The kick is drier than in disco. Little reverb on the sequence: it must stay centered and precise, while the synth strings go into a long 2 to 3 second plate. Delay is the main effect: dotted eighth on the bass, quarter note on the vocals. Pan the delay repeats left and right. An SSL-style bus compressor on the master at 2:1 with a fast release gives the pumping quality of the era. Cut the lows below 35 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: The modular system behind I Feel Love: eighth-note octave bass, kick, hi-hats and filtered white noise, all from the same machine, driven by a sequencer.
The usual modular Moog emulation for rebuilding the sequenced bass: sawtooth, low-pass at 300 Hz with a touch of resonance, short 80 ms envelope.
Enough for the Moroder bass: a sawtooth wave, a dotted-eighth delay behind it, and the gallop appears without a modular.
The acid leads and the gliding sirens. Today, the ARP Odyssey from the Korg Collection or the Korg ARP Odyssey reissue.
The slightly cold synth strings that replace the orchestra, with chorus and slow phaser; the Arturia Solina V emulation does the same job.
The early drum machine that holds the bed while the drummer plays on top; CR-78 samples in a Drum Rack are enough.
The SSL-style bus compressor on the master, 2:1 with fast release, for the deliberate pumping of the Munich productions.

reperes: Giorgio Moroder: From Here To Eternity (1977): the sequenced Moog bass that carries everything, and the vocoder.
Cerrone: Supernature (1977): the blend of tight played drums and cold synths, with the octave bass riff.
Silver Convention: Fly Robin Fly (1975): the simplicity of the vocals and the string arrangement that replaces the lyrics.
Munich Machine: Get On The Funk Train (1977): the Musicland sound, sequences and drums to a click over a whole side.
eurodisco.rythme: The rhythm section is drier and more regular than in disco. Kick on all four beats, snare on 2 and 4, often doubled with a clap. The hi-hat plays perfectly even eighth or sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats but less expressive. Few congas, more tambourine and cabasa. On some records, an early drum machine (Roland CR-78, Maestro Rhythm King) lays down the bed while the drummer plays on top. In your DAW, use a heavily quantized acoustic drum kit, or a mix of a played snare with a drum machine kick. Fills are rare: the tension comes from the synths, not from rolls.
eurodisco.sons: The modular Moog is the heart: sequenced bass, gliding leads, filtered white noise in the build-ups. The ARP Odyssey gives the acid leads and the siren effects. The strings are often a string synth (Solina, ARP String Ensemble) rather than a real orchestra, which gives that colder sound. The vocoder appears, and the female vocals are doubled, ethereal. An analog sequencer drives everything: in Ableton, a 16-step MIDI clip with filter automation does exactly the same job. Put a chorus on the synth strings and a slow phaser on the pads. What to aim for: precision and a slight coldness, not warmth.
sourcesOutils: Sound On Sound (Classic Tracks: Donna Summer, I Feel Love)
eurodisco.tempo: Euro disco sits a little above American disco: 120 to 132 BPM, often 125 to 128. Above all, the feel changes. Munich and Milan work to a metronome or a sequencer: the eighth notes are straight, with no swing. Set your project to 126 BPM, quantization at 100%, swing at zero. The groove no longer comes from the drummer but from the perfect repetition of a synth sequence and the small chord variations on top of it. Where disco breathes, euro disco pulses. If you use a played drum kit, it has to sound tight, recorded to a click, like Keith Forsey's drums for Giorgio Moroder.

eurotechno.arrangement: Five to seven minutes, thought out in 16-bar phrases. A 32-bar intro of drums and sub. The riff comes in at bar 33, the build-up starts at 49 with the snare roll, drop at 65 with crash and hoover. A 32-bar central breakdown: kick cut, strings or stabs alone, white noise riser over the last 8, roll, then a drop harder than the first. The second half is similar with a variation of the riff. A 32-bar drum outro. Unlike Detroit, here the drop exists and has to be felt. Unlike hardcore, keep the structure readable and leave bars to breathe after each drop.
eurotechno.basse: Two options. The first: a simple sub on the root, one note per beat or in eighth notes, generated by a Juno-106 or Operator, which leaves room for the riffs. The second, more typical: the bass is a rave riff played low on an Alpha Juno, sawtooth wave with PWM, in eighth or sixteenth notes, on two or three notes, filter at 800 Hz with resonance. It has to work without the kick during the breakdowns. Layer the two: sine sub below 80 Hz, riff cut at 100 Hz on top. Light sidechain on the riff, 4:1 ratio, 100 ms release. The bassline of Pullover is a good model: few notes, a lot of pressure.
etapes: At 135 BPM, lay down a 909 kick with a second kick for body, clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Create a sine sub on the root in eighth notes and an Alpha Juno or Serum bass riff on three notes.
Program a hoover: two detuned saws, noise, a pitch that drops one octave on the attack.
Sample a minor chord and play it as stabs on the offbeats, with a hall reverb.
Write a 4-bar snare roll with rising velocity before each drop.
Arrange in 16-bar phrases: intro, riff, build-up, drop, 32-bar breakdown, drop, outro.
eurotechno.mix: A mix loaded in the midrange: stabs and hoover dominate between 300 Hz and 3 kHz, the kick and sub alone occupy the low end. Cut the hoover at 150 Hz and the stabs at 200 Hz. Drum bus with Glue at 4:1 and 4 dB of reduction, Analog Clip saturation at 3 dB for pressure. Reverb on the claps, not on the kick. The riffs can be mono or slightly widened by a chorus, but keep the image centered. Kick at -8 dB, riff at -10, stabs at -12. Masters of the era were modest; today you can go up to -8 LUFS with a gentle limiter, without crushing the rolls, which must stay dynamic.

outils.pourquoi: The hoover, WhatThe preset: PWM sawtooth waves, chorus, pitch that drops on the attack; recreate it in Serum or Diva with two saws and noise.
Kick with sustain doubled by a second kick, clap on 2 and 4, snare rolls in sixteenth then thirty-second notes before each drop.
The sampler for the rave stabs: a sampled minor chord played across the whole keyboard, so detuned at the extremes, plus breakbeats under the kick.
Strings for the breakdowns and a simple sub on the root; TAL-U-NO-LX or the Roland Cloud Juno-106 are the usual emulations.
Modern rebuild of the hoover and the sawtooth bass riffs, filter at 800 Hz with resonance, one-octave pitch drop in 100 ms.
In FM for metallic stabs, and an eighth-note sine sub that leaves all the room for the riffs between 300 Hz and 3 kHz.
On the drum bus at 4:1 with 4 dB of reduction, followed by Saturator in Analog Clip at 3 dB for rave pressure.

reperes: Mescalinum United: Into Mekong Center (1989): heavy kick and synth riff, the bridge between Frankfurt and hardcore
Speedy J: Pullover (1991): a mono riff bass, strings, the Dutch rave structure in its pure form
Jaydee: Plastic Dreams (1992): organ and bass over ten minutes, the example of a riff that holds a whole track
Cygnus X: The Orange Theme (1993): the melodic build-up, the strings and the kick, what would become trance
eurotechno.rythme: 909 kick with more sustain than in Detroit, often doubled with a second kick for body. 909 clap on 2 and 4 with a short reverb, plus a layered 909 snare for the rolls. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats, ride on the strong phrases. Crash at the start of every 16 bars. The signature: snare rolls in sixteenth notes then thirty-second notes over the last four bars before a drop, with rising velocity. Add descending 909 tom fills at the end of 8-bar phrases. Sampled breakbeats (Akai S1000) can double the kick in the build-up sections, that is the rave heritage.
eurotechno.sons: The Alpha Juno hoover is the sound of the genre: WhatThe preset, sawtooth waves with pulse width modulation, built-in chorus, a pitch envelope that drops on the attack. Recreate it in Serum or Diva with two detuned saws, noise, and a pitch that falls one octave in 100 ms. The rave stabs: a minor chord sampled into an Akai S1000, played from a single key across the whole keyboard, so detuned at the extremes. Add sirens, pitched vocal snippets, Juno-106 strings for the breakdowns. Effects: medium hall reverb on the stabs, quarter-note delay on the sirens. In Ableton, Operator in FM makes good metallic stabs.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
eurotechno.tempo: Between 128 and 140 BPM, faster than Detroit and Belgium: Speedy J, Harthouse and the German raves push toward 135 or 140. No swing or almost none, the groove is straight and martial, and it is the hi-hat velocities and the rolls that give the energy. The feel is that of the rave: every 16-bar phrase has to move toward something. You read the tempo in the sixteenth-note hi-hats at full speed. If in doubt, 135 is the center of gravity. The tempo can rise by 2 BPM mid-track as in some live sets of the era, but in a DAW keep it fixed and work on intensity instead.

eurotrance.arrangement: Radio structure: 8-bar intro with the filtered hook, 8-bar verse, 8-bar pre-chorus with a roll, 16-bar chorus with the supersaw hook and the vocal, verse, chorus, 8- to 16-bar breakdown with piano and vocal alone, roll, doubled final chorus, clean ending. Club version: add a 16-bar intro of kick and hi-hat, a 16-bar outro, and double each chorus. The hook must be heard at least six times. The breakdown is short and only serves to relaunch. Anything that lasts more than 16 bars without a change gets cut.
eurotrance.basse: The pumped kick-bass: an offbeat bass sidechained so hard that it seems sucked in by every kick, 10:1 ratio, 70 ms release. A simple sawtooth, Virus or Triton, cutoff 350 Hz, on the root almost all the time, moving to the fourth or the sixth in the chorus. No sixteenth-note layer: the pumping is enough. Sine sub below 60 Hz. In the breakdown, the bass drops out completely. It does not have to be pretty, it has to pump with the kick on a club system and on a car radio. Cut at 80 Hz and saturate lightly.
etapes: Project at 140 BPM, 909 kick compressed hard on every beat, bright open hat on the offbeat, clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note tambourine.
Write an 8-bar whistleable hook in minor and play it on a simplified supersaw with portamento.
Lay down the offbeat bass sidechained at 10:1 on the root, with a sine sub underneath.
Record or pitch a female vocal singing the hook, compress it at 6:1 and add a chorus.
Arrange in a 3 minute 30 radio structure: 8-bar intro, verse, pre-chorus with roll, chorus, short breakdown, final chorus.
Push the master toward -5 LUFS with 2 dB more at 10 kHz and compare with a compilation from the era.
eurotrance.mix: Loud and bright, designed for radio compression. Kick in the center around -5 dB peak, bass glued to it by the sidechain. Vocal compressed and bright, +3 dB at 8 kHz, centered. The supersaw lead wide, cut at 200 Hz, compressed 4:1. Everything that is not kick, bass, vocal or lead sits low in the mix. Short reverb everywhere, 1.5 second decay. Master: glue compressor at 3:1, an EQ adding 2 dB at 10 kHz and 1 dB at 60 Hz, hard limiter around -5 LUFS. The result must sound as loud as the other tracks on a compilation: that is the genre's criterion.

outils.pourquoi: Rack version of the JP-8000: the Sandstorm hook comes from its factory preset. Simplified supersaw lead, 3 to 5 voices, light portamento.
Wide pads, strings and verse piano in Kontor's German studios. Korg Triton in the Korg Collection as software.
Leads and basses on the productions of Darude and JS16, the digital complement to the JP-8080 for whistleable hooks.
Female vocals locked in and pitched up a semitone or two, compressed 6:1: the characteristic vocal artifact of the genre.
Rompler with lead, pad and piano presets calibrated for radio dance: the shortcut for today's hands up and eurotrance producers.
Sandstorm was put together in Cubase VST: the DAW of eurotrance studios for three-minute radio structures.
Hard limiter on the master around -5 LUFS, to sound as loud as the other tracks on a compilation, the genre's criterion.

reperes: ATB: 9PM Till I Come (1998): the synth hook with portamento repeated to the point of obsession, over a pumped kick
Darude: Sandstorm (1999): the repeated sixteenth-note lead and the snare rolls every 8 bars, the instrumental euro trance formula
DJ Sammy & Yanou ft. Do: Heaven (2001): a pop song turned into euro trance, compressed vocal and radio structure
4 Strings: Take Me Away (Into the Night) (2002): the pitched vocal, the pumped kick-bass and the chorus that arrives before the one-minute mark
eurotrance.rythme: Pumped 909 kick: compressed hard, 8:1 ratio, with an accented click, often layered with a shorter sampled kick. Very loud open hat on the offbeat, as in hard trance, but brighter. Clap on 2 and 4 with a short reverb. 4-bar snare rolls before each chorus, sixteenth then thirty-second notes, with a reversed cymbal. Crash on the first beat of every 8-bar block. The pattern barely changes: the vocal and the lead provide the variation. Add an eighth-note tambourine for radio brightness.
eurotrance.sons: The simplified supersaw: a JP-8000 or a Korg Triton as a monophonic lead, 3 to 5 unison voices, playing a 4- or 8-bar hook that is easy to whistle, in minor, with light portamento. The female vocals are compressed hard, 6:1 ratio, often pitched up a semitone or two, with a chorus. The chorus is sung over the synth hook, or the hook itself is sung. Wide Triton pads, a piano in the verse. Simple effects: white noise build-up, impact, siren. No complex arpeggios: two notes in eighth notes are enough. Everything has to be recognizable in 5 seconds.
