eurotrance.tempo: 138 to 142 BPM, often 140, with a pumped pulse: the sidechain on the bass and the pads gives a mechanical sway that replaces the groove. Straight grid, full quantization. The feel is that of radio: everything has to arrive fast, the chorus at 45 seconds, no long intro. Count in 8-bar blocks, never 32. Darude's Sandstorm is around 136, ATB's 9PM Till I Come around 132: the genre is not the fastest in the family, but it is the most in a hurry. A radio version lasts 3 minutes 30, the club version 6 minutes with a 16-bar intro and outro.

fidgethouse.arrangement: Five to six minutes, electro 12-inch structure: 16- or 32-bar intro with the drums and a vocal, 8-bar build-up with a snare roll and a rising filter, drop at bar 33 with the twisted bass. The drop lasts 32 bars, then a 16-bar breakdown with the vocal alone in echo. Second drop with a variation of the bass (different LFO rate). The breakdowns are often jokes: a one-bar silence, a ridiculous vocal, a brutal return. Beat Repeat fills on the last 2 bars of each 8-bar block are essential. Short outro, 16 bars. The track is made to surprise, not to drift.
fidgethouse.basse: The twisted bass is the center of the genre, a precursor of the wobble. In Massive or Serum: two saw oscillators detuned by 15 cents, a 24 dB low-pass filter with 40% resonance, and a pitch envelope that drops 3 to 5 semitones over the first 30 milliseconds of each note. A square or sine LFO synced to the eighth or sixteenth note modulates the cutoff between 200 Hz and 2 kHz. The pattern is syncopated, in sixteenth notes with gaps, often a note and its fifth, with glides. Change the LFO rate every 2 bars. A soft distortion (Saturator at 6 dB) and a very obvious sidechain with a 200 ms release make the whole thing elastic.
etapes: Tempo 128 BPM, fat kick on the beats with one kick removed every 4 bars, gated clap on 2 and 4, hats swung at 66%.
Build the bass in Massive or Serum: detuned saws, pitch dropping 4 semitones in 30 ms, LFO on the cutoff at the eighth note.
Pitch a vocal up 6 semitones without formants, cut it into syllables and place them on a swung grid.
Put Beat Repeat on the percussion group with Chance at 20% and draw fills on the last 2 bars of each block.
Arrange as a 12-inch: intro 32, build-up 8, drop 32, breakdown 16, second drop with a different LFO, outro 16.
Saturate and compress hard, obvious sidechain, limiter around -6 LUFS.
fidgethouse.mix: Loud and dirty mix. Kick around -8 dBFS, bass right behind it, and the obvious sidechain is part of the aesthetic. The bass is saturated then compressed hard, 6:1 ratio, to stay constant despite the LFO. The pitched vocals are compressed at 4:1 with a high-pass at 300 Hz and an exciter in the highs. A multiband compressor on the master to hold the low end. Lots of stereo width on the percussion and vocals, mono below 120 Hz. Gated reverb on the clap, short and bright. Aggressive limiter, aim for -6 LUFS like the 12-inches of the era, with 3 dB of reduction. If it distorts a little, that is intentional. Compare with the 2007 Dubsided releases.

outils.pourquoi: The twisted bass of 2007: two detuned saws, 24 dB filter, square LFO on the cutoff between 200 Hz and 2 kHz.
Today's replacement for Massive for the same bass, with the pitch envelope dropping 4 semitones in 30 ms.
On the percussion group, Chance at 20%, Grid 1/16, and 1/32 fills on the last two bars of each block.
Two grooves rubbing against each other: MPC 16 Swing at 66% on the hats, Swing 8 at 58% on the bass.
Raise a rap vocal 6 semitones without formants for the chipmunk effect, then cut it into syllables on the grid.
Fat kick and gated clap; a tuned 808 kick layered underneath for body, samples or D16 emulation.
6 dB of drive on the bass before 6:1 compression, so it stays constant despite the LFO.

reperes: Switch: A Bit Patchy (2007): the sliding bass, the hiccups, the extreme swing, the whole genre on one 12-inch.
Fake Blood: Mars (2009): the looped chopped vocal, the surprising drop, the end of the blog house era.
Mr. Oizo: Flat Beat (1999): the ancestor, a talking bass and a hiccupping groove ten years before the name.
Format B: Like A Techmachine (2005): the German side, more techno, same taste for cuts.
fidgethouse.rythme: Fat 909 kick, often with a tuned 808 kick layer for body, on every beat but with one or two kicks removed every 4 bars for the hiccup effect. Clap on 2 and 4, big, with a 200 ms gated reverb. The closed hi-hat plays heavily swung sixteenth notes, 30 ms decay, with velocities jumping from 40 to 120. The open hat on the offbeats, often chopped by a Beat Repeat at 1/32 on one eighth note. The percussion is noises: mouth sounds, beeps, a cut-off shout. Use Beat Repeat with Chance at 20% and Grid at 1/16 on the percussion group to create random stutters. A one-bar pattern must never be symmetrical.
fidgethouse.sons: Pitched and chopped vocals are the signature: take a word or a phrase of rap or dancehall, raise it 5 to 7 semitones without preserving formants for the chipmunk effect, then cut it into syllables that you move around a grid of swung sixteenth notes. A second vocal lowered by 5 semitones gives the contrast. Video game beeps, sirens, crowd shouts, mouth noises, anything is welcome if it is short. A major chord stab, Juno or Analog, zero attack, very short, on the offbeats. Massive also provides stuttering square leads. Effects: Beat Repeat everywhere, sixteenth-note delay with a filter, flanger on the clap for the high-energy passages.
sources: Sonic Academy (Tech Tips, Electro / Fidget House Bassline)
sourcesOutils: Sonic Academy (Tech Tips Volume 6, Electro / Fidget House Bassline)
MusicRadar (How to make a Foamo-style fidget house bassline)
fidgethouse.tempo: 125 to 130 BPM, often 128, with exaggerated swing: 60 to 66% on the sixteenth notes, much more than the tech house it comes from. The feel is hiccupping, jerky, inherited from UK garage and 2-step: the hi-hats and percussion are pushed far back, and some bass hits land early. In Ableton, an MPC 16 Swing groove at 66% on the hats, plus a different groove (Swing 8 at 58%) on the bass so the two rub against each other. Add eighth-note silences in the middle of the bar. The track should feel like it stumbles and catches itself on every beat.

floridabreaks.arrangement: A Florida breaks track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and follows a simple club form. 16-bar intro on the 808 and the hi-hats, with a scratch. The sampled break and the bass come in at bar 17. A 32-bar section with the stabs. 16-bar breakdown: the 808 stops, a vocal and a stab remain, build-up with a hi-hat roll. 32-bar drop with everything. Second 16-bar breakdown with the scratch solo. Second 32-bar drop. 16-bar outro on the 808 alone. The changes are marked by an 808 hi-hat “roll” and a crowd shout. The track must stay joyful and direct from start to finish.
floridabreaks.basse: The round 808 basses of the brief: the 808 kick itself, with a long decay (600 ms to 1 s), tuned to the root, serves as the bass on the strong beats, as in Miami bass. On top, a funky synth line: a square or a saw on Analog or a Juno, low-pass filter at 500 Hz with a fast envelope, in syncopated sixteenth notes, on the root, the minor seventh and the octave, like a 1984 electro line. The long 808 kick and the synth bass alternate: kick on the strong beats, bass on the offbeats. An extra sub is rarely needed, the 808 handles the low end. Light sidechain of the synth bass by the kick.
etapes: Set Ableton to 135 BPM with 55% swing. Program an 808: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and the “a” of 3, clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Lengthen the 808 kick decay to 800 ms and tune it to the root: it is your bass on the strong beats.
Add an electro or funk break in the background, filtered at 150 Hz, and a funky synth bass in sixteenth notes on the offbeats.
Place a minor rave stab every 2 bars and a sampled scratch as percussion.
Arrange intro 16, break and bass 32, breakdown 16, drop 32, scratch breakdown 16, drop 32, outro 16.
Mix the 808 kick loud and mono, bumps at 60 Hz and 8 kHz on the master, -7 LUFS.
floridabreaks.mix: The Florida breaks mix is made for cars: the long 808 kick is the loudest element, mono, boosted at 55 Hz, and it is not sidechained. The synth bass is high-passed at 90 Hz so it does not fight with it. The 808 snare is snappy, boosted at 2 kHz, with a short gated-type reverb. The 808 hi-hats are bright, cut below 1 kHz. The sampled break is compressed and high-passed at 150 Hz, set back. The stabs are wide and bright. Master at -7 LUFS, with a 2 dB bump at 60 Hz and another at 8 kHz on the main bus, like a Miami bass master.

outils.pourquoi: Round kick, cowbell, clap and hi-hats of Miami electro; Roland Cloud TR-808 or D16 Nepheton as emulation.
Funky electro breaks and rave stab samples sequenced with swing, at 130-140 BPM, in the studios of Orlando and Tampa.
Scratches and lifting vocal phrases; the scene is first of all a DJ culture, with DJ Icey leading the way.
A rack of 808 samples or the 808 kit from Drum Synths for kick, snare, clap and cowbell under the break.
Funky synth line in syncopated sixteenth notes, square or saw, filter at 500 Hz with a fast envelope.
Replaces the Juno for the funky line and the minor-chord rave stabs, two saws and a resonant filter.
Packs of long tuned 808s and funk breaks at 130 BPM; the 808 bass is the held note under the break.

reperes: Dynamix II: Just Give The DJ A Break (1987): Miami electro with 808 and scratches, the turning point toward Florida breaks.
DJ Icey: Escape (1996): the funky break, the rave stabs and the round 808, the Orlando sound.
Rabbit in the Moon: Out of Body Experience (1994): the psychedelic, long side of the Florida raves.
Baby Anne: Bounce That Ass (2000): the 808 kick as bass, the cracking snare, pure club Florida breaks.
floridabreaks.rythme: The funky electro breaks of the brief: a sampled break (often an electro or funk break, mostly played whole) layered with 808 programming. 808 kick on beat 1, the “and” of 2 and the “a” of 3, 808 snare or clap on 2 and 4, 808 hi-hats in sixteenth notes with openings on the offbeats, and thirty-second-note hi-hat “rolls” on the last beat every 4 bars. Add 808 cowbells in a clave pattern, and scratches (cited in the brief) as percussion: a “baby scratch” on the “and” of 3. The brief cites the MPC60: program with 55% swing.
floridabreaks.sons: The brief cites the TR-808, the MPC60 and the turntables. The 808 provides kick, snare, hi-hats, cowbell, clap: in Ableton, a Drum Rack of 808 samples or the 808 kit from Drum Synths. The rave stabs are minor chords on a hoover or a sampled piano stab, played on the offbeat every 2 bars, inherited from the English raves. The scratches are recorded on a turntable or sampled: “ahh” and “fresh” phrases, chopped and looped. Add vocoded electro voices, laser noises, synth “zaps”, and a rap vocal phrase cut word by word. The sound is bright and joyful, not dark.
sources: Mateo Barbarossa, “The Golden Era of Florida Raves” (Substack)
floridabreaks.tempo: Florida breaks run between 130 and 140 BPM, often 135, faster than English nu skool. The feel is that of Miami electro: funky, bouncy, with a light swing (54 to 56%) on the sixteenth notes, and an 808 bass that bounces. What sets it apart from nu skool is the American DNA: 1985 hip-hop electro and Miami bass rather than techno. The hi-hats are chattier, the snare snappier, and the whole thing is made for big car systems and beach raves. Think of an 808 drum machine playing a break.

folktronica.arrangement: Tracks last 4 to 7 minutes and are built by accumulating loops: you start with the guitar alone, add a layer every 8 bars, up to 8 or 10 layers, then take some away. Loops of different lengths create changes without you writing them. The climax is not a drop but a density: everything plays, then a clean cut leaves a single spoken voice or a guitar. With The Books, the structure follows the spoken phrases: a collage that changes with every word. Plan a B section where the key changes or where the drum break is reversed. End on the starting sample alone, bare, to show where everything came from.
folktronica.basse: The bass is discreet and often absent from the sub: a sampled double bass, an electric bass played softly, or the low E string of an acoustic guitar isolated and looped. It plays little, held notes or folk patterns in quarter notes, root and fifth, with diatonic passing notes. Cut it at 200 Hz, but do not go looking for rumble: the genre is listened to on living room speakers and headphones. On Caribou's more danceable tracks, a round synth bass appears for 16 bars. A useful trick: sample a low acoustic guitar note into Simpler, set an 800 ms release, and play it as a bass. It sounds like an instrument that does not exist.
etapes: Record 2 minutes of acoustic guitar arpeggios with a mic, without a click, and find the tempo of the best phrase.
Slice the phrase in Simpler in Slice mode or in Granulator, and replay the slices in a new order over 3 bars.
Build a Drum Rack with recorded domestic noises, keys, table, breath, and a finely chopped jazz break.
Sample a low guitar note and play it as a discreet bass, root and fifth, with an 800 ms release.
Add a domestic field recording in the background and a spoken voice run through Grain Delay with random spray.
Arrange by accumulation: a layer every 8 bars up to 10, clean cut, end on the guitar alone, natural and dynamic mix.
folktronica.mix: The mix is natural, dynamic and detailed, without saturation or heavy compression: that is what separates it from lo-fi hip hop. Keep the transients of the clicks and strings. Light compression on the drum bus, 2:1, and nothing on the guitars. Cut the lows at 100 Hz on everything except the bass. The stereo field is wide and alive: each loop has its position and a slight automated pan. Short room reverb on the recordings to put them in the same space, a longer plate on the harp or the vocals. Master at -14 LUFS, very dynamic. Listen on headphones: the granular details at -30 dB are half the pleasure.

outils.pourquoi: Four Tet chops audio directly in the arrangement, without a sampler, with 10 to 14 tracks and factory presets. Warp and Slice do everything.
The raw material: 2 minutes of arpeggios recorded without a click, then cut into 100 to 300 ms slices.
Replay the guitar slices in another order, pitched or reversed, and a low note as bass with an 800 ms release.
Robert Henke's Max for Live granular device: 50 ms grains with random spray on a spoken voice or a harp.
Kitchen, street, children, keys on the table: the domestic field recordings that make the background and the Drum Rack of noises.
For Four Tet it serves as a sampler and a source of discreet pads, alongside Kontakt and Arturia's V Collection.
Harp, banjo, upright piano and toy instruments in libraries, to then put through the same slicing as the guitar.
For those who prefer to cut the slices on pads and play a jazz break out of order, before finishing everything in the DAW.

reperes: Four Tet: She Moves She (2003): the harp and the jazz break chopped into sixteenth notes, the loops drifting apart.
The Books: Take Time (2003): found voices pasted over an acoustic guitar and a cello, the structure that follows the words.
Tunng: Bullets (2007): the folk song with clicks and noises in place of drums, the pop version of the genre.
Caribou: Melody Day (2007): recorded and stacked acoustic percussion, more danceable and psychedelic.
folktronica.rythme: The kit is made of noises and fragments: a knock on a table, a key, a finger snap, a breath, sampled and played like a Drum Rack. The kick is soft, often a low tom or a filtered kick from a jazz break. The snare can be a rimshot, a snap or a percussive guitar cut. The hi-hats are granular clicks and mouth hisses. On top, a jazz drum break finely chopped, with sixteenth-note slices replayed out of order, as on She Moves She. Add recorded acoustic percussion: tambourine, shells, wood. The pattern can be irregular: 7 eighth notes looping against a kick in 4 beats.
folktronica.sons: Sampled acoustic guitar is the raw material: record 2 minutes of simple arpeggios with a mic, then cut them into 100 to 300 ms slices in Simpler in Slice mode or with a Granulator. Replay the slices in a different order, pitched, reversed. Harp, banjo, upright piano and toy instruments follow the same method. Granular slicing makes the textures: Grain Delay or Granulator on a spoken voice, 50 ms grains, with random spray. Domestic field recordings, kitchen, street, children, form the background, as with The Books, who paste in found voices from cassettes. Few synths: when there are any, it is a Rhodes or a discreet sine.
sourcesOutils: Sound On Sound (Four Tet / Kieran Hebden)
Noisegate (Four Tet, New Energy production details)
MusicRadar (Four Tet on presets and Ableton)
folktronica.tempo: 90 to 125 BPM, often with loops of irregular lengths: 3 bars, 5 beats, 7 eighth notes. What changes compared to downtempo is that the tempo is a consequence of the loop, not a starting choice: you sample a phrase of acoustic guitar, you loop it, and the tempo is that of the phrase. The swing comes from the recorded human playing, not from a setting. In Four Tet's work, layers of loops of different lengths drift against each other and create a groove that moves constantly. Program without swing, 50%, and let the recordings bring the imperfection. Try a 3-bar loop over a 4-bar kit: the offset makes the genre.

footwork.arrangement: A series of cuts. Intro of 4 to 8 bars, often the sample alone or the kick alone. The track comes in in blocks of 4 or 8 bars, but each block can remove an element rather than add one. Complete silences of one bar, or two beats, every 16 bars. An 8-bar breakdown with the sample alone and the sub, brutal return of the toms. Second half with a new sample or a new kick pattern. Length 3 to 5 minutes, clean ending or on the sample alone. The structure is not a build-up, it is a conversation between the kicks, the toms and the voice, with breaks that keep the dancers on alert.
footwork.basse: The tuned 808 sub, with a very long decay and glide, in lines of two or three notes that follow the kick pattern or contradict it. Or a held sine that changes note every 4 bars. Often the bass is the kick itself, with the pitch varying from one kick to the next: program the 808 kicks at different pitches (root, fifth, lower octave) so the kick line is also the bassline. No sidechain, no filter. The sub is loud, clean, and it is sometimes the only element left when everything else goes quiet. With DJ Rashad, the bass is often absent for whole bars and then comes back all at once.
etapes: Project at 160 BPM, 808 kicks in an irregular off-beat 2-bar pattern, with silences, and a clap on 3.
Program 808 toms in triplets answering the kicks, and tune the kicks to different pitches so they make the bassline.
Held 808 sub with glide, absent on some bars.
Sample a soul or R&B record, slice it into syllables and repeat one syllable in sixteenth notes over a bar, then another.
Build 4 minutes in blocks of 4 and 8 with one-bar silences, a sample and sub breakdown, and a second kick pattern.
Mix dry, sub up front, samples compressed and bitcrushed, toms spread, master at -8 LUFS.
footwork.mix: A dry mix, with the sub and the samples up front, everything else raw. The 808 sub alone in the low end, unfiltered, with a little saturation so it is audible on a phone. Short kicks with a click. Dry toms, no reverb, spread a little in stereo so the triplets read clearly. Samples compressed hard and sometimes bitcrushed to 12 bits, with a very short delay on the stutters. No long reverb, or just one on a stretched sample. Master saturated and limited to -7 to -8 LUFS. The legibility of the rhythmic layers matters more than cleanliness: if the toms and kicks mask each other, cut the toms below 200 Hz and turn down the hats.

outils.pourquoi: The tool of Teklife and young Chicago producers: 808 kicks in irregular patterns, triplet toms, brutal silences, all in the step sequencer.
As samples: kicks tuned to different pitches so the kick line is the bassline, triplet toms, sub with glide.
RP Boo's drum machine, with an Akai S01 sampler: the modest gear on which the first footwork tracks were made.
MPC2000XL, 2500 or 1000 for DJ Rashad and DJ Spinn, to chop the soul and R&B samples and play them on the pads.
The stutter is the main gesture: a syllable repeated in sixteenth notes over a bar, then another, sliced in Slicex or Simpler.
Repeats, slowdowns and rhythmic gates on the vocal samples, for stutter and cut effects without redrawing everything.
Nothing is synthesized from scratch: the material comes from old records and fragments of rap, cut into syllables and repeated to the point of hypnosis.

reperes: DJ Rashad: Feelin (2013): the soul sample in stutters over off-beat kicks and triplet toms, the masterpiece of the style.
RP Boo: Baby Come On (2013): the brutal silences and the kicks as melody, the architect of footwork in its most abstract form.
DJ Spinn: Dubby (2013): a reading of dub at 160, with the gaps as an instrument.
DJ Manny: Signals in My Head (2021): the next Teklife generation, more melodic, same rhythmic grammar.
footwork.rythme: The 808 kick in irregular 2-bar patterns, often off the beat: few kicks on beat 1, many on the “ands” and the “a”s, with brutal silences. Clap or snare on 3 (half-time) or on 2 and 4, sometimes absent. Sparse sixteenth-note hats, more often chopped rides or shakers. 808 toms in eighth- or sixteenth-note triplets, in rolls of 2 or 3 notes, placed against the kicks. A silence of the whole drum kit for one bar, without warning. The kick patterns are the melody of footwork: write them like phrases, with questions and answers between two bars.
footwork.sons: Samples of soul, R&B, jazz or rap, cut into syllables and short fragments, repeated to the point of hypnosis: one syllable in sixteenth notes over a bar, then another. The stutter is the main gesture, in Slicer or Simpler. Rhodes or piano chords sampled from a record, played as offbeat stabs. Spoken voices, dancers' calls. Video game sounds, sirens, noise. Rare pads, often a stretched sample. Nothing is synthesized from scratch: footwork is an art of sampling in FL Studio, with the basic 808 banks. The style does not look for beauty of sound, it looks for the vertigo of repetition.
sourcesOutils: Big Fish Audio, 6Blocc Footwork Juke Producer Tools
footwork.tempo: 160 BPM, almost always, sometimes 155 or 165. It is the speed of the battles. The feel is double: the dancers count in sixteenth notes at 160, but the track can also be heard in half-time at 80, like slow hip-hop, and the best tracks play on that ambiguity. The triplet toms against the binary kicks create a third grid. Nothing is humanized, everything is quantized, but the placement is so irregular that the track seems to stumble. Where juke changes every 8 bars, footwork can change every 2 and leave silences of a whole bar. Emptiness is a tool.

forestpsy.arrangement: A 32-bar intro can start without a kick, on a field recording, then the kick comes in softly. The body of the track moves forward in 16- or 32-bar sections where the textures replace each other, without the energy level changing much. The breakdowns are clearings: kick cut, the forest keeps rustling for 8 to 16 bars, then the kick returns without a roll, often on a single drum hit. Plan a denser section around two thirds of the way, with all the percussion at once. Aim for 8 to 9 minutes. The track should be mixable over 2 minutes at each end with the kick and bass alone.
forestpsy.basse: The round, woody bass of the brief comes from removing the sour distortion of darkpsy. Start from a triangle wave or a heavily filtered sawtooth (low-pass at 180 Hz, low resonance), with a soft tube saturation that adds round harmonics without grating. The pattern stays rolling in sixteenth notes, kick then three notes, but each note is a little longer (90 ms) and the release a little softer, which gives the “woody” side. Root in F or E, never higher. Add a sine sub and a slight bump around 120 Hz. Some tracks alternate with triplets, but the forest bass moves less than the darkpsy one: it is the ground, not a character.
etapes: Project at 150 BPM. Warm kick tuned to E around 58 Hz, 120 ms body, little click.
Rolling bass on E1 in sixteenth notes, triangle wave filtered at 180 Hz, soft tube saturation, 90 ms notes.
Record or gather field sounds and cut them into percussion: claves, seeds, wooden drums, played with varied velocities and a light swing.
Load a forest recording into Granulator, 40 ms grains with randomness, and play a pad held over 8 bars.
Add a tape delay with wow and flutter at a dotted eighth on the percussion, and a short dark reverb.
Arrange 9 minutes with an intro without kick, clearings without build-ups, and a dense section at two thirds.
forestpsy.mix: The warmth comes through the low mids: unlike darkpsy, let the bass live between 100 and 250 Hz, and do not carve this zone too much on the wooden percussion. Tube or tape saturation on the percussion bus to round off the transients. The field recordings go to the sides, with a high-pass at 300 Hz and a shared short reverb. Light compression on the master, 2:1 ratio, plus a gentle limiter around -8 LUFS: forest does not look for power but for depth. Listen on headphones to check that the micro-details remain audible, then on speakers to check that the kick has body.

outils.pourquoi: The field recorder: rain, insects, stream, cracking wood. These takes become the percussion and pads of the track.
20 to 80 ms grains on the field recordings, randomness on position and pitch, replayed as teeming pads.
Organic synthesized textures: comb filters, slow LFOs, pads swarming under the round bass.
The forest DAW for its sampling tools: Simpler in slices on the acoustic percussion, Echo in tape mode with wow and flutter.
The woody bass: triangle or sawtooth heavily filtered at 180 Hz, soft saturation, 90 ms notes a little longer than in darkpsy.
Short, dark undergrowth reverbs, 0.8 s, damped from 4 kHz, shared by the field recordings.
Wood and skin resonances on dry impacts: turns a click into the percussion of a forest creature.

reperes: Derango: Deranged (2005): the founding track, the round bass and the teeming organic details.
Fungus Funk: Total Confusion (2003): the humor and the moving textures, still close to darkpsy in speed.
Psykovsky: Sunya (2006): the density of micro-events and the way the sections follow each other without a drop.
Battle of the Future Buddhas: Twin Sharkfins (1997): the Scandinavian prehistory of the sound, rough and woody.
forestpsy.rythme: The forest kick is warmer than the darkpsy kick: tune it around 55 to 60 Hz, with a slightly longer body (120 ms) and less click, so it sounds like a foot striking the earth. Snare or rimshot on 2 and 4, but choose a wooden sample: claves, block, skin drum. The hi-hats are discreet, replaced by recorded shakers and seeds. The sampled acoustic percussion of the brief does all the work: a calabash, a water drum, snapped twigs, cut into short slices and replayed in sixteenth notes with varied velocities. Add drum fills at the end of phrases. The rhythm should seem played by a band of creatures, not by a machine.
forestpsy.sons: The granulator and the field recorder are the main instruments. Record yourself: rain, leaves, insects, stream, creaking doors. Cut these sounds in Granulator II or a granular sampler, with 20 to 80 ms grains, a little randomness on position and pitch, and replay them as pads. Absynth adds organic synthesized textures, with comb filters and slow LFOs. The delays are “organic”: a tape delay with wow and flutter, set to a dotted eighth, with a low-pass filter that darkens each repeat. The undergrowth reverbs are short and dark, 0.8 s time, damped from 4 kHz. Almost no melody: two or three recurring notes, played by a sampled wooden instrument.
sourcesOutils: Micro Genre Music, What is Forest Psytrance
Future Media Academy, Forest Music Production with Atropp
forestpsy.tempo: Forest runs a little slower than the darkpsy it descends from: 148 to 152 BPM, rarely more. The feel changes mostly through the material: the grid stays straight, but the sampled percussion keeps its natural imprecision, and you can add a light groove (52 to 54% swing in Ableton) on the percussion tracks only, never on the kick and bass. The track does not build tension toward a drop, it teems: the feeling is that of living ground where something is always moving. Count in 16-bar cycles, but let the textures run over odd lengths (5, 7 or 9 bars) so they never repeat identically.

freestyle.arrangement: It is a pop song: 8-bar instrumental intro with the orch hit, 16-bar verse, 8-bar pre-chorus, 16-bar chorus, then repeat, 8-bar bridge with a possible key change, doubled final chorus. Count four minutes for the radio version, six for the 12-inch, which extends the intro and adds an 808 percussion break in the middle. The most useful production trick: the drum cut for half a bar before each chorus, the vocal holding the note, and the return with a tom roll. The orch hits mark the section entries. The verses are emptier, DX7 bass and 808 alone, so the chorus feels huge.
freestyle.basse: The freestyle bass sound is the Yamaha DX7: a sharp, bright FM bass, with a clean attack and a short tail. In Operator, the Attack book describes the method for getting a DX-family bass: a modulator operator tuned one octave above the carrier, its level around -7 dB, a decay of about two seconds with sustain at zero, which gives a note that brightens on the attack and then closes. Write eighth and sixteenth notes that follow the chord, with octave jumps on the offbeats and chromatic passing notes at the end of phrases. Progressions in minor: i, VI, VII, v is the most common. The bass answers the 808 kick, which keeps the sub.
etapes: Tempo at 116 BPM, 808: kick on 1, the “and” of 2, steps 12 and 16, snare and clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, syncopated cowbell, claves over two bars.
In Operator, build a sharp FM bass (modulator one octave above, level -7 dB, decay 2 s, sustain zero) and play an i, VI, VII, v progression in eighth notes.
Place orch hits on the strong beats of the chorus, transposed to follow the chords, and a Juno pad behind.
Write a vocal melody in minor with a held note in the chorus, record it, double the third.
Arrange as a song: intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, with a drum cut before each chorus.
Mix the vocal in front, 1.8 s plate reverb, dry 808, 2 dB shelf at 10 kHz on the bus.
freestyle.mix: The mix is more produced than the rest of the family: the vocal in front of everything, compressed at 4:1 with a 5 ms attack, with a 1.5 to 2 second plate reverb and an eighth-note delay. The snare and clap get a gated reverb. The 808 kick stays dry, at -8 dBFS, with the DX7 bass right behind it, cut below 70 Hz. The pads are wide, in stereo, and filtered below 200 Hz to keep the low end clean. A slight shelf at 10 kHz on the bus gives the shine of the 1985 New York productions. Gentle bus compression, 2:1 ratio. Aim for -12 LUFS, the dynamics are part of the charm.

outils.pourquoi: Syncopated kick on 1, the and of 2 and steps 12 and 16, cowbell and claves in a simplified clave, toms for the fills; Stevie B used nothing else.
The sharp, bright FM bass of Let the Music Play, the electric pianos and bells of the choruses; Arturia DX7 V or Dexed for the original patches.
To recreate the DX bass: modulator one octave above the carrier, level around -7 dB, two-second decay and sustain zero.
The orch hit on every strong beat of the chorus, transposed to follow the chord; play it as a note in Simpler from a sample or from Arturia CMI V.
The favorite polysynth of New York freestyle studios for pads and chord stabs; Roland Cloud JX-3P is its emulation.
Held chord pads with chorus behind the vocal, filtered below 200 Hz; TAL-U-No-LX or Cherry Audio DCO-106 today.
The 1.5 to 2 second plate reverb on the melodramatic vocal, and in a short gated version on the snare and clap.

reperes: Shannon: Let the Music Play (1983): the sharp DX7 bass, the syncopated 808 and the chorus that set the genre's formula.
Debbie Deb: When I Hear Music (1983): the Miami version, drier, with the orch hits and an unadorned vocal.
Lisa Lisa and Cult Jam: I Wonder If I Take You Home (1985): the drum cut before the chorus and the doubled harmonies.
Stevie B: Spring Love (1988): late freestyle, wide pads and FM keyboards in the foreground.
freestyle.rythme: Always 808, but more ornamented. Kick on 1, on the “and” of 2 and on step 12, with an extra kick on step 16 to push forward. 808 snare on 2 and 4, doubled with a clap with plate reverb. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, open hat on the “ands” of 2 and 4. 808 cowbell in syncopated eighth notes, claves on a two-bar pattern, 808 congas (the toms tuned high) answering the kick. The fills are descending 808 toms and snare rolls, and above all cuts: the drums stop half a bar before the chorus, the vocal alone, then everything comes back. The breakdowns use breakbeats, inherited from hip-hop.
freestyle.sons: Two colors sign the style. The Fairlight orch hit on every strong beat of a chorus, often transposed to follow the chord: play it as a note in Simpler. DX7 keyboards for the rest: FM electric piano (the two-operator algorithm with low modulation and a light tremolo), bells, synthetic marimba. Add Juno or OB pads for the held chords, with chorus. The vocal is the star: a teenage, melodramatic lead, with harmonies doubled at the third and a long plate reverb. The melodies use the natural minor scale with held notes in the chorus. A small mono lead with portamento answers between the sung phrases.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter, DX-style FM bass in Operator)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter)
freestyle.tempo: Freestyle sits between 110 and 122 BPM: Let the Music Play runs around 116, most of the Fever and Cutting hits between 112 and 120. No swing on the 808, but the feel is more melodic than electro-funk because the vocal and the chords carry the track. The rhythmic signature is the Latin syncopation: the kick often anticipates beat 4 by a sixteenth note, and the cowbell and claves trace a simplified clave. It is the first genre in the family where the tempo is chosen for singing, not for rapping: leave room for long vocal phrases and breaths between bars.

frenchcore.arrangement: Tracks last 4 to 6 minutes and keep the tribe structure: 16- to 32-bar intro with kick and a bass pattern, then the lead comes in, then a 16- to 32-bar breakdown with the main melody without kick or at half tempo, build-up with a pitched kick roll, 32-bar drop where the kick bounces under the melody. Two or three cycles, each with a variation of the melody. Frenchcore breakdowns are often the most melodic moment of the track, with the melody played in full. End on kick and bass, 16 bars. What makes the track playable is the constant bounce: never interrupt it during the drops.
frenchcore.basse: The frenchcore bass is melodic, and that is what sets it apart from nu style: the kick tail and its bounce follow a real line, often root, minor third, fourth, fifth, over 4 or 8 bars. You build the tail with Operator or Serum: a sine with a little distortion, an 80 ms descending pitch envelope, Saturator at 18 dB, and you play it via MIDI, which lets you change the notes. The bounce follows the same note. Many producers add a separate saturated bass, a sawtooth filtered at 500 Hz, played in eighth notes on the offbeats, doubling the bounce. Sidechain from the kick attack, 8:1 ratio, 25 ms release.
etapes: Tempo 200 BPM. Build the attack (clipped 909, 50 ms) and the tail (saturated Operator sine, falling pitch, 220 ms decay), and glue them together.
On the next eighth note, place the tail alone at -6 dB with a 120 ms decay: the bounce. Bounce it into one sample.
Play the kick via MIDI following a 4-note bassline over 8 bars (root, minor third, fourth, fifth).
Add a clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, a pitched kick roll before each drop.
Create a melodic sawtooth lead with portamento, an 8-bar melody in harmonic minor, and a screech answering it.
Tribe structure: intro, lead, melodic breakdown, build-up, drop, second cycle with variation, ending. Clipper then limiter.
frenchcore.mix: The kick and its bounce take all of the low end and low mids, at -2 dB peak. The bounce is 6 dB lower than the attack and must stay audible: check it in mono. As the Attack book suggests for layered kicks, every change in the chain (distortion, EQ, transient) affects the whole, so set the kick in a loop while listening to the attack and the bounce together. High-pass at 35 Hz. The leads are high-passed at 300 Hz with a short reverb and a dotted-eighth delay. Light bus compression. Master: clipper then limiter, -5 to -6 LUFS. Compare with Dr. Peacock at the same level.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the frenchcore scene from Dr. Peacock to Sefa: the pierced kick is drawn in the Piano roll with pitch bend, then processed in a chain.
Today's method for the frenchcore kick: sine with a long pitch envelope, internal distortion, then resample and a second pass. Almost all the genre's tutorials start from there.
The origin of the kick, sampled then stretched: the “pierce” comes from a 909 whose tail is lengthened and tuned to the bass.
To set the kick's pitch curve by hand, point by point, before distorting it elsewhere. Useful for the melodic bounce specific to frenchcore.
Melodic saturated basses: sawtooth and sine in FM, played in eighth notes on the root, Saturator behind to make it rough.
On the kick after the resample, Drive 10 dB in Analog Clip, then an EQ to carve 250 Hz: it keeps the bounce without mud.
Screeches and tribe leads: sawtooth, band-pass filter, LFO on pitch. The screaming sound above the kick often comes from there.

reperes: Micropoint: Neurophonie (2000): the bouncing kick and the sped-up free party leads, the source.
Radium: The Beat Is Coming (2001): the very pronounced bounce and the screech answering the bass.
Dr. Peacock: Trip to Ireland (2015): the sampled traditional melody over the frenchcore kick, the style gone global.
Dr. Peacock & Sefa: The Universe (2019): the kick follows a real melodic bassline.
frenchcore.rythme: The frenchcore kick is the most recognizable in the family: an attack, then a saturated tuned tail, then a softer second hit on the offbeat, like a bouncing ball. The classic way to do it: your kick on the beat, and on the next eighth note the tail alone (without attack), pitched the same, at -6 dB, with a shorter decay. The whole thing bounced into a single sample one and a half eighth notes long. Kick on every beat, so a bounce on every offbeat. Snare or clap on 2 and 4, dry. Sixteenth-note hi-hats, discreet. Sixteenth-note kick rolls with rising pitch before each drop, inherited from tribe. The pattern changes little: it is the kick that moves.
frenchcore.sons: Screeches, as in nu style, but often more melodic, playing riffs that follow the bass. Sawtooth leads with portamento, inherited from tribe and psytrance, playing simple melodies in harmonic minor. Flute, violin and traditional music sounds (Irish, Balkan) sampled and sped up: Dr. Peacock made it his trademark. MC vocals in French or English. Samples from French films. Free party sirens. The hoover is rare. The overall sound is more musical and warmer than uptempo, with leads that really sing over the bounce of the kick.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
YouTube, frenchcore kick tutorials (TMPR Kicks and others)
frenchcore.tempo: Frenchcore runs between 190 and 210 BPM, most tracks around 200. In numbers that is close to uptempo and terrorcore, but the feel is unique: it bounces. The reason lies in the kick itself, which contains an offbeat, and in the free party heritage (tribe, 170-180 BPM with a bouncing kick) sped up. No swing in the grid, but a bounce in the sound. At 200 BPM, a beat lasts 300 ms and the kick with its bounce fills exactly that beat. Program at 200 BPM, sixteenth-note grid. The track should make you want to jump on the offbeats, not stomp on the beats.

frenchhouse.arrangement: A pop structure on a club base. 16-bar intro with the loop heavily filtered and the kick pumping. The filter opens over 16 bars, the bass comes in, the melodic chorus arrives early, around bar 33. 16-bar verse with the loop filtered halfway, 16-bar chorus with everything open. 16- to 32-bar breakdown: kick cut, loop pumping alone or vocoder a cappella, filter closing then reopening, brutal return of the kick. Second cycle, extended final chorus, short outro. Length 4 to 6 minutes, often less than disco house: it is radio house, with a short edit for the singles.
frenchhouse.basse: Sampled or replayed bass, in funky eighth notes with octaves, like disco house, but often processed through a talkbox or doubled by a well-filtered synth bass. The line is melodic and follows the chords of the loop. On One More Time, the bass is almost a counter-melody. Heavy sidechain on the bass (6:1 ratio, 200 ms release): it gets squashed by the kick and comes back up, and that pumping defines the sound. A sine sub underneath, also sidechained. Cut the sample's bass and replace it with your own if the two fight. The sub is round, never saturated.
etapes: Project at 124 BPM, a 2- to 4-bar disco loop locked to the grid, a short clean kick underneath, clap on 2 and 4.
Put a sidechain compressor on everything except the kick, 6:1 ratio, 200 ms release, until you hear the breathing.
Funky eighth-note bass with octaves, also sidechained, and a sine sub underneath.
Resonant low-pass Auto Filter and slow phaser on the loop, automated over 16 bars.
Write a 4-bar melodic chorus on synth or vocoder and place it from bar 33 in a 5-minute pop structure.
Mix round and warm, tape saturation on the bus, limiter at -8 LUFS, and make a 3 minute 30 radio edit.
frenchhouse.mix: The sidechain is the mix. A compressor on the bus of everything except the kick, triggered by the kick (4:1 to 8:1 ratio, 1 ms attack, 200 ms release), obvious enough that you hear the breathing. The kick itself is clean, short, with a click. The loop is filtered below 120 Hz and lightly saturated. The phaser is audible but not overbearing. The vocoded vocals are compressed hard and a little bright. The master is warm and round, with a bus compression that glues, tape saturation, and a limiter at -8 LUFS. The mix should sound like a record, not like a club track: balanced, pop, with the sidechain as the only aggression.

outils.pourquoi: Cheap stereo compressor on the master or on the sample bus, pushed hard with a 200 ms release, behind the pumping of Homework and Discovery.
MPC2000 or MPC3000 to chop and loop two bars of disco, played on the pads; the MPC grain is part of the sound.
Stereo analog rack filter associated with the filtered loops of the French touch; Auto Filter in resonant 24 dB does the same gesture in the DAW.
Filtered synth bass doubling the sampled bass, and simple pads; one of Daft Punk's analog synths along with the Oberheim OB-8.
The tube in the mouth on a bass or a lead, for the talking voice of Da Funk and the vocoded choruses; Heil Talk Box or Rocktron Banshee.
Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier on the sung vocals, as described in the lesson; replaces the hardware vocoders of the 1990s.
Slow phaser on the loop's strings, or an emulation of the Small Stone pedal; set very slow so the effect breathes over 8 bars.
Software emulation of the 3630, made to get the French touch compression without buying the rack; Justesse Sounds cites it along with Shy 90s Dynamix.

reperes: Daft Punk: One More Time (2000): the vocoded vocal, the pumping sidechain and a 90-second breakdown that makes you wait for the kick.
Etienne de Crecy: Am I Wrong (1996): the low-pass filter closing and reopening on a loop, the French gesture in its pure form.
Cheek: Venus (Sunshine People) (1996): the whole disco loop, with vocals and strings, pumped by the sidechain and left almost bare.
AIR: Sexy Boy (1998): the pop, vocoded side of the same scene, with a lead synth singing the melody.
frenchhouse.rythme: Simple drums, often a kick sampled from disco or a 909 with a short kick, clap or snare on 2 and 4, hats from the disco sample rather than from a machine. The particularity: the drums are caught in the sidechain with everything else, except the kick itself, which makes them pump. Add open 909 hats on the offbeats, a rim or a cowbell in syncopation. The fills are brutal cuts: everything stops for a beat, or the filter closes all at once. In the breakdowns, the kick disappears and the loop keeps pumping on a ghost kick, which builds anticipation.
frenchhouse.sons: The filtered and phased disco loop: a resonant low-pass that opens and closes, a slow phaser (Ableton's Phaser-Flanger, or a Small Stone emulation) on the strings, and the sidechain pumping over everything. Talkbox and vocoder (Ableton's Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier) on the vocals and sometimes on the bass. Simple sawtooth lead synths with a filter, in 4-bar pop melodies. A block-chord piano or Rhodes. Sampled strings played as chords. The vocals are sung, vocoded, or sampled from a record and replayed. Everything is warm, compressed, with an MPC grain: sampled at 44 kHz but with a little saturation and filtering to age it.
sourcesOutils: Gearnews, Alesis 3630: The Daft Punk Compressor
Justesse Sounds, How to Nail the French House Compression Style
Gearspace, French Filter/House, The Actual Filter
frenchhouse.tempo: Between 120 and 128 BPM, like the disco house it comes from. What changes is the breathing: the feel of the French touch comes from sidechain compression pumping on every kick, with a release that falls just before the next beat. At 125 BPM, a release of 200 to 250 ms on the compressor gives that back-and-forth that makes the whole mix “breathe”. The sampled loop keeps its own swing, the machine stays straight. Think pop: the choruses are melodic and sung, the phrases are 4 or 8 bars, and there is often a real synth melody on top of the loop.

fullon.arrangement: Full-on is the psy subgenre closest to a pop club structure. A 32-bar intro with kick, galloping bass and percussion. A first 32-bar section that sets up a secondary lead motif. First breakdown around bar 80, with pads, vocals and a 16-bar build-up: roll, filter, siren. Drop on the main lead, 32 bars. A longer second breakdown, 32 bars, with a different melody, a more spectacular build-up, final drop with the bass jumping to the octave. A 32-bar outro. Aim for 7 to 8 minutes. A good full-on track has a breakdown you recognize from the first note: that is where you should spend the most time.
fullon.basse: The galloping bass is the DNA of full-on. Take a sawtooth on a Virus or Serum, low-pass filter around 300 Hz with a snappy filter envelope, near-zero release. Program the gallop: kick on sixteenth 1, bass on 2, 3 and 4, then in the next beat kick on 1, bass on 3 and 4 only. Or the triplet version: kick on the first triplet, bass on the other two. The note stays on the root, F# or G in octave 1, but add jumps to the octave or the fifth during the last 4 bars of a section to announce the drop. A light overdrive in the low mids gives the “fat” Hom-Mega quality.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM. Layer a synthetic kick with a sampled click, compress at 8:1, tune to G.
Write the galloping bass: beat 1 kick then 3 sixteenth notes, beat 2 kick then 2 sixteenth notes, alternate over 2 bars. Sawtooth sound filtered at 300 Hz.
Add a big layered snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats on the offbeats, ride on the restarts.
Create a detuned 7-voice unison lead, eighth-note melody in G minor with upward bends, dotted-eighth delay.
Build a 32-bar breakdown with a pad, a sampled vocal and a 16-bar build-up (roll, filter, siren).
Arrange 7 minutes: intro, section, breakdown, drop, breakdown, drop, outro. Limit the master around -7 LUFS.
fullon.mix: Full-on is mixed loud and bright. Kick and bass compressed together on a bus with a fast compressor, 1 ms attack, 30 ms release, 4:1 ratio, then a little saturation. The lead needs space: cut the bass around 400 Hz with a dynamic EQ when the lead plays. The cymbals and hi-hats are louder than in darkpsy, with a bump at 10 kHz. Short reverb on the snare, long only on the breakdown pads. Use a powerful limiter on the master, aim for -6 to -7 LUFS, it is a genre that tolerates heavy compression. Check the mono sum: the galloping bass must stay clean on a festival sub.

outils.pourquoi: The galloping bass and the heroic leads of Hom-Mega: sawtooth unison, snappy low-pass filter, internal saturation. The TI is still on stages.
Infected Mushroom's first album is almost entirely multitracked Nord Lead; bright leads and short chord stabs.
The 8-bar build-up FX: noise sweeps, stretched granular textures, breakdown pads. Discontinued by NI but still installed everywhere.
The reference DAW of Israeli full-on, from Astrix to Vini Vici: MIDI programming of the gallop and automation of the snare rolls.
Replaces the Virus for the current generation: sawtooth bass with overdrive in the low mids, 7-voice unison leads.
The punchy full-on kick: clean click around 3 kHz, short body at 60 Hz, then 8:1 compression downstream.
Master limiter pushed to -6 or -7 LUFS: the genre handles heavy compression, but check the mono sum of the bass.

reperes: GMS: Juice (2001): the bass gallop and the saturated lead rising together, a perfect example of the full-on drop.
Infected Mushroom: Blink (2001): the richness of the lead layers and the way the breakdown prepares the return.
Blastoyz: Mandala (2019): current full-on, more compressed, with the bass jumping an octave before each drop.
The Delta: As A Child I Could Walk On The Ceiling (1997): proto full-on, still rough, to hear the origin of the gallop.
fullon.rythme: The full-on kick is punchier than that of basic psytrance: a clean click around 3 kHz, a short body around 60 Hz, compressed hard so it snaps on a big sound system at noon. Layer a click sample on a synthetic kick and compress the whole thing at an 8:1 ratio. The snare is big, layered with a clap and a short reverb, on 2 and 4. The hi-hats play the offbeats, but add rides and crashes on the restarts: full-on loves cymbals. The snare rolls before the drops are long, 8 bars, in sixteenth then thirty-second notes, with a high-pass filter that opens. Tuned toms punctuate the ends of phrases.
fullon.sons: The brief cites the Virus, the Nord Lead and Absynth. The heroic lead is a unison of 5 or 7 detuned sawtooth voices, low-pass filtered with moderate resonance, playing an eighth-note melody on a natural minor scale with long upward bends. Soft saturation and a dotted-eighth delay make it huge. Absynth is used for the build-up FX: noise sweeps and granular textures stretched over 8 bars. Add short chord stabs, vocal samples from films, synth sirens with rising pitch. The breakdowns use warm pads and a synth piano. Everything is bright, saturated, turned toward the top of the spectrum.
sourcesOutils: KVR Audio (Kulshan Studios psytrance Nord Lead banks)
fullon.tempo: Full-on runs at 145 BPM, sometimes 148, never below 142. The difference from the psytrance trunk is not in the number but in the bass: it gallops instead of rolling evenly. Two patterns share the genre. The first alternates kick then three sixteenth notes, then kick and only two notes, which gives an energetic limp. The second is ternary: kick then two eighth-note triplet notes, a true horse gallop. Some tracks switch from one to the other between sections. No swing: the pattern itself gives the bounce. Count in 16-bar blocks and plan changes every 16.

funk.arrangement: A funk track is a groove that hardly changes, with a bandleader calling the sections. Lay down a 2-bar groove and let it run; the form comes from adding and removing instruments, and from a different bridge (often on another chord, announced by the voice). Typical structure: intro on the groove with bass and drums, Clavinet and guitar come in, horns at bar 17, sung verse, a chorus that is just a collective shout, 4-bar drums-only break, bridge on the subdominant chord, return. Length 4 to 7 minutes. For an electronic producer, the key point is the break: 2 to 4 bars of bare drums, it is the track within the track, the one that hip-hop and house will sample.
funk.basse: The bass is the heart: slap or fingerstyle, it plays a 1- or 2-bar phrase in sixteenth notes, with very short cut notes (staccato) and silences as important as the notes. It leans on the root on the one, then circles around it with the octave, the minor seventh and the fifth, on a minor or Dorian scale. Use a sampled electric bass with articulations (Trilian, or the Ableton Electric Bass packs) and write short one-sixteenth notes with velocity 120 accents on the one and on the octave jumps. Slap can be simulated with a layer of slap sample or a fast compression (1 ms attack, 6:1 ratio) that squashes the attack. No sidechain: bass and kick lock the one together.
etapes: Set Ableton to 105 BPM with an MPC 16 Swing 57 groove and program a 2-bar drum pattern with ghost notes on the snare.
Write a bassline in short sixteenth notes, root on the one, silences, an octave jump on a syncopation.
Add a Clavinet in clipped sixteenth notes through Auto Filter as a wah, and a Rhodes playing ninth chords.
Program 3-note horn stabs on the syncopations and a tight strummed guitar.
Let the groove run for 5 minutes with a drums-only break and a bridge on another chord.
Mix dry, slow compression on the drums, gentle saturation, almost no reverb.
funk.mix: The funk mix is dry, warm and compact: little reverb, a round but not deep low end, rich mids. Cut everything below 40 Hz. The kick and bass share 60 to 120 Hz without ducking: set them with EQ, kick at 70 Hz, bass at 110 Hz. Bus compression on the drums with a slow Glue Compressor (30 ms attack, 0.4 second release, 3 dB) that keeps the transients. The bass gets a Compressor at 4:1 ratio with 4 dB of reduction and light tape saturation. A single short 0.7 second room reverb for the horns and the vocal. Everything goes through a gentle Saturator in Analog Clip and a limiter with headroom, target -12 LUFS.

outils.pourquoi: Seventh and ninth chords with stereo tremolo; Ableton Electric, Keyscape or Arturia Stage-73 V replace it, with Auto Pan at the eighth note.
The rhythm guitar of funk, in short sixteenth notes through a wah; Electric in Clavinet mode or Arturia Clavinet V, then Auto Filter in band-pass.
The envelope filter of Bootsy Collins and Bernie Worrell: the squelch that follows the attack; Auto Filter with Envelope at 60% reproduces it.
The voice going through a tube in the mouth with Zapp; today Ableton's Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier, or Antares Articulator.
The synth bass of Flash Light: Worrell stacks several Minimoogs, filter opened by velocity; Arturia Mini V or Analog with a sawtooth.
Electric bass with slap and fingerstyle articulations: one-sixteenth notes, accents at 120 on the one and on the octave jumps.
Rhodes and Clavinet in a single native device: dry, clipped Clavinet mode for the rhythm, round Rhodes for the chords, no sample library.
The MPC 16 Swing 57 groove applied to all the rhythm tracks, snare shifted by 10 to 15 ms: without this swing, funk sounds stiff.

reperes: James Brown: Get Up I Feel Like Being a Sex Machine (1970): the one, the choppy guitar, the bass that plays only what is needed.
The Meters: Cissy Strut (1969): the kick-snare dialogue in sixteenth notes, a break in every bar.
Parliament: Flash Light (1977): the bass played on a Minimoog by Bernie Worrell, funk goes synthetic.
Sly and The Family Stone: Thank You Falettinme Be Mice Elf Agin (1969): Larry Graham's slap bass, the birth of the style.
funk.rythme: Funk drums are played, so every hit is different. To reproduce them, take a dry acoustic kit (Drum Rack, 70s or Session kit), and program in sixteenth notes: kick on 1, then on syncopated positions like the “a” of 2 and the “and” of 3, never four regular hits. Snare on 2 and 4, with ghost notes (velocity 30 to 40) on the sixteenths around them: that is what makes the pattern breathe. Hi-hat in sixteenth notes with openings on the “a” of 4. Vary velocities between 70 and 110 on everything. Cissy Strut is a perfect exercise: kick and snare in dialogue, almost a breakbeat. Add congas and a cabasa in sixteenth notes at low volume for density.
funk.sons: The brief gives the Rhodes, the Clavinet and the talkbox. The Hohner Clavinet D6 is the rhythm guitar of funk: played in short sixteenth notes with a wah, you find it in Ableton's Electric (Clavinet mode) or in a sample, run through Auto Filter in band-pass with an LFO or an envelope for the wah. The Rhodes holds the seventh and ninth chords, with a stereo tremolo (Auto Pan at the eighth note, 40%). Zapp's talkbox, a voice going through a tube in the mouth, can be replaced by Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier, or by a talkbox plugin. The horns play short section stabs: horn section samples with a clean attack, in 3-note chords on the syncopations.
funk.tempo: Funk lives between 95 and 115 BPM, centered around 105. Sex Machine runs around 108, Cissy Strut around 90, Flash Light around 108. The secret is not the tempo but the subdivision: everything happens in sixteenth notes with a light swing of 55 to 58%, never straight, never triplet. The weight falls on the first beat, James Brown's famous one, and the rest of the bar is a conversation of syncopations that come back to land on it. In production, set Ableton's Groove Pool to an MPC 16 Swing 57 groove and apply it to all the rhythm tracks. A funk drummer plays the snare slightly behind the beat: shift it 10 to 15 ms to the right.

futurebass.arrangement: Pop format of 3 to 4 minutes. Intro of 8 to 16 bars with a piano or a voice. 16-bar verse with light drums. 8-bar build-up: snare roll, riser, opening filter, a one-beat silence. Drop of 16 or 32 bars: the chopped chords arrive with the snare on 3 and the sub. Second verse, second build-up, second drop with an extra vocal chop or a chord change. Short outro. The drop is the chorus: it has to be singable, with a vocal chop or lead melody on top of the chords. Everything is written for streaming and the stage.
futurebass.basse: A sine sub or a soft 808 that follows the root of the chords, in long half or whole notes, with a short glide between two notes. In Operator or Serum: sine, 5 ms attack, 200 ms release, a little saturation for presence on small speakers. The bass strictly follows the progression, no independent line. It is sidechained by the kick and by the snare, gently, 3:1 ratio. Sometimes it is chopped by the same LFO as the chords so they pump together. The kick carries the sub, the bass fills between the kicks. Nothing dark: it is a floor that supports the chords.
etapes: Set Ableton to 150 BPM, kick on 1, huge snare on 3, eighth-note hats with a roll every 4 bars.
Write a four-chord progression in 7ths in Serum with 7-voice unison and detune 0.3.
Chop the chords with an LFO on volume at 1/8, add an LFO on the cutoff, then OTT.
Lay down a sine sub following the roots, and a voice cut into syllables pitched up 6 semitones.
Arrange: piano intro, verse 16, build-up 8 with snare roll, drop 16 or 32, second drop.
Mix the chords wide and bright, mono sub, gentle sidechain, master around -6 LUFS.
futurebass.mix: Bright and wide. Supersaw chords wide in stereo, cut below 150 Hz, OTT at 30%, a +2 dB shelf at 10 kHz. Mono sub below 100 Hz, sidechain on kick and snare. Snare around -5 dB peak, with a reverb that stops at the sidechain. Vocal chops up front, 4:1 compression, de-esser. Sidechain visible but gentle: 3:1 ratio, 150 ms release, so everything pumps together. Limiter on the master with 4 dB of reduction, target between -6 and -7 LUFS. Check in mono: the supersaws lose width, keep a center layer with reduced unison.

outils.pourquoi: 7-voice supersaw, detune 0.3, four chords in 7ths, square LFO on volume at 1/8, LFO on the cutoff.
Flume's DAW, with the OTT preset of Multiband Dynamics on the chords and Simpler for the vocal chops.
Multiband at 30% on the supersaw chords to make them wide and bright before the gentle sidechain.
Midrange grit under the chords, plucks and bells, or the sine sub that follows the root.
Plays a vocal chop or a chord at half speed for a fill or a pre-drop, a signature move of the genre.
Multi-effect played live, cited by Flume, to twist a voice or a chord over 2 bars before the drop.
Wide reverb on the pitched vocal chops and the snare, with a sidechain that cuts it on the kick.
Voice cut into syllables, raised 5 to 7 semitones for the kawaii side, with delay and reverb behind.

reperes: Flume: Holdin On (2012): the chopped chords and the pitched vocal, the Australian template.
Cashmere Cat: Mirror Maru (2012): the soft, detailed side, vocal chops and harmony.
Wave Racer: Streamers (2013): sugary maximalism, arpeggios and video game sounds.
Flume: Never Be Like You (2016): the fully realized pop format, singable drop and gentle sidechain.
futurebass.rythme: Kick on 1, often doubled on the “and” of 2 or on 4, with a short sub. Snare on 3, huge: clap, acoustic snare, filtered white noise, 1 second reverb. Hats in eighth notes, with sixteenth-note or triplet rolls at the ends of phrases, a trap legacy. Soft percussion: snaps, finger clicks, a shaker. In the build-ups, an 8-bar snare roll that accelerates from eighth to thirty-second notes, and a white noise riser. After the drop, the drums are often absent for 2 bars to leave the chords alone. Drum kit from Serum or softened trap samples.
futurebass.sons: The chopped supersaw chord: in Serum, a saw oscillator with 7-voice unison, detune at 0.3, a four-chord progression in 7ths or 9ths, then an LFO on volume at 1/8 or 1/16, square or sawtooth shape, for the chopping. Add an LFO on the cutoff for the “wow” side. OTT on the chords. Pitched vocal chops: a voice cut into syllables in Simpler, raised 5 to 7 semitones for the kawaii side, with a delay and a reverb. Bells, plucks, synthetic flute, a piano in the intro. Gentle sidechain that makes it breathe. Massive or Serum, Ableton to assemble everything.
sourcesOutils: Magnetic Mag, Future Bass Producer's Toolkit: 11 Plugins You Should Own
Stealify Sounds, 10 Best Future Bass Effect Plugins
futurebass.tempo: Between 140 and 160 BPM in halfstep, which gives a feel of 70 to 80 BPM: the snare is on beat 3. 150 is a good center. The feel is that of a softer trap, with less dense hats and a bounce that comes from the chopped chords rather than from the drums. A little swing on the hats, 54 to 56%. What changes compared to UK bass: everything is melodic, pop, in a major key or a bright minor, and the bass gives way to the chords. The rhythmic signature is not in the drums but in the LFO that chops the chords into eighth or sixteenth notes.

futuregarage.arrangement: 4 to 6 minutes, no drop. A beatless intro of 30 to 60 seconds: rain, voice, pad. The drums come in without warning, often with a placement flaw. The sections come and go: the drums stop in the middle, a voice floats alone for 8 bars, then everything returns. No strict 16-bar blocks, rather irregular lengths. A track can contain two different pieces separated by a silence of a few seconds. End on the texture alone. It is not a DJ tool: it is a listening piece that keeps the pulse of the club in the background.
futuregarage.basse: A soft sine sub, without aggression, played in long half or whole notes, in minor. In Operator: sine, 20 ms attack, 300 ms release so the notes overlap slightly. No wobble, no Reese: the bass is a floor, not a character. Sometimes a second, warmer bass layer, a sampled 808 or a slightly saturated sub, run through a short reverb, which is forbidden elsewhere but here contributes to the veil. The bass does not really dialogue with the kick, it floats underneath. A note every 2 bars, a chord change every 8.
etapes: Set Ableton to 138 BPM, lay down a 2-step skeleton, then turn off quantization and move the hits by hand.
Replace the drum samples with found objects and run them through a short reverb and a filter at 8 kHz.
Add a vinyl crackle and rain track that plays continuously.
Lay down a sine sub in long notes, then a pitched vocal in a 5-second reverb with a filtered delay.
Arrange without a drop: beatless intro, irregular sections, drum stops, ending on the texture.
Mix while keeping the dynamics, saturate and filter the drums, target -12 LUFS.
futuregarage.mix: Deliberately lo-fi but controlled. High-pass at 200 Hz on everything except the kick and bass. Saturate the drums with Saturator in Analog Clip mode, then cut at 8 kHz. Let the reverb tails overlap, but watch the low end: cut the reverbs below 400 Hz. Keep the dynamics: no aggressive sidechain, gentle compression on the master bus, 2:1 ratio. Target around -12 LUFS, lower than the rest of the family. Resample the whole mix in an old format, 12 bits with Redux, then blend it back at 30% with the original. The big question of the mix: does it sound like a memory?

outils.pourquoi: Burial's audio editor: editing by ear, without a grid or MIDI, every hit placed and moved by hand in the timeline.
To imitate that editing: move the samples in the arrangement view, quantization off, 10 to 30 ms delays on the hits.
Time-stretching an R'n'B a cappella with artifacts, raised several semitones, before a 5-second reverb.
Pads filtered at 1 kHz with chorus, a chord held in the distance, and a soft sine sub in long notes.
Warm pads with built-in chorus, drowned in reverb; the TAL-U-NO-LX emulation gives its sound without the machine.
To assemble the garage breaks on pads, with MPC swing, then degrade everything to 12 bits.
12-bit reduction on the drums or on the whole mix, blended back at 30%, for the memory-of-a-club feel.

outils.nom: W. A. Production, Future Garage Foundation
outils.pourquoi: Vinyl crackle, veiled breaks, pads and Serum presets inspired by Burial and Mount Kimbie, to set the mood quickly.

reperes: Burial: Archangel (2007): the pitched, veiled vocal, the hand-placed drums, the continuous crackle.
Mount Kimbie: Maybes (2009): the collage of found objects and guitar, the garage rhythm in the background.
Joy Orbison: Hyph Mngo (2009): the club version of this sensibility, chopped vocal and swing.
Burial: Kindred (2012): the long form, two tracks in one, silences and returns.
futuregarage.rythme: A 2-step skeleton: kick on 1 and 2.5, snare on 2 and 4, swung hats. But every sound is a found object: a snare from a scratched record, a lighter, a key noise, a clap sampled in a street. Run the drums through a reverb at 20% and a short delay, then cut the highs at 8 kHz. Add a continuous layer of vinyl crackle, a separate track that plays for the whole length. Some hits are missing, others are doubled. Burial edited everything in Sound Forge, by ear, without a grid: imitate this by moving the samples in the arrangement timeline rather than in a MIDI clip.
futuregarage.sons: Pitched, ghostly vocals: an R'n'B a cappella slowed down or raised several semitones, time-stretched with artifacts in Simpler, drowned in a 5-second reverb and a filtered delay. Vinyl crackle, rain, street at night, field recordings, tape hiss. Massive or Juno pads filtered at 1 kHz, with a chorus. A distant piano or Rhodes playing two chords. Long reverbs on sends, with a high-pass at 400 Hz before the reverb so the low end does not drown. Everything is gray, damp and distant. An MPC or Ableton for the assembly, but the spirit remains that of collage.
sourcesOutils: Rekkerd, W.A. Production releases Future Garage Foundation
futuregarage.tempo: Between 130 and 140 BPM, 138 being the tempo of many Burial tracks. The patterns are those of 2-step, but the feel is blurry: the hits are placed by hand, off the grid, with delays of 10 to 30 ms that make the drums seem to stagger. In Ableton, turn off quantization or move the notes afterwards. The swing is not a percentage, it is human imprecision. What changes compared to the 2-step and dubstep it descends from: the energy is lowered, the hits are drowned in reverb and crackle, and the track sounds like a memory of a club more than a club.

futurehouse.arrangement: Pop structure for streaming. Intro of 8 to 16 bars with the filtered bass pattern and the kick. 16-bar sung verse with chords and hats. 8-bar pre-drop: sung chorus, rising pads, snare roll, silence. 16-bar drop: the pluck bass melody, kick, clap, chops. 16-bar verse 2, pre-drop, second 16-bar drop with a melody variation or an added lead, outro of 8 to 16. Length 3 to 4 minutes in the radio version, 5 minutes in the club version with extended intro and outro. The first drop arrives before the one-minute mark: the style is made for the first 30 seconds of a streaming listen.
futurehouse.basse: The filtered pluck bass: Spire or Sylenth1, one or two sawtooths with light unison, a low-pass filter with a fast envelope (attack 0, decay 150 to 250 ms) and resonance, which gives the pluck, then a soft distortion, a phaser or a moving formant for the talking effect. The pattern is a melody: eighth and sixteenth notes, within one octave, with passing notes and repetitions, over 2 or 4 bars, in a minor scale. Automate the cutoff on the melody for the accents. Pronounced sidechain (4:1 ratio, 150 ms release). A clean sine sub underneath, on the roots, held.
etapes: Project at 126 BPM, clean kick on every beat, layered clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hats with a slight shuffle.
In Spire or Sylenth1, create a pluck bass: sawtooth, resonant filter with fast envelope, light phaser, soft distortion.
Write a 4-bar bass melody in eighth and sixteenth notes, in minor, with repetitions, and automate the cutoff on the accents.
Add a sine sub on the roots, sidechain at 4:1, then pitched vocal chops and a sung chorus.
Build 3 minutes 30 in a pop structure with a melodic drop at bar 33 and a varied second drop.
Mix clean and bright, carve out 250 to 400 Hz, sparkle at 10 kHz, limiter at -7 LUFS, and check on a phone.
futurehouse.mix: A pop mix, clean and bright. The pluck bass up front, between 100 Hz and 5 kHz, with the clean sine sub underneath, sidechained together. Kick in the center, crisp, with a click at 4 kHz. Wide clap with a short reverb. Chops and leads spread out, with an eighth-note delay. Medium bus compression, an EQ that carves out 250 to 400 Hz for clarity, and some sparkle at 10 kHz on the master. Limiter at -6 to -7 LUFS, without audible clipping: the sound must stay clean. The vocal is mixed as in pop: heavy compression, de-esser, clearly audible reverb and delay. Check on a phone: the style lives on small speakers.

outils.pourquoi: The filtered pluck bass with fast envelope and resonance, plus the supersaw leads; the synth associated with Oliver Heldens and Don Diablo.
Same role as Spire, sawtooths in light unison, resonant filter moving on the bass melody, wide pads.
The dominant DAW of the Spinnin' and Heldeep generation, for 3 minute 30 pop structures with a melodic drop at bar 33.
For the talking bass with a formant or a phaser inside the synth, and the vocal chops pitched into a melody.
Preset rompler for plucks, pianos and bright pads, very common in future house and commercial dance studios.
Transparent limiter to hold -6 to -7 LUFS without audible clipping: the style lives on headphones and a playlist, not on a club system.
Future house banks from W. A. Production or Dance Midi Samples, a common starting point for the pluck bass before rewriting it.

reperes: Oliver Heldens: Gecko (2014): the pluck bass that seems to talk, played as a melody over a clean drop, the founding record.
Tchami: Promesses (2014): the deeper, vocal side, with a resonant filter moving on every note.
Don Diablo: On My Mind (2015): the pop structure and the melodic drop, future house calibrated for streaming.
Curbi: Discharge (2015): the most metallic and plucked bass, the Spinnin' sound at its most recognizable.
futurehouse.rythme: 909 or sampled kick, clean, with a click and medium sustain, on every beat. Layered clap on 2 and 4, with a snap and a short reverb. Closed hats in sixteenth notes with a slight shuffle, open on the offbeats, bright. A shaker or a percussion in sixteenth notes on the drop. Sixteenth-note snare fills over 2 bars before the drop, with white noise, a rising siren and a one-beat silence. On the drop, short syncopated percussion (rims, clicks) doubling the bass melody. The drums are clean and bright, mixed like pop: nothing sticks out, everything is crisp.
futurehouse.sons: Sylenth1 and Spire for everything: pluck bass, supersaw leads for the build-up, wide pads. Vocal chops pitched into a melody, with a formant shift, and a sung pop chorus. A piano or a synth pluck for the melodic chorus. Chord stabs on the drop. Build-up effects: white noise, siren, riser. Signature effects: the resonant filter moving on the bass, the phaser, the visible sidechain, the bright short reverb, the eighth-note delay on the chops. Everything is clean, bright, calibrated for headphones and a playlist. The drop is melodic, often an instrumental answer to the sung chorus, and that is what sets the style apart from the more aggressive electro house.
sourcesOutils: W. A. Production, Future House for Sylenth1 & Spire
Dance Midi Samples, Future House Presets for Sylenth1
futurehouse.tempo: Between 124 and 128 BPM, the clean house tempo of the Netherlands. The feel is square, light, without swing, with a slight shuffle on the hats (52 to 54%) that sets it apart from the heavier bass house. The pluck bass plays in eighth and sixteenth notes, like a melody, and it is this melodic pattern that defines the track. The sidechain is pronounced but musical. Pop song structure for streaming: short intro, drop at bar 33, sung chorus. Think melody before thinking bass: the future house drop is a melody played by a bass, not a bass riff.

futurepop.arrangement: A song in a trance structure, 5 to 6 minutes. DJ intro of 16 to 32 bars: kick, hi-hats, then the bass. First sung verse over the plucks and the bass. Pre-chorus with the pad and the snare roll. Chorus: the supersaw comes in, the vocal doubled, everything together. Second verse, chorus. Then a 16-bar breakdown without kick: the pad and the vocal alone, the supersaw melody comes back filtered, build-up with white noise and roll, then the last chorus, often doubled, with the lead melody added. 16-bar outro for the DJ. The emotion builds by accumulation, never by rupture.
futurepop.basse: A rolling bass between EBM and trance. Sawtooth on an Access Virus, a JP-8000 or Wavetable, low-pass filter at 500 Hz, in sixteenth notes, on the root. The typical pattern: the bass plays on the sixteenth notes that do not fall on the kick, which gives the trance roll, or in continuous sixteenth notes with the EBM accent on the octave. Sidechain from the kick, 6 dB, 120 ms release, for club pumping. The notes follow the chord progression: four minor chords, often i, VI, III, VII. A sine sub layer, in eighth notes, under the sawtooth. No heavy distortion: 3 dB of saturation at most.
etapes: At 132 BPM, program a club kick, clap and snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, open hat on the offbeats.
Write a progression of four minor chords and a rolling sixteenth-note bass on Wavetable, filter at 500 Hz, 6 dB sidechain.
Create a pluck for the verses and a Unison supersaw for the chorus, with a 3-second reverb and a dotted-eighth delay.
Sing a clear, in-tune melody, doubled on the chorus, with light pitch correction.
Program a snare roll and a white noise build-up over the 4 bars before each chorus.
Arrange over 5 minutes 30 with a 32-bar DJ intro, a 16-bar breakdown without kick and a doubled final chorus.
futurepop.mix: A polished club mix. Sidechain on the bass, the plucks and the pads, with different intensities: 6 dB on the bass, 3 dB on the pads. The kick is in the center, clean, with a sub down to 40 Hz. The supersaws spread wide, cut below 200 Hz to leave room for the bass. The vocal is up front, compressed in two stages (4:1 then 3:1), with de-esser, 2-second plate reverb and an eighth-note delay. Subtractive EQ on every element so everything stays clear despite the density. Master: 2:1 compression, light EQ lifting the air at 12 kHz, limiter. Aim for -7 LUFS, it is a loud and bright genre.

outils.pourquoi: VNV Nation's synth: chorus supersaws, rolling sixteenth-note basses, cold pads. Wehbba says it can do almost anything.
Seven detuned sawtooths, filter at 4 kHz, 3-second reverb: the genre's original supersaw. Roland Cloud JP-8000 as software.
Sixteenth-note plucks, 150 ms decay, to carry the verses, and softened EBM sequences as a filtered sawtooth.
The scene's historical sequencer, for trance structures in blocks of 8 and 16 bars with a 32-bar DJ intro.
VNV Nation's analog mono synth for the sub layer and the basses that keep the EBM heritage. Behringer Pro-1 as an affordable clone.
Unison mode for the supersaw, sawtooth bass filtered at 500 Hz with a 6 dB sidechain: the lesson's native solution.
Discreet pitch correction on the clear vocal, doubled on the choruses, for the club finish without grain.
7-voice Unison supersaw and bright plucks, the most common software synth among the scene's current producers.

reperes: VNV Nation: Beloved (2002): the chorus supersaw, the clear vocal, the trance structure carrying a song.
Covenant: Call the Ships to Port (2002): the rolling bass inherited from EBM under a pop melody.
Apoptygma Berzerk: Kathy's Song (2000): the verse pluck, the accumulation toward the chorus, the club finish.
futurepop.rythme: Clean club kick, a processed 909 or a synthetic kick with a crisp sub, on every beat. Clap and snare layered on 2 and 4, with a 1.5 second plate reverb. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes with alternating velocities of 100 and 60, open hat on the offbeats. Ride on the choruses. Snare rolls in sixteenth then thirty-second notes over the last 4 bars before each chorus, with an automated volume rise. A few light electronic percussion sounds, a rim or a click, on the offbeats of the verses. No distortion on the drums: everything is crisp, bright, calibrated for the club.
futurepop.sons: The supersaw is the sound of the chorus: seven detuned sawtooths on a JP-8000, a Virus or Wavetable in Unison mode, with a filter at 4 kHz, a 3-second reverb and a dotted-eighth delay. Sixteenth-note plucks (sawtooth, 150 ms decay) carry the verses. The pads are wide and cold, chorused sawtooths. The vocal is clear, in tune, melodic, doubled on the choruses with discreet pitch correction. Softened EBM sequences: the square bass becomes a filtered sawtooth. A few synthetic string arpeggios for emotion. Everything is produced with a club finish, without lo-fi grain.
sources: Equipboard and KVR forum (VNV Nation's gear: Access Virus)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros: Favourite bit of kit)
futurepop.tempo: Between 125 and 140 BPM, most often 128 to 135, straight, with a trance feel: four regular beats, open hat on the offbeats, snare rolls before the choruses.
