What sets futurepop apart from the electro-industrial it descends from: the grid is that of a club track, clean and regular, and the tempo never moves. What sets it apart from neighboring uplifting trance: it keeps sung verses and a sixteenth-note bass inherited from EBM. In your DAW, start at 132 BPM, full quantization, and think in blocks of 8 and 16 bars.

gabber.arrangement: A gabber track lasts 4 to 6 minutes, very square: a 16- or 32-bar intro with the kick alone, sometimes with a vocal sample announcing the track, then a hoover riff over 16 bars, then an 8- to 16-bar breakdown without kick where the vocal sample and the hoover answer each other, snare roll, return of the kick. Two or three cycles. The breakdowns are longer and more melodic than in hardcore techno: that is where the crowd sings. Many tracks use a half-tempo passage (kick on 1 and 3) before the final return, which lifts the room again. End on the kick alone, 16 bars.
gabber.basse: There is no bass in classic gabber. The tail of the crushed kick is the bass: when you clip a 909 with a long decay hard, the end of the sample becomes an almost square wave at the kick's pitch, and that pitch becomes the root of the track. So tune your kick: pitch the sample so its tail lands on the root (often between F and A, around 45-55 Hz fundamental, but heard mostly through its harmonics). The hoovers and stabs must be in the same key. If you want a truly clean low end, add an Operator sine below 60 Hz, sidechained hard (10:1 ratio, 50 ms release), but purists do not do it.
etapes: Tempo 175 BPM. Load a 909 kick with a long decay into Simpler, tune it to the root of the track.
Put Saturator in Hard Clip with 20 to 30 dB of Drive, listen to the tail turn into a note. Record the result as audio, reload it, clip it again.
Kick on every beat, 909 snare on 2 and 4 with a 2-bar sixteenth-note roll before each drop.
Create a two-note hoover riff (root and fifth, or root and minor third) in eighth notes, run through Overdrive.
Sample a film line, loop it over the breakdown, pitch it if needed.
Structure: 32 bars of kick, 16 of riff, 16 of breakdown, 32 of drop, breakdown, final drop, end on the kick. Hard limiter on the master.
gabber.mix: The whole mix is the kick. It occupies the entire range from -3 dB to -1 dB peak, and everything else slots into the gaps. As the Attack book points out, distortion adds frequencies that EQ cannot create: here you use it to fill the midrange with the kick itself. EQ after the distortion to cut below 40 Hz and soften around 3-4 kHz, where the clipping becomes painful. Snare compressed hard (8:1 ratio, 1 ms attack) so it cracks on top. No long reverb anywhere, except on the vocals in the breakdowns. Master: brutal limiter, -6 to -7 LUFS, distortion embraced. The track should sound crushed, that is the style.

outils.pourquoi: The 909 kick with gain all the way up, crushed into clipping then sent through a low-pass that you open as the track goes on. The starting point of every gabber kick, in hardware or via Drumazon.
The Rotterdam hoover, played as a one-eighth-note stab every two beats. The very sound of Poing and Alles Naar De Klote.
The rack sampler of the Rotterdam studios: resampled kicks, film voices and sirens replayed on the keyboard. Simpler or a Drum Rack replaces it today.
Stabs and small sawtooth basslines, chorus on, on the rare tracks that keep a bass under the kick.
The DAW of Dutch hardcore producers for twenty years: kick drawn by hand in the Piano roll then sent through Fruity WaveShaper to crush it.
Kick chain: Saturator, then Overdrive, then Redux at 12 bits to dirty it up, Auto Filter as a low-pass automated over 8 bars to open the kick.
Reload the resampled kick and pitch it across the keyboard for end-of-block variations; Operator handles the stabs when you have no Juno.
To design a synthetic gabber kick: steep pitch envelope, sine body, short click, then external distortion. Free alternative: Synsonic BD-909.

reperes: Rotterdam Termination Source: Poing (1992): a single spring sound and a clipped kick, all of gabber fits in this skeleton.
Euromasters: Alles Naar De Klote (1992): the crushed kick serving as bass and the vocal sample repeated like a slogan.
Neophyte: Braincracking (1996): the hoover turned into the main riff and the snare rolls before each return.
Paul Elstak: Luv U More (1995): the melodic side, piano and vocal, over the same crushed kick.
gabber.rythme: The gabber kick is no longer a distorted 909, it is a crushed 909: the waveform turns square from all the clipping, and the kick's tail becomes a held note. The classic method: a 909 kick in a Roland S-330 or an Akai, played through a console pushed into the red or through a pedal, re-recorded, played back even louder. In a DAW: Saturator in hard clip, Drive 25 dB, then EQ to remove the lows, then clip again. The kick on every beat, without exception. 909 snare on 2 and 4 well up front, sometimes a clap alone. Hi-hats almost absent or in heavily saturated eighth notes. Snare rolls over 2 or 4 bars before each drop.
gabber.sons: The Alpha Juno hoover, again, but played higher and louder, like a two-note riff. Rave stabs taken from the Juno-106 or sampled. Samples from films and cartoons in Dutch or English, shouted, repeated in loops. Sirens, sawtooth synth sounds with fast vibrato. Voices pitched up on Paul Elstak's happier tracks. All of it run through the same distortion as the kick so it blends. In Ableton: Overdrive on the synth bus, Redux at 8 bits on the samples, and Auto Filter with resonance at 30 for the sweeps. Few elements, but each one pushed to the max.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno)
Wavosaur, 5 free VST for hardcore gabber hardstyle kick (blog.wavosaur.com)
KVR Audio, Free hardcore kick vst forum (kvraudio.com)
Gearspace, Early hardcore gabber kick attempt (gearspace.com)
gabber.tempo: Gabber pushes between 160 and 190 BPM, with the bulk of the 1992-1996 Rotterdam output around 170-180. What changes compared to hardcore techno is that the tempo leaves room for nothing but the kick: at 180 BPM, a beat lasts 333 ms, and the kick has to fill almost all of that time. No swing, no nuance. The feel is that of hakken, the dance: the feet follow every kick, so every kick has to be identical. You program at 175 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, velocity 127 everywhere. The half-tempo passages (breakdowns with the kick on 1 and 3) let things breathe before going flat out again.

garagehouse.arrangement: It is a mixable song. A 16- to 32-bar DJ intro with drums and percussion, then the bass and organ settle in. A 16-bar sung verse, an 8-bar pre-chorus where the chords rise, a 16-bar chorus with backing vocals and strings. A 16-bar breakdown removes kick and bass to keep only the vocal, a pad and the shaker, often with a gospel ad lib, then the chorus returns at full power. Two or three cycles, an extended final chorus with ad libs, a 32-bar drum outro. Length 6 to 8 minutes in the club version. The dub version, without lead, with only the backing vocals, is almost mandatory.
garagehouse.basse: A round, played bass, or one that sounds like it: an electric bass preset or a Moog-type synth with a filter closed around 250 Hz, slightly slow attack, medium release. The line follows a real chord progression, four or eight bars, with chromatic passing notes between the roots and octave jumps on the last beat. Rhythm: quarter and eighth notes, with the first note often anticipated by a sixteenth before the beat, like a disco bassist. Avoid Chicago's tight sixteenth notes. Play it on a keyboard with velocity, or draw velocities between 70 and 110 to imitate that. Gentle compression, 3:1, to smooth it out.
etapes: Project at 122 BPM, softened 909 kit with doubled kick, snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hats with 56% swing, plus a conga loop and a shaker.
Write a progression of four minor 7 and major 7 chords over 8 bars, played as block chords on the M1 organ on the offbeats.
Play a round bass following the roots with anticipations before the beat and chromatic passing notes.
Record or sample a lead vocal and backing vocals, structured as verse, pre-chorus, chorus.
Assemble 7 minutes with a DJ intro, two song cycles, a vocal and pad breakdown, and a drum outro.
Mix the vocal up front with opto compression and hall, kick under the vocal, percussion spread out, and make a dub version without the lead.
garagehouse.mix: The mix is warm and wide. The vocal is centered, a little forward, with an opto compressor or an LA-2A emulation, a de-esser, a 2 to 3 s hall reverb and a quarter-note delay as a discreet return. The drums are quieter than on a Chicago track: the kick stays under the vocal, the snare has a short plate. The percussion is spread in stereo. Organ and piano slightly left and right, bass centered with a cut below 35 Hz. Gentle bus compression (2:1, slow attack) to glue without pumping. Aim for a mix that holds up on the radio as well as at the Zanzibar: balanced, with no harshness around 3 kHz.

outils.pourquoi: The Organ 2 preset in block chords and the percussive M1 piano: the keyboard of New York garage; Korg Collection M1 gives the exact plugin version.
Softened here: short kick doubled with a sampled acoustic kick, snare rather than clap, hats swung at 56% in the DAW.
Official remake of the M1 with its original banks; turn off the internal effects and replace them with a light chorus and some saturation, as the lesson advises.
The 12-bit sampler of Blaze and the New Jersey studios for disco a cappellas and conga loops; Simpler in slices today.
The opto compressor on the gospel vocal in front of the whole mix; a Universal Audio or Waves CLA-2A emulation plays the same role as a plugin.
When the organ is played rather than block-chorded on the M1; a drawbar organ plugin like Arturia B-3 V does the same in a DAW.
The round garage bass is played or imitates playing; record a bassist or draw velocities between 70 and 110 on a played-bass preset.

reperes: Ten City: That's The Way Love Is (1989): soul vocals and written strings over a house rhythm, the model of the garage song.
Crystal Waters: Gypsy Woman (1991): the M1 organ in chords on the offbeats and a three-syllable chorus that is enough.
Masters At Work: I Can't Get No Sleep (1993): the played bass and the layered percussion, the 909 keeping a low profile under the vocal.
Kerri Chandler: You Get Lost in It (2022): the garage formula held thirty years later, warm kick and organ chords intact.
garagehouse.rythme: The 909 is there but softened: short kick, often doubled with a sampled acoustic kick, snare rather than clap on 2 and 4, or both with the snare underneath. Swung sixteenth-note hats, open on the “and” of 2 and 4. What sets garage apart is the percussion layer: looped congas, sixteenth-note shaker, tambourine on the offbeats. These elements are sampled or played, never stiff. Add a light ride on the choruses. The fills are musical, a snare roll or a cut of everything except the shaker before a vocal entry. The drums serve the song, they do not dominate it.
garagehouse.sons: The Korg M1 organ (Organ 2 preset) in block chords, with its percussive tip, on the offbeats or as held chords. The M1 piano too, more percussive than the Rhodes of deep house. A discreet string pad under the choruses. The vocal is the main instrument: gospel lead, backing vocals in thirds, ad libs in the breakdowns, all doubled and lightly reverbed. If needed, sample disco a cappellas. A horn or string stab in syncopation for punctuation. In a DAW, an M1 plugin (Korg Collection) or a tonewheel organ with drawbars does the job; add a light chorus and a little saturation for period warmth.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, How to create classic house sounds with the Korg M1
Sounds of Ibiza, Essential Plugins for 90s Inspired House & UK Garage
garagehouse.tempo: Between 118 and 124 BPM, more laid-back than Chicago. The feel is that of a band playing: put 55 to 58% swing on the hats and percussion, and leave the kick straight. The keyboard parts are played by hand or humanized, with chords slightly ahead of or behind the beat by a few milliseconds. The groove comes from the bass anticipating the beat and from the shuffle of the hi-hats. A garage track breathes: it has bars where everything pulls back to let the vocal through. Think song arrangement as much as club arrangement, with a tempo that lets a gospel voice phrase without rushing.

germantrance.arrangement: No chorus: a structure built by accumulation and subtraction. A 64-bar intro where a sequence appears alone, then the drums come in one piece at a time. Each 32-bar block changes one parameter: the filter of an arpeggio, the chord of the pad, the appearance of a counter-arpeggio. A breakdown does not mean silence: the kick leaves, the sequence continues, the chord changes root, and the kick returns without a roll. Plan for 10 minutes and two or three 64-bar plateaus. The ending unravels slowly, the sequence stays alone for 32 bars. Cosmic Baby's Loops Of Infinity is a model of this kind of curve.
germantrance.basse: The bass is often a sequence: a closed 303 or an analog synth in sixteenth notes alternating root and octave, cutoff at 250 Hz, low resonance, with a short filter envelope on each note. It moves slowly: an accent shifted every 16 bars, a note that moves to the fifth. A sine sub holds the root. No aggressive sidechain: gentle compression, 3:1 ratio. The kick takes the sub-bass, the sequence occupies 80 to 300 Hz. Sometimes the bass is a held low pad, with no rhythm, and it is the arpeggios that carry the movement.
etapes: Project at 134 BPM, program an analog bass sequence in sixteenth notes, root and octave, filter closed at 250 Hz.
Add a Juno arpeggio in sixteenth notes on a three-note minor chord, then a counter-arpeggio in eighth notes an octave higher.
Lay down the 909 as a ground: kick, rimshot on 2 and 4, eighth-note ride, open hat on the offbeat.
Create an evolving pad with a 3-second attack and a slow LFO, and a 5-second reverb on a return.
Build 10 minutes in 32-bar blocks, one parameter per block, a breakdown that keeps the sequence and changes the root.
Tape-saturate the synth bus and let the master breathe around -10 LUFS.
germantrance.mix: A warm, analog mix, quieter than club music. Kick around -9 dB peak, bass sequence in mono, arpeggios in the center with their delays on the sides. Tape saturation on the synth bus to glue the layers. Wide pads, cut at 200 Hz, with a long 5-second reverb on a return. The arpeggios get a light sidechain from the kick, 2:1 ratio, to clear the downbeat. Little compression on the master, 1.5:1 ratio, limiter around -10 LUFS. The internal dynamics over 10 minutes matter more than the level. Keep some hiss and imprecision: the Eye Q records are not clinical.

outils.pourquoi: The synth of Oliver Lieb and the Eye Q studios: analog arpeggios in sixteenth notes, chorused pads. Roland Cloud Juno-106 or TAL-U-NO-LX as software.
Bass sequences and monophonic arpeggios with a filter that opens over minutes. Roland SH-01A or TAL-BassLine-101 for emulation.
Round kick, open hat, ride on the drop, with the slightly imprecise grain of the Eye Q records. D16 Drumazon or 909 samples.
A second acid melodic line, filtered low, on the Harthouse records. AudioRealism ABL3 or D16 Phoscyon 2 as software.
Strings and choirs on the long pads, M1 organ in the breakdowns. Korg M1 Software reproduces the presets of the era.
The central sampler of 1990s German studios for voices, breaths and cosmic textures. Ableton Simpler is enough today.
Arrives after 1997 on the productions of Paul van Dyk and Oliver Lieb for evolving pads and digital plucks.
Long delays at the quarter note and the dotted eighth, 45% feedback, filtered returns, with tape mode for analog hiss.

reperes: Cosmic Baby: Loops Of Infinity (1993): sequences that transform over ten minutes without ever falling into a chorus
Oliver Lieb: Subraum (1994): the sequenced bass and the long pads, german trance in its purest form
Komakino: Outface (G60 mix) (1993): the harder, darker side of the Frankfurt school, arpeggios over a dry kick
Paul van Dyk & Sue McLaren: Guiding Light (2020): what a pioneer keeps from that era in a current production
germantrance.rythme: The 909 serves as the ground, almost faded out. Kick on every beat, a clap or a rimshot on 2 and 4, a ride in eighth notes, an open hat on the offbeat. The drums change little over 10 minutes: sometimes the kick disappears for 32 bars, sometimes a tuned tom appears. The electronic percussion consists of short synth sounds, filtered noise, clicks, rather than percussion samples. No snare rolls. Transitions are made with reversed cymbals or with silences. A 2-bar drum pattern can carry the whole track if the synths move enough.
germantrance.sons: Analog arpeggios, Juno-106, SH-101 or their emulations, in sixteenth notes over three-note minor chords, with a filter that opens over whole minutes. The pads are long and evolving: two detuned oscillators, slow LFO on pulse width, 3-second attack, a Korg M1 for strings and choirs. No supersaw, no chorus section. The Attack book suggests automating the cutoff and the envelope decay of the arpeggio to give it life, and placing a more pronounced sweep at the end of a block: that is the german trance method. Long delays, a quarter note and a dotted eighth, 45% feedback, on filtered returns.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter 39 (arpeggios)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
germantrance.tempo: 130 to 140 BPM, with a feel of exploration rather than of a track: the pulse is straight, but the length is that of a journey, 8 to 12 minutes. No swing. You count in blocks of 32 and 64 bars, and a change can take a minute to happen. The difference from club trance: there is no goal, no drop to wait for. The tempo is a cruising speed. Cosmic Baby and Oliver Lieb write sequences that transform in small touches, like Tangerine Dream's sequencers. The feel comes from the sixteenth-note sequences running in circles, not from the drums.

ghettofunk.arrangement: A ghetto funk track lasts 3 to 5 minutes, short, like a party hip-hop track. 8-bar intro on the funk sample alone, or a scratch. 16-bar verse: break, sampled bass, horns. 16-bar chorus: wobble, vocal phrase, everything. 8-bar bridge with a solo scratch or a horn breakdown. Second verse, second chorus, and an 8-bar breakdown where only the vocal remains, stuttered, before the last chorus. Clean ending on a horn stab. The drop has to land before the first minute: it's made for festival DJs who mix fast. A “switch” from electric bass to wobble at the chorus makes the difference.
ghettofunk.basse: The light wobble basses from the brief: a dubstep bass, but soft and melodic. In Serum or Massive, a saw or a square with an LFO synced to eighth or quarter notes on the cutoff of a resonant low-pass filter, at 40% depth, no more. The line follows the riff of the funk sample, in quarter or eighth notes, over three or four notes (root, minor seventh, octave, fifth), in half-time relative to the break. A sine sub holds the root. Alternate between an electric bass sampled from the funk record for the verses and the wobble for the choruses. Light sidechain from the kick (3:1 ratio, 80 ms release).
etapes: Set Ableton to 108 BPM with a 60% MPC groove. Import a funk break and stack a hip-hop kick and snare on top.
Sample a two-bar horn or wah-wah guitar riff and pitch it into the key.
Create a soft wobble bass in Serum (eighth-note LFO on the cutoff, 40% depth) that follows the riff, plus a sub.
Add a funk vocal phrase as the chorus hook, scratches as percussion, and a little Beat Repeat on the vocal.
Arrange intro 8, verse 16 with sampled bass, chorus 16 with wobble, bridge 8, verse, chorus, breakdown 8, final chorus.
Compress the break with light pumping, contain the wobble with Multiband Dynamics, -7 LUFS.
ghettofunk.mix: The ghetto funk mix is loud and joyful, cleaner than big beat. The break is compressed (6:1 ratio, 3 ms attack, 80 ms release) with a little pumping, then lightly saturated. The stacked kick and snare are up front, the snare boosted at 2 kHz and 200 Hz. The wobble is high-passed at 80 Hz, with Multiband Dynamics to contain the filter resonance, and the sub is mono below it. The funk samples are high-passed at 250 Hz and gently compressed. Vocals and scratches are up front, with a short reverb. Master at -7 LUFS, with a little clipping: it has to sound loud on a festival system.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW for festival sets and productions: warped funk samples, wobble bass drops, everything arranged for live.
Pads to replay Funky Drummer breaks and horn riffs, light swing; A.Skillz comes from MPC culture.
Scratches recorded into the track and vocal phrases lifted from vinyl, a signature of the Bristol scene.
Light wobble basses, LFO synced to quarter or eighth notes on the filter, without the violence of brostep.
The wobble of the first Ghetto Funk records: saw, Daft filter, LFO on the cutoff, Dimension Expander.
Glitches and stutters on the vocals and sampled horns for the glitchy big beat side.
Moderate OTT on the bass and per-band compression on the funk samples to hold them at festival level.
A bit of 12-bit on the sampled breaks to recover the MPC grain of reworked funk records.

reperes: A.Skillz and Krafty Kuts: Tricka Technology (2003): funk breakbeat with scratches and rap vocals, before the term ghetto funk.
Featurecast: Ain't My Style (2010): the light wobble under a funk break, the genre's formula.
A Skillz: Sunshine (2009): the joyful soul sample, the bouncing bass, festival ghetto funk.
Stickybuds: Crowd Murder (2015): the glitchy, heavy side, the Canadian take on the style.
ghettofunk.rythme: The festive breaks from the brief: a funk break (Funky Drummer, a 1972 soul break) played almost in full at 108 BPM, with a hip-hop kick and snare stacked on top. Kick on the 1 and the “and” of 2, snare on 2 and 4, very snappy (boost at 2 kHz). Hi-hats from the break, plus an open hat programmed on the “and” of 4. Add scratches as percussion (a “transformer” on the “and” of 3), crowd claps, a tambourine. Fills are sampled snare rolls or break “stutters” made with Beat Repeat. The 60% MPC swing is mandatory: if it doesn't drag, it isn't ghetto funk.
ghettofunk.sons: The brief cites Ableton Live, the Akai MPC and turntables. Reworked funk samples: horns, wah-wah guitars, Hammond organs, James Brown screams, cut to one or two bars, pitched to fit the key, filtered, sometimes chopped with Beat Repeat. Vocals are rap or funk phrases (“get up”, “party people”) as the chorus hook, and sometimes a talkbox or a vocoder. Scratches are everywhere: phrases, percussion, transitions. Add played or sampled brass band horns, disco stabs, a boogie piano. The glitch comes from Beat Repeat on the vocals and Redux on the breaks: light, like a wink.
sources: Dance Music Northwest, “Getting to Know a Genre: Ghetto Funk” (dancemusicnw.com)
ghettofunk.tempo: Ghetto funk sits between 100 and 115 BPM, the slowest in the family alongside root breakbeat. The feel is party hip-hop: an MPC swing at 58 to 62%, a funk break that drags, a bass that bounces in half-time. What sets it apart from big beat, its parent, is the lower tempo and the light dubstep bass: the groove is that of a 1990 hip-hop track with a wobble underneath. Think of a festival brass band that invited a dubstep producer: festive, bouncy, a little glitchy, never dark.

ghettohouse.arrangement: A loop that cuts out and comes back. 8- to 16-bar intro with kick and clap, then the vocal arrives at bar 9 or 17 and repeats its phrase until the end. Every 8 bars, a change: an element comes in, an element drops out, a one-beat cut, the clap alone for 2 bars. An 8-bar break with the vocal and clap without kick, brutal return. Length 4 to 5 minutes, no elaborate outro, often a clean ending or a fade. The track is a tool for DJs and dancers, made to be cut and remixed live. Repetition isn't a shortcoming: it's the trance of the style.
ghettohouse.basse: An 808 bass: the 808 kick with a long decay, tuned to the root, playing a syncopated two- or three-note line, sometimes the same sound as the kick. Or a very simple square synth bass on one note in eighth notes. Notes are few, the root and the fifth, and the pattern is one bar long. On Feel My M.F. Bass, the bass is an 808 sub that glides down. No sidechain: the kick and the bass blend, it's intentional. Saturate it lightly (Saturator or a 12-bit bitcrusher) for the cassette grain. The low end is dirty and full, not clean.
etapes: Project at 135 BPM, 808 kit: kick on every beat plus a syncopated kick on the “a” of 4, dry clap on 2 and 4, hats in sixteenth notes.
808 bass: the kick with a long decay tuned to the root, syncopated two-note line, saturated.
Record or sample a three-word phrase and loop it over 2 bars, with a degraded pitch shift.
Add syncopated 808 toms over 2 bars and a simple organ stab.
Build 4 minutes in 8-bar blocks with a change in each block, one-beat cuts and a vocal and clap break.
Mix raw: mono, saturated vocal, bitcrusher and clipping on the master, at -8 LUFS.
ghettohouse.mix: The mix is raw, mono or close to it, with the kick and the vocal up front. Loud, unfiltered 808 kick with the 808 bass inside it. Dry clap, no reverb or a very short sampler reverb. The vocal compressed hard and saturated, with the background noise kept. No stereo space, no sophisticated effects. On the master, frank saturation (Saturator in Hard Curve or a cassette emulator), a light bitcrusher, a limiter that clips. Aim loud and dirty: -7 to -8 LUFS with audible clipping. If your mix sounds like a cheaply pressed Dance Mania record, a little distorted and too loud, you've nailed it.

outils.pourquoi: The backbone of DJ Deeon's tracks, pushed hard, syncopated kicks on the “a” of 4 and a very dry clap; D16 Drumazon 2 as a plugin.
Long-decay kick tuned to the root that serves as the bass, syncopated toms and cowbell; D16 Nepheton 2 or Roland Cloud TR-808.
DJ Funk's keyboard sampler for looping vocal phrases and stabs, with its onboard effects and its 1995 grain.
The two- or four-word phrases are shouted into an ordinary mic with the background noise kept; that's the sound, don't clean it up.
12-bit bitcrusher on the vocal and the 808 bass to recover the sampler and cassette grain of a Dance Mania pressing.
Hard Curve mode on the master with a clipping limiter, to aim for a dirty, distorted -8 LUFS, as the course asks.
The originals were recorded on the cheap to cassette through a saturated console; an emulator like Klevgrand DAW Cassette reproduces that haze.

reperes: DJ Funk: Pump It (1995): one phrase, an 808 kick and cuts every 8 bars, the Dance Mania formula in its purest form.
Paul Johnson: Feel My M.F. Bass (1995): the 808 bass gliding down under a dry clap, the dirty low end as a signature.
DJ Deeon: Freak Like Me (1996): syncopated sixteenth-note kicks and the chopped vocal, the bridge to juke.
Brandon: Shades On (2021): ghetto house revisited with modern production, same cuts, same economy.
ghettohouse.rythme: An 808 or 909 kick in four-on-the-floor, but with syncopated kick variations: an extra kick on the “and” of 2 or the “a” of 4, in sixteenth notes, that pushes the track. 808 or 909 clap on 2 and 4, very dry, sometimes doubled into a sixteenth-note roll. Closed 808 hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats. 808 toms in syncopated 2-bar patterns, which foreshadow juke. 808 cowbell, rim, clave in syncopation. No elaborate fills: a hard cut of everything for one beat, or the clap alone for 2 bars. Program on the grid without humanizing, it's the sound of the machine in its raw state.
ghettohouse.sons: Looped vocal phrases: two or four words, often obscene, recorded on a cheap mic or sampled from a rap or Miami bass record, repeated in a loop over 1 or 2 bars with variations in placement. A degraded pitch shift or time-stretch on the vocal. A simple synth or organ stab, a minor chord or a single note, syncopated. A siren, a crowd shout, a film sample. Nothing else: the track is a kick, a clap, a bass and a voice. The aesthetic is deliberately raw: 12-bit sampler, background noise, cassette saturation, clipping. A bitcrusher and a little white noise on the master bring that back in a DAW.
sourcesOutils: Red Bull Music Academy Daily, Interview: DJ Funk
ghettohouse.tempo: Between 128 and 140 BPM, and the tempo climbs over the years: 130 in 1994, 140 in 1998 when juke emerges. The feel is raw, mechanical, without swing: an 808 or a 909 looping with no humanization. What makes the groove is the syncopation of the kick and the vocal phrases, not the drums. The files are short and repetitive, 4 to 5 minutes, often made in an afternoon. Think in 4-bar loops and 8-bar blocks: ghetto house has no build-up, it has cuts. A track that sounds too clean or too polished is no longer ghetto house.

glitch.arrangement: Two strategies depending on the pole. With Fennesz, an ambient form of 6 to 10 minutes where a guitar melody is drowned under artifacts, with slow fades. With Raster-Noton, a minimal grid of 4 to 6 minutes that adds one element every 16 bars, mathematical, almost without fades: elements appear and disappear cleanly. Absolute digital silence, a few seconds of zeros, is an arrangement element. Transitions are cuts, not build-ups. Data.Matrix works like a demonstration: each new sound arrives alone, exact. Endless Summer, by contrast, is a song of which you only hear the ruins.
glitch.basse: Either a pure tone or a texture. With Alva Noto and Ikeda, the bass is a sub sine between 40 and 60 Hz, very short or sustained, with no harmonics, which appears as one more point on the grid. With Fennesz, there is no bass: the granulated guitar and the pads fill the low end, along with noise. With Pole, the dub side, a real slow dub bass under the clicks of a faulty filter. In every case, it's never a melodic line. Watch out for the short sine sub: it produces a click on the attack if it doesn't start at zero, which can be intentional. Keep it mono and check it on a system that can reach down to 40 Hz.
etapes: Choose your pole: drowned melody (Fennesz) or laboratory grid (Alva Noto). Here, the grid: tempo 125 BPM, 1/64 grid.
Make four error percussion sounds: a 1 ms click, a 4 ms burst of white noise, a 10 ms sine at 1 kHz, a 40 ms sine sub at 50 Hz.
Program a 4-bar pattern with five points per bar at most, each sound at a fixed stereo position.
Take any sample, cut it into 50 ms loops without crossfade and make it stutter with Beat Repeat, then resample the result.
Arrange over 5 minutes, adding one element every 16 bars, with two seconds of total digital silence in the middle, and transitions without fades.
Mix dry, extreme stereo, sub in mono, transparent limiter at -0.3 dB, and listen on two different systems.
glitch.mix: The peaks are harsh: a full-scale click can damage a tweeter, so use a transparent limiter with a ceiling at -0.3 dB on the master, and keep clicks at -6 dB maximum. No reverb on the artifacts, they stay dry and up front; reverb goes on the melodic layers only. Extreme stereo: one click hard left, the next hard right. The sub in mono. The final level can go up to -10 LUFS for Raster-Noton, or stay at -16 for Fennesz. Don't add dither by reflex: on pure sines and digital silence, it's audible, and so is its absence; choose. Test on several systems, the clicks change character with the tweeters.

outils.pourquoi: Oval's source: CDs painted or scratched with adhesive tape, played until they skip and recorded. An old Discman and a burned CD still do the job.
Fennesz granulates his guitar into a halo with it, Ikeda programs sines and pulses in it to the millisecond; Max for Live in Ableton.
Stuttering buffers and custom-built granulators, with the user ensemble library full of controlled-error tools.
A 32-step grid where you place blocks of stutter, reverse, tape stop and filter; the tool that set the standard for sequenced glitch.
Step effects sequencer with a random function to quickly find stutter patterns; the free version 1.3 only runs on Windows.
Free buffer effect that chops and loops at 50 ms without crossfade; Hysteresis from the same developer makes granular delays that run away into feedback.
1/64 grid with low chance on a sample cut into 50 ms loops, then resampling of the result; Grain Delay for continuous stutter.
Extreme downsampling for composed aliasing, dry, no reverb; Spectral Time in freeze and Corpus handle the resonances of the melodic layers.

reperes: Oval: Do While (1995): painted CDs that skip, turned into melodic loops, the origin of the genre.
Fennesz: Endless Summer (2001): a pop song of which you only hear the granulated ruins, melodic glitch.
Ryoji Ikeda: Data.Matrix (2005): clicks and sines placed to the sample, the laboratory grid.
Alva Noto: Uni Acronym (2011): Raster-Noton rigor with a voice, each click in its own stereo place and at its own frequency.
glitch.rythme: The percussion is made of errors: 1 ms clicks, 3 to 5 ms bursts of white noise, 10 ms sines, CD skips, buffer stutters. To make them: Beat Repeat on a 1/64 grid with a short decay, Buffer Shuffler, resampling a stutter, a Grain Delay with a high spray. Oval painted on CDs to make them skip: today, a sample cut into 30 to 100 ms loops without crossfade does the same. The kick, if there is one, is a 20 ms sine at 50 Hz. With Alva Noto, the pattern is minimal, four or five clicks per bar, and each click has its own frequency and stereo position. The rhythm is a grid of points, not a groove.
glitch.sons: The brief lists Max/MSP, Reaktor, the computer and the granulator. The sources are manufactured accidents: a recorded scratched CD, a file encoded to MP3 at 32 kbps then re-encoded five times, aliasing from Redux with extreme downsampling, a Grain Delay pushed until it stutters, a plugin crash captured by resampling. Fennesz granulates a guitar in Max/MSP until the melody is nothing more than a halo. Tools: Glitchmachines, Sugar Bytes Effectrix, dblue Glitch, Spectral Time in freeze, Corpus for resonances. A pure sine from Operator remains the most precise sound. The rule: no sound should sound like an instrument.
sourcesOutils: Cymatics, Glitch VST Plugins: 15 of the Best
Magnetic Magazine, Top VSTs for Glitches
glitch.tempo: Two opposite poles. No tempo with Oval and Fennesz, where the artifacts float over pads; strict, rigid tempo with Alva Noto and Ryoji Ikeda, 120 to 130 BPM, with clicks quantized to the sample. In both cases, the length of a buffer becomes a tempo: a fragment repeated every 20 ms gives a pitch of 50 Hz, repeated every 200 ms it gives a rhythm. That porosity between rhythm and pitch is what makes the genre. No swing, no humanization: the feel is dry, digital, exact. Choose your pole before you start, drowned melody or laboratory grid. A Raster-Noton track is programmed in thirty-second and sixty-fourth notes.

goatrance.arrangement: Build in a spiral, not toward a drop. A 32-bar intro lays down the kick and a first arpeggio layer. Every 16 or 32 bars, a layer is added (arpeggio 2, 303 line, FM lead) without any of them really disappearing: the density rises nonstop. Plan a key change in the middle of the track, often a minor third up, prepared by an 8-bar breakdown where only the arpeggios remain. Goa breakdowns are melodic, not silent: you cut the kick, keep the layers, and relaunch with a 909 roll. Aim for 9 minutes. A long ending, with the layers removed one by one, to let the DJ mix.
goatrance.basse: Goa bass isn't yet the rolling bass of psytrance: it's a TB-303 or analog sawtooth synth line, low-pass filtered around 300 Hz, playing sixteenth notes on the root with octave jumps and accented notes. The kick lands on the beat, the bass plays the next three sixteenths, but adds glides and accents (velocity 127) on the “a” of the beat, as the 303 does. Typical note: E or F, never higher than the second octave. Layer a second 303 with the resonance turned up playing the same line an octave higher: the two braided lines make the famous “acid goa”. Under all this, a simple sine doubles the root.
etapes: Open a project at 142 BPM, lay down a 909 kick four per bar and a 303 line in sixteenth notes on E, with accents on the “a” of each beat.
Program a first arpeggiator layer (sawtooth, up mode, sixteenth notes) on an E minor chord, then a second one a fifth higher in eighth notes.
Load Dexed or FM8, create an FM lead with ratio 2 and vibrato, write a 4-bar Phrygian melody on E.
Add alternating sixteenth-note hats, clap on 2 and 4, congas on a 2-bar pattern.
Arrange in a spiral: add a layer every 16 bars, place a key change to G minor halfway through.
Put a dotted-eighth delay on the arpeggios and a slow phaser on the pad, then mix each layer into its own band.
goatrance.mix: The period goa mix is crowded in the mids and lightly compressed: it was mixed to DAT without a mastering limiter. Today you can keep that spirit: leave some dynamics, don't aim louder than -10 LUFS. The challenge is making five layers of arpeggios coexist: give each its own band with a high-pass at 200 Hz and a bell boost near its brilliance frequency (2 kHz, 4 kHz, 8 kHz depending on the layer). Spread them in stereo with a different pan per layer and a light chorus. The kick and bass stay mono below 150 Hz. A little tape saturation on the master bus, applied gently, glues everything together and recalls the grain of cassettes.

outils.pourquoi: Goa's braided acid lines come from here: sawtooth, resonance up, accents and slides. Today replaced by AudioRealism ABL3 or D16 Phoscyon 2.
The Eastern FM leads, modulator ratio of 2 or 3, fast vibrato, played in Phrygian. Dexed, free, loads the same SysEx patches.
Short saturated kick, clap on 2 and 4, congas and rides for the plateaus. A 909 sample pack or D16 Drumazon 2 is more than enough.
Analog mono synth of Posford and the English school: filtered square basses and eighth-note sequences, with its internal sequencer looped over the kick.
Sampler-synth of Hallucinogen's first album: pads, documentary voices and sampled percussion, stacked on the arpeggio layers.
Free six-operator DX7 emulation: you set the short envelopes and integer ratios that give the goa color without hunting for a machine.
Its MIDI arpeggiators stacked on several tracks, each at its own speed, reproduce the goa spirals; Echo in dotted eighths on each layer.

reperes: Hallucinogen: LSD (1994): listen to how the arpeggio layers shift and how the FM lead comes in on top, it's the archetype of the goa sound.
Man With No Name: Teleport (1996): the acid bassline braided with the lead, and the build by accumulation, without a drop.
Juno Reactor: Laughing Gas (1993): the slower, more tribal side, sampled percussion and the 303 up front.
The Infinity Project: The Law (1991): proto-goa, still close to acid and EBM, to hear where the pulse comes from.
goatrance.rythme: The kick comes from a TR-909, short, with a little saturation on the click so it cuts through at 140 BPM. Four per bar, constant velocity. No snare in the rock sense: a 909 clap or a thin snare on beats 2 and 4, often buried in a short reverb. The closed hats play sixteenth notes alternating strong and weak (velocity 110 then 70), the open hat lands on the eighth-note offbeats. Add synthetic percussion: 909 congas or sampled tablas playing a 2-bar pattern, quarter-note rides during the plateaus. The rhythm stays simple: it serves as a carpet for the melodic layers.
goatrance.sons: Three families of sounds make goa. First the Yamaha DX7 or its emulation (Dexed, free, or FM8): FM leads with a modulator ratio of 2 or 3, a short attack envelope and a fast vibrato, played in Phrygian or harmonic minor scales for the Eastern color. Then the arpeggios: three to five layers of arpeggiators on thin sawtooths, each on a different interval (root, fifth, octave), with a dotted-eighth delay. Finally the TB-303 for the acid lines. The signature effects: a slow phaser on the pads, an eighth-note ping-pong delay, filter sweeps over 16 bars. The sampled voices come from documentaries or science fiction films.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (90's Psy/Goa trance and Ultimate Goa Trance technique threads)
Vintage Synth Explorer Forums (Astral Projection's synths)
goatrance.tempo: Set your project between 140 and 145 BPM. Goa doesn't swing: everything is quantized to straight sixteenth notes, with no groove or humanization. The feel comes from elsewhere: layers of arpeggios turning at different speeds (eighth notes on one layer, sixteenth notes on another, eighth-note triplets on a third) that shift against one another. Think in cycles of 8 and 16 bars, but with melodic phrases of 3 or 6 bars layered over the square cycle: that friction is what gives the impression of a spiral. A classic goa track lasts 8 to 10 minutes, sometimes more, without ever slowing down.

gqom.arrangement: Emptiness as structure. 16-bar intro with the hats and a sampled shout, then the triplet kick pattern comes in at bar 17. 16-bar blocks: a kick pattern, then a variation, then a complete silence of 2 or 4 bars, then the return. A 16-bar break with the chant and the reverb alone, a kick roll, return. Second half with a second, denser kick pattern or a siren. Length 5 to 7 minutes, often an abrupt ending. There is no build-up or drop: there are patterns replacing each other and silences separating them, and it's the surprise of the return that makes the track jump.
gqom.basse: Almost no bass in the house sense: the low end is held by the cavernous kick itself, whose decay and reverb fill the bottom. When there is a bass, it's a sine sub held on one note, with no melody, that appears and disappears by whole bars, or a saturated low drone. On some tracks, an 808 tom tuned low plays a note in triplets and acts as the bass. No sidechain, the kick and sub blend into one mass. The emptiness in the low end is intentional: a bar without kick or sub, then the return, that's what moves the track. Resist the urge to add a bassline.
etapes: Project at 125 BPM, dry sixteenth-note hats low in the mix, and a saturated 808 kick in eighth-note triplets (1/12 grid) over 2 beats then silence.
Add a second kick tuned lower that answers the first over 4 bars, and low toms as triplet accents.
Long, dark reverb (4 s hall, filtered at 3 kHz) on the kicks and toms.
Sample a Zulu shout or chant, pitch it down and repeat it with a delay.
Build 6 minutes in 16-bar blocks with complete silences of 2 to 4 bars between patterns, a chant and reverb break, a second kick pattern.
Mix dark: kick as the low end, no separate sub, cut above 12 kHz, saturation, master at -8 LUFS.
gqom.mix: A dark, cavernous mix, with lots of reverb and little brightness. The kick is loud, saturated, with a decay that fills the low end, and a long reverb on a filtered return. No clean separate sub: the kick is the low end. Hats low and dry, cut below 1 kHz. Shouts and chants in the center with a long reverb and a delay, compressed hard. Cut the mix above 12 kHz: gqom has no air, it has depth. Hard bus compression, frank saturation. Master at -7 to -8 LUFS with light clipping. The result should sound loud in a minibus taxi and in a dark club: low end, reverb and holes.

outils.pourquoi: DJ Lag has produced in FL Studio since 2010 on modest computers: triplet kicks on the 1/12 grid, complete one-bar silences.
As samples: cavernous kick with medium decay and deep toms tuned low, saturated and sent into a long, dark reverb.
A held dark sawtooth note or a saturated drone, the only synth in the track when there is one.
Banks of 808 kicks, toms, wood hits and whistles; the style is poor in elements, each sound is chosen for its depth.
Fruity Reeverb 2 or Valhalla VintageVerb, 3 to 5 s hall low-pass filtered at 3 kHz on the kicks and toms: emptiness is an instrument.
A syllable or a call, pitched down, repeated with a delay; recorded on a mic or taken from local records and videos.
Frank saturation on the kick and light clipping on the master around -8 LUFS, so the low end comes through in a minibus taxi.

reperes: DJ Lag: Ice Drop (2016): triplet kicks answering each other in a cavernous reverb, the record that defined gqom for the world.
Rudeboyz: Mercedes (2016): the silences and kick returns, emptiness as an instrument.
Distruction Boyz: Omunye (2017): gqom becoming a hit, with a chant and a simpler kick pattern.
DJ Lag: Trip To New York (2019): the more produced, heavier version, same architecture of triplets and holes.
gqom.rythme: The kick is the pattern: a heavy, cavernous kick (808 with medium decay, saturated, reverberated) in eighth-note triplets over 2 beats then silence, or in a broken pattern that avoids beat 1, over 2 or 4 bars. Two or three kicks tuned differently answer each other. No regular clap: low toms, muffled snares or wood hits as accents, in triplets. Straight sixteenth-note hats, dry, low in the mix, to provide the grid the triplets rub against. Sparse shakers. Complete one-bar silences. Fills are rising triplet kick rolls. The whole kit is dark, reverberated, in a big empty room.
gqom.sons: Cavernous drums: saturated 808 kicks and toms with a long, dark reverb (3 to 5 s hall, low-pass filtered at 3 kHz). Sampled Zulu shouts and chants, often a syllable or a call, repeated with a delay and pitched down. Sirens, car horn sounds, industrial noises, impacts. A rare synth: a held note from Massive on a dark sawtooth, or a dissonant stab in triplets. A spoken Zulu vocal with reverb. Nothing melodic, nothing warm. Gqom is made in FL Studio on modest computers, with 808 banks and samples: the sound is poor in elements and rich in space.
sourcesOutils: DJ Mag, DJ Lag: the gqom king conquers the globe
Red Bull, DJ Lag: Spewing Facts While Riding the Wave
Moziak, Meeting With The King: DJ Lag
gqom.tempo: Between 120 and 130 BPM, but gqom doesn't sound like 4/4 at that tempo: the kick is a triplet pattern, or a broken pattern, and the sensation is of a heavy, slow pulse that stumbles. No swing on the grid: the triplets are programmed at 1/12 and layered over the 4/4 of the hats. What distinguishes gqom from the afro house it came out of is emptiness: no round bass, no piano, no warm pads, and entire bars with nothing. Count in 4 bars for the kick patterns and in 16 for the changes. The track should be a little scary.

grime.arrangement: A grime instrumental is made for an MC: 2 minutes 30 to 3 minutes 30, structured in 8s and 16s. 8-bar intro with the riff alone, drums come in, 16 bars of verse, 8 of hook where one element changes, back to the verse. No long build-up or silent breakdown: changes are abrupt, a synth comes in, another drops out, the bass stops for 2 beats. Leave space between 1 and 4 kHz for the voice. A version without the main riff for 16 bars lets the MC breathe. Clean ending on a gunshot.
grime.basse: The bass is a square wave, blunt and monophonic: FL Studio's 3xOsc or a Triton. A square wave with a short 150 ms decay, no filter or a low-pass at 800 Hz, played as a melodic riff on syncopated sixteenths, often in minor with octave jumps. The gunshot bass: a very short, saturated note, on the same positions as the kick. Sine sub an octave below, only on the roots, in short notes. The bass riff is the main melody of the track, it must be memorable after one listen. It changes or stops every 8 bars.
etapes: Set FL Studio or Ableton to 140 BPM, syncopated sixteenth-note kick, clap or gunshot on 2 and 4.
Write a square bass riff in 3xOsc or Operator, over 8 bars, memorable, with octave jumps.
Add a cold sixteenth-note synth pattern and digital strings as stabs.
Put an exaggerated sidechain on the synths, 8:1 ratio, for the pirate radio effect.
Arrange in 8- and 16-bar phrases, an abrupt change at each phrase, a hole for the voice.
Mix dry and in mono, drums up front, saturated bass, master around -7 LUFS, test on a phone.
grime.mix: Dry, aggressive, all mids. Kick and snare up front, around -4 dB peak, no reverb. Square bass in mono, saturated with Saturator drive at 25%, cut below 60 Hz if you have a separate sub. Mono sine sub below 80 Hz. Cut the synths below 200 Hz. Hard parallel compression on the drums, 8:1 ratio, mix at 50%. Clipper on the drum bus for rawness. Leave a hole between 2 and 4 kHz with a -3 dB EQ bell on the synths for the MC. Master around -7 LUFS. Check on a small speaker: grime was made for radios and phones.

outils.pourquoi: Wiley and Jammer's workstation: Gliding Squares and AMS Feedback Lead presets for eskibeat. The Korg Collection Triton plugin replaces it.
FruityLoops, the workshop of the Bow teenagers: 8-bar patterns, 3xOsc on square, everything in the step sequencer.
The console software where Eskimo, Pulse Eskimo and JME's early work were born, recorded to MiniDisc then burned.
A blunt square wave, 150 ms decay, low-pass at 800 Hz, for the memorable bass riff and the gunshot bass.
E-mu rompler for percussion clicks, cold digital strings and orchestra stabs, the eskibeat palette.
To recreate the square bass and the octave-down sine sub today, in mono, with Saturator at 25% drive.

reperes: Wiley: Eskimo (2002): eskibeat, icy sounds, square and cold, the 8-bar phrase as the unit.
Dizzee Rascal: I Luv U (2003): the square bass and the gunshots, the unapologetic PlayStation production.
Lethal Bizzle: Pow Forward (2004): the 8-bar structure for ten MCs, raw energy.
Skepta: That's Not Me (2014): the return to the 2004 sound with a modern mix.
grime.rythme: Short digital kick, no sub, often on 1 then on syncopated sixteenths, the “a” of 2 or the “and” of 3. Dry, loud snare or clap on 2 and 4, sometimes replaced by a sampled gunshot, the famous “gunshot” sound. Low eighth-note hats, or none at all. Odd percussive sounds taken from a Korg Triton or FL Studio: wood hits, clicks, a pitched tom, a square bass note used as percussion. A 2-beat snare roll at the end of an 8-bar phrase. No reverb on the drums. Patterns change every 8 bars, with an element coming in or dropping out.
grime.sons: Square waves and raw synth sounds from FL Studio, Music 2000 on PlayStation or a Korg Triton: cold digital strings, bells, an orchestra “stab”, video game bleeps. Sirens, gunshots, a crowd shout. An icy sixteenth-note synth pattern, Wiley's eskibeat, with a droplet or ice-cube sound. The pirate radio sidechain: the whole mix pumps on the kick in an exaggerated way; imitate it with a sidechained compressor, 8:1 ratio, 150 ms release. No sampled sung vocal, the voice is the MC, live.
sourcesOutils: How We Get To Next, Ringtones and Playstations: The Tools of Grime's Low-Fidelity All-Stars
Complex, A Journey Through Wiley's Eskibeat
grime.tempo: 140 BPM, the speed of the garage it came from, but without swing: grime is square, cold and fast. Two feels coexist. The most common puts the snare on 2 and 4, which at 140 gives a fast flow under the MC. The second, darker one puts the snare on 3, as in dubstep. The basic unit is the 8-bar phrase, not the 2-bar loop: everything changes every 8, because the MC raps in 8s and 16s. Sixteenth-note grid, syncopated kicks, abrupt silences. What changes compared to 2-step: no more sensuality, the machine is naked, made for the voice.

happyhardcore.arrangement: A happy hardcore track runs 4 to 6 minutes and follows a song pattern: a 16- to 32-bar intro with kick and bass, a sung verse or a 16-bar piano breakdown, a build-up with a roll and a pitched vocal, a 32-bar chorus with everything in it, kick, bass, piano, lead, vocal. Second verse, second chorus, often with a key change a whole tone up for the last chorus, a real pop trick. Breakdowns are long and melodic: that's where the piano plays alone and the crowd sings. Ending on kick and bass, 16 bars. What makes the track playable is the recognizable chorus: people should be able to sing it.
happyhardcore.basse: The bouncing offbeat bass is the signature. On every offbeat eighth note (the “and” of each beat), a short note, 100 ms, square or sawtooth wave low-pass filtered at 400 Hz, an octave below the piano. In Operator: sawtooth, filter at 400 Hz, decay 120 ms, sustain 0. It follows the chords: the key's root on the first chord, then the root of each chord, in major or bright minor. No sidechain needed since it never lands on the kick. Add a short sine sub on the same notes if the mix lacks low end. This bass is what sets the genre apart from all the rest of hardcore: it's musical, not physical.
etapes: Tempo 170 BPM. Clean 909 kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on every offbeat.
Offbeat bass: Operator sawtooth filtered at 400 Hz, short notes on every “and”, following the chords.
Write a progression of 4 major chords (for example I, V, vi, IV) and play them as block chords on the M1 piano in syncopated eighth notes.
Sample a sung vocal, pitch it up 6 semitones without formants, place it on the chorus.
Add a monophonic sawtooth lead that doubles the vocal melody, with a dotted-eighth delay.
Arrange as a song: intro, verse, build-up, chorus, verse, chorus with key change, ending. Bright mix, gentle limiter.
happyhardcore.mix: The happy hardcore mix is bright and clean, the opposite of gabber. Kick at -4 dB peak, crisp, with a high-pass at 40 Hz. Offbeat bass lightly compressed, 3:1 ratio, so it stays even. Piano and vocals wide in stereo with a 2-second hall reverb, high-pass at 250 Hz on the reverb. Lots of highs: a +3 dB high shelf at 10 kHz on the melodic bus is not too much. Open hats forward, at -10 dB. Master: gentle bus compression, limiter around -8 LUFS. It should sound like sped-up pop, not like a wall. Compare with Hixxy and Sharkey.

outils.pourquoi: The rave piano: Piano 16 preset played as block chords on the beats, and the organ as a stab. Today the KORG Collection M1 emulation does the same job.
Helium-pitched vocals and sped-up breaks: sampled at 12 bits, raised 5 to 7 semitones without time-stretch, that's the color.
Clean 4/4 kick, just compressed, 909 snare on 2 and 4 with a clap: no distortion in the smiling branch.
With OctaMED or ProTracker, the machine of the English and Scottish bedroom producers of 1993-1996; the sped-up breaks often come from there.
Vocals loaded and transposed up 6 semitones in Classic mode without warp, to recover the helium pitch of a period sampler.
Sawtooth stabs and small offbeat basses in eighth notes, one note, short release, when you have neither an M1 nor a Juno.
For the modern take: supersaw leads and bright synthetic piano, with a wide chorus, on productions after 2000.

reperes: Hixxy and Sharkey: Toytown (1995): the pitched vocal, the piano and the bouncing bass, the whole genre in one track.
DJ Paul Elstak: Rainbow in the Sky (1995): the Dutch version, harder kick but a pop melody and chorus.
Slipmatt: Breaking Free (1996): pure 4/4 with open hats up front and a singable chorus.
Force and Styles: Heart of Gold (1998): the end of the era, cleaner production, full vocal and sawtooth lead.
happyhardcore.rythme: Clean 909 kick, barely saturated, on every beat: it's a clear, short kick (150 ms), with attack, not a crushed kick. 909 snare or clap on 2 and 4, with a short, bright reverb. Open hats on the offbeats, very present, it's the “tss” of the genre. Closed hats in sixteenth notes with velocity alternating 100 and 60. Snare rolls in sixteenth then thirty-second notes over 2 bars before each drop, with a velocity crescendo. In the UK period, a breakbeat (Amen or Think) sped up to 170 runs under the kick in the breakdowns and sometimes in the drops: slice it in Simpler in Slice mode and play it in eighth notes. Descending 909 toms at the end of blocks.
happyhardcore.sons: Rave pianos: the Korg M1 “Piano 1” preset (or any bright electric piano, with a chorus) played as block chords in eighth notes or in a syncopated rhythm, major chords in inversion, over 4 or 8 bars. Pitched vocals: sample a sung female vocal and pitch it up 5 to 7 semitones without preserving formants, the helium effect is intended. Rave stabs, softened hoovers, M1 strings. Simple, monophonic sawtooth leads for the main melodies, with a dotted-eighth delay. Cartoon and toy samples (Toytown). Cheerful sirens. Everything should be bright, in major, with lots of reverb.
sourcesOutils: W. A. Production, Happy Hardcore Hero (waproduction.com)
Rekkerd, Singomakers Happy Hardcore sample pack (rekkerd.org)
happyhardcore.tempo: Happy hardcore runs between 165 and 180 BPM, 170 being the reference tempo. Unlike gabber at the same tempo, the feel is light and bouncy: the 4/4 is there, but the offbeat bass gives the impression that the track jumps rather than pounds. The 1993-1995 UK period still mixes sped-up breakbeats with the 4/4 kick, the 1995-1998 period moves to pure 4/4. No swing on the kick, but a slight swing (52 to 54%) on the hats and breaks helps bring back the bounce. Program at 170 BPM, sixteenth-note grid. The track should smile.

hardcoretechno.arrangement: A hardcore techno track from that era runs 5 to 7 minutes, in 16-bar blocks. 32-bar intro, kick alone or kick and hat, for the DJ. Then the hoover or main stab comes in, 16 bars, then a breakdown: the kick stops, a siren or a pad rises, a 4-bar snare roll, and the kick returns on beat 1. Two or three of these cycles, each adding an element (vocal sample, second stab). 32-bar ending with the kick alone for mixing. What makes the track playable in a club is the clarity of the transitions: total silence for one beat just before the drop, it always works.
hardcoretechno.basse: There's often no separate bass: the distorted kick occupies the bottom of the spectrum and its decay acts as the note. When you add a bass, it's a short midrange stab, not a sub. A sawtooth oscillator from a Juno-106 or Operator, low-pass filtered at 300 Hz, played on the offbeats in eighth notes: the track's root, a single note, 80 ms release. Cut it below 100 Hz with a high-pass to leave the kick alone at the bottom. Light sidechain from the kick (4:1 ratio, 60 ms release) so it disappears under each hit. On 1991 tracks, the “bass” is sometimes just the kick pitched two octaves higher and replayed on the offbeats.
etapes: Set Ableton to 160 BPM. Load a 909 kick into Simpler, add Saturator (Drive 15 dB) then Overdrive then Saturator again, and have it play on all four beats.
Record the processed kick to audio (resampling), reload it into Simpler, distort it again. Two passes are enough to get the 1991 grain.
Add a snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hats on the offbeats, a sixteenth-note roll at the end of each 8-bar block.
Create a hoover in Wavetable or Serum: three detuned sawtooths, chorus, rising pitch envelope. Play a one-eighth-note stab every two beats.
Sample a film voice or a scream, distort it, place it at the start of each 16-bar block.
Arrange with 32 bars of intro, two build-up/breakdown/drop cycles, 32 bars of ending, and put a Saturator in Analog Clip on the drum bus.
hardcoretechno.mix: The kick dominates everything and is mixed first, around -6 dB peak on the track. Everything else is set relative to it. On the kick, a chain like the one the Attack book describes for hard techno works: light compression, amp-style distortion, reshaping of the transient, then final saturation with soft clip. No reverb on the kick, a little on the snare (short plate, 0.8 s). On the drum bus, a Saturator in Analog Clip mode at 2 dB of drive serves as a limiter, as the book suggests, rather than a bus compressor. Master: limiter around -8 LUFS integrated, it's a loud genre. For level references, listen to Marc Acardipane alongside your track.

outils.pourquoi: The kick of the whole genre: output pushed all the way, long decay, then distorted and resampled twice. Today often replaced by the D16 Drumazon or Roland Cloud TR-909 emulation.
The hoover, the What the patch, sawtooths through the internal chorus with a pitch glide at the start of each note. The main riff of the 1990-1992 period.
Stabs and midrange bass on a sawtooth filtered around 300 Hz, played on the offbeats. Chorus engaged to widen without adding a layer.
The Frankfurt and New York sampler: film voices, screams and sirens loaded then pitched. In Ableton, Simpler plays the same role.
Stacked with Overdrive in three light stages rather than a single violent stage, as the Attack book describes. Drive 15 dB, then Analog Clip on the drum bus.
To rebuild the hoover: three sawtooths detuned by 20 cents, chorus, pitch envelope of +12 semitones over 150 ms. Ableton's Wavetable does the same.
One-note sawtooth stab bass, 80 ms release, high-pass below 100 Hz to leave the kick alone at the bottom.
Resampling in one move: record the processed kick to audio, reload it into Simpler, distort again. That's the 1991 grain in two passes.

reperes: Mescalinum United: We Have Arrived (1990): the constantly sizzling kick and the rising stab, it's the model for everything that follows.
T99: Anasthasia (1991): listen to how the hoover serves as the main riff, with no melody, just a repeated glide.
Human Resource: Dominator (1991): the siren and the hoover answer each other over a kick that's still fairly clean, before Rotterdam crushed it.
Angerfist: Diabolic Dice (2023): the same vocabulary thirty years later, with a much longer kick and a modern mix.
hardcoretechno.rythme: The kick comes from a TR-909 (or a 909 sample) and plays on all four beats. What makes the genre is the chain: distortion, then bouncing the sample, then distortion again. The Attack book insists on stacking several stages of light distortion rather than a single violent stage, and that applies here to the letter. 909 snare on beats 2 and 4, often doubled with a clap. Closed hat in eighth notes on the offbeats, open hat on the offbeat of beat 4. Add sixteenth-note snare rolls on the last bar of an 8-bar block, velocity ramping from 60 to 127. Otherwise keep everything at a fixed velocity: nuance isn't the point.
hardcoretechno.sons: The signature sound is the hoover: an Alpha Juno patch (“What the”) made of sawtooths modulated by the internal chorus, with an upward pitch glide at the start of each note. You can recreate it in Serum or Wavetable with three sawtooths detuned by 20 cents, a chorus and a pitch envelope of +12 semitones over 150 ms. Otherwise, orchestra or film samples loaded into an Akai S1000 (or Simpler) and played as stabs, sirens, screams, and shouted vocals run through distortion. It all has to sound dirty: 12-bit bitcrush, a resonant filter sweeping over 8 bars. Nothing should stay clean except the snare.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno)
Gearspace, hardcore and gabber production forum (gearspace.com)
hardcoretechno.tempo: Early hardcore techno runs between 150 and 170 BPM. That's faster than the Frankfurt or New York techno it came out of, but still readable as techno: the kick remains a rhythm, not a continuous vibration. No swing, no humanization, everything on the grid in sixteenth notes. The feel comes from the brutality of the kick and from repetition. At 160 BPM, a bar lasts 1.5 seconds: every event must be short and dry. Set your DAW to 160 BPM, turn off any groove, and think in 16-bar blocks. If your track feels limp, it's never the tempo you need to raise, it's the kick you need to distort more.

hardhouse.arrangement: Long build-ups and long breakdowns. 32-bar DJ intro with kick and offbeat bass, then the hats. A first 32-bar plateau with the hoover riff. 32-bar breakdown: kick cut, pad and vocal, white noise rising, snare roll over the last 8, one beat of silence. Drop: everything comes back, kick, offbeat bass, hoover, crash. Second cycle with a different riff or a whole-tone modulation up, 32-bar outro. Length 6 to 8 minutes. The climax is the return of the kick, not the breakdown: the whole arrangement exists to make you wait for it.
hardhouse.basse: The pumping offbeat bass: a short note on every offbeat (the “and”s), never on the beat, with a filtered sawtooth sound, zero attack, 100 to 150 ms decay. On a single note, the root, with a jump of a fifth or an octave every 8 bars. The “pumping” comes from sidechaining to the kick, set hard (8:1 ratio, 100 ms release) so the bass gets crushed at each kick and bounces back in between. A second layer of sustained sine sub underneath, also sidechained. In the breakdowns, the bass stops and a pad replaces it. It's the same formula as hard trance and NRG, but with a rounder house sound.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM, hardened 909 with a saturated kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, loud sixteenth-note hats.
Offbeat bass on every offbeat, one note, short decay, sidechained hard to the kick, plus a sine sub underneath.
Program a two-bar hoover riff with an emulated Alpha Juno or an Operator with three detuned oscillators.
Add a siren and white noise rising over 32 bars, a snare roll with a crescendo and one beat of silence.
Build in 32-bar blocks: intro, plateau, long breakdown, drop, second cycle with a whole-tone modulation, outro, over 7 minutes.
Mix with the kick up front, a pumping bass, hard bus compression and a limiter at -8 LUFS.
hardhouse.mix: The kick is king, loud and saturated, compressed with its own limiter. The offbeat bass ducks under it with visible sidechain. Together, kick and bass form a single wave that must never stop. The hats are louder than in house, cut below 500 Hz, spread wide. The hoover occupies 500 Hz to 5 kHz, compressed hard and saturated, with a short delay. Reverb only on the clap and the vocals. Hard bus compression (4:1, 1 ms attack, fast release) and a limiter that works: aim for -7 to -8 LUFS. It's a mix of pressure, not finesse. Check that the kick-bass gallop stays clean in mono on a club system.

outils.pourquoi: The What The preset, PWM sawtooth with chorus: the hoover of Trade and Tidy Trax, played as a two-bar riff on the chorus.
Recent Alpha Juno-2 emulation by TAL, with the original hoover patch; the course also mentions Roland Cloud or an Operator with three detuned oscillators.
Short kick, tuned and saturated with a click at 3 kHz, clap layered with a snare, loud hats, toms rolling on the build-ups.
Offbeat bass on every offbeat, filtered sawtooth, 100 to 150 ms decay, in English studios of the mid-1990s; Bass Station II today.
Pads that replace the bass in the breakdowns and saturated chord stabs; TAL-U-NO-LX as a plugin, also cited by the course for the hoover.
Ableton's Compressor in sidechain on the offbeat bass and the sub, 8:1 ratio, 100 ms release: the pumping is half the style.
The sequencer of 1990s English hard house studios, on Atari then PC, for the 32-bar build-ups and the snare rolls.

reperes: Tony De Vit: Burning Up (1995): the kick and offbeat bass gallop and the build-up that seems never to end, the Trade model.
Tony De Vit: The Dawn (2000): the formula at its peak, with the hoover, the vocal and the breakdown that stretches the wait.
Jammin Gerald: Pump That Shit (1994): the rawer American side, where hardened house doesn't yet have the codes of English rave.
hardhouse.rythme: The hardened 909: short kick, tuned and saturated, with a pronounced click at 3 kHz, on every beat. 909 clap on 2 and 4, often layered with a compressed snare. Closed hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats, nice and loud. A ride or a crash on beat 1 of the choruses. 909 toms in long rolls on the build-ups, with rising pitch. Fills are violent: a 4-bar snare roll with a crescendo, one beat of silence, return. Add Latin or tribal percussion in sixteenth notes on the choruses for the Trade feel. The whole kit is compressed hard together.
hardhouse.sons: The Alpha Juno hoover (“What The” preset): a PWM sawtooth with chorus, played as chords or as a single gliding note, in a two-bar riff on the chorus. A plugin like TAL-U-NO-LX, Roland Cloud's Alpha Juno or an Operator with three detuned oscillators gets you there. Rising sirens at the end of build-ups, filtered white noise rising over 32 bars, crowd shouts, sampled and pitched female vocals. A block-chord piano can come back in the breakdown, a house legacy. A syncopated organ stab. Everything is treated with eighth-note delay and saturation. The style isn't afraid of cliché: the siren, the hoover and the vocal say “rave” with no detours.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, TAL-Pha emulates the Alpha Juno 2 behind the hoover
Gearspace, hard house trance production resources
hardhouse.tempo: Between 140 and 150 BPM, the fastest of the whole house family along with footwork. The feel is tense, straight, without swing: it's music for an endless club night where the DJ never stops. The signature rhythmic motif is the offbeat bass: every offbeat carries a short bass note, which creates a kick-bass-kick-bass gallop at 145 BPM. That gallop must sit perfectly on the grid. Build-ups last a long time, 32 or 64 bars, and so do breakdowns. Count your sections in 32s, not 16s: at this tempo, 16 bars go by in 26 seconds.

hardstyle.arrangement: A hardstyle track runs 4 to 6 minutes and tells a story in two drops: a 32-bar intro with kick and reverse bass, sometimes a screech, then a long 32- to 48-bar breakdown without kick where the supersaw melody develops, often with a spoken vocal, then an 8- to 16-bar build-up (kick roll, riser, one beat of silence), then the 32-bar drop: kick, reverse bass, screech or lead. Second, shorter breakdown, second drop with the full lead over the kick (the climax), 32-bar ending with kick and reverse bass. The breakdown is the emotional moment, the drop the physical one. DJs mix on the 4/4 intros and endings.
hardstyle.basse: The reverse bass: between each kick, on the offbeat, a bass sound with a slow attack that rises toward the next kick, like a kick played backwards. You make it by reversing the kick's tail (sample reversed, cut to one eighth note), or by synthesizing a saturated sawtooth with a 120 ms attack and a filter that opens. It's tuned to the same note as the kick, and together they form the bassline: kick on the root, reverse on the root, then both move up to the fourth at the chord change. There is no other bass in the drop. In the breakdowns, a sine sub can carry the chords under the supersaw, lightly sidechained.
etapes: Tempo 150 BPM. Make the tok: 909 cut at 50 ms, Saturator in hard clip. Make the tail: saturated Operator sine, pitch dropping over 100 ms then settling on the root, decay 250 ms.
Glue the tok and tail together, rebounce, process by bands: clean lows, distorted mids. Kick on every beat.
Reverse bass: reverse the tail, cut it to one eighth note, place it on every offbeat, same note as the kick.
Screech in Serum: sawtooth, resonant band-pass filter, distortion, sixteenth-note riff, high-pass at 400 Hz.
Supersaw lead in Sylenth1, 16-bar minor melody for the breakdown, with a long reverb.
Arrange: intro 32, breakdown 48 with lead and spoken vocal, build-up 16, drop 32, breakdown 16, final drop with lead over kick, ending 32. Clipper then limiter.
hardstyle.mix: The hardstyle mix revolves around the kick, which is mixed and processed like a melodic instrument: multiband so the bottom of the tail stays clean (30 to 100 Hz) and the mids are distorted, EQ to cut a narrow band where the tail sounds hollow, often around 250 Hz. Kick at -3 dB peak, reverse bass 3 dB below. Supersaw lead high-passed at 250 Hz, sidechained from the kick with a 150 ms release for the pumping. Screech high-passed at 400 Hz. Light bus compression, 2:1 ratio. Master: Ozone or Pro-L 2 around -6 LUFS, with a clipper before it. Compare your kick's tail with Headhunterz at the same level: that's the test.

outils.pourquoi: The modern hardstyle kick is drawn in it: sine with a pitch envelope, internal distortion in series, resample. Also the screeches and leads. Dominant since Serum 2.
Supersaw for the dramatic breakdowns and epic leads; the cheaper and still common alternative to Serum for melodies.
The origin: the 2000s hardstyle kick is a sampled 909, stretched, tuned to the root and distorted. Still the basis of many tail layers.
The DAW of the Scantraxx and Defqon scene: layered kick in the Piano roll, reverse bass as a reversed sample, arrangement in 32-bar blocks.
Synthesized sine kick, steep pitch envelope, then Saturator in Analog Clip with Drive at 8 dB: the starting point before moving to Serum.
On the kick tail, in three light stages, then FabFilter Saturn 2 or Decapitator if you want multiband; Drive between 30 and 60%.
Master limiter around -6 LUFS integrated, with Pro-Q 3 just before it for a high-pass at 30 Hz and a dip around 300 Hz.
Master: dynamic EQ, Exciter on the kick's mids, Maximizer. Nicky Romero's Kickstart 2 handles the sidechain on the leads.

reperes: Showtek: FTS (2007): the kick and reverse bass forming the bass, the spoken vocal, all of 2000s hardstyle.
Headhunterz: Psychedelic (2007): the screech as the main riff, listen to how it cuts through above the kick.
Noisecontrollers: Attack Again (2009): the long melodic breakdown then the drop with the lead over the kick.
Headhunterz: Dragonborn (2012): the kick tail changing notes to follow the melody, the euphoric climax.
hardstyle.rythme: The hardstyle kick is an instrument. Two parts: the “tok”, a short, snappy attack, 30 to 60 ms, often a clipped 909 or a synthetic click, and the tail, a tuned saturated wave that drops in pitch then settles on the root, 200 to 300 ms. Screech House's tutorials describe this split well, along with the key point: when you change the kick's note to follow the harmony, you pitch only the tail, never the tok, otherwise the attack loses its shape. Kick on every beat. Clap or snare on 2 and 4, set back. Hats in eighth notes. Pitched kick rolls before the drops. Half-time kicks (on 1 and 3) in the drop intros.
hardstyle.sons: The screech: a sawtooth run through a very resonant band-pass filter then a distortion, played as a high, piercing riff, often in sixteenth notes, in Serum or Sylenth1 with a Dist Unit on top. Dramatic supersaw leads for the breakdowns and main melodies: 7 detuned sawtooths in Sylenth1, hall reverb, playing rising minor melodies. Pianos and strings in the breakdowns. Vocals: epic spoken phrases, choirs, pop vocals in euphoric hardstyle. Risers, impacts, reverse cymbals. “Pitch bend” effects on the kick during rolls. The vocabulary is that of hard trance with a hardcore kick.
sources: Music Production Wiki, How to Make Hardstyle (musicproductionwiki.com)
sourcesOutils: hard cultr, Hardstyle Producer Plugins 2026: The Toolkit (hardcultr.com)
ADSR Sounds, How to Make a Hardstyle Kick in Xfer Serum (adsrsounds.com)
Music Production Wiki, How to Make Hardstyle (musicproductionwiki.com)
hardstyle.tempo: Hardstyle is played at 150 BPM, with the early years (2002-2005) around 140-145 and modern hardstyle sometimes at 155. It's the only tempo in the family that is really fixed: 150 is a convention, and kicks are designed for that tempo, with a tail that lasts exactly until the reverse bass on the offbeat. What sets it apart from gabber is the relative slowness that lets each kick be heard in full, and from hardcore techno, the total absence of dirt: everything is precise. No swing. Program at 150 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, and think in beats of 400 ms that the kick and the reverse bass share.

hardtechno.arrangement: Five to six minutes, kick almost constant. 16- to 32-bar intro of kick and hat for the DJ. Add the metallic percussion in 16-bar blocks. Breakdowns are short, 8 to 16 bars, often with a noise riser or a vocal element, and the kick comes back unannounced. The revival adds marked drops: 8 bars of build-up, one bar of silence, return. Keep three or four elements at once: with a kick like that, the emptier it is, the harder it hits. A variant is to strip everything except kick, clap and hat to let a synth in. 32-bar outro of kick alone.
hardtechno.basse: Often, the kick is the bass. Its sub layer at 41 Hz, boosted by Drum Buss with 20% Boom at that frequency, fills the whole bottom. If you want a separate bass, use the rumble: send the kick into a reverb at 100% mix, decay 5 to 9 s, cut everything above 150 Hz, saturate, then sidechain to the kick. You get a pumping low carpet. Revival alternative: a distorted sawtooth bass, sixteenth notes on the root, cut at 60 Hz to leave the sub to the kick. Always tune the bass to the kick's fundamental: use Ableton's Tuner to read the kick's note, then transpose. No reverb on a sub, no stereo.
etapes: At 150 BPM, build a three-layer kick (sub 41 Hz, body F#0, air 15 kHz) on a single bus.
Process the kick bus: Drum Buss, reverb on the click only, Amp Blues, transient shaper, Saturator 13 dB.
Place an electronic tom and a metallic impact just after kicks 1 and 3, with a roll before the last kick.
Run the tom through Devastor, Saturn and an EQ that brackets 70 Hz to 3 kHz with a resonant peak.
Add a clap on the kicks at velocities 50, 29, 100, 1 and a hi-hat on the offbeats with ghosts.
Mix around the kick at -4 dB, Saturator as a limiter on the bus, and arrange over six minutes with short breakdowns.
hardtechno.mix: Everything is mixed around the kick, set around -4 dB peak, the other elements around -6. The metallic tones sit on either side of the stereo field, the tom and the kick stay in the center. On the drum bus, no SSL compressor but a Saturator Analog Clip at 2 dB of drive with soft clip, used as a limiter: that's what gives the extra two dB of loudness. The distortions create aliasing peaks above 16 kHz: cut them. Watch 2 to 5 kHz, the fatiguing zone. Mono below 150 Hz. Masters in the genre are very loud, often above -7 LUFS, but the kick must remain the only element that moves the peak meter.

outils.pourquoi: Layered kick synthesis: Abyss preset for the sub at E0, pitch-modulated body at F#0, the beating between the two brings the kick to life.
The reference kick, saturated and compressed; as samples or via Drumazon, it serves as the body under the synthetic sub and as a source for claps and hats.
First distortion in the chain on toms and impacts, Pressurised preset, which brings up harmonics between 100 Hz and 1 kHz.
Multiband saturation in three Warm Tape bands, with LFOs on the crossovers so the distortion moves constantly.
The revival DAW: Drum Buss with Boom at 41 Hz, Amp in Blues mode, Saturator at 13 dB in soft clip, Tuner to read the kick's note.
Alternative to PunchBOX for drawing the kick's pitch curve by hand and adding a clean click, with a built-in clipper.
Screaming hoovers and leads of the 2020s revival, as well as sawtooth basses cut at 60 Hz under the kick.
On the kick bus, sustain at 65% to lengthen the body without stretching the tail beyond 300 ms at 150 BPM.

reperes: Dave Clarke: Red 2 (Wisdom to the Wise) (1994): the cutting kick and the snare roll that announce the style
Spiral Tribe: Probably Taking Drugs (1995): the speed of the free parties, distorted kick and loops
Arkus P: Hardtechno (2003): the crushed kick and percussive loops, the hinge with schranz
I Hate Models: Warehouse Memories (2019): the revival, huge kick, hoover and rave melancholy
hardtechno.rythme: The kick is a three-layer instrument: a sine sub at E0 (41 Hz), a pitch-modulated sine body at F#0, and an air layer above 15 kHz. The two low layers are slightly detuned to create a 2.5 Hz beating that brings the kick to life. In D16 PunchBOX or with three samples, then a single bus.
