Around it: an electronic tom just after kicks 1 and 3, then in a roll at 40, 1 before the last kick; a metallic impact on the same positions; a clap together with the kicks at velocities 50, 29, 100, 1; a snare on the offbeat of beat 1; a hi-hat on every offbeat at full velocity, with ghosts at 50 before beats 2 and 4.
hardtechno.sons: Percussion brutalized by distortion chains. Typical chain on a tom: Devastor 2, then Saturn 2 in three Warm Tape bands with LFOs on the crossovers, then EQ Eight bracketing between 70 Hz and 3 kHz with a 15 dB peak at 1.8 kHz, then Saturator Soft Sine to smooth it out. On the kick: Drum Buss, a reverb that only affects the click above 8 kHz, Amp in Blues mode with Treble and Presence maxed, Transient Master with sustain at 65%, Saturator at 13 dB of drive and soft clip. Metallic impacts pitched down 15 to 25 semitones and tuned to the key. For the revival, Serum for hoovers and screaming leads.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
hardtechno.tempo: From 140 to 160 BPM, sometimes more in the 2020s revival. No groove: the grid is straight, without swing, and that's intentional. At this speed a sixteenth note lasts less than 100 ms, so any humanization turns into blur. Movement comes from velocities and from the placement of percussion around the kick, not from timing. Take 150 as the center: 1990s warehouses ran between 140 and 150, the revival goes up to 155 or 160 with hoovers. Check that your kick has stopped ringing before the next one: at 150 BPM, a beat lasts 400 ms, so your kick's tail must not exceed 300 ms.

hardtrance.arrangement: Six to seven minutes, designed for impact. 16-bar intro of kick and hat, bass at bar 17, arpeggio at bar 33. A first short breakdown at bar 65: the kick leaves, the hoover or pad holds, 8-bar roll, drop with a crash. 32-bar plateau, a second, longer breakdown, 32 bars, with the main melody, roll, harder final drop, with the reverse bass coming in. 32-bar outro. Each drop must add an element: the hoover on the first, the reverse bass on the second. Build-ups are abrupt, comedowns don't exist.
hardtrance.basse: The early reverse bass: an offbeat bass note with a reversed, rising attack, like a sample played backwards, that sucks toward the next kick. Program a sawtooth with an amplitude envelope of 100 ms attack and zero release, one eighth note long, between each kick. Tune it to the kick's note. Alternative: a pumping kick-bass, offbeat bass sidechained at 10:1, 60 ms release. Saturate it lightly. It doesn't move: root for 32 bars, fourth on the breakdown. The sub belongs to the kick, the bass lives between 80 and 200 Hz.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM, distorted and compressed 909 kick on every beat, loud open hat on the offbeat, dry clap on 2 and 4.
Write an offbeat reverse bass: sawtooth, 100 ms attack, zero release, tuned to the kick.
Create a hoover: two sawtooths with PWM, chorus, pitch envelope dropping one octave, played as held chords.
Add a fast sixteenth-note arpeggio over two octaves and a short minor melody.
Arrange 7 minutes: short intro, two breakdowns with 8-bar rolls, each drop harder than the previous one.
Parallel-compress the drum bus and push the master toward -5 LUFS without losing the kick.
hardtrance.mix: Loud, compressed, almost clipped. Kick in the center around -5 dB peak, with saturation and fast compression. Open hat just below it. Bass in mono, glued to the kick by sidechain. The hoover is wide, cut at 200 Hz, with 4:1 compression to stay constant. Arpeggios compressed and placed in stereo. Drum bus with parallel compression blended at 40%. Master: glue compressor, 3:1 ratio, then a limiter working hard, around -5 LUFS. Be careful not to lose the kick's transient under the limiter: turn the rest down rather than pushing further. Reverb only on the breakdown.

outils.pourquoi: The hoover: pulse-width-modulated sawtooth, chorus, pitch dropping one octave. TAL-Pha emulates the machine, Phutura is free.
TAL's Alpha Juno 2 emulation: the What The preset and its PWM, for an exact hoover without hunting for the machine.
Fast arpeggios over two octaves, very open filter, and held chords on the offbeat. TAL-U-NO-LX as an emulation.
Sixteenth-note arpeggios and aggressive leads of the late 1990s for Kai Tracid. Arturia Jup-8000 V replaces it.
Hard compressed kick around -5 dB peak, with a short tail dropping in pitch to set up the early reverse bass.
Kicks, claps and sirens of 2000s German hard trance, still used for impacts and white noise risers.
Parallel compression on the drum bus blended at 40%, then a 3:1 ratio on the master before a limiter working hard toward -5 LUFS.

reperes: Kai Tracid: Trance And Acid (2002): the hard kick, the loud open hat and the fast acid arpeggio, German hard trance at its peak
Cosmic Gate: Exploration Of Space (2001): the abrupt build-up and the drop with a crash, between hard trance and anthem
Marlon Hoffstadt & DJ Daddy Trance: It's That Time (2023): the revival, same reverse bass and same aggressive euphoria, modern production
hardtrance.rythme: The kick is hard and compressed: a 909 with distortion and fast compression, 1 ms attack, 8:1 ratio, sometimes clipped. It holds the center on its own. The offbeat open hat is very loud, almost at the kick's level, with a 150 ms decay: it's the hard trance signature. Dry clap on 2 and 4, often doubled with a 909 snare tuned high. 8-bar snare rolls that accelerate, sixteenth then thirty-second notes, with a crash on the first beat of each 8-bar block. Little percussion: the trio of kick, open hat and clap is enough.
hardtrance.sons: The hoover: a Roland Alpha Juno with a pulse-width-modulated sawtooth, chorus maxed, pitch envelope dropping one octave in 200 ms. On a virtual synth, two detuned sawtooths with PWM and a wide chorus do the job. It plays chords or held notes on the offbeat. Arpeggios are fast, sixteenth notes over two octaves, Juno-106 or JP-8000, with a very open filter. Stabs, sirens, white noise risers. The melodic side exists but is short and aggressive, in minor, 4 or 8 bars. Short delay, one eighth note, and little reverb except on the breakdown.
hardtrance.tempo: 140 to 150 BPM, the fastest in the family, usually 145. Straight grid, no swing, with an energy that comes from compression and the offbeat rather than from groove. Blocks are 16 bars, build-ups are abrupt: 8 bars of roll and down you go. Kai Tracid and DJ Scot Project sit at 140-145, the later Cosmic Gate productions a bit slower. The feel is that of a rave: everything is loud, everything is square. The silences before the drops last one or two bars, never more, and each return of the kick should feel harder than the one before.

hinrg.arrangement: Hi-NRG keeps a song format stretched to 12-inch length: 6 to 8 minutes. 16- to 32-bar intro with the octave bass and drums, then a 16-bar verse, a rising pre-chorus, a 16-bar chorus with the OB-8 brass and backing vocals. A breakdown in the middle removes the kick and leaves the octave bass with a pad, then the syndrums descend in a fill and everything comes back. Modulating up a semitone for the last chorus is almost mandatory. End with 32 instrumental bars with the bass alone for the DJ. Each section should feel bigger than the previous one.
hinrg.basse: The genre's signature: the octave bass in eighth notes. On each eighth note, you alternate the low root and the root an octave up: low, high, low, high, eight notes per bar. The sound is a Juno-60 or Juno-106 sawtooth with the filter wide open, a short envelope, release at 50 ms for a clean staccato. The Juno's arpeggiator in octave mode does exactly that. The notes follow the chord progression, often four minor chords changing every bar. The kick lands with the low note, the high note falls between the kicks: that pumping is what creates the illusion of speed. Don't put a sub under this bass, it has to stay in the 80 to 200 Hz range.
etapes: Set 134 BPM, load LinnDrum samples: kick, snare, clap, hats, toms.
Program the kick on the beats, snare and clap on 2 and 4, hats in sixteenth notes, a descending tom fill every 8 bars.
Create the octave bass on a virtual Juno: eighth notes alternating low and high, sawtooth, release 50 ms, over four minor chords.
Add OB-8 brass as chorus stabs, a Juno pad with chorus, strings in a chromatic rise before the chorus.
Build intro, verse, pre-chorus, chorus, breakdown with syndrums, a semitone modulation for the finale.
Mix bright: loud hats, compressed bass, long plate on the vocal, gated reverb on the snare and toms.
hinrg.mix: A Hi-NRG mix is bright and compressed. The hats and tambourine are loud, around 8 to 12 kHz. The octave bass is compressed at 4:1, fast attack, so every note has the same strength. The kick is dry and short, cut below 40 Hz. The vocal is way up front, with a 2-second plate reverb and an eighth-note delay. The OB-8 brass is widened with chorus and wide panning. A short gated reverb on the snare and syndrums gives the early-80s touch. Compress the master with a bus compressor at 2:1 for light pumping, and aim for a club loudness louder than disco, around -10 LUFS.

outils.pourquoi: Firm, short kick, Linn snare doubled with a clap on 2 and 4; today, samples like Linn From Mars by Samples From Mars.
The eighth-note octave bass, sawtooth, open filter, release at 50 ms: the arpeggiator in octave mode plays that pumping by itself.
The most common Juno-60 emulation for the octave bass and chorused pads, the basic sound of the whole genre.
Big, bright synth brass for the chorus stabs, widened by chorus and wide panning; Arturia OB-Xa V replaces it.
Oberheim brass in software: two slightly detuned oscillators, a filter that opens on the attack, for the stabs that carry the chorus.
Patrick Cowley's main synth for the leads, glissandi and space noises that decorate his San Francisco productions.
The electronic toms with falling pitch that play the fills every 8 bars; recreate them with Operator, sine, pitch dropping 24 semitones.
The virtual syndrum: a sine with a pitch envelope that drops in 150 ms, a four-note descent on the last beat.

reperes: Patrick Cowley: Menergy (1981): the eighth-note octave bass and the syndrums, the template of the genre.
Sylvester: Do Ya Wanna Funk (1982): the huge vocal over a LinnDrum rhythm and synth brass.
Divine: You Think You're a Man (1984): the Stock Aitken Waterman version, everything is drier and faster.
Jessie Ware: Freak Me Now (2023): the modern take, with the same pumping bass and the same vocal drama.
hinrg.rythme: The LinnDrum is the reference machine: firm, short kick, Linn snare doubled with a clap on beats 2 and 4. Hats in sixteenth notes, open on every eighth-note offbeat. The tambourine doubles the hats. Syndrums (electronic toms with falling pitch) play the fills every 8 bars: a four-note tom descent on the sixteenths of the last beat. Add a light cowbell on the offbeats in the chorus. In your DAW, LinnDrum samples or a 909 kit will do; for the syndrums, an Operator with a sine and a pitch envelope that drops 24 semitones in 150 ms.
hinrg.sons: The Juno-60 and 106 provide the chorused pads and the octave bass. The Oberheim OB-8 supplies the synth brass, big and bright, for the chorus stabs. Syndrums are everywhere. The vocal is big, dramatic, female or falsetto, doubled and harmonized. Synth strings in chromatic rises before the choruses. Patrick Cowley added modular synth effects, glissandi and space noises. Today: TAL-U-NO-LX for the Juno, Arturia OB-Xa V for the brass, a sampled LinnDrum. The Juno chorus on everything except the bass is the color of the genre.
hinrg.tempo: Hi-NRG speeds everything up: 128 to 140 BPM, with a sweet spot around 132 to 135. It's the fastest genre in the disco family. The feel is mechanical and euphoric, straight eighth notes, no swing. The pulse is carried by the pumping eighth-note bass, which gives the impression of an even faster tempo. Set your project to 134 BPM, full quantization. Count in 8 bars, with syndrum fills announcing each change. The difference from euro disco: it's no longer the sequence that hypnotizes, it's the energy pushing toward the chorus.

hiphop.arrangement: A hip-hop track is a 4-bar beat running under a rap structure: 4- to 8-bar intro with the beat and a scratch, 16-bar verse, 8-bar chorus (a sample, a shout, a repeated phrase), second 16-bar verse, chorus, third verse or a bridge with a stripped-down beat, final chorus, outro on scratches. Length 3 to 5 minutes, up to 8 for the long versions of 1979. Variations come from mutes: drop the melodic sample for the last 4 bars of the verse, leave the drums alone at the start of the chorus. A 2-bar break without drums before each chorus creates impact. For an instrumental version playable in a set, duplicate the track without vocals and bring the melodic sample forward.
hiphop.basse: Early hip-hop bass is sampled with the break, or played by a bassist on the replayed groove (Rapper's Delight), or else the 808 kick acts as the bass. Choose: if you sample, leave the record's bass in the loop and cut it with a low-pass at 150 Hz to keep only the low end, then add a sine from Operator doubling the root. If you program, use an 808 kick with a long decay (400 to 800 ms) tuned to the track's key, played on the kick positions, and nothing else beneath it. 4:1 compression with 4 dB of reduction. The kick and bass don't duck each other: they overlap, and the kick wins through its transient.
etapes: Find or record 2 bars of funk drums, slice them in Simpler in Slice mode and rearrange them at 95 BPM with an MPC 58 groove.
Sample 2 beats of piano or horns, transpose them without Warp to tune them to the break, and run them through Redux at 12 bits.
Add an 808 kick tuned to the key, with a long decay, as the only bass, or keep the low end of the loop.
Program scratches or stabs on the transitions and a sampled shout for the chorus.
Structure over 4 minutes: intro, three 16-bar verses, 8-bar choruses, 2-bar breaks without drums.
Mix the drums up front, fast-compressed, a dry voice, master gently saturated at -10 LUFS.
hiphop.mix: The early hip-hop mix is raw and compact: kick and snare in front of everything, the voice just behind, the samples around. Compress the drums with a fast Compressor (3 ms attack, 80 ms release, 4:1 ratio, 4 to 6 dB) for snap, then Drum Buss with a little Drive. The 808 kick gets a Saturator and a boost at 60 Hz. The melodic sample is filtered from the top (low-pass at 8 kHz) and from the bottom (high-pass at 150 Hz) to make room. The voice: high-pass at 100 Hz, 4:1 compression with 6 dB of reduction, an eighth-note delay at 10%, almost no reverb. Master: Glue Compressor at 3 dB, gentle Saturator, limiter, target -10 LUFS for a modern version.

outils.pourquoi: The direct-drive turntable of Flash and Bambaataa: high torque, precise pitch, two of them and a mixer to isolate and loop the break.
The long kick tuned to the key, the dry snare, the cowbell of Planet Rock and Run-DMC; Roland Cloud TR-808 or D16 Nepheton.
The 12-bit, 26 kHz sampler that made the boom bap grain and the velocity swing; Inphonik RX1200 emulates it faithfully.
Roger Linn's 16 velocity-sensitive pads and sequencer, with MPC swing and imperfect quantization; Akai MPC Software or an MPC One today.
The funk break sliced up and replayed in a different order; Warp off to transpose a piano sample, the speed change makes the sound.
The SP-1200 grain without the sampler: 12 bits, rate at 26 kHz, then a low-pass at 10 kHz on the melodic samples and the break.
The SP-1200 emulation as a plugin: 12 bits, 26.041 kHz, SSM2044 filter and aliased transposition, four banks of eight pads like the original.
MPC 16 Swing groove at 58 to 62, Timing at 70%, snare 10 to 20 ms late: the head nod comes from there.

reperes: Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five: The Message (1982): drum machine and synth at a slow tempo, the voice telling a story.
Run-DMC: Peter Piper (1986): the looped Bob James break, the bells, the dry 808 drums up front.
Eric B. & Rakim: Paid in Full (1987): the sampled break, the record's bass kept, the voice sitting on the beat.
Public Enemy: Fight the Power (1989): the Bomb Squad's collage of dozens of samples, density as violence.
hiphop.rythme: Two methods, in historical order. First: the looped break. Find 2 bars of bare drums on a funk or soul record (or record some yourself), slice them in Simpler in Slice mode, and replay them while changing the order of the slices. Second: the 808 drum machine, long, deep kick, dry snare, sixteenth-note hats, cowbell, in the manner of Run-DMC and Bambaataa. Basic boom bap pattern: kick on the 1 and the and of 2, snare on 2 and 4, a pickup kick on the a of 3. Quantize at 90% only. Run the samples through Redux at 12 bits and 26 kHz for the SP-1200 grain. A scratch or a turntable hit on the 4 bridges back to the origins.
hiphop.sons: The brief lists turntables, the mixer, the MPC60, the SP-1200 and the TR-808. Sampling is the writing: a 1- to 4-beat fragment of piano, horns, guitar or voice, looped and transposed a few semitones to match the break. In Simpler, turn off Warp and transpose: the speed change is part of the sound. The SP-1200 grain comes from Redux (12 bits, sample rate at 26 kHz) and a low-pass at 10 kHz. Horn stabs, sirens and James Brown screams punctuate. The turntable is an instrument: a sampled scratch or one played via a controller, a crab scratch on the transitions. The MC's voice is in the center, dry, with words doubled at the end of phrases.
hiphop.tempo: Early hip-hop lives between 85 and 105 BPM, the tempo of the funk breaks DJs looped: Rapper's Delight at 110 over a Chic replay, The Message at 100 on a drum machine, Paid in Full at 97 over a sampled break. The feel comes from the sampler's swing: the SP-1200 and the MPC60 add a shuffle of 58 to 62% when you ask for it, plus a quantization imprecision that makes boom bap. In Ableton, use the Groove Pool with an MPC 16 Swing 58 to 62 groove and Timing at 70%. The snare is slightly late, 10 to 20 ms, the kick slightly early: that imbalance is what makes heads nod.

hiphouse.arrangement: Rap song structure on a house base: 16-bar DJ intro with drums and scratches, an 8-bar sung or chanted chorus that arrives early, 16-bar rapped verse, chorus, verse, 8-bar break without kick with a vocal sample and scratches, last chorus doubled, 16-bar drum outro. Length 4 to 6 minutes in the club version, with an instrumental mix for DJs. Choruses are slogans (“Turn Up The Bass”, “I'll House You”) repeated four times. Hip house doesn't build in steps, it alternates: clear verse, full chorus, hard cuts between the two.
hiphouse.basse: The standard house bass: synthetic, in octaves or in eighth notes on one note, filtered sawtooth, or a funk bass sample cut clean. The pattern is simple and repetitive, two bars at most, because the voice must stay readable. A period trick: a long 808 bass under the kick on the chorus, for hip-hop pressure, with the synth bass taking over on the verses. Stay on one note or a root-fifth back-and-forth, leaving silences on beat 1 so the kick comes through. Nothing melodic: the bass is an engine, the rap and the vocal sample do the rest.
etapes: Project at 122 BPM, four-on-the-floor 909 kick, 808 snare doubled with a sampled break snare, 808 hats in accented sixteenth notes.
Synth bass in octaves on one note, with a long 808 under the chorus.
Sample three or four syllables from an a cappella or a shout and play them syncopated, with a scratch on the “and” of 4.
Write or record a four-word chanted chorus and a 16-bar rapped verse, locking the rhymes to the beats.
Assemble verses and choruses over 5 minutes with a DJ intro, a kickless scratch break, and an instrumental version.
Mix the voice up front and compressed, keep the 12-bit grain of the samples, and check the result in mono.
hiphouse.mix: The voice up front, compressed firmly (6:1 ratio, fast attack) and doubled on the choruses, with a short eighth-note delay on the ends of phrases. The kick hits hard and dry, the breakbeat sample is cut below 100 Hz and mixed under the 909. The 12-bit samples keep their grain: don't clean them up, the crunch is part of the sound. A single short reverb on snare and stabs. Wide panning on the scratches and stabs, voice and bass in the center. Medium bus compression to glue the drum machine and the samples together. The mix must work in mono on a radio: check that the chanted chorus comes through even on a small speaker.

outils.pourquoi: 12-bit sampler at 26 kHz that gives rap a cappellas and breaks their dirty grain; a 12-bit bitcrusher or XLN RC-20 simulates it.
The 1988 studio sampler for chopping syllables, horn stabs and crowd shouts, played on the keyboard with varying pitch.
The clean four-on-the-floor kick under the rap, often doubled with a sampled break snare for the hip-hop smack.
Snare, accented sixteenth-note hats, syncopated cowbell and long 808 bass under the chorus, the direct legacy of the era's rap.
Scratches are percussion: a “fresh” or an “ah” scratched on the “and” of 4, recorded from the turntable or sampled.
Replaces the S900 and SP-1200 for slicing an a cappella into syllables and replaying them syncopated, with Redux for the 12-bit grain.
Common emulation of sampler and tape aging, to dirty up a clean sample as if it came out of an SP-1200.

reperes: Jungle Brothers: I'll House You (1988): the rap locking onto a house kick without losing any of its flow, and the slogan chorus.
Fast Eddie: Yo Yo Get Funky (1988): the Chicago version, with samples chopped in syncopation and a chorus repeated to the point of dizziness.
Tyree Cooper: Turn Up The Bass (1989): the 808 bass under the kick and the chanted voice on top, the style's formula at its peak.
hiphouse.rythme: A 909 or 808 kick in four-on-the-floor, but with hip-hop vocabulary around it: 808 snare or clap on 2 and 4, often with a breakbeat snare sample on top for the smack. 808 hats in sixteenth notes with accents, open on the offbeats. 808 cowbell in syncopation. A sampled breakbeat (SP-1200 or S900, mixed low) can double the 909 on the choruses for grain. Scratches act as percussion: a “fresh” or an “ah” scratched on the “and” of 4. Add descending 808 tom fills and two-beat drum cuts before the choruses, for the DJ feel.
hiphouse.sons: The sampler is the instrument: Akai S900 or SP-1200, or their emulations (Simpler's 12-bit modes, or a bitcrusher at 26 kHz). Rap a cappella samples chopped into syllables and replayed, horn stabs, crowd shouts, sirens. A house piano playing block chords on the choruses, an organ or synth stab on a major chord. Scratches, real or sampled, punctuate every four bars. A vocoder or a pitch shift on a key word. The rap itself is recorded dry, doubled on the choruses, with ad libs in response. What sounds hip house is the juxtaposition: a clean 909, a dirty hip-hop sample and a rapper shouting a club chorus.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, The 4 iconic samplers that changed musical history
Audio Plugin Deals, Classic Boom Bap & Lo-Fi Plugins SP1200/S950
hiphouse.tempo: Aim for 118 to 124 BPM, the standard 1988 house tempo, which is fast for a rapper. The feel must stay house, a straight four-on-the-floor kick, but the rap phrasing imposes an eighth-note reading with hip-hop syncopations. The real hip house trick: the rap is locked to the four-on-the-floor kick, not to a breakbeat, so it's chanted, hammered, with short rhymes landing on the beats. A slight swing of 52 to 54% on the hats recalls hip-hop without breaking the track. If you speed up a 90 BPM rap a cappella, prefer doubling it up to 120 by changing the placement rather than time-stretching it.

hitech.arrangement: Hi-tech is structured in short cells. A 16-bar intro lays down kick and bass in eighth notes. Then come sections of 8 or 16 bars, each with a new burst of micro-sounds and a bass variation. Breakdowns are very short, 2 to 4 bars, often a retrigger or a clean silence, then an immediate restart. Plan a longer breakdown in the middle (16 bars) with a glitchy lead alone, then a return with the bass in sixteenth notes, the most intense passage. Aim for 7 minutes: at this speed, longer becomes tiring. Keep 16 clean bars at the start and the end for the DJ, hi-tech gets mixed fast.
hitech.basse: Hi-tech bass comes from FM8 or Serum: an FM wave with a modulator at ratio 1 and an index modulated by the envelope, which gives a metallic attack and a clean body. Notes of 40 to 60 ms, zero release, pattern in eighth or sixteenth notes depending on the section. Root in F# or G, but hi-tech loves jumps: a bass pattern that changes note every two bars, with fast glides. Add pattern variations every 4 beats (two notes, then three, then a single long one). A separate sine sub holds the bottom, the FM bass occupies 150 to 600 Hz. Align the phase of the kick and the bass: at this speed, an offset turns into a hole.
etapes: Project at 180 BPM. 60 ms kick tuned to G around 70 Hz, click at 4 kHz, compressed hard.
FM bass in FM8 or Serum, ratio 1, 50 ms notes, eighth-note pattern on G1 with a note change every 2 bars.
Create a bank of 50 short FM micro-sounds, load it into a Drum Rack and program bursts of thirty-second notes with varied velocities.
Add a white noise snare on 2 and 4, FM hats in sixteenth notes and a 1-beat Beat Repeat every 2 bars.
Make a glitchy lead in Serum with a wavetable swept by a thirty-second-note LFO and a comb filter.
Arrange 7 minutes in 8-bar cells with 2-bar breakdowns, then limit in series until you reach -6 LUFS.
hitech.mix: The pushed limiters from the brief are real: hi-tech is mixed very loud, -5 to -6 LUFS, with a multiband limiter or several limiters in series, 2 dB each. For that to hold, every sound must be short and clean: high-pass at 300 Hz on everything that isn't kick or bass, and cut the reverb tails. The kick and bass are compressed together with a 20 ms release. The micro-sounds go into a bus with an EQ that scoops them around 2 kHz, where the kick's click must come through. The spectrum above 8 kHz is full: that's the fizz. Use an analyzer to keep the sum of the micro-sounds from creating a fixed bump.

outils.pourquoi: The raw material: a hundred FM micro-sounds of 50 to 200 ms, blips and springs, exported then machine-gunned in a Drum Rack.
FM basses at ratio 1 with a modulated index, glitchy leads swept by a thirty-second-note LFO, digital distortion at the output.
Micro-editing to the sample: Beat Repeat for retriggers, Drum Rack for bursts, warp for voices chopped into syllables.
Step effects sequencer: slices, reverses, upward pitch shifts, programmed in thirty-second notes over 2 bars.
The 60 ms kick tuned around 70 Hz, 10 ms pitch envelope, which disappears before the next note at 180 BPM.
The pushed limiters in series, 2 dB each, to hold -5 LUFS without destroying the fizz above 8 kHz.
Software modular synth for the bursts: FM and granular generators chained with per-voice effects, patched by the recent hi-tech scene.

reperes: Kindzadza: Roza Vetrov (2013): bursts of micro-sounds over a machine-gun kick, the reference for the Osom sound.
Kindzadza: Insoluble (2013): the FM bass changing pattern every 4 bars, and the one-bar breakdowns.
Mad Tribe: Sonic Mandala (2016): more playful hi-tech, with a glitchy lead serving as the chorus.
hitech.rythme: The kick is very short, 60 ms of body, tuned around 70 Hz, with a crisp click around 4 kHz: at 180 BPM it has to disappear before the next note. Make it in Operator or Serum with a very fast pitch envelope (10 ms) and compress it hard. Dry, bright snare on 2 and 4, often a very short white noise sample. The sixteenth-note hats here are FM micro-sounds rather than cymbals. Percussion comes in bursts: program sequences of 32 or 64 different micro-sounds in thirty-second notes, with varying velocities, to get that printed-circuit fizz. Use 1-beat retrigger fills (Beat Repeat) every 2 bars.
hitech.sons: FM8 and Serum are the tools. Micro-sounds are the raw material: create a hundred sounds of 50 to 200 ms in FM8 (blips, drops, springs, shards), export them and play them in a Drum Rack or Sampler with very dense sequences. Serum is for glitchy leads: a wavetable swept by a fast LFO synced to thirty-second notes, comb filter, digital distortion. The signature effects are retriggers, real-time granular slicing, upward pitch shifts, resonant filters swept over one beat. Sampled voices are chopped into syllables and reordered. Everything is ultra-edited: don't be afraid to spend an hour on 4 bars.
sourcesOutils: KVR Audio, Production Techniques forum (hi-tech FM leads)
Bandcamp, Gnosis Darkpsy and Hitech pack for Serum and FM8
hitech.tempo: Hi-tech starts at 170 BPM and commonly goes up to 190. At this speed, the grid changes meaning: a sixteenth note lasts 80 ms, so the classic rolling bass can no longer play three clean notes per beat. The genre therefore often switches to eighth notes (kick, bass, kick, bass) or keeps the sixteenths but with 40 ms notes, which sounds like machine-gun fire. No swing, no humanization: hi-tech celebrates machine precision. What changes compared to darkpsy is clarity: where darkpsy is dark and blurred, everything here is crisp, bright, cut to the sample. Think in 1-bar cells and 8-bar cycles.

hypnotictechno.arrangement: Eight to twelve minutes. 32-bar intro of textures and click. Kick at bar 33, tom at 65, bass at 97. After that the variations are tiny: a cutoff automation over 64 bars, a delay whose feedback rises from 30 to 60% over 32 bars, a bass note that changes at bar 161. No drop, no clear breakdown; at most 16 bars without kick around the two-thirds mark, where the tom and click carry on. Elements leave as slowly as they came in. For Dozzy and Neel, a track is an hour-long set compressed into ten minutes: each change should go unnoticed in the moment and be obvious in hindsight.
hypnotictechno.basse: A dark bassline in continuous sixteenth notes on the root, filtered at 200 Hz, with the notes that fall under the kick attenuated rather than removed. Or an undulating sub: Operator, a single sine oscillator in FM, a beat-synced LFO modulating the filter, two Gb notes: a short one on beat 1, a long one on beats 3 and 4. Auto Pan in tremolo mode at 40% for a gentle pumping that clears room for the kick. Drum Buss on the bus with Boom at 60% set to F# (46 Hz) for warmth. The bass almost never moves; it might change by one note every 64 bars, and that will be the event of the track. Mono, no reverb.
etapes: At 128 BPM, make a white noise kick: Simpler, SMP filter at 39 Hz, resonance 115%, one hit per beat.
Program an acoustic tom in sixteenth notes with gaps under the kick, start point pushed back into the tail.
Add a sixteenth-note click with Random and Velocity for the variations, then a ping-pong Echo.
Lay down a dark sixteenth-note bassline on the root, filtered at 200 Hz, mono.
Create a wood block in a three-hit cadence every two quarter notes, into Echo with reverb in the feedback.
Arrange over ten minutes with 64-bar automations, no drop, groove at 10%.
hypnotictechno.mix: A deep, dynamic mix. Modest kick, around -12 dB, the bass at -10, percussion between -14 and -20. A high-quality reverb or a convolution on a return, touching only the mids and highs (low cut at 400 Hz), for distance: more reverb, more depth. Drum Buss with Boom on the root and a gentle Glue at 2:1. No heavy saturation. The master around -10 LUFS with the dynamics preserved. Check that the sixteenth-note click and tom don't saturate the mids: a slight dip at 800 Hz on the tom helps. Background textures stay below -24 dB, almost inaudible alone, essential together.

outils.pourquoi: Donato Dozzy's sampler: looping, resampling and running long sequences live, a five-step melody against four beats.
Buchla or Eurorack for sequences that realign every five bars, with missing gates and varying velocities.
Simpler in self-oscillation at 39 Hz for the kick, Operator in FM for the sub, Random and Velocity on the click, Echo with reverb in the feedback.
The rack reverb in Dozzy's studio for depth, cut below 400 Hz on a return; a quality convolution reverb does the equivalent.
Almost inaudible here: synthesized hat on the offbeats and a modest kick around -12 dB, the speed comes from the click and the tom.
Slow arpeggios and pads held for four bars; Dozzy re-records it with the arpeggiator running for happy accidents.
Field recorder for the forest and water in the background, filtered between 300 Hz and 4 kHz, below -24 dB in the mix.

reperes: Donato Dozzy & Nuel: Aqua 1 (2008): the muffled percussion and the water, the birth of the Italian school
Abdulla Rashim: Weldiya (2011): the sixteenth-note tom and the dark bass, the Nordic version
Voices From The Lake: Iyo (2012): ten minutes of tiny variations, the absolute model of the style
Mike Parker: 17 Steps (Donato Dozzy Remix) (2013): the undulating FM sub and the shifting sequences
hypnotictechno.rythme: A kick made from white noise: Simpler with a noise sample, SMP low-pass filter closed at 39 Hz (D#) with resonance at 115%, the self-oscillation creates the note. One hit on every beat, Drum Buss after it. A low acoustic tom (Tom JupiterMop) in sixteenth notes with gaps where the kick hits and on the offbeats of beats 2 and 4; sample start point pushed back into the tail for an airy sound, 10 ms attack, 30 ms decay. An organic click in continuous sixteenth notes with Random (10% chance) and Velocity (random 15) for subtle variations. A wood block in a three-hit cadence every two quarter notes, into an echo. A synthesized hi-hat on the offbeats, decay at 1.5%.
hypnotictechno.sons: Long modular sequences: a five-step melody against a four-beat bar, which realigns every five bars, with missing gates that lower the velocity of some notes. A drone held for four bars on a Stutter Pad-type rack, which adds rhythmic movement in the highs. Forest or water field recordings, filtered, in the background. Muffled percussion run through Echo at a dotted eighth with the reverb placed in the feedback (8%), filtered between 300 Hz and 4 kHz: the cave effect. An Auto Filter at 6 kHz with a 4 Hz LFO on the wood block. Octatrack or Simpler for looping and resampling. No stabs, no hoovers.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
hypnotictechno.tempo: From 124 to 132 BPM, often 127 or 128. Very light groove, a template at only 10%, because movement doesn't come from swing but from the circling sixteenth notes and tiny variations. Time stretches out: think in sections of 32 or 64 bars, not 8. The feel is that of afterparties and forest clearings: everything pulses but nothing pushes. A sixteenth-note bassline and a sixteenth-note click are enough to give the speed; the kick can be almost inaudible. At 128 BPM, a 1.9 s reverb covers exactly one bar: set your spaces to these durations so the tails come back on the beat.

ibizatrance.arrangement: Seven to eight minutes. 32-bar intro with pad, delayed guitar and one percussion. The kick comes in filtered, then full, then the bass. The full guitar theme arrives around bar 65 and plays for 16 bars. Plateau. The breakdown, 32 to 48 bars: the kick leaves, piano and guitar play the theme, the pads widen, the sub stays. A reversed cymbal, the kick returns, the theme is doubled by an arpeggio. Second plateau. Slow withdrawal: the guitar is the last to leave. Also plan a 4-minute version without the intro for radio and the Café del Mar compilations.
ibizatrance.basse: A round, melodic bass, Juno-106, sawtooth and square, cutoff 400 Hz, release 250 ms, following a four-chord progression in major or bright minor. It plays eighth notes with passing notes toward the next chord, sometimes on the offbeat in the club sections. Light sidechain, 3:1 ratio, 150 ms release: the pumping exists but stays discreet. Sine sub below 60 Hz. During the breakdown, the bass stays in whole notes under the guitar. The Ibiza bass sings: try humming it. Cut at 50 Hz and give it some sustain.
etapes: Project at 132 BPM, four-chord major progression over 8 bars, softened 909 kick, soft clap, open hat, shakers and congas.
Record or program a clean guitar playing a 16-bar theme, dotted-eighth delay, chorus, plate reverb.
Write a singing Juno bass in eighth notes with passing notes, light sidechain, sub underneath.
Add an M1 piano in open chords for the breakdown and a sunny Juno pad, plus a filtered eighth-note arpeggio.
Arrange 8 minutes: intro without kick, full guitar theme, wide breakdown with piano, return with arpeggio, guitar outro.
Mix wide, tape saturation, limiter around -8 LUFS, and check in mono.
ibizatrance.mix: Wide and warm, wide-open production. Kick around -8 dB peak, bass almost at the same level, sub in mono. Guitar and piano very wide, with chorus and a 2.5-second plate reverb on separate returns. Pads cut at 250 Hz and opened out to the sides. Light tape saturation on the mix bus. Gentle master compression, 2:1 ratio, limiter around -8 LUFS: louder than balearic, quieter than uplifting. Check the stereo in mono, because the guitar delays can disappear. A bit of brightness at 12 kHz on the master for the sun.

outils.pourquoi: Clean sound through a dotted-eighth delay, 40% feedback, chorus and plate reverb: the sunny melody is played by the guitar, not by a lead.
Sampler to freeze the guitar and the voices, breaths and seagulls. Chicane sampled his guitar on a Roland S-760, same principle.
Balearic piano in open chords with the ninth for the breakdown. Korg M1 Software in the Korg Collection.
Sunny pads in major, two detuned oscillators, chorus, 2-second attack. Juno-6 for Energy 52, TAL-U-NO-LX today.
The Super JV rack used on Café del Mar for the strings and digital pads of 1990s Ibiza trance.
Filtered eighth-note leads and arpeggios on Café del Mar, the trance reminder under the balearic guitars.
Synced delays everywhere, tape mode, for the guitar and piano. Ableton Echo gives a close result for less money.
2.5-second plate reverb on separate returns for the guitar and piano, very wide, checked in mono.

reperes: Chicane: Offshore (1996): the delayed guitar and the sunny pad, the track that set the genre
Energy 52: Cafe Del Mar (1993): the melodic theme that stays pop over a club pulse, and the breakdown that widens
Agnelli and Nelson: El Nino (1998): the more club-oriented version, present kick and sunny theme, between Ibiza and uplifting
Energy 52: Cafe Del Mar (Tale Of Us Renaissance Remix) (2023): the same theme with a current production, to compare the mixes
ibizatrance.rythme: Softened but present 909 kick, 250 ms decay, filtered at 8 kHz. Soft clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeat at medium volume, ride in eighth notes on the plateau. Soft percussion: sixteenth-note shakers, eighth-note congas with ghost notes, a tambourine. Unlike pure balearic, the ride and hat give a continuous club pulse. The rolls before the returns are soft, a reversed cymbal and a conga roll or white noise, no thirty-second-note snare rolls. The basic pattern holds the whole track: variation comes from the synths and the guitar.
ibizatrance.sons: Clean electric guitar through delay, played or sampled on an Akai S1000, dotted-eighth delay with 40% feedback, chorus, plate reverb: that's the sunny sound. The balearic piano, Korg M1, in open chords with the ninth, plays the breakdown. The pads are sunny: Juno-106 with chorus, two detuned oscillators, 2-second attack, in major. Eighth-note arpeggios exist, filtered, to recall trance. Sampled voices, a breath, seagulls. Synced delays everywhere, long reverbs. The melody is played by the guitar or the piano, not by a synth lead.
ibizatrance.tempo: 128 to 136 BPM, between the balearic it descends from and the club trance it wants to please. Straight grid, a light swing tolerated on the percussion, 5 to 8%. The feel is sunny and wide: no tension, a progression that opens up. Chicane's Offshore and Energy 52's Cafe Del Mar sit in this zone. The difference from balearic: here the kick is present throughout, and the track is made for the end of a set on a big terrace, not for a living room. Count in 16-bar blocks, with 32-bar breakdowns that don't build but widen.

idm.arrangement: Free form, 4 to 7 minutes, no club drop. The track evolves by mutation: the break changes on every pass while the melody stays stable, or the reverse. That's the genre's tension: something beautiful laid over something broken. A frequent structure: beatless ambient intro, the break comes in and grows more complex over 32 bars, a rhythmless passage where the melody breathes, the break returns denser, then an abrupt ending or a long coda of pads. Windowlicker changes section halfway through like a film cutting. Write the melody and harmony first, then spend hours on the rhythm: it's the opposite of techno.
idm.basse: No standard, and it's a choice made per track. Clean sine sub under a chaotic break for Aphex Twin; detuned analog SH-101 or Juno bass for Boards of Canada, with a slight tape vibrato; a real electric bass played jazz-fusion style for Squarepusher. The common point: the bass is melodic and follows the harmony, minor chords with sevenths, Dorian and Lydian modes, childlike melancholy. It isn't systematically sidechained to the kick, since the kick itself moves all the time. On Roygbiv, it's a warm, round line carrying the chord; on Gantz Graf, there's almost no bass left, the texture fills the bottom.
etapes: First write a simple, melancholy melody in minor with sevenths on an emulated Juno, two voices detuned by 15 cents, at 92 BPM.
Program a 2-bar break with 808 and 909 hits, then slice it at the thirty-second note and reorder the slices by hand.
Add Beat Repeat on a 1/32 grid with chance at 30%, and a different fill every 4 bars.
Lay down a sine sub bass that follows the harmony, round, no sidechain.
Arrange over 5 minutes: beatless intro, a break growing more complex over 32 bars, a bare melodic passage, a denser return, an abrupt ending.
Mix the drums dry and saturated, the melody wide and wet, a low-pass at 12 kHz on the pads, level around -12 LUFS.
idm.mix: Contrast is the rule: dry, hard drums up front, no reverb, and blurry, wide, drenched melodies. Wide dynamics, no loudness war: -12 LUFS, sometimes lower. Saturation on the drum bus (Drum Buss, Saturator), deliberate bitcrushing, aliasing embraced. Autechre deliver raw mixes without smooth mastering; Boards of Canada put a low-pass at 10 kHz on everything and leave the hiss. The sub stays clean and mono even when the rest is dirty. Don't seek club coherence: each element can live in its own space. Listen back on headphones, it's the genre's listening format, and check that the micro-details of the break can be heard.

outils.pourquoi: The modern tracker, heir to OctaMED and ProTracker on the Amiga: break edits at the thirty-second note in columns, per-line retrigger and volume commands.
Autechre's tool since Confield: generative sequencers and programmed processing; in Ableton, Max for Live gives access to the same patches.
Autechre's virtual analog synth for cold melodies and percussion; a Nord Lead A1 or a well-tuned Ableton Wavetable stands in for it.
Simple, slightly sad melodies, two takes detuned by 10 to 20 cents; TAL-BassLine-101 or Roland Cloud SH-101 for the software version.
Pads and arpeggios with the original chorus, then run through a worn cassette the Boards of Canada way; TAL-U-NO-LX emulation.
The 16-bit sampler Richard D. James said he used on most of his early tracks; Simpler and Sampler with Redux recover that grain.
1/32 grid, chance at 30%, on the sliced 808 and 909 breaks; Grain Delay and Redux after it for artifacts, looped resampling until it degrades.
For repurposed sequencers and metallic FM percussion; the in-house alternative is Operator in FM with non-integer ratios.

reperes: Boards of Canada: Roygbiv (1998): simple hip-hop break, round bass and a weeping synth, worn tape as an aesthetic.
Aphex Twin: Windowlicker (1999): dense programming that stays danceable, the section change mid-track.
Autechre: Gantz Graf (2002): rhythm turned into texture, every hit edited, mutation at its extreme.
Plaid: Eyen (1999): the luminous melody and the clean break, the most accessible version of the genre.
idm.rythme: The edited break is the central gesture. Take a break or your own 808 and 909 hits, slice at the sixteenth or thirty-second note, reorder, reverse a slice, pitch each slice differently, add a different fill every 4 bars. In Ableton: Slice to New MIDI Track, Beat Repeat on a 1/32 grid with chance at 30%, Buffer Shuffler in Max for Live. Autechre push until the rhythm becomes a texture; Aphex Twin keeps the programming dense but stays danceable; Boards of Canada use a simple hip-hop break drowned in vinyl. What matters is that the pattern never comes back identical: the rhythm mutates on every pass.
idm.sons: The brief lists Amiga trackers and Max/MSP. Today: Renoise for the tracker feel, Ableton with Max for Live for the late period, Reaktor. Worn analog synths play the melodies: Juno-60, SH-101, Nord Lead, or their emulations, with 10 to 20 cents of detune between two voices. With Boards of Canada, everything goes through a worn cassette: wow and flutter, low-pass at 10 kHz, sampled children's and documentary voices. Identity effects: Grain Delay, Redux, Vinyl Distortion, looped resampling until the sound degrades. Operator in FM for metallic percussion. The melody is always simple and a little sad, even when the rhythm is ferocious.
sourcesOutils: Equipboard, Aphex Twin, Autechre and Boards of Canada
Gearnews, The Wizard of IDM: How to Sound Like Aphex Twin
idm.tempo: There's no typical tempo, which is the first difference from club music: from 80 BPM for Boards of Canada to 170 for Squarepusher, with bastard tempos along the way. The grid exists but it's broken: micro-offsets, triplets against straight time, bars in 7/8 or 5/4 for Autechre, tempo changes mid-track. The Amiga trackers in the brief worked in ticks and pattern speed, which produced those hiccuping rhythms; Renoise reproduces that today. With Boards of Canada, it's the opposite: a slow hip-hop tempo and a tape that wows, so a grid that floats. Pick your side before you write: the stuttering machine or the drifting tape.

illbient.arrangement: Tracks of 5 to 8 minutes built like a collage or a DJ mix: loops that layer, degrade, disappear. No drop: the strong moments are the drums coming in and out, as in dub, but the urban background never stops. A typical form: two minutes of fog and city noise, the break comes in, four minutes of variations where the break warps (filter, bitcrush, missing slices), the break leaves, a coda of pads and sirens. On a WordSound record, tracks flow into each other like a pirate radio show, with spoken interludes. Galactic Funk follows this mixing logic.
illbient.basse: An urban dub bass: the long 808 sub, with distortion that makes it menacing. Root held for one or two bars, occasional glide, notes in minor. With Techno Animal and Scorn, the bass is crushed: Saturator or Roar with heavy drive, then a low-pass at 150 Hz to keep only the mass. It's dirtier and more present than in ambient dub, less melodic too: it's pressure, not a line. The break's kick and the bass step on each other on purpose; if you want it clean, cut the break below 80 Hz and leave the bass alone at the bottom. The test: on headphones, the bass should seem to come from the building next door.
etapes: Record 5 minutes of the city on your phone (subway, street, rain), pitch the whole thing down 3 semitones and filter above 8 kHz: that's your background.
Take a drum break, slow it to 85 BPM without correcting the pitch, slice it at the eighth note in Simpler in Slice mode and reorder a few slices.
Write an 808 bass in D minor, one held note per bar, run through Saturator with heavy drive then a low-pass at 150 Hz.
Stretch a vinyl chord 8 times with Simpler in Texture mode, send it into a 6-second reverb: that's your grainy pad.
Arrange over 6 minutes: fog, the break comes in, progressive warping with Redux and filter, the break leaves, a coda of sirens.
Mix the break dry and up front, the bass in mono, the background wide, tape saturation on the master, level around -12 LUFS.
illbient.mix: Dirty, on purpose. The break dry and up front, no reverb, lightly compressed (4:1 ratio, 10 ms attack) to hold it; the pads behind, very wet. The bass in mono and distorted. A light Redux on the drum bus, tape saturation on the master, a low-pass at 12 kHz for the vinyl effect. Final level around -12 LUFS, louder than ambient dub, because it comes from hip-hop. City noises are placed wide in stereo, the drums in the center. Don't clean up the vinyl clicks, they are the texture. If the mix sounds like a demo recorded in a loft at 3 in the morning, you're there.

outils.pourquoi: DJ Spooky makes them skip with a piece of wire on the tonearm and plays records at 16 rpm: the slowed scratches and pads come from there.
The New York loft sampler; Spooky ran an S3000 with a Mac Quadra. Today, Simpler in Slice mode then resampling at 12 bits.
DJ mixer with built-in effects that DJ Spooky used as a studio console: delay and filter played live on the breaks and sirens.
The dub delay on the scratches and answering machine voices, long feedback; in the DAW, Ableton Echo in tape mode with the same filters on the repeats.
Slice mode to cut a break slowed to 85 BPM without correcting the pitch, Texture mode to stretch a vinyl chord eight times into a grainy pad.
Downsample to around 22 kHz and 12 bits on the drum bus for the grain of a period sampler; Vinyl Distortion adds the crackle, Saturator distorts the 808 bass.
On the pitched-down city recordings: wide spray, light random pitch, medium feedback, for the grainy fog behind the dry break.
The image-based resynthesis software DJ Spooky used with Hyperprism to twist samples and pads; a historic tool, still on sale.

reperes: Scorn: Deliverance (1992): the crushed bass and the crawling break, the British kinship of Mick Harris.
DJ Spooky: Galactic Funk (1996): collage as form, turntables, pads and city noise mixed like a radio show.
Sub Dub: Dancehall Malfunction (1996): Brooklyn dub with the hip-hop break, sound system bass and delays.
Techno Animal vs Dalek: Megaton (2000): the heaviest version, distorted bass and industrial beat, the limit of the genre.
illbient.rythme: Hip-hop breaks slowed down, filtered, pitched down 2 to 4 semitones, sliced and reassembled. Take a break, bring it to 85 BPM without correcting the pitch, cut it into eighth-note slices, reorder, and let a few hits double. The turntables are an instrument: a slowed scratch, the rumble of a spinning record, a record stopped by hand. The spectral scratches in the brief are a scratch run through a delay and a long reverb until only a breath remains. The rhythm degrades: progressive bitcrush, slices that vanish, then come back. With Scorn, the break becomes a slow, heavy mass; with Sub Dub, it keeps the dancehall.
illbient.sons: The brief lists turntables, the Akai S1000, the RE-201 and the mixing console. Today: a sampler (Simpler, Sampler) with 12-bit resampling (Redux, downsample to around 22 kHz), Vinyl Distortion for the crackle, Echo for the Space Echo, Grain Delay for grainy pads. City samples are the identity: subway, sirens, conversations, rain on a street, recorded on a phone then pitched down. The pads often come from a stretched record: a jazz or soundtrack chord time-stretched 8 times then run through a reverb. Radio and answering machine voices. Nothing comes from a clean preset: everything goes through at least two stages of degradation.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Textural Drone and Movement & Change)
Red Bull Music Academy Daily, Detuning the City: An Oral History of Illbient
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone chapter)
Tape Op, DJ Spooky: Electronic Music Production & Remix Culture
Red Bull Music Academy Daily, Detuning the City: An Oral History of Illbient
In Sheep's Clothing, The Story of Illbient in 5 Tracks
illbient.tempo: Between 75 and 95 BPM, the tempo of slowed-down hip-hop, not of reggae: that's the difference from ambient dub. The feel comes from the swing of the MPC or the Akai S1000 in the brief, 54 to 58%, and from sampled breaks that drag slightly behind the grid. In Ableton, apply an MPC 16 Swing 58 groove to your MIDI clips, or extract the groove from a break you like with Extract Groove, as the Attack book shows starting from a loop: the micro-offsets of the hits become a template for your own parts. The tempo can seem unstable because the vinyl loops play with wow. When there's no beat, you're in the fog: the city carries on in the background.

indiedance.arrangement: Indie dance keeps a song format: 5 to 7 minutes in the club version. A 16 to 32 bar intro with kick, Juno bass and a filtered guitar. A 16-bar verse with the treated vocal, an 8-bar pre-chorus where the pad rises, a 16-bar chorus or drop with the lead and the full guitar. Second verse, chorus. A 16-bar breakdown without kick, with the vocal and the arpeggios, then a sixteenth-note snare build-up and a euphoric return. A 32-bar outro with the rhythm section alone. The rise toward the chorus is the heart of it: each section must add a layer and some light.
indiedance.basse: The bass is a Juno-106 sawtooth with the chorus on, round and slightly veiled, inherited from italo. It plays an eighth-note riff, often the repeated root with an octave jump or a fifth, which changes with the chords every bar or every two bars. Medium release of 120 ms, low-pass filter at 600 Hz, a little portamento on note changes. It lands with the kick on the beats and fills the offbeats: it is a steady wall, not syncopation. Light sidechain from the kick, 3:1 ratio. Today: TAL-U-NO-LX or Diva. An electric bass played with a pick can double it for the rock side.
etapes: Set 116 BPM with 52% swing, load 808 samples and an acoustic snare into a Drum Rack.
Program the kick on the beats, the snare on 2 and 4 with a short reverb, eighth-note hi-hats, cowbell or tambourine.
Write an eighth-note Juno bass riff with chorus, over four minor chords, with a light sidechain from the kick.
Record or sample a guitar playing choppy chords with a dotted-eighth delay, and a vocal treated with chorus and delay.
Add a Juno pad and a sawtooth lead that only comes in on the chorus.
Structure it over 6 minutes with a verse, a rising pre-chorus, a chorus, and a breakdown with vocal and a snare build-up.
indiedance.mix: The indie dance mix is warm and wide. The chorus on the bass, the pads and the vocals gives the width; the kick and the sub stay mono. Compress the bass at 3:1 and the kick lightly, without obvious pumping. The guitars are doubled and panned left and right. The vocal goes through a dotted-eighth delay with 30% feedback and a 2-second reverb, then it is compressed at 4:1 to stay up front. The drum bus gets gentle saturation. The master aims for -9 LUFS for the club, with a limiter. Keep the top of the spectrum a little soft, around 10 kHz, for the retro side.

outils.pourquoi: The round, veiled bass inherited from italo, sawtooth with chorus, release at 120 ms, filter at 600 Hz, light portamento.
The most widespread virtual Juno on the scene for the bass, the pads and the sixteenth-note arpeggios, chorus on everywhere except the bass.
The other common emulation for a thicker Juno sound on the bass and the sawtooth lead that rises in the chorus.
The round 808 kick on all four beats, the snare or clap, and the cowbell; an 808 clone or samples also do the job.
The dotted-eighth delay with 30% feedback on the vocals and guitars, with Ableton's Chorus-Ensemble in front for the blur.
The virtual amp for the choppy guitar chords or the slightly driven single-coil riff, doubled and panned left and right.
The guitar, played or sampled, choppy chords and arpeggios, which brings the rock band side that synths alone do not have.

outils.nom: Samplesound Indie and Dark Disco Tools
outils.pourquoi: A pack of loops and one-shots cut for the scene, useful for electronic percussion and claps.

reperes: LCD Soundsystem: Dance Yrself Clean (2010): the patient build and the synth drop that explodes halfway through.
Hot Chip: Over And Over (2006): the eighth-note bass, the choppy guitar and the treated vocal.
Roosevelt: Sign (2021): the current version, Juno with chorus and guitar, tempo around 116.
The Rapture: House of Jealous Lovers (2002): rock nervousness over a club four-on-the-floor, with the cowbell.
indiedance.rythme: A TR-8 or an 808 clone holds the kick on all four beats, round but not huge. The snare is a real sampled rock snare, or an 808 with a clap, on 2 and 4, often with a short reverb. The hi-hats are in eighth or sixteenth notes, with an open one on the offbeat of 4. A sampled live drum kit can double the drum machine for the band feel. Cowbell, tambourine or shaker in eighth notes. In your DAW, a Drum Rack with 808 samples and an acoustic snare, a sixteenth-note snare fill before each chorus, a crash on the 1 of each section.
indiedance.sons: The guitars are sampled or played: choppy chords, arpeggios with a dotted-eighth delay, sometimes a driven single-coil riff. The vocals are treated with chorus, delay and reverb, often spoken or half-sung. The Juno synths handle the pads and the sixteenth-note arpeggios, and a sawtooth lead rises in the chorus. A TR-8 or an 808 clone for the rhythm section. Today: a virtual Juno, Ableton's Echo and Chorus-Ensemble on the vocals, a virtual amp like Amp and Cabinet on the guitars. The overall texture is warm and a little blurry, with lots of chorus.
sourcesOutils: ADSR Sounds (Indie and Dark Disco Tools)
indiedance.tempo: Indie dance stays below techno: 110 to 122 BPM, with many current tracks around 115 to 118. The feel mixes the stiffness of a drum machine with the energy of a band: straight eighth notes, little swing, 50 to 53%, but guitar and vocal accents that move. Set 116 BPM. The signature is a four-on-the-floor that feels like rock: the snare on 2 and 4 is blunt, and the eighth-note bass is a riff, not a funk groove. The track climbs toward a euphoric moment, a chorus or a melodic drop: that is what sets it apart from its dark cousin, dark disco.

industrial.arrangement: There is no club structure to follow. An industrial piece can last 3 minutes or 20. What holds it together: one or two elements that persist from start to finish (the pulse, the drone) and layers that arrive without transition, abruptly. Work in Arrangement view rather than in clips: lay down your base over 8 minutes, then cut out entire blocks to create hard breaks. Build-ups come from piling up saturation and volume, not from a filter opening. Place a spoken voice, a documentary excerpt, a text reading, right in the middle, without reverb. End with a hard stop or with a tape slowing down to silence.
industrial.basse: Industrial bass is often a drone rather than a line. Take a sawtooth on Analog, a single held note (E1 or F1), and move the low-pass filter slowly between 80 and 400 Hz with a free-running LFO at 0.1 Hz. Add a second oscillator detuned by 30 cents to get a slow beating. If you want movement, play monotonous eighth notes on a single note, like an engine, rather than a melody. There is no sidechain: the bass and the pulse can overlap, mask each other, get dirty. An electric bass recorded through a fuzz, a single repeated note, also works very well: that is the sound of Cabaret Voltaire.
etapes: Record three sounds from the world with your phone or a contact mic: struck metal, an engine, a voice reading a text. Import them into Ableton without Warp.
Build a quarter-note pulse at 100 BPM with the struck metal in a Drum Rack, saturated at 20 dB of drive, and let it run for 16 bars without variation.
Lay down a drone on Analog: a single note, two oscillators detuned by 30 cents, a low-pass filter that moves slowly.
Add the engine as an unquantized loop, at a free tempo, and the voice run through Echo then Vocoder, dropped 7 semitones.
Arrange over 6 minutes by cutting out entire blocks for hard breaks, and end with an automated tape slowdown.
Mix with two saturation stages on the master and an 8:1 compression that pumps, without chasing volume.
industrial.mix: The industrial mix accepts dirt, but chosen dirt. Saturate in series rather than with a single stage: Overdrive, then Saturator, then Amp in Bass mode, each stage between 6 and 10 dB of drive. Do not look for a clean sub: cut everything below 40 Hz and let the saturated low end live between 60 and 200 Hz. Heavy compression on the master, 8:1 ratio, 10 ms attack, 100 ms release, so everything pumps together. The vocals stay up front, dry, or with a short 0.8-second plate reverb. Aim for a modest level, around -12 LUFS: the fatigue must come from the timbre, not the volume. A layer of tape hiss, pink noise at -40 dB, glues the whole thing.

outils.pourquoi: Throbbing Gristle's tape delay: feedback pushed to 80%, smearing heads, to drown a reading voice. Ableton's Echo with Wobble on does the same job.
Chris Carter's modular, the heart of Throbbing Gristle's electronic sound. Today, Operator with an operator B at a 7.3 ratio gives those inharmonic broken-bell tones.
The effect Throbbing Gristle built from a magazine schematic, modulated tremolo and filter that chop the signal. Endangered Audio Research makes a reissue as a pedal.
Stuck on a radiator, a metal sheet or a chain, it captures objects without the room noise. Each recording becomes a sample that only you own.
The tape recorder behind Cabaret Voltaire's mangled loops: a 2 to 5 second loop running off tempo. In Ableton, turn off Warp and let it drift.
Drive at 20 dB on the struck-metal Drum Rack, then Redux at 8 bits behind it: the chain that breaks the definition and gives the factory grain.
A primitive 1978 drum machine: a metronome of quarter or eighth notes, without variation, for sixteen bars. CR-78 or Korg Mini Pops samples are enough.
After Echo, put the voice through Vocoder then drop it 7 semitones: the dehumanized documentary voice the genre invented on tape.

reperes: Throbbing Gristle: Hamburger Lady (1978): the voice run through delay and filter, the drone without a pulse, the emptiness around it.
Einstürzende Neubauten: Tanz Debil (1981): percussion on real metal, a raw pattern that does not vary.
Skinny Puppy: Assimilate (1985): the moment industrial becomes danceable, samples and distorted voice over a steady kick.
industrial.rythme: Forget the clean kick and snare pair. Historical industrial rhythms come from primitive boxes (Roland CR-78, Korg Mini Pops) or from struck metal. In a Drum Rack, replace the samples with recordings of objects: sheet metal, pipe, garage door, chain. Keep a simple pattern, steady quarter or eighth notes, without variation, for a long time: the monotony is intentional. Run everything through a Saturator at 20 dB of drive, then through a Redux at 8 bits to break the definition. Add a tape loop track, a 2 to 5 second sample looped without Warp, which runs alongside the pattern without syncing to it. Cymbals are rare: white noise filtered at 6 kHz replaces them.
industrial.sons: The sources are mangled voices, tapes, jury-rigged modulars and noises from the world. Record your voice, put it through Echo (feedback 80%, low-pass at 2 kHz, Wobble on), then through a Vocoder, then drop it 7 semitones. For the tape effect: Warp in Texture mode, large grain, then pitch automation for the slowdowns. For the modular: on Operator, an operator B at a 7.3 ratio modulating A at audio rate, which gives an inharmonic broken-bell tone. Field recordings are instruments in their own right: a contact mic stuck on a radiator, a struck object, a computer picked up by a coil, as experimental techno does. Each object becomes a unique sample that nobody else has.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Experimental Techno and Textural Drone chapters: recording objects, layered drones)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Experimental Techno and Textural Drone chapters)
Sound On Sound (Classic Tracks: Throbbing Gristle, Hamburger Lady)
MOD WIGGLER (Building a setup for an early industrial sound thread)
industrial.tempo: There is no required tempo. Many pieces run between 90 and 120 BPM, often without a clear grid, with tape loops that drift. What matters is the feel of a running machine: a mechanical pulse, sometimes just the metronome of a primitive drum machine, sometimes no pulse at all. In your DAW, turn off Warp on your audio loops: a 3.7-second sample that does not land on the bar is exactly the grain of the genre. If you want a pulse, use heavy quarter notes at 100 BPM, swing at zero, and let one layer drift at a free tempo on top. The rhythmic disagreement between layers is part of the aesthetic.

industrialrock.arrangement: Song format with very strong dynamics, 4 to 5 minutes. Intro on a machine loop or sampled guitar, 8 bars. Calm verse: loop, synth bass, whispered vocal, light electronic drums. Pre-chorus: the tension rises, the drums thicken. Chorus: a wall of guitars, screamed vocal, full hybrid drums. Second verse, chorus, a bridge that breaks everything (a solo piano, or a looping noise), a longer final chorus, an abrupt ending or a collapse into noise. The contrast between the electronic verse and the rock chorus is the engine, as in NDH, but with more samples and collage.
industrialrock.basse: Two layers. First the sampled guitar: record a two-bar riff, cut it up in Simpler in Slice mode, and replay it on the grid, which gives the robotic stiffness of the genre. Then a synth bass on Massive, cited in the brief, or on Wavetable: a sawtooth with a low-pass filter at 400 Hz and internal distortion, following the riff in unison an octave lower. An electric bass with fuzz can replace the synth. The lines follow the guitar: root, diminished fifth, minor second. Light sidechain on the kick. The synth bass holds the sub, the sampled guitar holds the mids.
etapes: At 100 BPM, program hybrid drums in a Drum Rack: acoustic kick doubled with a 909, a huge snare with a 1-second room, a machine noise loop in place of the hi-hats.
Record a two-bar guitar riff, slice it in Simpler in Slice mode and replay it on the grid with a Redux at 8 bits.
Program a bass on Massive or Wavetable that follows the riff an octave lower, filter at 400 Hz, internal distortion.
Record a whispered vocal for the verse and a screamed one for the chorus, with Overdrive at 8 dB and a delay.
Add two dialogue samples and a crushed breakbeat under the verses.
Arrange over 4 minutes 30: calm electronic verse, wall-of-guitars chorus, broken bridge, final chorus, collapse.
industrialrock.mix: A powerful rock mix, but with the digital artifacts left visible. Guitars doubled and panned wide, cut below 100 Hz. Drums with heavy parallel compression, 8:1 ratio, blended at 40%, for the crushed punch. Acoustic kick and 909 kick aligned. The distorted vocal stays intelligible: 6:1 compression before the distortion, then an EQ that lifts 3 kHz. The samples and loops sit back, filtered, so they do not compete with the guitars. Synth bass alone below 60 Hz. Master: 2:1 compression and a limiter, aim for -8 LUFS. Keep some digital noise and dirt: the genre is not clean.

outils.pourquoi: Trent Reznor's sampler-sequencer on The Fragile: guitars sampled and replayed on the grid, the robotic stiffness of the riffs.
Reznor sampled his drums in stereo on it with velocity splits: the genre's played-and-programmed hybrid drums.
Sawtooth synth bass, filter at 400 Hz, internal distortion, in unison with the riff an octave lower, and aggressive leads.
Slice mode on a two-bar guitar riff, replayed on the grid with a Redux at 8 bits: the native version of the MPC.
Working sampler and synth in the Nine Inch Nails studio in 1994, for the textures and pads that contrast with the guitars.
1990s resynthesis software used by Reznor, to twist samples and guitars until the digital artifact is left visible.
The DAW of the genre's massive rock productions, editing samples and film dialogue, parallel compression on the drums.
A 909 kick aligned under the acoustic kick, for the tight, dry punch of the choruses. Samples do the job.

reperes: Ministry: Thieves (1989): the sampled and looped guitar, the machine drums, the dialogue sample at the opening.
Marilyn Manson: The Beautiful People (1996): the robotic riff, the contrast between empty verse and massive chorus, the MTV format.
White Zombie: More Human than Human (1995): the heavy groove, the film samples, the synth bass under the guitar.
industrialrock.rythme: Hybrid drums: acoustic drum samples in an Akai MPC (or Drum Rack), played with the stiffness of the machine, plus electronic elements. A tight, dry kick, often doubled with a 909. A huge snare, with a 1-second room reverb, sometimes replaced by a metal impact. Eighth-note hi-hats, or a machine noise loop in their place. On top, sampled breakbeats crushed with Redux at 8 bits, cut into slices and replayed. Industrial percussion loops (sheet metal, chain) run under the verses. The fills are sample retriggers, not played rolls.
industrialrock.sons: The guitars are sampled, looped, distorted: a riff played once, then chopped and resequenced. A high-gain amp simulator, plus a Redux for digital grain. Massive provides the basses and aggressive leads, with its wavetables and built-in distortion. Noise textures, film dialogue samples and machine loops punctuate. The vocal is whispered in the verses and screamed in the choruses, with distortion (Overdrive at 8 dB) and a delay. A piano or a clean synth sometimes appears for contrast, as with Nine Inch Nails. The MPC of the era becomes a Drum Rack full of slices.
sourcesOutils: Equipboard (Trent Reznor, Nine Inch Nails The Fragile)
industrialrock.tempo: Between 90 and 140 BPM. Two feels dominate: the heavy mid-tempo around 95 to 110, with a snare that falls like a hammer, and the fast one around 130 to 140, Ministry style, with a double pedal. The groove is rock, but stiffened by the machine: swing at zero, sampled and played drums mixed together. What sets the genre apart from the industrial it descends from: there are songs with choruses, and the guitar is at the center. In your DAW, start at 100 BPM with a heavy feel. Program the drums on the grid, then record the guitars without quantizing.

industrialtechno.arrangement: Six to eight minutes, with no drop. A long 32-bar intro of textures and reverb before the first kick. Elements come in in waves of 16 or 32 bars and evolve through automation: a filter that opens over 64 bars, a reverb whose decay grows. Negative space is a tool: remove the kick for 16 bars and leave the textures, then bring it back alone, without a riser. No fills, no rolls. Only one strong event per track: an impact, a voice, a key change. End on the textures alone, 32 bars, for an ambient mix. The more patient the track, the harder it hits when it changes.
industrialtechno.basse: The bass is a rumble rather than a line. The classic rumble: kick sent into a dark reverb, low-pass filter at 150 Hz, distortion, sidechain. Or a modular or Wavetable synth drone on the root, held for 8 bars, with a slow LFO on the filter. Or else a white noise bass: Simpler with a noise sample, SMP filter closed at 39 Hz and resonance at 115% so that the self-oscillation produces the note. Cut everything that is not kick or bass below 100 Hz. The bass can disappear for 16 bars and leave a void: negative space is part of the style. Mono below 120 Hz, no exceptions.
etapes: At 132 BPM, lay down a heavy kick and route it to a reverb track at 100% (decay 9 s) sidechained to the dry kick.
Record three found sounds (metal, canvas, interference) and turn them into a tom, an impact and a noise hi-hat.
Create a rumble: kick into a dark reverb, low-pass at 150 Hz, Saturator, sidechain.
Add a Wavetable or modular drone on the root, slow LFO on the filter, 8 bars.
Run everything through Devastor or Saturator then a hangar reverb, and cut the returns below 200 Hz.
Arrange over seven minutes with no drop, a 32-bar intro of textures and only one strong event.
industrialtechno.mix: Distortion goes on the bus, not just on the tracks: a Saturator at 3 or 4 dB on the drum group, another on the master in parallel at 30%. Cut the reverb returns below 200 Hz or the low end turns to soup. Mono below 120 Hz. Watch 2 to 5 kHz: distortion chains create fatiguing peaks there, remove them with narrow notches. Keep some dynamics: a master around -8 or -9 LUFS is enough, the style is not played out in the loudness war but in the physical pressure of the kick. The kick stays around -6 dB peak and everything else below it. Listen on closed-back headphones to check that the textures do not crush the kick.

outils.pourquoi: Perc's tube distortion, he owns three of them: it is what gives attitude to the drum bus and the textures before the reverb.
A kick voice with two detuned VCOs, a VCA feeding back into the filter, noise and unstable sequences; Doepfer and Erica Synths Pico Drums to get started.
Cold, metallic synthetic percussion, sequenced live; the Analog Rytm is its heir for many current producers.
The base kick, with less click and more mass, sent into a 9 s reverb sidechained to the dry kick for the rumble.
Multiband distortion on found sounds and the bus, before Saturator and Amp, to turn a metal plate into percussion.
Reverb at 100% mix on a rumble track, Wavetable for the drones, Simpler self-oscillating at 39 Hz for a white noise bass.
A coil mic that picks up the electromagnetic interference of a computer or a neon light: raw material for noise hi-hats and textures.
A field recorder to capture a factory, a kitchen or struck metal, then resample and distort it in the DAW.

reperes: Regis: Blood Witness (1996): the gray, hammered loop, Downwards at its driest
Surgeon: Badger Bite (1997): the kick as a press and the metallic textures that loop around
Ancient Methods: The Seventh Seal (2007): industrial cathedral reverbs and a distant kick
Perc: Take Your Body Off (2014): noise as material, the distorted voice and the pumping kick
industrialtechno.rythme: The kick is a hydraulic press: less click, more mass, and a reverb. Create an audio track that receives the kick, Reverb at 100% mix, size 50, decay 9 s, low cut at 70 Hz, highs cut, then a compressor sidechained to the dry kick that crushes the tail on every hit. The bed breathes between the kicks. The percussion comes from found sounds: a struck painter's canvas for the kick, a metal plate, a coil picking up a computer's interference. Velocities between 52 and 127, routed to the cutoff and the volume. Hi-hats replaced by bursts of noise. Claps are rare, often drowned. A metallic impact pitched -15 semitones on beat 4.
industrialtechno.sons: Noise is a noble material: modular feedback, field recordings from a factory or a kitchen, electromagnetic interference picked up with a coil mic, saturated tape. Elektron Machinedrum for cold synthetic percussion. Process everything through distortion chains and huge reverbs: Devastor, Saturator, Amp, then a hangar reverb with 50 ms of pre-delay. Use resampling: record a texture, feed it back in, distort it again. Modular: a kick voice with two detuned VCOs, a VCA feeding back into the filter. Melodies, when there are any, are drones or dark two-note chords a minor second apart, heavily filtered.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
industrialtechno.tempo: From 128 to 140 BPM. 1990s Birmingham runs around 135 or 140, 2010s Berlin often around 130 to 135, Perc and Ancient Methods sometimes slower, around 128. No swing, but the groove is not stiff either: it comes from space, from reverb tails that spill onto the next beat and from textures with no sharp transient. You can break the bar: a 5/4 time signature with a kick on every beat gives a pounding that destabilizes without losing the track. Set your reverb decays to the tempo: at 132 BPM, a quarter note lasts 455 ms, and a 1.8 s reverb covers a bar.

isolationism.arrangement: A single mass that breathes for 10 to 20 minutes. No sections, no clean entries or exits: dark ambient stacks plateaus, isolationism has only one. The movement is a single very long gesture: a filter that closes over the whole length, a reverb whose mix goes from 30 to 90 percent, a layer that appears at minute 6 and that you only notice at minute 9. Start inside the sound, with no introduction, and end with a two-minute fade. On an album, the pieces flow into each other without silence. Nuuk works this way: a single landscape, and the cold rising.
isolationism.basse: The frozen sub: a frequency between 25 and 40 Hz, static, almost inaudible but felt in the body. It is the dub heritage put in the freezer: with Scorn, the dub bass becomes a motionless slab. A pure sine at 30 Hz at -15 dB, no modulation, no harmonics, and on top a drone between 60 and 120 Hz that moves by a few cents over several minutes. Nothing melodic, no intervals, a single pitch for the whole track. Check on a subwoofer that your frequency really comes out; below 30 Hz, most systems reproduce nothing, and earbuds even less. A layer at 60 Hz saves the listening on small speakers.
etapes: Record or download a gong, play it 24 semitones lower in Simpler in Texture mode with a long grain, and keep only the stretched attack.
Send it into an algorithmic reverb with 30 seconds of decay, or freeze it, and make that tail your continuous background.
Add a pure sine at 30 Hz at -15 dB and a drone at 60 Hz that drifts by a few cents over five minutes.
Cut the mids between 300 and 600 Hz, keep the air above 8 kHz, put everything below 120 Hz in mono.
Arrange a single gesture over 12 minutes: a low-pass that closes from 2 kHz to 400 Hz over the whole length, with no other section.
Export at -20 LUFS without a limiter and listen on headphones at low volume.
isolationism.mix: The cold is made with EQ: cut the warm mids between 300 and 600 Hz by 3 to 4 dB, keep air between 8 and 12 kHz so the reverb shimmers, and leave the sub isolated below 60 Hz. Very wide stereo on the reverbs, but mono below 120 Hz. Low final level, -20 LUFS, no limiter: the dynamics between the sub and the air are the subject. The Attack book recommends summing the low end of delays and reverbs to mono to avoid phase problems: essential when everything is reverb. No compression on the drones, just very slow manual gain riding. Check the result on headphones at low volume: that is how this genre is listened to.

outils.pourquoi: Thomas Köner's instrument: rubbed or scraped with a close mic, sometimes underwater, then slowed down and pitched 12 to 36 semitones lower down to the subliminal register.
The studio digital reverb of the 90s, the one behind huge frozen halls; its UAD Lexicon 480L emulation or Valhalla VintageVerb gives the same cold.
Concert Hall or Cathedral mode, 30-second decay, 1980s color for the loss of highs; it is the genre's cold room, on everything, as a send.
A reverb of unrealistic size with a freeze function: any gong or breath becomes an infinite tail that serves as a background for ten minutes.
To play a gong 24 semitones below its pitch with a long grain, keeping only the stretched attack; Hybrid Reverb in algorithm mode takes over behind it.
