Tape brings the hiss and the loss of highs that make the genre's freeze; Chow Tape Model, free, imitates that filtering and that slight wow in the DAW.
A free library that provides gongs, bowed strings and orchestral textures to slow down; enough to rebuild Permafrost without owning a single instrument.

reperes: Thomas Koner: Permafrost (1993): gongs slowed down until they become landscapes, no sharp attack, absolute cold.
Main: Rail (1994): guitar feedback processed into a drone, the rock lineage reduced to a motionless texture.
Scorn: Silver Rain Fell (1995): the frozen dub bass, a rhythm that barely exists, the link with Mick Harris's industrial side.
Thomas Koner: Nuuk (1997): a single mass of reverb that breathes through the whole track, isolationism in its purest form.
isolationism.rythme: No rhythm, and no spaced-out impacts like in dark ambient either. What stands in for a pulse is the attack of a slowed-down gong, so slow it lasts ten seconds, or the barely perceptible return of a mass of sub that swells and recedes. The industrial and dub lineage (Lull comes from Napalm Death and Scorn, Main from rock) shows in the material: guitar feedback, tape noise, but all frozen. One method: record a gong or a cymbal, slow it down four times with Simpler's Texture mode or a time-stretch without pitch preservation, and keep only the moment where the sound unfolds. The only transients are the ones the tape let through.
isolationism.sons: The brief gives gongs, the tape recorder and digital reverb. Gongs can be found as free samples (Spitfire LABS, orchestral libraries): play them 12 to 36 semitones lower, or bow them if you have a real one. The digital reverb of the 90s (Lexicon 480L, Eventide) can be found in Valhalla VintageVerb, Eventide Blackhole or Ableton's Hybrid Reverb in algorithm mode, with 30-second decays or freeze on. Main's guitar feedback goes through a tube amp then an infinite reverb pedal. Tape brings the hiss and the loss of highs. Forbidden here: anything that sings, any warm synth pad.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone and Movement & Change chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone chapter)
Gearspace (forum), Thomas Koner / isolationist production techniques
isolationism.tempo: No tempo, and even fewer events than in dark ambient. Where Lustmord tells of a crypt, Köner sets up a frozen landscape where nothing happens: change is measured in minutes, not seconds. Set up your session without a grid, in real-time display, and think in blocks of 3 to 5 minutes. The only movement is a low-pass filter that goes down from 2 kHz to 400 Hz over five minutes, or a reverb whose size slowly grows. No audible LFO: if you can hear a modulation, it is too fast. Permafrost holds for 12 minutes without anyone being able to say where it starts to change. Time does not flow, it freezes.

italodisco.arrangement: The format is a song stretched out for the club, 5 to 7 minutes. A 32-bar instrumental intro with the drum machine, the bass and the arpeggio, often a synth hook that will become the chorus. A 16-bar verse with the vocal, a 16-bar chorus with the hook and the pads. A breakdown in the middle with the vocoder or a lead synth solo over 16 bars, without kick or with the kick alone. A doubled final chorus. A 32-bar instrumental outro. The chord changes cycle over 4 or 8 bars and do not vary: the structure lives through what comes in and goes out, not through the harmony.
italodisco.basse: The bass is a Juno-106 sawtooth, sequenced in sixteenth or eighth notes, with octave jumps that follow the chord. A typical pattern: root on the first three sixteenths, octave on the fourth, repeated, then the note changes with the chord. Very short envelope, release at 40 ms, low-pass filter around 400 Hz with a little envelope that opens each note. No glide. The kick and the bass land together on the beats; between the beats, the bass traces the grid. It stays in the low mids, between 60 and 250 Hz, with little sub: the records of the era had none.
etapes: Set 120 BPM with no swing, load LinnDrum and TR-808 samples into a Drum Rack.
Program the kick on the beats, the clap on 2 and 4 with a 250 ms gated reverb, sixteenth-note hi-hats, a tom fill every 8 bars.
Write a sixteenth-note Juno bass with an octave jump on the fourth, over an i, VI, III, VII progression in minor.
Add a sixteenth-note arpeggio on a bright synth, a Juno pad with chorus, then a brassy lead that sings the hook.
Record or program a doubled vocal, and a vocoder answer for the breakdown.
Structure it over 6 minutes with 32 bars of intro and outro, then mix it dry and bright with a short delay on the vocal.
italodisco.mix: The italo mix is dry, bright and centered. The gated reverb on the clap is the only big spatial effect: the rest is rather dry with a short 120 to 250 ms delay. The Juno chorus gives the pads their width, leave the bass in mono. Compress the bass at 3:1 to even it out, but without pumping. The kick is short, cut below 45 Hz. The arpeggios are panned slightly right, the countermelodies left. The vocal is up front with an eighth-note delay and a short plate. Aim for a modest loudness, -12 LUFS: the style was never loud, it is clean. Cut the low end of the pads at 200 Hz to leave the bass alone at the bottom.

outils.pourquoi: Pads, bass and leads with the built-in chorus: the sawtooth bass, release at 40 ms, filter around 400 Hz, sequenced in sixteenth notes.
The dry rhythm with the pushed snare, kick on all four beats, toms descending in fills; the Oberheim DMX does the same job.
The clap, the eighth-note cowbell on the chorus and the fill toms, sampled into a Drum Rack alongside the Linn sounds.
The bright sixteenth-note arpeggios; today Ableton's Arpeggiator in up mode on a three-note chord gives the same result.
The common Juno emulation for every synth part, with the chorus on for the pads and off for the bass.
The more CPU-heavy alternative for a denser virtual Juno, useful on the bass and the brassy leads with an opening filter.
The digital reverb that gives the 200 to 300 ms gated reverb on the clap; Universal Audio sells an emulation, otherwise a short reverb with a gate.
The robot voice that answers the singer: a sawtooth carrier synth, the voice as modulator, like the Roland VP-330 of the era.

reperes: Charlie: Spacer Woman (1983): the gated clap, the sixteenth-note Juno bass and the vocoder, the whole manual on one record.
My Mine: Hypnotic Tango (1983): the bright arpeggio that never stops and the sentimental minor progression.
Mr. Flagio: Take a Chance (1983): the sequenced bass with octave jumps and the brassy lead.
Easy Going: Fear (1979): the moment Italian disco switches entirely to machines.
italodisco.rythme: LinnDrum or TR-808, never played drums. Kick on all four beats, dry. The clap is the central element: on beats 2 and 4, often doubled with a snare, and above all run through a 200 to 300 ms gated reverb that cracks. The hi-hats are closed in sixteenth notes, with an open hat on the offbeat of the fourth beat. A discreet 808 cowbell in eighth notes on the chorus. The fills are 808 or Linn toms descending over the last two beats every 8 bars. In your DAW, a Drum Rack with LinnDrum and 808 samples, and a short reverb with a gate on the clap only.
italodisco.sons: The Juno-106 with its chorus handles the pads, the bass and the leads. The Korg Poly-61 gives the bright sixteenth-note arpeggios. The vocoder is the robot voice that answers the singer. The leads are often a brassy sound, a sawtooth with an opening filter, played as a simple, singing melody. DX7-style bells appear after 1983. The vocals, male or female, are doubled and often in approximate English. Today: TAL-U-NO-LX or Diva for the Juno, an Ableton MIDI arpeggiator in up mode on a three-note chord for the Poly-61, Ableton's Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier synth.
sourcesOutils: Radio ITALOPOWER! (The Machines Behind Italo Disco)
italodisco.tempo: Italo disco is calmer than Hi-NRG: 115 to 125 BPM, often 118 to 120. The feel is that of a drum machine: full quantization, straight eighth and sixteenth notes, no swing. What gives the movement is the sixteenth-note synth arpeggios and the sequenced bass. Set 120 BPM and let the grid do the work. The signature is melodic and sentimental: four-chord progressions in minor, often i, VI, III, VII, that cycle through the whole track. The machine is dry, the melody is romantic: that contrast is what makes the style.

italohouse.arrangement: A pop song structure over a DJ intro. A 16-bar intro with drums and a filtered piano riff, then the bass. A 16-bar verse with organ and vocal, an 8-bar pre-chorus where the piano starts hammering, a 16-bar chorus with full piano, diva and brass. An 8 to 16 bar breakdown: kick cut, piano alone in long chords with reverb, snare roll, back to the chorus. Two cycles, a doubled final chorus, a 16-bar drum outro. Length 5 to 6 minutes. The chorus must arrive before the second minute: this is radio and rave house, not an end-of-night track.
italohouse.basse: The bass is in octaves, like the italo disco it descends from: root on the beat, octave above on the offbeat, in eighth notes, on the roots of the progression. A sawtooth or square synth sound, filter fairly open (800 Hz), zero attack, short decay so it bounces. A Juno or M1 bass preset (the famous “Pick Bass”) works. On the choruses, the bass follows the chord changes every two bars. It is louder and brighter than in deep house, with present mids around 500 Hz to blend with the piano. No deep sub: the track has to sound good in a seaside resort club.
etapes: Project at 121 BPM, a clean 909 with a four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hats and a sixteenth-note tambourine.
Write a progression of four major chords over 8 bars and hammer it out on the M1 piano in syncopated eighth notes.
Octave bass in eighth notes on the roots, filter open, short decay.
Sample a diva phrase or a soul a cappella, lock it to the tempo and replay it with pitch variations on the chorus.
Assemble a verse, pre-chorus and chorus with a DJ intro, a piano-only breakdown and a return with crowd cheers, over 5 minutes.
Mix the piano up front in the 1 to 6 kHz range, the vocal with a 2 s hall, and keep a bright, compressed master.
italohouse.mix: The piano is the lead and occupies 1 to 6 kHz with a little brightness added at 8 kHz. Moderate compression (3:1) on the piano so the hammered chords all have the same force. The diva vocal is very far forward, with a clearly audible 2 s hall reverb and an eighth-note delay on the ends of phrases. Kick and bass are clean but not dominant, cut below 40 Hz. Brass and strings spread in stereo, piano slightly left, organ right. On the bus, a gentle compressor and light saturation. The mix must be bright, a little harsh in the highs, like a 1990 CD: do not be afraid of 10 kHz.

outils.pourquoi: Piano 16 or Piano 8 hammering out major chords, Organ 2 on the verses, the Pick Bass preset in octaves: Ride On Time fits almost entirely inside it.
The official reissue, with the same numbered presets; add a chorus and a bright reverb and you have the 1989 Italian piano.
Clean, simple drums under the piano, four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, snare roll at the end of a block; Roland Cloud TR-909 for the plugin version.
The sampler for diva vocals cut from disco a cappellas, sped up and replayed with pitch variations, like Loleatta Holloway with Black Box.
A sawtooth bass preset in octaves with the filter open around 800 Hz, and string pads under the choruses.
To lock a diva phrase to the tempo and replay it varying the pitch key by key, in place of the S1000.
Glue Compressor or equivalent at 3:1 on the piano so every hammered chord has the same force, and a master as bright as a 1990 CD.

reperes: Black Box: Ride On Time (1989): the M1 piano pounded in quarter notes and the sampled diva, the manifesto of Italian piano.
Gino Latino: Welcome (1988): the octave bass inherited from italo disco under major chords, before the style had a name.
El Chico: House Music Lovers (1989): the more club-oriented version, where the piano punctuates rather than dominates.
Barry Can't Swim: How It Feels (2023): Italian piano house reread thirty years later, with modern production and the same euphoria.
italohouse.rythme: A simple, clean 909: four-on-the-floor kick, clap on 2 and 4, closed hats in eighth notes, open on the offbeats. Often a tambourine or a shaker in sixteenth notes for lightness, and a sampled conga loop very low in the mix. The fills are 909 snare rolls on the last bar of a 16-bar block, or a full beat of silence before the chorus. No breakbeat, no heavy percussion: the drums must never cover the piano. On the breakdowns, the clap is often kept alone in reverb with the piano, then the kick comes back on the chorus with crowd cheers.
italohouse.sons: The Korg M1 piano (Piano 16 or Piano 8 preset) hammering out major chords, thirds and sixths, in syncopated eighth notes or pounded quarter notes, with a little chorus and a bright reverb. That is the sound. The M1 organ (Organ 2) in held chords on the verses. A sampled diva vocal, often a soul or disco a cappella sped up and replayed on the sampler with pitch variations, like Loleatta Holloway on Ride On Time. Synth brass stabs, string pads, crowd cheers and sirens at the end of the build-up. A simple synth lead in octaves on the chorus. Everything is bright, colorful, a bit kitsch and fully owned.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar, Get the sound of Blackbox's Ride On Time
Sonicstate, Korg M1: Famous Sounds in Songs
Synthtopia, The Italo Dance House Piano Sound
italohouse.tempo: Between 118 and 124 BPM, slower than the British house it feeds. The feel is straight and joyful, with no swing or almost none, with a piano hammering out eighth-note chords that imposes a pop pulse. What makes the groove is not the drums but the bounce between the piano on the offbeats and the bass on the beats. Think Italian song before you think club: the melodies are in major, the progressions have four chords, the choruses come fast. If your track does not make you want to raise your arms by bar 33, the tempo is right but the writing is not there.

jcore.arrangement: A J-core track is a dense 3 to 5 minute montage, often 4, designed to be played note by note in a rhythm game: an 8 to 16 bar intro with the main melody, a 16 to 32 bar drop, a section change every 4 or 8 bars, a 16-bar breakdown with piano or Vocaloid, a build-up, a denser drop, often a change of tempo or style (a switch to gabber, dubstep, drum and bass), a return to the main theme, a brief ending. DJ intros and outros are short or absent: J-core is listened to and played, it is mixed less. What makes the track work is the main melody: it must be memorable despite the density.
jcore.basse: The offbeat bass of UK hardcore, one note per “and”, a Sylenth1 or Serum sawtooth filtered at 600 Hz, follows chord progressions more complex than in UK hardcore: borrowings from J-pop, seventh chords, frequent key changes. It is often doubled with a sub. On the harder passages, it disappears in favor of a tuned gabber kick tail. On the more dubstep or bass passages, a Serum growl takes its place. J-core bass is therefore several basses that follow one another, and the switch between them happens on beat 1 of a new block, with no transition. Sidechain from the kick everywhere, 5:1 ratio, 70 ms release.
etapes: Tempo 180 BPM. UK hardcore kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats, a dense fill every 4 bars with Beat Repeat.
Write an 8-bar main melody in sixteenth notes, in minor with a seventh chord, played by a supersaw.
Double it with a chiptune lead (Operator, square wave, fast vibrato) an octave above in some passages.
Offbeat bass in Serum following the chords, sub underneath, sidechain everywhere.
Add a Vocaloid voice or a chopped anime sample in 1-bar phrases, and video game sounds as punctuation.
Arrange it as a montage: intro 16, drop 32 with changes every 8, breakdown 16 with piano, build-up, 16-bar gabber passage, return of the theme, ending. Clean, bright mix.
jcore.mix: The J-core mix is clean and very full: lots of elements, each in its own zone. Kick at -4 dB peak. Sidechain on everything melodic. The chiptune leads are high-passed at 1 kHz and narrow in stereo, the supersaws wide. Vocaloid voice compressed hard, 6:1 ratio, with a high-pass at 200 Hz and a short reverb. The dense fills need a limiter on the drum bus so they do not blow up the master. Master: Ozone around -6 to -7 LUFS, very bright, high shelf at +2 dB. Check that the main melody stays audible during the fills: if not, turn down the fills, not the melody.

outils.pourquoi: Synthetic singing voices, Hatsune Miku first and foremost: melody typed in note by note, lyrics in kana, then pitched and chopped in the track.
The dominant DAW of the doujin circles and HARDCORE TANO*C: fast kick edits, Piano roll for rhythm game melodies.
Synthesized gabber kicks, sawtooth leads and screaming basses; Camellia's productions use it massively.
Chorus supersaws and bright arpeggios inherited from UK hardcore and trance, often doubled with a chiptune lead.
Voice and kick stutters at the ends of bars, Grid in thirty-second notes: the rhythm game speed comes from there.
Chiptune leads: pure square wave, no filter, short envelope, plus backup sine kicks with a pitch envelope.
A loud, bright master around -6 LUFS integrated, with Maximizer in IRC IV mode to hold the density of the drop.

reperes: DJ Sharpnel: Pretty Green Onions (2003): the gabber and anime sample strand, the foundation of J-core.
t+pazolite: Oshama Scramble (2016): density and fills, written for rhythm games.
Camellia: Exit This Earth's Atmosphere (2017): style and tempo changes within the same track.
Camellia: Ghost (2018): the main melody that survives a very dense montage.
jcore.rythme: The kick is either a clean, tuned UK hardcore kick or a crushed gabber kick depending on the strand, and many tracks switch from one to the other. On every beat, with bursts of sixteenth notes and pitched rolls. Clap on 2 and 4, snare with a bright reverb. Open hats on the offbeats, closed hats in sixteenth notes, plus hi-hat rolls in thirty-second notes. Breakbeats sometimes. The J-core signature is the very dense fills at the end of each 4-bar block: snare rolls, pitched kicks, retrigs, glitches, all at once. Beat Repeat with Grid at 1/32 and Variation at 50 percent does part of it on its own.
jcore.sons: Supersaw leads as in UK hardcore, but also chiptune leads: square and triangle waves with fast vibrato, sixteenth-note arpeggios, Game Boy sounds (Operator with a square wave and no filter envelope does that). Vocaloid voices, or pitched voices, or anime samples, chopped and repeated. Fast pianos. Synth strings. Screeches and growls on the hard passages. Video game sounds (coin, jump, laser). “Yeah” shouts and countdowns. The palette is huge, and the rule is contrast: a chiptune passage, then a supersaw passage, then a gabber passage, each with its own sounds.
jcore.tempo: J-core covers a wide range, from 170 to 200 BPM for the happy hardcore and UK hardcore strand, up to 220-250 for DJ Sharpnel's gabber and speedcore strand. Camellia often changes tempo within the same track. What sets it apart from UK hardcore is density: more notes, very fast sixteenth-note melodies, section changes every 4 or 8 bars, and writing designed for rhythm games (osu!, beatmania) where every note counts. No swing. Program at 180 BPM, with a thirty-second-note grid to be safe. The feel is that of anime pop that has had too much coffee.

jerseyclub.arrangement: 2 to 3 minutes, short-video format. The kick pattern arrives from the first bar or after 4 bars of vocal. 8-bar blocks: the vocal chop changes, the bed squeak comes in, the kick stops for a beat. A 4-bar breakdown with the vocal alone, then the kick comes back in a thirty-second-note roll. No long build-up, no festival drop: the track is a plateau of energy with cuts. Often built like a remix: the original's chorus in hiccups, the verse in club pattern. End on the vocal alone or a hard cut. Think of the dancer filming their feet.
jerseyclub.basse: The kick is often the bass: a short 808 with a 200 to 300 ms tail is enough. If you add a sub, a short sine that follows the kick pattern on beats 1 and 3 only, so it does not weigh down the bounce. The key is taken from the remixed vocal sample. No melodic bassline: the low end must stay light and dry so the triplet kicks remain readable. Sidechain the sub from the kick with a 40 ms release. One exception: remixes of rap tracks sometimes keep the original 808, slid and tuned, under the club pattern.
etapes: Set Ableton or FL Studio to 137 BPM, program the kick on steps 1, 5, 9, 12 and 15 of the sixteenth-note grid.
Layer three kicks: sub, mids, click, and put a clap on 2 and 4.
Add a bed squeak pitched to the key in a syncopated pattern against the kicks.
Chop an a cappella into syllables in Simpler and turn them into sixteenth-note hiccups.
Arrange in 8-bar blocks, a 4-bar breakdown with the vocal alone, the kick returning in a roll.
Mix the kick up front and mono, vocal behind, light gimmicks, master around -6 LUFS, test on a phone.
jerseyclub.mix: Kick up front, around -4 dB peak, the three layers aligned in phase and cut below 35 Hz, mono. Vocal chop just behind, 4:1 compression, high-pass at 200 Hz, a little brightness at 8 kHz. Bed squeak and gimmicks cut below 400 Hz, panned slightly. Dry clap, no reverb. No invasive sub: the low end stays clean and short. A clipper or a limiter with 3 to 4 dB of reduction, target around -6 LUFS. Check on a phone: Jersey club lives on tiny speakers, the kick must stay audible through its mids and its click, not its sub.

outils.pourquoi: The Newark DAW: kicks on steps 1, 5, 9, 12 and 15 of the sixteenth-note grid, rolls in thirty-second notes.
A short 200 to 300 ms kick in three layers, sub, mids, click, plus a clap on 2 and 4. Common 808 samples.
Bed squeaks, DJ shouts, water drops, R'n'B and rap a cappellas to chop, the genre's raw material.
Battery and Maschine kits with drums and vocal one-shots already in the Jersey bounce.
Chop an a cappella into syllables and make sixteenth-note hiccups, bed squeak pitched to the key.
A short sub on beats 1 and 3 only, or the original 808 of a rap remix, slid and tuned.
In the spirit of the early Brick Bandits, to play the chops and the kick pattern on the pads.

reperes: DJ Sliink: Vibrate (2013): the kick pattern and the vocal hiccups, the model of the 2010s.
Cookiee Kawaii: Vibe (2019): the viral breakthrough, original singing over the club mechanics, short format.
UNIIQU3: Microdosing (2018): the more produced version, layered kicks and bed squeak up front.
Lil Uzi Vert: Just Wanna Rock (2022): Jersey club in mainstream rap, kick and chop in the foreground.
jerseyclub.rythme: The kick pattern is the signature: on a sixteenth-note grid, kicks on steps 1, 5, 9, 12 and 15, that is beats 1, 2 and 3, then the “a” of 3 and the “and” of 4. This scheme, given by several Jersey club guides, creates the triplet bounce at the end of the bar. Layer three kicks: one for the sub, one for the mids, one for the click. Clap or snare on 2 and 4, sometimes only on 4. The bed squeak, a sampled creaking bed, plays a syncopated pattern against the kicks, often pitched to the key. Hats in eighth notes, kick rolls in thirty-second notes for the fills.
jerseyclub.sons: The bed squeak, a sampled creak that comes from the intro of a Trillville track produced by Lil Jon, played as a rhythmic pattern. Chopped vocal chops: one syllable repeated in hiccups over sixteenth notes, a word cut into three, a “hey” or a breath. Water drops, gun-cocking sounds, a DJ shout, a crowd “yeah”. Remixed rap and R'n'B a cappellas, since Jersey club is often a remix. FL Studio and Ableton, with an 808 kit and an MPC in spirit. Short, dry, funny sounds, with no reverb. The track must stay recognizable if you cut all the gimmicks.
sources: Orphiq, What Is Jersey Club? Sound, BPM, and Kick Pattern (orphiq.com)
Beats To Rap On, How to Make a Jersey Club Beat (beatstorapon.com)
sourcesOutils: Internet Tattoo, How to Make Jersey Club: Essential Plugins and Samples
Orphiq, What Is Jersey Club? Sound, BPM, and Kick Pattern
Splice Blog, UNIIQU3 on Sampling and the Sonic Identity of Jersey Club
jerseyclub.tempo: Between 130 and 140 BPM, 137 or 138 is a good starting point according to current production guides. The feel is bouncy: the triplet kicks and the vocal hiccups give a sway that Baltimore club does not have. No programmed swing, the grid is straight, but the kick pattern creates the bounce. What changes compared with the Baltimore club it descends from: the kick replaces the break as the engine, the vocal samples are chopped into rhythmic hiccups rather than shouted, and the format is short, designed for dancing on video. The track should make you want to move your feet within 2 seconds.

juke.arrangement: Frequent and cutting. An 8-bar intro with syncopated kick and hats, the chopped vocal arrives at bar 9, the triplet toms at bar 17. A change every 4 or 8 bars: new syllable, new kick pattern, rising toms, a beat of silence. An 8-bar breakdown with the vocal and the toms without kick, then a brutal return. A second half with a denser kick pattern or a lead. Length 3 to 5 minutes, hard ending. The track is a battle tool: every 8-bar section must give the dancers something new to follow. Juke tracks follow one another in a set through hard cuts, not long blends.
juke.basse: The 808 sub: an 808 kick with the decay at maximum, tuned to the root, playing a two- or three-note line in syncopation, with glides between the notes. The bass and the kick are often the same instrument, the short kick being an 808 with no decay and the bass the same 808 with a long decay. Or a sine sub with glide. Notes: root, fifth, octave below, in a 2-bar pattern. Saturate it slightly so the sub is audible on small speakers. No sidechain: the two blend. The bass does not follow a harmony, it is rhythmic, in dialogue with the triplet toms.
etapes: Project at 155 BPM, a short 808 kick in a syncopated 2-bar pattern, clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hats.
Program three 808 toms in eighth-note triplets (1/12 grid) answering the kick, over 1 or 2 beats per bar.
808 sub with a long decay and glide, a two-note syncopated line, saturated.
Sample a rap or R&B phrase, slice it into syllables and replay them in sixteenth notes with stutters.
Build 4 minutes in 8-bar blocks with a change in each block and a vocal and toms breakdown without kick.
Mix dry and loud, unfiltered sub, compressed vocal, toms slightly spread, master at -7 LUFS.
juke.mix: A loud, dry mix, dominated by the 808 sub and the vocal. The sub holds the low end alone, unfiltered, slightly saturated to come through on small speakers. The short kick is up front, with a click. Dry clap and toms, no reverb. The chopped vocal compressed hard (6:1) with a very short delay on some stutters. The triplet toms spread slightly in stereo for readability. No space, no long reverb. Master saturated and limited to -7 LUFS, with a little clipping. Check that the triplets stay readable against the sixteenth notes: if it turns to mush, lower the hats and cut the toms below 150 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: Short syncopated kick, 808 sub with the decay at maximum and glide, triplet toms: three roles for a single machine, almost always as samples.
The South Side Chicago DAW for programming triplets on the 1/12 grid and stacking binary kicks against ternary toms.
The native slicer to cut a rap or R&B phrase into syllables and replay them in sixteenth notes with stutters.
DJ Spinn and DJ Rashad's sampler-sequencer for chopping vocals and playing the 808s on the pads, before and alongside the computer.
Banks of already tuned 808 kicks, toms, claps and hats, loaded into the step sequencer; synthesis has no place here.
In Slice mode, the equivalent of Slicex for those who work in Live: one syllable per key, repeated over a beat.
Chopped vocal compressed at 6:1 and 808 sub slightly saturated to come through on small speakers, master limited to -7 LUFS.

reperes: DJ Slugo: Godzilla (2003): the triplet 808 toms against a syncopated kick, the layering that makes juke.
DJ Clent: Back Up Off Me (2004): the vocal chopped into stutters over 2 bars, the battle tool in its barest form.
DJ Gant-Man: Juke Dat Girl (2005): juke becoming an anthem, with a chanted phrase and a sliding 808 sub.
Traxman: Footworkin On Air (2012): the shift from juke to footwork, soul samples and already more abstract rhythms.
juke.rythme: A short 808 kick in a syncopated pattern: for example on the 1, the “and” of 2, the 3 and the “a” of 3, with variations every 2 bars. 808 clap on 2 and 4, or only on 3 for a half-time effect. 808 hats in sixteenth notes, sometimes in eighth-note triplets over 2 beats. The 808 toms in triplets: three toms at different pitches playing triplet rolls over 1 or 2 beats, answering the kick. Rim and cowbell in syncopation. No snare roll: the toms act as fills. This layering of binary sixteenth notes (kick, hats) and triplets (toms) is the signature. Program the triplets with the grid at 1/12 in FL Studio or Ableton.
juke.sons: The chopped vocal samples: a rap, R&B or ghetto house phrase cut into syllables and replayed in sixteenth notes or triplets, with fast repetitions of the same syllable (stutter) over one beat. The DAW's sampler (FL Studio's Slicer, Simpler in slices) is the tool. Short synth stabs, often a minor chord or a single note, in syncopation. A simple monophonic square-wave synth lead. Shouts, sirens, video game sounds. A rare pad on the breakdowns. Juke is made in FL Studio with 808 banks and samples: no elaborate synthesis, no sophisticated effects, just chopping and repetition.
juke.tempo: Between 150 and 160 BPM, the zone where ghetto house turns into juke. The feel is nervous and syncopated: the kick is no longer a steady four-on-the-floor, it plays sixteenth-note patterns with gaps, and the triplet 808 toms create a second grid on top. The “3 against 2” feeling is constant. No swing on the grid, everything is straight, the syncopation comes from placement. Think in 2-bar cycles for the kicks and 1-bar cycles for the chopped vocals. At 155 BPM, a bar lasts 1.5 seconds: changes must be frequent, every 4 or 8 bars, or the dancers lose interest.

jumpstyle.arrangement: The tracks are short, 3 to 4 minutes, in blocks of 8 and 16 bars: an 8 to 16 bar intro with kick and bass, melody over 16 bars, an 8-bar breakdown with the melody alone or a voice, the kick returns without a complicated build-up, a reverse cymbal is enough, melody over 16 bars, a second melody or a variation, a short breakdown, return, an 8-bar ending. No 48-bar breakdown as in hardstyle: the dancer does not want to wait. What makes the track useful is the repeated melody and the kick that almost never stops. Think of YouTube videos: the track must be danceable from the tenth second.
jumpstyle.basse: A light reverse bass, inherited from hardstyle, on every offbeat: shorter (one eighth note) and less saturated than in hardstyle, often a simple reversed tail sample with an 80 ms attack. Or a classic offbeat bass, a square wave filtered at 500 Hz, short note, as in bouncy techno. In both cases, it sits on the root and follows the melody's chord changes, often only root and fifth. No separate sub: the kick carries the low end. The kick-bass bounce at 145 BPM is exactly the rhythm of the dance, alternating jumps and kicks. If your bass is too complex, the dance does not work.
etapes: Tempo 145 BPM. Hardstyle kick shortened to 150 ms, dry, on every beat. Clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats.
Light reverse bass: reversed kick tail, cut to one eighth note, 80 ms attack, on every offbeat, same note as the kick.
An 8-note melody in eighth notes in Massive, sawtooth with unison, repeated over 8 bars.
Add short chord stabs on the offbeats and a one-word vocal sample at the start of each 8-bar block.
An 8-bar breakdown with the melody alone, the kick returning with a simple reverse cymbal.
Arrange over 3 minutes 30: intro 16, melody 16, breakdown 8, return 16, variation 16, breakdown 8, return, ending 8. Dry mix, kick up front.
jumpstyle.mix: The jumpstyle mix is simple and dry, with the kick up front: -3 dB peak, a well-present tok thanks to a +2 dB high shelf at 5 kHz on the kick. Reverse bass 4 dB below, in mono. Melody in moderate stereo with a short reverb (1 second) and a low-level eighth-note delay. Clap with a brief reverb. No complicated multiband, no aggressive sidechain: the kick and the bass do not overlap. Master: limiter around -7 LUFS. The track must sound clear on computer speakers, that is where it was listened to.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of Patrick Jumpen and Jeckyll & Hyde: dry kick, blocky melody in the Piano roll, a track wrapped up in three minutes for YouTube.
Simple sawtooth leads with unison, and the light reverse bass: a reversed sawtooth, a low-pass filter that opens over one beat.
A short, dry 909 kick, very lightly distorted, at 140-150 BPM: it is simplified hardstyle, the kick has to leave room to jump.
Simple epic supersaw melodies, a high octave, two chords, for the chorus everyone remembers.
Ready-to-use dance pads and plucks, typical of the fast-moving Belgian and Dutch productions of 2007.
A little curve on the kick to harden it without drowning it: jumpstyle wants a clean kick, not a gabber kick.

reperes: Da Boy Tommy: Candyman (2000): the Belgian forerunner, dry kick and blocky melody.
Patrick Jumpen: Holiday (2007): YouTube jumpstyle, simple melody, kick and reverse bass without variation.
Jeckyll and Hyde: Frozen Flame (2007): the more melodic version, with a real synth chorus.
Scooter: Jumping All Over the World (2007): the commercial takeover, the same bounce with an MC voice.
jumpstyle.rythme: The jumpstyle kick: a shortened, drier hardstyle kick, with a well-defined tok and a short tail, 150 ms, less distorted. On every beat, without exception, without rolls, without variation: the dancer counts on it. Clap on 2 and 4, fairly dry. Open hats on the offbeats, discreet. Closed hats in eighth notes. That is all, or almost. The only fills are reverse cymbals and one-beat cuts before section changes. Some tracks add half-time kicks (on 1 and 3) in the intro to mark an entrance, but once the dancing starts, the kick is on every beat until the end. Regularity is the technique.
jumpstyle.sons: Simple blocky melodies: a Massive sawtooth lead, with a little unison, playing a 4 to 8 note melody in eighth notes, in minor or major, repeated over 8 bars. Short synth chords on the offbeats, like softened stabs. Spoken or sampled voices: a word, a slogan, a shout. Pianos sometimes, in the style of Belgian dance. Sampled trumpet or organ sounds. A very softened hoover occasionally. The vocabulary is that of 2000s European commercial dance, put over a hardstyle kick: a melody you memorize in 4 seconds, bright sounds, nothing aggressive.
jumpstyle.tempo: Jumpstyle is played between 140 and 150 BPM, often 145, a little slower than the hardstyle it comes from. This tempo is the dance's: each beat corresponds to a jump, and the offbeat to the landing, so the kick and the offbeat bass must be perfectly steady. What sets it apart from hardstyle is simplicity: no dramatic breakdown, no screech, only the kick, the bass and a blocky melody. No swing, no velocity variation. Program at 145 BPM, eighth-note grid: the whole of jumpstyle fits into eighth notes. If you are wondering whether an element is too simple, it is not.

jumpup.arrangement: A jump-up track lasts 4 to 5 minutes, shorter than classic DnB, and follows a strict club format. A 32-bar intro with the vocal sample and the hi-hats, no bass. An 8-bar build-up with a roll. A 32-bar drop: beat plus bass, nothing else, or almost. A 16-bar breakdown with the vocal and a pad. A second 32-bar drop, often with a second bass or a pattern “switch” halfway through. A 32-bar outro. The drop must arrive before 1 minute 30 seconds: DJs mix fast. The vocal phrase comes back before each drop, like a chorus.
jumpup.basse: The jump-up bass is monophonic and carries the whole track. 1990s version (Zinc, Hype): a filtered square or saw on the Nord Lead, with the cutoff following a fast envelope, played in quarter or eighth notes on the root and the fifth, sometimes with an octave glissando. 2010s version (Hazard, Macky Gee): an FM bass or a wavetable in Serum with an LFO synced to an eighth or quarter note on the cutoff, which gives the bouncing “wobble”. In both cases, a separate sine sub below 60 Hz holds the note. The bass plays on the offbeats, in call and response with the kick: kick on the beat, bass on the “and”.
etapes: Set Ableton to 174 BPM. Program a martial two-step: short 909 kick, cracking snare, eighth-note hi-hats at fixed velocity.
Create a bass on Serum or Operator: saw or FM, low-pass filter with an eighth-note LFO on the cutoff.
Write the line on the offbeats, root and fifth, in call and response with the kick.
Add a sine sub below 60 Hz playing the same notes, and a hip-hop MC sample to launch the drop.
Arrange intro 32, build-up 8, drop 32, breakdown 16, second drop 32 with a bass switch, outro 32.
Compress the bass hard, put a clipper on the master, and test on a phone.
jumpup.mix: The jump-up mix is loud, simple and centered. The bass is the loudest thing in the track, high-passed at 80 Hz and compressed hard (8:1 ratio, 1 ms attack), with the sine sub just below, mono. The kick is sidechained to the bass or the other way around depending on the school, but either way they never play at the same time. The snare is boosted at 1 kHz and 6 kHz, with no reverb. Few elements, so no conflicts: each sound has its own band. The master is very loud, -5 to -6 LUFS, with a clipper before the limiter. Check that the bass comes through on a phone: jump-up is also played on tiny speakers.

outils.pourquoi: The monophonic trampoline bass: saw, resonant filter, fast envelope, pitch bend; it is the True Playaz sound.
Simple Apache breaks, hip-hop samples and hook vocals chopped on the sampler for the DJ-calibrated drops.
Super Sharp Shooter and the early Aphrodite records were made on this tracker, with two Amiga 1200s in parallel.
The sequencer of the Ganja and Frontline scene: intro structure, 32-bar drop, bass switch every 16 bars.
The modern jump-up bass: saw or square, 24 dB filter, LFO synced on the cutoff, short notes and Hazard-style pitch bend.
A sine sub under the main bass, locked to the same note, for weight on a club system.
Simple, effective breaks, scratches and rapper vocals; modern jump-up packs provide kicks and snares already calibrated.

reperes: DJ Zinc: Super Sharp Shooter (1996): the rap sample, the bouncing bass, the record that defines True Playaz jump-up.
Aphrodite: Style From The Dark Side (1997): trampoline bass and a simple break, the pure format.
Hazard: Machete (2007): the FM bass jumping from one offbeat to the next, the 2000s revival.
DJ Hazard: Mr Happy (2008): the calibrated drop, silence then bass, the track every dancefloor demands.
jumpup.rythme: The simple, effective breaks of the brief: kick on the 1 and the “and” of 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth or sixteenth notes at constant velocity. The kick is a short, dry 909 or a kick sample from a break, the snare is loud, cracking, with a peak at 1 kHz and lots of attack. A hip-hop break (often Apache or a break from Ultimate Breaks and Beats) can play in the background, pitched and compressed, for the hip-hop side. The fills are sixteenth-note snare rolls on the last bar before the drop, with a reversed crash cymbal. The beat almost never changes: it is the bass that moves.
jumpup.sons: The brief cites the Akai S3000, the Nord Lead and Cubase: the True Playaz studio. The Nord Lead gives the bass (saw, 24 dB low-pass filter, 30% resonance, filter envelope with a 200 ms decay). The hip-hop samples come from American rap records: an MC shouting a phrase, a scratch, a brass stab. The DJ-calibrated drops of the brief mean a clear vocal phrase before each drop, a noise build-up, and a beat of silence before the bass. Add sirens, laser sounds and crowd cheers. In Ableton, Operator in FM mode (1:1 ratio, modulated feedback) or Serum with an LFO on the cutoff make the modern bass.
jumpup.tempo: Jump-up runs at 170 BPM for the Ganja and True Playaz era, and 174 to 175 for the 2010s wave. The feel is a bounce: everything is designed so the bass jumps from one beat to the next. The two-step is simple, without ghost notes, almost martial, and the bass occupies the offbeats. No swing. What sets jump-up apart from the rest of DnB is its deliberate simplicity: a single bass pattern, a single beat, and a vocal hook that launches the drop. If your track needs more than ten tracks, you are doing too much. Jump-up is direct, short and loud.

jungle.arrangement: A 1994 jungle track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and is structured like a sound system tune. A 16 to 32 bar intro with the vocal sample, a pad and fragments of the break. First drop at bar 33: full break and sub at the same time, with no build-up. The first pass holds for 32 bars, then a 16-bar breakdown where only the vocal remains, with a final roll. A second drop with a different break or a more complex chopping pattern. The track often contains a “switch”: the bass changes note or pattern in the middle of a section, without warning. The ending is a 16-bar break-only outro for the DJ.
jungle.basse: Jungle bass is a sound system sub: a pure sine or an Operator triangle between 40 and 55 Hz, played slowly. Classic pattern: root on beat 1 for a dotted quarter note, silence, then a drop to the fourth below on the “and” of 3, like a slowed-down roots reggae line. Two notes per bar are often enough. Add an octave above with a very soft filtered square for small systems, and a whole-tone downward pitch bend on the long notes, a dub “wobble” effect. Since the break's kick is light in the low end, the sub fills the whole space below 80 Hz without sidechain. Cut it cleanly before each roll so the drop can breathe.
etapes: Set Ableton to 160 BPM. Import the Amen and a second break, Slice to MIDI by transients.
Rewrite the break changing the pattern every 2 bars: shifted snare, double kicks, a roll on bar 8.
Create an Operator sub around 45 Hz on a two-notes-per-bar reggae pattern, with a downward pitch bend on the long notes.
Slow down a ragga a cappella in Texture mode and cut it into phrases for the intro and the breakdowns.
Add a sampled piano stab one bar in four and a sound system siren on the transitions.
Arrange intro 32, drop 32, breakdown 16, drop 32, outro 16, and saturate the breaks bus before mixing the sub underneath.
jungle.mix: The breaks go in the foreground, saturated and compressed hard: a fast compressor (attack 0.5 ms, release 40 ms, ratio 8:1) on each break, then a shared bus with a Glue Compressor and a little Overdrive at 20%. Filter each break differently: the main one full, the second high-passed at 400 Hz, the third band-passed around 2 kHz. The sub stays alone below 80 Hz, mono, uncompressed. The ragga vocals need a high-pass at 200 Hz and a dotted-eighth delay with 30% feedback. Do not chase cleanliness: a little noise, a light downsample (Redux 12 bits) and a master at -8 LUFS with a gentle limiter give the sound of the era.

outils.pourquoi: The heart of jungle: Amen chopped and time-stretched to 160 BPM, ragga vocals made grainy by its 12-bit stretch.
The tracker of Aphrodite, Omni Trio and Urban Shakedown: breaks typed in at the sixteenth note, two Amigas side by side for more tracks.
The MIDI sequencer driving the S950 when the budget went beyond the Amiga; note-by-note editing of the Amen slices.
A kick doubled under the Amen for weight on a sound system; a 909 sample or D16 Drumazon is enough.
Slice to MIDI by transients on the Amen, then rewriting the slices; it is the modern equivalent of Akai chopping, with Redux behind it for grain.
A reggae sine sub in long notes under the breaks, an octave below the played bass, with a little Overdrive on the bus.
On the bus of the stacked breaks, to make them breathe together before an Overdrive at 20%.
An emulation of the Yamaha CS01 with cheap built-in effects, perfect for an old school wobble bass and sound system sirens.

reperes: Shy FX: Original Nuttah (1994): UK Apache's voice, the sub falling in dotted quarter notes, the Amen changing every two bars.
Remarc: RIP (1994): the craziest Amen chopping of the era, every bar is a new pattern.
M-Beat: Incredible (1994): General Levy on the mic, the jungle formula entering the UK charts.
Nia Archives: Baianá (2022): jungle revisited, clean breaks and a modern sub, the 1994 structure held with today's tools.
jungle.rythme: The dissected Amen is the main subject. Cut the break into 16 slices per bar in Simpler or with Slice to MIDI, then rewrite it: the break's kick on beat 1, the snare on beats 2 and 4, but also a snare shifted one sixteenth note before beat 4, and pairs of fast kicks on the “and” of 3. Change the pattern every 2 bars: that is what Remarc and Shy FX did. Use two or three breaks stacked at different pitches (Amen, Think, Hot Pants), each filtered differently. No four-on-the-floor 909 kick: the break's kick is enough, doubled if needed with a short sampled kick. Thirty-second-note snare rolls announce the drops.
jungle.sons: The brief cites the Akai S950, the Amiga, the TR-909 and Cubase: a bedroom studio. The S950's time-stretch on the ragga vocals gives that grainy texture: in Ableton, warp in Texture mode (Grain Size 40 ms, Flux 20%) on a slowed-down dancehall a cappella. The vocals are snippets of Jamaican toasting, sound system sirens and crowd cheers. Add piano or brass stabs sampled from reggae records, played one bar in four. A single synth is enough: a thin pad on Analog for the intros. When in doubt, remove the synth and add a sample. Jungle is music made from records, not keyboards.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (Slicing Breakbeats Like Nia Archives, jungle bass with BA-1, Make Your Own Jungle FX)
jungle.tempo: Jungle settles between 155 and 165 BPM, with 160 as the center of gravity in 1994. That is slower than the drum and bass that would follow, and the groove sways more: the breaks are played in full, with their original swing, and you feel the drummer behind them. The feel comes from the coexistence of two speeds: the break running in sixteenth notes, and the reggae bass falling in dotted quarter or half notes, as if it were at 80 BPM. This half tempo for the bass and the vocals is what makes jungle danceable for a sound system crowd. Keep this double meaning in mind with every decision.

kosmische.arrangement: A kosmische piece takes up one side of a record, 18 to 22 minutes, and is built like a journey: 3 to 5 minutes of pads and noises without a pulse, then the sequence appears, gently, filtered. It opens up gradually over 5 minutes, a second sequence layers on top, a Moog lead melody comes over it. Halfway through, the sequence changes key or pattern, which renews attention. The return to calm takes another 4 minutes. For an 8-minute version playable in a set, keep this curve but compress it: 2 minutes of intro, sequence at bar 33, second sequence at bar 65, key change at bar 97, a 2-minute exit. Never cut abruptly: everything comes in and goes out through filter and volume.
kosmische.basse: The bass is a low sequence repeating one or two notes with a Moog timbre: sawtooth, 24 dB filter with a little resonance, fast filter envelope. In Analog, choose a sawtooth, Filter LP4, cutoff at 300 Hz, resonance 25 percent, filter envelope with a 200 ms decay and a modulation amount of 40 percent. Program it in eighth notes on a low D or A (D1, A1), and shift the key by minor thirds every 32 bars to give the impression that the landscape is turning. The bass and the percussion sequence share the same clock, so the bass needs no sidechain. Add a light Chorus to widen it, but keep the sub in mono.
etapes: Program an 8-step sixteenth-note sequence in Analog, sawtooth, resonant filter, on a single note, at 70 BPM.
Add an eighth-note bass sequence on D1, same clock, and let them run for 4 minutes while automating the cutoff.
Lay down Mellotron or filtered choir pads, very wide, with a slight pitch wobble.
Send the sequence into a dotted-quarter tape echo and a 2-second reverb.
Build the journey: 2 minutes of intro without a pulse, sequence, second sequence, key change, long exit.
Mix with a slow Auto Pan on the pads, cut 300 Hz, gentle Saturator on the master.
kosmische.mix: The mix must be deep and dark, with very wide stereo on the pads and a well-centered sequence. Apply a slow Auto Pan (0.1 Hz, 30 percent) on the pads so they breathe. The sequences get the tape echo and a medium hall reverb (2 seconds). Compress little: a Glue Compressor on the master with 1 to 2 dB of reduction is enough. The spectrum is crowded in the low mids (200 to 500 Hz) because of the organs and the Mellotron: cut them by 3 dB where the bass plays. Gentle tape saturation on the whole mix brings the cohesion of the 1974 Virgin records. The final level stays low, around -14 LUFS, because the dynamics between the intro and full flight are part of the journey.

outils.pourquoi: The heart of Phaedra: eight steps in sixteenth notes, oscillators drifting as they warm up; Behringer sells a Eurorack copy, Arturia Modular V emulates it.
The tape keyboard of choirs, strings and flutes that makes the pads on Rubycon; Arturia Mellotron V or a Mellotron sample pack in Simpler.
Schulze's first synth: filter sweeps, ring modulation, gliding oscillators, for the cosmic noises of the pulseless introductions.
The organ holding the chords under the sequences with Schulze and Tangerine Dream, often with vibrato, to be replaced by a chorused organ sample.
The software emulation of the Moog modular and its sequencer: program an 8-step line, 24 dB filter, and automate the cutoff over minutes.
For the melodic sequence and the bass: sawtooth, Filter LP4 at 300 Hz, resonance 25 percent, filter envelope with a 200 ms decay.
The software Minimoog for the lead melody that comes over the sequences: two detuned oscillators, glide, played by hand without quantizing.
The tape echo that turns each sequence into a rhythmic web: tape mode, triplet or dotted quarter, feedback 50 percent, high-pass in the loop.

reperes: Tangerine Dream: Phaedra (1974): the Moog sequencer that goes out of tune and becomes landscape, the gradual entry of the pulse.
Tangerine Dream: Rubycon Part One (1975): the Mellotron pads and the sequence that opens up over ten minutes.
Klaus Schulze: Mindphaser (1976): the slowness of the intro then the loose drums joining the sequencer.
Cluster: Sowiesoso (1976): the soft, melodic, short version, with discreet drum machines.
kosmische.rythme: There are no drums on most Berlin School records before 1977. The rhythm is the sequence itself: an 8-note line in sixteenth notes played by an oscillator with a short envelope, 150 ms decay, which acts as melodic percussion. Make it with Analog or with a Moog plugin (Arturia Mini V, or Operator with sawtooths), resonant low-pass filter at 800 Hz, and automate the cutoff over 32 bars to open and close the sequence. Layer a second 8-step sequence at a different rate (eighth-note triplets) to create crossed patterns. When drums do appear, as with Schulze after 1976, they are played loosely, with toms, and stay discreet behind the machine.
kosmische.sons: The brief gives the Moog modular and its sequencer, the EMS Synthi AKS, the Mellotron, Farfisa organs and tape echo. The Mellotron, a keyboard that plays back tapes of choir or strings, is the signature of the pads: use a Mellotron pack or any choir sample run through a low-pass filter at 4 kHz with a slight pitch wobble (LFO on pitch at 0.3 Hz, very low). The Farfisa organ holds the chords, often with vibrato. The Synthi AKS produces the cosmic noises: filter sweeps, gliding oscillators, ring modulation. The tape echo, set to a triplet or a dotted quarter note, turns each sequence into a rhythmic web: Echo in tape mode, feedback 50 percent, high-pass filter in the loop.
kosmische.tempo: What changes compared with krautrock: no more drummer, the pulse comes from an analog sequencer. The tempo is often slow on the surface, 60 to 90 BPM, but the sequencer runs in sixteenth notes, which gives a felt pulse of 120 to 180 pulses per minute. The Moog 960 sequencer had eight steps: so program sequences of 8 sixteenth notes, not 16, and let them run. The feel is perfectly mechanical, without swing, but the tempo drifts: analog oscillators and clocks moved slightly. Automate your project tempo by plus or minus 1 BPM over minutes, or add a very slow LFO on the pitch. Phaedra was recorded with a Moog that went out of tune during the take.

krautrock.arrangement: A krautrock track lasts 6 to 12 minutes and evolves by accumulation, not through marked sections. Lay down the drums and the bass from the first bar and never remove them, or almost never. Add an element every 16 or 32 bars: the organ, then the guitar, then the synth noises, then a second guitar. Halfway through, remove everything except drums and bass for 8 bars, then bring everything back at once. The ending is often a fade or a collapse of slowed-down tape. To make it playable by a DJ, keep a 16-bar intro with drums alone and an identical ending. Faust's pieces, more deconstructed, splice together fragments recorded separately: you can imitate this by cutting the track into two different moods linked by a noise.
krautrock.basse: Krautrock bass is an electric bass played in eighth or quarter notes on a single note, sometimes two, for minutes. It is the hypnotic pillar: Hallogallo holds almost the entire track on a single chord. To produce it, use a sampled bass (Electric Bass in the Ableton packs, or Trilian in Fingered mode) on an E (E1) or a D (D1), in eighth notes at a constant velocity of 90, with a note that rises to the fifth or the minor seventh every 8 bars. Add an Amp in Bass mode, a light Compressor at 4:1 ratio with 10 ms attack, and a low-pass cut at 3 kHz for roundness. The bass and the kick must blend, not duck: no sidechain.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM and finger-drum the motorik pattern on an acoustic kit for 8 bars, without quantizing at 100 percent.
Record a bass on a single note in eighth notes, with a note change every 8 bars.
Lay down an organ held on two chords and a guitar or a guitar sample into a tape echo.
Create a Synthi sound with Analog: resonant self-oscillating filter, cutoff automated by hand.
Stretch everything over 8 minutes, adding an element every 16 bars and a drop-out halfway through.
Mix with Glue Compressor on the drums, Saturator on the master, a shared plate reverb.
krautrock.mix: The mix aims for the sound of a band in a room in 1972: little deep low end, dense mids and fairly wide stereo. Run the drum bus through Drum Buss with a little Drive and the Boom parameter at zero, then visible bus compression (Glue Compressor, ratio 4:1, attack 10 ms, release Auto, 3 to 4 dB of reduction) to pump gently. Tape saturation on the master, Saturator in Analog Clip mode or a tape plugin, rounds off the transients. Cut everything below 40 Hz. The reverb is short and everywhere: a shared send to a 1.2-second Reverb, Plate type. The final level stays modest, around -12 LUFS, with dynamics. A light tape noise floor over the whole mix is welcome.

outils.pourquoi: The combo organ held in open chords on Hallogallo and with Can; recreate it with an organ sample in Chorus-Ensemble and Amp, or Arturia Farfisa V.
The tape recorder Conny Plank used as a delay: a makeshift tape echo on Rother's guitar, today Ableton Echo in tape mode.
The plate in Plank's studio, set short on almost everything: a 1.2-second Plate-type Reverb on a shared return is enough.
The gliding, hissing electronic noises of Cluster and Harmonia: self-oscillating filter and joystick, to imitate with Analog and drawn automation.
The synth for the Synthi noises and the first pads: one oscillator, resonant self-oscillating filter, cutoff automated by hand over 32 bars.
A dry acoustic kit, finger-drummed without quantizing at 100 percent, for Dinger's motorik or Liebezeit's tribal playing.
The tape echo on the guitar and the organ: tape mode, dotted quarter note, feedback 50 percent, with a slow Phaser behind it for Plank's homemade phasing.
The electric bass in eighth notes on a single note for ten minutes: Fingered mode, constant velocity 90, into Amp in Bass mode and a 4:1 Compressor.

reperes: Neu!: Hallogallo (1972): motorik in its purest form, ten minutes on one chord, the guitar coming and going in the echo.
Can: Vitamin C (1972): Jaki Liebezeit's drumming, dry and tribal funk, the bass that does not move.
Harmonia: Watussi (1974): motorik meeting Cluster's synths, the primitive drum machine.
Faust: It's a Rainy Day Sunshine Girl (1972): stubborn repetition and studio collage.
krautrock.rythme: The motorik pattern is simple: kick on 1, 2, 3 and 4 plus an extra kick on the “and” of 4, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hat in continuous eighth notes. All the richness comes from the consistency of the hi-hat and the velocity variations. To reproduce it without a drummer, take a sampled acoustic kit (Drum Rack, Session kit or a 70s kit), finger-drum the pattern on a pad or a keyboard rather than with the mouse, then keep the imperfections. Add a second open hi-hat track that comes in by 8-bar phrases. With Can, the playing is more percussive and tribal: add congas and a rimshot snare. No clap, no 808: it is a drum kit in a room, with two ambient mics.
krautrock.sons: The brief talks about organ, Moog modular, EMS Synthi AKS, tape and tape echo. The organ is central: a Farfisa or a Vox Continental held in open chords, reproduced with Electric or with a combo organ sample run through a Chorus-Ensemble and an Amp. The Synthi AKS gives the electronic noises that glide and hiss: recreate them with Analog, one oscillator, a self-oscillating filter, and a hand-drawn cutoff automation. The guitar, often processed with tape delays and phasing, can be imitated with a sustained guitar sample, Echo in tape mode at a dotted quarter note and a slow Phaser. Conny Plank is the producer who defined the sound: plate reverb and short echoes on everything, a slightly dirty color.
krautrock.tempo: Motorik runs between 120 and 140 BPM, straight, without swing, but played by a human drummer: Klaus Dinger in Neu! or Jaki Liebezeit in Can. What creates the trance is consistency over ten minutes with micro-variations in intensity, never a spectacular fill. In production, keep a strict grid at 130 BPM and add 4 to 8 ms of random delay on the hi-hats with Velocity and Note Length, or the Groove Pool at only 20 percent. The feel must stay forward, almost rushed. Some tracks, like Vitamin C, lean instead toward a dry funk at 100 BPM with drums that stay on the one. Pick one of the two camps: motorik or broken funk, not both.

latinfreestyle.arrangement: A pop song structure, like freestyle, but with an extra section: the mambo or percussion break, 8 to 16 bars after the second chorus where the brass plays a looped riff over congas, timbales and bell, with no vocal and little or no bass. That is the dance moment of the track, keep it. An 8-bar intro with the clave and a brass riff, a 16-bar verse, a 16-bar chorus, second verse, chorus, percussion break, final chorus with ad libs. Four minutes for radio, six for the maxi with the extended break. The timbale rolls mark each chorus entry.
latinfreestyle.basse: The bass follows the salsa tumbao: it anticipates, playing the root on the “and” of 2 and the fifth or the root on beat 4, often leaving beat 1 empty. That is what sets Latin freestyle apart: the bass does not land with the kick, it pulls forward. A plucky DX7 sound as in freestyle, or a rounder Minimoog for the Miami Sound Machine side. Longer notes than in freestyle, in dotted quarter notes. A minor progression with dominants: i, iv, V7, i. Cut below 70 Hz, the 808 kick holds the sub. A 2 dB sidechain from the kick avoids collisions on the rare occasions they land together.
etapes: Tempo at 120 BPM, choose a 2-3 son clave and program it on the 808 claves over two bars.
Place the kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and step 12, snare and clap on 2 and 4, congas in tumbao, bell on the chorus, eighth-note hi-hats.
Write a tumbao bass that anticipates the “and” of 2 and the 4, progression i, iv, V7, i.
Add a two-bar synth brass riff in response and an eighth-note montuno on a synth piano.
Record the vocal and backing vocals in Spanish and English, then build a 16-bar percussion break after the second chorus.
Mix with wide percussion, the vocal up front and the brass doubled.
latinfreestyle.mix: The mix resembles that of freestyle, vocal up front, but the Latin percussion needs space: wide panning, congas left, timbales right, bell in the center, claves slightly right. A short 600 ms plate reverb on the percussion, a longer 1.8 s one on the vocal. The brass is doubled and offset by 15 ms between left and right. 808 kick at -8 dBFS, bass cut below 70 Hz, compressed at 3:1 to hold the anticipations. Cut the congas below 150 Hz so they do not muddy the low end. Gentle 2:1 bus compression. The result must stay bright and lively, with more air than pure freestyle.

outils.pourquoi: Kick, snare and above all the claves that play the 2-3 son clave from start to finish; the tuned toms serve as backup congas.
Plucky tumbao bass and synth brass sections with a 20 ms attack and slight detune, answering the vocal; Arturia DX7 V today.
For an FM brass: medium modulation and a modulator envelope that rises slowly, then an eighth-note montuno on an FM piano.
A pack of clean congas, timbales, bongos and bells for the tumbao, the cascara and the timbale rolls that open the choruses.
Brass and pads doubled with chorus, offset by 15 ms between left and right; TAL-U-No-LX is more than enough.
The rounder bass of the Miami Sound Machine side, in dotted quarter notes that anticipate the “and” of 2; Arturia Mini V or the Moog Minimoog Model D plugin.
A short 600 ms plate on the wide-panned Latin percussion, a longer 1.8 s one on the lead vocal.

reperes: Miami Sound Machine: Dr. Beat (1984): the 808 and Latin percussion blended, synth brass answering the vocal.
Miami Sound Machine: Conga (1985): the percussion break and the unabashed clave, the mainstream version.
TKA: Maria (1986): the New York club side, tumbao bass and melodramatic vocal.
The Cover Girls: Show Me (1986): the doubled backing vocals and the pop structure, the formula at its peak.
latinfreestyle.rythme: The 808 keeps the kick, snare and hi-hat, but the top end is taken by the Latin percussion: congas in tumbao (open on the “and” of 2 and on 4, muted elsewhere), timbales for the fills and the cascara on the cymbals, campana (bell) in a bongo bell pattern on the choruses. Kick on 1, on the “and” of 2 and on step 12, as in freestyle, but with one more hit on step 8 when the clave is 2-3. Snare on 2 and 4, doubled clap. The 808 claves play the clave from start to finish. Thirty-second-note timbale rolls open the choruses. Look for clean sampled Latin percussion packs, or 808 toms tuned as congas.
latinfreestyle.sons: Synth brass is the master color: trumpet and trombone sections played on a DX7, a Juno or an Oberheim, with 20 ms attacks and a slight detune, playing two-bar riffs in answer to the vocal. In Operator, an FM brass patch needs medium modulation with a modulator envelope that rises slowly. Add a piano or a synth playing a montuno, a syncopated arpeggio pattern on the chord, in eighth notes. The backing vocals alternate Spanish and English, doubled and wide. The orch hit is still present on the choruses. The pads are less present than in freestyle: the space is taken by the percussion.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter)
latinfreestyle.tempo: Same range as New York freestyle, 112 to 126 BPM, Conga runs around 120. What changes is the clave: the whole track is organized around a 3-2 or 2-3 son clave, played by the 808 claves or a sampled wood block. Decide the direction of the clave from the first bar and lock the kick, the bass and the brass to it. The feel is a little more danced, with accents on the “and” of 2 and on beat 4 that come from salsa. No swing on the grid, but you can push the Latin percussion 10 to 15 ms ahead for the nervous energy of the congueros.

latinhouse.arrangement: A structure that blends house and salsa. A 16-bar DJ intro with kick, hats and congas, then the clave and the bass. A 16-bar verse with the piano montuno and the vocal, a 16-bar chorus with the brass and the coro. A 16 to 32 bar breakdown: kick cut, montuno and percussion alone as in a mambo, a timbale or piano solo, a brass build-up, the kick returns. Second cycle, final chorus with pregón, a 16-bar drum outro. Length 5 to 7 minutes. The kickless breakdown is the Latin moment of the track, and the return of the kick the house moment: that alternation defines the style.
latinhouse.basse: The bass is in tumbao or in house, often both alternately. Tumbao: it plays on the “and” of 2 and on 4, anticipating the next chord, not on beat 1, which gives the Cuban sway; an electric bass or baby bass sound, or a synth with a slow attack. House: eighth-note octaves on the roots for the choruses. On You Used to Hold Me, the bass is a house synth line; on Some Lovin', it is played. It follows a I-IV-V progression or a two-chord montuno. Gentle compression, no synthetic sub, the bass must stay within 60 to 250 Hz and let the low congas ring.
etapes: Project at 125 BPM, program a 2-3 son clave on a muted track, then a four-on-the-floor 909 kick with a clap on 2 and 4.
Add congas in tumbao, timbales with cascara, bongos, guiro and cowbell, each 2-bar pattern aligned with the clave.
Write a 2-bar piano montuno over two chords, in syncopated octaves and thirds.
Tumbao bass on the “and” of 2 and on 4 for the verses, house eighth notes for the choruses.
Add brass stabs on the clave accents, a Spanish vocal with a coro, and a kickless mambo breakdown with a timbale solo.
Assemble 6 minutes with a DJ intro, two cycles and an outro, then mix the percussion up front with a shared room reverb.
latinhouse.mix: A lively mix, with the percussion up front. Kick in the center below 100 Hz, bass between 60 and 250 Hz. Congas slightly left, bongos right, timbales in the center, guiro and maracas wide, all with a shared short room reverb. Piano montuno on the right with a little brightness at 5 kHz, brass in the center compressed firmly (4:1) so the stabs crack. Vocal up front with a short hall and an eighth-note delay. Medium bus compression, light saturation. Master at -9 LUFS. Watch out for 200 to 400 Hz where congas, bass and piano meet: filter the congas below 150 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: Tumbao on the congas, cascara and abanicos on the timbales, bongos in martillo: played in clave or sampled, they sit up front in the mix.
Four-on-the-floor kick and clap on 2 and 4 under the Afro-Cuban section, the house part that holds the club dancers.
Piano montuno in syncopated octaves and thirds over two chords, with a little brightness at 5 kHz; otherwise a sampled acoustic piano.
The sampler of the New York studios of Cutting and Strictly Rhythm for chopping salsa and boogaloo records, brass and coros.

outils.nom: House of Loop Latin Percussion Session
outils.pourquoi: Over 200 hits and 80 loops of congas, bongos, timbales, guiro and cowbell, to build the 2-bar clave patterns in a Drum Rack.
To play realistic brass stabs on the clave accents and a solo flute or violin, when you have no musicians.
A 2-3 son clave programmed on a muted track in Ableton to line up every percussion part, as in the first step of the course.

reperes: Ralphi Rosario: You Used to Hold Me (1987): a Chicago track with Latin percussion and piano, the hybrid before the label.
Liberty City: Some Lovin' (1992): the piano montuno and the tumbao bass over a house kick, the Murk formula from Miami.
David Morales: In de Ghetto (1996): brass and Afro-Cuban percussion in a big-room club version.
Armand Van Helden: Witch Doktor (1994): the harder, sample-based side, where Latin percussion becomes a dancefloor weapon.
latinhouse.rythme: 909 kick four-on-the-floor, 909 clap on 2 and 4, closed hats in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats. Then the Afro-Cuban section: congas in tumbao (slap on the “and” of 2, two open notes on 4 and the “and” of 4), timbales with cascara on the bell and abanicos as fills, bongos in martillo, guiro in eighth notes, cowbell on the beats or in clave, maracas. Each instrument is a 2-bar pattern in clave. The fills are timbale abanicos, a roll with an accent on the crash. On the breakdown, the kick stops, the percussion and the piano carry on, like a mambo. A sampled percussion breakbeat can replace all of it.
latinhouse.sons: The piano montuno: a two-bar pattern in octaves and thirds, arpeggiated in syncopation on the clave, over two chords (for example D minor and G7), played on acoustic piano or on the M1 with a little brightness. The brass, sampled or played: trumpet and trombone stabs in chords on the clave accents, brass montunos on the choruses. A solo flute or violin. Vocals in Spanish, sung or spoken, with call-and-response backing vocals (“coro” and “pregón”). A house synth stab as a reminder of the club. Effects: room reverb on the percussion, a short hall on the brass, an eighth-note delay on the vocals. The sampler is used to chop salsa and boogaloo records.
sourcesOutils: House of Loop, Latin Percussion Session
Soundtrack Loops, Latin Percussion Loops and Samples
latinhouse.tempo: Between 122 and 128 BPM, but the tempo matters less than the clave. Everything locks to a 2-3 or 3-2 son clave: a two-bar pattern that places the accents and that the piano montuno, the congas and often the bass respect. Program the clave on a muted track and line up your other patterns with it. The kick stays a straight four-on-the-floor, that is what makes it house and not salsa, but everything above it swings in clave. Light swing, 52 to 54%, the played or humanized percussion brings the rest. Phrases are 8 bars long, in 2-bar clave cycles.

lentoviolento.arrangement: The tracks are long, 5 to 8 minutes, and evolve very slowly: a 16 to 32 bar intro with kick and bass, the melody comes in, repeated over 32 bars, a 16-bar breakdown without kick with the melody and a pad, the kick returns without a build-up, just on beat 1, melody again, a minimal variation (one note changes, a countermelody appears), breakdown, return, long ending. No drop, no roll, no riser: that would be too fast. What makes the track hypnotic is the length of each section and the slowness of the changes. A lento DJ mixes on 32-bar intros and outros; at this tempo that is over a minute.
lentoviolento.basse: The bass follows the hardstyle principle: the kick tail carries the note, and a reverse bass or an offbeat bass answers. But at 100 BPM, you can add a real dance bassline: a square wave or a sawtooth filtered at 400 Hz, playing a simple eighth-note pattern, root, root, fifth, root, as in Italian dance. In Operator: sawtooth, filter at 400 Hz, decay 200 ms. It is slightly saturated. Sidechain from the kick, 4:1 ratio, 150 ms release, long enough for the pumping to be felt at this tempo. A sine sub under everything, on the same notes, if the kick is not enough at the bottom.
etapes: Tempo 100 BPM. Hardstyle kick with a long tail (400 ms), distorted, on every beat. Clap on 2 and 4 with a medium reverb.
Offbeat kicks with the tail only, -6 dB, for the sway.
Eighth-note dance bass in Operator, root-root-fifth-root pattern, filtered at 400 Hz, sidechained with a 150 ms release.
A 4 to 8 note sawtooth melody with portamento, in minor, repeated over 32 bars without change.
Add a folk sample (accordion, guitar) or a slowed-down voice as a countermelody from the second half onward.
Arrange over 6 minutes: intro 32, melody 32, breakdown 16, return, minimal variation, breakdown, return, ending 32. Moderate limiter.
lentoviolento.mix: The kick takes all the lows and low mids, at -3 dB peak, with its tuned tail well present. At 100 BPM, there is room between the hits, so leave a short reverb (0.8 seconds) on the kick, which would be impossible at 160. Bass sidechained under it. Melody in the center, with an eighth-note delay and a medium reverb. Gentle bus compression, 2:1 ratio, 300 ms release. Master: limiter around -7 LUFS. The kick must stay heavy without becoming aggressive: if the distortion stings at 3 kHz, cut it, lento is violent through weight, not through the highs.

outils.pourquoi: The practical DAW for the genre: heavy slowed-down kick, melody looped in the Piano roll, tempo at 100-120 BPM without time-stretch.
A lengthened, distorted 909 kick, played in heavy quarter notes at 110 BPM: each hit lasts, the slowness makes the violence.
The Italian dance melodies: workstation leads and plucks, played simply and repeated to the point of hypnosis. Gigi D'Agostino's keyboard at the time.
Sawtooth dance leads with light unison and short plucks for the simple blocky melodies over the slowed-down kick.
A long synthesized sine kick with a slow pitch envelope, plus a sine bass that follows the melody note for note.
Drive at 8 to 10 dB on the slowed-down kick so it keeps its presence at a tempo where every hit is heard naked.

reperes: Gigi D'Agostino: Silence (2004): the heavy slow-motion kick and the repeated melody, lento defined.
Gigi D'Agostino: Momento Contento (2007): unapologetic slowness and the contrast between melodic softness and the weight of the kick.
Luca Noise: Potenza Adeguata (2009): the more hardstyle version, tuned kick and reverse bass slowed down.
Gigi D'Agostino: Bla Bla Bla (1999): before lento, listen to the repeated melody that will become the method.
lentoviolento.rythme: The lento kick is a hardstyle or hardcore kick, distorted, with a long tuned tail, played at 100 BPM: at this tempo, you can let the tail last 400 ms and it fills the space. On every beat, or sometimes on 1 and 3 only with a softer kick on 2 and 4. Clap or snare on 2 and 4, often with a medium reverb. Hi-hats in eighth notes, sometimes in sixteenth notes to give a little movement under the slowness. Offbeat kicks with the tail only, inherited from hardstyle, which give a sway. No rolls, or very rare ones. The pattern barely changes: it is the repetition that hypnotizes.
lentoviolento.sons: Italian dance melodies: simple sawtooth leads, in minor, with a little portamento, playing 4 or 8 note themes repeated endlessly. In Sylenth1 or a Korg Triton: sawtooth, filter at 4 kHz, eighth-note delay. Dance pianos. Accordions and sampled folk instruments, a D'Agostino trademark. Voices pitched down, or spoken, slowed down. Acid samples (slow TB-303). String pads. Everything is simple and repeated: the melody must fit in one breath and repeat 32 times without changing. The contrast between the softness of the melodies and the heaviness of the kick is the subject.
lentoviolento.tempo: Lento violento drops to between 85 and 115 BPM, most Gigi D'Agostino tracks between 90 and 105. It is hardstyle and Italian dance slowed down by almost half, and at this tempo, each kick becomes an event lasting over 600 ms. The feel is heavy, hypnotic, almost a march: nothing is rushed, everything repeats. No swing, but a slight delay on the melodies (10 to 20 ms) gives that dragging feeling. Program at 100 BPM, eighth-note grid. Think in 4-bar loops repeated for a very long time: the technique is resisting the urge to add things.

liquiddnb.arrangement: Liquid is arranged like a song laid over a DnB form. A 32-bar intro with Rhodes, vocal and pads, without drums or with only shakers. A 64-bar drop that is actually a verse and a chorus: the chords cycle in 4 or 8 bar loops and the vocal leads. A 32-bar breakdown: Rhodes and vocal alone, often with a chord change toward the relative major. A second drop with a countermelody or a string line. A 32-bar outro. The key thing: the chord progression is present from start to finish, it is what structures the track, not the drops. Make it last 5 to 6 minutes.
liquiddnb.basse: Liquid bass is round, not distorted. An Operator sub as a sine or triangle, with a 5 ms attack and a 150 ms release, playing a melodic line: root, third, fifth, octave, in syncopated eighth notes, sometimes with a glissando. It follows the chords, like a soul bass. On top, a second soft layer: the same patch with a saw low-pass filtered at 300 Hz and a little chorus, or a Massive bass (cited in the brief) with a Daft filter and a slow LFO. No screaming Reese. The bass is sidechained from the kick at a 3:1 ratio with a 70 ms release, just so the kick can breathe.
etapes: Set Ableton to 172 BPM. Write a progression of four seventh chords on Electric (for example Fm7, Db maj7, Ab maj7, Eb9).
Program a soft two-step with a round rimshot, and add a jazz break filtered at 500 Hz with 56% swing.
Create an Operator sub that follows the chords in syncopated eighth notes, with a 5 ms attack and a 150 ms release.
Add a sung vocal (royalty-free a cappella) with a dotted-eighth delay and a 2.5 s reverb.
Lay down Analog strings in the background, 400 ms attack, and sixteenth-note shakers.
Arrange intro 32 without drums, drop 64 as verse and chorus, breakdown 32 on Rhodes and vocal, second drop, outro 32.
liquiddnb.mix: The liquid mix favors warmth. A softer kick than in neurofunk, high-passed at 45 Hz, no click. The sub holds the low end alone, mono. The Rhodes is high-passed at 150 Hz so it does not fight the bass, and gets gentle compression (2:1 ratio, 20 ms attack). The vocal goes to the foreground, with a de-esser and an EQ that cuts 300 Hz. The background breaks are parallel compressed, but less than in hard DnB. Longer, more present reverbs: 2 to 3 s on the chords and the vocal. Master at -8 LUFS, softer than club level, to let the song's dynamics live.

outils.pourquoi: The genre's soul chords, played with tremolo and a little phaser; Ableton Electric or a Rhodes sample in Sampler does the job.
Muted breaks and sampled soul loops on the first Good Looking and Hospital records, before the move to the DAW.
A round bass with a Daft filter and a slow LFO, no distortion; the synth of High Contrast and Netsky in the 2000s.
The genre's historical sequencer in London, for long arrangements with a 32-bar intro without drums.
Rhodes samples, jazz guitars and pitched sung vocals; dotted-eighth delay and a 2.5 s reverb behind them.
A sine sub that follows the round bass note for note, or a saw filtered at 300 Hz with a little chorus.
Synth strings from two saws with a 400 ms attack and warm pads in the background of the breakdowns.
A dotted-eighth delay on vocals and Rhodes; Rudimental put it almost everywhere, Galaxy preset for the ambient pads.

reperes: LTJ Bukem: Music (1993): the floating pads and the gliding break, the origin of the genre's whole soft side.
High Contrast: If We Ever (2004): a soul sample, a chorus that sings, liquid getting radio play without losing its tempo.
Calibre: Even If (2003): restraint, a round bass and Rhodes chords that are enough to hold six minutes.
