Hybrid Minds: Halcyon (2020): modern liquid, vocal produced like a pop song, clean sub and muted breaks.
liquiddnb.rythme: The muted breaks of the brief: a two-step with the kick on the 1 and the “and” of 3, snare on 2 and 4, but the snare is rounder, often a rimshot or a break snare with lots of body at 200 Hz, and little attack at 5 kHz. The hi-hats are a jazz or funk break (Think, Apache, Soul Pride) high-passed at 500 Hz and played in full under the programmed drums, with light swing. Add sixteenth-note shakers, a tambourine on the offbeats, and snare ghost notes at velocity 35. The fills are break rolls, not synthetic edits.
liquiddnb.sons: The Fender Rhodes is the instrument of the genre: major seventh and minor ninth chords, played by hand or programmed with varied velocities, with a light tremolo and a little plate reverb. In Ableton, Electric does the job; otherwise a Rhodes sample in Sampler. The vocals are sung, not toasted: a soulful female or male voice, with a dotted-eighth delay and a 2.5 s reverb. Add sampled or synthetic strings (Analog, two saws, 400 ms attack), sampled jazz guitars, and warm pads. High Contrast sampled soul and disco records: look for chords, not breaks.
liquiddnb.tempo: Liquid keeps the DnB tempo, 170 to 174 BPM, but changes the feel. The two-step is softer, with real swing of 55 to 58% on the hi-hats and ghost notes, and a background break often played in full to bring human feel. Where neurofunk counts in sixteenth notes, liquid counts in 2-bar units: the chords change every 2 or 4 bars, as in soul. The fast tempo becomes a conveyor belt under a song at 87 BPM. If your track works at half speed, with its chords and its vocal, you are in the right feel.

lofihiphop.arrangement: The tracks are short, 2 to 3 minutes, made for playlists and continuous streams. A 4-bar intro with the sample alone and the crackle, beat at bar 5, first change at bar 21: a filter closing or an added melody. No drop, no long breakdown: a one-bar pause without drums is enough to relaunch. The form is A A B A, with the B changing a chord or pitching the sample. Many producers end abruptly, on a bar of sample alone followed by an end-of-record noise. If you are aiming for a lofi stream, keep constant energy from start to finish: the track must never wake the listener up.
lofihiphop.basse: The bass is round and short: an 808 with a 300 to 500 ms decay, or an Operator sine with a little saturation. It plays few notes, often the root and the minor third in quarter notes, and follows the kick while sometimes sliding to the next note with a 50 ms portamento. Cut it at 250 Hz: it must stay under the sample. On Nujabes productions, the bass is often a double bass or an electric bass sampled along with the jazz, replayed note by note. To do this, isolate a bass note from the sample, put it in Simpler and replay a simple line. Sidechain is pointless: the kick is short and the bass has room.
etapes: Choose a tempo of 82 BPM and turn off quantization: play the kick and the snare by hand over 2 bars, without correcting.
Cut a piano or Rhodes sample into 4 bars, pitch it down a semitone and run it through a low-pass at 8 kHz plus a simulated cassette.
Add a short 808 or sine bass, root and minor third in quarter notes, under the sample.
Lay down a vinyl crackle at -40 dB and a very low domestic noise, rain or coffee, across the whole track.
Arrange over 2 minutes 30: intro with sample alone, beat at bar 5, a change at bar 21, abrupt ending.
Mix dirty and soft: master low-pass at 10 kHz, tape saturation, master at -14 LUFS.
lofihiphop.mix: The mix is deliberately dirty and soft. Cut everything above 10 kHz, add tape saturation on the master bus, and compress the drums at a 4:1 ratio with a slow 30 ms attack to let the transient through. The samples are mono or nearly so, and the stereo comes from the chorus and the ambient noises. Kick around -12 dB, bass at -14, sample at -16, and vinyl crackle at -40: present but never in the way. The master stays low, -14 LUFS, which the platforms handle well. Listen on a phone: if the bass disappears, add a harmonic at 100 Hz with a Saturator.

outils.pourquoi: J Dilla's machine: quantization off, kick and snare played by hand, swing that smears. An MPC One or Ableton with the Groove Pool is enough.
A 12-bit sampler with 10 seconds of memory: you record the record at 45 rpm then repitch it, hence the veil. Decimort 2 for the grain.
The pocket sampler of Madlib and of Donuts, with its Vinyl Sim effect. Goodhertz Vulf Compressor is built on that compression.
Noise, cassette wobble, bitcrush and saturation on the piano sample, the most common of today's lo-fi plugins.
Free, it puts vinyl crackle at -40 dB across the whole track. Ableton Vinyl Distortion does the same in Live.
Simpler to replay a bass note isolated from the sample, Operator for the sine, Drum Rack for the short kit, Groove Pool for the swing.
Ninth and eleventh chords with lots of chorus to replace the jazz sample and avoid rights issues. Keyscape or Lounge Lizard in software.
Tuned 808 kick and bass, 300 to 500 ms decay, 50 ms portamento between notes. Samples in a Drum Rack are enough.

reperes: J Dilla: Time: The Donut of the Heart (2006): the soul sample cut on the fly, the kick early and the snare late, all by hand.
Nujabes: Aruarian Dance (2003): the sampled and looped jazz guitar, the clean but supple beat, and the bass replayed underneath.
Nujabes: Feather (2005): the piano in a 4-bar loop with laid-back rap, the reference for melodic lofi.
Madlib: Slims Return (2003): Blue Note jazz chopped with abrupt cuts, sampler grain and irregular swing.
lofihiphop.rythme: The kit is short and muffled. A kick from a soul break or a tuned 808, run through a low-pass at 3 kHz, with a 150 ms tail. The snare is a blend of break snare and clap, heavily filtered, almost a dull thud. The hi-hats are in eighth notes with irregular velocities, between 40 and 90, sometimes a sixteenth note that appears to surprise. The classic 2-bar pattern: kick on the 1, the “and” of 2 and the “a” of 3, snare on 2 and 4, but the second bar changes one note. Add a shaker or a faint rimshot, and snare ghost notes at velocity 30 before the 4. Little percussion: the crackling vinyl acts as hi-hats.
lofihiphop.sons: The veiled jazz sample is the heart: a piano, a Rhodes or a guitar taken from a record, cut into 2 or 4 bars, slowed down by one or two semitones, then run through a low-pass at 8 kHz and a cassette simulation with wow and flutter. RC-20 Retro Color, Vinyl Distortion or Ableton's Vinyl add the hiss. A Rhodes played in ninth and eleventh chords, with lots of chorus, replaces the sample if you want to avoid rights issues. Add domestic noises: rain, a page turning, coffee being poured, very low in the mix. The melodies are simple, in Dorian mode or minor, two chords looping. No wide pads: lo-fi is small and intimate.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (plugins for Boom Bap and Lo-Fi Hip Hop)
lofihiphop.tempo: 70 to 90 BPM, and human feel above all. What changes here compared with trip-hop is the unquantized feel: J Dilla turned off the quantization on his MPC3000 and played the pads by hand. The result: the kick arrives a little early, the snare a little late, the hi-hats hesitate. In Ableton, play the pattern on the keyboard without quantizing, or apply an MPC 16 swing 62% groove, then shift the snare by 20 ms and the kick by -10 ms. The tempo should feel drunk but stable. Avoid perfect grids: if everything lands dead on, it has failed.

lofihouse.arrangement: A simplified deep house structure. A 16-bar intro with veiled drums and a filtered pad, then bass, then vocals. Elements come in every 16 bars, without a build-up. A 16-bar breakdown: kick cut, pad and vocals with the reverb opening up, the kick returning without a transition or with a roll. A second plateau, a 16-bar outro. Length 5 to 7 minutes. Many tracks are shorter, made quickly, with a single idea: a 4-bar loop that keeps turning and wears out. The arrangement is deliberately simple, almost naive, and the nostalgia comes from repeating a loop that already seems old.
lofihouse.basse: A supple deep house bass, in eighth notes with rests, on the roots of minor 7 chords, with a round synth sound (Juno, SH-101, or Analog) filtered at 200 to 300 Hz. What changes: it is slightly out of tune (a few cents), saturated, and its envelope is soft. It follows a 2 or 4 chord progression over 4 or 8 bars, with a few passing notes. Light sidechain. Add a little noise and a light wow (slow pitch modulation, 0.2 Hz, a few cents) for the tape effect. The low end is full but veiled: no clean sub, the bass and kick blend a little.
etapes: Project at 121 BPM, 707 and 909 kit with a long-decay kick, a clap with sampler reverb, hats with varying velocity and 58% swing.
Write a progression of 2 minor 7 chords over 4 bars, as a held Juno pad with chorus and a filter at 5 kHz.
Round bass in eighth notes with rests, detuned by a few cents, saturated.
Sample a phrase of 1990s R&B, stretch it, filter it, and repeat it with a long delay.
Assemble 6 minutes without a build-up, bringing in one element every 16 bars, with a pad and vocal breakdown.
Run the whole mix through a cassette chain: tape saturation, heavy compression, bitcrush, low-pass at 10 kHz, hiss, master at -11 LUFS.
lofihouse.mix: The mix is squashed and veiled, and that is the point. The whole track goes through a cassette chain: tape saturation, heavy compression (ratio 6:1 or more, slow attack), light bitcrush, a low-pass filter at 10 or 12 kHz, and a little white noise or hiss throughout. The kick is saturated and blends into the bass. The reverb is long and dirty, often a single one on everything. The stereo image is narrow. The master is not loud, -10 to -12 LUFS, but heavily compressed, which gives that feeling of an overdriven cassette recording. Resist the urge to clean up: if the mix starts to sound clean, put the saturation back.

outils.pourquoi: Saturated, veiled 707 hats, clap and rim, the drums of DJ Boring and Mall Grab; Roland Cloud TR-707 or a sampled kit in a Drum Rack.
Long-decay kick, saturated and filtered above 8 kHz, toms for rolls; D16 Drumazon 2 as a plugin, run through the cassette chain.
A Tascam Portastudio or an ordinary deck, the mix bounced onto it and recorded back: compression, hiss and wow that make the style.
The course builds the cassette chain with Saturator, Redux and a low-pass at 10 kHz on the master, then a little white noise.
Noise, wow and flutter, bitcrush and filter in a single plugin, the most widespread emulation for degrading pads and R&B samples.
A simple cassette emulator on the whole mix, saturation and high-end loss, for those without a tape deck.
Minor 7 pads with chorus, detuned by a few cents and filtered at 5 kHz; TAL-U-NO-LX or Arturia Jun-6 V as a plugin.
To sample vocals and pianos from records with the grain of an old sampler; Simpler with Redux does the same in Live.

reperes: DJ Boring: Winona (2016): a veiled pad loop and a sampled vocal that turn until they wear out, the record that defines the style.
Ross from Friends: Talk to Me You'll Understand (2015): saturated 707 drums under filtered deep house chords, the memory of house.
Mall Grab: Menace II Society (2016): the faster, more rave version, same cassette chain, more energy.
DJ Seinfeld: U (2017): the pad and the stretched vocal, lo-fi as openly embraced melancholy.
lofihouse.rythme: Saturated 707 and 909 emulations: a 909 kick with a slightly long decay, saturated and filtered above 8 kHz, a 707 or 909 clap with sampler reverb, 707 hats in sixteenth notes with varying velocity, open on the offbeats, all run through tape saturation and a light bitcrusher. A 707 rim or cowbell in syncopation. A shaker or a breakbeat lifted from a record, very low in the mix. Fills are saturated 909 tom rolls or cuts. What matters is the processing: the whole kit goes through a cassette chain (Ableton's Tape, or Saturator plus Redux plus a low-pass filter at 10 kHz) that squashes and veils it.
lofihouse.sons: Veiled pads: Juno or a digital strings preset (D-50, M1), in minor 7 and 9 chords held over 4 or 8 bars, run through chorus, a low-pass filter at 5 kHz, wow and flutter, and a long reverb. A Rhodes or a piano sampled from a record, with noise. Vocals sampled from 1990s R&B or soul, stretched, pitched, filtered, often a single phrase repeated with a delay. Field recordings, vinyl noise, cassette hiss. A rare lead, often a simple sine synth melody with vibrato. The processing makes the sound: tape saturation, 12-bit bitcrush, low-pass filter, long reverb, wow and flutter on everything.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace, Hazy Lo Fi House Hardware Only
lofihouse.tempo: Between 118 and 126 BPM, often a little slower than the deep house it descends from, and above all slightly off: the machines are a touch out of tune, the tempo can drift by 0.1%, and the hat swing is pronounced (56 to 60%). The feel is that of a rediscovered cassette: elements land a few milliseconds late or early, loops repeat with small imperfections. Humanize timing and velocity by hand, or leave mistakes in. A lo-fi house track sounds like a memory of house: the tempo should give that floating feeling, not energy.

lounge.arrangement: Tracks last 4 to 6 minutes and follow a jazz standard form: a 16-bar A theme, an 8-bar B theme, back to A, then a solo or variation, then the final theme. The beat comes in from bar 1 or after 4 bars of percussion alone. Changes arrive every 8 bars: a solo instrument takes the melody, the flute, then the trumpet, then the vibraphone. The breakdown, around the middle, removes the drums and leaves the double bass and percussion for 8 bars, like a bass solo. End on a final theme and a clean ending, with a held chord and a cymbal: no fade, lounge ends like musicians do.
lounge.basse: The double bass is the signature instrument. Sampled or played with a plugin like Trilian or an orchestral library, pizzicato, with a woody note and a slight finger noise. The line is the bossa one: root on 1, fifth on 3, sometimes the third in between, in dotted quarter notes and eighth notes. On mambo or cha-cha, the tumbao: root on the "and" of 2 and fifth on 4, never on 1. Cut it at 250 Hz but keep a little midrange at 800 Hz for the wood. 3:1 compression to even it out. The bass is mixed quieter than in trip-hop: it walks, it doesn't rumble. A soft bass synth can double it an octave below.
etapes: Pick 105 BPM, program a 3-2 clave and a bossa rimshot over 2 bars with a dry, clean kick.
Add Latin percussion, bongos, cabasa and shaker, with varied velocities but no added swing.
Write a pizzicato double bass on root and fifth, with a little finger noise, and cut it at 250 Hz.
Lay down a vintage organ in short chords on the offbeat and a sampled vibraphone or flute on the theme.
Arrange like a standard: A theme, B theme, flute solo then trumpet solo, double bass breakdown, clean ending.
Mix hi-fi and wide, instruments placed as on stage, short plate, bright master at -12 LUFS.
lounge.mix: The mix is hi-fi and wide, like a well-recorded jazz record. No saturation, no bitcrusher: that is what separates it from downtempo. Place the instruments in the stereo field as on stage: double bass in the center, percussion on the right, vibraphone on the left, brass slightly right. A 1.5-second plate reverb on the brass and vibraphone, a short room on the drums. Gentle compression, 2:1, on each instrument, and a bus compressor doing just one dB. The kick stays at -12 dB and the double bass at -12 too. The master around -12 LUFS, bright but not harsh: a touch of shelf EQ at +1 dB above 10 kHz.

outils.pourquoi: Pizzicato double bass with finger noise and wood at 800 Hz, in a bossa line with the root on 1 and the fifth on 3.
If you have a double bass player, a mic in front of the bridge replaces any plugin: a played tumbao beats a programmed one.
Short chords on the offbeat with a slow Leslie. IK Multimedia Hammond B-3X or Arturia B-3 V give the same organ in the DAW.
Vibraphone, flute, muted brass and "ah-ah" choirs played from libraries, to replay exotica without sampling records.
Brushes and rimshot in continuous sixteenth notes, a clean jazz kit with no dust: the drums the style calls for.
A dry, filtered kick with no sub, under the brushes and the 3-2 clave. 909 samples in a Drum Rack are enough.
To cut an Italian singer or a spy film clip and drop it tongue-in-cheek over the theme.
A 1.5-second plate on the brass and vibraphone, a short room on the drums: a hi-fi mix placed as on stage.

reperes: De-Phazz: The Mambo Craze (1999): sampled mambo brass on a clean beat, tongue-in-cheek and real groove together.
Tosca: Suzuki (2000): the round double bass and held chords, Viennese lounge in its gentlest form.
Nicola Conte: Bossa Per Due (2000): bossa nova replayed with flute and nylon guitar, the jazz standard form.
Gotan Project: Epoca (2001): bandoneon and tango over an electronic bass and a 100 BPM beat.
lounge.rythme: The kit is clean, with no dust: that is the difference from downtempo. A dry, short kick with no sub, more like a jazz kit kick or a filtered 909. The snare is often replaced by a rimshot or brushes on the snare, in continuous sixteenth notes with an accent on 2 and 4. Closed hi-hats in eighth notes at even velocity, clean. On top, the Latin percussion: bongos, cabasa, shaker, guiro, and a crisp 3-2 clave. The bossa pattern over 2 bars: kick on the 1 and the "and" of 2, then on the "and" of 3 and on 4, rimshot on the clave. A clean programmed beat under hand-played percussion makes the lounge blend.
lounge.sons: Exotica and bossa samples give the color: vibraphone, flute, light strings, "ah-ah" choirs, muted brass, cut from records of the 1950s-1960s or replayed with libraries. The vintage organ, a Hammond with a slow Leslie or a Farfisa, plays short chords on the offbeat. The Rhodes is present but more discreet. Add a nylon guitar playing bossa chords, a muted trumpet, an accordion or a bandoneon if you are aiming for tango. The effects are clean: short plate reverb, light delay. The kitsch is embraced: a sample of an Italian singer or a clip from a James Bond film comes in tongue-in-cheek, but the mix stays serious.
lounge.tempo: Lounge runs between 95 and 120 BPM, livelier than chill-out, its parent. What changes: the groove comes from Latin music, bossa nova, mambo, slow samba. The bossa feel is a pulse of steady sixteenth notes with a 3-2 clave pattern that shifts the accents. Set the swing to just 52 or 54%: bossa is straight, the sway comes from the accents, not from lateness. On more tango-flavored tracks like Gotan Project, the tempo sits around 100 with a pulse of marked quarter notes. Lounge should make you want to nod your head with a drink in your hand, not really dance.

lowercase.arrangement: Pieces of 10 to 40 minutes where silence is a section. The typical form: a thin noise floor, around -50 dBFS, that never stops, and sporadic events placed on top of it. No build-up, no peak: if the listener notices a progression, that is already too much. A new texture can replace the previous one at minute 12, without a transition, as if you had changed rooms. Think installation rather than track: the music must work in a place, while someone reads. The record is often a single piece, or a numbered series without titles, like Chartier's Series.
lowercase.basse: The low end is almost absent. When it exists, it is a pure sine between 25 and 40 Hz at a very low level, felt rather than heard, or a dull mass of filtered noise. Chartier often plays both extremes at once: a sub sine and a hiss around 12 kHz, with nothing in between. No bass notes, no harmony. Be careful: below 30 Hz, most speakers produce nothing, and a sub at -30 dB disappears completely on a laptop. Own it: the piece doesn't have to sound everywhere. If you want the low end to be felt, raise it to around 45 Hz and accept that it becomes audible.
etapes: Stick a piezo contact mic on a sheet of paper or a book, plug it into an interface with the gain very high, and record 10 minutes of rubbing and silence.
In the DAW, turn off the grid, switch to seconds, and select 8 to 10 micro-events that you space 20 to 60 seconds apart.
Add a floor: the background noise of your recording, band-pass filtered around 4 kHz, at -50 dBFS, continuous.
Generate a 35 Hz sine in Operator with a 5-second attack and a 10-second release, and make it appear two or three times in total.
Arrange over 15 minutes without any build-up, with an abrupt texture change halfway through.
Export at 24 bits without compression or limiter, peaks around -24 dBFS, and check that the piece goes unnoticed in the background in a quiet room.
lowercase.mix: The mix is an exercise in extreme levels. Peaks between -20 and -30 dBFS, no normalization, no compression, no limiter: anything that raises the level destroys the intention. The noise floor of your chain becomes a choice: either you remove it with a gate or a denoiser, or you keep it as a backdrop, but decide. Export at 24 bits with dither, because at 16 bits sounds at -60 dB degrade. Listen on headphones at a normal volume: if you hear everything distinctly, it is too loud. The stereo image is wide and precise, each micro-event in an exact spot. A simple test: play the piece in the background in a quiet room, it should almost disappear.

outils.pourquoi: Stuck on paper, wood or a window, it captures the tiny rubbing sounds of Forms of Paper; a piezo costing a few dollars into a clean preamp is enough.
Very quiet preamps to push the gain to the maximum on empty rooms, neon lights and fans without the chain's noise taking over.
The environment named in the brief: microscopic granulation, resonant filters and composed silences programmed patch by patch, or via Max for Live in Ableton.
For granulation and barely audible DSP: Grain Cloud Delay or a homemade ensemble that slices a micro-event into spaced-out particles.
A pure sine without modulation, 35 Hz, 5-second attack, 10-second release, appearing twice in fifteen minutes: the only synth allowed.
A very narrow band-pass, Q of 20, to isolate a resonance in a recording or filter the noise floor around 4 kHz at -50 dBFS.
Spectral freeze turns a click or a breath into a thin pad without reverb, which respects the genre's ban on long tails.
To decide on the background noise: remove it surgically or keep it as material, Bernhard Günter style. Then export at 24 bits with dither.

reperes: Bernhard Günter: Untitled I/92 (1993): background noise as material, tiny sounds separated by long silences, the first milestone.
Richard Chartier: Series (2000): sines at the extremes of the spectrum, almost nothing in the middle, the rigor of the Line label.
Steve Roden: Forms of Paper (2001): book pages rubbed on contact mics, designed for a library, the manifesto of the genre.
Taylor Deupree: Northern (2006): the warmer side of 12k, tiny loops and hiss, the most accessible way in.
lowercase.rythme: No percussion, but tiny strikes: the rubbing of a page, a finger on a contact mic, a relay click, amplified by 30 to 40 dB. Roden recorded book pages with contact mics, that is all the material of Forms of Paper. Place these events rarely, one or two every 30 seconds, and leave the rest to the background noise. Chartier works differently, with pure sines at the extremes of the spectrum and grains of noise that appear and then fade. To make this: Operator with a single sine, an envelope with a 5-second attack, or a granulator with 5 to 20 ms grains on a recording of silence. Every sound must stay at the threshold of audibility.
lowercase.sons: The brief names the contact mic, the computer and Max/MSP. A piezo costing a few dollars stuck on paper, wood or a window, into a clean preamp, is enough to start. A field recorder captures empty rooms, fans, neon lights. In the DAW: generated sines (Operator without modulation), a very narrow band-pass (Q of 20) to isolate a resonance, Ableton's Spectral Time in freeze, Reaktor or Max for microscopic granulation. A long delay with low feedback to space out the repeats. The background noise of the mic and preamp is a material in its own right: Günter uses it as a backdrop. No long reverb, no pad synth.
sources: Line imprint, Steve Roden's essay on Forms of Paper (lineimprint.com)
sourcesOutils: Line imprint (Bandcamp), Steve Roden, Forms of Paper and six sound installations
Wikipedia, Steve Roden and Forms of Paper
lowercase.tempo: No tempo, and the silences are composed: 10 seconds, 40 seconds, a minute of almost nothing, decided to the second. Turn off the grid, switch the timeline to seconds and work as if editing a film. Where drone fills time, lowercase empties it: the piece is a thin line of noise on which micro-events rarely arrive. No pulse, no LFO; if there is a cycle, it is that of a recorded fan or hard drive. With Roden, time is that of a hand rubbing a page. The listening format matters: Forms of Paper was designed for a library, it had to fit into a place without disturbing it.

makina.arrangement: A makina track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and follows the hard trance structure: a 32-bar intro with kick, bass and hi-hats, the hoover or a stab coming in over 16 bars, a long 32-bar breakdown without kick where the main melody develops with a pad and a vocal, a build-up with a 4-bar snare roll and a riser, a 32-bar drop with kick, bass, hoover and melody. A shorter second breakdown with the piano, a second drop with the full melody and a countermelody. A 32-bar ending with kick and bass. What makes the track playable is the build-up: the 4-bar roll and the silence before the drop are mandatory.
makina.basse: The offbeat bass, as in happy hardcore and bouncy techno, but with a particular timbre the scene describes as higher and more piercing: a sawtooth or a square wave filtered at 700 Hz instead of 400, with more resonance, played on every "and", a short 120 ms note. In Analog: sawtooth, filter at 700 Hz, resonance at 30 percent, 120 ms decay. It follows the chords of the melody, in minor, often root, minor sixth, fourth, fifth. A short sine sub on the same notes if the low end is lacking. No sidechain: it never falls on the kick. The kick-bass bounce is the same as in bouncy techno, but higher.
etapes: Tempo 170 BPM. A 909 kick saturated at 10 dB, 150 ms decay, on every beat. Snare on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeat.
Offbeat bass filtered at 700 Hz with resonance, a short note on every "and", following 4 chords in minor.
Alpha Juno hoover (or recreated in Serum) playing an 8-bar melody in minor, with long reverb.
Supersaw in Sylenth1 doubling the melody an octave above in the drop, plus a pad in the breakdown.
A 4-bar snare roll in sixteenth then thirty-second notes with a velocity crescendo before each drop, plus a riser.
Arrange as hard trance: intro 32, hoover 16, breakdown 32 with melody and vocal, build-up, drop 32, breakdown, final drop, ending 32. Limiter on the drum bus and on the master.
makina.mix: The makina mix is harder than happy hardcore and more melodic than gabber: kick peaking at -3 dB, saturated but with a clean low end thanks to a high-pass at 40 Hz. The offbeat bass 4 dB below, with its resonance cutting through the midrange. Hoover and supersaw wide in stereo, high-pass at 250 Hz, a 2 to 3 second hall reverb cut below 400 Hz. Vocals heavily compressed with a dotted eighth delay. Snare rolls with a limiter on the drum bus so they don't blow up the master. Master: limiter around -7 LUFS. Compare with Ruboy or Xque at the same level, and check that the hoover doesn't mask the bass.

outils.pourquoi: The hoover, everywhere in 1990s Catalan mákina as a stab and in build-ups, pitched upward on the drops.
A hard 909 kick, 909 snare and 4/4 hi-hats: the rhythmic base from Valencia to Barcelona, around 160-170 BPM.
Simple epic leads and workstation pianos, played as four-note riffs over the breakdowns; the KORG Collection M1 replaces it today.
The sequencer of Spanish studios in the Bit Music and Max Music era, to drive the 909, the Alpha Juno and the M1.
For the Newcastle scene and current productions: supersaw for the epic leads and plucks for the simple melodies.
Rebuilding the hoover and the pitched leads: three detuned sawtooths, chorus, a rising pitch envelope.
6 to 8 dB of drive on the kick to harden it the Spanish way, without going as far as gabber clipping.

reperes: Megabeat: Es Imposible, No Puede Ser (1989): the Valencian source, before the word makina existed, listen to the kick and the simple melody.
Ramirez: Terapia (1995): 1990s makina, melodic hoover and a snare roll before the drop.
Ruboy Vs. Radium: End Of Universe (2021): modern makina meets frenchcore, an epic melody over a hard kick.
Puchy Vs Barris: La Llave De La Fiesta (2021): current production, supersaw and a piercing offbeat bass.
makina.rythme: A saturated 909 kick, hard, with attack, somewhere between bouncy techno and gabber: Saturator at 10 dB, a little clipping, 150 ms decay. On every beat. A 909 snare on 2 and 4, with a short reverb. Open hi-hats on the offbeat, as in all melodic hardcore, fairly upfront. Closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes. The makina signature is the fast, long snare rolls, 4 bars of sixteenth notes then thirty-second notes with a velocity crescendo, before every drop, and often a kick roll too. Descending 909 toms. The drum pattern is that of hard trance, played with hardcore sounds.
makina.sons: The Alpha Juno hoover, played as a melodic lead, not as a two-note riff: whole 8-bar melodies in minor. Epic supersaw leads, sawtooths stacked at 5 or 7 voices in Sylenth1 or in a Korg M1 for the period sound, with a long reverb, playing rising themes. M1 stabs. Pianos in the breakdowns. Vocals sung in Spanish or English, with lots of reverb, often a repeated phrase. On the Newcastle branch, MC vocals rapped on top. Sirens, white noise risers, impacts. Everything is dramatic: minor chords, rising melodies, long reverb.
makina.tempo: Spanish makina runs between 150 and 180 BPM, with 1990s Catalan production often around 160-170, and the Newcastle branch around 170-175. What sets it apart from hardcore techno, its contemporary, is a stronger link to hard trance: epic melodies, long breakdowns, build-ups. What sets it apart from happy hardcore is a harder kick and more dramatic melodies, in minor, never childlike. No swing. Program at 170 BPM, sixteenth-note grid. The feel is that of a stadium: every melody must be singable by a thousand people.

melodictechno.arrangement: Seven to eight minutes. A 32-bar intro with kick and filtered arpeggio. Bass at 33, held melody at 49. First breakdown at 65: 16 bars without kick, arpeggio and pad, a riser over the last 8, a roll, the drop at 81 with a crash. A 32-bar plateau. Second breakdown at 129, longer, 32 to 48 bars: pad alone, then the pluck comes in as a dialogue, the bass-lead returns without kick, a white noise build-up over 16 bars, one bar of silence, final drop. A 32-bar outro. The melody must evolve in each section: transposition, an added note, an octave. It is the only genre in the family where the breakdown is the most important moment of the track.
melodictechno.basse: Two layers. A dedicated sub: a pure sine (Operator or an empty sampler putting out a sine), in sixteenth notes on F#0 (around 50 Hz), with the first note of each beat removed where the kick plays, EQ cutting below 30 Hz at 24 dB per octave, LFO Tool with the first node at zero to kill the tail under the kick. On top, a held bass-lead: Monark, Sub 37 or Diva, two inverted saws detuned by a third of a semitone and a few cents, noise at 30%, filter with contour at 50%. It plays long notes: F#3 over two bars, A3, G#3, then D4 and C#4 to end the phrase. Low cut at 270 Hz, a 5.9 s reverb, sidechain ducking.
etapes: At 122 BPM, lay down a clean kick, a clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocities.
Create a sine sub in sixteenth notes on F#0, removing the first note of each beat.
Program a seven-note chord with a tension note in Diva, arpeggiate it in sixteenth notes, then edit the MIDI.
Add a held bass-lead (detuned saws, noise 30%) over an 8-bar phrase, long reverb.
Apply LFO Tool or sidechain as gentle ducking on the arpeggio, pad and bass-lead.
Arrange over eight minutes with two breakdowns, the second one 32 bars long, build-up and drop.
melodictechno.mix: A polished production. Gentle sidechain on everything that isn't the kick: pad, arpeggio, bass, with a curve that comes back up over 200 ms. Sub mono and dry, no effects. Wide arpeggios and pads, reverbs on returns cut below 300 Hz. Cut the bass-lead at 270 Hz and the arpeggio below 30 Hz with a 2 dB boost at 105 Hz for body. Light bus compression (Glue 2:1) and a master around -8 LUFS with Ozone or Pro-L 2, without crushing the breakdown, which must sound at least 3 dB softer than the drop. Watch 200 to 400 Hz, the zone where pads and bass-lead fight. The kick stays dry and short so it doesn't crowd the melody.

outils.pourquoi: The genre's synth: a seven-note arpeggio in sixteenth notes, a two-oscillator pluck with chorus, a bass-lead with two detuned saws.
Stephan Bodzin's held bass-lead, long notes over two bars, cut at 270 Hz with a 5.9 s reverb and gentle ducking.
The drawn sidechain on arpeggio, pad and bass-lead, first node at zero to kill the tail under the kick, recovery in 200 ms.
Cinematic pads with unison saws and a slow attack, and widely shared presets from the Afterlife scene.
Minimoog emulation for the bass-lead when you don't have the Sub 37, filter with contour at 50% and noise at 30%.
A clean kick layered with a sub and a click, a clap on 2 and 4 with a short plate; as samples rather than the machine.
Operator for the sine sub in sixteenth notes, Wavetable for the pads, Stereo Delay at 45%; Logic and its Quick Sampler are the other school.
Final limiter around -8 LUFS, with Ozone before it, without crushing the breakdown, which must stay 3 dB below the drop.

reperes: Kolsch: Grey (2013): the minor arpeggio and the pad rising, the melody as the drop
Tale of Us: North Star (2013): the pluck in dialogue and the endless breakdown, the Afterlife model
Stephan Bodzin: Singularity (2015): the held Moog bass-lead, arpeggio and strings, the analog sound of the genre
Massano: The Feeling (2022): the festival version, huge sidechain and a noise build-up
melodictechno.rythme: A clean, calibrated 909 kick, layered with a sub and a click, four-on-the-floor. Clap and snare layered on 2 and 4, with a short plate reverb. Closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocities (100, 60, 80, 60), open on the offbeat of beat 4. A discreet percussion or shaker. Few elements: the rhythm serves the melody. A 4-bar snare roll before each drop, a crash on arrival. During the breakdowns, keep a hi-hat or a shaker to hold the pulse. Duck everything that isn't the kick with LFO Tool or Ableton's sidechain, drawing a curve that dips on the downbeat.
melodictechno.sons: The arpeggios: in Diva, a seven-note chord on C (C0, C1, D#1, C2, C#2, E2, C3) where the C# brings the dark tension, run through an arpeggiator in sixteenth notes over two octaves, exported to MIDI then edited: some notes raised by two octaves, others lowered by one. Cutoff automation every bar, more pronounced at the end of the 4 bars, and automation of the envelope decay. Stereo Delay at 45%. A two-oscillator Diva pluck with chorus, reverb and delay to answer in call and response. Cinematic pads (Serum or Wavetable, unison saws, slow attack). Sub 37 for the bass-lead. Gentle sidechain on everything.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
melodictechno.tempo: 120 to 126 BPM, the slowest tempo in the family along with dub. A light groove on the hi-hats (16th swing at 10 or 15%) and gentle sidechain everywhere to give the characteristic pumping. The feel is cinematic: the track is designed for a festival, not an afterparty, so every 16-bar section must announce the next. Arpeggios in sixteenth notes give the perceived speed even at 122. Lock the delays to the dotted eighth to widen the arpeggios. Unlike progressive house, the kick stays techno, dry and present; unlike peak time, the tempo never goes above 126 and leaves the melody room to breathe.

miamibass.arrangement: The tracks are party anthems: a call-and-response chorus within the first 16 bars, short verses, a chorus that keeps coming back. Allow five to six minutes for a 12-inch, four for a radio edit. The typical breakdown cuts everything except the 808 kick, which plays a bassline alone for 8 bars, then the vocals return on a snare roll. Transitions are made with shouts and rolls, not filters. Add sections where the sampled breakbeat takes the place of the 808 to change the color. Plan a 16-bar intro and outro with drums and 808 bass for DJs, as in the rest of the family.
miamibass.basse: Here the bass and the kick are the same sound: the 808 kick tuned chromatically. Sample an 808 kick with a long decay, load it into Simpler or Sampler, and play it like a note. Dynamix II, in an interview for Roland, describes a 909 kick stuck onto the tail of an 808, put in a sampler and played at several pitches: that is the recipe. Write basslines in quarter and eighth notes on two or three notes, often root, fourth and fifth, in a low key like F or G. Tune the sample so the fundamental falls between 35 and 45 Hz. No synth on top: everything low comes from the 808. Check the sustain of each note on headphones and on a subwoofer.
etapes: Tempo at 130 BPM. Sample an 808 kick with a very long decay, load it into Simpler and tune it so low C falls around 40 Hz.
Play a three-note bassline in quarter and eighth notes with this sample, keeping the sustain of each note.
Add a clap and snare on 2 and 4 run through Redux at 12 bits, hi-hats in sixteenth notes, open hat on the "and" of 4.
Record a call-and-response chorus with several voices, shouted, and double them.
Program snare rolls in thirty-second notes before each section change and a breakdown where only the 808 plays.
Mix with the 808 on top, a 3 dB shelf at 50 Hz, and check on a subwoofer.
miamibass.mix: The mix reference is the car subwoofer. The 808 kick-bass must dominate: place it at -4 dBFS peak, everything else 6 dB below. Boost the 40 to 60 Hz zone with a 3 dB shelf, and cut below 30 Hz so you don't waste headroom. Compress the 808 on its own, 4:1 ratio, a slow 30 ms attack to keep the transient, 200 ms release, so that each note holds at the same level. The vocals are loud and compressed hard, 6:1 ratio. No reverb except a short delay on the shouts. Strict mono below 150 Hz. Listen to your mix on a subwoofer or with a sub enhancer: if the 808 disappears, the whole genre disappears with it.

outils.pourquoi: The kick with maximum decay, a second or more, tuned below 40 Hz: it is both the drums and the bass of the genre, set for the car subwoofer.
The 12-bit sampler that sequenced Luke Records productions and gave the claps and breakbeats their grain; imitate it with Redux at 12 bits and 26 kHz.
The scene's other sampler, for the breakbeats doubling the 808 on the choruses and the snare rolls built by hand.
Where Dynamix II stuck a 909 kick onto the tail of an 808 to replay it chromatically as a bassline on the keyboard.
Load a long 808 kick, tune it so the fundamental falls between 35 and 45 Hz, and play the bass in quarter and eighth notes like a note.
Bit depth reduced to around 12 and sample rate to around 26 kHz on claps and vocals to get the SP-1200 crunch without the machine.
A Roland Cloud pack of long, pre-tuned 808 kicks and dry claps, a quick starting point for a playable 808 bassline.

reperes: 2 Live Crew: Throw the D (1986): the sustained 808 kick as bass and the call-and-response vocals, the template of the genre.
Dynamix II: Just Give the DJ a Break (1987): the tuned 808 kick played as a bassline, with scratches at the ends of bars.
DJ Magic Mike: Drop the Bass (1989): the snare rolls and the sub dropping below 40 Hz.
Tag Team: Whoomp There It Is (1993): the radio version of the style, a chorus shouted by the crowd from the first minute.
miamibass.rythme: The 808 kick is the centerpiece, with the decay pushed to the maximum, a second or more, set to drop below 40 Hz. Typical pattern: kick on 1, on the "and" of 2 and on step 12, but each hit is a long note that almost overlaps the next. A dry 808 snare on 2 and 4, often replaced by an SP-1200 clap sampled at 12 bits for the grain. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, even velocities, open hat on the "and" of 4. Add snare rolls in thirty-second notes before section changes, a hallmark of the style. Breakbeats sampled on an SP-1200 or MPC60 sometimes double the 808 on the choruses.
miamibass.sons: The 12-bit SP-1200 and the Akai MPC60 give the grain: run your samples through Ableton's Redux with the bit depth reduced to around 12 and a sample rate of 26 kHz to imitate it. The vocals are shouted, in call and response, recorded as a group and often doubled: a leader, a crowd that answers. Scratches punctuate the ends of bars. The melodies are minimal, a synth stab or a two-note sample, because the space is taken by the sub. Sirens, lasers and whistles act as effects. The 808 cowbell and the bell remain present. On 1990s tracks, a pad or a sampled piano riff slips in, but the core remains vocals, 808 and clap.
sources: Roland Articles: Dynamix II, On Miami Bass, the TR-808, and Finding the Perfect Tempo (articles.roland.com)
sourcesOutils: Roland Articles (Dynamix II, On Miami Bass, the TR-808, and Finding the Perfect Tempo)
miamibass.tempo: Faster than its parents: between 120 and 135 BPM, with a sweet spot around 128 to 132 for club tracks, and up to 140 for later tracks. No swing on the grid, but a nervousness that comes from the hi-hat in sixteenth notes and the vocals shouted on every beat. The feel is that of an outdoor party: everything is loud, everything is upfront. Unlike electro-hop, the kick is no longer percussive but sustained: each hit lasts a dotted eighth or more, which gives the fast tempo a sense of heaviness. So program your bars thinking about the length of the kick notes, not just their position.

microhouse.arrangement: Six to eight minutes, but the arrangement happens at the level of detail. There is rarely a clear breakdown: elements come in and out in small touches every 4 or 8 bars. Start with the kick and three micro-sounds, add a new one every 8 bars up to twelve, then remove them in a different order. Luomo writes real songs: verse and chorus with a fragmented vocal that gradually reassembles itself. A good technique: record eight minutes of jamming with the mutes in Session view, then edit the result. The climax is often the moment when the bass holds a long note. End on the clicks alone, without kick, for 16 bars.
microhouse.basse: A soft, round sub, never aggressive: a pure sine or a triangle in Operator, with a 2 ms attack to avoid the click and a 100 ms release. The pattern is short, one or two notes, often on the offbeats as in house, but more discreet in the mix. With Luomo, the bass is almost a voice: long, gliding, with an 80 ms portamento between two notes. Stay in the octave between F0 and F1. A variant: a sung bass or a vocal fragment pitched down two octaves, run through a low-pass filter at 150 Hz. Light sidechain, 2 dB of reduction, so it dances with the kick without pumping.
etapes: Record ten minutes of radio or voices, then cut 30 fragments of 20 to 200 ms into a Drum Rack.
Tempo 123 BPM, a short kick on the beats, replace clap and hats with clicks and pops, 60% groove on everything.
Add a soft sine sub on one or two notes on the offbeats, light 2 dB sidechain.
Program twelve tracks of micro-sounds with two or three notes each, precisely panned, never all together.
Record an eight-minute jam with the mutes, then edit and tighten the result.
Mix with a discreet kick, high-pass at 300 Hz on the fragments, very light compression.
microhouse.mix: The microhouse mix is airy and detailed. The kick is not the loudest element: place it around -14 dBFS and let the micro-sounds occupy 2 to 8 kHz. High-pass at 300 Hz on all fragments, except the sub and the kick. Precise panning: each click has its place in the stereo field, between 40% left and 40% right, and the panning can move with Auto Pan at 0.1 Hz. No heavy compression on the bus: a Glue at 1.5:1 with a 30 ms attack is enough. Use a multiband compressor on the sub to keep it stable. The transients of the clicks must stay intact: no aggressive limiter, aim for -10 LUFS. A light tape or saturation on the master brings the organic side.

outils.pourquoi: Born at the same time as the genre: Session view to jam the mutes, warp to lock the fragments, the same groove on every track.
Slice a loop into 32 slices and keep the first twenty milliseconds of each: every pad becomes a click or a pop.
Via Max for Live, generate random click sequences and buffer players; the historical tool of the German glitch scene.
Robert Henke's Max for Live granulator: a vocal fragment becomes a shimmering texture, grains of 20 to 50 ms.
On the vocal fragments, spray and a random pitch of two semitones, low feedback, for glittering tails.
Record the radio, conversations or a room: Akufen carved his micro-samples out of hours of FM tape.
A soft sine sub between F0 and F1, 2 ms attack, 100 ms release, an 80 ms portamento for the Luomo-style sung bass.

reperes: Isolée: Beau Mot Plage (1999): a sampled guitar, a slow swing, details that come in one by one.
Luomo: Tessio (2000): a whole song in fragments, the voice reassembles itself as the minutes go by.
Farben: Discfunction (1998): Jan Jelinek cuts soul into confetti, the groove is in the pops.
Pantytec: Into The Duster (1998): the Perlon school, tiny sounds and a round bass, the model for 2000s minimal.
microhouse.rythme: A dry, very short kick (150 ms), often a filtered 909 sample or a kick synthesized in Operator with a sine and a fast pitch envelope. No straight clap: instead, clicks, pops, fragments of noise on beats 2 and 4, each 30 to 80 ms long. The hi-hat is replaced by noise cuts or bits of vinyl in sixteenth notes. The principle: each hit is a piece of something else, a consonant, a bit of radio, a tic. In Drum Rack, slice a loop into 32 slices and keep the first 20 milliseconds of each. Program at least twelve tracks of micro-sounds, each with two or three notes per bar, never all at once.
microhouse.sons: Microsampling is the central technique. Record the radio, conversations, records, then cut fragments of 20 to 200 ms and play them as notes in Simpler or Drum Rack. Granulation in Grain Delay or Granulator gives textures that shimmer. Vocals are chopped into syllables, spread across a bar, with a random pitch of plus or minus two semitones via the Random MIDI effect. Max/MSP and Max for Live are used to generate random sequences of clicks. Add a held chord, Juno or Analog, heavily filtered and distant, for warmth. Effects: a short ping-pong delay in sixteenth notes, a tiny 300 ms reverb on the clicks, a light chorus on the vocal fragments.
sourcesOutils: Paul Harkins, Microsampling: From Akufen's Microhouse to Todd Edwards (academic chapter)
microhouse.tempo: 120 to 126 BPM, slower than tech house, with a pronounced shuffle: 58 to 62% on the sixteenth notes. The feel is silky, almost swaying, because nearly every element sits on the sixteenth-note grid and the swing shifts them together. In Ableton, put the same groove on every track, not just the hats: a groove extracted from an old Chicago house record works very well. The micro-samples are so short that their placement makes the whole groove: shifting a click by 10 ms changes the feel. Listen to Isolée: the tempo seems to float because the elements breathe inside the swing.

microtechno.arrangement: Five to eight minutes, built on cycles rather than sections. Pick three pattern lengths, for example 16, 12 and 7 steps, and let them run: the point where they all line up again becomes your structure, here 336 steps, or 21 bars. Add or remove an element at each realignment. No breakdown in the DJ sense: a silence of exactly one bar, cut clean, serves as a breath. Brinkmann builds variations on a theme: the same loop with one parameter changing, over seven-minute tracks. Automate a single parameter per section, the pitch of a click or the speed of an LFO, in jumps, not curves. A clean ending, on an isolated click.
microtechno.basse: Pure sine waves. The bass is a sine at 45 or 55 Hz, with no harmonics, playing one note in eighth or sixteenth notes with very short envelopes (1 ms attack, 80 ms decay): a pulse more than a line. With Brinkmann, it can be a held drone modulated by a square LFO synced to the sixteenth note, which chops it. A second sine at 110 Hz, an octave higher, plays a 7-step pattern against the 16-step one to create a low-end polyrhythm. No filter, no saturation: the purity of the sine is the sound. In Operator, a single oscillator A set to sine, everything else at zero. Check the phase against the kick to avoid cancellations.
etapes: In Operator, build a 60 ms sine kick, a sine sub at 50 Hz and three clicks from filtered impulses at 1, 4 and 9 kHz.
Tempo 130 BPM, grid without swing, kick on the beats, clicks on cycles of 5, 7 and 16 steps.
Add a sine at 110 Hz on a 7-step pattern against the bass in eighth notes, and check the phases.
Generate a texture in Granulator or a Reaktor patch, very low, panned to the extreme.
Structure the track on the realignment points of the cycles, add or remove an element at each, cut clean at the end.
Mix without compression or reverb, spectrum hollowed out in the middle, export at 24 bits 48 kHz.
microtechno.mix: An austere, physical mix. The low sine sits in the center, around -10 dBFS, in mono, and it is what moves bodies. The clicks are at -20 dBFS but with their transients intact: no compression, no limiter on them. The spectrum has a hole: sub below 100 Hz, nothing between 150 Hz and 1 kHz, clicks and sines above. Calculated panning: left, right, center, without movement, or a square Auto Pan synced to the sixteenth note on a click. No reverb, no saturation. A safety limiter at -0.5 dBFS with no gain, aim for -12 LUFS. Export at 24 bits and 48 kHz minimum: the clicks contain highs that suffer from digital compression. The silence between events must be total.

outils.pourquoi: Patches of impulses run through a resonant filter, counters for cycles of 5, 7 and 16 steps; the tool of SND and Raster-Noton.
Pure sines, noise and envelopes driven by counters; build your own click generator rather than a synth.
A single sine oscillator, everything else at zero: a 60 ms kick, a sub at 50 Hz, a second sine at 110 Hz over 7 steps.
A grid without swing, sample-level editing to align phases, export at 24 bits and 48 kHz.
Brinkmann played scratched records with a second tonearm to create his offsets; a copy of the loop shifted by a sixteenth note and a half imitates it.
A granular texture from a noise sample, very low in the mix and panned to the extreme, the only non-sine material.
A square shape synced to the sixteenth note on a click: left, right, no transition, calculated panning.

reperes: Thomas Brinkmann: Isch (2000): clicks and a sine, a groove born from mechanical offsets.
SND: Travelog (2002): precisely measured rhythms on strange subdivisions, no fat, a real groove.
Robert Hood: Minus (1994): techno already reduced to a pulse and a 1.5-beat pattern, the starting point.
Alva Noto: Xerrox Phaser Acat 1 (2007): test signals as material, the Raster-Noton side.
microtechno.rythme: The kick is reduced to a short 50 to 80 ms sine, or to a filtered impulse, on every beat or only on 1 and 3. No snare: digital clicks of 2 to 10 ms, generated in Max/MSP or Reaktor by an impulse run through a resonant filter, on beats 2 and 4 and on isolated steps. The hi-hat is replaced by a very short filtered white noise in sixteenth notes, or by higher clicks. The basic pattern remains techno, but each element is reduced to its smallest audible form. Program three click voices at different pitches (1 kHz, 4 kHz, 9 kHz) on cycles of 5, 7 and 16 steps. Edit at the sample level to align the phases.
microtechno.sons: DSP and granulation, not traditional synths. Reaktor or Max/MSP to build a patch that generates impulses, sines and noise with envelopes controlled by counters. Granulator or Grain Delay on a noise sample for crackling textures. Held sines between 2 and 8 kHz, very low in the mix, serve as static harmonics. Alva Noto uses test signals (calibration tones, measurement impulses) as musical material. An extreme edit: cut a 1-second sample into 64 slices and replay them in a calculated order. The only accepted effect is a short sixteenth-note delay with no feedback, to double a click. No reverb, unless as a radical choice.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Minimal Techno and Step-sequences chapters, Robert Hood's 1.5-beat pattern)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Minimal Techno and Step-sequences chapters)
microtechno.tempo: 125 to 135 BPM, faster and straighter than microhouse: no swing, the grid is bare and that is intentional. The movement comes from mathematics: patterns of different lengths (5, 7, 12 steps) layered over the 16-step grid, which only line up again after dozens of bars. Brinkmann played records with two tonearms to create phase offsets; you can shift a copy of your loop by a sixteenth note and a half. With SND, the tempo seems unstable because events fall on unusual subdivisions, sixteenth-note triplets against straight time. Rigor is the groove.

minimalprog.arrangement: Nine to eleven minutes. Structure by subtraction: start with kick, bass and pluck together, then remove elements rather than add them. A 32-bar intro, the bass coming in at 33, the delayed pluck at 65. The breakdown is long, 32 bars, without kick, where the pad and delays fill all the space and the bass filter closes and then reopens. The kick's return at bar 161 is soft, without a roll. The second half repeats the first with a transposed pattern or a different bass note. Filter automation over 64 bars everywhere, never over fewer than 16. A 32-bar outro with the delays draining away. Nothing should ever surprise.
minimalprog.basse: The round, sustained bass carries everything. A saw or square oscillator in Analog or a Juno clone, low-pass filter at 200 Hz, resonance 15%, with a held note in eighth or sixteenth notes on the root, F1 or A1, note length 80%, almost legato. A second sine oscillator an octave below for the sub. The pattern changes one note every 4 or 8 bars: the minor third or the seventh, never more. Gentle sidechain, 250 ms release, 3 dB. A very light chorus widens the bass above 200 Hz. The filter cutoff is automated over 64 bars, from 200 Hz to 800 Hz, and that slow opening is what replaces the build-up.
etapes: Tempo 122 BPM, a round kick with no click, hi-hat in eighth notes on the offbeats, a soft rimshot on 2 and 4, groove at zero.
Program the round bass in eighth notes on F1, notes at 80%, a sine sub below, gentle sidechain, filter automated from 200 to 800 Hz over 64 bars.
Write a three-note pattern on a soft pluck and send it into a dotted eighth / quarter note dub delay, 45% feedback.
Add very quiet ghost percussion of which you only hear the delays, and a heavily filtered minor pad.
Arrange ten minutes by subtraction, a 32-bar breakdown without kick, a soft return, automation never under 16 bars.
Mix kick and bass at the same level, the rest 12 dB below, long reverb on a return, low-pass at 12 kHz on the master.
minimalprog.mix: A deep, soft mix with no aggression. Kick around -12 dBFS, bass at the same level, the kick-bass pair making up 70% of the energy. Everything else is 12 dB lower and lives in the delays and reverbs. A long reverb, 3 to 5 seconds, on a return, with a high-pass at 400 Hz, fed by the pluck and the ghost percussion at 20%. Delays filtered in their loop so they get darker with each repeat. A gentle low-pass at 12 kHz on the master for a muffled feel. Light compression on the bus, Glue at 2:1 with a 30 ms attack. Aim for -10 LUFS with plenty of dynamics. Mono below 150 Hz, but generous width above, the delays in stereo ping-pong.

outils.pourquoi: Groove at zero, filter automation over 64 bars, synced delays: the movement comes from curves, not placement.
The round, sustained bass: saw or square, filter at 200 Hz, resonance 15%, a sine an octave below for the sub.
Pads and basses with its chorus; the TAL-U-NO-LX emulation replaces the machine in most prog studios.
A soft three-note pluck, attack 0, 300 ms decay, filter at 1 kHz, sent into the dub delay.
Dotted eighth on the left, quarter note on the right, 45% feedback, low-pass at 3 kHz in the loop: the delay that fills the grid.
A 3 to 5 second reverb on a return, high-pass at 400 Hz, fed by the pluck and the ghost percussion.
Chops a chord into rhythmic grains and drives crossfader scenes over ten minutes; Simpler in slice mode does the same.
A round kick with no click, 300 ms decay, a soft rimshot on 2 and 4: the 909 filtered rather than raw.

reperes: Nathan Fake: The Sky Was Pink (Holden mix) (2004): a ten-minute build through filter and delay, the model of the genre.
Trentemoller: Moan (2006): the round, sustained bass, the distant voice, the patience of the construction.
Extrawelt: Soopertrack (2007): a three-note pattern that keeps turning, the movement comes only from the delays.
Fairmont: Gazebo (2005): the Border Community side, a stripped-down melody and a plateau arrangement.
minimalprog.rythme: A round 909 kick, no click, 300 ms decay, on every beat. No straight clap: a rimshot or a soft click on 2 and 4, very low. The closed hi-hat plays eighth notes on the offbeats, soft, with an open hat that appears only in the high sections. Ghost percussion is the signature: very short, very quiet sounds (block, muffled conga, beep) placed on isolated sixteenth notes, at 30% volume, often audible only through their delays. A shaker in sixteenth notes with a slow fade-in over 8 bars. A low tom on the last step of every 2 bars. Program few notes and send them into synced delays: the repeats are what fill the grid.
minimalprog.sons: A two or three note pattern played by a soft pluck (Wavetable, attack 0, 300 ms decay, filter at 1 kHz) sent into a synced dub delay, dotted eighth on the left and quarter note on the right, 45% feedback, with a low-pass at 3 kHz in the loop. A discreet pad, a minor chord with a fifth, 2-second attack, heavily filtered, in the background. Field recording textures (rain, wind) run through a big reverb. An Octatrack or a Simpler in slice mode to chop a chord into rhythmic grains. A single-note held lead that rises over 64 bars with a filter and volume, like a riser that lasts half the track. No sound is bright: everything is kept below 6 kHz.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Movement & Change chapter, long automation and filter LFOs)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Movement & Change chapter)
Transition Studio (Top 10 Plugins for Progressive House & Melodic Techno)
Ableton Templates (Hernan Cattaneo, Cid Inc Style Progressive House)
minimalprog.tempo: 120 to 124 BPM, the slowest in the family along with microhouse, and the straightest feel: little or no swing, 52% at most, because the movement comes from delays and automation, not from note placement. The pulse is round and steady, made for warm-ups and long sets. What distinguishes minimal prog from minimal tech is patience: nothing changes before 16 bars, and often 32. In Ableton, leave the groove at zero and work instead with slight delay offsets: an Echo set to a dotted eighth on a percussion creates the sway. Think of the track as a landscape crossed slowly.

minimaltech.arrangement: Ten to twelve minutes, with no drop structure. The track is a stretch that evolves as details circulate in the stereo field. Start with kick, sub and a click; add a micro-percussion every 8 bars; once six or seven elements are running, start removing one while you add another. The breakdown is a reduction to 16 bars of sub and delays without kick. Automate the panning of the percussion with Auto Pan at different speeds (0.05 Hz, 0.08 Hz) so everything circulates. Duplicate the loop across the whole length, then, in each 8-bar block, change one note or one sample. The track doesn't peak: it drifts.
minimaltech.basse: A round sub bass, more present than in microhouse. A sine or a triangle in Operator, with a little soft saturation for harmonics, plays sixteenth or eighth notes on a single note, F1 or G1, with gaps on the beats. The fake sidechain technique works well: instead of a compressor, draw a volume automation that dips 6 dB over the 100 ms following each kick. A second pattern comes in every 4 bars with a passing note, the fourth or the seventh. The swing also applies to the bass, unlike tech house. Low-pass filter at 250 Hz, resonance 10%, cutoff modulated very slowly by an LFO over 8 bars.
etapes: Tempo 126 BPM, a round kick on every beat with Boom around 46 Hz, closed hi-hat on the offbeats, swing groove at 55%.
Add a sub in sixteenth notes on one note with gaps on the beats and a fake sidechain drawn as automation.
Program a low tom, a click on the sixteen steps and a wood block, all with Velocity Random at 15.
Send a percussion into an Echo set to a dotted eighth at 100% wet, filtered between 300 Hz and 4 kHz.
Make the percussion circulate with Auto Pan at different speeds and stretch to ten minutes, replacing one element every 8 bars.
Mix warm: kick and sub up front, percussion 10 dB below, light tape saturation on the master.
minimaltech.mix: The mix is warm and centered on the low mids. Kick around -12 dBFS, sub just below, everything else 10 dB lower. A Drum Buss on the percussion, Boom at 50% around 46 Hz, comp on, to glue the small sounds. The delays are filtered between 300 Hz and 4 kHz so they don't clog the mix. A short reverb, 0.6 s, only on the clap and the wood block. The stereo field is wide for the percussion but mono below 150 Hz. Parallel compression on the drum group, 10 ms attack, 100 ms release, 30% mix. No aggressive limiter, aim for -10 LUFS, to keep the swing of the transients. A little tape saturation on the master makes the whole thing rounder.

outils.pourquoi: A groove extracted from an old Chicago record or Notator 16B Swing, Random at 5% in the Groove Pool, Auto Pan everywhere.
Dry digital beeps, clicks and toms, with its per-track LFOs: the grain of the Perlon and Minus micro-percussion of the 2000s.
A round kick on every beat, often via Roland Cloud; the clap replaced by a rimshot or a block.
The discreet dub delay: dotted eighth, 30% feedback, filtered between 300 Hz and 4 kHz, at 100% wet on a percussion.
Boom at 50% around 46 Hz on the percussion group, comp on, to glue the small sounds to the kick.
A sine or triangle sub in sixteenth notes on F1, with the fake sidechain drawn as volume automation.
MIDI effects on the click and the tom: Random at 15 on velocity, a 10% chance on pitch, nothing stays static.
Two or three percussion parts at different speeds, 0.05 and 0.08 Hz, so the details circulate in the stereo field.

reperes: Daniel Bell: Baby Judy (1995): a groove made of almost nothing, a pitched voice, the origin of the Perlon sound.
Plastikman: Ping Pong (2003): delays bouncing from one ear to the other over a bare loop.
Richie Hawtin: Minus Orange (1998): Minus precision, a kick, a beep, and the movement in the stereo field.
Chris Stussy: Blueprint (2024): the current reinterpretation, more house, with the same rolling micro-percussion.
minimaltech.rythme: A round kick, 909 or synthesized, on every beat, with a slight boost of the fundamental around 46 Hz in Drum Buss. A discreet clap on 2 and 4, often replaced by a rimshot or a block. The heart is the micro-percussion: a low tom in sixteenth notes with gaps where the kick hits, a click filling the sixteen steps with random velocities, a wood block on three steps every two quarter notes. A Machinedrum or its samples give this dry digital grain. The closed hi-hat plays on the offbeats, very short decay. Make the velocities move with the Velocity MIDI effect, Random at 15, and the pitch with Random at a 10% chance so nothing is static.
minimaltech.sons: The sounds are small, dry and numerous. The discreet dub delay is the signature: an Echo set to a dotted eighth, 30% feedback, with a high-pass filter at 300 Hz and a low-pass at 4 kHz in the loop, set to 100% wet on a percussion so you only hear the bounces. An organic click (wood, clock, finger) run through an Auto Filter with a slow LFO at 6 kHz comes alive on its own. A Machinedrum, or Ableton's factory samples, provides short digital beeps and noises. A two-note chord, held and heavily filtered, very far back in the mix, gives depth. Villalobos uses pitched fragments of voices or field recordings. Vinyl crackle across the whole bar adds a pad.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Deep Techno, Movement & Change chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Deep Techno, Movement & Change chapters)
Red Bull Music Academy Daily (Playhouse: An Interview With Ricardo Villalobos)
minimaltech.tempo: 124 to 127 BPM, with the heaviest swing in the family after microhouse: 58 to 62% on the sixteenth notes, applied to the hats, the percussion and often the bass. This meaty swing is the difference from Hood's minimal, which is straighter. The feel is that of an afterparty: it rolls, it sways, without ever pushing. In Ableton, a groove extracted from an old Chicago record, or Notator 16B Swing between 40 and 60%, gives this result. Add a little timing randomness (Random at 5% in the Groove Pool) so the percussion never lands the same way twice. The track must be able to run for ten minutes without getting tiresome.

minimaltechno.arrangement: A minimal track lasts seven to ten minutes and lives on a single loop that transforms. Structure in 32-bar blocks: 32 of kick and sub for the DJ, the hi-hat and wood block coming in, then the pluck. The breakdown is not a dramatic silence but a subtraction: remove the kick for 8 or 16 bars and let the sub and percussion run. Automate a single parameter over 64 bars, the pluck cutoff for example, from 400 Hz to 4 kHz. Duplicate your one-bar loop eight times and change one note in each copy. End the way you started, kick and sub alone, for the next mix. Nothing rises, everything circulates.
minimaltechno.basse: The minimal bass is a sub that pulses between the kicks, not a melodic line. Tune everything to a single note, for example G# or F, kick included: in Simpler, transpose by a few semitones until kick and sub merge. Place the sub on steps 4, 7, 12 and 15 of a sixteen-step grid, so just before or after the kicks, never on them. A sine LFO synced to the sixteenth note on the volume gives a tremolo that breathes. For the Hood version, take an SH-101 or a clone in Operator, square wave, low-pass filter closed around 200 Hz, and sequence one note over a length of three sixteenth notes to create an offset against the kick.
etapes: Set Ableton to 129 BPM, pick a key (F or G#) and create a one-bar loop with a kick on every beat.
Add a sub tuned to the same note, placed between the kicks on steps 4, 7, 12 and 15, with a volume LFO at the sixteenth note.
Lay down a hi-hat in eighth notes, a wood block and an 808 tom: six sounds in total, then apply an MPC groove at 60%.
Sequence a one or two note pluck over 1.5 beats and listen to the loop run for three minutes without touching anything.
Compress the drum bus in parallel (Glue 40%, Drum Buss 45%) and check the tuning of all the low end.
Unfold over eight minutes by subtraction: mute and bring back, automate a single filter over 64 bars.
minimaltechno.mix: The kick is the reference, around -12 dBFS peak, everything else below it. On the drum bus, a Glue Compressor with a slow 30 ms attack and a ratio of 10, mixed in at only 40%: the transients get through, the body settles. After it, a Drum Buss with soft drive at 25% and Boom at 30% tuned to the fundamental of your key, 43.7 Hz for F, in parallel at 45%. Check the tuning of everything low: in a genre this bare, a sub detuned by a semitone is heard immediately. High-pass at 30 Hz on the master, no reverb in the low end, and keep 6 dB of headroom before the limiter. The stereo image stays narrow, the movement comes from time, not width.

outils.pourquoi: The kick on every beat and the hi-hat in eighth notes come from it; today you go through Roland Cloud TR-909 or D16 Drumazon 2.
Robert Hood's mono synth, bought at a pawnshop: a square pluck sequenced over 1.5 beats, or its emulation TAL-BassLine-101.
The Groove Pool with MPC 16 Double Down at 60% gives the machine offset, and Session view is for jamming the mutes.
A sine for the sub tuned to the fundamental, or a square filtered at 200 Hz to clone the 101 without hardware.
On the drum bus in parallel at 45%, Boom tuned to the fundamental (43.7 Hz for F), soft drive at 25%.
A slow 30 ms attack, ratio 10, mixed in at 40%: the transients get through and the body of the loop settles.
Its quantization at 60% swing on sixteenth notes is the reference minimal groove, used as is in Live.
For Hawtin's acid version, a three-note line, low resonance; a TT-303 clone or a Behringer TD-3 does the job.

reperes: Robert Hood: Museum (1994): a single loop, a pluck and a kick, all the movement comes from what is removed and brought back.
Plastikman: Spastik (1993): a drum machine alone, snare rolls that speed up, no bass or melody.
X-102: Phoebe (1992): the precision of Mills and Hood before Minimal Nation, the rigor of the grid as an aesthetic.
Boris Brejcha: Happinezz (2019): the modern, melodic version, more elements but the same short-pattern logic.
minimaltechno.rythme: A four-on-the-floor kick on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 of a sixteenth-note grid, and that is almost all. Take a 909 kick or an acoustic kick, cut the click above 1 kHz and bring up a little body around 160 Hz. Two layers are enough: a low one, and an airy one of which you keep only the tail with a 250 ms fade-in. Add a wood block on the beats and on two offbeats, a low 808 tom on a single step, and a hi-hat in eighth notes duplicated with two different start points to create a sway. Six sounds maximum. If you mute an element and nothing is missing, delete it. The clap is often absent.
minimaltechno.sons: A palette of six sounds, chosen for their character: a little dirt in the waveform, a little room air, a slow modulation. The synth, if there is one, plays a short pluck: Wavetable or Operator, 0 ms attack, 120 ms decay, no sustain, sequenced over 1.5 beats so the pattern realigns every three bars. On a wood block, a very slow LFO at 0.07 Hz on the pitch imitates an old machine drifting out of tune. The Velocity MIDI effect with Random at 5 makes each kick slightly different. Discreet effects: a ping-pong delay set to a dotted eighth at 100% wet on a click, a short reverb on the wood block, nothing on the kick. No pad, no vocal.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Minimal Techno, Step-sequences, Movement & Change chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Minimal Techno, Step-sequences, Ask the Pros chapters)
Magnetic Magazine (Essential Plugins for Producing Minimal Techno)
minimaltechno.tempo: Between 128 and 130 BPM, the zone of Hood and Hawtin. The groove doesn't come from a classic swing but from a machine offset: in Ableton, load an MPC 16-type groove at 60%, it delays and softens some of the sixteenth notes. The feel stays straight, almost dry, and all the movement lies in micro-variations: a velocity that shifts by five values, a sample that starts a little later. Think in one-bar loops, not four-bar patterns. If you want it harder, go up to 132, but never go below 126. Your loop must hold for thirty seconds without getting tiresome before you add anything.

minimalwave.arrangement: A 3 to 5 minute song: a 4 or 8-bar intro with the drum machine and bass, a 16-bar verse with the vocal, an 8-bar chorus with the synth chord, a second verse, chorus, an instrumental bridge where the synth melody plays alone, a last chorus, an abrupt ending or a fade. No build-up, no club breakdown: the structure is that of pop. The drum machine never stops except perhaps for one bar before the last chorus. Add a second voice to the chorus or a countermelody. Record live: synth and vocal played in one take, with the mistakes. Four tracks maximum: drums, bass, synth, vocal.
minimalwave.basse: The bass is a monophonic synth, MS-20, SH-101 or Pro-One, with a saw or square wave, a resonant low-pass filter around 400 Hz and a short envelope. It plays repeated eighth or sixteenth notes on the root, sometimes with an octave jump, sequenced on an SQ-10 or played by hand. The basslines are simple and cold: root, fifth, minor third, over chords that change every 2 bars. No sub: cut below 60 Hz. A chorus (Juno or pedal) widens the bass. Unlike the whole minimal family, the bass is a melodic line that carries the song, not a pulse that carries the kick.
etapes: Tempo 118 BPM, a TR-606 or its samples: kick on the beats, snare on 2 and 4 with an eighth-note echo, hi-hat in eighth notes, a single pattern.
Program or play a monophonic bass in eighth notes on an MS-20 or a clone, resonant filter around 400 Hz, with chorus.
Write a three-chord progression on a Juno or a Poly-800 and a one-note melody repeated in the high octave.
Record a deadpan vocal, without vibrato, in one take, with a short echo and a spring reverb.
Arrange as a song: intro, verse 16, chorus 8, verse, chorus, instrumental bridge, chorus, ending.
Run everything through a four-track cassette simulation, dry and narrow mix, -16 LUFS, no limiter.
minimalwave.mix: The mix is a 1982 bedroom mix: dry, narrow, a little dull. Record or run everything through a cassette simulation (hiss, low-pass around 12 kHz, light saturation, wow). No sidechain, no modern compression: a single gentle compressor on the vocal, 3:1 ratio. The drum machine is mono in the center, the bass next to it, the synth slightly left, the vocal in the center with an echo on the right. Little low end: high-pass at 60 Hz on everything. Spring reverb or a short plate on the vocal and snare. Low level, -16 LUFS, with dynamics. The result should sound like a cassette found in a box, not like a master. If it's too clean, it has failed.

outils.pourquoi: Basses in eighth notes, resonant filter around 400 Hz, noises and synthesized drums; the MS-20 mini or Arturia MS-20 V replace it.
A thin kick and a noisy snare, a single one-bar pattern; the CR-78 and the Boss DR-55 play the same role.
The bedroom four-track cassette recorder: hiss, wow and natural compression, drums, bass, synth and vocal, one track each.
The analog sequencer companion to the MS-20: twelve repeated bass steps, octave jumps by hand during the take.
A cheap 1982 polyphonic for the three chorus chords, built-in chorus, no memory so it is played live.
The other affordable polyphonic of 1983 to 1985, thin and cold sounds, perfect for a verse pad.
Naive one-note melodies repeated in the high octave and a toy drum machine: the Solid Space sound.
A cassette simulation to run the whole mix through: low-pass around 12 kHz, light saturation, wow, when you don't have a Portastudio.

reperes: Crash Course in Science: Flying Turns (1981): a stiff drum machine, toy synths and a barking voice, the bare sound.
Oppenheimer Analysis: The Devil's Dancers (1982): the cold pop song, bass sequence and deadpan vocal, bedroom production.
Martin Dupont: Just Because (1984): the French version, naive melodies and cassette, the reference for vocals.
Solid Space: Destination Moon (1982): Casio and a cheap drum machine, the cassette spirit in all its simplicity.
minimalwave.rythme: A primitive drum machine and nothing else: TR-606, CR-78, DR-55, or their samples. A thin analog kick, no sub, on beats 1 and 3 or on every beat. A 606 snare, short and noisy, on 2 and 4, often with an analog echo in eighth notes to widen it. Closed hi-hat in eighth or sixteenth notes, open on the offbeat of beat 4. A single one-bar pattern, rarely varied, sometimes a snare fill in sixteenth notes every 8 bars. If you don't have a drum machine, synthesize your drums in an MS-20 or Operator: a sine with falling pitch for the kick, white noise filtered at 2 kHz with a 100 ms decay for the snare.
minimalwave.sons: Monophonic synths and one cheap polyphonic: MS-20 for basses and noises, Juno-6 or Poly-800 for chords, Casio for naive melodies. Simple sounds, one waveform, one filter, no effects except a chorus and a tape echo. A repeated one or two note synth melody, in the high octave, square wave without resonance. The vocals are deadpan, spoken or sung without vibrato, often in French or German, with a short echo and a spring reverb. The four-track cassette recorder is an instrument: record your tracks onto it (or through a tape simulation) for the hiss, the wow and the natural compression. A little tape saturation on everything.
sources: Wave Alchemy (MS-20 mini Drum Synthesis Guide)
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (Synth pop people, what's your gear?)
Wave Alchemy (MS-20 mini Drum Synthesis Guide)
minimalwave.tempo: Between 100 and 130 BPM, often 110 to 125: this is bedroom pop, not club music. No swing: 1980 drum machines couldn't swing, and the stiff feel is part of the charm. The tempo is often a little unstable because the machines weren't synced: a synth played by hand over a running drum machine. To reproduce this, play your synth lines live without quantizing, or quantize at only 70%. Song structure: verses and choruses, 3 to 5 minutes. The rhythm can also be a very slow 4/4, 90 BPM, for the coldest tracks.

morningfullon.arrangement: Morning full-on is built around an emotional breakdown. A 32-bar intro with kick, bass and hi-hats. A first 32-bar section with an arpeggiated pluck. First breakdown around bar 96: kick cut, major pad, ethereal vocal, the main melody exposed alone over a pad, for 16 to 32 bars, then a 16-bar build-up with a roll, riser and filter, and the drop with the Sylenth1 lead over the bass. A longer second breakdown, with a variation of the melody and a piano chord, a bigger build-up, a final drop with all the layers. A 32-bar outro. Aim for 8 minutes. An anthem is recognized by its first build-up: take more care over it than anything else.
morningfullon.basse: The softened full-on bass of the brief: the pattern is still kick then three sixteenth notes, but with less distortion and more roundness. On Sylenth1 or Serum, a sawtooth filtered at 250 Hz, low resonance, medium filter envelope, very light tube saturation. Notes of 80 ms, soft release. The bass follows the chords of the melody, which is rare in psy: when the pad moves from the root to the subdominant, the bass changes note too. A bright major or relative minor key: A major, F# minor, D major. A separate sine sub. Gentle sidechain from the kick, 80 ms release, gives a light pumping that suits the pads.
etapes: Project at 140 BPM in A major. A round kick tuned to A around 55 Hz, a soft snare on 2 and 4 with a 1 s reverb.
Softened rolling bass on A1: kick then three 80 ms sixteenth notes, sawtooth filtered at 250 Hz, light tube saturation, gentle sidechain.
