Write a 4-chord progression in A major on a wide pad, and make the bass follow the chord changes.
Create a 6-voice unison Sylenth1 lead and a singing 8-bar melody in eighth and quarter notes, dotted eighth delay.
Record or sample a vocal, run it through a 4 s reverb and an octave pitch shifter, place it in the breakdown with a piano.
Arrange 8 minutes around two emotional breakdowns with 16-bar build-ups (roll, riser, filter).
morningfullon.mix: The mix is bright and wide. Kick and bass mono below 150 Hz, with the gentle sidechain. The leads and pads are very wide, widened by a chorus and a stereo utility, but their mono sum must stay correct: check it. The vocals have a high-pass at 300 Hz and a long reverb on a send. Bus compression on the drums, 4:1 ratio. The limiter on the master aims for -7 LUFS, like full-on, but with more dynamics kept in the breakdowns: automate the limiter's input gain so the breakdown is 2 dB lower and the drop hits. A master EQ with a slight bump at 10 kHz gives the morning light.

outils.pourquoi: The synth of the genre: bright major leads made of unison sawtooths, arpeggiated plucks, light on the CPU. Hundreds of psy presets exist.
Softened full-on bass, a sawtooth filtered at 250 Hz, and build-up FX: white noise sweeps, sine risers over 8 bars.
Arranging 8 to 16-bar build-ups, automating the limiter's input gain so the drop hits after the breakdown.
The scene's other DAW, still dominant among the Israeli producers of Hom-Mega, for MIDI programming of the leads.
A long 4 s reverb on the ethereal vocals and breakdown pads, on a send, with a high-pass at 300 Hz on the return.
Sampled or recorded female vocals, corrected then doubled an octave up, for the isolated words in the breakdowns.
A bright, wide master: a slight bump at 10 kHz, a stereo imager on the highs, limiter around -7 LUFS.

reperes: Ace Ventura: Rebirth (2008): the emotional breakdown and the rising major melody, a reference of the genre.
Vini Vici: The Tribe (2015): the ethereal vocal and the build-up that prepares a drop recognizable from the first note.
Astrix: Deep Jungle Walk (2016): the softened full-on bass under a bright melody, current production.
Infected Mushroom: Bust A Move (2000): the ancestor, still nocturnal in its sound but already euphoric in its melody.
morningfullon.rythme: The kick is round, less piercing than the night full-on kick: tuned around 55 Hz, a 150 ms body, a moderate click. A soft snare or clap on 2 and 4, with a slightly longer reverb than usual (1 s) for brightness. Hi-hats on the offbeats, a clear open hat on the "and" of 2 and 4, ride during the plateaus, generous crashes on the restarts. The percussion is light: shakers, tambourines, discreet congas in sixteenth notes. The snare rolls are long, 8 to 16 bars, with a high-pass filter that opens and a velocity crescendo, because the build-up is the central moment of the genre. Add impacts and reversed cymbals on the drops.
morningfullon.sons: Sylenth1 is the synth of the genre: bright major leads made of unison sawtooths, 4 to 8 voices, low-pass filter open, with a dotted eighth delay and a long reverb. Play singing melodies in eighth and quarter notes, in major, rising toward the third and the fifth. The pads are wide and warm, with chorus. Ethereal vocals: a sampled or recorded female voice, run through a 4 s reverb, a delay and a pitch shifter an octave up, played as isolated words or "ah" sounds. Bright plucks in sixteenth-note arpeggios on the chord. Serum is used for build-up FX: white noise sweeps, sine risers over 8 bars. Nothing dark: even the FX are bright.
sourcesOutils: Dance Midi Samples, Spectro Senses Sylenth1 Psytrance banks
Myloops, Top 15 VST Plugins for Psytrance Production
morningfullon.tempo: Morning full-on slows down slightly compared to night full-on: 138 to 143 BPM, with 140 as the center. The grid stays straight, but the energy changes: the classic rolling bass often replaces the gallop, more regular, softer, and the track breathes more. What distinguishes it from full-on is the major key and the slightly lower tempo. What distinguishes it from uplifting trance is that the psy bass in sixteenth notes remains the engine, not the trance offbeat bass, and that the kick remains a tuned psy kick. Count in 32 bars. A track lasts 7 to 8 minutes and aims for the sunrise.

musiqueconcrete.arrangement: A concrète study lasts 3 to 12 minutes and is organized in contrasting sections rather than build-ups. Think in tableaux: a first tableau on a single object explored from every angle (speed, direction, filter), a second tableau that brings in another object and makes them converse, a third tableau of saturation where everything is layered, then an abrupt return to silence or to the bare initial object. Transitions are made by hard cuts, never by an 8-bar fade. What makes the piece listenable is repetition: a recognizable loop that comes back three times gives the audience something to hold on to. Symphonie pour un homme seul strings together short, clearly separated movements in this way, worth listening to as a model of structure.
musiqueconcrete.basse: No played bass, but a manufactured one. Take any recorded sound, an engine, a voice, a rumble, and slow it down by two or three octaves in Simpler with Warp mode turned off: the pitch drops with the speed, exactly like a tape recorder switched from 38 to 9.5 cm/s. You get a textured low mass, far more alive than a sine wave. Filter above 200 Hz with EQ Eight so only the foundation remains. Bring it in in waves with slow volume automation, with no repeated note. If you want to converse with club music, add an Operator sine holding a low C (C1), and let the concrete sound modulate its volume via an Envelope Follower.
etapes: Record 20 minutes of everyday sounds with your phone: kitchen, street, transport, doors.
Import everything into Ableton, cut five short objects and seven long ones, name them after what they evoke.
Load the short objects into Simpler in Slice mode and program three loops of different lengths (3, 5 and 7 beats).
Slow down a long object by two octaves for the bass, and reverse another for a backdrop.
Edit five tableaux in Arrangement view, with clean cuts, no fades.
Mix with extreme panning, a reverb on a return, and export without a limiter.
musiqueconcrete.mix: The mix must keep the dynamics: no limiter crushing everything. Aim for peaks at -6 dBFS and a low average level, around -20 LUFS, so the silences carry weight. The essential processing is placement in space: hard panning, one object fully left, another fully right, then automated movements with Auto Pan at a very slow speed (0.05 Hz). Use EQ to isolate narrow bands, for example a band-pass from 800 to 1200 Hz on a train recording, which makes it abstract. Gentle compression (2:1 ratio, 30 ms attack) on the main bus glues the fragments back together. Keep the hiss and the editing clicks: perfect cleanup kills the genre.

outils.pourquoi: The founding tool of the GRM: you cut the tape with scissors, flip it, change the speed from 38 to 19 cm/s to drop an octave.
Schaeffer's keyboard loop player: twelve playback speeds to transpose a recorded fragment, the direct ancestor of Simpler in Classic mode.
The first sampler: a record cut with a groove that closes on itself repeats a sound endlessly, the loop before tape.
Today's editing and transposition: Warp off, Reverse and Slice reproduce the three historical gestures, slowing down, reversal, cutting.
The GRM's own plugins: Shuffling, Freeze, Comb Filters and Doppler extend tape manipulation into the digital domain, widely used in electroacoustic teaching.
The material comes from the real world: capture doors, trains and kitchens at 24 bits, or with a phone if nothing better is at hand, before cutting.
To stretch and granulate a sound object: high Spray and random Pitch turn a creaking door into a cloud, without an external plugin.
Tape grain and record crackle: Saturator in Analog Clip to round off, Vinyl Distortion in small doses to dirty up the silence.

reperes: Pierre Schaeffer: Étude aux chemins de fer (1948): the locomotive loop, mechanical rhythm becoming music through repetition and cutting.
Pierre Henry: Variations pour une porte et un soupir (1963): a single sound object varied across an entire record, a lesson in sound design through variation.
Pierre Henry: Psyché Rock (1967): concrète montage laid over rock drums and bass, a direct bridge to the dance floor.
Bernard Parmegiani: L'Instant mobile (1975): the articulation of sounds in the stereo field and the sense of gesture.
musiqueconcrete.rythme: The rhythm is born from the sound objects themselves: a locomotive, a creaking door, a sigh. Record everything that slams, rubs or whistles around you with your phone or a portable recorder. In Ableton, drop each sound into Simpler and slice it (Slice mode). A car door becomes your snare, a faucet your hi-hat. Then program a short pattern, three or four hits, and loop it with an odd clip length: 3 beats, 7 sixteenth notes. Reverse every other slice (Reverse) and halve the playback speed to get a low hit. Reversal, speed change and the clean cut are the three historical gestures of scissors and tape.
musiqueconcrete.sons: The material is the recorded world. The machines in the brief are the tape recorder, the turntables and the phonogène (a keyboard that changes the playback speed of a loop). Today, these three tools fit into Simpler and Sampler: transposition, looping, reverse playback. The tape grain can be recreated with Saturator in Analog Clip mode and a little Vinyl Distortion for crackle. The key gesture remains scissor editing: cut your recordings into fragments of 50 to 500 milliseconds and paste them end to end in Arrangement view without crossfades. The splice click is part of the style. Add a Grain Delay for stretching and a long Reverb (4 to 8 seconds) on a return, used sparingly, to reveal the space of a sound.
musiqueconcrete.tempo: There is no tempo in the dance sense: musique concrète is thought of in durations and gestures, not BPM. Yet Schaeffer invented the loop with the locked groove, and a loop has a duration that becomes a pulse. In your DAW, turn off the grid or set it to an arbitrary tempo (for example 100 BPM) only so that your loops stay aligned with each other. The feel comes from irregularity: a 1.7-second loop against a 2.3-second one creates a cycle that only repeats after many minutes. If you want one foot on the dance floor, keep a rhythmic drone at 120 BPM under your montage, as Pierre Henry did in Psyché Rock.

ndh.arrangement: A song format calibrated for stadiums, 3 minutes 30 to 4 minutes 30. An intro on the electronic sequence alone or on a guitar riff, 8 bars. Verse: sequence, synth bass, vocal, stripped-back drums. Pre-chorus: the drums build. Chorus: wall of guitars, choirs, everything together. Second verse, chorus, a calm bridge with piano or pad, a doubled last chorus, a clean ending. The contrast between the electronic verse and the guitar chorus is the main mechanism: the emptier the verse, the harder the chorus hits. Plan one beat of silence before the first chorus. Everything is designed to be sung along.
ndh.basse: The bass follows the guitar in unison. The guitars are tuned low, drop C or drop B, and play palm-muted eighth notes on the root. The electric bass doubles them exactly, with light distortion. Underneath, a square synth bass (Nord Lead or Analog) plays the same note an octave lower in sixteenth notes, which gives the machine feel under the wall of guitars. The lines are simple: root, minor second, diminished fifth, back. High-pass the electric bass at 60 Hz, and let the synth bass hold the sub. Light sidechain from the kick on the synth only.
etapes: At 110 BPM, program metal drums: kick on quarter notes, a huge snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes, with a saturated 909 kick under the acoustic kick.
Write a sixteenth-note sawtooth sequence on Analog or a Nord Lead, on a single note, running the whole time.
Record or program a guitar riff in drop C, palm-muted eighth notes, doubled on each side, with a high-gain amp simulator.
Add an electric bass in unison and a square synth bass an octave lower.
Record a deep, declaimed vocal, 6:1 compression, short room reverb, and write a chorus to be sung along.
Arrange over 4 minutes: empty electronic verse, wall-of-guitars chorus, calm bridge, doubled last chorus.
ndh.mix: A modern metal mix, dense and loud. Quadruple-tracked guitars, panned hard left and right, cut below 100 Hz and above 10 kHz. The acoustic kick and the 909 kick aligned in phase, the sum stays centered. Snare with parallel compression. The vocal is in the center, compressed in two stages, with a de-esser. The electronic sequence sits between 1 and 4 kHz, where the guitars leave a gap: carve it deliberately into the guitars with a -3 dB bell. Master bus: 2:1 compression then a limiter. Aim for -8 LUFS, it is a loud genre. The synth bass is the only element below 60 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: A high-gain amp simulator for drop C guitars, doubled on each side, with a high-pass at 100 Hz on each take.
Metal kick and snare samples for the massive drums, a huge snare on 2 and 4 with a 1.2-second room.
Square sixteenth-note sequences, a filtered sawtooth on a single note, running under the empty verses before the wall of guitars.
The sequencer of German rock and metal studios, where drums quantized at 100% and guitars at 90% coexist.
A saturated 909 kick layered over the acoustic kick, aligned in phase, for electronic weight under the metal drums. Samples are enough.
Modern high-gain amps and cabinets, an alternative to Guitar Rig for a dense, clean wall of guitars, cut above 10 kHz.
Heavy mode with Cabinet after it: the native solution if you don't have a dedicated simulator, to quadruple-track and pan hard.
To thicken certain words of the deep declaimed vocal, with a pitch shift an octave down mixed in discreetly.

reperes: Rammstein: Du Hast (1997): the electronic sequence opening alone, then the wall of guitars on the chorus, the deep declaimed vocal.
Oomph!: Augen Auf (2004): the more melodic side, with more upfront synths and a pop chorus.
Eisbrecher: Verrueckt (2008): the empty verse over a sequence, the massive chorus, pure NDH mechanics.
ndh.rythme: Massive metal drums: kick and snare samples in the style of Superior Drummer, or a Drum Rack with acoustic drum samples. Kick on quarter notes or in doubled sixteenth notes, a huge snare on 2 and 4 with a 1.2-second room reverb. Hi-hats in eighth notes, ride on the choruses, china on the downbeats. Under the acoustic kick, layer a saturated 909 kick for electronic weight. A sixteenth-note sequence (synthetic percussion or electronic hi-hat) runs on top the whole time. The toms play rolls before the choruses. Drum breaks are square, never jazzy.
ndh.sons: High-gain guitars, tuned low, recorded twice on each side: an amp simulator (Guitar Rig 7, Neural DSP, Ableton's Amp in Heavy mode) with a high-pass at 100 Hz. Square electronic sequences on a Nord Lead: sixteenth notes of filtered sawtooth, or a two-note arpeggio, running under the verses. Sampled string pads, choirs, sometimes a piano or a music box for the intros. The vocal is deep, declaimed more than sung, with rolled Rs, recorded close to the mic, with 6:1 compression and a short room reverb. A vocoder or a pitch shift an octave down thickens certain words.
ndh.tempo: Between 90 and 130 BPM, with many tracks around 100 to 120 with a heavy, almost half-time feel. The groove is straight and square, locked to the grid like modern metal. Du Hast is around 125 BPM, Sonne slower. What distinguishes NDH from electro-industrial: the drums are metal drums, real or sampled, and the guitar is the main instrument. In your DAW, start at 110 BPM. Quantize the drums at 100% and the guitars at 90% to keep a little life. The electronic sequence in sixteenth notes must stay perfectly rigid under the guitars.

neogoa.arrangement: The neo-goa spiral is even longer than the goa one: 10 minutes is common. A 32-bar intro with kick, 303 bass and a first arpeggio layer. Every 16 to 32 bars, a layer is added and an automation opens. A first melodic breakdown around bar 128, without kick, with the arpeggios alone and the lead, 16 bars, then back in. A key change in the middle, often a minor third up, then a return to the original key toward the end. The peak is reached in the last third, with all six layers at once. A long ending, layers removed one by one. For playability, plan 64 bars of intro and outro with a steady bass.
neogoa.basse: The acid bass in sixteenth notes: on a software TB-303 (ABL3, D16 Phoscyon, or Operator with portamento and accents), a sawtooth or a square, a resonant low-pass filter around 300 Hz, a pronounced filter envelope. Kick on the beat, bass on the next three sixteenth notes, but with accents (velocity 127) and slides programmed as on a 303, and octave jumps on the "a" of the beat. Root in E, F or F#. Layer a second 303 line an octave above, with higher resonance and a short delay, playing a variation: the two lines braided together. A separate sine sub for sustain. Automate the cutoff frequency over 16 bars for the build-ups.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM. A 909 kick tuned to E, a clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in alternating sixteenth notes, 909 congas over 2 bars.
Software 303 bass on E1: kick then three sixteenth notes with accents and slides, resonant filter at 300 Hz, a second 303 an octave above.
Program three arpeggiators on thin sawtooths, patterns of 8, 12 and 16 steps, dotted eighth delay, different panning.
Create a supersaw or FM lead and write an 8-bar Phrygian melody with vibrato and bends.
Automate the filter of each layer over 32 bars and plan a key change to G minor halfway through.
Arrange 10 minutes as a spiral: one layer every 16 bars, a melodic breakdown without kick, peak in the last third, long ending.
neogoa.mix: Neo-goa benefits from modern mixing without giving up the aesthetic: more clarity than the originals, but no crushing limiter. Each arpeggio layer gets a high-pass at 250 Hz and its own band (2, 4, 6 kHz), with different panning and a delay in the sides. The lead stays in the center. Kick and bass mono below 150 Hz, the two 303 lines separated by their octave and their EQ. Light bus compression on the percussion, 3:1 ratio. Aim for -8 to -9 LUFS: neo-goa labels like Suntrip keep their dynamics. A gentle tape saturation on the master recalls DAT without copying its flaws. Check the balance in mono, because six stereo layers can cancel each other out.

outils.pourquoi: Supersaw and thin waveforms for the arpeggio layers and the lead; the goa revival uses it as hardware or via Roland Cloud JP-8000.
The two braided acid lines, programmed accents and slides; today almost always AudioRealism ABL3 or D16 Phoscyon 2.
The most faithful 303 emulation for the sixteenth-note bass with octave jumps, cutoff automated over 16 bars.
The DX7-style FM lead, vibrato and bends in Phrygian or harmonic minor, free and faithful to the vocabulary of 1995.
Six MIDI arpeggiator tracks of different lengths, 8, 12 and 16 steps, each with its own dotted eighth Echo and its own panning.
The goa kick, clap and congas, as samples or via D16 Drumazon 2, better placed in the spectrum than in 1995.
Another 303 emulation with built-in distortion and arpeggiator, for the second acid line an octave above.

reperes: Filteria: Sky Input (2004): the return of the 1995 sound with modern precision, six braided arpeggio layers.
Khetzal: Corolle (2005): Eastern melodies and spiral structures, the Suntrip aesthetic.
Median Project: Constellation (2020): current neo-goa, arpeggios and 303 in a clear mix.
Filteria: Bring Everything But Whistles (2021): the complexity of the layers and filter automation pushed over several minutes.
neogoa.rythme: The kick is the goa kick, but better produced: a 909 or a synthetic kick tuned around 55 Hz, short, with a clean click, moderately compressed. A 909 clap on 2 and 4 with a short reverb. Hi-hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocity, an open hat on the eighth-note offbeats, ride during the plateaus. The synthetic percussion: 909 congas, sampled tablas, bells, in 2 or 4-bar patterns. What changes compared to 1995 is the care: each percussion has its place in the spectrum, and the fills are programmed with precise velocities. Snare rolls stay moderate: neo-goa restarts are driven by the arpeggios, not the drums.
neogoa.sons: JP-8000 and TB-303 as the brief says, in emulation. Old-school layered arpeggios: three to six arpeggiator layers on thin sawtooths or JP-8000 waveforms, each with a pattern of a different length (8, 12, 16 steps), a dotted eighth delay and its own panning. The lead is a JP-8000 supersaw or an FM lead (Dexed), played in the Phrygian or harmonic minor scale with vibrato and bends. The long spiral structures are built through automation: each layer has its filter opening over 32 bars. The FX are period-correct: slow phaser, flanger, resonant filter sweeps, science-fiction voices. No modern liquid FX, no psytrance squelch: neo-goa stays faithful to the vocabulary of 1995.
sourcesOutils: Discogs, New Releases Oldschool Goa and Neo Goa thread
neogoa.tempo: Neo-goa picks up the tempos of 1995: 142 to 148 BPM, a little faster than the original goa, because today's producers grew up with psytrance. The grid is straight, no swing. What distinguishes it from historical goa is precision: the arpeggio layers are quantized to the sample and the offset cycles are calculated rather than accidental. What distinguishes it from psytrance is the rejection of the rolling bass in favor of an acid bass in accented sixteenth notes, and a spiral structure rather than drops. Count in 16 bars, but layer phrases of 3, 5 and 6 bars. A track lasts 9 to 12 minutes.

neurofunk.arrangement: A neurofunk track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and is structured like club DnB, but with more movement in the drops. A 32-bar intro with drone, percussion and a build-up. A 64-bar drop where the bass changes pattern every 8 bars and timbre every 16: this is where the genre stands out, the bass is a solo. A 32-bar breakdown with a cold lead or pad and a build-up made of white noise and a snare roll in thirty-second notes. A second drop with two basses in dialogue. A 32-bar outro. Mark every 8 bars with an edited drum fill or a "stutter" effect on the bass.
neurofunk.basse: The heart of it: a resampled multiband Reese, as the brief says. Start from the Reese recipe in Attack Magazine's book (two oscillators detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide, unison), but in Serum or FM8. Record to audio, then split into three bands with Multiband Dynamics or three EQs: below 100 Hz, 100 Hz to 1 kHz, above. Process each band separately: the low end stays clean, the mids get distortion and a moving filter, the highs a phaser or FM. Glue it back together, re-record, repeat. Write the line in syncopated sixteenth notes on the root, with short notes that change "timbre" through wavetable position automation. A separate sine sub holds the low end.
etapes: Set Ableton to 174 BPM. Program a two-step with a stacked kick (click plus 909 body) and a snare of four aligned samples.
Create a Reese in Serum (two oscillators detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide, unison 5) and record it to audio.
Split it into three bands, distort the mids, phase the highs, leave the low end clean, glue it back together and re-record.
Write the bassline in syncopated sixteenth notes and automate the wavetable position per note.
Add a tuned sine sub, a cold drone and FM8 percussion.
Arrange intro 32, drop 64 with a bass change every 8, breakdown 32, second drop in dialogue, outro 32.
neurofunk.mix: The neurofunk mix is the most surgical in the family. Kick and sub are tuned: the sub plays the fundamental, the kick is set so its body falls an octave above. The Reese is high-passed at 120 Hz and compressed by band. Every bass sound is mono below 200 Hz and stereo above (Utility in Mid/Side mode, or an EQ Eight in M/S). Sidechain all the mids from the kick at a 3:1 ratio, 50 ms release. The drum bus gets a clipper before the limiter. Master at -6 or -7 LUFS, with two limiters in series to hold that level without distorting. Check every bass on a spectrum analyzer: nothing should stick out between 80 and 120 Hz except the kick.

outils.pourquoi: The reference synth for neuro: modulated wavetables, FM between oscillators, filters in series, then audio export for resampling.
Metallic, shifting FM basses, non-integer ratios, feedback: the Noisia texture before the Serum wave.
A modular block-based synth for the documented resampling chains: sampler, wavetable, distortion and filters in a single window.
A 6-voice unison Reese with the Monark filter, as in the book, a starting point before the distortion passes.
With the OTT preset on the resampled bass, to squash the three bands and bring out every movement in the mids.
Surgical cuts between the sub and the mids of the bass, high-pass at 90 Hz on everything that isn't the sub.
Precision drum edits: bursts of sixteenth and thirty-second notes at the ends of phrases.
Mono below 120 Hz on the bass and sub, controlled width on the resampled mids.

reperes: Noisia: Stigma (2007): the talking bass over a motionless two-step, every note a different timbre.
Noisia: Machine Gun (2010): the call-and-response bass dialogue, and a drop that changes every 8 bars.
Black Sun Empire: Arrakis (2004): Dutch neurofunk, science-fiction drones and a distorted Reese.
Mefjus: Blackout (2013): precision drum edits and a perfect mono/stereo mix, the standard of the 2010s.
neurofunk.rythme: The neurofunk two-step is edited with surgical precision. Kick on beat 1 and on the "and" of 3, snare on 2 and 4, with a very short ghost snare on the sixteenth note before 4 every other bar. The kicks are stacked: a 5 ms transient click, a 909 body at 90 Hz, and sometimes a short tail. The snare is a stack of three to four samples aligned to the sample, with no reverb. The hi-hats are programmed in sixteenth notes with micro-variations of velocity and pitch (±2 semitones). The fills are break edits in thirty-second notes on the last beat of bar 16, with a delay in Beat Repeat.
neurofunk.sons: The brief names Serum and FM8. Serum is used for the Reese (Basic Shapes wavetable, two oscillators, unison 4 to 7, Bend warp) and for moving basses thanks to its tempo-synced LFOs. FM8 gives the metallic basses and the timbres that "talk": two operators, 1:2 ratio, feedback modulated by an envelope. The documented resampling chains in the brief are the method: each sound goes through three to five stages recorded to audio. Add synthetic percussion (FM blips, clicks), impacts, drones. Noisia made this vocabulary standard: basses that converse with each other, like two voices, in call and response over a bar.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Basslines chapter, Reese bass)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable chapter)
Attack Magazine (Halftime Drops In The Style Of Nikki Nair)
neurofunk.tempo: Neurofunk is played between 172 and 174 BPM, fixed tempo, no swing. What distinguishes it from techstep is the word "funk": the beat is still a two-step, but the bass is syncopated and moves in sixteenth notes, like a funk line played by a robot. The groove comes from the interaction between the drums, which stay still, and a bass that bounces on the offbeats and changes timbre with every note. Count in sixteenth notes and think of each bass note as a percussion hit. The feel must stay cold and functional: nothing is there for emotion, everything is there for movement.

newage.arrangement: An instrumental song of 4 to 6 minutes, with a memorable theme, a verse and a chorus, exactly like pop. A 20-second intro of nature or pad, the theme stated on piano or flute, a chorus with strings, a bridge that modulates, the theme returning with one more layer, a fade-out ending. The build-up comes from accumulating instruments, never from a filter or tension. Chariots of Fire is the exact form: a rhythmic piano motif, a theme that enters, a modulation, an ending that rises. On an album, the pieces answer each other through themes. No excessive length: the track must work on the radio or in a shop.
newage.basse: A soft, held synth bass, half or whole notes on the root of each chord, barely audible as a line. Sometimes no bass at all: the piano or harp covers the low end. The harmony is tonal and bright, in major, with major sevenths and suspended chords, I, V, vi, IV progressions, a tonic pedal under changing chords, a modulation up a whole step before the end. That is the fundamental difference from ambient: here the music goes somewhere and resolves. On tracks with a beat, a fretless bass or a round held sub. No saturation, a low-pass at 150 Hz, everything must stay clean and warm.
etapes: Load a D-50 or M1 preset (a Fantasia-type pad, a choir) and a piano, set the tempo to 68 BPM in 4/4.
Write a progression in D major, I, V, vi, IV, with major sevenths, one held bass note per chord.
Compose an 8-bar theme on piano or pan flute, played by hand and quantized at 80 percent.
Add a harp in eighth-note arpeggios and a sea recording under the whole track at -30 dB.
Arrange in 5 minutes: nature intro, theme, chorus with strings, a bridge that modulates up a whole step, the theme returning, fade.
Mix with a smooth reverb, a brightness shelf at 8 kHz, gentle compression, final level around -13 LUFS.
newage.mix: Clean, bright, wide. A long reverb on almost everything, a +2 dB shelf above 8 kHz for brightness, a round but discreet low end, no saturation. Gentle pop-style compression, 2:1 ratio, slow attack, medium release, for a steady level without pumping. Target -12 to -14 LUFS, which stays quiet. The instruments are spread across the width: piano in the center, wide strings, harp on the right, flute on the left, nature all around. Soften 3 kHz if the flutes get piercing. The goal is zero fatigue over an hour of looped listening in a spa: if anything catches the ear, it is too much. Check on small living-room speakers.

outils.pourquoi: The Fantasia and Pizzagogo presets are the sound of the genre on their own; Roland Cloud D-50 reproduces them note for note with the built-in chorus and reverb.
The Universe preset, the choirs and the digital piano of a thousand relaxation albums; Korg Collection M1 includes the original banks and the Korg Wavestation completes it.
The smooth, long reverb of the 80s, the one that makes harps and flutes sparkle; UAD Lexicon 224 and Valhalla VintageVerb give its grain.
Concert Hall mode with the 1980s color, 5 to 8 second decay, on almost everything, with a stereo chorus and a wide delay after it for the background pad.
Sampled harp, pan flute, smooth strings and "Aah" voices, from the Factory Library or an orchestral library; the eighth-note harp arpeggios come from there.
Sea, birds, stream under the whole track at -30 dB; the free libraries from the BBC and Freesound offer long, clean takes.
Wave sequences and shifting pads of the 90s, very present in late new age; Korg Collection Wavestation makes it available in the DAW.

reperes: Kitaro: Silk Road (1980): soft synths and an Eastern melody, the theme moving over a pad, the Japanese model.
Vangelis: Chariots Of Fire (1981): the perfect instrumental song form, piano motif, theme, modulation.
Enya: Orinoco Flow (1988): dozens of layers of voices and pizzicato, the pop production of new age.
Enigma: Sadeness Part I (1990): the slowed hip-hop break under Gregorian chant, the new age beat variant.
newage.rythme: Often no drums, and when there are some, they are muted: a soft drum machine (LinnDrum, TR-707) with a kick on 1 and 3 and a snare drowned in a gated reverb, or world percussion in shaker and tabla. Enigma and Deep Forest added a hip-hop break slowed to 80 BPM under Gregorian or Pygmy chants: that is the new age beat variant of the early 90s. In contemplative pieces, the rhythm comes from the harp or piano arpeggio in eighth notes, and from recorded ocean waves that return every 8 seconds. No aggressive hi-hats, never a dry clap: everything is wrapped up.
newage.sons: The brief names the Roland D-50, the Korg M1 and the harp. The presets of the era make the genre: Fantasia and Pizzagogo on the D-50, Universe and the choirs on the M1, available today in Roland Cloud and the Korg Collection. Add pan flutes, smooth strings, "Aah" voices, a sampled harp, and nature recordings: sea, birds, stream, under the whole track at -30 dB. The reverbs are smooth and long, Lexicon 224 style, which you can find in Valhalla VintageVerb, with a stereo chorus and a wide delay. No distortion, no tape hiss: new age wants crystal, not patina. Green-House shows today's version, with soft synths and plants.
sourcesOutils: Ableton Forum, Resurgence of the Korg M1 and Roland D-50 in new music
Gearspace (forum), What synth for this sound? (New age, mid 90's feel)
Vintage Synth Explorer (forum), Korg M1 vs Roland D-50
newage.tempo: Between 60 and 90 BPM, or outright rubato, without a grid, as with Vangelis. The reference tempo is that of a resting pulse, 60 to 70 BPM, which explains its use for relaxation. Bars in 4/4 or a gentle 6/8, arpeggios in steady eighth notes that rock you. Unlike ambient, there is a clear pulse and a melody that moves forward, but everything is rounded off: no swing, chords slightly behind the beat, rallentandos at the ends of phrases. If you play on a keyboard, keep your imprecisions rather than quantizing everything; if you program, quantize at 80 percent. The track should give the impression of a calm musician, not a machine.

newbeat.arrangement: New beat is designed for the DJ. A 16-bar intro of kick and hi-hat, then the bass, then the vocal sample that serves as the hook. The structure is a stack: every 8 bars, an element comes in or goes out. A breakdown in the middle removes the kick and leaves the deep voice over the pad for 8 bars, then a 909 tom roll brings everything back. Allow 5 to 6 minutes. The choruses are instrumental, carried by the orchestra hit and the slogan. No filter build-up or snare roll: the tension comes from the slowness and the repetition of the sample. End on 16 bars of kick and bass for the next mix.
newbeat.basse: The relaxed EBM bass. Square or sawtooth wave, one note, but in eighth notes rather than sixteenth notes, or in sixteenth notes at 108 BPM, which comes to the same feel. The low-pass filter is more closed than in EBM, between 200 and 500 Hz, with pronounced resonance and a longer release (250 ms): the note bounces instead of snapping. A slight 30 ms glide between notes adds the rubbery side. The lines often descend in minor: root, seventh, sixth. The bass follows the kick without sidechain, and its fundamental is locked to that of the transposed 909 kick, often around E1 or F1.
etapes: Program an EBM pattern at 125 BPM: a 909 kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4, a square bass in sixteenth notes.
Lower the tempo to 108 BPM with the audio clips in Warp Re-Pitch, and transpose the bass down three semitones.
Record a spoken phrase and pitch it down 6 semitones. Sample an orchestra hit, play it every two downbeats.
Add an open hi-hat on the offbeats and a 909 tom roll before each chorus.
Arrange as a stack over 5 minutes 30, with a vocal and pad breakdown in the middle, 16-bar intro and outro for the DJ.
Run the samples through a low-pass at 8 kHz and let the kick dominate the mix.
newbeat.mix: The low end is king: the slowed 909 kick occupies 50 to 120 Hz and the bass sits just above it. Cut the bass below 50 Hz to leave the kick alone. A big reverb on the snare and the hits, 2 seconds, plate. The vocal samples go through a low-pass at 8 kHz and light saturation, 4 dB, to sound as if played from slowed-down vinyl. Moderate compression on the drum bus, 3:1 ratio. Keep the mix dark: little top end above 10 kHz. The result should feel slower and heavier than it really is. A Saturator in Analog Clip on the master, 2 dB of drive, adds the final layer of weight.

outils.pourquoi: The Belgian kick, long Decay and Tune lowered by two semitones so it becomes round and fat at 108 BPM. D16 Drumazon 2 or Roland Cloud TR-909 in software.
The sampler for orchestra hits, moans and slogans played slowed down. Simpler with Redux at 12 bits and a low-pass at 8 kHz recaptures that grain.
The other 12-bit sampler in Belgian studios in 1988, cheaper than the Emax, for deep voices pitched down 5 to 7 semitones.
A few slow acid lines, filter half open, under the rubbery bass. Roland Cloud TB-303 or D16 Phoscyon 2 as emulation.
A single held minor chord, filtered, with the built-in chorus, for the genre's rare pad. TAL-U-NO-LX is the reference emulation.
The Atari ST MIDI sequencer that drove the 909, the sampler and the 303 in the opportunistic studios of the time, the direct ancestor of Cubase.
Program an EBM pattern at 125 BPM, switch the audio clips to Warp Re-Pitch and drop the tempo to 108: the 33 rpm accident reproduced in one move.

reperes: A Split Second: Flesh (1986): listen to the 45 rpm version and then the slowed-down version, it is the birth of the genre in a single record.
Confetti's: The Sound Of C (1988): commercial new beat, a hook sample, a heavy 909 kick, a stacked structure.
Tragic Error: Tanzen (1988): the deep voice over a dragging tempo, the bouncing bass.
newbeat.rythme: The TR-909 dominates, but slowed down and often transposed downward. A 909 kick on every beat, long Decay, Tune lowered by two semitones: it becomes round and fat. A 909 snare on 2 and 4, with a big 2-second reverb. Open hi-hat on the offbeats, in eighth notes, which gives the sway. 909 tom rolls before the choruses. A handclap doubled on the snare. The pattern stays very simple, more stripped down than EBM: no metallic percussion, no sixteenth-note hi-hats. Instead, add orchestra hits sampled on the Emax or Simpler, played on the first beat every two bars.
newbeat.sons: New beat lives on samples: moans, erotic phrases, repeated slogans, sirens, orchestra hits. The Emax and Akai of the era are replaced by Simpler with Redux at 12 bits. The deep voice is a male voice pitched down 5 to 7 semitones, spoken slowly. A few TB-303 acid lines appear, but slow, filter half open. Pads are rare: one held minor chord on a Juno, filtered, is enough. The rule of the genre: anything that sounds too fast or too bright is pitched down three semitones. A global low-pass at 8 kHz on the samples bus recreates playback at 33 rpm.
sources: Discogs and Are.na (Flesh page, playback at 33 rpm and pitch +8)
sourcesOutils: Gearspace (What synthesizers and drum machines were used for the New Beat style thread)
Discogs (Sound Of Belgium, New Beat Sampler)
newbeat.tempo: Between 105 and 115 BPM, sometimes 100. That is the essential difference from EBM: everything is slowed down by about 20%. The feel drags, heavy, almost lazy, but stays straight, no swing. The historical trick is easy to reproduce in Ableton: program an EBM pattern at 125 BPM, then lower the global tempo to 108 with your audio clips in Warp Re-Pitch mode. Everything drops three semitones and thickens, exactly like the record played at 33 rpm. Keep that heaviness: don't try to compensate by speeding up the hi-hats. The quarter note at 110 BPM should sound like a heavy step, and the sixteenth-note bass like a rubber bounce.

nitzhonot.arrangement: A 32-bar intro, kick and bass alone, then the hi-hats. Around bar 32, the arpeggio arrives. First breakdown as early as bar 64: kick cut, strings and lead exposed alone for 16 bars, a snare roll, the kick returning with the full melody. The track then strings together two or three cycles of 32 bars of plateau and 16 of breakdown, each breakdown presenting a variation of the main melody. The last breakdown is the longest and most grandiose, with the strings in full chords. A quick outro, 16 to 32 bars. A track lasts 6 to 8 minutes. Nitzhonot hides nothing: the melody is there from the first minute.
nitzhonot.basse: The nitzhonot bass is simpler than the rolling bass: two forms coexist. The first is an offbeat line in eighth notes, kick on the beat and bass on the "and", a sawtooth sound filtered at 250 Hz, as in hardtrance. The second takes the goa pattern in sixteenth notes, kick then three notes, but with a rounder, less acid sound, on a JP-8000 or Nord Lead. Choose one and keep it for the whole track. Root note in E or F#, and the bass follows the chord changes of the melody, unlike psytrance, which stays on one note. A sine sub under the main bass is necessary, because the long kick takes up a lot of space.
etapes: Project at 150 BPM. Program a long synthetic kick with a pitch envelope from 200 to 50 Hz, saturated, four per bar.
Write an offbeat bass in eighth notes on E1, sawtooth filtered at 250 Hz, a sine sub underneath.
Load a 7-voice supersaw and write an 8-bar Phrygian melody on E, long and singing.
Add synthetic strings in chords over 4 bars, a sixteenth-note arpeggio and a loud open hi-hat on the offbeats.
Arrange in short cycles: 32 bars of plateau, 16 of breakdown with the kick cut and a snare roll, three times in a row.
Mix the kick loud with a high-pass at 150 Hz on everything else, wide strings, master around -9 LUFS.
nitzhonot.mix: The period mix is direct, a little dirty, and that is part of the charm. The kick is loud, louder than in current psytrance, and its long tail forces a severe high-pass on everything else, around 150 Hz. Don't compress it too much: its dynamics give the hammering feel. The supersaw takes the mids, between 500 Hz and 5 kHz, with a medium reverb. The strings go wide in stereo, with a chorus. No sophisticated sidechain: a simple compressor on the bass, triggered by the kick, 4:1 ratio, 100 ms release, is enough. The master can stay around -9 LUFS to keep the rough edge of Phonokol productions.

outils.pourquoi: The supersaw of the Eastern leads, seven detuned sawtooths, played in Phrygian without irony. Roland Cloud offers its official emulation.
Round offbeat basses in eighth notes and synthetic string pads; the quintessential Israeli studio synth of 1998.
A period sampler for Eastern chants, grandiose strings and 909 snares: replayed on a keyboard, run through a long reverb.
The sequencer of Phonokol and Trust in Trance: direct arrangement, snare rolls before each restart, no sophisticated automation.
To remake the laser kick today: sine, pitch from 200 to 50 Hz in 40 ms, 250 ms decay, outright saturation after it.
The JP-8000 emulation with the same supersaw oscillator; otherwise any 7-voice unison in Serum or Sylenth1 will do.

reperes: Eyal Barkan: Good Morning Israel (1998): the hard kick, the unapologetic Eastern melody and breakdowns returning every 32 bars.
Power Source: Goaway (1997): still close to goa in its arpeggios, but already with the nitzhonot kick and eighth-note bass.
Sandman: Witchcraft (1997): the grandiose strings and the rising supersaw, a template for Israeli uplifting.
Shiva Shidapu: Power of Celtic (1997): the openly borrowed melody and the euphoric restart, to understand why the psy scene snubbed the genre.
nitzhonot.rythme: The kick is the signature: hard, long, with a pitch that drops fast, in the spirit of the hardtrance of the time, almost a "laser kick". Make it in Operator or a synthetic kick: a sine with a pitch envelope going from 200 Hz down to 50 Hz in 40 ms, a 250 ms decay, then outright saturation. It falls on every beat without nuance. The open hi-hat on the eighth-note offbeats, at a high volume, gives the beach trance feel. A clap or snare on 2 and 4, often doubled with a 909 snare. Snare rolls in sixteenth notes before each restart, a crash on the first beat of each drop. Little extra percussion: the kick and the hi-hat do the work.
nitzhonot.sons: The brief names the JP-8000, Nord Lead, Akai S3000: a 1998 trance studio. The main lead is a JP-8000 supersaw (or its emulation, or any 7-voice unison) played in a Phrygian or harmonic minor scale, with long, singing melodies, without irony. Stack on top grandiose synthetic strings on a sampler or a Nord Lead pad, and an arpeggiator in sixteenth notes on the chord, with an eighth-note delay. A discreet TB-303 line adds a little acid. Sampled vocals, often Eastern chants, go through a long reverb. No granular textures, no liquid FX: everything is melodic and upfront.
sources: Wikipedia, Nitzhonot article (tempo and kick references)
nitzhonot.tempo: Nitzhonot pushes a little harder than the goa it comes from: 145 to 155 BPM, some tracks up to 160. The feel is square, almost hardtrance: no layering of offset cycles as in goa, but neatly aligned 8-bar phrases, made for raising your arms. What changes compared to the full-on that will follow it is simplicity: a single rhythmic pattern, a single heavy kick, a melody that takes up all the space. Count in 16 bars, and plan short breakdowns that come back often, every 32 or 48 bars, because the genre lives on its euphoric restarts.

nudisco.arrangement: Nu-disco is arranged like a club track: 6 to 8 minutes. A 32-bar intro with kick, percussion and filtered bass, building gradually as the filter opens. A 32-bar main section with the full sample or melody. A 16- to 32-bar breakdown without kick, where the strings or the Juno pad take over, with a white noise build-up and a snare roll. Drop: everything comes back with the filter open. A second main section, then a 32-bar outro with the drums alone. Unlike the original disco, there is no verse: the track lives through its build-ups and breakdowns.
nudisco.basse: The bass is played and then replayed in MIDI, or sampled from a record and transposed. The sound is a round electric bass, or a virtual Moog with a low filter. The pattern is syncopated as in disco, in sixteenth notes with octave jumps, but locked tighter to the kick. The low-pass filter is automated: closed at 200 Hz in the intro, open at 2 kHz in the drop. Sidechain is the difference from the original: compress the bass from the kick with a 4:1 ratio and a 100 ms release so the kick can breathe. Cut the bass below 40 Hz and add a sine sub on the root if the club demands it.
etapes: Set 120 BPM with 56% swing, import a disco drum break and slice it to MIDI, then layer a 909 kick on the beats.
Add a clap on 2 and 4, an open hat on the offbeats, congas and shaker in sixteenth notes.
Write a round, syncopated sixteenth-note bass, sidechained from the kick at 4:1, with an automated low-pass filter.
Sample disco strings or brass, filter them, and add a Juno pad and a Rhodes or a recorded funk rhythm guitar.
Build 7 minutes: a filtered 32-bar intro, main section, breakdown without kick with a build-up, drop, outro.
Parallel-compress the drum bus, saturate the samples, master with a limiter at -9 LUFS.
nudisco.mix: The nu-disco mix is modern: sidechain on the bass and pads gives the pumping, saturation and parallel compression on the drums give the punch. Send the drum bus into 8:1 parallel compression blended at 30%. Saturate the disco samples to thicken them and glue them with an EQ that cuts below 100 Hz. The kick is louder than in the original disco, with a clean sub around 50 Hz. A short reverb on the stabs, a long 3-second one on the strings in the breakdown. Modern mastering aims for -8 to -9 LUFS for the club, with a limiter like Pro-L 2. Keep the sub in mono.

outils.pourquoi: Slice to New MIDI Track to chop a disco break and replay it with swing under a clean kick, plus the sample edits the scene is built on.
The automated low-pass filter on string and brass samples, closed at 200 Hz in the intro, open at 2 kHz in the drop.
Pads and sixteenth-note arpeggios in the style of Todd Terje or Lindstrøm; TAL-U-NO-LX is its usual emulation.
The virtual Juno for chorused pads and leads, with light sidechain from the kick for the modern pumping.
The bass played and then replayed in MIDI, round, syncopated with octave jumps, locked tighter to the kick than in the original disco.
The virtual Fender Rhodes for block chords, with chorus and a short reverb.
A real funk rhythm guitar recorded in sixteenth notes: that is what separates a serious track from a simple edit.
The modern mastering limiter, around minus 8 or minus 9 LUFS for the club, with the sub kept in mono.

reperes: Todd Terje: Inspector Norse (2012): the sixteenth-note Juno arpeggio and the filter build-up.
Lindstrom: I Feel Space (2005): the cosmic pad and the round sidechained bass over 8 minutes.
Spiller: Groovejet (2000): the filtered disco sample under a house kick, the original formula.
Breakbot: Baby I'm Yours (2012): the recorded funk rhythm guitar and the Rhodes, the played side of the genre.
nudisco.rythme: The rhythm blends two worlds: a played disco drum loop, sliced and replayed, and a 909 or 808 kick underneath on every beat. A modern clap doubles the sampled snare on 2 and 4. The open hats on the offbeats come either from the sample or from an open 909 hat. Add congas, shaker and tambourine in swung sixteenth notes. In Ableton, slice a disco break with Slice to New MIDI Track, keep the hits you like, place them on the grid with swing, and layer a clean kick. Fills are sampled snare rolls or white noise build-ups.
nudisco.sons: Filtered disco samples are the raw material: strings, brass, choirs, funk rhythm guitars, run through an automated low-pass or high-pass filter. The Juno-106 provides the pads and leads, as with Todd Terje or Lindstrøm, with sixteenth-note arpeggios. The Fender Rhodes plays the chords. A recorded funk rhythm guitar is what separates a serious track from a simple edit. Today: Ableton Live for the edits, Auto Filter for the filters, TAL-U-NO-LX for the Juno, Electric for the Rhodes. The signature effects are the filter, the sidechain and a dotted-eighth delay on the stabs.
sourcesOutils: Magnetic Magazine (Satin Jackets' 5 Favorite Plugins For Producing Nu-Disco)
KVR Audio (forum: plugins for retro disco, nu disco and funk)
nudisco.tempo: Nu-disco sits between 112 and 125 BPM, often 118 to 122. The feel is more human than house: 55 to 58% swing on the sixteenth notes, often inherited from a played disco drum loop. Set 120 BPM with 56% swing. What separates nu-disco from the original disco is precision: the kick is on the grid, everything else floats around it. The rhythmic signature is still four-on-the-floor with an open hat on the offbeats, but the kick is more present and the groove is set up for the mix. Count in 8- and 16-bar phrases, as in house.

nuitalo.arrangement: Nu-italo returns to the pop format: 4 to 6 minutes, with a 7-minute extended version for DJs. A 16-bar intro with the arpeggio and the pad, the drums come in at bar 9. A 16-bar verse with the doubled vocal, a 16-bar chorus with the synth hook and the bells. Second verse, chorus. A 16-bar breakdown without kick, with the vocal and pads, a gentle build-up. Final chorus, 16-bar outro with the arpeggio alone. The structure is a song's: the melody matters more than the build-up. Chromatics sometimes stretches it into a slow ballad; Italoconnection keeps the club format.
nuitalo.basse: The bass is a Juno-106 or a faithful emulation, in eighth or sixteenth notes jumping octaves as in italo, but cleaner and softer. Sawtooth with a little chorus, low-pass filter at 500 Hz, 60 ms release. The pattern follows a sentimental four-chord progression in minor: i, VII, VI, VII for example. Light sidechain from the kick, 2:1 ratio, gives the modern pumping without overdoing it. A sine sub layer on the root, at -12 dB, adds what the original lacked. Ableton's Arpeggiator in up mode over one octave turns a single held note into the italo bass.
etapes: Set 116 BPM without swing, load clean LinnDrum samples into a Drum Rack with a short gated reverb.
Program the kick on the beats, clap and snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, discreet toms every 8 bars.
Write a Juno bass in eighth-note octaves over a sentimental minor progression, with light sidechain and a sub layer.
Add a sixteenth-note arpeggio with delay, a chorused Juno pad, DX7 bells for the hook.
Record a doubled, whispered female vocal with a long reverb and a dotted-eighth delay.
Structure 5 minutes in pop format, mix clean with a transparent limiter at -10 LUFS.
nuitalo.mix: The nu-italo mix is clean and modern. Long reverbs, 3 to 5 seconds, on vocals and pads, with a 40 ms pre-delay to keep clarity. Chorus on everything Juno, except the bass, which stays mono. The kick and sub are clean, cut below 30 Hz, but present. Compress the vocal at 4:1 with a de-esser; it should be soft and up front. The drum bus gets 2:1 glue compression. The master is treated like a current pop track, -10 LUFS, with a transparent limiter, without the original's saturation. Keep a slight bump at 12 kHz for the shimmer of the bells.

outils.pourquoi: Chorused pads, eighth-note octave bass, sixteenth-note arpeggios: the same machine as the original, or its faithful emulation.
Roland's official emulation for a sound as close as possible to the original, chorus included, on pads and arpeggios.
The reference virtual Juno for the clean sawtooth bass, 60 ms release, filter at 500 Hz.
The alternative for a denser Juno on long pads with 3- to 5-second reverb.

outils.nom: Samples From Mars Linn From Mars
outils.pourquoi: The LinnDrum sampled cleanly: tight kick, clap and toms, with a soft gated reverb of 150 to 200 ms.
The shimmering DX7 bells and FM electric pianos, with a slight bump at 12 kHz in the mix.
In up mode over one octave, it plays the italo bass from a single held note, and the three-note arpeggios with dotted delay.

reperes: Sally Shapiro: I'll Be by Your Side (2006): the whispered, doubled vocal, clean nostalgia over an italo bass.
Chromatics: In the City (2007): Johnny Jewel's slowed tempo and long reverbs.
Italoconnection: Metropoli (2015): the faithful reconstruction, LinnDrum and Juno in club format.
Glass Candy: Digital Versicolor (2007): the Juno arpeggio and the gated clap played with restraint.
nuitalo.rythme: The LinnDrum is sampled, clean and tight. Kick on every beat, rounder than the 1983 one thanks to a light sub layer. Linn clap and snare on 2 and 4 with gated reverb, but softer, 150 to 200 ms. Sixteenth-note hi-hats, open on the offbeat of beat 4. Linn tom fills every 8 bars, more discreet. A sixteenth-note shaker. In your DAW: good-quality LinnDrum samples, a short gated reverb, and gentle compression on the drum bus. Unlike italo, dryness is not the goal at any cost: a small room reverb on the whole kit ties it together.
nuitalo.sons: The Juno-106 or its emulations does everything: chorused pads, bass, arpeggios. Sixteenth-note arpeggiators on three-note chords, with a dotted-eighth delay. The female vocal is doubled, often whispered, with a long reverb and a delay: Sally Shapiro and Chromatics are the models. DX7 bells and FM electric pianos. A restrained sawtooth lead. Today: TAL-U-NO-LX, Diva or Roland Cloud Juno-106, Dexed for the bells, a sampled LinnDrum. The difference from the original: everything is soft, clean, with long reverbs and unapologetic nostalgia.
sourcesOutils: Radio ITALOPOWER! (The Machines Behind Italo Disco)
nuitalo.tempo: Nu-italo takes the italo tempo: 115 to 125 BPM, but with a preference for the low end, 112 to 118, among melancholic producers like Johnny Jewel or Sally Shapiro. The feel is perfectly on the grid, no swing, with added softness: the attacks are less harsh than in the original. Set 116 BPM, full quantization. The signature is still sixteenth-note arpeggios and an octave bass, but played with modern restraint. What separates it from the original italo: cleanliness, unapologetic nostalgia, a tempo often a little slower and longer pads.

nujazz.arrangement: The form follows jazz: a theme stated, then solos or variations over the changes, then the theme. On the house version, 6 to 8 minutes with a 32-bar intro of kick and percussion, the sample or theme at bar 33, 32-bar solos, and a breakdown where the kick disappears to leave the bass and the Rhodes. On the broken beat or orchestral version, 5 to 10 minutes with a slow build in layers, like a suite. Change the harmony every 8 bars, with a modulation around the middle. Leave room for the soloists: a 16-bar trumpet solo is an arrangement element in its own right.
nujazz.basse: Played double bass is the reference, pizzicato, in walking bass lines or a funky ostinato. On St Germain's Rose Rouge, the electric bass loops under the vocal sample for the entire track. Write 2-bar lines in eighth notes with chromatic passing notes, root, third, fifth, sixth, seventh, like a jazz bassist. Use Trilian or a double bass library with finger noise, or a recorded electric bass. Cut at 250 Hz but keep 700 Hz for the wood. 3:1 compression and a little tube saturation. In broken beat, the bass is a round synth, Moog or Operator, that plays the kick's syncopations and leaves silences.
etapes: Pick your side: jazzy house at 124 BPM or broken beat at 105 BPM, and program the matching kit over 2 bars.
Lay a sampled or played jazz kit, ride and brushes, over the programmed kit, without quantizing it.
Write a 2-bar double bass line in eighth notes with chromatic passing notes, or loop a bass sample.
Learn 4 Rhodes voicings, major seventh, minor ninth, thirteenth, sus4, and play an 8-bar progression.
Add a soloist, muted trumpet or saxophone, over 16 bars, and a jazz vocal sample if you are aiming for house.
Arrange like a standard: intro, theme, solos, breakdown without kick, final theme, then mix clean, natural, with no saturation.
nujazz.mix: The mix is natural and hi-fi, like a jazz record with a house kick. Little compression on the played instruments, 2:1 with a slow attack, to keep the transients. The programmed kick is compressed and placed at minus 10 dB in house, lower in broken beat. The double bass at minus 12 dB, the Rhodes at minus 16. Short room reverb on the drums, a 2-second plate on the horns and vibraphone. Place the instruments in stereo as on stage. Cut the Rhodes and horns at 150 Hz. Master around minus 10 LUFS in house to hold up in the club, minus 14 in orchestral. No distortion: nu jazz is clean, which is what separates it from lo-fi and trip-hop.

outils.pourquoi: The harmonic heart: major seventh, minor ninth, thirteenth, sus4. Spectrasonics Keyscape or AAS Lounge Lizard if you don't have one.
Pizzicato double bass in walking lines with chromatic passing notes, or a looped electric bass in the style of Rose Rouge.

outils.nom: Played electric bass or double bass
outils.pourquoi: The mix of machine and musician is the signature: a real recorded 2-bar line, compressed 3:1, beats any plugin.
The house kick on every beat under the jazz drums, with open hats on the offbeat. Samples in a Drum Rack.
Jazz drums with ride and brushes, played unquantized over the programmed kit humanized by 10%.
Muted trumpet, saxophone and trombone as a section when you don't have a guest musician on hand.
In broken beat, the round synth bass that plays the kick's syncopations and leaves silences, sine plus triangle.
A 2-second plate on the horns and vibraphone, a short room on the drums: a natural mix without distortion.

reperes: St Germain: Rose Rouge (2000): the Marlena Shaw vocal loop, the electric bass ostinato and the trumpet over a house kick.
Cinematic Orchestra: Channel 1 Suite (1999): the double bass, played drums and strings over a programmed beat, the orchestral version.
Koop: Waltz for Koop (2001): the light swing, the vibraphone and the vocal, Scandinavian nu jazz as a standard.
Kruder & Dorfmeister: Bug Powder Dust (1996): the looped double bass and the dub beat under a rap, the bridge between Vienna and jazz.
nujazz.rythme: Two possible kits. In jazzy house: a 909 or sampled kick on every beat, open hats on the offbeat, a jazz rimshot and sampled brushes swinging on top, plus congas. In broken beat: the kick is syncopated, on the 1, the “a” of 2 and the “and” of 3, the snare on 2 and the “a” of 4, the hi-hats in sixteenth notes with shifted accents. In both cases, add a real jazz drum kit, sampled or played, with ride and brushes, under or over the programmed kit. The mix of machine and drummer is the genre's signature. Humanize the programmed kit by 10% in timing, and leave the played drums untouched.
nujazz.sons: The Rhodes is the harmonic heart, but played with real jazz chords: major seventh, minor ninth, dominant thirteenth, sus4. Learn 4 voicings and repeat them. The horns, muted trumpet, saxophone, trombone, come from guest musicians or well-played orchestral libraries. Jazz samples are used as on Rose Rouge: a vocal or piano phrase looped, whole, recognizable. Add a vibraphone, a flute, strings for The Cinematic Orchestra. Effects are sober: plate reverb, a little delay. In the Scandinavian scene, analog synths and colder electronic sounds blend with acoustic piano.
nujazz.tempo: Nu jazz lives at two tempos: jazzy house around 120 to 128 BPM, like St Germain, and broken beat around 100 to 110 BPM, like Jazzanova. What changes compared to downtempo is speed and rhythmic complexity: the accents fall off the grid, on offbeat sixteenth notes. 58 to 62% swing on the sixteenth notes, but with displaced accents rather than a simple delay. On the house version, keep a straight 4/4 and leave the swing to the hi-hats and percussion. The feel is that of a jazz drummer playing house: precise, but free on the subdivisions.

nuskoolbreaks.arrangement: A nu skool breaks track lasts 5 to 7 minutes and follows a club house form. A 32-bar intro of break and percussion, with a build-up over the last 8. The bass enters at bar 33, for 32 bars. A first 16-bar breakdown with the stab and the vocal, a filter that closes and then opens. A 32-bar drop with everything. A central 32-bar breakdown with pad and vocal, a long build-up. A second 64-bar drop with a bass variation. A 32-bar outro that removes the bass, then the hi-hats. Mark every 8 bars with a fill or an FX. The track must mix with house: intro and outro with the break alone, no bass.
nuskoolbreaks.basse: The modulated electro basses of the brief: a saw or square on a Nord Lead or on Analog, with a resonant low-pass filter whose cutoff is modulated by a fast envelope (150 ms decay) and a slow LFO, plus soft distortion. The line plays syncopated eighth notes, often on the “and” of the beats, on the root and the minor seventh or the fifth, with a one-octave glide at the end of the phrase. A separate sine sub holds the note below 60 Hz. Since the break's kick is dry and short, the sidechain is light (3:1 ratio, 60 ms release). This bass is what foreshadows electro-house and melodic dubstep: moving, tense, clean.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM. Program a break with 909 sounds: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and the “a” of 3, snare on 2 and 4.
Add electro percussion (808 cowbell, rimshot, clave) on the offbeats, panned.
Create a bass on Wavetable or Analog: saw, resonant filter with a fast envelope and a slow LFO, a syncopated eighth-note line.
Add a sine sub below 60 Hz, a minor stab on the offbeats on Analog, and a spoken voice through Vocoder.
Arrange intro 32, bass 32, breakdown 16, drop 32, breakdown 32, drop 64, outro 32, with a fill every 8.
Mix clean: every percussion element in its place, bass cut at 100 Hz, gentle Glue on the drums, -8 LUFS.
nuskoolbreaks.mix: The nu skool mix is clean and wide, like a tech-house record. The programmed kick occupies 50 to 100 Hz, the sub below, the electro bass high-passed at 100 Hz and compressed at 4:1. Each percussion element has its own EQ and its place in the panorama: cowbell left, rimshot right, hi-hats in the center. The stabs and pads are wide (Chorus-Ensemble or Utility Width at 130%) and cut at 200 Hz. Light sidechain on the bass and pads. Short reverb on the snare, medium on the stabs. Drum bus with a gentle Glue Compressor (2:1 ratio). Master at -8 LUFS, without pumping: the opposite of big beat.

outils.pourquoi: Tense electro basses: saw or square, resonant filter modulated by a fast envelope and a slow LFO, a syncopated eighth-note line.
Clean programmed breaks and electro percussion (cowbell, rimshot, clave) replayed from chopped samples.
Dry kick and snare on the grid at 130 BPM, without MPC swing: the almost techno restraint that separates the genre from big beat.
The sequencer of Marine Parade and TCR for long arrangements: intro 32, drop 64, breakdown 32, without rave collage.
The modern electro bass: saw, resonant filter, LFO on the cutoff, with Operator as a sine sub below 60 Hz.
Minor stabs on the offbeats and wide pads, two detuned saws, to replace the Nord Lead.
A spoken voice run through the vocoder for the Stanton Warriors' robotic side, with Utility for width.
On the drum bus, 4:1 ratio, for a precise club hit without the overt pumping of big beat.

reperes: Stanton Warriors: Da Virus (2001): the gliding electro bass, the vocoded vocals, breakbeat entering the house clubs.
Plump DJs: The Funk Hits the Fan (2000): dry programmed break and offbeat stabs, the TCR sound.
Adam Freeland: We Want Your Soul (2003): the spoken vocal, the tense bass, the mainstream format of nu skool.
Evil Nine: Cakehole (2003): the dark electro side, the modulated bass that foreshadows electro-house.
nuskoolbreaks.rythme: The clean programmed breaks of the brief: no whole sample, but a kick, a snare and hi-hats from a 909 or short samples, programmed into a break pattern. Kick on beat 1, the “and” of 2 and the “a” of 3 (the sixteenth note before 4), snare on 2 and 4. Closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocity, open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4. Add electro percussion: 808 cowbell, rimshot, clave, on the offbeats. A sampled break can play in the background, heavily filtered, for movement, but the skeleton is programmed. Fills are 909 snare rolls in sixteenth notes rising in velocity.
nuskoolbreaks.sons: The brief cites the Akai S3000, the Nord Lead, the TR-909 and Cubase: the studio of an English producer in 2000. The Nord Lead provides the basses and synth stabs: short minor chords, saw with a filter that opens on the attack, played on the offbeats. The 909 provides the skeleton. The S3000 handles the vocal samples: a spoken phrase from a film or radio, filtered, or a vocoder. Add wide pads on Analog, build-up FX (filtered white noise) and vocal “stutters”. In Ableton, Wavetable with an LFO on the filter makes the bass, Operator makes the sub, and Vocoder on a spoken voice gives the robotic side the Stanton Warriors love.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (Mixing A Breaks Track, Layering Vinyl Drum Breaks)
nuskoolbreaks.tempo: Nu skool breaks runs between 125 and 135 BPM, the tempo of house and progressive, with 130 as the standard. The feel is clean, precise, almost techno: no MPC swing, no dragging funk break. What separates it from big beat is restraint and modernity: the breaks are programmed, the basses are electro, and the groove comes from the syncopation of the bass and percussion, not from heaviness. Think of an electro or tech-house track whose 4/4 kick has been replaced by a dry break. Set swing to 0 and find the groove in the placement.

nustylegabber.arrangement: A nu style track runs 4 to 5 minutes and follows the logic of big venues: a 16- to 32-bar intro with kick and a motif, then a long breakdown, 32 bars, where the kick stops and the MC or the melody carries everything, with an 8-bar build-up (roll, riser, one beat of silence), then the drop: kick, screech, bass, 32 bars. A second breakdown, often shorter, a second drop with variation. End on the kick alone, 16 bars. What makes the track playable at a festival is the silence just before the drop and the first kick landing right on beat 1, louder than anything before it. Plan one clear “climax” per track.
nustylegabber.basse: The bass is the kick's tail, but this time it is designed, not endured. You build it separately: a sine or triangle from Operator at the root, with a pitch envelope dropping one octave over 100 ms, run through Saturator at 15 dB then EQ, and you glue it behind the attack. The track is written in the key of the kick, often between E and G, root around 40-50 Hz. Chord changes are made by pitching the kick's tail, not by adding a bass: a kick in E for 8 bars, then a kick in G for 8 bars. No separate sub, it would double the tail. Cut everything below 35 Hz.
etapes: Tempo 160 BPM. Build the attack: a 909 kick cut at 60 ms, Saturator in hard clip.
Build the tail: Operator sine at the root, a falling 100 ms pitch envelope, Saturator at 15 dB, 280 ms decay. Glue it behind the attack and bounce it to a single sample.
Process the kick by bands: EQ Eight to cut below 35 Hz, distortion on the mids, light clipping on the top.
Add a clap on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hats, offbeat kicks (tail only, minus 8 dB).
Create a screech in Massive or Serum, a 4-note sixteenth-note riff, high-passed at 300 Hz.
Structure: 32-bar intro, 32-bar breakdown with vocal or melody, 8-bar build-up, 32-bar drop, second breakdown, drop, ending. Clipper then limiter on the master.
nustylegabber.mix: The nu style mix is clean, which separates it from gabber: the kick is distorted but controlled. The common method, which the Attack book describes for hard techno, is to process the kick by bands: the low end stays clean, the mids are distorted, the top is lightly clipped. Multiband Dynamics or an EQ with three bands and a different distortion on each. Kick at minus 3 dB peak, everything else below it. The screech is high-passed at 300 Hz so it never touches the kick. Sidechain on everything melodic (4:1 ratio, 100 ms release). Master: Ozone or Pro-L 2 at around minus 6 LUFS, with a clipper before the limiter. Compare with an Angerfist track at the same volume.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the Masters of Hardcore scene: a kick drawn and then chained through Fruity WaveShaper and Fruity Parametric EQ 2, the project organized around the kick.
To synthesize the long kick: sine with a pitch envelope, then internal distortion, resample. The screeches come from there too, sawtooth and FM.
The classic nu style screeches: Scrawl or sawtooth oscillator, resonant band-pass filter, distortion, fast LFO on pitch.
The starting point is still a sampled 909 kick, pitched and lengthened: the tuned tail of the nu style kick is a stretched, distorted 909.
Limiter on the master at around minus 6 LUFS integrated, with Pro-Q 3 before it to clean up the kick's low end below 40 Hz.
Maximizer and dynamic EQ on the master, plus the Exciter module to add mids to the kick on big-venue tracks.
Controlled distortion by band: compress the kick's low end, let the top distort. EQ Eight afterwards to scoop 200 to 400 Hz.
Backup synthesized kick: sine, steep pitch envelope, then Saturator in Analog Clip. A good starting point before Serum.

reperes: Neophyte: Army Of Hardcore (2003): the kick becomes long and tuned, the shift from gabber to nu style.
Angerfist: Raise Your Fist (2006): the screech as a riff and the MC vocal as a chorus, the Masters of Hardcore model.
Evil Activities: Nobody Said It Was Easy (2007): a real sung, melodic breakdown before the kick returns.
Tha Playah: Why So Serious (2009): listen to the kick's tail changing notes to follow the harmony.
nustylegabber.rythme: The nu style kick is built in layers, and that is the big difference from gabber: a short, snappy attack (“punch” or “tok”), often a clipped 909, then a separate tail, a saturated waveform tuned to the root that lasts 250 to 300 ms. The two are glued and processed together, then resampled several times. The kick plays on every beat. On top, a snare or clap on 2 and 4, set back. Eighth-note hi-hats on the offbeats, fairly discreet. Offbeat kicks with only the tail, lower in volume, which add a bounce. Snare and kick rolls over 4 bars before each drop, accelerating.
nustylegabber.sons: The screech, a distorted, piercing lead made of a highly resonant sawtooth run through distortion and then a band-pass filter, played as a fast riff and pitched over the kicks. In Massive: a sawtooth, Scream filter, distortion in series, 4-voice unison. More melodic leads in stacked sawtooths, for the anthems. MC vocals, rapped or shouted, often in English, with an eighth-note delay and light distortion: the MC chorus is the hook of the tracks. Dark orchestrations, choirs, sampled strings for intros and breakdowns. The hoover survives, but softened. Lots of reverse cymbals and risers for transitions.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (chapters Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz)
Screech House, hardstyle and hardcore kick tutorials (screechhouse.com)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno)
Screech House, hardstyle and hardcore kick tutorials (screechhouse.com)
Neroz Productions, Uptempo and Hardcore courses (nerozproductions.com)
nustylegabber.tempo: Nu style, or mainstream hardcore, drops back to between 150 and 170 BPM, with the bulk of the Masters of Hardcore output around 160-165. That is slower than 1990s gabber, and the slowdown changes everything: at 160 BPM, a beat lasts 375 ms, and the kick can finally have a real tuned tail, long, filling all the space up to the next hit. The feel is heavier, more martial, closer to hardstyle than to hakken. No swing, but a new attention to placement: kicks are sometimes nudged 5 ms early to hit harder. Program at 160 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, and let the kick ring.

orchestraltrance.arrangement: Nine to twelve minutes. A 32-bar intro with kick, bass and a filtered string ostinato. A first plateau with harp and brass. A first short break. The big breakdown, 96 bars or more: the strings play the theme slowly, the choirs come in, a section in whole notes, a one-tone modulation, timpani, a mixed roll. Drop: kick, bass, string ostinato doubled by the supersaw, brass, full theme, 48 bars. A last stripped-down plateau, then a 32-bar exit. The breakdown is the slow movement of a symphony: give it its own curve, with a climax before the final roll.
orchestraltrance.basse: Uplifting offbeat bass on the drop, Virus or Sylenth1 sawtooth, 120 ms decay, 5:1 sidechain, over a rich harmonic progression: vi, IV, I, V, with passing chords and inversions. It is doubled by EastWest cellos and double basses in whole notes or eighth notes, which add weight and warmth. In the breakdown, the synth bass disappears and the low strings hold the harmony alone. Sine sub below 60 Hz on the drop. Cut the bass at 90 Hz and the low strings at 60 Hz so they don't fight the sub.
etapes: Project at 138 BPM, a rich four-chord progression with inversions, a 16-bar theme written for strings.
Load EastWest libraries or equivalents: violins in a sixteenth-note ostinato, harp arpeggios, held brass, choirs, timpani.
Lay down uplifting drums and an offbeat bass on the drop, with cellos doubling the bass.
Write the breakdown as a slow movement: theme on strings, choirs, a section in whole notes, a one-tone modulation, timpani.
Double the string ostinato with a supersaw on the drop only, 4 dB below.
Arrange 10 minutes, put the whole orchestra in a single hall reverb and high-pass each section.
orchestraltrance.mix: Orchestral layers mask each other easily: high-pass each section, strings at 200 Hz, harp at 300 Hz, brass at 150 Hz, and reserve the low end for the kick, the sub and the cellos. A single hall reverb return for the whole orchestra, 4-second decay, 30 ms pre-delay, so everything sounds in the same room. Light sidechain on the strings, 2:1 ratio. Supersaw wide but 4 dB below the strings. Kick around -6 dB peak. Compression on the orchestral bus, 2:1 ratio, 30 ms attack. Master: glue compressor, limiter around -7 LUFS. The grandeur comes from the dynamics of the breakdown, not from the level.

outils.pourquoi: Violins and violas in a sixteenth-note ostinato, held brass, choirs: the reference orchestral library for producers following Andy Blueman.
Recent version with more string and woodwind articulations, for the main theme played by the strings and then taken up by the supersaw.
The player for third-party orchestral libraries, harps and woodwinds included, with articulation control via keyswitch.
Eighth-note harp arpeggios over two octaves, dotted-eighth delay, high-passed at 300 Hz so it doesn't mask the strings.
The supersaw as reinforcement: doubles the strings on the drop, 4 dB below them, for power without taking the orchestra's place.
Classic trance plucks and pads under the orchestra, lightly sidechained, as with Daniel Kandi and Ferry Tayle.
A single hall reverb return for the whole orchestra, 4-second decay, 30 ms pre-delay, so all sections sound in the same room.

reperes: Tiesto: Elements of Life (2007): strings in ostinato doubled by supersaw and the symphonic breakdown, the genre taken to the stadium
Andy Blueman: Sea Tides (2009): the breakdown written as a slow movement, with modulation and choirs, the fine craftsmanship of the style
Daniel Kandi: Breathe (2007): uplifting tipping into orchestral, harp and strings over an offbeat bass
Ferry Corsten: Punk (2002): sampled brass and strings as reinforcement for an anthem, before the full formula
orchestraltrance.rythme: On the drop, the drums are uplifting drums: clean 909 kick, clap and snare on 2 and 4, open hat, ride. What gets added is orchestral percussion: timpani on the first beats of the 8-bar blocks, an orchestral bass drum reinforcing the kick on the drop, a marching snare rolling during the breakdown, struck cymbals instead of crashes. During the breakdown, the timpani and an orchestral snare in soft sixteenth notes hold the tempo without a kick. The build-up rolls mix the 909 snare and accelerating timpani.
orchestraltrance.sons: Strings in ostinato, EastWest violins and violas in sixteenth notes, playing the chord arpeggio: this replaces the trance pluck. The harps play eighth-note arpeggios over two octaves, the brass holds the chords on the drop, the choirs widen the breakdown. The woodwinds, flute or oboe, sometimes carry the theme. The supersaw is reinforcement: it doubles the strings on the drop for power, nothing more. Classical progressions, modulations, cadences. A long 4-second hall reverb on the orchestral parts, a dotted-eighth delay on the harp. The main theme is written to be played by the strings, then taken up by the supersaw.
orchestraltrance.tempo: 136 to 140 BPM, the uplifting tempo, but the feel is that of a score: you think in movements, not blocks. Straight grid. The breakdown can last 3 minutes and contain a key change, a slowing of the harmony, a section in whole notes. Andy Blueman writes tracks of 10 to 12 minutes. Count in 8-bar phrases that match melodic phrases, and plan a one-tone modulation upward for the final drop. The difference from uplifting: the breakdown's time is not a build-up toward the drop, it is a slow movement with its own logic.

peaktimetechno.arrangement: Six minutes, readable. A 32-bar intro of kick and hi-hats for the DJ. Bass at 33, stab at 49, plateau at 65. Breakdown at 97: 16 bars without kick, stab and vocal, an 8-bar noise riser, a 4-bar roll, one bar of silence or a sub drop, drop at 113 with everything. A 32-bar plateau, a second, longer breakdown at 161 with the bass-lead alone, build-up, final drop, 32-bar outro. Each section is 16 or 32 bars, never anything else. Two drops, no more. It is a Beatport-shelf architecture, but it works because the crowd knows exactly when to jump. Add a tom fill every 8 bars on the plateaus.
