peaktimetechno.basse: An FM sub with Operator: carrier A on coarse 1, modulator B on coarse 2 at -40 dB, 24 dB low-pass filter at 2 kHz with 2.8 dB of drive in Sine mode for warmth. A low-high pattern jumping octaves: one G per beat, you remove the first, raise the third by an octave, then shift the notes by hand so they stick to the swung hi-hat. Sub mono, dry, no effects at all. On top, a bass-lead: Saturn 2 in five bands (crossovers at 100, 300, 1000, 5000 Hz), then Saturator, an audible reverb, an EQ that controls the lows and boosts presence, a compressor at the end of the chain. It becomes the track's hook.
etapes: At 130 BPM, build a three-layer kick (tuned sub, body, click) with Drum Buss on the bus.
Create an FM sub in Operator (coarse 1 and 2, modulator at -40 dB, 2 kHz filter with drive) in an octave pattern.
Add a bass-lead processed by Saturn in five bands, Saturator, EQ, compressor.
Program a dark stab in Serum in a syncopated pattern and a group of rhythmic synths.
Make a 16-bar white noise riser and a 4-bar snare roll.
Arrange in 16- and 32-bar sections, two breakdowns, two drops, a loud master with clipper and limiter.
peaktimetechno.mix: Loud mastering: the master aims for -6 to -7 LUFS with a limiter (Pro-L 2) and a clipper before it, without the kick losing its transient. Dominant kick at -4 dB peak, sub at -8, everything else below -10. Strong sidechain on the bass-lead and stabs, 150 ms release. Sub mono below 100 Hz, highs widened with an imager or a Utility at 120% above 3 kHz. Drum bus with Glue at 4:1 and gentle saturation. Surgical EQ on the bass-lead to avoid 200 to 400 Hz. The riser must cut out at the exact moment of the drop, cleanly. Compare your drop with a Drumcode track at the same volume: if it feels softer, it's the kick, not the master.

outils.pourquoi: A three-layer kick on a bus with Drum Buss, Analog for the white noise build-ups, Glue at 4:1 on the drums, Utility widened above 3 kHz.
Dark stabs: two saws, closed filter, short decay, a one-key minor chord played in a syncopated pattern; also the hoovers on the rave side.
FM sub: carrier coarse 1, modulator coarse 2 at -40 dB, 24 dB low-pass at 2 kHz with 2.8 dB of Sine drive, in an octave pattern.
Five bands (100, 300, 1000, 5000 Hz) on the bass-lead before Saturator, EQ and compressor: this is what becomes the hook.
The clearly audible reverb on the bass-lead and stabs, and a short 0.8 s plate on the clap.
The kick body, toms in a descending fill at the end of 8-bar phrases, a snare roll over 4 bars before the drop; as samples.
The loud master of the Beatport shelf, -6 to -7 LUFS, with a clipper before it so the kick keeps its transient.
To synthesize the short sub tuned to the key and the definition click, to layer under a 909 body.

reperes: Amelie Lens: Higher (2017): the clean kick, the dark stab and the vocal, the complete peak time recipe
Enrico Sangiuliano: Astral Projection (2018): the bass-lead as a hook, Drumcode-calibrated build-ups and drops
Charlotte de Witte: Doppler (2018): the sub pumping under a mono riff, maximum efficiency
I Hate Models: Daydream (2018): the melancholic hoover and the kick up front, the rave version of peak time
peaktimetechno.rythme: A calibrated, layered kick: a short sine sub tuned to the key, a 909 or synthesized body, a click for definition, on a bus with Drum Buss. Closed hi-hats on the offbeats or in sixteenth notes, open hat on the last offbeat, ride on the plateaus. Clap on 2 and 4 with a short 0.8 s reverb. 909 toms in a descending fill at the end of 8-bar phrases. A snare roll in sixteenth notes then thirty-second notes over 4 bars before the drop, rising velocity. A swung hi-hat that makes the bass slide: place the sub notes slightly late so they lock to the hi-hat rather than the grid.
peaktimetechno.sons: Dark stabs in Serum: two saws, closed filter, short decay, a minor chord on a single key, played in a syncopated pattern. A group of rhythmic synths that switch on and off depending on the section. White noise build-ups: Analog with noise only, a filter that opens over 16 bars, auto-pan. A one-phrase vocal, pitched, with delay. Impacts and sub drops at the moment of the drop. The kick is treated as an instrument: reverb on the click only, transient shaper, saturation. Everything is clean and loud: few elements, each one polished. A rave hoover is coming back in recent productions for the anthem side.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
peaktimetechno.tempo: From 128 to 135 BPM, most often 130 or 132. 5 to 10% swing on the hi-hats at most, the rest straight. The feel is that of the main room at midnight: efficiency, readability, every move signposted. The sixteenth notes of the hi-hats and bass give the speed; the tempo itself stays below the hard techno line. Lock your risers and rolls to exactly 8 and 16 bars. At 130 BPM, a bar lasts 1.85 s: a 16-bar build-up lasts 30 seconds, which is the maximum to keep a dancefloor in suspense. Don't go below 128: you tip into melodic.

phillysoul.arrangement: The Philly song is an architecture: an 8- to 16-bar instrumental intro where the strings state the theme, a 16-bar sung verse with light rhythm section, a rising pre-chorus, an 8- or 16-bar chorus with backing vocals, second verse, chorus, a modulating bridge (often one tone up), a final chorus repeated with ad-libs, a long 1- to 2-minute outro where the groove rolls and the singer improvises. It is this instrumental outro, on Love Is the Message or TSOP, that the disco DJs extended. Length 4 to 6 minutes, up to 10 for the long versions. Transitions are made with snare rolls, harp glissandos and string build-ups. For a club version, cut the vocal and extend the outro to 5 minutes.
phillysoul.basse: The Philly bass is a Fender played fingerstyle, more melodic than funk: it walks, it sings, it connects the chords with passing notes. At disco tempos, it plays steady eighth notes with the octave on the weak beat; on ballads, whole notes and descending chromatic lines. Use a fingerstyle bass sample (Trilian, or an electric acoustic bass from the Ableton packs) with medium sustain and a little release. Write lines that follow the chord changes every 2 bars, with a third or a fifth as an approach note before each change. Gentle compression (3:1, 3 dB) and a low-pass at 2.5 kHz for roundness. No saturation, no synth: the bass must sound like a 1973 session musician.
etapes: Program Earl Young's beat at 120 BPM: kick on all four beats, hi-hat opening on each offbeat.
Write an 8-bar progression in major seventh chords and a melodic fingerstyle bass that connects them.
Lay down a Rhodes with tremolo and a sixteenth-note wah guitar.
Write separate string parts, violins in a motif, cellos in countermelody, with an orchestral library.
Build the song format with a modulating bridge and a 2-minute instrumental outro.
Mix wide, shared Plate reverb, strings high-passed at 200 Hz, dynamic master at minus 14 LUFS.
phillysoul.mix: The Sigma Sound sound is silky and wide: strings in a wide-open stereo field, compact drums in the center, vocal up front with a 2.5-second plate reverb. Use a shared Plate reverb for the strings, brass and vocal, and a short 0.9-second room for the drums. The strings get a high-pass at 200 Hz to leave room for the bass, and a slight dip at 3 kHz to stay soft. Bus compression on the rhythm section (Glue, 2:1, 2 dB) and firmer compression on the vocal (4:1, 5 dB). The master stays dynamic, minus 14 LUFS, with gentle tape saturation and a one-dB bump at 12 kHz for air. No aggressive limiter: the string crescendos need room to rise.

outils.pourquoi: The plate reverb of Gamble and Huff's studio, shared by the strings, brass and vocal; Hybrid Reverb or Reverb in Plate type at 2.5 seconds.
Ronnie Baker's bass with MFSB: played fingerstyle, walking, melodic, with approach notes before each chord change every 2 bars.
Major seventh and ninth chords with tremolo, under the strings; Ableton Electric or Keyscape, with a slow Auto Pan.
Free and enough to write separate string parts: violins in a rising motif, violas and cellos in countermelody, harp glissando.
The native alternative for silky strings: legato sections, high-pass at 200 Hz to leave room for the bass, slight dip at 3 kHz.
The fingerstyle bass that sounds like a 1973 session musician: medium sustain, a little release, gentle 3:1 compression, low-pass at 2.5 kHz.
A well-recorded acoustic kit for Earl Young's beat: kick on all four beats, hi-hat opening on each offbeat, rolls at the end of phrases.
Two spaces: a short 0.9-second room for the drums, a 2.5-second plate shared by the strings, brass and vocal.

reperes: MFSB: TSOP The Sound of Philadelphia (1974): Earl Young's drumming, the string motifs, disco before the word existed.
The O'Jays: Love Train (1972): the walking bass, the group chorus, the irresistible pop structure.
Harold Melvin and The Blue Notes: The Love I Lost (1973): the open hat on the offbeats, considered one of the first disco beats.
Billy Paul: Me and Mrs. Jones (1972): the Philly ballad, silky strings and Rhodes, slowness with soul.
phillysoul.rythme: Earl Young's drumming with MFSB is what invented the disco beat: kick on all four beats, snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hi-hat opening on each offbeat (the “and”), which gives the characteristic pshh. Load a well-recorded acoustic kit and program this pattern at 120 BPM, with the open hat at velocity 80 and the closed one at 100. Add discreet snare ghost notes, sixteenth-note congas, a tambourine on the eighth notes and a cabasa. Fills are snare and tom rolls at the end of 8-bar phrases, more orchestral than in funk. A vibraphone or bells sometimes double the rhythm. Everything is played: vary velocities and timing by a few milliseconds.
phillysoul.sons: The brief names the Sigma Sound studio, the Rhodes, the Clavinet, the electric bass, the drums, and the MFSB orchestra with its written strings. The strings are the sound of the genre: violins in high sustained lines or repeated eighth-note motifs, violas and cellos in countermelodies. Use a string library (Ableton Orchestral Strings, or Spitfire BBC Discover, free) and write separate parts, not block chords: a violin motif rising over 4 bars, a cello descending. Add soft brass in held chords, a vibraphone, a harp glissando at transitions, and a sixteenth-note wah guitar. The Rhodes holds the major seventh and ninth chords, with tremolo. Backing vocals in thirds double the lead vocal in the chorus.
phillysoul.tempo: Philly soul slows down and softens funk: ballads at 65-80 BPM and upbeat tracks at 110-125 BPM, like Love Train or TSOP, which foreshadow disco. The sixteenth-note swing is lighter than in funk, 52 to 55 percent, almost straight, with drums playing ahead of the beat and a hi-hat that starts opening on the offbeats. What changes compared to funk: the pulse becomes steady on all four beats, the kick loses its syncopations, and the orchestra imposes very square 8-bar phrases. At a slow tempo, the strings and the vocal stretch time; at a fast tempo, the snare on 2 and 4 carries the dance. In a DAW, groove MPC 16 Swing 54 and rounded velocities.

postdisco.arrangement: A post-disco track is a long groove, 6 to 9 minutes, arranged by subtraction. A 16-bar intro with bass and drums alone. The keyboard comes in, then the vocal, over 16-bar sections that resemble verses and choruses but with little harmonic contrast: often a single chord, or two. A dub break in the middle: the drums stay, everything goes into the echo, 16 bars. The bass returns, then the vocal. A long 32-bar outro with the bare groove. The experimentation is in the production, not in the structure: a track can hold on a single bass note for eight minutes.
postdisco.basse: The electric bass is up front, often the main element of the track. It is minimal: a two-bar pattern on one or two notes, played slap or with a pick, repeated without variation. Think of ESG or the Peech Boys: the root in eighth notes with an octave, a silence, a passing note. Record a real bass if you can; otherwise an electric bass sampler with contrasting velocities and very short notes for the slap. Compress it at 5:1 with a fast attack so it snaps. It talks with the kick, but above all with the void: what it doesn't play counts as much as what it plays.
etapes: Set 112 BPM with 54% swing, load an acoustic drum kit and compress it hard with gated reverb on the snare.
Program the kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats in eighth notes, cowbell in eighth notes, no fills.
Record or program a minimal electric bass on one or two notes, slap or with a pick, compressed at 5:1.
Add Prophet-5 minor-chord stabs on the offbeats, a thin guitar with delay, a vocal processed through an echo.
Build 7 minutes by subtraction: bass and drums alone, gradual entries, dub break, bare groove in the outro.
Mix dry: bass as loud as the kick, tight drum bus, dynamics preserved.
postdisco.mix: The post-disco mix is dry and compressed, with a loud bass. Compress the drum bus at 4:1 with a 10 ms attack for tightness, then gated reverb on the snare alone. The bass is compressed at 5:1 and placed as loud as the kick, around 80 to 150 Hz. The kick is cut below 45 Hz. The Prophet stabs get an eighth-note delay and a short plate. The vocal gets heavy treatment: tape echo or gated reverb, never neutral. The master stays dynamic, -13 LUFS, with light tape saturation. The space comes from what is missing: don't fill the spectrum, leave holes.

outils.pourquoi: The minor-chord stabs on the offbeats and the short pads that replace the vanished strings.
The Prophet-5 emulation for the stabs and the sawtooth lead, with an eighth-note delay and a short plate behind.
The other common Prophet-5 emulation, for the same stabs and pads, with the original factory presets.
The electric bass up front, a two-bar pattern played slap or with a pick, compressed at 5:1 so it snaps.
The drum machine that doubles or replaces the drummer, electronic claps and cowbells, in a Drum Rack under the acoustic kit.
The first drum machine of the New York records at the turn of 1980, sampled under the played drums for the machine side.
The 200 ms gated reverb on the snare and on the Peech Boys' vocals; a short reverb with a gate is enough today.
Tape echo on the vocal, in the manner of Arthur Russell, and the delay on the thin single-note guitar.

reperes: ESG: Moody (1981): the one-note bass, the dry drums and the void, the minimal template.
Peech Boys: Don't Make Me Wait (1982): gated reverb, synth stabs and production as an instrument.
D Train: Keep On (1982): the electric bass up front over a groove without strings, the hinge toward boogie.
Was (Not Was): Wheel Me Out (1980): the dry drums, the repeated bass and the experimental studio.
postdisco.rythme: The drums are dry, compressed, close-miked, often with gated reverb on the snare. Kick on 1 and 3 or on all four beats but shorter, a firm snare on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats in eighth or sixteenth notes with few open ones. A cowbell or clave in eighth notes, sparse congas. The first drum machines (LinnDrum, CR-78) sometimes double or replace the played drums. In your DAW, a heavily compressed acoustic drum kit, with a 200 ms gated reverb on the snare, and a CR-78 or LinnDrum Drum Rack underneath for the machine side. No ornamental fills.
postdisco.sons: The Sequential Prophet-5 replaces the strings: minor-chord stabs on the offbeats, short pads, a sawtooth lead. The guitar is thin, in choked chords or single notes with a delay. The vocal is more direct, sometimes spoken, often processed: Arthur Russell ran his voice through echoes, the Peech Boys through gated reverbs. The first drum machines add electronic claps and cowbells. Studio effects are used as instruments: gated reverb, tape delay, filters. Today: Arturia Prophet V or u-he Repro-5, Ableton's Echo, a reverb with a gate.
sourcesOutils: The Vinyl Factory (Arthur Russell, World Of Echo)
postdisco.tempo: Post-disco slows down a little and strips back: 105 to 120 BPM, with many tracks around 110 to 115. The feel is still played, but drier and tenser than disco, with a light 53 to 55% swing on the sixteenth notes. Set 112 BPM. The signature is space: fewer elements, each one louder. The kick is no longer necessarily on all four beats, the snare on 2 and 4 cracks on its own, and the groove holds on three elements: drums, bass, one keyboard. It is rhythm-section music, not orchestral music, and the silence between the notes is part of the pattern.

powerelectronics.arrangement: A power electronics piece is a recorded performance, then edited. Prepare your three chains (feedback, oscillator, voice), start recording, and play for 10 minutes, manipulating the gains, filters and pedals. Then cut. The most common form: a wall that settles in over 30 seconds, holds, then a voice that comes in and out in bursts, then a rupture into near-total silence, then the wall returns louder. Dynamic contrast is the main tool: from silence to maximum in one second. Count on 5 to 12 minutes. The titles and lyrics carry the meaning: they are as important as the sound.
powerelectronics.basse: The low end is a hostile drone. A lab oscillator, or Operator as a pure sine, between 30 and 60 Hz, held without interruption, saturated until it turns square. Add a second oscillator 2 Hz apart for a slow beating that makes the room vibrate. No notes, no line: a single frequency that rises or falls very slowly, via automation over 3 minutes. No-input mixing feedback also provides a natural low end: the howl of a console looped into itself often settles around 50 to 100 Hz. The relationship to rhythm doesn't exist, since there is no rhythm: the low end is the floor on which everything else screams.
etapes: Create a feedback loop in Ableton: a return track sent to itself, Utility for the gain, EQ Eight and Overdrive in the loop. Raise the gain until it whistles.
Lay down a drone on Operator, sine at 45 Hz, saturated in Hard Curve until it becomes a square wave, with a second oscillator at 47 Hz for the beating.
Record a screamed vocal into a dynamic mic, run through Pedal in Fuzz, Overdrive, then a tape delay feeding back at 90%.
Record a 10-minute performance playing the gains, filters and mutes live, without grid or metronome.
Edit the recording into a 7-minute piece with a rupture into silence and a louder return.
Finish with a high-pass at 30 Hz, a hard clipper, a cut of the peaks between 2 and 5 kHz and a mono check.
powerelectronics.mix: Everything is clipped, but methodically. High-pass at 30 Hz on the master so you don't destroy the speakers. A hard clipper (Saturator in Hard Curve with Soft Clip off) at the end of the chain, rather than a limiter that would pump. Check mono compatibility: stereo feedback often cancels out, a Utility in mono below 300 Hz fixes the problem. Watch the spectrum analyzer: distortions in series create resonant peaks around 2 to 5 kHz that genuinely hurt the ears, cut them by 6 dB. The final level is loud, minus 6 LUFS, but the real volume is set at the gig. Keep a moment of silence in each piece to give the noise meaning.

outils.pourquoi: A small console for no-input mixing: output sent back into an input, gain raised slowly until it howls, which often settles between 50 and 100 Hz.
A distortion pedal chained with two others, on the screamed vocal as on the oscillators, until the origin of the signal is lost.
High-pass and low-pass filters pushed into self-oscillation, external input to make a mic scream through it: the synth of noise scenes since 1978.
A dynamic mic that takes the scream at arm's length, before Pedal in Fuzz, Overdrive and a tape delay feeding back at 90%.
On metal, glass or a radiator, for textures. The book also describes a telephone coil that picks up interference from devices.
The tape delay that runs into feedback on its own when you raise the feedback, a source of irregular pulses without a drum machine.
Pure sine at 45 Hz saturated in Hard Curve until it squares off, plus a second oscillator at 47 Hz for the slow beating that makes the room vibrate.
Amount 100%, square shape, rate 4 Hz on the noise track: the only mechanical pulse allowed in the genre.

reperes: Whitehouse: Wriggle Like a Fucking Eel (2003): the processed scream, the pushed oscillators, the theatricality of excess.
Genocide Organ: Mind Control (1995): the wall settling in, the speech samples, the oppressive slowness.
Pharmakon: Self-Regulating System (2019): the contemporary side, body and feedback, dynamics from silence to scream.
powerelectronics.rythme: No drums. Rhythmic events come from elsewhere: a square LFO at 6 Hz cutting a drone, feedback that starts oscillating in jolts, a voice screaming in bursts. In Ableton, put an Auto Pan with Amount at 100%, square shape, rate 4 Hz, on your noise track: you get the genre's mechanical pulse. A Gate with a high threshold on a feedback signal creates irregular pulses. If you want an impact, a gunshot or sheet-metal sample, run through three distortions, played by hand without quantization. Regularity is the enemy: every hit should land a little too early or too late.
powerelectronics.sons: Three sources: feedback, oscillators, voice. No-input mixing in Ableton: create a return track, send it to itself with a Utility to control the gain, put an EQ and a distortion in the loop, and slowly raise the gain until it whistles. The oscillators: Operator in sine, sawtooth or noise, pushed into a chain of pedals (Pedal in Fuzz, then Overdrive, then Saturator in Hard Curve). The voice: screamed into a dynamic mic, run through the same chain, with a tape delay feeding back at 90%. A contact mic on metal gives textures. Each source is processed until its origin is lost.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone chapter: layered drones, effects on drones)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Textural Drone and Experimental Techno chapters)
Vintage Synth Explorer (Power electronics / noise thread)
Gearspace (Additional gear for harsh/rhythmic noise thread)
powerelectronics.tempo: There is no tempo. Power electronics is played in free time, without a grid, without a regular pulse. What separates the genre from the industrial music it descends from: it refuses even the machine pulse. The only measure is duration: blocks of noise from 2 to 15 minutes. In your DAW, turn off the metronome, work in Arrangement view without a grid (Ctrl+4 to turn off snap), and think in seconds. If a pulse appears, it comes from a square-wave low-frequency oscillator chopping a signal at 2 or 8 Hz, not from a drum machine. Changes happen when you decide, by hand, during a live take.

progpsy.arrangement: Prog psy is a trajectory. A 32- to 64-bar intro: kick, offbeat bass, hi-hats, then a filtered pad that opens up. The body unfolds in 32-bar sections where one element comes in and another goes out, without a break. A first breakdown around bar 128, where the kick disappears but the bass continues muted under a pad that opens up, for 16 to 32 bars, then the kick returns on a simple crash, with the lead. The second, longer breakdown introduces the main melody. Aim for 9 minutes. Playability comes from long, stable intros and outros: the prog psy DJ mixes over 2 or 3 minutes.
progpsy.basse: The round offbeat bass is the genre's identity. On Virus or Serum, a sawtooth with a low-pass filter at 200 Hz, moderate resonance, a filter envelope that opens on each note and closes again in 120 ms. The note lasts almost a full eighth note, with a 60 ms release, which gives the bounce. Kick on the beat, bass on the “and”. Add variations: an extra sixteenth note before the next kick every 2 bars, or a passing note on the fifth. Root in F or G, but the bass follows the pad's chord changes. Soft sidechain triggered by the kick, 3:1 ratio, 150 ms release, makes the whole thing breathe.
etapes: Project at 138 BPM. A round kick tuned to F around 50 Hz with a 200 ms body.
Offbeat bass on F1: notes on the “and” of each beat, sawtooth filtered at 200 Hz, 60 ms release, soft sidechain from the kick.
Add sixteenth-note hi-hats with varied velocities, an open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4, shakers with 52% swing.
Create a pad with two detuned oscillators and automate its filter over 32 bars, add a long reverb.
Write a melodic eighth-note pluck in F Dorian with a dotted-eighth delay, and a discreet arpeggio filtered low.
Arrange 9 minutes as a trajectory: long intro, two breakdowns where the bass continues under the pad, stable outro.
progpsy.mix: The mix is airier than psytrance: fewer elements at once, more stereo space and more reverb. Kick and bass stay mono below 150 Hz, but the bass can have a little width above 300 Hz via a light chorus. The soft sidechain is also applied to the pads and leads, with a 200 ms release, to create discreet pumping. Light bus compression, 2:1 ratio, on the percussion. No aggressive limiter: aim for -8 to -9 LUFS to keep the dynamics of the automations. A long shared reverb (3 to 4 s) on the pads and leads, with a 40 ms pre-delay, gives depth.

outils.pourquoi: The round offbeat bass: sawtooth, low-pass at 200 Hz, filter envelope closing in 120 ms. There are plenty of progressive psy Virus banks.
Evolving pads with two detuned oscillators, filter automated over 32 bars; the sound of the Swedish school, Atmos, Ticon, Vibrasphere.
Pads and intros with analog grain, slow filter movement; used for the long 4-minute build-ups that define the genre.
The modern offbeat bass and the soft eighth-note plucks, dotted-eighth delay behind, in the Israeli wave of the 2010s.
Pads with slow LFOs on the table position; Echo alongside for delays synced to the dotted eighth.
The soft sidechain drawn by hand: release around 150 ms on the bass, 200 ms on the pads, for discreet pumping.
A long shared reverb, 3 to 4 s with 40 ms of pre-delay, on the pads and leads for depth.

reperes: Atmos: Klein Aber Doctor (1999): the offbeat bass and the gradual entry of layers, the founding Swedish sound.
Vibrasphere: Erosion (2003): pads automated over minutes and melodic light.
Ace Ventura & Astrix: Pranava (2019): the Israeli version, more melodic and more compressed, with a piano breakdown.
Space Safari: Fun Key (2000): the groove of discreet percussion under the offbeat bass.
progpsy.rythme: The kick is round and deep, tuned around 50 Hz, with a 200 ms body: it has room, since the bass doesn't play on the next sixteenth note. A soft clap or snare on 2 and 4, with a short reverb. The discreet groove percussion of the brief: sixteenth-note hi-hats with very differentiated velocities, a short open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4, lightly swung shakers, spaced-out wooden percussion, playing 2-bar patterns. No spectacular snare rolls: transitions are made with filters and by pulling elements out. A ride during the plateaus adds air.
progpsy.sons: Virus and Nord Lead for evolving pads: two slightly detuned oscillators, a low-pass filter whose frequency is automated over 32 bars, a chorus and a long reverb. The leads are soft, often short-decay plucks played in eighth notes with a dotted-eighth delay, in minor or Dorian scale, with luminous melodies. The FX are slow sweeps, not squelches. Add layers of discreet sixteenth-note arpeggios, filtered low. The Israeli school of the 2010s adds ethereal vocals and piano chords in the breakdowns. In Ableton, Wavetable with its slow LFOs and Echo do the job. Everything is automated: filter, reverb send, stereo width.
sourcesOutils: Dance Midi Samples, Spectro Senses' Access Virus Progressive Psytrance banks
Myloops, Top 15 VST Plugins for Psytrance Production
progpsy.tempo: Prog psy slows down: 134 to 140 BPM, with 138 as the center. The bass leaves the rolling pattern for the offbeat: kick on the beat, bass on the eighth-note offbeat, which gives a sway rather than a wheel. A light swing (51 to 53%) on the percussion is accepted, never on the bass. What changes compared to psytrance is the long timescale: phrases are 32 or 64 bars, automations last minutes, and the track is a trajectory rather than a series of sections. What changes compared to psytech is the bounce of the offbeat bass and the presence of melody. A track lasts 8 to 10 minutes.

progressivebreaks.arrangement: A progressive breaks track lasts 7 to 9 minutes. A 32-bar intro: percussion, a filtered pad. The bass enters at bar 33 for 32 bars. A first 32-bar build-up: the pad opens, an arpeggio appears. A first 32-bar breakdown: the drums drop out, the strings or vocal arrive, the pad rises. The break returns for 64 bars with everything, often with a chord change to the relative major in the middle. A second, longer breakdown, 48 bars, with a full melodic theme. A final 64-bar return. A 32-bar outro. Each change is anticipated 8 to 16 bars ahead by a filter or reverb automation.
progressivebreaks.basse: The round basses of the brief: a saw or triangle on an Access Virus (cited in the brief) or on Analog, with a low-pass filter at 300 Hz without resonance, a 10 ms attack and a 200 ms release. The line is simple and hypnotic: root in eighth notes, with an octave on the “and” of 4, or a dotted-quarter pattern that follows the break's kick. It changes note every 8 or 16 bars to follow the harmony (often i, VI, III, VII in minor). A sine sub underneath. Soft sidechain from the kick (3:1 ratio, 100 ms release), for breathing, not for pumping. The bass must be able to hold 64 bars without getting tiresome.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM. Program a soft break with rimshot on 2 and 4, soft-velocity hi-hats, shakers and congas in the background.
Create a round bass on Analog (saw, filter at 300 Hz, 200 ms release) in eighth notes on the root, plus a sub.
Lay down a minor ninth pad on Wavetable in unison, and automate the cutoff over 32 bars.
Add sampled strings and an ethereal vocal for the breakdowns, and a slow arpeggio on a Juno or Analog.
Arrange intro 32, bass 32, build-up 32, breakdown 32, drop 64, breakdown 48, drop 64, outro 32.
Mix the break back, automate the reverb sends, and keep -9 LUFS for dynamics.
progressivebreaks.mix: The progressive mix is spacious and soft. The break is mixed back, at -6 dB below the pads, with gentle compression (2:1 ratio). The round bass and the sub occupy the low end, mono, with light sidechain. The pads are wide (Utility Width 140%, or a Mid/Side chorus) and high-passed at 200 Hz, with a 4 to 6 s reverb and a 60 ms pre-delay. The strings and vocal come forward in the breakdowns. Automate the reverb send: it rises in the breakdowns and drops back in the drops. Master at -9 LUFS, with dynamics: the build-ups need headroom to be felt. No clipper.

outils.pourquoi: Round saw or triangle basses filtered at 300 Hz and unison pads whose filter opens over 32 bars; Wehbba keeps it on every track.
Hybrid-style sampled strings and clean mid-tempo breaks loaded from library music records.
The sequencer of the Distinctive and Hooj Choons era for long trajectories at 130 BPM, eight minutes per track.
A slow eighth-note arpeggio under the breakdowns, built-in chorus; TAL-U-NO-LX or Analog replace it easily.
A minor ninth pad in 4-voice unison, cutoff automated over 32 bars, in place of the Virus.
Round bass (saw, 300 Hz filter, 200 ms release) and two detuned saws with Chorus-Ensemble for the pads.

outils.nom: Spitfire Audio BBC Symphony Orchestra Discover
outils.pourquoi: Orchestral strings for the breakdown melodies, in the spirit of Hybrid's sessions with orchestra.
A long 6 s reverb on the ethereal vocal and strings, with Utility to widen the pads without touching the bass.

reperes: Hybrid: Finished Symphony (1999): the strings carrying the theme, the clean break underneath, the build-up over several minutes.
Way Out West: The Gift (1996): the ethereal vocal and the rising pad, the prototype of progressive breaks.
Hybrid: If I Survive (1999): the sung vocal and the break, the song version of the genre.
Way Out West: Apollo (1996): the round eighth-note bass and the long breakdown, the end of the night set to music.
progressivebreaks.rythme: The clean mid-tempo breaks of the brief: a programmed pattern with 909 sounds or soft samples. Kick on beat 1 and the “and” of 2, snare on 2 and 4, often a rimshot rather than a loud snare. Sixteenth-note hi-hats at soft velocity (80 and 50), open hat on the “and” of 4. Add sixteenth-note shakers, a tambourine, and tribal percussion (congas, bongos) in a 2-bar loop, very low. A sampled break can run in the background, high-passed at 1 kHz, for texture. Fills are rare: a reversed cymbal over 2 bars before a change, a soft snare roll every 32.
progressivebreaks.sons: The Virus is the genre's synth: wide unison pads, saw with built-in chorus, a filter opening over 32 bars. In Ableton, Wavetable in 4-voice unison or Analog with two detuned saws and Chorus-Ensemble. The progressive pads play minor chords with ninths and sus4, held for 4 bars. Sampled strings, Hybrid's signature: string sections (orchestral samples or recordings) playing a melody over the breakdowns. Add a slow eighth-note arpeggio on a Juno, an ethereal female vocal with a 6 s reverb, and long build-up FX (white noise filtered over 16 bars). No short stabs: everything is sustained.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros, Access Virus TI)
progressivebreaks.tempo: Progressive breaks is played between 128 and 134 BPM, like the progressive house it is the syncopated variant of. The feel is long and floating: the breaks are clean and discreet, and the attention goes to the pads rising over 32 or 64 bars. What separates it from nu skool is the timescale: where nu skool changes every 8 bars, progressive changes every 32, and a build-up can last two minutes. No swing. The break is there to avoid the 4/4 kick, not to grab the ear. Think of an end-of-night journey where the landscape moves slowly.

progressivehouse.arrangement: The journey. A 32- to 64-bar intro with kick, hats and one percussion part, the bass fades in. Each 32-bar block adds a layer: a pad, an arpeggio, a second percussion part, the melody. The overall filter opens continuously. Two-thirds of the way through, a 32- to 64-bar breakdown: kick cut, pads and arpeggios alone, a very slow build-up, possibly the melody in the clear, then the kick returns with everything open. A last 32-bar plateau, a gradual descent over 64 bars, outro. Length 8 to 10 minutes. There is only one peak and it has to be earned. Sasha and Digweed's sets are built on these tracks that rise across three records.
progressivehouse.basse: The round sequenced bass: a filtered sawtooth or square (JP-8000, Virus, or Analog in Ableton), filter at 300 Hz with an envelope that opens it slightly on each note, in sixteenth or eighth notes on one or two notes, with octaves. The line moves slowly: a 2-bar pattern that changes one note every 8 bars, and a modulation toward the fourth or sixth in the middle of the track. Light sidechain with the kick, 3:1 ratio. A sine sub underneath, held. The bass must turn like a wheel: it is what hypnotizes, more than the drums. Automate the cutoff over 32 bars so it opens with the track.
etapes: Project at 127 BPM, round 909 kick, low-velocity hats, a sampled conga loop with a 3/16 delay.
Round sixteenth-note bass with octaves on one note, filter at 300 Hz, sine sub underneath.
Stack two pads in chords held for 8 bars with filters opening at different speeds, and an arpeggio with a 3/16 delay and long reverb.
Write an 8-bar melody for the peak and save it.
Build 9 minutes in 32-bar blocks: one layer per block, a long breakdown two-thirds through, a single peak, a descent over 64 bars.
Mix wide and deep, one long filtered reverb, gentle bus compression, master at -10 LUFS.
progressivehouse.mix: A deep, wide mix. Kick in the center, round, without an exaggerated click. Bass in the center with the sub, cut below 35 Hz. The pads are wide and spread, filtered below 200 Hz so they don't clog. The percussion is spread and sent to a 3/16 delay and a medium reverb. A single long reverb (4 to 6 s, low-passed at 6 kHz) for the pads and arpeggios. Gentle bus compression (2:1, slow attack), no audible pumping. Light, invisible sidechain on pads and bass. Master at -9 to -10 LUFS: the style likes dynamics, an over-squashed track loses its depth. Control 200 to 400 Hz: three stacked pads quickly clog the mix.

outils.pourquoi: Filtered Supersaw for the stacked pads and the round sequenced basses, Sasha's synth in the Xpander era.
Pads and basses with a filter opening over 32 bars, built-in synced delays; the Virus TI later, or Ableton's Wavetable with unison.
The sampled conga and tribal percussion loops, played in 2-bar layers with a 3/16 delay on top.
The sequencer of the English Guerilla and Deconstruction studios for building 9 minutes in 32-bar blocks, one layer per block.
Wide pads, arpeggios and stretched textures for today's progressive producers, who find sampled Juno, Jupiter and Virus sounds in it.
Ableton's Delay or Valhalla Delay at 3/16 on almost everything, percussion, arpeggios, stabs: this is what gives the style its roll.
A single long 4 to 6 s reverb, low-passed around 6 kHz, on pads and arpeggios, for depth without clogging the mix.

reperes: Sasha: Xpander (1999): the turning sequenced bass, the stacked pads and the peak arriving after five minutes, the style at maturity.
BT: Flaming June (1997): the arpeggios with 3/16 delay and the melody saved for the peak, the melodic side.
Lost: Baz De Conga (1990): looped tribal percussion under English house, before the word progressive existed.
Meduza: Piece of Your Heart (2019): what the word means in the 2010s charts, a short structure and a pop vocal.
progressivehouse.rythme: A round 909 kick, not too loud, on every beat. Clap or snare on 2 and 4, often discreet, replaced by a rim or a percussion hit. Closed hats in sixteenth notes at low velocity, open on the offbeats. The rhythmic core is the layer of tribal percussion: sampled congas, bongos, shakers, played in two-bar loops with 3/16 delays doubling them, mixed low and spread in stereo. These percussion parts come in one by one over 64 bars. Fills are hat cuts or percussion rolls, not loud 909 toms. A discreet ride can come in at the peak. Everything is soft, steady, deep.
progressivehouse.sons: Stacked pads: two or three pads (JP-8000 filtered Supersaw, Virus, or Wavetable with unison) in chords held for 4 or 8 bars, each with its own filter opening at different speeds. Arpeggios or sixteenth-note sequences, with a 3/16 delay and a long reverb, that appear as the filter opens. A simple lead, an 8-bar melody, saved for the peak. Processed percussion sounds, sampled and stretched ethereal vocals, wind noises. Signature effects: 3/16 synced delay on almost everything, long filtered reverb, slow phaser, a low-pass filter rising over 64 bars. Nothing saturated, nothing brutal: progressive is a style of pads and layers.
sourcesOutils: GearBook, Progressive House and the Birth of Trance
Production Music Live, Best VST Plugins For Progressive House
progressivehouse.tempo: Between 124 and 130 BPM in 1992, 126 to 128 today. The feel is steady and hypnotic, with a light swing on the percussion (52 to 55%) and a perfectly straight kick. What sets progressive apart is the long timescale: phrases are 32 bars, build-ups 64, tracks 8 to 10 minutes. Delays synced to dotted eighths (3/16) create a polyrhythm that gives the feeling of moving forward without anything changing. Nothing is abrupt: each element arrives with a fade or a filter opening. Count your sections in 32s and build the track like a journey, with a single peak two-thirds of the way through.

progressivetrance.arrangement: Ten minutes that dramatize nothing. A 64-bar intro for the DJ with drums and filtered bass. One layer every 16 bars: arpeggio 1, pad, arpeggio 2, pluck. The first breakdown removes the kick but keeps the filtered bass and the arpeggios. Unlike uplifting, the breakdown adds an element instead of stripping everything out. The drop is a return of the kick without a crash, without a roll, almost discreet. A second, longer breakdown in the middle, with a chord change. Then the layers are removed in reverse order. The track is a trajectory: at any moment, something is appearing or disappearing.
progressivetrance.basse: The rolling bass is the signature. A Virus or JP-8000 sawtooth, cutoff around 350 Hz, eighth notes on the root with added sixteenth notes on beats 2 and 4, or alternating root and octave in continuous sixteenth notes. Tight sidechain from the kick, 6:1 ratio, 120 ms release: the pumping is what makes it roll. The bass follows the chord progression, root, sixth, fourth, fifth over 8 bars. A second sine sub layer holds whole notes below 60 Hz. High-pass the main bass at 80 Hz and leave the sub alone at the bottom.
etapes: Project at 131 BPM, short kick on every beat, thin clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats with velocities 100/60.
Write the rolling bass: eighth notes on the root with added sixteenth notes, 6:1 sidechain from the kick, sine sub underneath.
Program three arpeggios on the same chord progression, in eighth notes, sixteenth notes and dotted eighths, short plucked sounds, each in its own stereo position.
Add a pad with a slow LFO on the cutoff and a pluck with ping-pong delay.
Spread it over 10 minutes: one layer every 16 bars, two breakdowns that keep the bass, a symmetrical removal.
High-pass everything except kick and sub, then check that the track is constantly moving.
progressivetrance.mix: The progressive mix is clean and deep. Kick around -9 dB peak, sidechained bass just below it. Everything that isn't kick or bass is high-passed at 150 Hz minimum. Light sidechain on the pads and arpeggios too, 2:1 ratio, so the kick can breathe. Arpeggios placed at different stereo positions: one left, one right, one center. Long reverb on a single return, 4-second decay, 40 ms pre-delay, and ping-pong delay on another. Little saturation. Master around -9 LUFS, without squashing: depth demands dynamics.

outils.pourquoi: Plucks and evolving pads, slow LFO on the cutoff, built-in ping-pong delay. The Virus stays in the rack of many progressive producers, with no official emulation.
The virtual synth of the Anjunabeats sessions: short plucks for the layered arpeggios, moderate unison, no huge supersaw.
Generates the three arpeggio layers in eighth notes, sixteenth notes and dotted eighths, then convert to MIDI to move a few notes by an octave, the Attack book's method.
Plucked arpeggio, short bass preset, two detuned oscillators, cutoff and decay automation: the melodic arpeggio patch detailed by Attack Magazine.
Ducking drawn on each beat for the arpeggios and pads, more precise than a sidechain compressor. Nicky Romero Kickstart does the same thing.
Arpeggios and pads on the Platipus and Hooj Choons records of the 1990s. Arturia Jup-8000 V replaces it in the DAW.
The historic sequencer of British and Dutch trance, still used by Above & Beyond for their ten-minute trajectories.
The long reverb on a single return, 4-second decay, 40 ms pre-delay, which gives depth without drowning the arpeggios.

reperes: F2: Dominica (1994): the rolling bass and the filtered arpeggios, early progressive on Platipus
Sasha & John Digweed: Northern Exposure (1996): how a mix builds ten minutes without ever breaking the flow
Gabriel And Dresden: Tracking Treasure Down (2006): the breakdown that adds instead of removing, and the discreet drop
Tinlicker & Helsloot: Because You Move Me (2021): the modern version, more melodic, with the bass still in eighth notes
progressivetrance.rythme: The kick is less dominant than in uplifting: a short 909 or a drier sampled kick, 200 ms decay. The snare is replaced by a thin clap or a rimshot, at low volume. The hi-hats are in sixteenth notes with varied velocities, 100 then 60, to create the roll. Discreet percussion: shakers, a filtered conga, a metallic tick shifted onto the sixteenth note. No 8-bar snare roll: build-ups are made with filtered white noise and reversed cymbals. A 4-bar drum block should feel like it rolls on its own.
progressivetrance.sons: The arpeggios are layered: a first one in eighth notes, a second in sixteenth notes, a third in dotted eighths, each with a different timbre and filter. The Attack book recommends short, plucked sounds for arpeggios, instant attack and brief decay, and converting the arpeggiator to MIDI to move a few notes by an octave: that is exactly the technique here. The pads evolve slowly with an LFO on the cutoff, an 8-bar period. Virus plucks with ping-pong delay. No huge supersaw, or else low in the mix. The melodies are short and repeated, never an anthem.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter 39 (arpeggios)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
progressivetrance.tempo: 128 to 134 BPM, barely faster than the progressive house whose patience it borrows. Straight grid, but the groove comes from the rolling bass in eighth and sixteenth notes, not from the drums. A track is conceived over 10 minutes and in 32-bar blocks: each block changes only one thing. The feel is fluid, never jerky, and transitions are made with filter fades rather than cuts. Above & Beyond and Jaytech are around 130-132, Way Out West and Quivver a little lower in the 1990s. If the track feels static, add a layer of sixteenth notes, not tempo.

prototechno.arrangement: The proto-techno track is long, 5 to 9 minutes for Kraftwerk, 8 to 13 for Moroder, built on a single motif. Typical structure: a 16-bar intro with the beat and bass alone, entry of the main melody, a vocoded verse, return of the theme, an intermediate section where a new motif is layered on top, a bridge with a sound effect (train, siren, computer), everything returns, a long exit where the elements disappear one by one. Each section lasts 16 or 32 bars and starts exactly on the first beat. There is no drop, only clean additions. For playability in a DJ set, keep a 32-bar intro and exit of pure beat. The melodies return identical every time: mechanical repetition is the message.
prototechno.basse: Two schools in the brief. Kraftwerk: a short Minimoog bass, in quarter or eighth notes, on a single note per chord, round tone, filter at 400 Hz, 150 ms decay, no resonance. Moroder: the sequenced sixteenth-note bass alternating root and octave, the famous I Feel Love line reused in The Chase, played by a modular Moog driven by a sequencer. For the second, program a sawtooth in Analog, filter at 600 Hz with a little resonance, a short filter envelope, and a sequence of 16 sixteenth notes that jumps an octave every other note. Run it through a short dotted-eighth delay at 20 percent to make it shimmer. In both cases, the bass and the kick play together on the beat, without sidechain.
etapes: Build a purely synthetic percussion kit in Operator: sine kick, noise snare, short hi-hat, and program a straight beat at 120 BPM.
Pick your side for the bass: Minimoog in quarter notes (Kraftwerk) or a sixteenth-note octave sequence (Moroder).
Write a 4-bar melody on a two-oscillator mono lead, with glide, and play it by hand.
Record a spoken phrase and vocode it with a sawtooth carrier playing the chords.
Assemble 7 minutes through clean 16- or 32-bar additions, with a sound bridge in the middle.
Mix dry, no reverb on the beat, bass in mono, master at minus 12 LUFS.
prototechno.mix: The proto-techno mix is dry, centered and clean, without the reverb of the kosmische records. Little low-mid, a clean bass, clear highs. Each sound is a distinct object: no layering, one source per track. Light compression on the kick (4:1 ratio, 5 ms attack) to hold its place, and a percussion bus with Drum Buss with Transients at plus 20 percent for snap. The vocoded voice gets a quarter-note delay at 15 percent and a short 0.8-second reverb, nothing else. On the master, a Glue Compressor at 2 dB of reduction and a gentle limiter, target minus 12 LUFS. One thing to add today: cut below 30 Hz and check that the sixteenth-note bass stays in mono, because 1970s club systems were mono.

outils.pourquoi: Kraftwerk's melody and bass: two detuned oscillators, filter at 2 kHz, 60 ms glide, mono; Arturia Mini V or Behringer Model D.
The vocoder for the robot voice, with its built-in strings; Kraftwerk also used the EMS Vocoder. Roland Cloud VP-330 or Ableton's Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier.
The custom 32-step sequencer of Trans-Europe Express: the first quantized control voltages, the mechanical stiffness that becomes style.
The octave bass of I Feel Love and The Chase: a sixteenth-note sequence triggered by a click on tape, retuned constantly during the take.
The cold strings behind the melodies: sawtooths run through an ensemble chorus; Ableton's Chorus-Ensemble in Ensemble mode on a sawtooth pad.
To build a purely synthetic percussion kit like Kraftwerk before the 808: sine kick dropping from 80 to 50 Hz, filtered noise snare.
Speak a short phrase, Analog sawtooth carrier playing the chords, 24 bands, Formant at zero, then a quarter-note delay at 15 percent.
The Moroder sequence: sawtooth, filter at 600 Hz with a little resonance, 16 sixteenth notes jumping an octave every other note.

reperes: Kraftwerk: Trans-Europe Express (1977): the metallic beat imitating the train, the melody repeated identically, the vocoder.
Giorgio Moroder: The Chase (1978): the sequenced octave bass, the mechanical disco that would last all the way to techno.
Yellow Magic Orchestra: Computer Game (1978): video game bleeps as instruments, Japanese precision.
Telex: Moskow Diskow (1979): the Belgian drum machine beat, the detached voice, a pop proto-techno.
prototechno.rythme: Kraftwerk built their percussion with synths and homemade pads, before the TR-808: bare electronic sounds, clicks, filtered noise, no samples. Build your kit with Operator or Analog: a sine kick with a pitch drop from 80 to 50 Hz in 40 ms, a snare made of white noise band-passed at 1.5 kHz with a 120 ms decay, a very short noise hi-hat. Basic pattern: kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4, eighth- or sixteenth-note hi-hats at fixed velocity. Trans-Europe Express adds a syncopated metallic motif that imitates a train: a filtered noise on the “and” of each beat. Moroder, for his part, uses a real drummer or a machine playing straight disco with an open hat on the offbeats.
prototechno.sons: The machines of the brief: vocoder, drum machine, Minimoog. The vocoder is the genre's voice: sing or speak a short phrase and run it through Ableton's Vocoder with a sawtooth carrier from Analog playing the chords, 24 bands, Formant at zero. The main melody comes from the Minimoog: two slightly detuned sawtooth oscillators, filter at 2 kHz, 60 ms glide, played monophonically. The pads are cold, Polymoog- or ARP Solina-style synth strings, recreated with chorused sawtooths (Chorus-Ensemble in Ensemble mode). YMO adds video game bleeps, short square waves made with Operator. Effects: a slow phaser on the pads, an eighth-note delay on the bleeps, and nothing excessive: every sound must stay readable and clean.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Detroit techno chapter)
prototechno.tempo: Proto-techno is kosmische learning to dance: tempos from 110 to 130 BPM, with a fully quantized drum machine or sequencer pulse. Trans-Europe Express moves at around 112 BPM, Moroder's The Chase runs at 125, Telex's Moskow Diskow hits at 122. No swing: the stiffness is the style, the man-machine embraces the grid. What separates it from the synth-pop that followed: here, the beat is the subject, not the accompaniment to a song. The feel comes from repeating a 2-bar motif for 6 minutes, with tiny variations. In your DAW, turn off all groove, set velocities to 100 everywhere and let the machine dictate. Only one element can be played by hand: the Minimoog melody.

psybient.arrangement: A track lasts 8 to 12 minutes and is conceived as a landscape you travel through. A 2-minute intro without a beat: pad, nature noise, a flute in delay. The kick arrives gently, alone, then the bass, then the world percussion, each element 16 or 32 bars apart. The plateau lasts 4 minutes with texture variations, never a drop. A 1- to 2-minute breakdown around two-thirds of the way strips everything except the pad and a delay fading out slowly. The return can change key or rhythm, like a new landscape. The ending is long, 2 minutes of pad alone. Think in albums: the tracks flow into each other without silence.
psybient.basse: The round dub bass is the ground of psybient: an Operator sine or a Moog with a little triangle, gentle saturation, 600 ms release, notes held for 1 or 2 bars. It plays root and minor seventh, with slow 200 ms glides between the notes. Unlike psytrance, it doesn't pulse in sixteenth notes: it rolls. Add a send to a delay filtered at 400 Hz with 50% feedback for the dub moments. Cut it at 200 Hz, place the kick on the root and bring the bass in just after with a soft 2 dB sidechain, 300 ms release. In the passages without a beat, a very low drone bass at 40 Hz holds the ground alone.
etapes: Create an evolving pad in Absynth or Wavetable, LFO at 0.02 Hz on the wave position, and let it run over 32 bars at 85 BPM.
Record or find nature sounds, water, forest, and lay them in the background with a slowly moving filter.
Synthesize a round kick in Operator, pitch from 80 to 45 Hz in 80 ms, and a held sine bass on root and minor seventh.
Sample a flute or world percussion, chop it in Simpler and send it into a Space Echo at 60% feedback.
Run a voice or a piano through Granulator, 30 ms grains, and automate the pitch over 16 bars for the psychedelic texture.
Arrange over 10 minutes as a landscape: 2 minutes without a beat, spaced-out entries, plateau, long breakdown, ending on the pad alone.
psybient.mix: The mix is deep and detailed: many layers at very low volume, long reverbs, 8 to 12 seconds, with different pre-delays to create several distances. Each sound has its place in the stereo field, and the granular textures have automated panning. The kick and bass are clean, compressed together on a bus at a 3:1 ratio. Cut the pads at 150 Hz and the textures at 300 Hz. No heavy saturation: finesse is the goal, which separates psybient from the rawer psydub. Master at minus 12 or minus 14 LUFS, and check on headphones: that is how the genre is listened to. A transparent limiter, 1 dB of reduction maximum.

outils.pourquoi: The reference for evolving pads, 30-second envelopes and morphing. Discontinued in 2022: Omnisphere or Massive X take over.
Cosmic pads, sampled world instruments and granular mode in the same synth: today's Swiss army knife of psychill.
Granulator III on a voice, Grain Delay, Beat Repeat on the rain, Simpler for the world percussion, Echo for the dub.
Flute, didgeridoo and dub rimshot at a dotted eighth with 60% feedback. Ableton Echo or Roland Cloud RE-201 as emulation.
Carbon Based Lifeforms' virtual modular for the random textures of Stochastic, with a Moog One alongside.
Synthesized kick with pitch from 80 to 45 Hz in 80 ms, and a held sine bass, 600 ms release, 200 ms glides.
LFO at 0.02 Hz on the wave position: the pad that changes over 32 bars without anyone hearing when. Ableton's Wavetable does the same.
Sitar, tabla, Tibetan voices, udu and frame drum in a Kontakt library, to run through the Space Echo afterwards.

reperes: Carbon Based Lifeforms: Photosynthesis (2006): the slow pulse, the round bass and the pad that evolves without you knowing when.
Shpongle: I Am You (2005): Raja Ram's flute in delay, the world percussion and the baroque sound design.
Solar Fields: The Road to Nothingness (2005): the very fine layers, the discreet kick and the depth of the Ultimae mix.
Asura: Lost Eden (2001): the sampled voices, the slow dub and the cathedral reverbs.
psybient.rythme: The kick is round, deep, a tuned 808 or a kick synthesized in Operator with a pitch dropping from 80 to 45 Hz in 80 ms, long 400 ms decay. A dub snare or rimshot on 3, with a Space Echo at a dotted eighth with high feedback. The percussion is sampled world percussion: tabla, udu, djembe, frame drum, chopped in Simpler and replayed in 2-bar patterns with humanized velocities. Add granular rhythmic textures: a rain sound chopped into sixteenth notes by a Beat Repeat or a gate. Hi-hats are rare, replaced by shakers and filtered noises. The beat comes in after 2 minutes and never stays frozen: keep a filter or a delay constantly automated.
psybient.sons: Long evolving pads are the main material: Absynth remains the reference, with its 30-second envelopes and morphing, but Wavetable or Serum with very slow LFOs on the wave position do the job. A pad should change over 32 bars without anyone hearing when. Add world instruments: flute, didgeridoo, sitar, Tibetan voices, sampled and run through a Space Echo or Ableton's Echo with 60% feedback. Fine granular sound design creates the psychedelia: Granulator or Grain Delay on a voice or a piano, grain size 20 to 50 ms, pitch rising slowly. Nature sounds, forest, water, insects, serve as a permanent background, filtered and modulated.
psybient.tempo: Between 70 and 100 BPM when there is a beat, with many passages without a pulse. What changes compared to downtempo is the awareness of long time: tracks last 8 to 12 minutes and the tempo is a frame for the delays, not a dance constraint. On Shpongle's more rhythmic tracks, a dub groove at 90 BPM in half-time with lots of syncopation. With Carbon Based Lifeforms, a slow pulse at 80 BPM with a kick on every beat, almost a heartbeat. Light swing, 54%. Lock all the delays to the tempo, in dotted eighths and quarter notes, and let the pads ignore the grid.

psybreaks.arrangement: A psybreaks track lasts 6 to 8 minutes and follows a psytrance form over a break. A 32-bar intro with effects and percussion, the rolling bass enters at bar 33 with the break. A 32-bar passage with the neuro bass answering. A 32-bar breakdown: the break stops, the rolling bass can continue alone or stop, an acid lead rises, a delay runs away. A 64-bar drop with everything, and a neuro bass variation every 16. A second, longer 32-bar breakdown, with a white noise build-up. A second 64-bar drop. A 32-bar outro. Every 8 bars is marked by an effect or a fill.
psybreaks.basse: The modulated neuro-psy basses of the brief: the heart of the genre. In Serum, a saw or a simple wavetable, 24 dB low-pass filter with a fast envelope (attack 0, decay 80 ms), very short sixteenth notes on the root, like a psytrance bass. Since the break's kick and snare are short, the bass rolls without interruption on the offbeats and goes silent on the beats where the kick hits. On top, a second neuro bass: Reese or FM, with LFOs on the filter and the wavetable position, resampled, playing a 2-bar phrase in answer to the rolling bass. A sine sub below 60 Hz. Strong sidechain on the rolling bass from the kick (6:1 ratio, 40 ms release).
etapes: Set Ableton to 138 BPM. Program a clean break: kick on 1 and the “and” of 2, dry snare on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats.
Create a rolling bass on Serum: saw, 24 dB filter, 80 ms decay, short sixteenth notes on the offbeats, 6:1 sidechain from the kick.
Create a neuro bass (Reese or FM with LFO, resampled) that answers the rolling bass over 2 bars.
Add psy FX: dotted-eighth delay at 60% feedback, acid lead, zaps in counterpoint, triplet percussion.
Arrange intro 32, bass 32, answer 32, breakdown 32, drop 64, breakdown 32, drop 64, outro 32.
Mix clean: rolling bass mono between 40 and 300 Hz, sends filtered at 300 Hz, -6 LUFS without clipping.
psybreaks.mix: The psybreaks mix is surgical, like neurofunk but at 138 BPM. The kick and the rolling bass alternate with millimeter precision thanks to the short sidechain. The rolling bass is mono, high-passed at 40 Hz and low-passed at 300 Hz, compressed at 8:1. The neuro bass is cut at 120 Hz and wide above. The sub is mono. Every effect is filtered so it doesn't touch the low end. Delays and reverbs are on sends with a high-pass at 300 Hz. The drum bus gets a Glue Compressor at 4:1 and light saturation. Master at -6 LUFS with a clean limiter, no clipping: the genre wants clean.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of Hedflux and the Broken Robot scene: clean breaks at 135-140 BPM and basses resampled to audio, Freeze then Flatten.
Rolling neuro-psy bass: saw or wavetable, 24 dB filter, 80 ms decay, FM between oscillators, short notes on the offbeats.
Modulation and distortion chains in a single instrument for moving basses and psychedelic FX.
Sampled breaks and FX on the first records of the English breaks scene, before the full move to software.
Bursts of sixteenth notes at the end of phrases and on the FX, for the genre's hyper-surgical rhythm.
On the drum bus, 4:1 ratio, with sidechain on the rolling bass from the kick (6:1 ratio, 40 ms release).
Surgical cuts between kick, sub and rolling bass; production in this genre is judged on how clean the low end is.

reperes: Hedflux: Nonstop (2008): the rolling psytrance bass under a break, the complete psybreaks formula.
Hedflux: Sacral (2011): the neuro-psy sound design, every sound short and in its place, surgical production.
Colombo: Bombafunk (2011): the funkier, breaks side of the style, a bouncing bass and psychedelic effects.
Neurodriver: Sidewinder (2009): the neuro bass answering the rolling bass, the bridge between neurofunk and psytrance.
psybreaks.rythme: The clean breaks of the brief: a programmed pattern with short, precise sounds. Kick on beat 1 and on the “and” of 2, snare on 2 and 4, very dry and precise, with a peak at 1.5 kHz. Closed hi-hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocity, open hat on the “and” of 4. Add synthetic percussion (clicks, blips, pitched rimshots) following a triplet motif every other bar, for the psychedelic side. A second sampled break can run in the background, cut at 1 kHz. Fills are sixteenth-note rolls with rising pitch, and snare “stutters” via Beat Repeat. The basic pattern doesn't move: the bass and the effects move.
psybreaks.sons: The brief cites Ableton Live, Serum and the Akai S3000. Serum provides the basses and leads: wavetables with position modulation, FM between oscillators, filters moving in sixteenth notes. The psychedelic FX are those of psytrance: dotted-eighth delays with 60% feedback and a rising filter, synced phasers and flangers, 303 or resonant square “squelches”, white noise build-ups, synth sounds spinning in the panorama. Hedflux uses acid leads and short “zaps” in counterpoint to the bass. Add a filtered spoken voice and a little reverse. The brief's hyper-surgical production: every sound is short, clean, and has its place.
sources: Dirty Hippy Studio, “Production Talk with Hedflux” (dirtyhippystudio.com)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable chapter)
psybreaks.tempo: Psybreaks is played between 135 and 140 BPM, a little faster than nu skool, in the low zone of psytrance. The feel is precise and rolling: the break is clean, without swing, and the bass follows a continuous sixteenth-note pulse, like a psytrance bass that has lost its 4/4 kick. What separates the genre from nu skool is that hypnotic bass engine and the psychedelic sound design on top. Think of a psytrance track whose kick has been replaced by a break: the bass rolls, the breaks syncopate, the effects swirl.

psychedelictrance.arrangement: An intro of 16 to 32 bars with kick, bass and hi-hats sets up the engine. Then 32-bar sections: each section introduces a new element (lead, FX, percussion) and removes another so the density stays stable. A first breakdown around bar 96, without kick, where the liquid FX and a long delay take all the space for 8 to 16 bars, then a build-up with roll and filter, and the kick returns with the main lead. A second, longer breakdown two-thirds of the way through the track. End with a 32-bar outro with kick and bass alone. What makes a track playable: clean first and last 32 bars, without melody, for the mix.
psychedelictrance.basse: The rolling bass is what defines psytrance: the kick plays the first sixteenth note, the bass plays the next three, each note lasting 60 to 80 ms with a very short release. The sound starts from a sawtooth (Nord Lead, Virus or Serum) low-pass filtered around 250 Hz with a little resonance, plus a fast-decaying filter envelope that opens each note. A little saturation in the 100 to 300 Hz range so it comes through on small speakers. Typical note: F or F#, in octave 1. A sine below 60 Hz can double the root. The kick and bass form a single instrument: set them together, soloed, until the pattern turns like a wheel.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM. Lay down a short kick tuned to F and write the kick, bass, bass, bass motif in sixteenth notes on F1.
Build the bass in Serum or Operator: sawtooth, low-pass at 250 Hz, filter envelope with 80 ms decay, very short release, light saturation.
Add a snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats on the offbeats, a sixteenth-note percussion with varied velocities.
Create a filtered unison lead and play a 4-bar phrase in eighth notes with a dotted-eighth delay.
Program a liquid FX: noise and an oscillator in a resonant filter swept by an LFO, with ping-pong delay.
Arrange over 8 minutes in 32-bar sections, with two breakdowns without kick and a build-up with a snare roll.
psychedelictrance.mix: The kick and bass occupy the entire low end: below 200 Hz, nothing else. High-pass every other track at 200 Hz minimum. If the bass masks the kick, add a short sidechain (50 ms release) or shift the first bass note by a few ms. The lead is narrow and bright: a high-pass at 400 Hz, a bump at 3 kHz. The FX live on the sides: widen them with a stereo utility, but keep the center for kick, bass and snare. Parallel compression on the drum bus, 4:1 ratio, slow attack to keep the transients. Aim for around -8 LUFS on the master with a transparent limiter. Listen in mono regularly: the bass has to sound just as good.

outils.pourquoi: The virtual analog synth of 2000s psytrance: rolling sawtooth bass, three-voice unison leads, liquid FX through filter sweeps.
Basses and leads for the whole Israeli scene, with its built-in effects. Psytrance patch banks still exist for it.
The historic psytrance sequencer, still dominant in Israel: fine MIDI editing of the sixteenth-note bass and filter automation.
The modern rolling bass: sawtooth, low-pass around 250 Hz, fast filter envelope; an audio-rate LFO on the wavetable for talking basses.
Psy kick synthesis: body tuned to the bass root, tail cut at 150 ms, click layered separately.
Synthetic kicks and FM squelches with a falling pitch envelope; Wavetable takes over for thin leads and FX.
High-pass at 200 Hz on everything that isn't kick or bass, dynamic EQ to carve the bass when the lead plays.

reperes: Hallucinogen: Gamma Goblins (1998): the rolling bass established as the engine, and leads talking with the FX.
Infected Mushroom: Return of the Shadows (1999): clean digital production, sculpted breakdowns, the build-up of the first section.
Shpongle: Dorset Perception (1998): to hear the same liquid textures used without the kick, useful for your breakdowns.
Koma Club: Palpitating (1995): the transition between goa and psytrance, the bass already more regular.
psychedelictrance.rythme: The psytrance kick is short and round, with a pronounced click and a tail no longer than 150 ms: it has to leave room for the three bass notes that follow. Tune it to the bass root. On beats 2 and 4, a dry snare or a clap layered with a snare, without a long reverb. Closed hi-hats fall on the eighth-note offbeats, with an open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4. Add short percussion in sixteenth notes (shakers, rimshots, small blips) but with varied velocities so they don't clog the spectrum. Snare rolls build over 4 bars before each relaunch, in sixteenth notes then thirty-second notes.
psychedelictrance.sons: The brief names the Nord Lead and the Virus: these are the synths that gave psytrance its thin leads and liquid FX. The typical lead is a 3-voice unison sawtooth, low-pass filtered with an envelope that opens on each note, played in sixteenth or eighth notes with a delay synced to the dotted eighth. The liquid FX are resonant filter sweeps on noise or oscillators, with a fast LFO on the cutoff frequency and a ping-pong delay. Add “squelches”: short notes with a falling pitch envelope. In Ableton, Operator and Wavetable do this job very well. Short vocal samples, processed with delay and reverse, punctuate the breakdowns.
sourcesOutils: Myloops, Top 15 VST Plugins for Psytrance Production
Integraudio, Top 10 Goa and Psytrance Plugins
psychedelictrance.tempo: The psytrance trunk is played between 140 and 148 BPM, with 145 as the reference point. Everything is quantized straight, no swing: the sense of movement comes from the rolling bass and the delays, not from groove. What changes compared to goa is the rhythmic unit: the whole track rests on a one-bar motif repeated with digital precision, kick on the beat, bass on the next three sixteenth notes. The tempo never moves within the track. Think in 8-bar blocks for variations and 32 for sections. A track lasts 7 to 9 minutes, with a liquid, continuous feel rather than a stepped one.

psycore.arrangement: Psycore doesn't follow a club plan. An 8- to 16-bar intro can be a simple rising noise. Then blocks of 4, 8, 12 or 16 bars follow one another: a passage at 180 with rolling bass, an explosion at 220 with an eighth-note kick, a 2-beat silence, a half-tempo passage with a heavy bass, a glitch burst. Tempo changes are programmed by automation or by sixteenth-note blocks that simulate doubling. Still plan a “theme” that comes back two or three times, otherwise the track becomes a catalog. Aim for 6 to 7 minutes. Playability is relative: a few stable bars at the start and end are enough, the scene is used to brutal mixes.
psycore.basse: The ultra-fast hollowed-out bass of the brief: an FM wave or a sawtooth on Serum or FM8, with crisp distortion and a band-pass filter around 400 Hz that makes it “hollowed out”, meaning hollow and aggressive. Notes of 30 to 40 ms, zero release, in sixteenth notes on the 180 passages and eighth notes on the 220 passages. It often merges with the kick: same bus, same distortion, the kick becoming one bass note among others. Root in G or A, but the bass makes octave jumps and two-octave glissandos. Still keep a clean sub below 60 Hz on a separate track, otherwise the low end becomes noise without body.
etapes: Project at 200 BPM. Layer a short psy kick with a saturated speedcore kick, tune them to G.
Hollowed-out bass in Serum: distorted sawtooth, band-pass at 400 Hz, 35 ms notes in eighth notes, octave jumps every 2 bars, separate sine sub.
Make glitch bursts: FM micro-sounds in thirty-second notes, Beat Repeat on the drums with pitch rising over 1 bar.
Create noise filtered by a random LFO and a piercing FM siren, chop a vocal sample into 20 ms fragments.
Build blocks of different lengths (4, 8, 12 bars) with sixteenth-note passages simulating 400 BPM and 2-beat silences.
Set a theme that returns three times, then mix with clipper and limiter toward -5 LUFS while keeping the sub clean.
psycore.mix: Psycore is saturated by choice, but a mix saturated everywhere turns to mush. Reserve the distortion for the layers that carry it (kick, bass, noise) and keep the sub and the high micro-sounds clean. Kick and bass on a bus with a crushing compressor, 10:1 ratio, then saturation. High-pass at 400 Hz on everything else. The master limiter is pushed, -5 LUFS, but with a clipper before it so the transients don't pump. Use a dynamic EQ to carve the noise around 2 to 4 kHz when the kick hits. Listen in fragments at low volume to check that the events stay readable: total saturation should remain an experience, not fatigue.

outils.pourquoi: The hollowed-out bass: FM or sawtooth, crisp distortion, band-pass around 400 Hz, 30 ms notes in sixteenth notes at 180 BPM.
Piercing sirens with very fast vibrato and sines rising until they disappear; the direct legacy of Russian hi-tech.
Beat Repeat on the whole kit with rising pitch, Redux for bitcrushing, retriggers in sixty-fourth notes: this is where destruction gets programmed.
Step-based glitch sequencer: chopping, reverse, tape stop and crush on 20 ms vocal fragments.
The speedcore kick: sine saturated until it squares off, 100 ms body, bump around 100 Hz, played in sixteenth-note bursts.
Clipper before the master limiter: the kick's transients hold at -5 LUFS without pumping.
Dynamic EQ that carves the noise between 2 and 4 kHz when the kick hits, so the chaos stays readable.

reperes: Kindzadza: Waves From Inner Space (2005): darkpsy tipping into speed and noise, an already fragmented structure.
Psykovsky: Tanetsveta (2007): the density of sound design and tempo changes mid-track.
psycore.rythme: The psycore kick is a hybrid: a short tuned psy kick, layered with a distorted speedcore kick, that is, a sine saturated until it turns square, with a 100 ms body and a bump around 100 Hz. On the fastest passages, the kick plays in eighth or sixteenth notes (bursts), not only on the beats. The snare is clipped white noise. The hi-hats are replaced by bursts of glitched micro-sounds, as in hi-tech but even denser, with retriggers in thirty-second and sixty-fourth notes. Fills are explosions: Beat Repeat on the whole kit, with rising pitch, for one bar. The rhythm should feel like it is about to collapse.
psycore.sons: Serum and FM8 for the sounds, but above all the destruction effects: bitcrusher, Redux, digital saturation, pushed comb filter, real-time granulator. Glitch and noise are instruments: white noise filtered by a random LFO in thirty-second notes, a vocal sample chopped into 20 ms fragments and reordered, sines rising in pitch until they disappear. The leads are piercing FM sirens with very fast vibrato. The sampled voices come from horror films and cartoons, played too fast or too slow. The black humor comes through contrast: a childlike sample followed by an explosion of noise. Nothing lasts more than 4 bars without being transformed.
sourcesOutils: The Hard Data, Psycore cross-subcultural hybrids
psycore.tempo: Psycore starts around 180 BPM and climbs to 200, 220, sometimes 250. The grid becomes almost abstract: at 220 BPM a sixteenth note lasts 68 ms, an eighth note 136 ms. The genre exploits this by changing tempo within the track, doubling or halving the tempo by section, layering a kick at 200 BPM over a bass playing at 100. What changes compared to hi-tech is the fragmented structure: no more regular 8-bar cycle, but blocks of different lengths. What changes compared to speedcore is that the rolling psy bass and the sound design stay at the center. Think in events, not sections.

psydub.arrangement: Psydub takes its time. A 16- to 32-bar intro on a pad and a world instrument, without kick. The kick and bass come in, then the track unfolds in 16-bar sections where the instruments take turns. The breakdowns are passages where kick and bass disappear and the delays keep spinning, sometimes for 32 bars. Plan a “dub mix” of a theme: the same flute phrase replayed with the Space Echo cranked. A more rhythmic section around two-thirds of the way, with all the percussion. Aim for 9 minutes or more. For a chill festival set, a long ending with the delay alone is perfectly playable.
psydub.basse: The deep dub bass of the brief: a sine or triangle with a soft attack (10 to 20 ms), a long decay and a low-pass filter at 120 Hz. No distortion, or very little tube saturation. The lines follow the dub tradition: long notes on the root, a drop of a fifth at the end of the phrase, sometimes silences on the first beat. Root in D, E or F, in octave 1 or 0. The relationship to the kick is loose: the bass can anticipate the kick or follow it by an eighth note. Trilian or a played electric bass also work. Add a very light chorus above 200 Hz for roundness, and let the bass hold the note until the next one arrives.
etapes: Project at 90 BPM. Deep kick tuned to E around 48 Hz, pattern with kick on 1 and the “and” of 2, snare or rimshot on 3.
Sine bass with a 15 ms attack on E1, long notes, a drop of a fifth at the end of each 4-bar phrase.
Add sampled world percussion in sixteenth notes with 57% swing, send the rimshot into a tape delay at the dotted eighth.
Record or sample a flute or a sitar, play an 8-bar theme, send it into the Space Echo with high feedback.
Stretch a chant in a granulator to make a pad, add organ skanks on the offbeats with spring reverb.
Arrange 9 minutes with an intro without kick, 16-bar sections, a 32-bar breakdown with delay alone, a long ending.
psydub.mix: Depth is the priority. The kick and bass are mono, well forward, with an EQ that lets the sub breathe down to 30 Hz. A high-pass at 100 Hz on everything else. The spring reverb on the percussion and the long reverb on the pads are two different spaces: don't mix them. The Space Echo goes on a send, with the return wide in stereo. Gentle compression on the percussion bus, 3:1 ratio, slow attack. No need for a pushed limiter: aim for -10 to -12 LUFS, chill music is not a loudness contest. The master can go through gentle tape saturation for glue. Listen on a subwoofer: the sub should be round, never muddy.

outils.pourquoi: The central instrument: dotted-eighth delay, high feedback, tape wobble. In software: Universal Audio RE-201 or Arturia Delay TAPE-201.
Echo in tape mode on a send, send automation every 4 beats on a rimshot: live dubbing inside the DAW.
Granular pads: a chant stretched into a cloud, slow LFO on the filter, under the deep basses.
Sampled world instruments and Eastern pads, sitar, bansuri, chants, with its own delays and built-in granulator.
The held dub bass: electric bass or sine with a soft attack, long decay, light chorus above 200 Hz.
Simon Posford's multi-effects unit, present all over Shpongle: pitch shifts, modulated delays and slowed-down liquid FX. H3000 Factory as a plugin.
Two separate spaces: short plate or spring mode for the percussion, long hall for the pads, never mixed.

reperes: Shpongle: Divine Moments of Truth (1998): the blend of world instruments, delays and psy textures in slow motion.
Ott: Rogue Bagel (2003): the deep dub bass and the Space Echo used as an instrument on the percussion.
Shpongle: Tickling the Amygdala (2023): current psydub production, denser and cleaner.
Young American Primitive: Sunrise (1993): the prehistory of the genre, chill goa with the same delays.
psydub.rythme: The kick is deep and long, tuned around 45 to 50 Hz, with a 300 ms body: it has all the room it needs. Often an acoustic dub kick sample, doubled with an 808 kick. Basic pattern: kick on 1 and on the “and” of 2, snare on 3, with a cracking dub rimshot. The hi-hats are thin, in swung sixteenth notes, often replaced by shakers and world percussion: tablas, udu, dumbek, chopped and replayed. The percussion goes through a tape delay, with an automated send: one rimshot hit sent into the Space Echo every 4 beats. Tuned toms at the ends of phrases. The groove should make you want to nod your head, not jump.
psydub.sons: The Space Echo RE-201 is the central instrument, real or emulated (Echo in Ableton with tape mode, or a dedicated emulation): dotted-eighth delay, high feedback, a darkening filter, and that wobble that makes each repeat breathe.
