Send everything into it at times: snare, vocal, flute, chord. The world instruments of the brief, sampled or played: bansuri flute, sitar, oud, didgeridoo, chants. Absynth and granulators make the pads: a vocal sample stretched into a cloud, a slow LFO on the filter. The chords are dub skanks on an organ or an electric piano, with a delay and a spring reverb. Add the liquid FX of psytrance, but slowed down and stretched.
psydub.tempo: Psydub drops to between 70 and 100 BPM, with many tracks around 85 to 95. The feel is half-time: the snare falls on 3, not on 2 and 4, which gives an impression of deep slowness even when the hi-hats play sixteenth notes. Swing is welcome, 55 to 60% on the percussion, and the played instruments bring their natural micro-delays. What changes compared to the psytrance it comes from is the relationship to time: delays at the dotted eighth and dotted quarter create long cycles layered over the slow tempo. A track lasts 7 to 12 minutes and is never in a hurry.

psytech.arrangement: Psytech is arranged like club techno. 32-bar intro: kick, hi-hats, rolling bass. Add a modular sequence at bar 33, a drone at bar 65. A first short breakdown around bar 96: kick cut for 8 bars, the sequence continues in the dub delay, the kick returns on a crash. A 64-bar main section with all layers, then a second, longer breakdown, 16 bars, with a low-pass filter that closes then reopens the whole mix. 32-bar outro, kick and bass. Aim for 7 minutes. The track's function comes first: the techno DJ must be able to mix it with hypnotic techno without anything sticking out.
psytech.basse: The straight rolling bass: kick on the first sixteenth note, bass on the next three, 70 ms notes, short release, exactly as in psytrance but at 134 BPM, which makes it clearer and heavier. The sound is less aggressive: a saw on Serum or an FM sine on Operator, low-pass filter at 200 Hz, a touch of saturation. The book suggests an FM sub on Operator with a tempo-synced LFO that modulates the timbre in rhythm: it works very well here, with an Auto Pan in pumping mode set around 40% to let the kick breathe. Root in F# or G. The modular sequences from the brief can take over from the bass in some sections: an eighth-note line on an analog oscillator, filtered and sequenced.
etapes: Project at 134 BPM. Dry 909 kick tuned to F#, clap on 2 and 4, closed hi-hats on the offbeats, panned slightly apart.
Straight rolling bass on F#1: kick then three sixteenth notes, saw filtered at 200 Hz, 70 ms notes, Auto Pan pumping at 40%.
Create a 16-step modular sequence (Operator plus a sample and hold LFO on pitch and filter), in eighth notes.
Add a drone on a note held for 4 bars and a dub delay on a send on a percussion, high feedback, filtered.
Measure the psychedelic FX: one squelch per section, a filter sweep over 16 bars, a short voice in a delay.
Arrange 7 minutes like club techno: 32-bar intro, short breakdowns by filter, 32-bar outro.
psytech.mix: The mix follows techno codes: kick up front, bass just behind, both mono below 150 Hz. The book places the main kick and the low-end group within a few dB of each other, and keeps the whole low-end group unpanned: apply that principle. The clap is moderate; the hi-hats are set by lowering the listening volume until you can barely hear them, then raising them until they sit just right, a trick from the book that rests the ears. Bus compression on the drums, 4:1 ratio, slow attack. Delays and reverbs go to the sides, with a high-pass at 300 Hz. Limiter around -8 LUFS, no more: psytech is mixed alongside techno, it must have the same dynamics.

outils.pourquoi: Dry kick tuned around 55 Hz, clap on 2 and 4, club hi-hats; a 909 sample pack or D16 Drumazon 2 replaces the machine.
8- or 16-step sequences on an analog oscillator, modulated resonant filter, sample and hold on pitch: the hypnotic material.
FM sub with a tempo-synced LFO modulating the timbre, the Attack Magazine book's trick for psychedelic bass.
Auto Pan in pumping mode around 40% on the sub, Echo in tape mode on the stabs, Operator plus sample and hold LFO rack without a modular.
The straight rolling bass at 134 BPM: saw, low-pass at 200 Hz, 70 ms notes, a touch of saturation.
Semi-modular cited by the book's techno producers: a single sequenced, filtered line that carries a whole section.
Dub delays on an automated send, high feedback, low-pass filter on the repeats, to measure out the psychedelic FX.

reperes: X-Dream: Panic in Paradise (2004): the shift from psytrance to a hardened club sound, straight bass and dry kick.
Son Kite: Colours (2004): the club groove under measured psy textures, with hypnotic sequences.
Neelix: Disco Decay (2005): the track function and club percussion, before the term drifted commercial.
Ace Ventura: Presence (2008): the border with psy-prog, useful to hear what separates the straight bass from the offbeat bass.
psytech.rythme: The dry techno kick: a TR-909 sample or a synthetic kick tuned around 55 Hz, short, with a sharp attack, compressed so it snaps. Four per bar. 909 clap on 2 and 4, with a very short reverb. The club percussion from the brief: closed 909 hi-hats on the offbeats, open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4, a discreet ride, a percussion in sixteenth notes (rimshot, conga, short tom) with velocities that make the groove. Attack Magazine's book on psychedelic techno offers a useful idea: pan the hi-hats slightly apart, one closed on the left, the open one a little to the right, to open the image without touching the center. No snare rolls: transitions are techno, by filter and by subtraction.
psytech.sons: Modular synth, Serum, Ableton and the TR-909. The modular sequences: an 8- or 16-step line on an oscillator, with a resonant low-pass filter whose envelope is modulated by a voltage sequencer, and a sample and hold on pitch. Without a modular, an Ableton rack with Operator and a sample and hold LFO does the same thing. The dub delays: Echo in tape mode, high feedback, automated send on a percussion or a stab, with a filter. The psychedelic FX are measured: a single squelch per section, a filter sweep over 16 bars, a short voice sample in a delay. A background drone, on a single note held over 4 bars, brings the hypnotic side. Nothing should crowd the spectrum: psytech breathes.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Psychedelic Techno chapter (hi-hat mixing, FM sub on Operator, Auto Pan)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Psychedelic Techno chapter and Ask the Pros, favourite bit of kit)
KVR Audio, Psy Trance Production Gear thread
psytech.tempo: Psytech is played between 130 and 138 BPM, the tempo of club techno, never that of psytrance. The grid is straight, with no swing: the groove comes from the bass rolling in steady sixteenth notes, as in psytrance but slower, and from club percussion. What changes compared to psy-prog is precisely this straight bass: kick then three sixteenth notes, never the offbeat. What changes compared to Zenonesque is the track's function: the piece is a DJ tool, with clean sections and a kick that never moves. Count in 16 and 32 bars, as in techno. A track lasts 7 to 8 minutes.

raggacore.arrangement: Tracks run 3 to 5 minutes and follow the logic of riddim and dub rather than rave: intro with the vocal sample and a siren, entry of the Amen and the bass, 8- or 16-bar sections alternating full breakbeat, half-time skank and gabber kick bursts. The breakdowns are dub moments: the drums stop, the delay and reverb take the vocal, then everything slams back in. No classic build-up, no 4-bar snare roll: transitions are abrupt, one siren blast and off it goes again. What makes the track playable is the recognizable vocal sample and the regular return of the full Amen.
raggacore.basse: The bass comes from dancehall and jungle: a sine sub or a reese (two detuned saws through a low-pass at 300 Hz) playing a short, syncopated line, in minor, with notes landing on the offbeats and the “and” of 3. Often a 2-bar pattern: root, minor seventh, root, fifth. In Operator: sine plus a saw an octave up, filter at 300 Hz. It is lightly saturated and sometimes distorted during the breakcore passages. Sidechain from the gabber kick, 8:1 ratio, 40 ms release, so the kick gets through. In the half-time passages, the bass takes more room and plays longer notes, as in a riddim.
etapes: Tempo 180 BPM. Load an Amen into Simpler in Slice mode, reorder it over 2 bars with sixteenth-note retrigs.
Add a crushed gabber kick on beats 1 and 3, plus a burst of 4 sixteenth notes at the end of each 4-bar block.
Reese bass or sub in Operator, syncopated 2-bar pattern in minor, sidechained from the kick.
Sample a dancehall acapella, speed it up to 180 in Complex mode, cut it into 2-bar phrases, chop it with Beat Repeat.
Add a sound system siren, an offbeat skank stab, and a dub delay on a send with feedback at 60 percent.
Arrange in 8- to 16-bar sections alternating full break, half-time skank and bursts, with dub breakdowns. Moderate limiter.
raggacore.mix: The raggacore mix is deliberately dirty but the low end must stay readable: sub in mono, cut above 120 Hz, at -6 dB peak. The gabber kick on top at -3 dB, high-pass at 45 Hz. The Amen high-passed at 150 Hz to make room, with 10 dB of saturation and heavy compression (8:1 ratio, 3 ms attack) so it snaps. The ragga vocal up front, compressed, with a high-pass at 300 Hz and the delay on a send. A Redux at 12 bits on the drum bus for grit. Master: limiter around -7 LUFS, dirtier than jungle but not as much as gabber. Listen to Aaron Spectre for the balance.

outils.pourquoi: The Amen and ragga acapellas sampled at 12 bits then sped up 20%, which gives the genre's pitched toast and grainy break.
Source of the dancehall acapellas and sound system sirens: sampled from the 12-inches, pitch pushed to +8 before recording.
The most common DAW among 2000s breakcore producers for chopping the Amen in Slicer and reassembling it fast.
The modern tracker, very present in breakcore: retrigger, per-line sample slicing, fast editing above 180 BPM.
On the Amen track: Grid in sixteenth notes, Chance 30%, Pitch Decay for the typical stutters and pitch drops.
12 bits and downsampling on the ragga vocals and the break to recover the grit of a vintage sampler.
Slices the Amen in Slice mode and replays the slices from the keyboard; Operator adds the occasional gabber kicks as a distorted sine.

reperes: DJ Scud: Total Destruction (1998): breakcore taking on ragga, saturated Amen and chopped vocal.
Aaron Spectre: Look Out Fi Liar (2006): raggacore defined, sped-up toast, chopped Amen and occasional gabber kicks.
Bong-Ra: Suicide Speed Machine Girl (2005): the most violent version, bursts and distortion on everything.
Shitmat: Killababylonkutz (2004): humor and dub, sirens and delay on a shredded Amen.
raggacore.rythme: The Amen break sped up to 180 BPM and chopped: in Simpler in Slice mode, or by cutting each hit manually, you reorder the break over 2 bars with displaced snare hits, sixteenth-note retrigs, reversals. On top, a crushed gabber kick replaces the break's kick on some beats, often 1 and 3, or in a burst of 4 on one beat like a punch. The Amen snare is saturated and doubled with a dry ragga snare. Dancehall rimshots on the offbeats. Beat Repeat at 1/16 and 1/32 for the glitches. The skank sections drop to half-time, snare on 3, with the break continuing at half strength.
raggacore.sons: Ragga and dancehall acapellas, sped up to 180 BPM (Warp in Complex or Texture mode in Ableton) and often pitched up 2 or 3 semitones: the toast becomes a machine gun. Cut into 2-bar phrases, repeated, chopped with Beat Repeat. Sound system sirens, horns, “brrap” shouts. Dub sounds: dotted-eighth delay with feedback at 60 percent, spring reverb, sweeping filter. Skank stabs (a short minor chord on organ or sampled guitar) on the offbeats. Samples from kung-fu films and cartoons. Everything is saturated and a bit lo-fi, as if the sound system were pushed too hard.
raggacore.tempo: Raggacore runs between 160 and 220 BPM, often 175-190, which is the ragga jungle tempo pushed one notch further. What sets it apart from happy hardcore and gabber is that the grid is not a regular 4/4: it is a breakbeat, most often the Amen, chopped, with gabber kicks landing wherever the producer wants. The feel alternates between the dancehall skank (accent on 3, syncopations) and breakcore bursts. A light swing on the Amen chops (the break naturally has one) and none on the gabber kicks. Program at 180 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, with half-time sections for the skank.

raggajungle.arrangement: A ragga jungle track lasts 5 to 6 minutes and is structured around the voice, like a dancehall song. 16-bar intro: a cappella vocal, siren, a filtered break. Drop at bar 17: whole break, sub, vocal carrying on. The verse lasts 32 bars. Then a “rewind”: everything stops, the voice repeats a phrase, a roll, and the drop starts again. A 16-bar breakdown keeps the sub and the voice, without the break. Second verse with a different or pitched break. 16-bar outro on the break alone. The vocal hook comes back at every drop. The track must let the DJ rewind it himself on the sound system.
raggajungle.basse: The dub sub from the brief: the slowest bass in the family. An Operator sine or a square low-pass filtered at 150 Hz, between 40 and 55 Hz, playing a real reggae line: root on 1, fifth on the “and” of 2, back to the root on 4, then silence, like a slowed-down Sly and Robbie bassline. Notes last a dotted quarter note, with a 200 ms release. Add a whole-tone glide on the first note of each phrase. The break kick is light: the sub holds the low end without sidechain. Cut the sub dead before each “rewind”, and bring it back on the first beat after the vocal.
etapes: Set Ableton to 165 BPM. Import a dancehall a cappella, cut it into phrases, pitch it up +2 semitones if needed.
Lay down a fairly whole Amen with cuts that follow the ends of phrases, and a 909 rimshot on 3.
Create an Operator sub on a reggae line (root, fifth, root, silence) in dotted quarter notes, 200 ms release.
Add a siren (Operator saw with a 2-octave pitch envelope) and a sampled organ skank on the offbeats.
Arrange a 16-bar intro on the voice, 32-bar drop, rewind with roll, 16-bar breakdown on sub and voice, second verse, 16-bar outro.
Compress the voice hard with a filtered delay, leave the sub alone in the low end, and keep the master at -8 LUFS.
raggajungle.mix: The ragga jungle mix puts the voice in front of everything. High-pass it at 150 Hz, compress it hard (6:1 ratio, 3 ms attack) so it stays constant, and add a dotted-eighth delay with a low-pass filter at 3 kHz, feedback 35%. The sub is alone below 80 Hz, mono, and it is the loudest element of the track after the voice. The breaks are compressed and saturated (Overdrive 25%) but sit behind the voice, high-passed at 100 Hz. A spring reverb (Reverb in short mode, or a spring sample) on the sirens and stabs gives the dub sound. Master at -8 LUFS, with room for a live MC.

outils.pourquoi: Amen and dancehall vocals slowed down or sped up in the sampler: the 12-bit grain is part of the Congo Natty sound.
The tracker of Rebel MC and the 1994 pirates: a cappella stuck onto breaks typed in column by column.
Sequencer to drive sampler and sub, with the a cappellas laid out like MIDI to switch toasters every 16 bars.
The track is judged on a wall of bass: the sub must get through a stack and the siren be played live by the MC.

outils.nom: Dancehall a cappellas and sound system sirens
outils.pourquoi: Vocals by Top Cat, General Levy or riddim versions, cut into phrases, plus sirens, gunshots and rewinds.
Warp in Texture mode (Grain Size 40 ms) on an a cappella to recover the S950's grainy stretch.
Dub sub in long whole or half notes, with a little Overdrive so it can be heard on small speakers.
To build your own dub sirens: tri-saw-pulse oscillator, LFO on pitch, tube distortion and delay.

reperes: Shy FX & UK Apache: Original Nuttah (1994): UK Apache's flow leads, the sub drops in dotted quarter notes, the break follows the voice.
Dead Dred: Dred Bass (1994): the bass up front, a single bouncing sub pattern, the track rests on it.
Top Cat: Ruffest Gun Ark (1995): the Jamaican deejay on an Amen, the pure ragga jungle format.
Congo Natty: Junglist (1995): London's Jamaican culture proudly claimed, sirens and dub sub.
raggajungle.rythme: The Amen and the toasted breaks from the brief: an Amen or a Think played fairly whole, at 165 BPM, with the cuts following the ends of the vocal phrases rather than the grid. Break kick on 1, snare on 2 and 4, and an extra snare on the “and” of 4 at the end of a phrase. Add a 909 rimshot on 3 for the dancehall side, and a bell or a reggae timbale sample once per bar. Snare rolls come in when the deejay says “rewind” or “selecta”. A variant uses the “bam bam” pattern (kick on 1, the “and” of 2, and 4) under the break, for Jamaican weight.
raggajungle.sons: Ragga and dancehall a cappellas are the raw material: Top Cat, General Levy, or royalty-free vocals from a Jamaican deejay, cut into phrases, played at their original pitch or pitched up +2 semitones to fit the tempo. Sound system sirens are oscillators that rise and fall (Operator, saw, 2-octave pitch envelope over 1 s) with an eighth-note delay. Add foghorns, laser shots, a sampled “pull up”, and a guitar or organ skank sampled from a reggae record, played on the offbeats. The brief cites the S950, the Amiga and Cubase: sample everything, play little.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine (Make Your Own Jungle FX)
raggajungle.tempo: Ragga jungle runs between 160 and 170 BPM, the tempo of 1994-1995 jungle. What sets it apart from jungle in general is that the voice leads: the feel is dictated by the flow of the Jamaican deejay, who counts in 80 or 85 BPM, half the tempo. The breaks are therefore less chopped than with Remarc, to let the voice breathe, and the bass follows a slowed-down dancehall pulse (the “one drop” or the “bam bam” rhythm). Think sound system: the track must work like a sped-up reggae version, with the voice in front and the drums behind, and room for the live MC to jump in.

reggae.arrangement: A reggae track is a song on a riddim: 4-bar intro often played by the horns or the organ, 8- or 16-bar verse, 8-bar chorus with backing vocals, second verse, chorus, bridge or horn solo, chorus, outro on the riddim with the instrumental B-side in mind. The instrumental version, the version, is produced at the same time as the song: keep your stems to make it. Length 3 to 4 minutes. The riddim does not change chords during the whole track, or has only two: the variation comes from the sung melody, the horns, and instruments coming in and dropping out. Snare rolls announce each section. For an electronic producer, the 2-bar riddim is the basic module on which everything is built.
reggae.basse: The bass is the foundation: a Fender played fingerstyle, muffled, deep, with a 2-bar riff that defines the whole riddim. It plays few notes: root, fifth, octave, sometimes the minor third, with long silences and a note held on 3. Aston Familyman Barrett with Marley or Robbie Shakespeare are the references. Use a sampled fingerstyle bass (Trilian, Ableton packs), cut everything above 1.2 kHz, boost 3 dB at 80 Hz, and compress at 5:1 with 5 dB of reduction and a 250 ms release for even sustain. Write the riff before anything else: it gives the riddim its name and ten different songs will reuse it. No sidechain, no saturation.
etapes: First write a 2-bar bass riff on two chords, fingerstyle, with silences and a note held on 3, at 72 BPM.
Program a one drop on an acoustic kit with rimshot, hi-hats accented on the offbeats, varied velocities.
Add a guitar skank and an organ bubble on the offbeats, shifted 8 ms ahead.
Lay down horns in short answering phrases and a spring reverb on the snare.
Structure the song over 3 minutes 30, then export an instrumental version from the same stems.
Mix for the sound system: mono bass at 80 Hz, soft kick, dynamic master at -14 LUFS.
reggae.mix: The reggae mix is made for the sound system: bass and kick in the center, huge, dry, the rest lighter and a bit higher in the spectrum. Cut below 35 Hz, boost the bass at 80 Hz, keep it mono. The kick is muffled, soft, with little attack: low-pass at 4 kHz on the kick. The rimshot snare gets the spring reverb (short, 0.6 seconds). The guitar skank and the organ are panned to each side, with a high-pass at 300 Hz. The voice gets a short echo doubling (80 ms) and 4:1 compression. The master stays dynamic, -14 LUFS, with a Glue at 2 dB: on a sound system, the amp makes the volume, not the limiter. Check on a subwoofer that the bass is round and not muddy.

outils.nom: Fender Jazz Bass and Ampeg SVT
outils.pourquoi: Aston Familyman Barrett's bass: flatwound strings, highs cut, played fingerstyle, muffled and round, for a 2-bar riff that defines the riddim.
The organ for the bubble, that sixteenth-note pattern alternating between the hands; Arturia B-3 V or an organ sample in Auto Filter, panned to one side.
The short spring on the rimshot and the horns at the Black Ark; Hybrid Reverb with the Spring algorithm at 0.6 seconds replaces it.
The echo chamber for doubling the voice at 80 ms and for the answering horns; Ableton Echo in tape mode with low feedback.
The sampled fingerstyle bass: cut everything above 1.2 kHz, 3 dB boost at 80 Hz, 5:1 compression with a 250 ms release for even sustain.
A dry acoustic kit recorded for the one drop, the rockers and the steppers, rimshot snare, short hi-hat, no clap.
Multi-sampled rhythm guitar dedicated to the skank: short, choked chords on the offbeats, with envelope and pickup settings.
The native spring: short Spring algorithm on the snare and the horns, nothing on the bass, which stays mono, dry and huge.

reperes: Toots & The Maytals: Pressure Drop (1969): the shift from rocksteady to reggae, the lively skank and the soul voice.
Burning Spear: Marcus Garvey (1975): the slow, deep one drop, the answering horns, the bass carrying everything.
Junior Murvin: Police and Thieves (1976): Lee Perry's Black Ark sound, the falsetto voice in the echo, the spongy riddim.
Bob Marley & The Wailers: Could You Be Loved (1980): the rockers, the wah guitar, the clean radio-oriented production.
reggae.rythme: Three drum patterns to know, all played on a dry acoustic kit with the snare played as a rimshot (cross-stick): the one drop, kick and rimshot together on 3, nothing on 1, hi-hat in eighth notes with accents on the offbeats; the rockers, kick on all four beats with the rimshot on 3; the steppers, kick on all four beats, heavier, which will lead to dub steppers. Program with varied velocities (kick 100, rimshot 90, hi-hats 60 to 85) and add short snare rolls before section changes. The percussion, bongos, cabasa, bell, plays continuously at low volume. The hi-hat is dry and short. No clap, no drum machine: the drums of Sly Dunbar or Carlton Barrett are those of a musician.
reggae.sons: The brief gives the sound system, the console, the spring reverb, the echo chamber and the electric bass. The skank is the harmonic sound: a guitar in short chords on the offbeats, choked dry, doubled by an organ (Hammond or Farfisa) playing the bubble, a sixteenth-note pattern alternating left hand and right hand. In Ableton, Electric in organ mode or an organ sample with an Auto Filter, and a sampled or played guitar. The horns play short lines answering the voice. The short spring reverb sits on the snare and the horns, the echo chamber on the voice for doubling. The melodica, nyabinghi (hand drums) and backing vocals in thirds complete the palette. The voice is up front, warm, with answering backing vocals.
sourcesOutils: KVR Audio (reggae and dub VST forum)
reggae.tempo: Reggae plays between 60 and 90 BPM felt, often written as 120 to 180 in sixteenth notes by electronic producers. Israelites or Pressure Drop, still close to rocksteady and ska, run at 120 with a straight pulse; Marcus Garvey and Police and Thieves slow down to around 70 to 75 felt. The feel rests on two things: the one drop, with the weight on 3 and not on 1, and the skank, those guitar and organ chords struck on the offbeats. The swing is light, 52 to 55 percent, and the band plays slightly ahead on the offbeats and behind on 3. In Ableton, set 72 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, and shift the skanks 8 ms to the left.

rhythmicnoise.arrangement: Count on 6 to 8 minutes, mixable. 16-bar intro on a metal loop alone, then the distorted kick comes in all at once, with no build-up. Every 16 bars adds or removes an element by mute. The breakdowns remove the kick and let the noise textures run for 8 or 16 bars, often with a filter sweep on the noise, then the kick returns brutally, sometimes with a thirty-second-note retrigger on the last bar. No chorus, no structuring melody: the form is that of techno, but the tension comes from the density of the noise. End with the kick alone for 16 bars, then a dead stop.
rhythmicnoise.basse: There is often no separate bass: the distorted kick is the bass, its saturated tail fills 60 to 200 Hz. If you want a sub, put a held sine on the kick's fundamental (often F0 or E0), very short, only on the beats, and cut the distorted kick below 50 Hz so they don't fight. Another option: a noise drone band-pass filtered around 150 Hz, pumping in sidechain on the kick with a 150 ms release. The result is a low end with no note, only weight. No bass melody: the slightest melodic line would pull it back toward EBM.
etapes: At 135 BPM, take a 909 kick and stack Overdrive 15 dB, Saturator Hard Curve 12 dB, Pedal Fuzz and Redux 6 bits, until you get a square block.
Program four-on-the-floor plus kicks on sixteenth notes 2 to 4 of the third beat, all at velocity 127. Add an 80 ms burst of white noise on 2 and 4.
Sample a chain or a sheet of metal, loop it in eighth notes, saturate it, and add noise clicks in sixteenth notes as hi-hats.
Treat the kick in three bands: clean sub below 70 Hz, crushed mids, air above 7 kHz.
Arrange over 7 minutes with 16-bar mutes, with two kickless breakdowns where the noise runs, and brutal returns.
Saturate the drum bus in Analog Clip, cut the resonant peaks between 1 and 5 kHz, and check the mix in mono.
rhythmicnoise.mix: The challenge is keeping weight despite the clipping. Treat the kick in three bands, as the book describes for hard techno: keep the sub below 70 Hz clean and unsaturated, crush the mids, and add a touch of air above 7 kHz. High-pass at 150 Hz on everything that is not the kick. Use a Saturator in Analog Clip as a limiter on the drum bus, 2 to 3 dB of drive. A final limiter on the master, but with only 2 dB of reduction: the saturation has already done the work. Hunt down the resonant peaks between 1 and 5 kHz created by the serial distortions, with a narrow EQ. Aim for -6 LUFS. Check in mono.

outils.pourquoi: Hand-built granular noise generators and loop processors, the tool cited by the brief and by the scene's forums.
The 1990s Amiga tracker: short samples, 64-step patterns, thirty-second-note retriggers. Renoise is its direct heir today.
Multiband distortion with filters, described in the book for hard techno kicks: crushes the mids while keeping the sub clean below 70 Hz.
Four-band distortion with extreme algorithms, recommended on rhythmic noise forums to turn a 909 kick into a square block.
Two serial distortion stages and a convolver, for the metal loops and the 80 ms white noise bursts on 2 and 4.
8-bit hardware bitcrusher with filter, for degrading the noise hi-hats and extreme repitches live.
Hard Curve at 12 dB after an Overdrive at 15 dB, then Pedal in Fuzz and Redux at 6 bits: the stack that turns the kick into a square wave.
The raw material for the kick before the four distortion stages, as samples, all at velocity 127. Its saturated tail replaces the bass.

reperes: Imminent Starvation: Nord (1999): the kick turned into a block of distortion, the relentless pattern, the scrap-metal textures.
Converter: Denogginizer (2000): tracker precision, retriggers, organized violence.
P·A·L: Gelöbnis (1994): the slower, ritual side, where the metal loop carries the track.
rhythmicnoise.rythme: The kick is a product of distortion. Take a 909 or a synthetic kick, then stack three or four stages: Overdrive at 15 dB, Saturator in Hard Curve at 12 dB, Pedal in Fuzz, Redux at 6 bits. The kick becomes a square wave with a buzzing tail: that is the sound. Four-on-the-floor, plus syncopated kicks on sixteenth notes 2 to 4 of certain beats, like the gallop described in the book for processed techno. The snare is a burst of distorted white noise, 80 ms, on 2 and 4. The hi-hats are noise clicks in sixteenth notes. Add metal loops (chain, sheet metal) sampled and looped in eighth notes, saturated. No velocity nuances: everything is at 127.
rhythmicnoise.sons: Distortion across the whole chain is the instrument. Reaktor, cited in the brief, is used for granular noise generators and loop processors; in Ableton, Grain Delay with random pitch and Spectral Time do a similar job. Metal loops, engines, sirens, filtered white noise sweeps replace the synths. If a melody appears, it is noise passed through a resonant filter whose frequency is sequenced, or a Vocoder with noise as the carrier. The historical trackers left a habit: sample short, play the samples at different pitches, retriggers in thirty-second notes. Check the spectrum after every extreme repitch, aliasing above 16 kHz is common.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Hard Techno and Processed Techno chapters: multiband kick, serial distortions, kick gallop, aliasing after repitch)
Gearspace, Rhythmic Noise/Power Noise Techniques and Theory thread
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Hard Techno and Processed Techno chapters)
Gearspace (Good Software/Hardware For Rhythmic/Power Noise and Rhythmic Noise/Power Noise Techniques and Theory threads)
rhythmicnoise.tempo: Between 120 and 150 BPM, crushed four-on-the-floor, straight, with no swing at all. Some tracks run at 90 BPM with a double-speed pattern, which amounts to the same feel. What sets rhythmic noise apart from the power electronics it descends from: the grid is back, and it is relentless. What sets it apart from neighboring industrial techno: the kick is no longer a kick, it is a block of distortion. In your DAW, start at 135 BPM, full quantization, and think like the scene's Amiga trackers: 64-step patterns, repeated, with variations by mute and retrigger rather than by nuance.

riddim.arrangement: Short, 2 minutes 30 to 3 minutes 30. 16-bar intro with a vocal element and the drums coming in. 8- to 16-bar build-up. 32-bar drop: the same triplet bass pattern, with a timbre change at bar 16. 8- to 16-bar breakdown, second build-up, second drop with a different pattern or a “switch-up” to another tempo for 8 bars. Abrupt ending. The hypnosis comes from repetition: don't add elements to fill space. If you're bored at bar 24, that's a good sign, the mosh pit crowd is into it.
riddim.basse: A hammer bass, short and square. In Serum: a square oscillator or a simple wavetable, a little FM from the second oscillator, amplitude envelope with a 100 to 150 ms decay, a very short pitch envelope for the attack. A single LFO, or none. A 2-bar pattern in triplets, on one or two notes, the root and sometimes the minor third or the fourth. A separate sine sub that follows the notes. The pattern stays the same for 32 bars, the only variations being a change of filter or amount of FM every 8 bars. Resample the bass to freeze the sound and cut it with scissors.
etapes: Set Ableton to 150 BPM, eighth-note triplet grid, dry 4/4 kick and snare on 2 and 4.
Create a square bass in Serum with light FM, short decay, fast pitch envelope.
Write a 2-bar triplet pattern on one or two notes, with a separate sine sub following it.
Resample the bass, add a filter variation every 8 bars, nothing more.
Arrange: 16-bar intro, 8-bar build-up, 32-bar drop, 8-bar breakdown, second drop with a different pattern.
Sidechain everything to the kick, clip the bass, crush the master to around -4 LUFS.
riddim.mix: Deliberately crushed mastering. Kick and bass share the low end: kick around 60 Hz with no sub, sine sub below 80 Hz, mono. Everything is sidechained to the kick with a fast 50 ms release. Mid bass saturated then run through a clipper. Loud, dry snare. No long reverb, a very small delay on the vocals. Multiband compression on the master, limiter with 6 to 8 dB of reduction, target between -4 and -5 LUFS. Check that the bass doesn't mask the kick: offset the kick by a sixteenth note from the bass if the two overlap, or cut the bass during the kick.

outils.pourquoi: Hammer bass: square or simple wavetable, light FM, 100 to 150 ms decay, short pitch envelope, triplet pattern.
The riddim scene's DAW: eighth-note triplet grid, 2-bar pattern copied 16 times, fast resampling.
The other workshop: 1/8T grid, resampling the bass to cut it with scissors, filter automation every 8 bars.
Multiband on the mid bass to make it flat and present before the clipper, high depth setting.
Clipper on the saturated bass and on the drum bus, for the deliberately crushed mastering, before the limiter.
Limiter with 6 to 8 dB of reduction, target between -4 and -5 LUFS, while checking that the bass doesn't mask the kick.

outils.nom: W. A. Production, Pumped Serum Riddim & Dubstep Essentials
outils.pourquoi: Serum presets of riddim basses, to dissect a hammer patch and start again from its internal effects chain.

reperes: Getter: Head Splitter (2014): the shift from brostep toward minimalism, a pattern that hammers.
Infekt: Raptor (2017): pure riddim, square triplet bass, minimal drums, total repetition.
Phiso: Jotaro (2016): the hammer pattern and the switch-up, the mosh pit reference.
Virtual Riot: Energy Drink (2015): more detailed sound design that stays within the riddim frame.
riddim.rythme: Short, dry kick, 4/4 or on 1 and 3, with a pronounced click and no sub, around 60 Hz. Sharp snare on 2 and 4 or on 3, without much reverb, layered with a dry clap. Hats almost absent or in very low eighth notes. A few metallic percussions in triplets to reinforce the bass pattern. The drums are minimal and dry: they are there to frame the bass, which plays the role of main percussion. Snare rolls in the build-ups as in brostep, but shorter, 8 bars. One rule: if you mute the bass, what remains should be a boring drum loop. That's intended.
riddim.sons: Serum and FL Studio or Ableton, almost nothing else. Short vocal shouts, a “yeah” or a pitched word, placed once per phrase. Metallic clicks, lasers, sirens in the build-ups. A sub drop before the drop. The sounds are dry, without reverb, with almost no space. A secondary bass pattern, higher-pitched, sometimes answers the main one at the end of a phrase. The aesthetic embraces repetition and rawness: no elaborate melodic intro, no supersaw, a theme of 4 notes at most. A filtered noise texture can fill the 8 bars of build-up.
sources: EDMProd, How to Make Riddim like Subtronics in 5 Easy Steps (edmprod.com)
sourcesOutils: Plugin Boutique, Pumped Serum Riddim & Dubstep Essentials
EDMProd, How to Make Riddim like Subtronics
riddim.tempo: Between 140 and 150 BPM, often 150 today. The kick is frequently in 4/4 rather than halfstep, or else kick on 1 and 3 with snare on 2 and 4, which brings riddim closer to heavy techno than to dubstep. The signature is the triplet feel: the bass plays in eighth-note or sixteenth-note triplets, on a 1/8T grid in Ableton. No swing, everything is hard-quantized. What changes compared to brostep: variation disappears, a 2-bar pattern repeats 32 times, hypnosis replaces the roller coaster. The higher tempo and the triplet give the hammer feel.

rominimal.arrangement: Ten to fourteen minutes, with no drop and no clear breakdown. The track is a 4-bar loop that transforms through micro-variations: each 8-bar block changes a hit, a pan, a volume, a delay. Elements come in very gradually, over a 16-bar fade-in. There are rarely more than six audible elements at once. The breakdown, if there is one, is a gentle 16-bar reduction where the kick drops 6 dB without disappearing. Rhadoo lets 32-bar stretches run without changing anything except a pan. Record a 15-minute jam in Session view with mutes and sends, then cut the beginning and the end. The track must be playable from the beginning or from the middle.
rominimal.basse: A discreet, almost subliminal sub bass: a pure sine on F0 or G0, two notes over 2 bars, long, with a 10 ms attack. It never plays a dense rhythmic pattern. Often a second, higher and shorter bass, between 100 and 200 Hz, plays an isolated note on an offbeat, like a tonal percussion. The sub is lightly sidechained (2 dB, 200 ms release) so it pulses with the kick without audible pumping. A slight downward pitch bend of 1 semitone on the attack makes it feel alive. Low-pass filter at 120 Hz. On Arpiar records, the bass is sometimes a sampled double bass or a very muffled synth: the organic before the electronic.
etapes: Record ten minutes of real sounds (room, street, objects) and cut about thirty organic fragments of 50 to 200 ms.
Tempo 125 BPM, round acoustic kick with a 5 ms fade-in, muted rimshot on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note shaker with undulating velocities, extracted groove applied at 40%.
Add a discreet sine sub, two long notes over 2 bars, 2 dB of sidechain.
Place the organic percussion over 4 bars, shifted 5 to 15 ms after the grid, with a filtered dub delay.
Lay a filtered field recording as a pad and a sampled piano chord every 8 bars.
Jam for fifteen minutes with mutes and sends, edit, and mix it muted at -12 LUFS with the kick at -14 dBFS.
rominimal.mix: A muted, dynamic mix, designed for vinyl. Kick around -14 dBFS, softer than anywhere else in the family, sub just below, organic percussion at -24 dBFS. No hard saturation: tape or a warm preamp, that's all. Low-pass at 10 kHz on the master, high-pass at 35 Hz. Short room reverb, 0.4 s, on the percussion at 10%, to place it in a real space. Wide, moving panning, very slow Auto Pan (0.03 Hz) on two or three percussions. Almost no compression, Glue at 1.5:1 with 0.5 dB of reduction. Aim for -12 LUFS. The result should sound like a room where someone is playing, not like a computer.

outils.pourquoi: Micro-loops from an old jazz record, slices and scenes: the machine most cited by the Arpiar scene for live sets.
Field recorder for a Bucharest street, an empty room, drops: the intimate field recording placed as a pad.
Groove extracted from a house record applied at 40%, Random at 3%, fifteen-minute jam in Session view with mutes and sends.
Slice mode on a piano or double bass fragment, cut at 100 ms, low-pass at 6 kHz, undulating velocities.
Very round analog kick and muted percussion with a sample layer; found in many Romanian studios.
Dotted-eighth dub delay, feedback 35%, low-pass at 2 kHz, on the congas and the wood for space.
Tape emulation on the master instead of any hard saturation: the mix should sound like a room, not a computer.
A pack of organic percussion, sub basses and tiny elements cut for this groove, when you don't record yourself.

reperes: Petre Inspirescu: Sakadat (2007): muted percussion that varies with each cycle, a sub that breathes, the Arpiar manifesto.
Rhadoo: Arhiva (2012): a twelve-minute track where only the panning and the delays move.
Cristi Cons: Glassdance (2013): fragments of glass and jazz in micro-loops, the goldsmith side of the genre.
Dan Andrei: Vino (2011): a clean groove and a distant chord, the school's more house-oriented version.
rominimal.rythme: A very round kick, often an acoustic kick or a 909 filtered below 2 kHz, with a 5 ms fade-in to soften the attack, on every beat. No clap: a muted rimshot, a wood knock or a mouth sound on 2 and 4, very low. The percussion is organic and muted: congas, bongos, shakers, wood, all recorded or sampled, cut at 100 ms, run through a low-pass at 6 kHz. A shaker in sixteenth notes with undulating velocities (60, 90, 70, 100). A very soft closed hi-hat on the offbeats. Program over 2 or 4 bars so the percussion never repeats identically, and vary one hit per cycle: that is the infinite micro-variation.
rominimal.sons: The intimate field recording is the signature: a distant conversation, a Bucharest street, an empty room, recorded on a phone or a Zoom, filtered and placed very low as a pad. Tiny organic sounds: drops, rubbing, wood, glass, cut into 50 to 200 ms fragments and played as percussion. An Octatrack or a Simpler in slice mode makes micro-loops from an old jazz record. A sampled held piano or Rhodes chord, heavily filtered, on one note every 8 bars. Dub delays synced to the dotted eighth, feedback 35%, on the percussion, with a low-pass at 2 kHz. No bright synth, no lead: everything is muted, below 8 kHz.
sources: Telekom Electronic Beats (A 10-Track Beginner's Guide To Rominimal)
rominimal.tempo: 123 to 126 BPM, with a clean, discreet swing: 54 to 57%, never exaggerated, but applied with watchmaker precision to the percussion. The feel is that of a jazz drummer playing slightly behind: the organic percussion is shifted 5 to 15 ms after the grid, the kick stays on it. In Ableton, extract the groove from an old house record and apply it at 40% to everything except the kick. Add Random at 3% in the Groove Pool. Unlike Berlin minimal, ro-minimal is made for ten-hour sets: the track must be mixable over its whole length, with no moment that snags. Time should dissolve.

schranz.arrangement: Seven to eight minutes, cut for long, physical sets. 32-bar intro of kick and tops. The loops come in one by one every 16 or 32 bars and almost never leave. Events are rare: an 8-bar breakdown where only the kick stops, a glitched vocal appearing halfway through, a filter opening over 64 bars. No drop in the rave sense: when the kick returns, nothing else has changed. Think in two-minute plateaus rather than in phrases. 32-bar outro of kick and one loop. The track is a DJ tool: everything must be mixable at any moment.
schranz.basse: No separate bass in the classic sense. The kick group, after processing, peaks around -2 dB and occupies the bottom of the spectrum alone. What acts as bass are the distorted loops in the low mids, between 100 and 300 Hz, cut below so they don't fight with the kick. If you want a rumble, send the main kick into a short, dark reverb, cut above 200 Hz, saturate it and sidechain it to the kick. In Chris Liebing's style, an acid line or a synth sequence can occasionally replace the loops, but it stays in the mids. Tune the loops to the kick's note by ear, not by the pack's label.
etapes: At 150 BPM, create a kick group: main kick, faded offbeat kick at -20 dB, sidechained sixteenth-note kicks.
Cut two beats from an eight-bar percussion loop and roll it with an automated Auto Filter.
Saturate the loop in a chain: Amp, Reverb, EQ, VolumeShaper, Echo, then cut below 300 Hz.
Add saturated clap, low hi-hat, open hat and ride, all around -10 dB, as a continuous blanket.
Cut three chops from a vocal, stick them together over two beats, duplicate over one bar, distort.
Arrange in plateaus over eight minutes, a single 8-bar breakdown, Saturator on the drum group.
schranz.mix: Main kick at -10 dB, secondary kicks around -20, kick group at -2 dB peak in the dead center. The high elements all hit around -10 dB and form a continuous blanket; the tops group is set around -5 dB. Only a little width: clap and low hi-hat spread 10%, open hat and ride 25%. On the main drum group, Saturator Analog Clip at 2 dB of drive and 45% mix for cohesion. The danger is mud: cut each loop below 200 or 400 Hz. The master is dense and loud, but the kick must stay above the blanket of noise, otherwise everything turns gray.

outils.pourquoi: Crushed main kick, doubled with offbeat and sixteenth-note kicks at -20 dB; Chris Liebing uses the D16 Drumazon emulation.
The period sampler for cutting two beats from an eight-bar loop and rolling it continuously; Simpler in Ableton does the same.
Hand-drawn pumping on the saturated loops, locked to the kick, instead of a classic sidechain.
Band-pass with a slow LFO or an 8-bar automation on each loop: the moving filter replaces the fills.
First stage of the Amp, Reverb, EQ Eight, VolumeShaper, Echo chain; Boost and Crunch preset to make the loops rough.
The historical DAW of the 2000s German scene, still used by some schranz producers.
Chris Liebing's synth for the rare acid lines or sequences that occasionally replace the loops in the mids.
The pack used in the book for the percussion loops and vocal chops to distort; replace it with your own recordings as soon as possible.

reperes: Chris Liebing: The Real Schranz (1999): the name and the recipe, rolled loops and crushed kick
DJ Rush: Motherfucking Bass (2001): the speed and the raw vocal, Chicago pressure passed through Germany
Spirallianz: Blast Food (2000): saturated loops rubbing together, with no melody
Chris Liebing: Auf Und Ab (2003): the filter rising and falling over minutes, the plateau arrangement
schranz.rythme: The kick group has three parts: the main kick at -10 dB, an offbeat kick reduced to -20 dB with its attack faded (or a reversed kick, the hard house legacy), and sixteenth-note kicks at -20 dB in sidechain that fill the space. Above, the tops form a blanket of noise at -10 dB: clap, low closed hi-hat, open hat and ride doubled, all saturated. The percussion comes from loops: take a two- or four-beat loop from an eight-bar sample, roll it with an automated band-pass filter, saturate it in a chain. Several loops offset by a sixteenth note from each other create the grinding. No fills: variation comes from the filter.
schranz.sons: The crushed TR-909 and Akai S3000 sampler loops run through distortion chains: Amp, then Reverb, then EQ Eight, then VolumeShaper for pumping, then Echo. The filters move constantly: Auto Filter with a slow LFO or an automation over 8 bars. For the hook, a glitched vocal: three chops from an eight-bar vocal sample, stuck together into a two-beat phrase, duplicated over one bar, the last chop with no fade to accent a vowel. Make your own high-end textures by recording dead leaves or rice in a bag, then distort them: commercial packs don't have that scratch. Cubase remains the historical DAW, but Ableton does all of this.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
schranz.tempo: Between 145 and 155 BPM, with no groove at all. Schranz is a trance of matter: the tempo is a wall and nothing should stray from it. Where hard techno plays with percussion velocities, schranz rolls saturated loops continuously; the feel comes from the loops rubbing against each other and the moving filters, not from programming. At 150 BPM, a bar lasts 1.6 seconds, which makes a one-bar loop hypnotic in less than a minute. The main kick is doubled with offbeat kicks and low-level sixteenth-note kicks that create a constant pulse: this roll is what defines the style.

skweee.arrangement: Short tracks, two to four minutes, arranged quickly and without showing off. 4-bar intro with the bass alone or the drums alone, entry of the other, melody after 8 bars, pad after 16, then alternation: melody alone with drums, bass alone with drums, everything together. The breakdown removes the drums for 4 bars and lets the bass glide. No build-up, no drop, no DJ outro: the track stops when it has said what it had to say. The variations are melodic, a different pitch bend, a note that changes, not structural. Think of an instrumental funk track played by one person on one machine.
skweee.basse: The bass is the heart of skweee: round, detuned, squeaky. A simple monophonic synth, SH-101, MS-20, or Ableton Analog with two oscillators, square and saw, detuned by 10 to 15 cents, low-pass filter at 300 Hz with strong resonance, filter envelope with a 200 ms decay and an 80 to 120 ms portamento for the glides. Play eighth and quarter notes with glides of a fifth or an octave, pitch bends on the wheel, and silences. The squeak comes from the resonance opening on each attack. Naive minor keys, basslines that almost sing. No separate sub: this bass does everything, down to 45 Hz.
etapes: Tempo at 92 BPM, MPC 16 Swing 62 groove, dry drum machine: kick on 1 and the “and” of 2, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes with gaps.
Build a mono bass with two detuned oscillators, filter at 300 Hz with strong resonance, 100 ms portamento, and play eighth notes with glides and silences.
Write a naive square-wave melody with pitch bends, on the same synth.
Add a short pad in simple chords and a synth noise as percussion, still on the same instrument.
Arrange short: bass alone, drums, melody at 8 bars, pad at 16, alternations, hard stop around three minutes.
skweee.mix: Almost no mixing: the genre claims minimal processing, it is even its definition. Dry drums at -8 dBFS, resonant bass at the same level, melody 3 dB below. Light saturation on the bass, 3 dB of drive, for the squeak. No sidechain, or a very light one of 1 dB. Chorus on the pad, short delay on the melody, a small spring reverb on the snare. Bus compression 2:1, gentle. Mono below 100 Hz. Don't correct the low end that spills a little from the resonant bass: it is part of the sound. Master around -12 LUFS, with no aggressive limiter. If you spend more than an hour on the mix, you have probably betrayed the genre.

outils.pourquoi: Daniel Savio's favorite synth, from which he drew the drums, bass and melodies of a whole track: the very definition of the genre.
Round bass that squeaks thanks to the strong resonance opening on each attack, 100 ms portamento; Korg Collection MS-20 today.
The scene's other simple mono, bass and naive square-wave melody with pitch bends on the wheel; TAL-BassLine-101 or Roland SH-01A.
Two oscillators, square and saw, detuned by 10 to 15 cents, resonant filter at 300 Hz, 200 ms decay: the skweee bass in a single instrument.
The fallback single instrument: short FM noises as percussion, video game melodies and a short pad, all on the same track.
A dry, thin drum machine for the swung boom bap pattern, four bare drum tracks; the Oberheim DMX or the 808 also do the job.
The MPC 16 Swing 62 groove applied to the kit for the heavy swing at 92 BPM, the bass left a few milliseconds behind the kick.

reperes: Eero Johannes: We Could Be Skweeeroes (2008): the round, squeaky bass and the naive melody, a manifesto of the style.
Randy Barracuda: Ghetto Ghouls (2009): the dry drum machine and the heavy swing, with a single synth doing everything.
Mesak: Horrostaja (2010): bass glides and silences, Finnish restraint.
Ivan Senkevich: Rei (2025): the recent continuation, same economy of means, pitch bends and bare drums.
skweee.rythme: A dry drum machine: 808, 606, DMX or the synth's own percussion. Kick on 1 and on the “and” of 2, or on step 11, in a boom bap pattern: never four-on-the-floor. Snare or clap on 2 and 4, thin, a little late. Closed hi-hat in swung eighth notes, with gaps, and a rare open hat. One or two more elements at most: a bell, a rimshot or a filtered synth noise as percussion. The rule of the genre is restraint: four to five drum tracks, each one bare, without layers. Variations are made by removing a hi-hat hit, not by adding a fill. Program two bars, no more, and let them loop.
skweee.sons: The principle is to squeeze as much juice as possible out of simple gear: Daniel Savio described his practice of using a single synth for a whole track, drums, bass, melodies and pads included. Take a single instrument, Analog, Operator or a virtual SH-101, and do everything with it. Naive square-wave melodies, like a video game, played in eighth notes with pitch bends, a short pad in simple major or minor chords, and synth noises used as percussion. Light effects: chorus, short delay, a spring reverb or a small room. No vocoder, no vocals or almost none, no samples: that is what sets skweee apart from the rest of the family. Three to six tracks per song, never more.
skweee.tempo: Skweee is slow: 80 to 105 BPM, hip-hop tempo, with a marked swing of 58 to 62% on the sixteenth notes or an MPC 16 Swing 62 groove. It is the only genre in the family, along with late electro-funk, to leave so much air between the hits: the kick and the snare have room, and the bass takes advantage of it to stretch out. The feel is heavy, a little twisted, like funk played in slow motion by a computer. Some tracks go up to 110 BPM when crossing into electro, but the reference remains 92 BPM. Don't quantize everything: let the bass drag a few milliseconds behind the kick.

soulfulhouse.arrangement: A soul song in a club version. DJ intro of 16 to 32 bars with drums, percussion and a Rhodes motif. 16-bar verse with bass and voice, 8-bar pre-chorus with rising strings, 16-bar chorus with backing vocals, horns and piano. 16- to 32-bar breakdown: kick cut, instrument solo or vocal ad lib over Rhodes and percussion, conga roll, return of the chorus. Bridge modulated up a whole tone for the last chorus, extended ad libs, 32-bar drum outro. Length 7 to 9 minutes in the club version, with an instrumental dub and a radio edit. The track must stand as a song without the kick: that is the soulful test.
soulfulhouse.basse: A played bass: electric bass, or a synth that imitates it (Moog, or a fingered bass preset with a slow attack). The line is funky and melodic, follows a jazz progression of 4 or 8 chords, with walking lines between the roots, chromaticism, anticipations ahead of the beat and ghost notes. Quarter notes and eighth notes, never tight sixteenth notes. Play it on the keyboard with velocity or record a bassist. Gentle compression (3:1, slow attack) and a little tape saturation. It converses with the Rhodes and the voice, as in a soul band. No synthetic sub underneath, the bass holds the low end alone.
etapes: Project at 123 BPM, softened 909 drums with snare and clap on 2 and 4, hats swung at 56%, plus congas in tumbao, shaker and tambourine.
Write a 4-chord jazz progression (minor 9, major 7, dominant 13) over 8 bars and play it on the Rhodes with open voicings.
Play an electric or imitated bass, in quarter and eighth notes, with walking lines and anticipations.
Record a lead vocal and backing vocals in thirds, with ad libs, in a verse, pre-chorus, chorus structure.
Add written strings and a horn stab, and a flute or sax solo for the breakdown.
Assemble 8 minutes as a club song with DJ intro, solo breakdown, modulated bridge, and mix warm with the voice up front and dynamics.
soulfulhouse.mix: A soul record mix, warm and balanced. The voice up front, opto compression and de-esser, 2 s hall reverb, backing vocals spread in stereo and a little behind. Rhodes and piano left and right, bass in the center below 200 Hz, round kick with no click. Percussion spread with a shared room reverb. Wide strings filtered below 300 Hz, horns in the center with firm compression. Gentle bus compression (2:1), light tape saturation to glue. Master at -10 to -11 LUFS: the style likes dynamics and depth. Control 250 to 500 Hz, where Rhodes, bass, congas and voice meet.

outils.pourquoi: Minor 9 and dominant 13 chords in open voicings, light chorus: the central keyboard; Spectrasonics Keyscape or Arturia Stage-73 V as a plugin.
M1 organ and piano for the garage side, Kenny Dope's keyboard in the early days of Masters At Work; Korg Collection M1 today.
Softened, round kick, snare and clap together on 2 and 4, hats swung at 56%, under played Latin percussion.
Replaying conga loops and horn stabs, not hiding the writing; the S950 and the SP-1200 at Kenny Dope's before it.
Louie Vega's DAW for recording singers, strings and horns in studio sessions, with the gospel voice up front.
Played by a bassist with walking lines and ghost notes, or imitated by a fingered preset with a slow attack, with no synthetic sub underneath.
LA-2A emulation on the lead vocal with a de-esser, then a 2 s hall; gentle 2:1 compression on the bus to keep the dynamics.

reperes: Masters at Work: To Be in Love (1997): India's voice, the piano and Latin percussion, the reference for soulful at its peak.
Blaze: Lovelee Dae (1997): the played bass and Rhodes chords cycling under a murmured vocal, the intimate side.
Kerri Chandler: Rain (1998): Kerri's warm kick under a piano and a voice, how deep and soulful meet.
Frankie Knuckles: The Whistle Song (1991): soulful without vocals, a flute melody and jazz chords over soft drums.
soulfulhouse.rythme: A softened 909 or a sampled kit: round kick on every beat, snare and clap together on 2 and 4, swung sixteenth-note hats, open on the “and” of 2 and 4. A ride on the choruses. Latin percussion is essential: congas in tumbao, bongos, shaker, tambourine, guiro, bell, played or as 2-bar loops, with swing. The fills are conga or timbale rolls, or a one-beat stop where only the voice continues. In the breakdown, the kick stops, the percussion stays and the voice improvises. The drums serve the song and leave room for the musicians.
soulfulhouse.sons: Played Rhodes and piano, in jazz chords: minor 9ths, major 7ths, dominant 13ths, with open voicings and passing chords. The Korg M1 for organ and piano for the garage side. Written strings and horns, in lines and stabs, played or from realistic libraries. A funky rhythm guitar in muted eighth notes. A gospel lead vocal, with backing vocals in thirds and sixths, ad libs, and often call-and-response singing. An instrument solo (flute, sax, piano) in the breakdown. Effects: hall reverb on the voice and strings, chorus on the Rhodes, a discreet quarter-note delay. The S3000 sampler is used to replay percussion loops or stabs, not to hide the writing.
soulfulhouse.tempo: Between 120 and 126 BPM, with a band feel: this is house played by musicians, or that sounds like it. Swing of 55 to 58% on the hats and percussion, straight kick, but the keys and bass are played by hand and keep their micro-offsets. The groove comes from the bass that anticipates and the Latin percussion that sways. The voice phrases freely on top, with ad libs that ignore the grid. What sets soulful apart from the garage it descends from: more jazz in the chords, more Latin percussion, and a more composed production, with horn and string arrangements written rather than sampled.

spacemusic.arrangement: Space music uses the song format, 4 to 7 minutes, with a real melody laid out from the start. Typical structure: 30-second intro of phased pads, entry of the sequence and the drum machine, main theme played twice, B section with another theme or a modulation, return of the theme, coda of pads. Each part is 8 or 16 bars, like a song. Transitions go through a filter sweep or a spatial sound effect (filtered white noise, resonance sweep) rather than a rhythmic break. The theme must be memorable on first hearing: long notes, simple intervals, a 4-bar motif repeated. For the ambient side of Structures from Silence, forget all that and let one chord evolve for 30 minutes.
spacemusic.basse: The bass is a synth note held or in eighth notes, less aggressive than in kosmische, rounder. The Eminent 310 or the ARP 2600 were often used: saw, very closed filter (200 Hz), no resonance, slow envelope. In Analog or Operator, play the root of each chord in whole notes or eighth notes, with a 100 ms portamento between notes for the gliding feel. The harmonic progression matters more than the rhythmic pattern: Oxygène cycles through four minor chords that change every 4 bars, and the bass follows. Add a slow phaser to the bass as to everything else, but leave a clean sub underneath with a sine doubled an octave lower. No sidechain, the drum machine is too discreet to need it.
etapes: Choose four cycling minor chords and play the root on the bass in whole notes with portamento.
Build a pad of detuned strings and run it through a Phaser at 0.2 Hz, then a 5-second reverb.
Program a sixteenth-note arpeggio with Arpeggiator in Up-Down on the same chords.
Add a small drum machine in Operator, very discreet, kick on 1 and 3.
Compose a 4-bar theme with long notes on a saw lead and play it by hand.
Assemble into a 5-minute song format with filter sweep transitions.
spacemusic.mix: The mix is wide and bright, with lots of reverb and phasing, clearer than kosmische. Each pad gets its own reverb, long (4 to 6 seconds) with a 40 ms predelay to keep definition. The lead is centered, with a dotted-eighth stereo delay at 25 percent. The low end stays clean: cut the reverb below 200 Hz with an EQ on the return. The phasing on the pads creates moving frequency notches, let them be, it's the signature. Light bus compression (2:1, 2 dB) and a gentle limiter with 1 dB of headroom are enough. Target -12 LUFS. Lift the highs above 10 kHz by a dB or two with a gentle slope for the bright side of the Dreyfus records.

outils.pourquoi: The home organ whose string section makes the Oxygène pads; no common emulation, rebuild it with detuned saws and a phaser.
The phaser Jarre puts on the Eminent: slow sweep, medium feedback, the breathing of the pads; Ableton's Phaser-Flanger at 0.2 Hz does the job.
The semi-modular behind Jarre's leads and basses: saw, resonant filter, portamento; Arturia ARP 2600 V or the Behringer 2600 clone today.
The spatial sound effects of Oxygène: filtered white noise, resonance sweeps, beeps; use it for transitions between sections instead of breaks.
Vangelis's polyphonic on Pulstar: two layers, ribbon, aftertouch controlling the vibrato; Arturia CS-80 V remains the reference emulation.
The preset drum box of Oxygène Part IV: short, noisy sounds, almost subliminal; Mini Pops samples or a very discreet Operator kit.
Phasing on the pads, the bass and almost everything: Phaser mode, rate 0.2 Hz, for the moving frequency notches, the genre's signature.
To imitate the CS-80: two detuned oscillators, PWM, LFO on pitch modulated by aftertouch, then a 5-second reverb with predelay.

reperes: Jean-Michel Jarre: Oxygène Part IV (1976): the phased Eminent pad, the discreet Mini Pops drum machine, the simple theme that sticks.
Vangelis: Pulstar (1976): the expressive CS-80 lead, the wide electronic percussion, reverb on everything.
Ashra: Sunrain (1976): Göttsching's melodic sequences, a bridge between kosmische and pop.
Steve Roach: Structures from Silence (1984): the tempo-less side, one chord breathing for half an hour.
spacemusic.rythme: The drum machine is present but in the background, a color more than an engine. Jarre used a Korg Mini Pops: short, noisy, slightly toy-like sounds. Reproduce it with samples of 1970s preset drum boxes or with Operator: sine kick with a short 100 ms decay, snare as noise filtered at 2 kHz, hi-hat as very short 30 ms noise. Simple pattern, kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes, at an almost subliminal volume. The real rhythm comes from the arpeggiated sequences, as in kosmische, but more melodic: 16 sixteenth-note arpeggios on a minor chord, played by an Arpeggiator in Up-Down mode. Vangelis adds bigger electronic percussion, synthetic timpani hits on the strong beats.
spacemusic.sons: The machines from the brief are the ARP 2600, the Eminent 310 and the Yamaha CS-80. The Eminent 310 is a home organ whose string section, run through a Small Stone phaser, gives Jarre's signature pads: recreate it with an organ string sample or a pad of detuned saws, then Phaser-Flanger in Phaser mode, rate 0.2 Hz, medium feedback. Vangelis's CS-80, with its ribbon and aftertouch, gives the singing leads of Pulstar: a two-layer polyphonic synth, PWM, pressure-controlled vibrato, which Wavetable imitates with two slightly detuned oscillators and an LFO on pitch modulated by aftertouch. The melodies are played on an ARP 2600-type lead: saw, resonant filter, portamento. Add a long, wide reverb everywhere.
sourcesOutils: Sound On Sound (Jarre, 30 Years of Oxygène)
spacemusic.tempo: Space music keeps the pulse of kosmische but makes it pop: tempos between 100 and 125 BPM, sequences in eighth or sixteenth notes, and above all a melody that sticks in your head. Oxygène Part IV beats around 120 BPM with a discreet drum machine. The feel is clean, with no tempo drift: this is the generation of digital sequencers and the first stable clocks. One nuance to keep: the sequences are often played by hand on top of the machine, so a slight human offset of a few milliseconds on the main melody, ahead of the beat, brings it to life. For the ambient pieces of Steve Roach or Jonn Serrie, there is no tempo at all anymore, only pads.

spacesynth.arrangement: A spacesynth track is instrumental and is built like a film theme: 5 to 7 minutes. 16-bar cosmic intro with pads, lasers and sound effects without kick, then the bass arpeggio comes in, then the 707 drums. 16-bar theme A on the bright lead, 16-bar theme B higher or lower, return of theme A. Cosmic breakdown in the middle: the drums stop, the pads, a cascade of arpeggios and lasers remain, over 16 bars. Theme A comes back transposed up a whole tone. 32-bar instrumental outro for the DJ. Each new section arrives with a crash and a tom fill.
spacesynth.basse: The bass is an octave arpeggio in sixteenth notes, more mechanical and more continuous than in italo. A typical one-bar pattern: low root, octave, root, fifth, and back, sixteen notes per bar. The sound comes from a Roland JX-8P or a Juno, saw with a little square, very short envelope, 30 ms release, filter at 500 Hz with some envelope. Use Ableton's Arpeggiator in up-down mode over one octave with a two-note chord, or write the sixteenth notes by hand. The bass follows the chord each bar and only stops in the cosmic breakdown. The kick and the first note land together; in between, the arpeggio is the engine.
etapes: Set 126 BPM with no swing, load TR-707 samples: kick, snare, clap, hi-hats, toms.
Program kick on the beats, snare and clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats, descending tom fills every 8 bars.
Create the sixteenth-note bass arpeggio on a JX- or Juno-type synth, root, octave, fifth, over a four-chord progression in minor.
Write an 8-bar main theme on the bright lead, then a theme B, with cascading pads behind.
Make lasers with Operator: sine, pitch falling 36 semitones in 150 ms, delay and long reverb.
Assemble cosmic intro, theme A, theme B, drumless breakdown with lasers, transposed reprise, 32-bar outro.
spacesynth.mix: The spacesynth mix is bright and wide. The leads and lasers get a long 3 to 4 second reverb and a delay synced to the dotted eighth. The arpeggiated bass stays dry, in mono, compressed at 3:1 so every sixteenth note has the same weight. The hi-hats are loud and clear around 10 kHz. The snare and toms have a 250 ms gated reverb. Pan the pads very wide with chorus, and the chord arpeggios in crossed stereo. Cut the low end of the pads at 250 Hz. On the master, a light bus compressor and an EQ gently rising above 8 kHz for the shimmer. Aim for -11 LUFS.

outils.pourquoi: The bright leads and synth brass that carry the main theme; Laserdance used its big brother, the Super JX-10. Roland Cloud offers the emulation.
The snappy FM basses, the bells and the shimmering electric pianos that fill the verses.
The free DX7 emulation that loads the original banks: bells, FM basses and pianos, with nothing to program.
The dry digital kick, the short snare and the clap doubling it on 2 and 4, with a 250 ms gated reverb.
The electronic toms for the descending fills every 8 bars; recreate them with Operator, a sine and pitch falling 12 semitones in 200 ms.
The signature lasers: a sine or a saw whose pitch drops 36 semitones in 200 ms, with a delay behind it.
The octave bass arpeggio in sixteenth notes, the track's continuous engine, saw and 30 ms release; TAL-U-NO-LX replaces it.
The vocoder for Laserdance's robot voices; today, Ableton's Vocoder with a saw carrier.

reperes: Laserdance: Humanoid Invasion (1986): the sixteenth-note bass arpeggio, the lasers and the heroic theme.
Koto: Visitors (1985): the cascading pads and the bright lead playing a film theme.
Koto: Jabdah (1986): the very dry 707 rhythm and the melody transposed in the last third.
Space: Magic Fly (1977): the ancestor, the spacey instrumental theme before drum machines.
spacesynth.rythme: The Roland TR-707 is the machine: dry digital kick, short snappy snare, sixteenth-note hi-hats with an open hat on the offbeats. The 707 clap doubles the snare on 2 and 4. Simmons-style electronic toms play descending fills every 8 bars, and a crash marks each section. A rimshot or a cowbell can hold the eighth notes in the verses. In your DAW, 707 samples or a very dry 909 kit; for the toms, an Operator with a sine whose pitch falls 12 semitones in 200 ms. Add a short gated reverb on the snare and toms, that's the sound of 1986.
spacesynth.sons: The JX-8P gives the bright leads and synth brass that carry the main theme. The Yamaha DX7 brings the snappy FM basses, the bells and the shimmering electric pianos. Laser effects are the signature: a sine or a saw whose pitch drops 36 semitones in 100 to 300 ms, with a delay behind it. The spatial sound effects are filtered white noise rising and falling, resonance sweeps, reverb explosions. Cascading pads play chord arpeggios over two octaves. Vocoders or robot voices sometimes pass through. Today: Dexed for the DX7, a virtual Juno for the JX, Operator for the lasers.
spacesynth.tempo: Spacesynth runs a little faster than the italo that spawned it: 122 to 130 BPM, often 125 to 128. Everything is on the grid, no swing, with a constant sixteenth-note pulse in the bass arpeggios. The feel is that of a science-fiction film theme played by a drum machine. Set 126 BPM, full quantization. The signature is melodic: a main theme you can sing, played like a heroic lead, and an arpeggiated bass that never stops. Where italo has a singer, spacesynth has an 8-bar instrumental theme that comes back like a chorus.

speedcore.arrangement: Tracks are short, 2 to 4 minutes, and often built like a performance: introduction with the kick at a “normal” tempo (200-250 BPM), then successive accelerations, each block faster than the last, until complete fusion. Then a brutal return to a slow tempo, sometimes a real break with a sample, then back in. Some tracks actually change tempo in the DAW (BPM automation) rather than simulating it with retrigs: in Ableton, tempo automation on the Master track does this. Speedcore isn't really mixed by DJs, so no need for a long intro. The track is a demonstration: show what you do with speed.
speedcore.basse: There is no bass. Or rather, the burst of kicks becomes the bass: when you chain kicks at a rate of 20 Hz, you create a 20 Hz wave, which is a note. Producers play with this: varying the speed of the burst changes the perceived pitch. You can exploit it: a 1/32 burst at 300 BPM gives 40 Hz, roughly an E1. Otherwise, a layer of white noise low-pass filtered at 150 Hz, held continuously and distorted, fills the low end without competing with the kicks. No sine sub, it would be swallowed. If you insist on a bassline, a single square-wave note, sidechained with a 20 ms release, so it disappears between each hit.
etapes: Tempo 300 BPM. Gabber kick shortened to 100 ms, distorted, high-pass at 50 Hz.
Kick on every beat for 8 bars, then a 2-bar burst in sixteenth notes, then back.
Automate the tempo: rise from 250 to 400 BPM over 16 bars with the Master automation, listen to the fusion.
Add white noise low-pass filtered at 150 Hz, distorted, as a continuous low-end layer.
Sample a video game or anime voice, place it as an announcement before each acceleration.
End at 3 minutes with a 1/64 burst that becomes a drone, then a dead silence.
speedcore.mix: Mixing speedcore means mixing one thing, the kick, and keeping the fast repetition from turning the low end to mush. High-pass at 50 Hz on the kick, otherwise the bursts make the sub vibrate constantly. As Attack's book reminds us, the shape of a sound (its envelope) must be thought of in relation to the tempo: here it is vital, a 200 ms kick at 600 BPM overlaps three times. So cut the decay down to the sample. No reverb, none, it makes mud at this speed. Limiter on the master at -5 LUFS, distortion embraced. Check the mix in mono: at this rate, stereo adds nothing and can cancel hits.

outils.pourquoi: The machine of Nasenbluten and Bloody Fist: 4-track tracker, 8-bit samples, tempo pushed beyond what the hardware was designed for. The dirty sound is the signature.
Kick sampled once then replayed in thirty-second-note bursts until it fuses into a drone. The 909 is the material, no longer the rhythm.
The DAW of modern speedcore: Piano roll to draw kick bursts at 300 BPM and above, tempo settable to four digits without flinching.
The modern tracker: speed, per-line retrigger and sample effects, the direct heir of the Amiga for anyone who wants the original workflow.
Bit and sample rate reduction on the drum bus to recover the 8-bit grain of the trackers.
Grid in thirty-second notes, Chance at 100% at the ends of blocks: fused kick bursts without drawing every note.
Tempo can go up to 999 BPM, which is enough for most tracks; beyond that, double the tempo in the notes rather than in the transport.

reperes: Moby: Thousand (1993): the progressive acceleration up to a thousand beats, the founding concept, listen to how the kick becomes a sound.
Nasenbluten: Intellectual Killer (1995): the Australian tracker sound, short kicks and 8-bit samples, the hinge toward speedcore.
m1dy: Speedcore Dandy (2003): the Japanese version, pop samples and joyful bursts, the genre as a game.
The Berzerker: Reality (2000): speedcore and death metal fused, kicks and blast beats merged.
speedcore.rythme: The kick must be very short: 60 to 120 ms, otherwise the hits overlap and the low end turns to mush. Cut the decay, keep mostly the attack and a bit of body, distort to the max. At 300 BPM on all four beats, you get the basic pulse. Then the bursts: kick in eighth notes, sixteenth notes, thirty-second notes, over 1 to 4 bars, often accelerating (eighths, then sixteenths, then thirty-seconds). In Ableton, Beat Repeat with Grid at 1/32 and a short Gate does this live. Snare almost absent or a single hit per bar. The rhythmic breaks are clean cuts: total silence for one eighth note, then back in. The genre lives on the contrast between drone and isolated hits.
speedcore.sons: Speedcore has few sounds because it has no room. Anime or Japanese film samples with m1dy, metal samples and screams with The Berzerker, video game samples. Very short synth sounds, like beeps. Sirens. Swept white noise. Everything in 8 or 16 bits, with the aliasing of Amiga trackers, which you can recover with Redux. The hoover is rare, too long for the tempo. What matters is the attack of each sound: everything must have a sharp transient, otherwise it drowns. Many producers use FL Studio for how easily it programs retrigs and rolls: the Piano roll at 1/64 is your friend.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
speedcore.tempo: From 250 BPM, up to 1000 and beyond. It is no longer really a tempo, it is a frequency: at 600 BPM, ten kicks per second, and the ear no longer hears hits but a drone. What sets speedcore apart from terrorcore, then, is that the kick becomes a texture, and the producer plays with the passage between the two states: fused bursts, then back to distinct hits. Technically, you can stay at 300 BPM in your DAW and program kicks in sixteenth notes to simulate 1200 BPM. The trackers did it with retrig commands. No swing, of course: here swing sounds like an engine fault.

speedgarage.arrangement: A 5 to 7 minute club track. 32-bar DJ intro with drums and one element, often the filtered organ. The warp bass arrives at bar 32 or 48, it's the first big moment. Ragga vocal as a hook every 16 bars. Breakdown in the middle: the bass and kick drop out, leaving the organ and the voice, 16 bars, then a snare roll and the bass returns alone for 4 bars before the kick. A second, shorter breakdown around the three-quarter mark. 32-bar outro with kick and hats. Think of the rewind: the moment the bass comes back should make people want to put the needle back at the start.
speedgarage.basse: The warp bass is the genre's DNA, inherited from jungle. Build a Reese: two saws detuned in opposite directions, +0.1 and -0.1 semitone, in mono with glide on, in Massive or Serum. Run it through a low-pass with the cutoff around 400 Hz and a little resonance, and modulate the cutoff with an envelope or a slow LFO. The “warble” comes from the pitch glide: write long notes that slide down a semitone or a fourth. Under this Reese, a sine sub an octave lower plays the roots in eighth notes. The Reese chapter of Attack Magazine's book details this recipe: opposite detuning, mono glide, 6-voice unison, filter movement.
etapes: Set the project to 132 BPM, TR-909 kit: 4/4 kick, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats.
Build a Reese in Massive or Serum: two saws detuned in opposite directions, mono, glide, low-pass at 400 Hz.
Write long bass notes that slide down, with a sine sub an octave below in eighth notes.
Lay down M1 organ stabs and a ragga sample in a 2-bar loop.
Arrange: 32-bar intro, bass drop, 16-bar breakdown with the bass returning alone.
Mix the sub in mono, saturate the Reese, sidechain to the kick, master around -7 LUFS.
speedgarage.mix: The bass is up front, the sub dominates and the kick slips underneath. Set the sub around -6 dB peak, mono below 120 Hz with Utility. The Reese occupies 100 to 600 Hz: saturate it with Saturator or an amp, drive at 30%, so it comes through on a small system. Sidechain the bass from the kick, 4:1 ratio, 1 ms attack, 80 ms release. Kick cut below 40 Hz, no higher, its fundamental must stay. Organ and voice high-passed at 250 Hz. Short reverb on the snare, 0.8 s. Light drum bus compression. Master around -7 LUFS, a Limiter with 2 to 3 dB of reduction at most.

outils.pourquoi: Full kick on all four beats, clap, 909 open hat on the offbeats and snare rolls at the end of phrases. Samples or D16 Drumazon 2 as a plugin.
The book's Reese: two wavetables detuned to +0.1 and -0.1, mono with glide, 6-voice unison, Blue Monark filter moving slowly.
The other synth for the warp bass: two saws in opposite directions, low-pass around 400 Hz, slow LFO on the cutoff, notes sliding down.
Organ 2 stabs louder and simpler than in UK garage, M1 piano for the euphoric moments. Korg Collection plugin.
12-bit sampler for ragga vocals, sirens and disco strings taken from vinyl, with the 1997 grain. Redux imitates its crunch.
Drive at 30% on the Reese so it carries between 100 and 600 Hz on a small system, while keeping the sine sub clean underneath.
Warp basses, kicks, vocals and sirens for speed garage and 4x4, useful for comparing your Reese to references of the genre.

reperes: Double 99: RIP Groove (1997): the warp bass sliding under a straight 909 kick, the genre's model.
187 Lockdown: Gunman (1997): the western sample and the organ, the arrangement in 8-bar blocks.
Serious Danger: Deeper (1997): the slowly undulating Reese, the pitched vocal and the breakdown in the middle.
Tina Moore: Never Gonna Let You Go (1997): the remix that tipped an R'n'B vocal into speed garage.
