speedgarage.rythme: A full TR-909 kick, on all four beats, with the click clearly present. 909 snare or clap on 2 and 4, with a short reverb that snaps. 909 open hat on every offbeat, closed hat in shuffled sixteenth notes. Ride or shaker in eighth notes to fill in. At the end of each 8-bar phrase, a snare roll in sixteenth or thirty-second notes, sometimes a timbale build-up. Add syncopated rimshots borrowed from US garage and pitched tom hits. The jungle breaks are not in the drums here, they are in the bass: the drums stay house drums, clean and regular, leaving room for the low end.
speedgarage.sons: Korg M1 organ stabs, as in UK garage, but played louder and simpler. M1 house piano for the euphoric moments. Sampled ragga and dancehall vocals, a phrase or two, often pitched and chopped into a loop. Sirens, vinyl spin-backs, rewind noises. Timbales and bells for the fills. Disco strings sampled from an old 12-inch, filtered. The TR-909 for the whole kit. The common thread: direct sounds, no complicated sound design, everything serving the contrast between bright house up top and a jungle bass rumbling below.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter, Reese bass (wavetable)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter, Reese bass (wavetable)
MusicRadar, How to create a Korg M1-style organ bass sound
speedgarage.tempo: Between 130 and 135 BPM, with a dead-straight 4/4 kick: speed garage is squarer than the UK garage that follows it, the energy comes from the bass and not from the swing. Still keep a moderate 909 shuffle on the hats, 54 to 56%, the rest almost quantized. The feel is New York house pushed by jungle pressure: the kick runs straight ahead, the bass undulates underneath. Rhythmic signature in 4/4, 8-bar phrases with a snare roll at the end of each block. What changes compared to its parent: less rhythmic finesse, more power, a tempo slightly higher than the house of the time.

suomisaundi.arrangement: There is no mandatory structure, but there is a principle: the unexpected turn. A 16-bar intro sets up a normal psy motif, then at bar 17 an absurd sample changes everything. Alternate track passages (kick, rolling bass, lead) with jam passages (guitar, funk bass, sampled drum break). The breakdowns are for telling a joke: a dialogue sample, a silence, a return on a trumpet sample. Plan at least one passage where the tempo or time signature changes. Aim for 7 to 9 minutes. To stay playable, keep 32 bars of straight psy at the start and the end: the madness is in the middle.
suomisaundi.basse: The suomi bass can be a rolling psy bass, but it often slides toward funk: lines in eighth and sixteenth notes with leaps of a fifth and an octave, chromatic passing notes, slides. The brief mentions a monophonic synth: an SH-101, a Pro-One or an emulation, saw and square mixed, resonant low-pass filter at 300 Hz, portamento set for the slides. A played, lightly saturated electric bass can double or replace it on a passage. Root in E or A, but the bass follows chord progressions, sometimes major, which psytrance never does. Still keep a stable sine sub under the madness.
etapes: Project at 145 BPM. Lay down a psy kick and a classic rolling bass on E1, to have a base that dances.
Load a mono synth (SH-101 emulation), set the portamento and write a funk bassline with slides and octave leaps, swing at 56%.
Chop three absurd samples (voice, cartoon, old record) and play them pitched on a sampler.
Record a guitar or a nasal synth playing a major melody with a wrong note, through a pedal distortion.
Add sampled drum breaks, offset triplet fills and a 4-bar passage in 7/8.
Arrange as a jam: 32 bars of straight psy, absurd turn, funk passage, back to psy, joke in the breakdown, straight outro.
suomisaundi.mix: DIY production is not an excuse for a dirty mix, but an aesthetic choice: tape saturation on the master, a little background noise, cheap plate reverbs. The kick and the bass stay clean and centered, because the track still has to make people dance. The rest can be mixed “weird”: a lead only on the left, a sample suddenly too loud, a guitar compressed to death. Parallel compression on the sampled drum breaks for the funk. Avoid the modern transparent limiter: a slightly colored limiter, set around -9 LUFS, suits the genre better. The final test: does it sound like a group of friends in a basement, but with a sub that works?

outils.pourquoi: The mismatched mono from the brief: saw and square mixed, resonant filter at 300 Hz, portamento for the funk bass slides.
Another second-hand mono typical of Finnish studios; nasal leads and basses that go off the rails, played by hand.
The sampler full of wacky samples: cartoons, Finnish TV, old records, replayed pitched on the keyboard.
The unapologetically cheap pedal: electric guitar or synth run through it, then recorded as is, noise included.
Beat Repeat to chop up a whole bar, Simpler for the sampled breaks, Vocoder for the absurd voices; modern DIY goes through it.
Juno-60 emulation for the disco chords hidden under the kicks, with the original chorus that sounds instantly vintage.
Nasal leads and transposed video game melodies: two operators, integer ratio, without worrying about being pretty.

reperes: Texas Faggott: Impastil (2003): the funk under the psy kick, the absurd samples and the studio you can hear.
Haltya: Hero (2005): twisted video game melodies and sudden arrangement turns.
Luomuhappo: Rauhaa Veljet (2004): unapologetically homemade production, with mismatched synths.
Texas Faggott: Harry Blotter (2005): the joke as track structure.
suomisaundi.rythme: The kick stays a psy kick, short and tuned, but it coexists with sampled drum breaks, hand-played snare fills, acoustic kit cymbals. Snare on 2 and 4, but sometimes moved to the “and” of 3 for a beat. The hi-hats play funk sixteenth notes, with openings on the offbeats and ghost notes. Add absurd percussion: a car horn sample, a spoon on a glass, a laugh cut short. The fills are “tricky”: triplet rolls that land an eighth note too early, Beat Repeats that chop up a whole bar. The rhythm should surprise at least once a minute.
suomisaundi.sons: The principle: mismatched hardware synths, wacky samples, cheap effects. Use what you have: a Juno emulation for disco chords, an Operator for nasal leads, an electric guitar recorded through a 20-dollar distortion pedal. The melodies are twisted: major scales with wrong notes, transposed polka or video game melodies, arpeggios that go off the rails. The samples come from cartoons, Finnish TV shows, old records: chop them and replay them pitched. The effects are unapologetic: a pedal flanger, a digital delay whose repeats degrade, a vocoder. The listener should hear the studio and the smile.
suomisaundi.tempo: Suomisaundi runs between 140 and 150 BPM, but it is the only psy subgenre where tempo is not a rule: some tracks change tempo along the way, others slip in a bar of 7/8 or a half-time passage. The groove is different too: there is hidden funk underneath, so a swing of 54 to 58% on the percussion and the bass is welcome. What changes compared to the whole family is the attitude: the structure is a jam, not a plan. Count in 8 bars, but allow yourself phrases of 6 or 10 when the joke calls for it.

synthfunk.arrangement: This is band music: 4- to 8-bar intro on the Linn and the bass, 16-bar verse with the talkbox or the voice, 8- to 16-bar chorus with the brass and backing vocals, bridge with a synth or talkbox solo, final chorus with ad libs. Count on four to six minutes, the long versions keep a 32-bar instrumental groove at the end. Transitions happen through Linn fills (toms and rolls) and one-beat cuts where only the voice speaks. The groove doesn't change tempo or kick: it's the chords and layers that move. Keep empty bars for the answers: the voice asks, the bass answers.
synthfunk.basse: The bass is a Minimoog, or a Prophet-5 in unison, imitating slap: two layered sounds, a deep saw with a filter closed at 200 Hz for the thumb, and a brighter sound with a filter open at 2 kHz and a 60 ms decay for the pop. Play in sixteenth notes with silences: funk lives in the gaps. Typical one-bar pattern: root on 1, silence, octave on the “a” of 1, root on the “and” of 2, minor seventh on 4. Add portamento on a few notes and octave slides. Keys in E or A minor, with seventh chords. Cut only below 40 Hz, the Linn kick is short and leaves room.
etapes: Tempo at 108 BPM, LinnDrum kit, MPC 16 Swing 58 groove: kick on 1 and the “and” of 3, snare and clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes, snare ghost notes at velocity 40.
Build a slap bass on a virtual Minimoog with two layers, deep thumb and bright pop, and write a sixteenth-note pattern with silences in E minor.
Lay down minor 9 chords on an Operator FM piano and OB brass in ninths, 30 ms attack.
Record a voice through a talkbox or a narrow-band vocoder for the chorus.
Add a clavinet in muted eighth notes and a Moog lead with portamento for the bridge.
Arrange like a band: intro, verse, chorus, bridge with solo, final chorus, instrumental outro groove.
synthfunk.mix: A 1982 studio mix: the Linn dry but compressed, snare with a 400 ms gated reverb, short kick at -8 dBFS. Moog bass in the center, compressed at 4:1 with a 20 ms attack to keep the slap's pop, and light saturation. Talkbox and voice up front, with an eighth-note delay. Brass and FM piano wide in stereo, with chorus. A slow 3:1 bus compression glues everything, like an SSL console. Cut the pads below 200 Hz. The mix must have body between 100 and 250 Hz, where the bass and the snare live: don't thin it out. Master around -12 LUFS, the dynamics carry the groove.

outils.pourquoi: Roger Troutman's talkbox, a tube in the mouth connected to a saw synth; the MXR M222 Talk Box is the common version today.
Two-layer synth slap bass, deep thumb filtered at 200 Hz and bright pop, and the talkbox source at Zapp; Arturia Mini V today.
8-bit samples of real drums with built-in shuffle, huge snare on 2 and 4; the Linn LM-1 with Prince, sampled kits in Drum Rack today.
The small FM synth Roger Troutman plugged into his talkbox on the early albums, with a hard brass preset.
FM electric piano with tremolo and bells, for the minor 9 chords; Arturia DX7 V or Dexed take over the patches.
To recreate the FM piano: low modulation ratio or E.Piano preset with tremolo, the method from the FM Synthesis chapter of Attack's book.
In unison for Zapp's basses and synth strings; u-he Repro-5 or Arturia Prophet-5 V replace it easily.
Synth brass in ninth chords with a 30 ms attack, wide in stereo with chorus, the signature of Cameo and Midnight Star.

reperes: Zapp: More Bounce to the Ounce (1980): the talkbox and the Moog bass, a groove that doesn't move for five minutes.
The Gap Band: Outstanding (1982): the swung Linn and the ninth chords, the boogie model.
Midnight Star: Freak-a-Zoid (1983): the robotic vocoder and the slapped synth bass, the junction with electro-funk.
Cameo: Word Up (1986): the huge Linn snare with gated reverb and the synth brass.
synthfunk.rythme: LinnDrum or LM-1: 8-bit samples of real drums, dry and compressed. Kick on 1 and on the “and” of 3, with funk variations (a kick on step 8 or step 15). Linn snare on 2 and 4, huge, often doubled with a Linn clap and a gated reverb in 1983. Closed hi-hat in swung eighth notes, with openings on the “and” of 4. Linn cowbell and cabasa in sixteenth notes. The production trick is velocity: program the hi-hats with at least three levels, and add snare ghost notes at velocity 40 on steps 7 and 15. With Prince, the Linn is treated with a flanger or low pitch on the snare.
synthfunk.sons: The talkbox is the voice of the genre: a tube in the mouth connected to a synth, often a Minimoog on a saw. Today, a narrow-band vocoder or a talkbox plugin (TAL-Vocoder in talkbox mode, or a formant filter driven by a voice) gets close to the effect, but nothing replaces a real tube. The DX7 provides the FM electric piano: in Operator, a low modulation at a 1:14 ratio or an E.Piano preset, with tremolo. The Oberheim OB-8 gives the synth brass in ninth chords, 30 ms attack. Add a clavinet or a rhythm guitar in muted eighth notes, a Moog lead with portamento, and synth strings. The chords are rich: minor 9, dominant 7 with a sharp 9.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (FM Synthesis chapter)
synthfunk.tempo: Synth-funk is the slowest in the family: 96 to 115 BPM, More Bounce to the Ounce around 108, Word Up around 118 at the top end. It is also the only genre in the family with real swing: the LinnDrum and the Linn LM-1 have built-in shuffle, and patterns were often played on the pads. Apply a swing of 54 to 58% on the sixteenth notes, or an MPC 16 Swing 58 groove in Ableton. The feel is heavy and laid back: the snare lands a little after the beat. It is the bridge between played funk and programmed funk, and the tempo must let a bassist play slap.

synthpop.arrangement: Strict song format, 3 minutes 30 to 4 minutes 30: 8-bar instrumental intro that lays out the synth riff, 16-bar verse, 8-bar pre-chorus, 8- or 16-bar chorus, second verse, chorus, 8-bar bridge with a modulation or a new pad, last chorus doubled, outro on the riff. The instrumental riff is as important as the sung melody: Just Can't Get Enough and Enola Gay are recognized by their riff before the voice. Tom breaks at the end of sections announce each change. For a club-playable version, prepare an extended remix in the manner of the 1982 maxi singles: 32-bar intro of beat and bass, the song, then a 32-bar outro with the riff repeated.
synthpop.basse: The bass is played on a synth, often in eighth or sixteenth notes, and follows the song's chords: it changes note every 2 or 4 bars. The brief gives the Juno-60 and Juno-106: a saw oscillator plus sub, filter at 500 Hz, fast envelope, a little Juno chorus for width. In Ableton, Analog or a Juno plugin (TAL-U-NO-LX) does the job. The typical line: root in eighth notes with a jump to the octave on the “and” of 4, or a Moroder-style sixteenth-note line for dance tracks. The DX7 brings the snappy FM basses, the Bass 1 preset with its pick attack: in Operator, a 1:1 ratio with a modulation index on a very short envelope.
etapes: First write a 2-bar synth riff and a singable chorus melody, on four chords.
Program a LinnDrum or 808 beat at 120 BPM with a tom roll at the end of every 8 bars.
Lay down a Juno bass in eighth notes following the chords, with a jump to the octave on the “and” of 4.
Add chorused pads and a DX7 bell in Operator for the counter-melodies.
Record the voice, compress it hard, and build the verse-chorus-bridge format over 4 minutes.
Mix with gated reverb on the snare, wide chorus on the pads, voice up front.
synthpop.mix: The synth-pop mix is bright, very stereo on the chorused pads, with the voice in the center and up front. The kick and bass share the low end without obvious sidechain, but with complementary EQ: kick bump at 60 Hz, bass bump at 100 Hz. The gated reverb on the snare is the signature effect of 1982 to 1985: Reverb in Gate mode, or Hybrid Reverb with a Gate after it. The pads get a 3 second Hall reverb. Compress the voice firmly (4:1 ratio, 6 dB of reduction) and add an eighth-note delay at 15 percent. On the master, a Glue Compressor at 2 dB and light tape saturation. Target -11 LUFS for a modern version, but keep the LinnDrum transients, which must stay snappy.

outils.pourquoi: The chorused pads and the eighth-note bass: saw plus sub, filter at 500 Hz, Chorus II; TAL-U-NO-LX or Roland Cloud Juno-60 today.
The 8-bit real-drum samples on Don't You Want Me: dry kick, snappy snare, descending tom rolls; Linn From Mars in Drum Rack.
The deep kick and claps of the more dance-oriented tracks; Roland Cloud TR-808 or D16 Nepheton, kick on every beat, clap on 2 and 4.
The bells, electric pianos and snappy FM bass of 1983 to 1985 (Bass 1 preset); free Dexed or Arturia DX7 V.
Short orchestral and vocal samples played in chords, the luxury of ZTT and OMD; Simpler with a sample reduced to 8 bits via Redux.
The most widespread and inexpensive Juno emulation: oscillator, sub, chorus I and II, for the bass following the chords and the wide pads.
The free and open DX7 that reads the original SysEx banks: load the factory presets for period bells and FM basses.
Native FM for the bells (1:3.5 ratio) and the snappy bass (1:1 ratio, index on a very short envelope), with no third-party plugin.

reperes: The Human League: Don't You Want Me (1981): the LinnDrum, the synth bass following the chords, the perfect pop structure.
Depeche Mode: Just Can't Get Enough (1981): the synth riff recognizable in one second, the chorused pads.
Soft Cell: Tainted Love (1981): two synth notes as a gimmick, minimalism serving the voice.
Orchestral Manoeuvres in the Dark: Enola Gay (1980): the drum machine beat up front and the melody that won't let go.
synthpop.rythme: The brief cites the LinnDrum and the TR-808. The LinnDrum (1982) brings 8-bit samples of real drums: dry kick, snappy snare, short hi-hat. The 808 brings the deep kick and the claps. Load a LinnDrum or 808 kit into Drum Rack and program: kick on 1 and 3 (or on every beat for dance tracks), snare or clap on 2 and 4, hi-hats in eighth notes, with an open hat on the “and” of 4. Add electronic toms as a fill at the end of each 8-bar section: that's the signature of the era, a descending LinnDrum tom roll. The percussion must stay clean and reverberated with a gated reverb: Reverb with Gate on, 1.5 second decay, gate cutting at 200 ms.
synthpop.sons: The machines: Juno-60, Juno-106, DX7, TR-808, LinnDrum, Fairlight. The Juno gives the chorused pads and block chords, the warm color of the genre: saw, filter at 3 kHz, Chorus II. The DX7 gives the bells, electric pianos and FM basses of 1983-1985, to recreate with Operator in 2-operator FM, 1:3.5 ratio for the bells. The Fairlight brings short orchestral and vocal samples: Simpler with a sample reduced to 8 bits via Redux, played in chords. The leads are simple, a square wave or a mono saw with vibrato. Period effects: chorus on everything, dotted-eighth delay on the leads, gated reverb on the drums. The voice is up front, with a 2 second plate reverb.
synthpop.tempo: Synth-pop keeps the song format: tempos from 100 to 135 BPM, centered around 120. Don't You Want Me runs around 118, Just Can't Get Enough around 126, Tainted Love around 145. The beat is machine-quantized (LinnDrum or TR-808) but the sung melody carries the expression: the tempo serves the voice, not the dancefloor. One difference from the parent proto-techno: the verse-chorus structure imposes energy changes every 8 bars, so the feel varies within the same tempo. A light 54 percent shuffle on the hi-hats shows up with some bands, but the norm stays straight. Program the chorus first: if the beat doesn't carry the chorus melody, change the tempo.

techhouse.arrangement: Six to seven minutes, classic DJ structure in 16-bar blocks. 32-bar intro with kick, hats and one percussion, the bass comes in at bar 33. First drop at bar 65 with the vocal and all the percussion. Breakdown halfway: remove the kick and bass for 16 bars, keep the filtered vocal with a high-pass rising from 200 Hz to 2 kHz, then a snare roll over the last four bars. The return of the kick is the big moment. Contemporary tech house often has two breakdowns and a vocal that comes back every 8 bars. 32-bar outro, back to hats and kick. Change one percussion every 8 bars to keep the set alive.
techhouse.basse: The round looped bass is the signature. A Bass Station or its clone, or Operator with a sine and a square wave mixed, low-pass filter at 300 Hz, low resonance. The pattern plays on the offbeats: one note on each upbeat eighth, sometimes an added sixteenth note before beat 3. Note length 60%, never legato, so the kick breathes in between. Pitch one octave above the sub, between F1 and A1; a two-bar variation changes a single note, the fifth or the minor seventh. Sidechain from the kick with a 120 ms release to carve out space. It is this offbeat bass that creates the house sway under the techno kick.
etapes: Tempo 126 BPM, 909 kick on the beats, clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hat with a Swing 16 groove at 57%.
Program the round offbeat bass with Operator or a Bass Station, notes at 60% length, sidechained from the kick.
Layer three dry percussions (conga, shaker, block) on the free sixteenth notes, without reverb.
Cut a one-second vocal into four pieces and loop them over one bar with an eighth-note delay.
Build the arrangement in 16-bar blocks: 32-bar intro, drop, 16-bar breakdown with filter, second drop, 32-bar outro.
Mix kick and bass together, compress the percussion group, aim for -8 LUFS on the master.
techhouse.mix: The tech house mix is clean and dense in the low mids. Kick around -10 dBFS peak, bass 3 dB below, sidechain visible but not pumping. A high-pass EQ at 100 Hz on all the percussion, at 200 Hz on the vocals. Compress the percussion group with a 10 ms attack, 50 ms release, 4:1 ratio, to glue it. Light saturation (Saturator at 3 dB) on the bass so it comes through on small systems. Short reverb, 0.8 s plate, only on the clap and the vocal, at 15%. On the master, a Glue at 2:1 with 1 dB of reduction, then a limiter aiming for -8 LUFS integrated for the platforms. Check mono below 120 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: The genre's dominant DAW: Swing 16 groove at 57% on the hats and percussion, kick and bass left straight.
Round kick with a short tail, clap and hi-hats: 909 samples remain the foundation, often via Roland Cloud or D16 Drumazon 2.
The round offbeat bass: sine and square mixed, low-pass filter at 300 Hz, short notes at 60% length.
Modern basses and stabs, with an LFO on the cutoff for variations; its tech house presets have been everywhere since 2015.
To design a kick tuned to the key, 250 ms decay, controlled click, instead of hunting for the right sample.
One-knob sidechain on the bass and stabs, release around 120 ms; Xfer LFOTool or Cableguys VolumeShaper do the same.
High-pass at 100 Hz on all the percussion, at 200 Hz on the chopped vocals, and mono control below 120 Hz.
The machine of the Wiggle pioneers and Terry Francis: dry percussion played on the pads, MPC swing inherited by DAWs.

reperes: Paperclip People: Throw (1994): Carl Craig's filtered disco loop, a rolling groove that never stops.
Peace Division: Feel It (2001): the tight percussion and round bass of the London school, zero melody.
Fisher: Losing It (2018): festival tech house, a chopped vocal, a long breakdown and a bass that comes back like a punch.
As One: We No Longer Understand (1995): the deep, Detroit side of early British tech house.
techhouse.rythme: 909 kick on every beat, rounder than in techno, with a short 250 ms tail. The clap or snare lands on beats 2 and 4, often doubled with a rimshot offset by a sixteenth note. The closed hi-hat plays sixteenth notes with alternating velocities of 100 and 60, the open hat on the eighth-note offbeats. What sets tech house apart is the layer of dry percussion: congas, shakers, blocks, all short and without reverb, placed on the free sixteenth notes. A shaker in swung sixteenth notes with a 20 ms fade-in becomes the engine. Add a discreet ride on the eighth notes for the high sections. Everything must be tight: no sample longer than 300 ms.
techhouse.sons: Few synths, lots of percussion. The chopped vocal hook has been central since the 2010s: take a one-second phrase, cut it into three or four pieces, repeat them in a one-bar pattern, with a band-pass filter around 1 kHz and an eighth-note delay at 20%. A short stab, a minor chord on Juno or Analog, attack 0, decay 200 ms, on a single offbeat per bar. Simple riser effects: white noise filtered over 8 bars, a reversed crash. An MPC or its emulation makes the percussion livelier than the perfect grid. Add a tonal beep or blip in eighth notes on a single note as the common thread, very far back in the mix.
sourcesOutils: Integraudio (Best Plugins For Techno, Electro & UK Garage)
We Make Dance Music (Must-Have Plugins for House Music Production)
techhouse.tempo: 124 to 128 BPM, where house and techno meet. Unlike minimal techno, the swing is embraced: between 55 and 58% on the sixteenth notes, the hi-hat and percussion benefit from it, the kick stays straight. The feel is rolling, a continuous pulse that makes you want to walk rather than jump. In Ableton, a Swing 16 groove at 57% applied only to the hats and percussion does the job. Don't put swing on the bass, it must stay square to lock with the kick. 2010s tech house often goes up to 126 or 127 BPM; the 1990s Wiggle versions ran closer to 125. The track must roll, never force.

technobass.arrangement: Techno bass is made for DJs who mix fast: intros of 16 to 32 bars with the 808 alone, 16-bar sections, short breakdowns. A track lasts five to six minutes. Ghettotech is shorter, three to four minutes, and moves every 8 bars: new vocal phrase, new stab, kick switching from syncopated to four-on-the-floor. Use mutes as structure: cut the kick for 4 bars, keep the synth bass, relaunch on a roll. The vocoded chorus returns three or four times. No long build-up or drop: the tension comes from the speed and the repetition of the voices. End on the 808 alone to allow mixing.
technobass.basse: Two basses coexist. The first is the tuned 808 kick, as in Miami, but played shorter and in faster eighth-note patterns. The second is an electro synth bass: saw or square, low-pass filter at 300 Hz with a fast envelope, playing sixteenth notes in octave leaps on the root, Detroit-style. It takes the place of the melody as much as of the bass. Minor key, often A or D. Alternate the two: the held 808 during the chorus, the synth bass during the verses. Cut the synth bass below 80 Hz, leave the 808 alone underneath. Light sidechain of the bass from the kick, 3 dB of reduction, for clarity at high tempo.
etapes: Tempo at 138 BPM, 808 in Drum Rack: kick on 1, the “and” of 2 and step 12, clap on 2 and 4, sixteenth-note hi-hats with accents on the offbeats.
Sample a long 808 kick, tune it and play an eighth-note bass on two notes for the chorus.
Write a sixteenth-note synth bass with octave leaps for the verses, filter at 300 Hz, 6 dB of saturation.
Add minor chord stabs on the offbeats and a cold held pad.
Record a phrase, vocode it, then cut it into syllables in Simpler and replay it rhythmically.
Arrange in 16-bar sections with kick mutes, rolls before the relaunches, and an intro and outro with the 808 alone.
technobass.mix: The mix inherits from Miami bass for the low end and from techno for the rest. 808 at -5 dBFS peak, sub down to 35 Hz, cut below 30. The stabs and the synth bass are saturated: Ableton's Saturator or Overdrive, 6 dB of drive, so they cut through at high tempo. Light bus compression, 2:1 ratio, 10 ms attack, 50 ms release. The chopped voices are compressed hard and run through an eighth-note delay at 20% dry/wet. Tight panning, everything almost centered: the style plays on big mono systems. Short reverb on the clap only, 200 ms. The final level can be louder than electro-funk: aim for -9 LUFS integrated for club tracks.

outils.pourquoi: Fast, precise 808 at 138 BPM, kick with a medium 300 ms decay so it doesn't overlap; Behringer RD-8 or an 808 kit in Drum Rack today.
Its clap and hi-hats stacked on the 808 bring Detroit's techno layer; 909 samples in Drum Rack are enough.
For Aux 88's science-fiction lyrics or DJ Assault's obscene phrases, before chopping the voice into syllables.
In Slice mode, cut the vocoded phrase into one-syllable fragments and replay them rhythmically: that is the chopped ghettotech voice.
The electro synth bass in sixteenth notes and octave leaps, filter at 300 Hz with a fast envelope, and the short 200 ms minor stabs.
6 dB of drive on the synth bass and stabs so they cut through at high tempo; Overdrive does the same job more aggressively.
DJ Godfather's scratches and Databass's battle tools are done on this turntable, to be recorded at the end of the bar.
Analog drum machine that several producers in Attack's book call the 808/909 of their generation, handy for playing these patterns live.

reperes: Aux 88: Bass Magnetic (1993): the science-fiction vocoder, the fast 808 and the techno stabs, the cosmic pole of the style.
DJ Assault: Ass N Titties (1996): the ghettotech pole, repeated chopped voices, four-on-the-floor kick at high speed.
DJ Godfather: Player Haters in Dis House (1998): the scratches, the mutes every 8 bars and the fast editing.
HiTech: ZOOTED (2023): Detroit's next generation, same 808, same speed, voices treated like percussion.
technobass.rythme: Fast, precise 808. Two families of patterns: the classic electro pattern (kick on 1, the “and” of 2, step 12) for the Aux 88 side, and four-on-the-floor with a kick on every beat for the ghettotech side. In both cases, snare or clap on 2 and 4, closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes with accents on the offbeats, open hat on the “and” of each beat. The kick has a medium decay, 300 ms: enough for weight, not enough to overlap at this speed. Add 808 toms in two-bar patterns, an occasional cowbell, and thirty-second-note snare rolls before the breakdowns, inherited from Miami. A 909 clap on top of the 808 snare adds the techno layer.
technobass.sons: The vocoder comes back to the forefront, with science-fiction lyrics at Aux 88 and obscene lyrics at DJ Assault: in both cases, a chopped voice. Cut your vocal phrases into one-syllable fragments in Simpler in Slice mode and play them rhythmically. Scratches punctuate, but the real Detroit marker is the synth stabs: short minor chords, on a saw, with a 200 ms decay, played on the offbeats as in the local techno. Add a cold Juno- or OB-type pad, lasers, spaceship sound effects. The 808 kit can be doubled with 909 elements (clap, hi-hat) for brightness. Stay dry, no long reverb.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Ask The Pros chapter, favourite bit of kit)
Wikipedia, AUX 88 and DJ Assault articles
technobass.tempo: Detroit speeds up Miami: between 130 and 150 BPM for Aux 88's techno bass, and up to 155 or 160 when it tips into ghettotech with DJ Assault and DJ Godfather. Strict grid, no swing, the 808 quantized to the sixteenth note. The difference from Miami bass lies in the feel: the speed makes the hi-hat almost continuous and the syncopated kicks come closer to a techno pulse. Ghettotech tracks sometimes add a four-on-the-floor kick borrowed from Chicago ghetto house, played at 150 BPM, which completely changes the dance. Start at 138 BPM, the balance point between electro that walks and techno that runs.

technobodymusic.arrangement: Mixable techno structure, 6 to 7 minutes. 32-bar intro with kick, hi-hat and the bass coming in gradually as the filter opens. The voice arrives around 1 minute 30. Alternate 16-bar sections: bass alone with kick, bass plus voice, kickless breakdown where the bass and voice swirl in the reverb, brutal return of the kick. A good method: record an 8-minute jam while manipulating the filter, distortion and mutes live, then edit within that recording. The track must be playable in concert as well as in a DJ set. 32-bar outro of kick and bass.
technobodymusic.basse: This is the signature. SH-101 or MC-202, or their software equivalent (Roland Cloud, TAL-BassLine-101, Analog), saw plus square, sequenced in sixteenth notes with an accent pattern: on the 101, the accent opens the filter and hardens the note. Typical pattern: root on three steps, octave on the fourth, or root, root, minor seventh, root. A slide now and then. Then distortion: a pedal (Pedal in Fuzz mode, 30% gain) or an Overdrive at 12 dB, all filtered at 3 kHz. Moderate sidechain from the kick, 4 dB, so the two coexist. The bass is almost as loud as the kick.
etapes: At 130 BPM, sequence a sixteenth-note bass on an SH-101 emulator with an accent pattern, then run it through Pedal in Fuzz mode.
Build a saturated 909 kick, plus a 100% wet reverb track sidechain-compressed by the kick.
Add a clap on 2 and 4, a sixteenth-note hi-hat and a metallic impact repitched down 15 semitones with hangar reverb.
Record a shouted three-word vocal, Overdrive at 10 dB, 5-second metallic reverb, dotted-eighth delay.
Record an 8-minute jam playing the filter, distortion and mutes, then edit it into a 6 minute 30 structure.
Process the kick in three bands and saturate the drum bus in Analog Clip to finish.
technobodymusic.mix: The kick goes through three-band processing, as the book describes for hard techno: split at 70 Hz and 7 kHz, saturate the mids separately (Saturator, Hard Curve, 10 dB, 45% mix), then recombine. The distorted bass is cut below 45 Hz to leave the kick alone at the bottom, and its energy lives between 80 and 500 Hz. The voice is far back in the reverb but its attack stays up front thanks to 6:1 compression. On the drum bus, a Saturator in Analog Clip with 2 dB of drive acts as a limiter. Master around -8 LUFS, this is club music. The kick's reverb layer is mixed 10 dB below the dry kick.

outils.pourquoi: The signature bass: saw plus square, sixteenth-note sequence with accents that open the filter. TAL-BassLine-101 or Roland Cloud SH-101 in software.
1983 step sequencer with a slight timing drift and a per-step accent, the machine of the Berlin scene's live sets.
Stage drum machine for hard 909 kicks and claps, playable in concert. Failing that, 909 samples in Drum Buss with Drive at 40%.
Analog drum machine with Steiner-Parker distortion on the output, for the dirty kicks and industrial percussion of live sets.
Fuzz mode at 30% gain on the sequenced bass, then a filter at 3 kHz: the distortion inherited from DAF and Nitzer Ebb.
Plate or cistern impulse response, 5 seconds, to drown the shouted voice in metal, with a dotted-eighth delay.
The tube distortion Perc calls essential to his records: three units in his studio, for dirtying basses and the drum bus.
Layered kick synthesis with built-in distortion, the hard techno kick described in the book, to be processed afterward in three bands.

reperes: Phase Fatale: Anubis (2017): the distorted sequenced bass up front, the techno kick, the voice far off in the metal.
Kontravoid: Undone (2019): the more melodic side, with a sequence pattern that serves as a chorus.
Years of Denial: Suicide Disco (2019): the drowned shouted voice, the tempo that holds the dancefloor, the concert format.
Fixmer McCarthy: Freefall (2002): the direct ancestor, Nitzer Ebb meets Terence Fixmer's techno.
technobodymusic.rythme: A big techno kick, with the layered kick technique: a saturated 909, plus a reverb layer on a separate track, 100% wet, 9 seconds of decay, sidechain-compressed by the kick itself so it breathes between hits. Clap on 2 and 4 with a short metallic reverb. Closed hi-hat in sixteenth notes, open on the offbeats. Industrial percussion: a metal impact repitched down 15 semitones with hangar reverb, as the book describes for hard techno. The pattern is simpler than electro-industrial: four-on-the-floor, nothing more, the complexity is in the bass.
technobodymusic.sons: The voice is shouted, then drowned: Overdrive at 10 dB, then a long metallic reverb (Hybrid Reverb with a plate or cistern impulse response, 5 seconds) and a dotted-eighth delay. The lyrics are short, repeated, in German, English or French. Other sounds are rare: a saturated synth stab, a filtered white noise sweep for transitions, a second sequence pattern an octave higher for the choruses. Hard drum machines: TR-8S, Drumbrute, or 909 samples run through Drum Buss with Drive at 40%. The metallic reverb is the shared space of every element except the kick.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Warehouse Techno chapter: reverb layer on the kick; Hard Techno chapter: multiband processing and metallic percussion)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Warehouse Techno, Hard Techno and Ask The Pros: Favourite bit of kit chapters)
Studio Brootle (EBM Bassline Tutorial, Nitzer Ebb / Phase Fatale)
DJ Mag (The unstoppable influence of EBM)
Bandcamp Daily (13 Striking Contemporary EBM Releases)
technobodymusic.tempo: Between 125 and 135 BPM, straight, with techno energy but EBM weight. The feel often comes from hardware sequencers (MC-202, SH-101) that have a slight timing drift and a per-step accent. In Ableton, you can imitate this with a sixteenth-note groove at 8% swing and 10% velocity randomization. What sets the genre apart from EBM: the kick is a techno kick, not an 808, and the track is designed to be mixed. What sets it apart from techno: the sequenced bass takes the place of the lead. Start at 130 BPM.

techstep.arrangement: Techstep drops the emotional breakdown. 32-bar intro: drone, machine noises, an isolated kick that lands in unpredictable places. Drop at bar 33: two-step and Reese at the same time. The section lasts 64 bars and the only variation is the bass, which changes filter or note every 16. The middle breakdown is short, 16 bars, and replaces the bass with a higher drone. Second drop with a second version of the bass, more distorted. 32-bar outro that lets the bass die out over the kick. Over 6 minutes, everything revolves around the gradual transformation of a single sound.
techstep.basse: The heart of the genre: the distorted, resampled Reese. Start with two saws detuned 10 to 20 cents in opposite directions, mono, as described in the Reese chapter of the Attack Magazine book, but then get out of the synth. Record the Reese to audio, run it through an Overdrive (Drive 50%, Tone 40%), a slowly moving low-pass filter, and another distortion. Re-record, filter again, re-record. Each pass adds harmonics and takes away dynamics. The final bass is a long note that vibrates on its own, on the root and the fifth, with a separate sine sub below 60 Hz. Kick and bass don't touch: kick above 80 Hz, sub below.
etapes: Set Ableton to 170 BPM. Program a two-step with a 40 ms kick and a dry snare, with no break behind it.
Create a Reese in Analog or Serum: two saws detuned 15 cents in opposite directions, mono, short glide.
Record it to audio, run it through Overdrive then a moving Auto Filter, and Freeze then Flatten. Repeat twice.
Add a sine sub below 60 Hz that follows the same note, and high-pass the Reese at 100 Hz.
Sample machine noises and a line of science fiction film dialogue, very low in the mix.
Arrange intro 32, drop 64, breakdown 16, drop 64, outro 32, changing the bass filter every 16 bars.
techstep.mix: Techstep sounds dry because nothing has reverb, except the atmospheres. The drums are compressed hard (ratio 10:1, attack 0.3 ms, release 30 ms) and get 30% saturation. The resampled Reese fills the whole midrange, from 100 Hz to 3 kHz, and it is the loudest element of the track after the kick. The sine sub stays mono at -3 dB below the Reese. High-pass everything that isn't bass at 150 Hz. An EQ on the main bus cuts 1 dB at 400 Hz to remove the veil. The master aims for -7 LUFS, light clipping accepted on the kick. Check it all on closed headphones: that is where the genre lives.

outils.pourquoi: The No U-Turn Reese: two saws detuned 15 cents, mono, glide, then recorded to audio and reworked outside the synth.
Serial resampling: the distorted Reese is loaded back into the sampler, refiltered, replayed, three or four passes.
The sequencer of 1997 studios: dry two-step breaks programmed by hand, 40 ms kick, snare with no tail.
Dry kick and snare that replace the break behind the bass, often as samples rather than from the machine.
The modern Reese: detuned saws, filter, then Freeze and Flatten between each step to reproduce the resampling passes.
Two detuned saws, low-pass filter and slow LFO for the starting Reese, before the distortion chain.
Multiband distortion at the end of the chain, after Saturator and Overdrive at 50%, for the Wormhole-style spinning bass.
Low-pass that moves slowly on the audio Reese, between two distortions, then resampling; that is the movement of the genre.

reperes: Ed Rush & Optical: Wormhole (1998): the Reese that turns like an engine, two-step drums without an ounce of fat.
Dom & Roland: Thunder (1998): the isolated kick in the intro, the bass resampled until it becomes noise.
Photek: UFO (1995): the prototype, breaks still complex but the cold atmosphere and the rumbling sub already there.
Konflict: Messiah (2000): the bass spinning on two notes, techstep tipping over into neurofunk.
techstep.rythme: Two layers and no more. A very short kick with no sub, its energy between 80 and 120 Hz: a 909 with the decay at minimum, or a break kick sample cut at 40 ms. A dry, short snare with no reverb, boosted at 200 Hz and 4 kHz, often an isolated Think or Amen sample compressed to the extreme. Minimal hi-hats: every other sixteenth note at constant velocity, or a simple open hat on the offbeats. What replaces the ghost notes is metallic percussion: a pitched rimshot, a pipe hit, placed once per bar. Fills are cuts, not rolls: remove the kick for two beats before a drop.
techstep.sons: The brief cites the Nord Lead and the Akai S3000, the techstep duo. The Nord Lead provides the raw material of the Reese, the S3000 resamples and refilters it: that is the “serial filtering and resampling” of the brief. In Ableton, a chain of Analog into Saturator into Auto Filter into Roar, with Freeze then Flatten between each step, reproduces the process. The atmospheres come from science fiction samples: dialogue from dystopian films, machine noises, metallic drones, played very low in the mix. A single melodic synth, often a held note with a resonant filter, replaces the pads. No piano, no sung vocals, no warm color.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Basslines chapter, Reese bass)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Reese bass wavetable and Broken Beat Techno chapters)
techstep.tempo: Techstep runs at 170 BPM, barely slower than classic DnB, but it sounds colder because everything is square. The two-step is played with no swing, no full break behind it, and sixteenth notes are rare: the beat breathes through its silences. The feel is that of an industrial machine: kick on the 1, snare on 2 and 4, and a kick on the “and” of 3 that hits like a piston. The difference from the parent genre is the absence of warmth: no drummer ghost notes, no shimmering hi-hats. The groove comes from the bass turning in on itself and from the contrast between its movement and the stillness of the drums.

techtrance.arrangement: Six to seven minutes, designed for mixing. 32-bar intro of techno drums, the bass comes in at bar 17. The arpeggio arrives filtered and opens over 32 bars. Only one real break, short, 16 bars, with the kick coming back through a noise roll rather than a silence. No two-minute breakdown. The track is a series of plateaus: each 32-bar block swaps one element for another rather than stacking. Long 32-bar ending with drums alone for the next DJ. Changes happen on bar 1 of each block, clean, with no fade.
techtrance.basse: The bass is on the offbeat as in the rest of the family, but more aggressive: a Virus sawtooth with distortion, cutoff at 500 Hz, medium resonance. It stays on the root, with no chord progression, or alternates with the fifth every 8 bars. Often the bass is doubled by a saturated sixteenth-note line, close to a closed 303, rolling underneath. Tune the kick and the bass to the same note. Hard sidechain, ratio 8:1, release 80 ms. High-pass at 70 Hz and let the distorted kick take the sub.
etapes: Project at 139 BPM, layer a 909 kick and a distorted kick tuned to the root, dry clap on 2 and 4, metallic open hat.
Write a saturated offbeat bass on the root and double it with a closed sixteenth-note line.
Program a 4-note acid arpeggio in sixteenth notes with high resonance and short delay, no supersaw.
Add metallic percussion, short minor stabs and a white noise riser.
Arrange 7 minutes in plateaus: drum intro, clean entries every 32 bars, a single short break, long outro.
Saturate the drum bus in parallel and push the master toward -6 LUFS without losing the kick.
techtrance.mix: Loud and dirty. Kick in the center, around -6 dB peak, with saturation before the compressor. Bass in mono, kick and bass glued by a hard sidechain. Parallel distortion on the drum bus, blended at 30%. The arpeggios are compressed hard, ratio 4:1, to stay up front. Little reverb: short, dry delays, high-passed at 500 Hz. The master bus gets a glue compressor, ratio 2:1, attack 10 ms, then a limiter toward -6 LUFS. Make sure the kick stays clean despite the saturation: it is what has to come through on a techno system. Cut everything else below 120 Hz.

outils.pourquoi: Tense acid arpeggios, FM modulation on the filter, high resonance, dark stabs on the offbeat: the central synth of tech trance.
To design the massive techno-style kick: fast-falling pitch, long body, saturation before the compressor, around -6 dB peak.
Distorted hi-hats and clap, ride in eighth notes. 909 samples processed with a bitcrusher or parallel distortion, rather than the clean machine.
Sawtooth arpeggio, short delay, filtered without wide supersaw. Arturia Jup-8000 V or Sylenth1 for the software version.
Parallel distortion on the drum bus, drive 30%, transients lifted: the dirty side without losing the kick's transient.
Hard sidechain drawn between kick and bass, plus volume shaping on the arpeggios so they stay up front without a compressor.
The DAW of the Dutch tech trance studios of the 2000s, still used by Marco V and Mark Sherry.
On the master, ratio 2:1, attack 10 ms, before the limiter toward -6 LUFS: glues drums and arpeggios without pumping.

reperes: Kai Tracid: Liquid Skies (1999): the tense acid arpeggio over a hard kick, the hinge between acid trance and tech trance
Marco V: Godd (2001): the kick that leads, the short repeated motif and a single break, the tech trance formula at its peak
Yoji Biomehanika: Ding-A-Ling (2000): the Japanese version, faster and dirtier, metallic percussion up front
techtrance.rythme: The kick is techno: a 909 layered with a longer, distorted, saturated kick with a 300 ms tail tuned to the root. The clap is dry and loud on 2 and 4. The offbeat open hat is harder, more metallic, often a saturated 909. Add metallic percussion: a filtered bell tick in sixteenth notes, an offset rimshot, a sheet-metal noise at the end of the bar. The ride is present but compressed. Snare rolls exist but are short, 4 bars, and often replaced by white noise rising in resonance. Think techno: the drums must stand on their own for 32 bars.
techtrance.sons: Little sugar: the arpeggios are acid and tense, Virus or JP-8000 sawtooth with FM modulation on the filter, high resonance, short delay. Short, dark, minor stabs on the offbeat. White noise risers and sirens. No wide supersaw, or else filtered and pushed to the back. The melodic side is limited to a repeated 4-note motif, transposed once per block. The Attack book points out that the arpeggio must stay short and plucky so it doesn't spill over in the mix: here that is vital, because everything is saturated. Tube distortion or a light bitcrusher on the stabs. The effects are impacts and filter sweeps rather than reverbs.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter 39 (arpeggios)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
techtrance.tempo: 136 to 142 BPM, the tempo of trance with the aggression of techno. Straight grid, no swing, and a heavy pulse: the kick leads, not the melody. Count in 16-bar blocks and keep a constant energy plateau: where uplifting rises and falls, tech trance stays high. Marco V and Mark Sherry sit around 138-140. The feel must stay tense, with no breathing room: if a techno DJ can mix it with hard techno, you've got it. Build-ups are short, 8 bars maximum, and comedowns almost nonexistent.

terrorcore.arrangement: Tracks are shorter than gabber, 3 to 5 minutes, and much less structured for the DJ. Brief intro, sometimes a horror sample alone for 8 bars, then the kick arrives all at once, with no build-up. Breaks are rare and short: 4 to 8 bars of vocal sample or drone, then a brutal return. The burst passages (eighth-note kick) last 2 to 4 bars and are placed like exclamation marks. What holds the track together is escalation: each section must be denser than the previous one. Still plan 16 bars of kick alone at the start and the end if you want a DJ to mix it.
terrorcore.basse: As in gabber, the bass is the tail of the kick. But at 220 BPM the tail is too short to carry a note, so terrorcore does it differently: a layer of distorted noise, a very low sawtooth drone, or a second slow kick (once per bar) with a long decay that acts as a drone. In Operator: a square wave on the root, an octave below the kick, held continuously and run through Saturator at 20 dB, with a low-pass at 200 Hz. Sidechain from the kick at ratio 6:1, release 40 ms, so it pumps on every hit. The effect you want is a permanent dull pressure under the kicks, not a bassline.
etapes: Tempo 210 BPM. Take your gabber kick, shorten its decay to 250 ms, and add one more distortion stage (Pedal in Fuzz).
Kick on every beat, plus a 2-bar eighth-note pass at the end of each 16-bar block.
Create a square wave bass drone, an octave below the kick, saturated and sidechained.
Sample three lines or screams from a horror film, pitch them down, Redux at 8 bits, place them at the start of the blocks.
Add a fast alarm-like hoover, two notes in eighth notes, resonant filter.
Arrange as an escalation over 4 minutes, with breaks of 4 bars maximum, and a limiter pushed hard on the master.
terrorcore.mix: The terrorcore mix is saturated from start to finish. The kick takes all the lows and the midrange, at minus 1 dB peak. As the Attack book notes, each stage of distortion brings out peaks, and you have to hunt them down with EQ afterwards: at 220 BPM these peaks quickly pile up into a tiring mush, so cut a narrow band around 2.5 kHz and another around 5 kHz. No fine compression, the distortion does the work. A single limiter on the master, pushed to minus 5 LUFS. The vocal samples come through thanks to a high-pass at 800 Hz, not thanks to volume. Don't aim for cleanliness: Delta 9 or DJ Skinhead sound deliberately filthy.

outils.pourquoi: Source of the kicks, sampled then distorted until the rhythm becomes a continuous assault beyond 200 BPM. Today a 909 sample is enough.
The hoover sped up and pitched up, played in bursts of sixteenth notes to add panic above the kick.
With ProTracker or OctaMED, the 8-bit tracker behind the hardest and dirtiest productions of the 1990s. The lo-fi grain comes from there.
The sequencer of the New York and German branch: MIDI control of the sampler and the 909, arrangement in 16-bar blocks.
Bitcrush at 8 or 12 bits on the kick and on the horror samples to recover the crunch of period trackers.
Fuzz mode on the kick after Saturator: the guitar distortion adds the aggressive midrange that the 909 kick doesn't have on its own.
Sawtooth sirens and stabs with a pitch envelope, played in a fast loop to hold the tension between two kick salvos.

reperes: Delta 9: Real Hardcore (1994): New York speed and the kick that no longer has time to finish.
DJ Skinhead: Extreme Terror (1995): the vocal sample as a threat, the kick bursts, the absence of any comfortable break.
Nasenbluten: Intellectual Killer (1995): the Australian version, on a tracker, with 8-bit samples and black humor.
Disciples of Annihilation: New York City Speedcore (1996): the hinge toward speedcore, the burst becomes the rule.
terrorcore.rythme: The kick is the gabber kick, but with a shorter decay so it holds at 220 BPM, and an even more total distortion: more midrange, more fizz, almost white noise on every hit. Kick on every beat, then on every eighth note during the “burst” passages. Snare on 2 and 4, often replaced by a second kick pitched higher. Rolls become longer and faster: thirty-second notes over 4 bars. Add kicks on isolated offbeats to break the regularity, like a punch that lands early. The hi-hats almost disappear: the top of the spectrum is filled by the distortion of the kick itself.
terrorcore.sons: Terrorcore borrows its samples from horror films: screams, laughter, killers' lines, slasher dialogue, all pitched down a fifth and distorted. The hoover is there but played faster and higher, like an alarm. Minor sawtooth pads with lots of filter resonance, heavily saturated. Industrial noises: sheet metal, machines, feedback. Producers of the time worked on Amiga trackers and Cubase, so the samples are short, 8-bit, with aliasing: reproduce it with Redux at 8 bits and a sample rate divided by 4. No melody, only two- or three-note motifs on a loop.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
terrorcore.tempo: Terrorcore starts where gabber stops: 190 to 250 BPM, often around 200-220 in the New York productions of Industrial Strength. At these speeds a beat lasts less than 300 ms and the kick no longer has time to finish before the next one, which creates that continuous pressure with no breathing room. No swing, no nuance, but one new thing compared to gabber: double-time passages where the kick switches to eighth notes, which gives the impression of 400 BPM. Program at 210 BPM, sixteenth-note grid, and use the eighth-note kick passage as the final weapon. The bar becomes very short, so think in blocks of 32.

trance.arrangement: An early trance track lasts 7 to 9 minutes. 32-bar intro with kick and hi-hat for the DJ, then the bass comes in at bar 33 and the filtered arpeggio at 49. Each 16-bar block adds a layer or opens a filter. A first breakdown around bar 97: the kick disappears, the pad and the arpeggio stay, the chord changes once. Return with all elements for 32 bars, a second shorter break, a last plateau, then gradual withdrawal mirroring the intro. No chorus in the pop sense: the build-up is the chorus. Automate the cutoff over 32 bars rather than over 4.
trance.basse: The trance bass sits on the offbeat: a short note on every off eighth, in the gap between two kicks. That is the sway of the genre. A sawtooth or a square with cutoff around 300 Hz, low resonance, short decay envelope, 150 to 200 ms. Stay on the root for 8 bars, then move to the sixth or the fourth to open the chord. The kick keeps the bottom of the spectrum below 80 Hz, the bass lives between 80 and 250 Hz: high-pass it at 60 Hz. A second layer of light sixteenth notes, filtered higher, gives the speed. Gentle sidechain from the kick, ratio 4:1, release 100 ms.
etapes: Set the project to 134 BPM and place a 909 kick on every beat, a clap on 2 and 4, an open hat on the offbeats for 8 bars.
Write the offbeat bass on the root (A minor, for example), a short eighth note between each kick, decay 150 ms.
Program an A minor chord across three octaves, run it through the arpeggiator in sixteenth notes, up mode, two octaves, then convert to MIDI and move two notes per bar to break the regularity.
Add a detuned pad with a 1.5-second attack holding the chord, and a 3/16 delay on the arpeggio.
Stretch everything over 8 minutes: 32-bar intro, entries every 16 bars, a break without kick at bar 97, a return, a withdrawal.
Automate the arpeggio cutoff over the whole length, from low to high, and listen to the whole track before touching the mix.
trance.mix: The early trance mix is drier than that of the 2000s. 909 kick on top, around -8 dB peak, everything else below it. Bass in mono, cut at 60 Hz. The arpeggio is narrow in the center, its delays wide on the sides. The pad takes the full width but cut it at 200 Hz so it doesn't mask anything. Light drum bus compression, ratio 2:1, attack 30 ms. Gentle tube saturation on the 303 for warmth. A limiter on the master to get to around -9 LUFS, but let it breathe: the MFS and Eye Q records weren't squashed. A single reverb on a return, predelay 20 ms, decay 3 seconds.

outils.pourquoi: The synth of the supersaw and of trance arpeggios: seven detuned sawtooths, filter opened slowly. Today its Arturia Jup-8000 V emulation does the same job.
Long, round kick on every beat, clap and ride in eighth notes. Roland Cloud TR-909 or D16 Drumazon replace the machine, or 909 samples in a Drum Rack.
Softened, low cutoff and moderate resonance, it serves as a second melodic line behind the arpeggio. AudioRealism ABL3 or D16 Phoscyon 2 in software.
Enough for a trance arpeggio: sawtooth, instant attack, short release, cutoff automated over 16 bars, in sixteenth notes via Live's MIDI Arpeggiator.
Juno-60 emulation: wide two-oscillator pads with the Juno chorus, attack of 1 to 2 seconds, the warm layer under the arpeggio.
The historic Juno of the Frankfurt studios for analog pads and arpeggios. Roland Cloud Juno-106 or TAL-U-NO-LX give the same chorus.
Delay synced to the dotted eighth and the quarter note, feedback 30 to 40%, high-pass on the returns: it's what makes the arpeggio spin in space.
A single long reverb on a return, decay 3 seconds, predelay 20 ms, reserved for the pads. Inexpensive and present in almost every trance session.

reperes: Age of Love: The Age of Love (1990): the sixteenth-note arpeggio and the pad that opens at the break, the whole vocabulary of the genre is already there
Zyon: No Fate (1992): the offbeat bass and the build-up in 16-bar steps, never a chorus
Delerium: Silence (Tiesto Remix) (2000): what the formula became ten years later, with a two-minute breakdown and a vocal
trance.rythme: The kick comes from the TR-909, long and round, on every beat. The 909 snare lands on beats 2 and 4, often doubled by a 909 clap offset by a few milliseconds. The closed hat plays offbeat eighth notes, the open hat marks the “and” of each beat with a decay of 200 to 300 ms. Add a 909 ride in continuous eighth notes from the first drop: that is what gives the rave feel. Little extra percussion, a rimshot or a tom at the end of each 8-bar block. Fills are snare rolls in sixteenth notes on the last bar, then in thirty-second notes to announce the build-up. Keep it simple: everything that really moves happens in the synths.
trance.sons: Three families of sounds. First the arpeggio, in sixteenth notes, on a minor chord of three or four notes, played by a sawtooth synth with instant attack and short release. The JP-8000 is the reference, Operator or a virtual Juno will do the job. Then the pad, wide, two detuned oscillators, attack of 1 to 2 seconds, chorus. Finally the softened TB-303: low cutoff, moderate resonance, light saturation, it serves as a second melodic line rather than an acid scream. Over all that, delays synced to the dotted eighth and the quarter note, feedback 30 to 40%, high-pass filter on the returns. The long reverb is reserved for the pads.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, chapter 39 (arpeggios)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production
trance.tempo: Early trance runs between 130 and 138 BPM, with no swing: the grid is straight, sixteenth notes quantized at 100%. The feel comes from accumulation, not from groove. Count in blocks of 8 and 16 bars and think of each section as a step. Age of Love sits around 130, Zyon a little faster. Pick a tempo and don't move: hypnotic repetition demands a fixed pulse. The offbeat eighth notes of the bass give the sway, the sixteenth notes of the arpeggio give the perceived speed. If your track seems to drag, it isn't the tempo you need to raise, it's the arpeggio you need to open with the filter.

trapedm.arrangement: Festival format of 3 to 4 minutes. 16-bar intro with strings or a vocal. 16-bar build-up: snare roll, riser, filtered horn that opens, one beat of silence. 32-bar drop in halfstep: 808, snare on 3, horn as the hook. Calmer 16-bar verse, with triplet hats. Second build-up, second drop with a growl or a key change. End on a sub drop. The drop hook is a repeated 2-bar phrase, often a three-note horn. Harlem Shake is a model of structure: the drop arrives fast and the track doesn't bother with nuance.
trapedm.basse: The 808 is the bass. An 808 sample or a sine in Serum with a decay of 1 to 2 seconds, a short pitch envelope for the click, and saturation for the harmonics. Tune it to the key of the track. Write the notes on the kick positions, with long notes that slide from one note to the next with a 100 ms glide. A two- or three-note line in minor, with octaves. Sometimes an 808 doubled by a clean sine sub. The drop is often carried by a growl or a horn rather than a bass melody, the 808 stays as the foundation.
etapes: Set Ableton to 145 BPM, 808 kick on 1 and on syncopations, layered snare on 3, hats in eighth notes.
Add hat rolls in triplets and thirty-second notes at the ends of phrases.
Tune an 808 to the key, 1.5 s decay, 100 ms glide, notes on the kick positions.
Create a huge horn in Serum, saturated, as a 2-bar hook, plus a vocal shout on 3.
Arrange: intro 16, build-up 16 with snare roll, drop 32, verse 16, second drop.
Mix the 808 loud and mono, snare up front, brass sidechained, master around -5 LUFS.
trapedm.mix: 808 loud and mono, around -5 dB peak, cut below 30 Hz, saturated to come through on phones. Kick with a click around 4 kHz layered over the 808, or the 808 is the kick. Snare and clap around -4 dB peak, with the mids pushed at 1 kHz. Hats cut below 500 Hz and bright. Brass in stereo, cut below 200 Hz, sidechained by the kick and the snare. OTT on the brass and the growls. Limiter with 5 to 6 dB of reduction, target between -5 and -6 LUFS. Make sure the 808 and the kick don't cancel each other out in phase, shift one of them if needed.

outils.pourquoi: Long tuned kick, clap, triplet hats and cowbell: Ableton's Drum Machines kit or 808 samples stand in for it.
The historic trap tool: thirty-second-note hat rolls in the piano roll, 808 patterns every 2 bars.
Sine with a 1 to 2 s decay, pitch envelope for the click and saturation for the 808; brass and growls for the drop.
Tuned 808 in three layers, sub, synth and sample, with a 100 ms glide between notes.
Baauer's DAW for Harlem Shake: 30-second loops, manipulated audio clips, a drop that arrives fast.
Huge brass and a horn hit as a 2-bar hook, saturated and sidechained by the kick and the snare.
Sidechain drawn on the 808 and the brass, short release, for clean pumping without a compressor.
On the brass and the growls to squeeze them and make them present in a mix that aims for -5 LUFS.

reperes: Baauer: Harlem Shake (2012): the direct structure, the horn hook and the drop that arrives right away.
TNGHT: Higher Ground (2012): pitched horns and 808s, where Glasgow meets Atlanta.
RL Grime: Core (2014): festival trap fully realized, long build-up and massive drop.
Hudson Mohawke: Thunder Bay (2011): the link with wonky, brass and broken rhythm.
trapedm.rythme: 808 kick on 1, then on the “a” of 2 and the “and” of 4, with a pattern that varies every 2 bars. Snare or clap on 3, layered: 808 clap, acoustic snare, a rimshot, short reverb at 0.7 s. 808 hats in eighth notes, with rolls in sixteenth notes, sixteenth-note triplets and thirty-second notes at the ends of phrases, varying the velocity. Open hat on the “and” of 2. In the build-up, an 8 to 16-bar snare roll and a riser. On the drop, the drums can drop out for a beat to leave a horn alone. FL Studio is the historic tool, Ableton does just as well.
trapedm.sons: Huge synthetic brass, a rising horn “hit”, in Massive or Serum, saturated and sidechained. Festival supersaw lead for the build-up. Sampled vocal shouts, a “hey” on 3, a rap phrase pitched down. Sirens, foghorn, sub drop before the drop, white noise riser. A Serum growl in call and response in the drop. Full 808 kit: kick, snare, clap, hats, cowbell. Cinematic strings in the intro. Everything is big, thick, and aimed at the stadium. Contrast between melodic intro and brutal drop, as in brostep.
sourcesOutils: Output, 9 Best Plugins for Trap Beats
MusicTech, Creating Planet's Mad, Baauer's frantic in-the-box brainchild
Ableton Blog, Making Harlem Shake in Live
trapedm.tempo: Between 140 and 150 BPM in halfstep, which gives a feel of 70 to 75 BPM, or counted directly at 70 or 75 in some projects. The snare lands on 3, the kick on 1 and on syncopations. The feel comes from Atlanta trap: heavy, slow, with hats that speed up in triplets and rolls. No swing on the grid, but the triplet hats create the bounce. What changes compared to UK bass: the grammar of Southern rap, the 808 as the central instrument, and festival build-ups with a drop. What changes compared to future bass: the hardness, the brass, no softness at all.

tribalhouse.arrangement: An accumulation. 32-bar intro with kick and a single percussion, then a new layer every 8 or 16 bars: congas, toms, timbales, shaker, bell. Around bar 96, all the layers are running. 32-bar break: kick cut, the percussion continues, a high-pass filter rises, a tribal voice appears, a timbale roll, then the kick returns alone, then everything. Second plateau with a pad or a stab added, outro that removes the layers one by one over 32 bars. Length 8 to 10 minutes. The tension comes from density: the track is stronger at the end than at the start because there are more drums, not because the volume rises.
tribalhouse.basse: Minimal: a held note or a two-note motif in eighth notes, often a sine sub or a heavily filtered sawtooth (200 Hz), which gives the root and nothing else. On many tracks the bass is a low-tuned tom or a long 808 kick acting as bass. Light sidechain with the kick. No melodic line: the percussion takes up all the rhythmic space, and an active bass would muddy it. A note change every 16 or 32 bars is enough to mark the sections. When you want more, use a percussive bass with short notes on beats 2 and 4, like a low conga, rather than a line.
etapes: Project at 127 BPM, dry 909 kick four-on-the-floor, a 909 tom in a 2-bar syncopated pattern in place of the clap.
Add a tumbao conga loop, sixteenth-note bongos and a timbale for accents, each humanized by plus or minus 10 ms.
Minimal bass: a sine sub held on the root, note change every 32 bars.
Layer a shaker, a bell in 3 against 4 and a sampled tribal voice with delay.
Build 9 minutes by accumulation, a layer every 8 or 16 bars, with a 32-bar break without kick where the percussion stays.
Mix by separating each percussion in stereo and in frequency, shared room reverb, kick alone below 100 Hz.
tribalhouse.mix: A mix that separates the percussion in space. Each layer has its stereo place: congas left, bongos right, timbales in the center slightly forward, shaker wide. Filter each percussion so it occupies one band: congas 150 to 500 Hz, bongos 500 Hz to 2 kHz, shaker above 4 kHz. The kick in the center, alone below 100 Hz with the sub. Bus compression on the percussion group (4:1, attack 10 ms) to glue them, and a little saturation. A shared short room reverb on all the percussion for space. Preserved transients: no limiter that's too hard, the percussion must snap. Check that the layers don't mask each other in mono.

outils.pourquoi: Played or sampled in 2- or 4-bar loops, tumbao and accents: the style is made of layered hand instruments.
The dry four-on-the-floor kick and above all the toms tuned to different pitches that replace the clap in a syncopated pattern.
The sampler of Danny Tenaglia's and Junior Vasquez's New York studios for stacking percussion loops and tribal shouts.
Drum machine with its Latin percussion cards, common in 1990s house productions for programmed congas and bongos.
Libraries of congas, bongos, toms and shakers designed for tribal; one loop per layer, each filtered into its own frequency band.
To organize dozens of percussion hits, tune them and humanize them by plus or minus 10 ms, like an expanded Drum Rack.
A single shared short reverb (Valhalla Room or Ableton's Reverb) on all the percussion to place them in the same space.

reperes: Danny Tenaglia: Elements (1998): layers of percussion piling up over 10 minutes, the bass almost absent and tension through density.
Danny Tenaglia: Music Is The Answer (1998): the same percussive architecture under a vocal, the track that defined the Twilo sound.
Junior Vasquez: Get Your Hands Off My Man (1994): the harder, vocal side of New York tribal, 909 toms and chanted vocal.
Danny Tenaglia: The Space Dance (2023): the tribal formula intact twenty-five years later, with a modern mix.
tribalhouse.rythme: The 909 kick four-on-the-floor, dry and loud. Little or no clap: the backbeat role is held by a tom or a timbale. The 909 toms in a 2-bar syncopated pattern, tuned to different pitches. On top, congas sampled or played as a 2- or 4-bar loop (tumbao, with the slap on the “and” of 2 and the open tones on 4), bongos in sixteenth notes, timbales for accents, a continuous shaker, a bell. Each layer is a short motif that cycles, and the layers overlap in 3 against 4 or 6 against 8. Fills are timbale or tom rolls. On the break, the kick stops and the percussion carries on alone, that is the high point of the track.
tribalhouse.sons: The percussion is the sound: congas, timbales, bongos, djembes, shakers, bells, sampled or played (Latin percussion libraries or the Drum Rack kits). Tuned 909 toms. Sampled tribal voices, shouts, chants, breaths, often pitched and run through a delay. A dark pad on a held minor chord, far in the background, or a drone. Rare, dark synth stabs. Signature effects: eighth-note delay on the percussion, short room reverb on the congas to place them in a space, a rising high-pass filter on the breaks, slow phaser on the shaker. Harmony is almost absent, what remains is atmosphere and tension.
sourcesOutils: Gearspace, Tips late 90s early 00s tribal house percussion
Recording Arts Canada, Evolution of Tribal House
tribalhouse.tempo: Between 125 and 130 BPM, a little faster than classic house, so the percussion can run. The feel is that of a drum circle sitting on a straight kick: the kick stays at 50% swing, but each percussion layer has its own placement, some slightly ahead, others a few milliseconds behind, and it is this friction that creates the groove. Use loops played by hand when you can, or humanize the timing by plus or minus 10 ms. The track is long, 8 to 10 minutes, and the tension builds through the accumulation of layers, not through a synth build-up. Think in 4-bar cycles for the polyrhythms.

triphop.arrangement: Trip-hop is a song as much as a track: 4 to 6 minutes, verse, chorus, bridge, but all slowed down. The beat often only appears after 8 bars of atmosphere, a lone sample, an a cappella vocal or a scratch. The chorus isn't louder: it's denser, with the strings and the bass dropping an octave. The bridge, around two thirds of the way in, cuts the beat and leaves the vocal with the Rhodes and the reverb. End with a fade on the break alone with the crackling vinyl. Changes are slow, every 16 bars, and the melancholy comes from repetition: a minor chord that keeps returning without ever resolving.
triphop.basse: The bass is dub, bigger and darker than in downtempo: it goes below 50 Hz and takes up almost all the low end. Electric bass played with the thumb or a sine wave synth with tube saturation, low-pass filter at 200 Hz, long release of 500 ms to 1 s. It plays held notes, half notes and whole notes, often on the root and minor seventh, with a silence on the 1 of every other bar, which lets the sound system breathe. It sometimes lands on the beat where the kick isn't, as in dub. No sidechain: the kick and the bass overlap and that mass is what you are after. Compress hard, ratio 4:1, so the level doesn't move.
etapes: Find a funk drum break and slow it down by 20% without time-stretching, then run it through Redux at 12 bits to veil it.
Lay down a saturated sine bass in held notes, root and minor seventh, with a silence on the 1 of every other bar.
Add a cinematic sample, strings or organ, cut into 2 bars and pitched down.
Record or sample a softly sung female vocal, and send it to a 3-second plate with 40 ms predelay.
Write the structure like a slow song: atmospheric intro, verse, denser chorus, bridge without beat.
Mix dark: cut everything at 150 Hz except kick and bass, compress the break hard, keep the master at minus 12 LUFS.
triphop.mix: The mix is dark, heavy in the low mids, with the top of the spectrum veiled. The break goes through tape saturation or a light bitcrusher, and the drum bus is compressed heavily, ratio 4:1, attack 10 ms, so the snare breathes in the reverb. The bass and the kick take all the space below 150 Hz, everything else is cut at 150 or 200 Hz. The vocal is up front, with gentle compression and a de-esser, but its reverb is very long and arrives a little late, predelay 40 ms. The master stays dynamic, minus 12 LUFS, and a bit of background noise is welcome: silence that's too clean breaks the illusion. Check on headphones: that is where the genre is heard.

outils.pourquoi: The sampler given to Geoff Barrow by Massive Attack: a break slowed down inside it loses top end and gains grain. Ableton Redux imitates this veil.
Funk breaks slowed down by 15 to 30% played on the pads, in 12 bits, with the dragging swing. An MPC One does the same job.
Turntable for digging samples and scratching cut phrases. Portishead pressed their own parts onto vinyl to scratch them afterwards.
Bitcrusher set to 12 bits and 26 kHz on the break to recover the definition of a 1990 sampler without buying one.
Free: crackle, dust and wow on the cinematic sample. Ableton Vinyl Distortion plays the same role with a groove noise.
Colder than in downtempo, with a slow phaser, in held chords under the vocal. Keyscape or Lounge Lizard in software.
3 to 4-second plate with 40 ms predelay on the female vocal, which makes it float behind the beat.
The period sequencer that drove the S1000 over MIDI, with recording on Alesis ADAT. Ableton or Logic today, with the same samples.

reperes: Massive Attack: Unfinished Sympathy (1991): the soul vocal and real strings over a slowed-down break, the model of the trip-hop song.
Portishead: Glory Box (1994): the slowed-down Isaac Hayes sample, the tremolo guitar and the broken voice in the reverb.
Tricky: Aftermath (1994): the dragging bass, the almost absent beat and the vocal murmured right up against the mic.
Sneaker Pimps: 6 Underground (1996): the John Barry sample, the dry break and the pop structure at a tempo of 80.
triphop.rythme: The slowed-down drum break is the center. Take a funk or soul break, slow it down by 15 to 30% without clean time-stretching: the pitch drops, the sound darkens, that's intended. A 12-bit sampler like the Akai S1000 did this on its own; today Redux or a bitcrusher at 12 bits and 26 kHz do the same. Filter the break at 8 kHz. Lay a heavy kick on top and a dry snare with lots of plate reverb, cracking on 3 only. Few programmed hi-hats: those of the break are enough. Add atmospheric scratches, not rhythmic ones: a rubbing record, a cut phrase. Percussion is rare and spaced out, a conga or a reversed cymbal every 4 bars.
triphop.sons: The Rhodes is there, but colder, with a slow phaser. What sets trip-hop apart is the female soul vocal, fragile, sung close to the mic, drowned in a 3 to 4-second plate and a quarter-note delay. The samples are cinematic: spy film strings, organ, theremin, a slowed-down John Barry theme. Portishead pushed the gesture as far as pressing parts onto vinyl to scratch them afterwards: you can imitate this with Vinyl Distortion and a looped groove noise. Western-style tremolo guitar, melodica, a veiled piano. Everything goes through a high-pass at 100 Hz and a low-pass at 10 kHz to leave the low end to the bass and the top end to the noise.
sourcesOutils: MusicRadar (Unpacking the dark, sample-based sound of trip-hop)
triphop.tempo: Go down further: 65 to 90 BPM, with the feel of slowed-down hip-hop. What changes compared to downtempo is the heaviness: trip-hop doesn't swing to please, it drags. Keep a moderate swing, 55 to 58%, but play with lateness: shift the snare 15 to 25 ms after the beat, so it seems to fall like something heavy. The kick stays on the grid. Many tracks are written in half-time at a tempo of 140 to 170, which is the same thing as 70 to 85 with the snare on 3. A good trick: program at 90 BPM, then slow down to 82 without warping the samples, so the breaks get veiled.

twilightpsy.arrangement: Twilight keeps the track structure of full-on with the weight of darkpsy. 32-bar intro: kick, bass, hi-hats, one metallic percussion. First 32-bar section with an acid lead answering the bass. First short break around bar 80, 8 to 16 bars, with a dark pad and a vocal, then a brutal 4-bar build-up and a heavy drop. The track runs through two or three cycles of this kind, each drop introducing a more aggressive lead. The last drop is the hardest, with the bass in saturated eighth notes. 32-bar outro. Aim for 7 minutes. Keep the kick and bass steady over the first and last 32 bars for mixing.
twilightpsy.basse: The hardened full-on bass: the pattern stays kick then three sixteenth notes, but each note is more distorted and shorter (60 ms). In Serum or Absynth, a sawtooth with a low-pass filter at 300 Hz, a fast filter envelope, then a frank distortion in the low mids (250 to 600 Hz) that gives the nasty side. Add pattern variations every 4 beats: a triplet bass note, an octave jump, a descending glissando. Root in F# or G. The sub stays clean, a separate sine. In the last 4 bars before a drop, the bass can switch to heavy eighth notes with stronger distortion, to announce the hit.
etapes: Project at 148 BPM. Punchy kick tuned to G around 55 Hz, 130 ms body, layered with a metallic click, compressed at 8:1.
Hardened rolling bass on G1: kick then three 60 ms sixteenth notes, sawtooth filtered at 300 Hz, distortion in the low mids, separate sub.
Add a heavy layered snare on 2 and 4, sheet-metal percussion in sixteenth notes and a saturated open hat.
Create an acid lead in Serum: square, resonant filter, overdrive, 2-bar phrases in G Phrygian in sixteenth notes.
Build metallic FX (impacts with reversed reverb, rising FM screams) and a dark pad in Absynth for the breaks.
Arrange 7 minutes in cycles of section, short break, brutal build-up, drop, with the last drop on saturated eighth-note bass.
twilightpsy.mix: The twilight mix is dense and aggressive, but organized. Kick and bass on a compressed and saturated bus, mono below 150 Hz. The acid lead takes the mids, 500 Hz to 4 kHz, and the bass is carved out in that zone by a dynamic EQ when the lead plays. The metallic FX are bright and wide, out on the sides, with a high-pass at 400 Hz. Parallel compression on the drums, ratio 6:1, blended at 30%. Limiter pushed hard on the master, aim for -6 to -7 LUFS, with a clipper before it to hold the kick transients. Listen in mono to check that the bass distortion doesn't create a fixed bump around 400 Hz. The result must be powerful on a festival system in the early morning.

outils.pourquoi: The hardened full-on bass: sawtooth, low-pass at 300 Hz, frank distortion between 250 and 600 Hz, 60 ms notes.
Dark break pads and FM screams with rising pitch; the metallic FX inherited from darkpsy go through its comb filters.
