The DAW of the Cape Town scene: Corpus for the sheet-metal sounds, Saturator on the kick-bass bus, Beat Repeat for the brutal rolls.
Aggressive acid leads in the TB-303 style but harder: accents, slides, high resonance, then an overdrive behind.
The punchy 130 ms kick tuned around 55 Hz, pronounced click, layered with a metallic click sample.
Master limiter toward -6 or -7 LUFS, with a clipper before it to hold the kick transients on a festival system.
Dynamic EQ that carves out the bass between 500 Hz and 4 kHz when the acid lead plays.

reperes: Rinkadink: Rabbit From Darkside (2004): the hardened bass and answering acid leads, the Cape Town sound at its peak.
Broken Toy: One Toy Soldier (2005): late-night humor and short breaks that relaunch brutally.
Xerox and Illumination: Gravity (2005): the metallic FX and the punchy kick, on the border of darkpsy.
twilightpsy.rythme: The punchy kick of the brief: longer than the darkpsy kick (130 ms of body), tuned around 55 Hz, with a pronounced click and heavy compression, ratio 8:1. Layer a synthetic kick and a metallic click sample. Heavy snare on 2 and 4, layered with a clap and a touch of distortion, short reverb. The hi-hats play the offbeats, with a saturated open hat on the “and” of 2 and 4. The percussion is metallic: samples of sheet metal, springs, pipes, played in sixteenth notes with varied velocities. Snare rolls before the drops are short and brutal, 4 bars, with rising pitch. Add reversed crashes on the restarts.
twilightpsy.sons: Absynth, Serum, Ableton. Aggressive acid leads: a sawtooth or a square wave into a resonant low-pass filter, high resonance, a filter envelope that opens hard, with accents and glides like a TB-303 but harder, saturated by an overdrive. Play them in sixteenth notes on a Phrygian scale, with 2-bar phrases that answer the bass. The metallic FX: sheet metal sounds processed through a comb filter and a short delay, metal impacts with reversed reverb, FM “screams” with rising pitch. Absynth produces dark pads for the breaks. The sampled vocals are late-night dialogue, ironic or menacing. It all has to sound hard but precise.
sourcesOutils: Psymedia, 30 influential South African psytrance albums
twilightpsy.tempo: Twilight is played between 145 and 150 BPM, straddling full-on and darkpsy. The grid is straight, with no swing. What sets it apart from full-on is weight: the bass gallops less and hits harder, often in straight sixteenth notes with heavy accents, and the leads aren't looking for the heroic melody but for aggression. What sets it apart from darkpsy is readability: there are drops, breaks and a track energy, not a drift. Count in 16 and 32 bars. Tracks last 7 to 8 minutes and are built for festival dawn, when the crowd is tired but still wants to pound.

ukbass.arrangement: A 6 to 7-minute DJ tool, a single idea that evolves. Long intro of 32 to 48 bars that sets up the groove element by element. The sub arrives late, bar 32 or 48, without warning. No drop, switches instead: one element replaces another every 16 bars. A 16-bar break in the middle that keeps the sub and one percussion. The second half introduces a new sound, often the chopped vocal. 32-bar outro. The track must work mixed for 2 minutes with another track: the changes are frequent enough to hold up on their own, discreet enough to be mixed.
ukbass.basse: A dominant sine sub, played in long notes or syncopated eighth notes, sometimes with a very slow LFO on the volume or cutoff, one cycle per 2 bars. The bass acts as melody: two or three notes in minor, with silences. With Blawan or Untold, the bass becomes raw, an FM synth or a saturated square wave. Another approach, from the Attack Magazine book: start from a bass sample, transpose it in Complex Pro, then run it through an EQ, a Vinyl Distortion and an amp at a low mix to give it grain. Discreet sidechain. The kick and the sub answer each other rather than doubling each other.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM, choose garage swing on a house grid or a halfstep, lay down a syncopated kick.
Program ten dry, short percussion sounds, never all together, with widely varied velocities.
Create a dominant sine sub on two or three notes, with a slow LFO on the cutoff, one cycle per 2 bars.
Add a sound you built yourself: FM, resampling or a chopped and pitched vocal.
Arrange in switches every 16 bars, intro of 32 to 48, no drop, outro of 32.
Mix dry, mono sub, intact transients, a single reverb send, master around -9 LUFS.
ukbass.mix: Space and dynamics. Mono sub below 100 Hz, clean, around -6 dB peak. Kick lighter than the sub. Percussion cut below 200 Hz, with intact transients: slow-attack compression, 30 ms, or no compression. No visible sidechain. A little tape saturation on the drum bus. Reverb on a single send, used on one or two elements. Master around -9 LUFS, with a Glue Compressor at 2 dB of reduction and a transparent limiter. The mix must sound dry in a club, with the lows coming up from the floor and the rest staying precise and readable.

outils.pourquoi: Editing and the book's chain: bass sample in Complex Pro, EQ Eight, Vinyl Distortion, Amp at 20% mix, Hybrid Reverb.
FM synthesis for raw basses and sounds that exist nowhere else, then looped resampling.
Dominant sine sub with a very slow LFO on the cutoff, one cycle per 2 bars, two or three notes in minor.
The groove: ten dry percussion sounds played on the pads, never all together, with widely varied velocities.
Joy Orbison's mono synth: aggressive filters for synthetic percussion and scratchy basses.
Used by Blawan, with a modular system: FM or saturated square basses, sequenced from a Beatstep Pro.
The book's grain on a sampled bass: Tracing Model at 10 kHz, Pinch Soft, drive at 1, before the Bass amp.
Pitched toms, rimshots and dull claps as dry percussion, without reverb. Samples or Ableton's Drum Machines.

reperes: Joy Orbison: Hyph Mngo (2009): garage swing on a house grid, the chopped vocal, the sub that rises late.
Untold: Kingdom (2008): dry, syncopated percussion, raw bass as melody.
Ramadanman: Blimey (2008): halfstep tipping toward house, rhythmic minimalism.
Mosca: Bax (2011): the return of vocal garage in a UK bass frame, syncopated kick and hook.
ukbass.rythme: Dry, short percussion with no reverb: rimshots, wood blocks, dull claps, pitched 808 toms, a house kick or a saturated 909 kick. The kick is often syncopated rather than four-on-the-floor: on 1, the “a” of 2, the 3, then a gap. Snare or clap on 2 and 4 with swing, or a single one on 3. Hats are rare, replaced by percussion in syncopated sixteenth notes with widely varied velocities. One percussive element plays a polyrhythmic pattern of 3 sixteenth notes over a grid of 4. The patterns are detailed but stripped back: ten sounds, never all together, in Ableton or on an MPC.
ukbass.sons: Experimental club sound design: FM in Operator, looped resampling, recorded percussion, a vocal cut into syllables and pitched as in Joy Orbison. Massive for the basses, MPC for the groove, Ableton for editing. Short synth stabs, a distant piano chord, an unrecognizable jazz sample. A grainy texture in the background, a breath. A three-note melodic motif played by a noisy sound. The watchword: each track has a sound that exists nowhere else. Short delay on the percussion, reverb on a single element, not everywhere. No supersaw, no growl.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter (sampled bass, EQ, Vinyl Distortion, amp)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter
Telekom Electronic Beats, Blawan On Impatience, Anxiety And How He Makes No-Frills Techno
Clash Magazine, 9 NextGen UK Bass Producers With Incredible Sound Design
ukbass.tempo: UK bass doesn't have a tempo but a range: from 125 to 135 BPM, 130 being the most common. Often a house grid at 128 with garage swing, 56 to 60%, or a halfstep at 130 with the snare on 3. The feel is dry, precise, syncopated, with silences that count as much as the hits. What changes compared to the dubstep it comes from: the tempo comes back down, 4/4 returns without being mandatory, and rigor replaces the wobble. Each track picks its own compromise between house, garage, techno and grime. The only common denominator: the English sub bass and the refusal of formula.

ukfunky.arrangement: 5 to 6-minute track. 32-bar percussive intro: the percussion patterns come in one by one, then the kick. The bass arrives at 32, the vocal at 48 or 64. 16-bar blocks. A 16-bar break where the drums stop and the vocal stays over a pad or a stab, then the percussion comes back alone for 8 bars before the kick. No brutal drop: elements coming in and out make the arrangement. 32-bar percussion outro for the DJ. The vocal hooks come back every 32 bars. Write an instrumental version for mixing.
ukfunky.basse: A round, short bass, somewhere between the sub and a house bass. In Massive or Logic's ES2: sine or triangle with a little saturation, attack 0, decay 200 ms, short release. Write a funky line in syncopated sixteenth notes, in minor pentatonic, that follows the kick on some hits and contradicts it on others. The 3+3+2 pattern works well: three notes landing on 1, the “a” of 1, the “and” of 2. The bass plays with the percussion like a bassist with a percussionist. No wobble, no Reese: it's a dance bass, not a subwoofer bass.
etapes: Set Logic or Ableton to 130 BPM, lay down a syncopated kick and a clap on 2 and 4.
Stack three percussion patterns in sixteenth notes: congas, cowbell, shaker, each with its own syncopation.
Write a round bass in minor pentatonic, in syncopated sixteenth notes, 3+3+2 pattern.
Add a 4-bar female vocal hook and a marimba or steel drum answering it.
Arrange: 32-bar percussive intro, gradual entries, break with the vocal, return of the percussion.
Mix the percussion separated and panned, mono sub, vocal up front, master around -8 LUFS.
ukfunky.mix: The percussion must be clean and distinct: cut each one below 150 Hz, place them at different positions in the stereo field, compress the percussion bus with a 3:1 ratio and 20 ms attack to keep the transients. Kick and bass in the center, mono sub below 100 Hz, light sidechain. Vocal up front, gentle compression, short plate reverb. A little tape saturation on the master bus. Master around -8 LUFS. Check that the percussion doesn't mask the vocal between 2 and 5 kHz. The mix must stay airy, it's a genre of light, not pressure.

outils.pourquoi: The DAW of the funky scene: three stacked percussion patterns, bass in the ES2, marimba and steel drum in the EXS24.
The other tool of 2008 producers, for programming congas, cowbell and shaker in syncopated sixteenth notes.
Roska loads his kicks, snares and percussion into it on all his projects, with varied velocities per pad.
Three volumes of kicks, snares, percussion, leads and basses from the pioneer of the genre, in 24 bits, with MIDI.
Round bass, sine or triangle with a little saturation, decay 200 ms, in minor pentatonic on a 3+3+2 pattern.
Bright synth stabs, Roska-style noisy lead, and the round bass when you're not in Logic.
Sampler for marimba, kalimba, soca brass and the female vocal hook, played dry with a short delay.

reperes: Kyla: Do You Mind (2008): the female vocal as lead over soca percussion, the genre's pop hook.
Roska: Squark (2009): the instrumental, rough side, stacked percussion, noisy lead.
Donae'o: Party Hard (2009): the syncopated kick and club euphoria, male vocal hook.
Roska & Untold: Myth (2010): the meeting with UK bass, funky percussion and darker bass.
ukfunky.rythme: Syncopated kick: on 1, on the “and” of 2, on 3, and sometimes on the “a” of 3, or four-on-the-floor depending on the track. Snare or clap on 2 and 4, or a rimshot on 3 for a more broken feel. Then the percussion: congas in sixteenth notes with a tumbao pattern, bongos, cowbell on the offbeats, shakers, a wood block. Stack three different percussion patterns in Logic or FL Studio, each with its own syncopation. Hats in simple eighth notes. The percussion is dry and bright, panned left and right, with varied velocities. A percussion roll, not a snare roll, at the end of a phrase.
ukfunky.sons: Female vocals as lead, sung, with no extreme pitching, often a short phrase repeated as a hook. Marimba, steel drum, kalimba sampled in Logic's EXS24 or Simpler for the tropical color. Bright synth stabs, soca brass, house piano for the euphoric moments. A noisy synth lead for the rougher, Roska-style side. Discreet sirens and MC shouts, a pirate radio legacy. Logic and FL Studio are the scene's historic tools. Little reverb, a short delay on the percussion, dry and bright sounds. Sound design counts for less than rhythmic richness.
sourcesOutils: Native Instruments Blog, Roska: Kick, Snares, Kontakt
Bandcamp, Roska UK Funky Sample Pack
ukfunky.tempo: Between 128 and 132 BPM, 130 is the center. The feel is swaying and tropical: the patterns borrow from soca, dembow and South African house. The kick isn't always four-on-the-floor, it's often syncopated. The swing is moderate, 55 to 57%, but the groove comes mainly from layering three or four percussion patterns in sixteenth notes, each with its own syncopation. The 3+3+2 rhythm in sixteenth notes, typical of dembow, often shows up in the congas or the bass. What changes compared to 2-step: Latin and African percussion replaces the shuffle, and light replaces shadow.

ukgarage.arrangement: A UK garage track lasts 5 to 7 minutes in the club version, 3 minutes in the radio version. 16 or 32-bar intro: beat alone with hats, then the bass. The first vocal or the organ arrives at bar 32. Structure in 16-bar blocks, break around bar 64 where everything drops out except the vocal and a pad, then the kick returns with a snare roll. Breaks are short, 8 bars, no endless build-up. Vary by subtraction: remove the kick for 4 bars, keep the bass. End with 32 bars of beat and bass for the DJ mix. Also think about the dub version without vocals, that's the historic DJ use.
ukgarage.basse: The UK garage bass is a round sub, usually a sine or a triangle with very few harmonics, played in short notes. In Operator or Serum: one sine oscillator, a light drive, attack 0, decay 200 to 400 ms, short release. Write a line that moves: root, fifth, octave, minor seventh, on syncopated eighth and sixteenth notes that avoid the kick. The bass answers the kick rather than doubling it. Minor key, often F or G minor. Sometimes add a second, fatter layer, a filtered sawtooth with cutoff at 300 Hz, for the choruses. Light sidechain from the kick, ratio 4:1, release 100 ms, just enough to let the kick through.
etapes: Set Ableton to 130 BPM, load a short 909 kick, a clap and two hi-hats, lay down the four-on-the-floor and an MPC 16 Swing groove at 58%.
Program the hi-hats in sixteenth notes with varied velocities and an open hat on the offbeats.
Write a sine bass in syncopated eighth notes that avoids the kick, in minor, over 2 bars.
Add M1 organ stabs on a syncopated pattern and a chopped R'n'B vocal, pitched +3 semitones.
Arrange in 16-bar blocks, with an 8-bar break and the kick returning on a snare roll.
Mix kick and sub together, lightly saturate the drum bus, glue it all with the Glue.
ukgarage.mix: The garage mix is warm, full in the low mids, with a kick that doesn't dominate. Set the kick around -8 dB peak, the sub just below, with a high-pass at 30 Hz. The hi-hat is bright but not aggressive: a shelf at 8 kHz on the drum bus and a little tape saturation, Saturator in Analog Clip mode. Cut the bass below 40 Hz, cut the organ and the vocal below 200 Hz. Parallel compression on the drum bus, ratio 4:1, attack 10 ms, mix at 30%. A Glue Compressor on the master with 2 dB of reduction to glue it all together. Aim for around -8 LUFS for a club master, keeping the dynamics of the swing intact.

outils.pourquoi: The 16-bit sampler of the 1996 garage studios: chopped R'n'B vocals, stabs and kicks go through it. Today Simpler in Complex Pro mode does the same job.
The Organ 2 preset for the organ stabs and the house piano in the choruses. The Korg M1 plugin from the Korg Collection replaces the machine.
Short kick on all four beats, clap and open hat on the offbeats. 909 samples or the D16 Drumazon 2 emulation are more than enough.
MPC 16 Swing grooves between 58 and 62% on the hi-hats, Simpler to pitch the vocals, Glue Compressor on the master.
The MPC swing is the garage swing: program the hats on it, or apply its extracted grooves in Ableton to recover the shuffle.
One sine oscillator, decay of 200 to 400 ms, for the round sub that answers the kick. Ableton's Operator does the same.

outils.nom: Loopmasters, MJ Cole UK Garage & House
outils.pourquoi: Pack by MJ Cole: swung drum kits, Rhodes chords, vocal chops already pitched, ready for Simpler or a Drum Rack.

reperes: Double 99: Ripgroove (1997): the swing of the hats against the four-on-the-floor kick, and the bass answering the kick.
MJ Cole: Sincere (1998): the fine craftsmanship of chopped vocals and chords, a clean and musical arrangement.
Artful Dodger: Re-Rewind (1999): the radio structure with break and rewind, the organ and the pitched vocal.
Tuff Jam: Need Good Love (1997): the dub version, close to US house but with the British shuffle.
ukgarage.rythme: Short, dry four-on-the-floor kick, TR-909 or a house kick sample, with no long tail. Clap or snare on beats 2 and 4, often a clap layered with a 909 snare pitched a little high. The heart of the groove is the hi-hat: closed hat in swung sixteenth notes with uneven velocities, and an open hat on the offbeat of each beat. Add shakers and syncopated rimshots, a conga on the last sixteenth note of beat 2. The signature pattern: open hat between the kicks, snare sometimes skipped to surprise. Use short samples, no reverb on the kick, a small room on the snare. Everything goes through in the spirit of an Akai S2000: 16-bit samples, a little grainy.
ukgarage.sons: The Korg M1 organ is the signature sound: chords as short stabs, played syncopated, often with the Organ 2 preset. You'll find it in the M1 plugin or in any rompler. The M1 house piano too. The vocals: take an R'n'B a cappella, cut out syllables and pitch them +2 to +5 semitones in Simpler in Complex Pro mode to keep the natural timbre. Repeat a word on a rhythmic pattern with a dotted eighth delay. Add string stabs, short filtered pads, a few sirens and rewind noises for the pirate radio spirit. The samples stay short and mid-heavy, no heavy pads that crush the groove.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter (transposing a sample in Complex Pro and processing)
sourcesOutils: Internet Tattoo, UKG VST: The Best Synth Plugins for UK Garage
MusicRadar, MJ Cole on the making of UKG classic Sincere
Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production, Basslines chapter
ukgarage.tempo: Set your project between 128 and 135 BPM, 130 is the classic starting point. What makes UK garage is the swing: in Ableton, apply an MPC 16 Swing groove between 58 and 62% on the hi-hats and percussion, much less on the kick. The feel must stay round and danceable, never stiff. The sixteenth notes are pushed back, the eighth notes stay almost straight. Compared to the New York garage house it descends from, everything is faster and more nervous, but the four-on-the-floor kick stays present most of the time. Don't quantize everything at 100%, leave 5 to 10% of freedom on the percussion so the loop breathes.

ukhardcore.arrangement: The UK hardcore track is a trance song at 172: 32-bar intro with kick, bass and a pluck, 16-bar sung verse with kick, 8-bar pre-chorus without kick with the vocal and the supersaw, 8-bar build-up with roll and riser, 32-bar chorus with everything, kick, bass, supersaw, vocal. Long break in the middle, 32 bars, with the vocal and a piano or a pad, no kick, then a build-up, then the last chorus, sometimes with a key change. 32-bar ending on kick and pluck. Length 5 to 7 minutes for club versions, 3 to 4 for radio. The sung chorus is the center.
ukhardcore.basse: The offbeat bass of happy hardcore, but fatter and longer: one note per “and”, 150 ms, a sawtooth with unison in Sylenth1, filtered at 600 Hz, with a bit of distortion. It follows the supersaw chords, often a four-chord progression in minor (vi, IV, I, V in the relative major key) over 8 bars. Underneath, a sine sub on the same notes, sidechained from the kick (ratio 5:1, release 80 ms) so it doesn't fight with the kick's tuned tail. Some tracks replace the offbeat bass with a hardstyle reverse bass in the drop: that's a variant, not the rule.
etapes: Tempo 172 BPM. Tuned kick with a short tail on every beat, clap on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats.
Offbeat bass in Sylenth1, sawtooth with unison, filtered at 600 Hz, following 4 chords in minor. Sine sub sidechained underneath.
7-voice supersaw in Sylenth1, 2-bar held chords, long reverb, high-pass at 200 Hz.
Record or sample a full sung vocal over 16 bars, compress it hard, dotted eighth delay.
Add a pluck in a sixteenth-note arpeggio and a lead with portamento doubling the chorus melody.
Arrange as a trance song: intro 32, verse 16, pre-chorus 8, build-up 8, chorus 32, break 32, build-up, final chorus, ending 32. Wide, bright mix.
ukhardcore.mix: The UK hardcore mix is that of commercial trance: wide, bright, compressed. Kick at minus 4 dB peak, sub sidechained under it. Supersaw very wide in stereo, high-pass at 200 Hz, with a 3-second hall reverb cut below 400 Hz. Vocal compressed at a 4:1 ratio then limited, up front, with a de-esser. Light sidechain on the supersaw and pads from the kick for the typical pumping. Bus compression, Glue at a 2:1 ratio. Master: Ozone or Pro-L 2 toward minus 7 LUFS, with a high shelf of plus 2 dB for brightness. Compare with Darren Styles at the same level.

outils.pourquoi: The synth of the genre since 2005: 7-voice detuned supersaw, wide unison, for the chorus leads and rising pads.
The original supersaw, borrowed from trance: the lead of Styles & Breeze or Darren Styles comes from this oscillator or its software copy.
The DAW of the UK hardcore scene: kick, offbeat bass and verse-chorus arrangement, with the Piano roll for pop melodies.
Ready-to-use trance pianos, plucks and pads, widely used in Raver Baby and Monstercat productions to work fast.
Bright, loud master: EQ, Exciter in the top end, Maximizer toward minus 7 LUFS, all built in. Pro-L 2 as the last stage for the peaks.
On the drum bus and on the synth bus separately, to glue the polished production the genre has expected since 2000.
Kicks, claps and build-up effects from the trance-house generation of the 2000s, still the basis of many UK hardcore kits.

reperes: Scott Brown: Elysium Plus (2000): the turning point, happy hardcore becoming cleaner and more trance.
Styles and Breeze: You're Shining (2004): the supersaw and the full pop vocal, UK hardcore defined.
Styles & Breeze: Heartbeatz (2005): the complete song structure with a chorus that carries the whole track.
Darren Styles: Save Me (2006): the polished production, the long break and the 8-bar build-up.
ukhardcore.rythme: UK hardcore kick: longer than the happy hardcore kick (200 ms), with a slightly tuned tail and gentle saturation, somewhere between the hardstyle kick and the trance kick. On every beat. Clap on 2 and 4, doubled by a snare with reverb. Open hats on the offbeats, always, but mixed lower than in happy hardcore. Closed hats in sixteenth notes with alternating velocity. 4-bar snare rolls before the drops, accelerating (eighths, sixteenths, thirty-seconds), plus a crash on beat 1 of the drop. Offbeat kicks with only the tail in some drops, inherited from hardstyle. The grid is that of happy hardcore, the production is that of trance.
ukhardcore.sons: The supersaw: in Sylenth1 or a JP-8000, 7 sawtooths detuned by 25 cents, low-pass filter at 8 kHz, long reverb, played as held chords or as an eighth-note melody. It's the main sound of the drops. Thinner single-sawtooth leads with portamento for the main melodies. Plucks (sawtooth, decay 80 ms) in sixteenth-note arpeggios. Full sung pop vocals, often female, with heavy compression, reverb and dotted eighth delay, not pitched: that's the big difference from happy hardcore. Pianos sometimes, but discreet. White noise risers, impacts, reverse cymbals at every transition.
sourcesOutils: KVR Audio, forum Anyone produce UK hardcore? (kvraudio.com)
ukhardcore.tempo: UK hardcore stays at the happy hardcore tempo, 170 to 175 BPM, but with the production precision of trance: everything is quantized, clean, wide. What changes compared to 1990s happy hardcore isn't the tempo, it's the sound: the supersaw replaces the piano, the full pop vocal replaces the pitched vocal, and the kick is longer and more tuned. No swing. Program at 172 BPM, sixteenth-note grid. The feel is that of sped-up trance: build-ups are long, drops are wide, and the bounce of the offbeat bass remains, but more discreet under the wall of supersaw.

ukhouse.arrangement: More movement than American house. 16-bar intro with breakbeat and samples, the 909 kick arrives at bar 17. The piano comes in in 8-bar blocks, as does the sampled vocal. 16-bar break where the 909 stops, the breakbeat continues, the pad rises, a voice speaks; then a tom roll and everything comes back with the piano. Two or three of these cycles. Length 5 to 7 minutes, with a longer dub version. The track must surprise: a new sample every 16 bars, a bass change in the last third. English hardcore and garage will grow out of these cuts and these breaks.
ukhouse.basse: A simpler, more pushed bass than in Chicago: often a disco or funk bass sample on one note, replayed on the sampler, or a synth sawtooth in eighth notes on one note with an octave. A Juno or D-50 bass preset does the job. Stay in eighth or sixteenth notes on one or two notes, the Italian piano and the samples provide the harmony. On 808 State or A Guy Called Gerald tracks, the bass becomes a more melodic synth, with a bit of glide and a moving filter. The sub is more present than in Chicago: add a sine an octave below, England already has sound systems.
etapes: Project at 125 BPM, 909 four-on-the-floor with clap on 2 and 4, plus a sampled breakbeat loop, cut below 150 Hz, locked and mixed underneath.
Eighth-note bass on one note with an octave, and a sine sub an octave below.
M1 piano or piano sample in syncopated major block chords, way up front.
Sample three vocals or sounds from disco and films, slice them in Simpler and play them while varying the pitch.
Build 6 minutes with changes every 8 bars, a break with the breakbeat alone, and a tom roll on the return.
Mix loud: 909 in front of the break, piano in the 2 to 5 kHz range, mono sub, Glue at 4:1 on the master.
ukhouse.mix: The mix is louder and brighter than Chicago, with a piano that cuts through in the 2 to 5 kHz range and a breakbeat that fills the mids. The 909 kick must sit in front of the break: compress the drum bus with a fast attack so the 909 dominates, and a light sidechain on the break. The samples keep their 16-bit grain: a little bitcrush if needed. The reverb is short on the piano, longer on the vocals and the pad. The sub is clean and mono. On the master, frank compression (Glue at 4:1) for rave energy. The result must sound loud on a pirate radio cassette, not clean.

outils.pourquoi: The 1988 16-bit stereo sampler on which breakbeats, film vocals and Italian pianos are chopped and replayed on the keyboard.
Kick and clap in front of the sampled breakbeat, open hats on the offbeats, descending toms on the fills, the foundation of English rave.
The Italian house piano in major block chords and the organ, way up front in the 2 to 5 kHz range on the 1989 and 1990 records.
The digital pads and bass presets mentioned in the course for the breaks, a colder sound than the Chicago Juno.
Sampler sequencer that A Guy Called Gerald used with his S950 and S1000 to build his tracks entirely on machines.
Replaces the Akai S1000: Slice mode on a break or a film vocal, played on the keyboard while varying the pitch, as the course describes.
Funky Drummer, Amen, Think: the funk breaks that double the 909, cut below 150 Hz; available from Loopmasters or Splice, or sampled from the record.

reperes: S'Express: Theme From S'Express (1988): the collage of disco samples, vocals and brass over a 909, English house as montage.
Bomb The Bass: Beat Dis (1988): stacked breakbeats and film samples, the line between house and hip-hop fading away.
Coldcut: Doctorin The House (1988): Yazz's vocal over a house piano and sampler cuts, the rave hit of the Summer of Love.
Ralphi Rosario feat Xavia Gold: You Used To Hold Me (1987): the Chicago record the English adopted and copied for its piano and vocal.
ukhouse.rythme: 909 kick four-on-the-floor, 909 clap on 2 and 4, but underneath a sampled breakbeat loop (Funky Drummer, Amen, Think, or any funk break) chopped, locked to the tempo and played across the whole bar. Cut the break below 150 Hz to keep only the snares and hats, and mix it at 40% under the 909. On the track's breaks, remove the 909 and leave the breakbeat alone. Add open 909 hats on the offbeats, a cowbell or a syncopated rim, and drum cuts of one eighth note before each 8-bar block. Descending 909 tom fills and sampled crowd shouts.
ukhouse.sons: The Italian house piano: an M1 piano or a piano sample, major block chords in syncopated eighth notes, in thirds and sixths, way up front. A sampled brass or string stab. Vocal samples from disco, soul or films, cut into syllables and replayed on the S1000's keyboard, with the pitch varying by key. Crowd shouts, sirens, rave noises. A synth pad (Juno, D-50) under the breaks. A vocoder or a pitch shift on a phrase. The mix is deliberately eclectic: a bright piano, a dirty breakbeat, a soul vocal and a siren in the same bar. The sampler is the instrument, the Akai S1000 or today Simpler in slices.
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, article A Guy Called Gerald & Graham Massey (808state.com)
Equipboard, A Guy Called Gerald's Studio Equipment
ukhouse.tempo: Faster than Chicago: 122 to 128 BPM in 1988-1990, sometimes more. The feel is energetic and a little homemade, because everything goes through the sampler: breakbeat loops layered over a 909, with the slight wobble that comes from a sample lined up by hand. Put a light swing on the machine but let the sampled loops impose their own groove, even if the two rub against each other. That friction between grid and breakbeat is what sets English house apart from Chicago house. Structure in 16 bars, but with more frequent changes, every 8, as in a pirate radio set.

upliftingtrance.arrangement: Seven to nine minutes. 32-bar intro with kick, bass and a pluck, for the DJ. First 32-bar plateau with a secondary melody. First short 16-bar break. Return, then around bar 129 the big breakdown: everything stops except the pads, the piano introduces the theme, the supersaw takes it up in chords, the snare starts its roll 16 bars before the end. Drop: the kick returns with the full theme on supersaw, 32 to 48 bars of climax. A last stripped-down plateau, then a 32-bar exit. The breakdown takes up a quarter of the track: that's the rule of the genre.
upliftingtrance.basse: The offbeat uplifting bass: a Virus or Sylenth1 sawtooth, a short note on every off eighth, decay 120 ms, cutoff 400 Hz. It follows the chord progression, often vi, IV, I, V in the relative minor, changing every 2 bars. A second layer in sixteenth notes, filtered lower, adds the roll. Sine sub in whole notes below 60 Hz. Sidechain from the kick, ratio 6:1, release 100 ms, for the characteristic pumping. High-pass the bass at 90 Hz, leave the sub alone at the bottom. During the breakdown, the bass disappears completely or remains as a filtered low pad.
etapes: Project at 138 BPM, clean 909 kick, clap and snare on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats, ride in eighth notes.
Write the offbeat bass on a vi, IV, I, V progression, with sub and 6:1 sidechain.
Compose an 8-bar stepwise melody and play it on a 7-voice supersaw, in octaves, with chorus and reverb.
Build the breakdown: pads, piano, theme, then a snare roll over 16 bars with filtered white noise.
Arrange 8 minutes around the breakdown placed at two thirds, with 32-bar intro and exit for the DJ.
Widen the supersaw, put the low end back in mono, push the master toward -6 LUFS.
upliftingtrance.mix: Loud, bright and wide. Kick in the center around -6 dB peak, sub in mono. Supersaw very wide, but high-passed at 150 Hz and with the frequencies below 200 Hz put back in mono. Sidechain on the supersaw and the pads too, ratio 3:1. A bump at 3 kHz on the lead so it cuts through. Long reverb on one return, ping-pong delay on another, both cut at 400 Hz. Master bus: glue compressor, ratio 2:1, EQ adding 1 dB at 10 kHz, limiter toward -6 LUFS. Make sure the drop is at least 3 dB louder than the breakdown, otherwise the effect fails.

outils.pourquoi: The origin of the supersaw: seven detuned sawtooths for the lead and the breakdown chords. Arturia Jup-8000 V reproduces the exact oscillator.
The synth most present in uplifting templates: 7-voice unison supersaw, 30% detune, plucks for the sixteenth-note arpeggios.
A brighter, more modern supersaw than Sylenth1, with its built-in unison and chorus: leads and chords of current uplifting productions.
Wide breakdown pads and digital plucks on Ferry Corsten and Armin van Buuren records since 1999.
For white noise risers, cutoff automated from 500 Hz to 15 kHz over 16 bars, and modern wavetable plucks.
Snare rolls, impacts, reversed cymbals and trance kicks: the library that supplied the transitions of 2000s uplifting.
Master limiter toward -6 LUFS after the glue compressor, in Modern mode to keep the kick transient at the drop.
The reference DAW of Dutch and British uplifting studios, with its precise MIDI functions for stepwise build-ups.

reperes: Gouryella: Gouryella (1999): the supersaw in octaves, the immense breakdown and the releasing drop, the uplifting manifesto
Rank 1: Airwave (1999): the stepwise melody and the sidechained offbeat bass, the model for all the anthems that followed
Push: Universal Nation (1998): the harder, darker version, before the formula softened
Cold Blue: The Mile (2019): uplifting today, same structure, cleaner and wider production
upliftingtrance.rythme: Clean, punchy 909 kick, no distortion, decay 300 ms, with a click in the attack. On 2 and 4, a clap and a snare layered. Open hat on the offbeats, ride in eighth notes, closed hat in sixteenth notes at low volume. The snare roll is the signature: over the last 16 bars of the breakdown, the snare goes from eighth notes to sixteenth notes then to thirty-second notes, with the volume rising and a high-pass filter opening. Crash on every first beat of an 8-bar block. A one-bar reversed cymbal before each drop. No tribal percussion: everything is 909 or clean samples.
upliftingtrance.sons: The JP-8000 supersaw, or Sylenth1 with 7 unison voices and 30% detune, plays the main lead in octaves and the breakdown chords. Short attack, 300 ms release, chorus. The breakdown pads are wide, with a 6-second reverb. Short plucks in sixteenth-note arpeggios, with ping-pong delay at the dotted eighth. A piano for the breakdown. The melodies are major or in a bright minor, stepwise, climbing over 8 bars toward the highest note. Filtered white noise for the build-ups, cutoff automated from 500 Hz to 15 kHz over 16 bars. Impact and reversed cymbal on the drop.
upliftingtrance.tempo: 138 BPM, almost a law, with a tolerance of 136 to 140. Straight grid, no swing, 100% quantization. The feel comes from tension and release: an uplifting track is built around a breakdown of 90 seconds to 2 minutes, and everything else serves to get there or to come out of it. Count in 16-bar blocks for the plateaus and in 32 for the breakdown. The climax should land around two thirds of the way through the track. Ferry Corsten and Armin van Buuren have been at 138 since the late 1990s. Aly & Fila sometimes push to 140. Don't go beyond: past that, it's hard trance.

uptempo.arrangement: Tracks are 3 to 4 minutes, shorter than nu style, and go straight to the point. 16-bar intro, 16 to 32-bar break with the sample or the melody and a very pronounced build-up (kick roll, riser, silence), 32-bar drop where the kick puts on the show with its bursts and cuts, a shorter second break, second drop, quick ending. Uptempo DJs mix fast, so intros and endings are short, 8 to 16 bars. What makes the track effective is the variety of the kick during the drop: a new pattern every 4 bars, with a burst fill every 8. The editing is the track.
uptempo.basse: As in nu style, the kick tail carries the note, and the track is written in its key. But uptempo also inherits a bouncing bass from frenchcore: the kick tail replayed on the offbeats, or a separate saturated bass, square wave or filtered sawtooth, played in eighth notes on the offbeats between the kicks. In Serum: a sawtooth, unison at 2, distortion, low-pass at 400 Hz, note held for one eighth. Sidechain from the kick, ratio 8:1, release 30 ms, so it disappears under each hit. Chord changes are made by pitching the kick tail and the bass together, often root then fourth or fifth.
etapes: Tempo 200 BPM. Take a nu style kick, shorten the tail to 200 ms, raise the midrange distortion a little.
Kick on every beat for 4 bars, then a burst fill in sixteenth notes with rising pitch on the last beat.
Add a bouncing bass on the offbeats, hard sidechained, in the key of the kick.
Create an aggressive screech in Serum, 8-note riff in sixteenth notes, two distortions in series.
Sample a funny phrase or a meme, chop it, place it in the break and as an answer to the screech.
Short structure: 16 intro, 24 break, 32 drop, 16 break, 32 drop, 8 ending. Clipper then limiter on the master.
uptempo.mix: The uptempo mix is that of the loudness war: everything is clipped, compressed, bright. Kick at minus 2 dB peak, processed by bands as in nu style but with more top end: a distortion on the 2 to 6 kHz band so the bursts cut through on big systems. High-pass at 40 Hz. The screeches are high-passed at 400 Hz and compressed hard. As the Attack book points out, saturation at the output of the drum bus gives a few extra dB of perceived loudness: here it's a hard clipper, not a soft clip. Master: clipper, then limiter, toward minus 4 to minus 5 LUFS. Check that the kick bursts don't make the limiter pump: if they do, shorten their tail.

outils.pourquoi: The whole uptempo kick is built inside it: pitched sine, internal distortion in series, then resampled to “pierce” it. Most of the genre's kick presets are for Serum.
The DAW of Partyraiser, F.Noize and the whole scene: Piano roll for quick kick edits, Fruity WaveShaper for crushing.
The transfer curve drawn by hand on the kick: it's FL Studio's native distortion tool that almost all uptempo tutorials use.
After each distortion stage, a dip around 300 Hz and a high-pass at 35 Hz, otherwise the kick at 200 BPM turns into mush.
Saturated screeches: sawtooth, resonant band-pass filter, distortion, then a very fast LFO on the pitch for the scream.
A pack of kicks ready for uptempo, terror and gabber when you want to compare your synthesized kick to what plays in clubs.
Loudness war mastering: limiter pushed toward minus 5 LUFS integrated, with True Peak disabled so you don't lose the kick's peak.

reperes: Partyraiser: La Bomba (2013): nu style speeding up, bouncing kick and party sample.
Partyraiser and Destructive Tendencies: Sound Becomes One (2016): the drop as an edit of kick patterns.
F. Noize: Rock the Party (2018): kick bursts and screeches, the style at maturity.
Deadly Guns & Dimitri K: Game Over (2021): very loud mastering and kick fills every 8 bars.
uptempo.rythme: The uptempo kick is a sped-up frenchcore or nu style kick: short attack, saturated tuned tail, but cut around 200 ms. On every beat. The signature is the “pierced” kicks or “rolls”: bursts of kicks in sixteenth notes over 1 or 2 beats, with a rising filter or pitch, used as fills. Offbeat kicks with only the tail, as in frenchcore, which give the bounce. Snare on 2 and 4, often a dry clap. Hi-hats in eighth notes. What's new is the editing: the kick patterns change every 2 or 4 beats, with cuts, retriggers and pitched kicks. Think fast video editing, not a loop.
uptempo.sons: Saturated screeches, even more piercing than in nu style, made in Serum with a harsh wavetable, a resonant filter and two distortions in series, played in very fast riffs. Simple melodic leads for the anthems, in stacked sawtooths. Lots of samples of memes, TikTok voices, film lines, pitched and chopped: humor is part of the genre. MC vocals. Crowd shouts, police sirens, horns. Reverse kicks and risers. Everything is short and tightly edited. The hoover is absent. The overall sound is bright and compressed, closer to EDM mastering than to dirty gabber.
sources: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2, Hard Techno, Schranz chapters)
sourcesOutils: Attack Magazine, The Secrets of Techno Production (Drum Processing 1 and 2)
Neroz Productions, Uptempo and Hardcore course (nerozproductions.com)
ON POINT SAMPLES, Uptempo Kick Generator Plugins (onpointsamples.com)
uptempo.tempo: Uptempo takes nu style and pushes it to between 190 and 230 BPM, with a lot of production around 200-210. What sets it apart from terrorcore, even at similar tempos, is that the kick remains the nu style and frenchcore kick, tuned and long, not the crushed gabber kick. At 200 BPM a beat lasts 300 ms and the kick tail has to be shortened so it doesn't overlap. The feel is party, not terror: the rhythms bounce. No swing. Program at 200 BPM, sixteenth-note grid. Many tracks play with half-tempo passages (100 BPM felt) for the breaks.

usdeephouse.arrangement: No drop, no white noise build-up. 32-bar intro with kick, hats and a held chord that opens with the filter. Elements are added one by one every 16 bars: bass, Rhodes, shaker, vocal. The track reaches its fullness around the halfway point, then a 16-bar break removes the kick and leaves the chords and the vocal, without tension, like a breath. The return is gentle, sometimes just the kick without the hats. Length 6 to 9 minutes, with an outro that removes the elements in reverse order. The harmonic progression can modulate once, to the relative major, for the last third. The rule: the track must be beautiful at any minute picked at random.
usdeephouse.basse: An SH-101 bass or equivalent (Analog, Cloud SH-101, TAL-BassLine) in sawtooth or square, filter at 200 to 400 Hz, a little glide between notes. The line is melodic: it follows the chords but with passing notes, sevenths and ninths, like a jazz bassist. Rhythm in eighth notes with silences, or dotted quarter notes, never tight sixteenth notes. On Can You Feel It, the bass is almost a second melody in dialogue with the chords. Let it breathe: a 2-bar line with two held notes and three passing notes is enough. Very light sidechain from the kick, just to clarify the low end.
etapes: Project at 120 BPM, softened 909 kit (kick without click, soft clap, low-velocity hats with 55% swing), everything at low volume.
Write a progression of two or four minor 7 and major 9 chords over 8 bars, played on the Juno with chorus, held over whole bars.
Double the chords on the Rhodes with open voicings and a slow tremolo, then open the Juno filter with automation over 16 bars.
Write an SH-101 bass in eighth notes with silences that converses with the chords, adding passing notes.
Spread it over 8 minutes, adding an element every 16 bars and a break without kick in the middle.
Mix warm: full low mids, a single long filtered reverb, tape saturation on the bus, master at -11 LUFS.
usdeephouse.mix: A warm, enveloping mix, with full lows and low mids. The chords occupy 200 Hz to 2 kHz, the bass 60 to 200, the kick 50 to 80 with little attack. Don't scoop the low mids, that's where the style lives. Gentle compression everywhere, 2:1 ratios, slow attacks, and tape saturation on the bus (Saturator, or a tape plugin like Satin or Ableton's Tape) to round things off. The reverb is the glue: a single return, long hall, low-passed at 5 kHz, sent from chords, Rhodes and vocal. The master isn't loud: -10 to -12 LUFS, with dynamics. Cut the top above 15 kHz if it gets too bright.

outils.pourquoi: Bass, chords and melody of Can You Feel It all come from a single Juno-60, with its chorus; TAL-U-NO-LX or Arturia Jun-6 V for the software version.
The other half of Larry Heard's studio in 1984; in deep house you muffle it: short decay, click reduced around 4 kHz, low-velocity hats.
Seventh and ninth chords in open voicings with slow tremolo; Electric in Ableton or Spectrasonics Keyscape for a sampled Rhodes.
The melodic monophonic bass with glide, filter between 200 and 400 Hz; Roland Cloud SH-101 or TAL-BassLine-101 replace it in the DAW.
The Juno-60's successor for held pads in minor 7 chords, filter opening over 16 bars, chorus switched on.
Modeled analog synth that today's deep house producers reach for for Juno chords and round basses when they want more than a strict emulation.
Tape saturation on the bus to round off the whole mix, in place of a tape machine; the course suggests Satin or Saturator for this role.

reperes: Mr. Fingers: Can You Feel It (1986): held Juno chords opening over a melodic bass, the whole grammar of deep house in one track.
Mr. Fingers: Mystery of Love (1985): the bass as a second melody and the drums staying back behind the harmony.
Kerri Chandler: Bar A Thym (1998): Kerri's typical warm, round kick, and a chord repeated to the point of hypnosis.
Moodymann: Black Mahogani (2004): Detroit deep house, soul samples and dirty drums, mixed like a jazz record.
usdeephouse.rythme: The muffled 909: kick with short decay and a cut around 4 kHz to remove the click, 909 snare replaced by a soft clap or a rim, closed hats in sixteenth notes at low velocity (60 to 80), a discreet open hat on the offbeats. Often a rounder 808 kick instead. Add a shaker or a conga very low in the mix for movement. No spectacular fills: cutting the hats for one bar is enough. The full drum kit takes up 30% of the mix; if you hear it before the chords, it's too loud. Make sure nothing snaps: deep house is music of sustain, not transients.
usdeephouse.sons: The heart is the chord: Juno-60 or Juno-106 with chorus, in minor 7, major 7 and 9 chords, held or stabbed in syncopation, with a filter that opens slowly over 16 bars. A Rhodes (Electric in Ableton, or a Mark I sample) plays the same chords with open voicings and a slow tremolo. A string pad far in the background. Touches of acoustic piano in response. Vocals are rare, whispered or spoken, or a sampled and muffled gospel phrase. Signature effects: analog chorus, dotted quarter delay with low feedback, long reverb but filtered above 6 kHz so it doesn't sparkle. Everything is soft, a little veiled, never bright.
sourcesOutils: Vice, Larry Heard Talks Us Through the Making of Can You Feel It
Roland Articles, Sound Behind the Song: Can You Feel It
Output, Best Plugins for House Music
usdeephouse.tempo: Aim for 118 to 123 BPM, never faster. This is house that takes its time, and the feel is supple, almost slow to the ear despite the tempo. Moderate swing on the hats (54 to 56%), straight kick, chords often slightly behind the beat, by 10 to 20 ms, which gives the “laid back” effect. Chords held over one or two full bars slow down the perception. The track should be able to play at the end of the night or at home. Where Chicago “jacks”, deep house floats: each element is a little less loud, a little less sharp, and the drums step back behind the harmony.

vocaltrance.arrangement: Two versions. The club version runs 7 minutes: 32-bar instrumental intro, first verse over reduced drums, pre-chorus with build-up, chorus on the full drop with supersaw chords, 32-bar breakdown with the second verse over piano, roll, final chorus, exit. The radio version runs 3 minutes 30: 8-bar intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, short breakdown, chorus. The drop serves as the chorus: the vocal sings its hook over the kick and the supersaw. Plan a 16-bar instrumental passage where the vocal theme is taken up by a synth.
vocaltrance.basse: The offbeat bass follows the song's chords, often four chords over 8 bars, changing every 2 bars: Sylenth1 or Virus, sawtooth, cutoff 400 Hz, decay 120 ms, 5:1 sidechain. The verse can simplify it to sub whole notes, the chorus brings it back to full offbeat. A filtered sixteenth-note layer during the chorus only. Cut at 90 Hz, sine sub below. The bass must never share frequencies with the vocal: nothing above 300 Hz. In the breakdown, it disappears and lets the piano hold the harmony.
etapes: Choose or record a female vocal, find its natural tempo, set the project to around 134 BPM.
Write the four-chord progression and the verse, pre-chorus, chorus structure over 8 bars each.
Process the vocal: two-stage compression, de-esser, dotted eighth delay, plate reverb, harmonies on the chorus.
Lay down 909 kick, clap and hi-hats, offbeat bass reduced on the verse and full on the chorus.
Add supersaw chords under the chorus, piano on the verse and the breakdown, arpeggiated plucks.
Arrange a 7-minute club version and a 3 minute 30 radio version, then carve the mix around the vocal.
vocaltrance.mix: The vocal is in the center, up front, around -10 dB peak, with an EQ that cuts 300 Hz and adds 2 dB at 5 kHz. Everything else makes room: the supersaw is cut by 3 dB between 2 and 4 kHz, the piano is slightly offset. Light sidechain on the pads from the vocal, ratio 2:1, so it comes through. Kick around -7 dB, sub in mono. Vocal reverb on a separate return, cut at 300 Hz. Gentler master compression than uplifting, ratio 2:1, limiter toward -7 LUFS for the club and -8 for radio. Check that the lyrics are intelligible on a phone.

outils.pourquoi: For the female lead vocal: a Neumann U 87 or a Rode NT1 in a dry booth, before two-stage compression at ratio 3:1 then 4:1.
Pitch correction of the vocals and harmony doubles for the chorus, more discreet than the hard Auto-Tune of pitched eurotrance vocals.
De-esser around 6 kHz on the compressed vocal, essential when you add 2 dB at 5 kHz so it sits in front of the supersaw.
Supersaw in held chords under the vocal, filtered sixteenth-note plucks for movement: the instrumental carpet of the chorus.
Supersaw chords of the vocal anthems from 1998 to 2004, from Delerium to Oceanlab. Arturia Jup-8000 V in software.
Wide pads and plucks of Anjunabeats and Armind productions, often on the same track as Sylenth1.
2-second plate reverb on a separate vocal return, cut at 300 Hz, with a dotted eighth delay on certain words.
DAW of the vocal trance studios, with built-in VariAudio to fix the pitch of takes without an external plugin.

reperes: Alice Deejay: Better Off Alone (1998): the short vocal hook that comes back on the drop like a chorus, the formula in its simplest form
iiO: Rapture (2001): the vocal up front, the discreet offbeat bass and the supersaw as a carpet, not a lead
Luminary: Amsterdam (2004): the verse on the breakdown and the chorus on the drop, the trance song structure at its peak
Armin van Buuren feat. Bonnie McKee: Lonely For You (2019): the modern version, radio production and compressed vocal
vocaltrance.rythme: The drums are those of uplifting but held back: clean 909 kick, clap and snare on 2 and 4, open hat on the offbeats, ride in eighth notes, no extra percussion. What changes: during the verse, the drums simplify, sometimes kick alone or kick and hi-hat, so the vocal dominates. The snare roll before the chorus is shorter, 8 bars, and follows the rising vocal. Fills must never land on a sung phrase. In the radio version, the drums come in from bar 8.
vocaltrance.sons: The female lead vocal, recorded on a condenser mic, compressed in two stages, ratio 3:1 then 4:1, with a de-esser at 6 kHz, a dotted eighth delay on certain words and a 2-second plate reverb. Doubled harmonies and widened backing vocals on the chorus. The supersaw plays held chords under the vocal, not a lead: it's the carpet of the chorus. The piano carries the verse and the breakdown, often a sampled piano with hall reverb. Sylenth1 plucks in sixteenth-note arpeggios, filtered, for movement. Wide pads. The instrumental lead only exists in the passages without vocals.
vocaltrance.tempo: 132 to 138 BPM, a little below uplifting, to give a vocal room to breathe: at 138, the syllables trip over each other. Straight grid. The feel is that of a song: verse, pre-chorus, chorus, and these sections drive the arrangement more than the 16-bar blocks do. Above & Beyond and Oceanlab sit around 132-134, Delerium and its remixes closer to 136. Take the vocal first: its natural tempo decides the track's. If you slow down or speed up a recorded vocal, stay within 3% to keep the timbre.

wonky.arrangement: Short format, 2 to 4 minutes, beat tape spirit. No DJ intro, the track often starts on the beat or on a sample. 8 or 16-bar sections that change quickly: a lead comes in, the bass stops, a vocal sample goes by. A 4-bar break where only a synth plays an out-of-tempo phrase. Abrupt ending or a fade on tape noise. The ideas are dense: three or four strong sounds per section, no more, but each with its bends and variations. A longer version can exist for the DJ, but the original format is for listening and mixtapes.
wonky.basse: A detuned sub bass that slides: sine or triangle in Operator or Massive, mono with a glide of 80 to 150 ms, played in overlapping notes so the portamento does the work. Detune the bass by 10 to 20 cents relative to everything else, or modulate its pitch with a slow, light LFO. A long 808 with glide between two notes is also a good base. Write a line in minor pentatonic with whole-tone bends. The bass is often the melody, played on off-grid positions too. Gentle saturation, a little amp, so it comes through on a small speaker.
etapes: Set Ableton to 80 BPM, play a kick and a snare on the pads without quantizing, keep the snare late.
Add hats swung at 66% with gaps and ghost notes, a triplet fill every 4 bars.
Create a mono sine bass with a 100 ms glide, detuned by 15 cents, in minor pentatonic with bends.
Lay down a bright FM lead with portamento and vibrato, played on the wheel, plus a pitched soul sample.
Arrange in short 8-bar sections, a 4-bar out-of-tempo break, abrupt ending.
Mix the sub first, crushed and saturated drums, wide synths, master around -8 LUFS.
wonky.mix: The sub first: mono sub, around -6 dB peak, everything else organizes itself around it. Drums saturated and compressed hard, ratio 6:1, attack 3 ms, for a heavy, crushed sound, then a little Redux or tape saturation for the MPC side. Bright synths but cut below 300 Hz, panned wide. A compressor on the master bus with 3 dB of reduction and tape saturation. Master around -8 LUFS. Don't correct the off-grid placements in the mix: they're the point. Listen on cheap earbuds: the bass must still slide and the leads must still sting.

outils.pourquoi: Drums played on the pads without quantizing, snare 20 to 40 ms late, the Dilla legacy Hudson Mohawke claims.
Hudson Mohawke's DAW: pitch bend and vibrato automation drawn by hand on the leads.
The workstation whose factory drum kits make the sound of Butter and early HudMo, garish and compressed.
Bright, detuned FM leads, bells, sliding basses; Dexed, which is free, loads its sound banks.
MPC 16 Swing groove at 66 or 70%, then hits moved by hand by 15 to 40 ms; Push to play the pads.
Mono lead with portamento and vibrato played on the wheel, chords with saturated colors, sine bass detuned by 15 cents.
FM for DX7-style leads and the mono sub bass with a glide of 80 to 150 ms.

reperes: Flying Lotus: GNG BNG (2008): the drunk drums and the smeared bass, the Los Angeles version.
Hudson Mohawke: Fuse (2009): the garish leads and the bends, the Glasgow color.
Rustie: Ultra Thizz (2011): maximalism, stacked synths and elastic rhythm.
Zomby: Spliff Dub (2008): the detuned bass and the 8-bit, the link with UK bass.
wonky.rythme: 808 kick or a heavy kick sample, placed on 1 and on offset positions, the “a” of 2, the “and” of 3, never quite on the grid. Snare or clap on 2 and 4 but 20 to 40 ms late, layered with a rimshot or a snap. Hats in eighth notes or swung sixteenth notes with gaps and ghost notes, sometimes in triplets for a bar. A tambourine or a shaker playing an even more swung version. Fills in sixteenth-note triplets at the ends of 4-bar phrases. Play the drums on the pads of an MPC or a Push without quantizing, then keep what holds up.
wonky.sons: Bright, detuned synths: DX7-style FM leads, 8-bit chiptune, a mono lead with portamento and vibrato played on the pitch wheel, in Massive or Operator. Synth chords with highly saturated colors, almost kitsch, video game sounds, bells. Soul or R'n'B samples chopped and pitched. Mouth noises, synthetic brass, a finger snap. All of it in an MPC or Ableton. The modulations are played by hand: pitch bend, vibrato, filter, recorded as automation. The contrast between bright colors and a dirty bass is the hallmark of the genre.
sources: Resident Advisor, The Art of Production: Hudson Mohawke
wonky.tempo: Hip-hop tempos: between 70 and 90 BPM, or double that, 140 to 180, depending on how you count. The watchword is off the grid. In Ableton, turn off quantization or apply an MPC 16 Swing groove at 66 or 70%, then move hits by hand by another 15 to 40 ms. The snare arrives late, the kick is sometimes early, the hats stagger. The feel is drunk, warped, but held together by a constant pulse. What changes compared to UK bass: the halved tempo, the legacy of the MPC beat and J Dilla, and a palette of garish colors instead of London gray.

zenonesque.arrangement: Zenonesque moves forward through micro-variations. 32-bar intro: kick, bass, one micro-FX. Then, every 8 bars, something changes slightly: a percussion comes in, a grain changes pitch, the bass filter moves. No section stands out clearly from the previous one, but after 64 bars everything has changed. The breaks are breaths: the kick disappears for 8 bars, the bass carries on muted, a field recording takes its place, and the kick comes back without warning. Plan a denser section around two thirds of the way through, then a gradual descent. Aim for 9 minutes. Zenon DJs mix long: keep 64 stable bars on each side.
zenonesque.basse: The rubbery mid-tempo bass is the heart of the Zenon sound. In Serum: a sawtooth or a square wave with a low-pass filter at 150 Hz, resonance raised for the bounce, and a filter envelope with a 5 ms attack and 150 ms decay. The pattern is an elastic offbeat: bass on the “and” of each beat, but with notes of different lengths (an eighth note, then a short sixteenth, then a dotted eighth) that create the rubbery feel. Add a little gentle saturation and a slow LFO on the cutoff frequency, over 4 bars. Root in E or F, very rarely other notes. A gentle sidechain from the kick, release 120 ms. The sub stays separate and clean.
etapes: Project at 128 BPM. Round kick tuned to E around 50 Hz, 180 ms body, muffled rimshot on 2 and 4.
Rubbery bass in Serum on E1: square filtered at 150 Hz with resonance, offbeat notes of varied lengths, slow LFO on the filter, gentle sidechain.
Add skin percussion and shakers in sixteenth notes with 55% swing and lots of low velocities.
Slice a field recording in Granulator II with 20 ms grains and play micro-FX in sixteenth notes with random pitch.
Create an industrial drone of noise filtered around 800 Hz, very low, and a few dark 2-note stabs with short reverb.
Arrange 9 minutes in micro-variations every 8 bars, with breaths without kick and 64 stable bars on each side.
zenonesque.mix: The mix is dark, muffled, deep. Kick and bass in mono below 150 Hz, with the gentle sidechain that makes it breathe. The bass can be fairly loud, because the rest of the spectrum is sparse. The micro-FX go out to the sides, with a high-pass at 400 Hz and a shared short reverb. The industrial drones are very low, 20 dB below the kick, but always present. Light bus compression on the percussion, ratio 2:1. A gentle limiter toward -8 LUFS is enough. Cut the highs above 12 kHz on the textures for the muffled effect, and keep brightness only on two or three micro-sounds. Listen at low volume: the groove must stay readable with the kick and bass alone.

outils.pourquoi: The rubbery bass: square or sawtooth, low-pass at 150 Hz with resonance, 150 ms filter envelope, slow LFO over 4 bars.
The DAW of the Zenon scene: Granulator III on field recordings, Simpler for the organic percussion, slow swung groove.
Field recorder for workshop, street and ventilation atmospheres, which become micro-FX and muffled industrial drones.
Grains of 15 to 40 ms on a field take, played in sixteenth notes with random pitch: the micro-FX of the genre.
Short dark reverbs, 0.5 to 1 s, damped from 3 kHz, shared by the micro-FX out on the sides.
Gentle drawn sidechain, release 120 ms, that makes the elastic bass breathe under the round kick.
Granular and glitch ensembles like Grainstates or Molekular for textures that move forward through micro-variations.

reperes: Sensient: Madman's Playroom (2009): the elastic bass, the granular micro-FX and progress through mutations, the manifesto of the sound.
Krumelur: Minimal Animal (2005): the slow tribal groove and the sampled organic percussion.
Tetrameth: The Eclectic Benevolence (2008): the muffled industrial atmospheres and the short reverbs.
Fractal Joke: Welcome To The Cloud (2022): zenonesque today, more glitched, with textures processed in real time.
zenonesque.rythme: The kick is round and deep, tuned around 50 Hz, with a 180 ms body and little click: it has to melt into the floor. The snare is often absent, replaced by a muffled rimshot or a wooden percussion on 2 and 4, with a short, dark reverb. The sampled organic percussion of the brief: skin drums, shakers, claves, played in sixteenth notes with swing and lots of low velocities, like a hand tapping. The hi-hats are discreet, filtered low. Add granular micro-FX as percussion: clicks, drops, short grains in sixteenth notes, with random pitch variations. The rhythm must be hypnotic and slightly unstable.
zenonesque.sons: Serum, Ableton and the field recorder. The granular micro-FX: take a field recording (street, workshop, machine), slice it in Granulator II with grains of 15 to 40 ms, play short notes in sixteenth notes, with randomness on the pitch. The muffled industrial atmospheres: drones of noise band-pass filtered around 800 Hz, very low in the mix, with a slow LFO. Processed field recordings: rain, ventilation, footsteps, run through a filter and a short delay. No melodic lead: resonant blips of 2 or 3 notes, short dark stabs. The reverbs are short, 0.5 to 1 s, dark, damped from 3 kHz. Everything should sound like a factory at night, heard from afar.

zenonesque.tempo: Zenonesque is played between 126 and 132 BPM, the slowest tempo of the danceable psy genres. The feel is a slow tribal groove: 53 to 56% swing on the percussion, ghost notes, patterns that breathe. What changes compared to psy-prog is the absence of a melodic trajectory: the track moves forward through micro-variations of texture, every 4 or 8 bars, rather than through build-ups. What changes compared to psytech is the slowness and the elasticity: the bass bounces, it doesn't roll. Count in 8-bar cycles, but think of each cycle as a slight mutation of the previous one. A track lasts 8 to 10 minutes.
